state: 阶段1制作清单及实现基线；最新已制作覆盖另见 docs/phase2/coverage.json
scope: 固定来源587个数学节点；仅电脑、本地；年级与年龄字段不参与分组、抽样或批次排序。
authoringNotes: 批次是制作顺序，不是锁定孩子的学习顺序。入口先提供与当前任务有关的短操作；遇到基础困难时沿来源关系返回或补做。被引用的基础尚未制作时不得做空跳转，须补一个真实可操作的准备任务，且不因此自动给该源节点记完成。
分组是本地适配；来源边按原方向和理由保留。
93 个共用教具/情境方向可以继续拆分；实际课程数量在制作和试用后确定。
教学内容来源及许可保留 vendor/os-taxonomy/LICENSE、LICENSE-CONTENT 与各示例说明。
阶段2记录实耗后估算工期，本清单不虚报日期或课时。

themes.title: 数与运算
themes.description: 多少、怎样分，以及数的不同样子。

themes.title: 图形与空间
themes.description: 拼一拼、转一转，发现形状的关系。

themes.title: 测量与变化
themes.description: 选一个单位，把世界的大小说清楚。

themes.title: 规律与推理
themes.description: 找到规律，也说清楚为什么。

themes.title: 数据与可能性
themes.description: 向数据提问，探索不确定的事。

count.title: 数、分与配对
count.learnerAction: 移动实物或计数物，配对、分组、合并后说明数量。
count.transferRequirement: 更换排列、物品和总数，重新构造而不是认同一幅图。
count.mathReview: 一一对应、总数守恒、合分关系和零的处理。
count.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

number-line.title: 数轴与距离
number-line.learnerAction: 放置点、走等长步或标出区间，比较位置与距离。
number-line.transferRequirement: 更换端点、刻度和数值，解释坐标及距离。
number-line.mathReview: 等距刻度、方向、负数顺序、端点和舍入边界。
number-line.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

place-value.title: 数位与交换
place-value.learnerAction: 把一组小单位换成一个大单位，将模型与数位记录联动。
place-value.transferRequirement: 换数量级或表示方式；需要进退位时自己安排交换。
place-value.mathReview: 交换前后数值守恒、零占位、小数位值及算法适用范围。
place-value.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

symbol-system.title: 数量与记号
symbol-system.learnerAction: 把数量、数词和不同记号来回编码并解释规则。
symbol-system.transferRequirement: 用新数值编码或纠正一条有歧义的记录。
symbol-system.mathReview: 记号规则、适用范围和数值保持。
symbol-system.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

structure.title: 排列与数的结构
structure.learnerAction: 构造阵列、因子组合或数集，寻找结构并提供反例。
structure.transferRequirement: 给出新数或边界例，检验自己的规律。
structure.mathReview: 因子是否穷尽、素数及一的区别、平方立方及无穷概念边界。
structure.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

operation.title: 操作、算式与检查
operation.learnerAction: 把计算步骤与模型对应，比较不同方法并定位错误。
operation.transferRequirement: 换数值或问题条件，自己选方法，再用另一种方法核对。
operation.mathReview: 运算性质、顺序、符号和估算误差，不以速度代替理解。
operation.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

array.title: 成组、阵列与平均分
array.learnerAction: 构造等组或行列，把乘除和余数放回实际分配过程。
array.transferRequirement: 改变总量、每份大小或组数，决定余下部分怎样处理。
array.mathReview: 等组条件、行列乘积、除法含义和情境中的余数。
array.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

model.title: 情境建模与规划
model.learnerAction: 选出有关量，搭建模型，执行方案并解释取舍。
model.transferRequirement: 换情境、增加无关信息或改变约束，修正模型。
model.mathReview: 假设、单位和结果合理性；开放解释不能只按关键词判定。
model.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

fraction.title: 同一整体的分割与组合
fraction.learnerAction: 固定整体，构造等份，选择、重组并解释几分之几。
fraction.transferRequirement: 改变整体形状或把连续量换成离散数量，仍能说明单位份。
fraction.mathReview: 整体一致、等份条件、单位分数、分子分母的含义。
fraction.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

fraction-line.title: 等长与同一点
fraction-line.learnerAction: 调整分割或数轴刻度，让不同分数在同一位置重合并说明原因。
fraction-line.transferRequirement: 换分母、改用分数条或数轴，说明比较及等值。
fraction-line.mathReview: 零点与整体对齐、分割等距、不用分子分母同时加一冒充等值。
fraction-line.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

fraction-decimal.title: 分割、百格与小数联动
fraction-decimal.learnerAction: 在数轴、百格和数字之间来回表示同一数量。
fraction-decimal.transferRequirement: 换成新数量或不同教具，独立建立对应。
fraction-decimal.mathReview: 十分位百分位、尾零、大小比较与同一整体。
fraction-decimal.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

ratio.title: 保持比例的共同变化
ratio.learnerAction: 拖动成对量或分配条，使相对关系保持，比较不同方案。
ratio.transferRequirement: 换配方、总量、百分率或单价，自选共同单位。
ratio.mathReview: 加法关系与倍数关系区分、百分比基准和比例不变量。
ratio.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

shape.title: 拼搭、分类与属性
shape.learnerAction: 组合或改变图形，对照属性分类并找出反例。
shape.transferRequirement: 旋转、拉伸或换外观后判断类别是否改变。
shape.mathReview: 定义属性与颜色朝向分离；分类包含关系及反例。
shape.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

construction.title: 几何构造与约束
construction.learnerAction: 用可追踪的尺规、长度和角度约束构造图形，检查可行性。
construction.transferRequirement: 换参数，识别无解、多解或适用条件。
construction.mathReview: 作图精度、三角形条件、定理假设和近似误差。
construction.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

coordinate.title: 位置与坐标
coordinate.learnerAction: 在方格或空间中定位、描点与描述移动，交换读图和制图角色。
coordinate.transferRequirement: 更换坐标、原点、路线或情境，解释两个数各代表什么。
coordinate.mathReview: 坐标顺序、象限、刻度和移动前后的位置。
coordinate.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

transform.title: 平移、对称与缩放
transform.learnerAction: 直接移动、翻折、旋转或缩放图形，追踪不变和改变的量。
transform.transferRequirement: 换图形或变换中心，预测后构造并验证。
transform.mathReview: 对应点、距离与角度保持、缩放对长度和面积的不同影响。
transform.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

angle.title: 转角、测量与拼角
angle.learnerAction: 转动射线、比较或拼合角，先预测再量取。
angle.transferRequirement: 改变边长、朝向或关联图形，独立判断和解释。
angle.mathReview: 角与边长无关、量角器起点、直角平角周角及角和条件。
angle.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

solid.title: 立体、展开与截面
solid.learnerAction: 直接旋转、搭建、折展或切开立体，关联各视图。
solid.transferRequirement: 换形状或折法，先预测再检查面、边及截面。
solid.mathReview: 拓扑计数、遮挡、合法展开图与截面的几何一致性。
solid.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

measure.title: 比较、测量与单位
measure.learnerAction: 选择属性和单位，估计后测量或换单位，解释精度。
measure.transferRequirement: 换工具、量程或非整刻度值，检查单位是否合适。
measure.mathReview: 单位迭代无空隙、读数起点、换算、误差和量纲。
measure.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

area.title: 铺满、围边与重排
area.learnerAction: 铺单位方格、展开边界、剪拼重组，比较面积和周长。
area.transferRequirement: 构造同面积不同周长或新复合图形，解释所用方法。
area.mathReview: 面积守恒、重叠与遗漏、周长和内边界的区别、公式条件。
area.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

volume.title: 填充、拆层与拆合
volume.learnerAction: 旋转、填充和拆层计数，构造与分解立体并留下计划。
volume.transferRequirement: 换尺寸、形状与视角，在揭示之前独立规划计数或分解。
volume.mathReview: 单位立方体、隐藏块、层数乘积、无重叠分解；面积不能当体积。
volume.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

time.title: 钟面、时间轴与日历
time.learnerAction: 拨钟、安排事件、沿时间轴量经过的时长。
time.transferRequirement: 跨整点、跨日或更换钟面表示后重新安排。
time.mathReview: 六十进制、时刻与时长、日期边界和上午下午。
time.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

money.title: 等值支付、找零与预算
money.learnerAction: 组合货币、模拟交易或比较预算，解释选择和核算过程。
money.transferRequirement: 换价格和约束，估算再精确计算，并检查找零。
money.mathReview: 货币单位、整数分的精确计算、税率折扣基准；不同币制不可静默互换。
money.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

pattern.title: 规则生成与反例
pattern.learnerAction: 拖放或生成序列，找最小重复片段或增长规则。
pattern.transferRequirement: 换起点、问远处一项、构造能推翻猜测的例子。
pattern.mathReview: 有限例子不唯一确定规则；区分观察、猜测与一般说明。
pattern.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

algorithm.title: 执行、修改与追踪规则
algorithm.learnerAction: 执行简单指令或小表格，逐步追踪生成的数并修正算法。
algorithm.transferRequirement: 换输入或边界，检查遗漏、重复和停止条件。
algorithm.mathReview: 规则精确定义、过程可追踪、输出集合与终止条件。
algorithm.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

balance.title: 相等与未知量
balance.learnerAction: 用平衡或对应模型表现未知量，保持两边关系并求解。
balance.transferRequirement: 改变未知量位置或条件，建立关系后再检查解。
balance.mathReview: 等号对称、等量变换、检验代回；模型不适用时需说明。
balance.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

algebra.title: 式子的不同表示
algebra.learnerAction: 用拼块、面积或符号改写表达式，将每步改写与关系对应。
algebra.transferRequirement: 换值、参数或结构，检查改写是否恒等或只在特定条件成立。
algebra.mathReview: 同类项、分配律、定义域和恒等式与方程的区别。
algebra.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

function.title: 两个量、表格与图线
function.learnerAction: 改变输入，建立表格和图像，比较不同变化关系。
function.transferRequirement: 换参数或让孩子反向从图像建立关系。
function.mathReview: 坐标和单位一致、离散连续区别、斜率及二次关系的条件。
function.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

explain.title: 作品、说明与质疑
explain.learnerAction: 借已有数学任务选择表示、留下推理作品，比较说明并回应反例。
explain.transferRequirement: 换一个任务，说明工具和推理为何仍适用或需要改变。
explain.mathReview: 按每个源目标保留解释证据；没有可靠判断时记录为待评，不宣称掌握。
explain.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

data-collect.title: 问题、分类与记录
data-collect.learnerAction: 明确问题，设计类别，收集或整理一组可核查的数据。
data-collect.transferRequirement: 换问题或加入异常记录，修改收集方案与分类。
data-collect.mathReview: 数据来自哪里、每条是否计入、类别互斥完备及缺失和重复。
data-collect.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

data-display.title: 数据与多种图表
data-display.learnerAction: 用同一份原始记录构造表和图，切换并回答真实比较问题。
data-display.transferRequirement: 换数据、比例尺或表达目的，选图并解释限制。
data-display.mathReview: 总量、图例、刻度、单位一致；连续数据不能任意当类别处理。
data-display.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

statistics.title: 分布、代表值与抽样
statistics.learnerAction: 拖动数据点或重抽样，观察代表值、差异及推断如何变化。
statistics.transferRequirement: 更换偏斜、离群值或抽样方法，比较结论的可靠程度。
statistics.mathReview: 统计量定义、样本总体、误差与变异；相关不能自动当因果。
statistics.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

chance.title: 预测、试验与模拟
chance.learnerAction: 先预测可能结果，再重复试验，比较短期结果与长期模式。
chance.transferRequirement: 换装置或次数，解释不确定性而非背下固定频率。
chance.mathReview: 概率范围与和、等可能条件、随机性和可重现的测试种子。
chance.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

chance-tree.title: 列举结果与条件变化
chance-tree.learnerAction: 构造结果树或集合图，计数并比较有无放回或条件变化。
chance-tree.transferRequirement: 更换条件，检查漏列重列及独立性假设。
chance-tree.mathReview: 互斥完备、交并关系、分支概率及依赖条件。
chance-tree.status: 制作假设，待阶段2及各批验证

local-fractions.label: 本地分数活动
local-fractions.reuse: 复用已有分割、数轴、百格、任务草稿与证据记录的适用部分。
local-fractions.limit: 只有 EXISTING 中三个源节点有早期完整活动；A03 仍为预览；新目标必须新增任务和验证。

hidden-cubes.label: Hidden Cubes
hidden-cubes.reuse: 旋转、填充、拆层、先提交后揭示及任务选择/计分分离。mt_d7XktBQPxm 是示例明确锚点。
hidden-cubes.limit: 其他体积、展开、截面目标只借部分教具代码；不能由数隐藏块推定全目标覆盖。源码尚未接入本地应用。

bee-builder.label: Bee Builder
bee-builder.reuse: 精确二维图形、边界展开、共享边和等面积比较的适用部分。
bee-builder.limit: 蜂巢示例不是所有形状或面积节点的完整课程；不将二维目标强制做成三维。保留素材许可说明。

sampleRoutes.title: 同一个量的不同写法

startingActivity.title: Cut it fair, then count the unit
learnerActions: Take one whole bar (a chocolate bar works well) and cut it into equal parts, e.g. 6, checking that the parts are genuinely equal in area before accepting them.
Shade ONE part and name it as a quantity: 'this is one-sixth, 1/6'.
Build 2/6, then 3/6, by copying that single 1/6 piece and counting as you go, saying 'two one-sixths, three one-sixths' and writing the label each time.
Reset the sixths bar to show 2/6, then set an identical bar beside it, cut into 4 equal parts, and shade 2 parts on it (so you have 2/6 next to 2/4).
Slide the two shaded regions over one another to compare how much chocolate each shows, and state which is more and why.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: a/b is a copies of an equal part whose size is fixed by the denominator; shading the same NUMBER of parts does not give the same amount, because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole (so 2/6 < 2/4).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area model — a bar or circle partitioned into b equal parts, a shaded
Fraction strips of a single unit size
Length / number-line jump of size 1/b iterated a times
Set model — a of every b·k objects
Cuisenaire rods where a rod is chosen as the whole
commonMisconceptions: Equal-parts ignored — any b pieces are called bths regardless of size (IES Roadblock 1.2)
Counting shaded parts mechanically without grasping that numerator and denominator together name one quantity (IES caution)
Reading the denominator as a group SIZE ('thirds = groups of three') rather than the number of equal parts
Whole-number bias — a bigger denominator means a bigger part or a bigger value
Non-unit fraction taken as a unit fraction — for 3/4 shading just one part
Calling every fractional part 'a half'
constraints: Always hold the whole fixed and require parts to be equal when naming fractions: equal in AREA for area models, equal in length for length/number-line models, equal in number for set models; differently-shaped pieces of an area model are acceptable only if they are genuinely equal in area.
Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a named quantity before non-unit fractions a/b.

When comparing the AMOUNTS two models show by counting shaded parts, this is only valid when the wholes are the same size; state this explicitly, especially in trap questions mixing a small and a large whole. Note that fractions as numbers remain comparable regardless (3/4 > 1/2).

A static reference such as a fraction wall can label parts ('one of six equal parts = 1/6') but does not let the learner enforce equal parts or iterate the unit themselves; treat it as a reference layer alongside active partitioning, not a substitute for it.

Recognition-only tasks (identify/match) and sorts confirm classification/fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or justification; pair them with a construct-and-explain step.

Keep the work in the plane (area/length/set); a third spatial dimension is not needed for this planar concept and can obscure equal-area partitioning. This is a scoped limitation here, not a universal claim about 3D media.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: routinely ask 'how big is ONE part?', not only 'how many are shaded?'

activityReferences.title: Plumb-line on stacked thirds and sixths lines
Re-partition toggle: the point that does not move

startingActivity.title: Plumb-line on stacked thirds and sixths lines
learnerActions: Stack a 0–1 line divided into thirds directly above a 0–1 line divided into sixths, carefully aligned at 0 and 1.
Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and drop a vertical plumb-line straight down to the sixths line.
Name the fraction on the sixths line that sits at exactly the same point (4/6), and state in words: two different names, one position.
Repeat for other target points and record each equivalent pair you find.
Say aloud why the shared point means the two fractions are equal in size.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions are different names for the SAME point on the number line; same position means same magnitude.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Stacked / aligned 0–1 number lines (IES Figure 4)
One line with dual labels above and below (1/2 above, 4/8 below at one point)
Fraction strips of different unit sizes compared by length
Fraction wall
commonMisconceptions: Cannot accept two differently-written fractions as the same point (IES Roadblock 2.3)
Cannot locate an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. finding 1/2 as 3/6 on a sixths line)
'Different numbers can't name the same amount' — denies equivalence altogether
Additive drift — thinks 1/2 and 2/3 are equivalent because you 'add 1 to each'
Whole-number bias — 2/4 must be bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are larger
constraints: Target understanding (REPRESENTATIONAL): learners should locate, generate and explain equivalents, not just recognise them.

A fraction wall or stacked-line reference that only highlights a family (e.g. tap 1/2 -> highlights 2/4, 3/6, 4/8) is a useful recall/reference scaffold but does not let the learner re-partition, so it cannot by itself build the crux differently-partitioned case; use it alongside, not instead of, re-partitioning work.

Verification/matching/sorting tasks consolidate and assess classification but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a family or an explanation of why the point does not move; pair them with construction activities.

Full understanding requires generating a correct family for 1/2 AND explaining equivalence as re-partitioning that preserves position AND correctly rejecting a non-equivalent (e.g. recognising that no fraction written in fifths equals 1/2, since no fifths mark lands on it). Reading off a single aligned equivalent is only partial.
Fraction strips and card cutouts have slight physical thickness; treat them as approximations to the ideal zero-thickness lengths and points on an idealised number line.

Re-partitioning only yields an equivalent when each unit part subdivides evenly to the point: 1/2 can be named in sixths (3/6, each half split into three) but cannot be written as any whole number of fifths, so no fifths mark lands on 1/2. Keep this condition explicit — never describe a half as simply 'absent from the line'.

Predict then reconcile on the number line

startingActivity.title: Shade, name it twice, and pin one point
learnerActions: On a 10×10 hundredths grid, shade 27 of the 100 squares; write the fraction (27/100) and the decimal (0.27) for the exact same picture, side by side in a place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns.
Mark where this amount sits on a 0-to-1 number line; confirm 27/100 and 0.27 land on the same single point.
Now shade just 7 squares. Write the fraction (7/100) and decide the decimal. Predict and then check: does it write as 0.7 or 0.07?
Compare where 0.7 would fall on the number line versus where your 7 shaded squares sit — notice 0.7 lands far past 7 hundredths, exactly at seven tenths.
Toggle between 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 and place each on the number line to confirm all three mark the identical point.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A decimal and its fraction are one number wearing two names; the place after the point fixes the denominator, so the placeholder zero in 0.07 holds the tenths place empty and is not decoration.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundredths grid shaded and labelled with both the fraction and the decimal
Place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns beside the fraction
Number line where 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 mark the same point
Contrasting pairs 3/10 = 0.3 vs 3/100 = 0.03 to spotlight the placeholder zero
Bidirectional fraction↔decimal cards for matching
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero — writing 7/100 as 0.7 (or reading 0.07 as 7/10), ignoring that the place fixes the denominator.
Treating a decimal and its fraction as different numbers — not seeing 0.3 and 3/10 as the same quantity at the same point.
Reading the digits after the point as an ordinary whole number ('0.27 means twenty-seven') rather than as 27 hundredths.
Mapping the numerator straight after the point regardless of denominator, so 3/10 and 3/100 both become 0.3.
Thinking annexing a zero changes the value (0.3 vs 0.30 seen as different).
constraints: The represented objects are planar (grid, number line, place-value chart); depth carries no meaning here, so flat representations are appropriate and a 3D model adds cost without conceptual gain for this objective.

The static annotated reference grid supports and reinforces but does not let the child drive the shading or test a wrong placement, so it should accompany, not replace, the interactive shading and prediction tasks.

The convert/match/locate check-up assesses the output; on its own it does not build the equivalence insight and can be passed by a digit-copying rule on tenths alone — include the 7/100 item and an explanation question so a hollow rule is exposed.
Read decimals in place-value language ('twenty-seven hundredths', 'three tenths') rather than 'point two seven', so the fraction meaning stays audible.

Treat 0.3 = 0.30 as naming one value: annexing a zero after the last decimal place does not change the amount; distinguish this from the placeholder zero in 0.07, which does change the value by shifting the digit's place.
Recognising and writing decimal equivalents of tenths and hundredths is the stated curriculum objective; the activities serve it but do not themselves prove any one medium is superior.

startingActivity.title: Shade a quarter: finding 0.25 on the hundred grid
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid of 100 squares, split the whole into four equal groups and shade one group to make a quarter.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: A quarter of 100 is 25 squares, so 1/4 and 0.25 name one and the same value — a fact the child can rebuild for 1/2 and 3/4 rather than recall blindly.

commonMisconceptions: Digit-copying: writing 1/4 as 0.14 or 0.4 (treating numerator/denominator digits as decimal digits).
Denominator-as-count on the grid: shading 4 squares for 1/4 (reading 1/4 as 4/100 = 0.04).
Believing 0.25 > 0.5 because '25 > 5' (whole-number bias across the decimal).
Treating the fraction and its decimal as different, unrelated values.
Recalling the facts with no grounding, so errors cannot be self-checked.
constraints: Target learners are roughly ages 8–9; this is conceptual work on recognising and writing decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4. The Year 4 statutory expectation to recognise and write these decimal equivalents is the curriculum anchor (its source was flagged unverified).
Insist that recall is backed by the 25/100 reasoning: a child who recalls 1/4 = 0.25 but cannot justify it on the grid, or grounds one landmark but not the family, has only partial understanding.

A static reference card showing the three shadings with labels is useful for review, but on its own it does not let a child shade, predict, or test wrong answers; use it as a reference scaffold alongside active shading, not as a replacement for it.

Recognition and matching tasks check whether the facts are known and can diagnose digit-copying (0.4/0.14 distractors) and denominator-as-count, but they do not by themselves build the grid-grounded reasoning or elicit the child's own justification.

An interactive grid that recolours as the child shades, counts squares, and shows the linked number-line point is one effective way to make the mechanism concrete, but it is an example, not a required tool; paper hundred grids and a drawn number line serve the same purpose.
Distinguish the mathematical idea (a value named two ways) from any particular display: the number-line point and the grid are representations of the same single value.

startingActivity.title: Predict, then unpack: how many cubes fill the block?
learnerActions: Look at a solid built from unit cubes — e.g. a 3×3×3 block shown so only three faces are visible — and PREDICT how many unit cubes make it up, stating your reasoning before building or unpacking.
Build the solid from real unit cubes (or take an existing one apart), peeling off one layer at a time to expose the middle.
Count by structuring: find how many cubes are in one layer (a 3×3 layer = 9), then how many layers (3), reaching 3 layers of 9 = 27.
Identify any cube touched by no outside face — the one hidden dead-centre — and say where it is and how many such hidden cubes there are.
Compare your first prediction with the unpacked total, and explain what you missed if they differ.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Volume counts EVERY cube that fills the solid, including cubes hidden at the back and buried in the interior — not just the cubes whose faces you can see. Organising the count into iterable layers lets you neither miss nor double-count cubes.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Unit cube (1×1×1)
Open box packed with unit cubes
Layer / row / column structuring of a solid
Predict-then-unpack activity
Isometric 3D cube diagram (with hidden cubes)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses volume with area or surface area (counts faces or squares rather than the space filled).
Counts only the visible/outside cubes and misses hidden interior cubes (Battista & Clements Strategy C).
Double-counts cubes along shared edges and triple-counts corners when reading a 3D drawing.
constraints: Build volume from packing real unit cubes into open boxes, counting with no gaps or overlaps, before introducing any formula.
Explicitly contrast volume (cubes filling space, cubic units) with area/surface area (squares covering a surface, square units).
Use 'cubic unit' language and correct notation (e.g. cm³, m³) from the outset.

A fixed/static isometric picture can introduce and assess the idea but cannot be manipulated to reveal occluded cubes; use a built model, rotatable solid, or predict-then-unpack to make the hidden interior accountable when the hidden count is the learning target.

Count-the-cubes recognition items (e.g. multiple choice or slider) can assess the skill but do not by themselves elicit the learner's structuring strategy or independent account of hidden cubes; pair with explain-your-reasoning or build tasks.
Recognition-only responses do not require the learner to construct or justify the layer structure; include construction and explanation for the conceptual objective.

Interactive transparency, layer-peeling and predict-then-reveal counters are optional illustrative supports, not mandatory apparatus; real cubes that can be built and unpacked can serve the same roles, while a clear isometric drawing can introduce or assess the idea but cannot by itself reveal hidden cubes.
Keep the ~21 figure only as a learner misconception (edge double-counting); the distinct visible count for a 3×3×3's three shown faces is 19, and this must never be offered as a correct answer.

startingActivity.title: Fill a box and count by layers
learnerActions: Fill a small open box (or transparent container) whose inside length, width and height are whole numbers of centimetres with centimetre cubes so they pack in snugly, leaving no gaps.
Find the number of cubes in the bottom layer (for a 4 by 3 base, count 4×3 = 12).
Count how many identical layers stack to fill the box (e.g. 2 layers), then add 12 for each layer: 12, 24.
Write the volume with its unit: 24 cm³. State explicitly why it is cm³ and not cm².
Predict the count before filling, then check by filling; investigate any mismatch to find double-counted or missed cubes.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Measuring volume means counting all the unit cubes that fill the solid. Organising them into layers (one layer multiplied by the number of layers) is more reliable and efficient than counting one-by-one, and counting only the visible faces misses hidden cubes. The unit is 'cubes', so it is recorded in cubic units.

keyRepresentations: Layer-by-layer count (one layer × number of layers)
Centimetre cubes filling a container
Isometric cube diagram
Cubic-unit notation (cm³, in³)
commonMisconceptions: Counts only visible cubes and misses hidden interior cubes (Strategy C).
Double-counts cubes on shared edges and corners.
Records volume in square units (cm²) instead of cubic units (cm³).
constraints: The objective is a spatial measuring procedure: learners must actually count and structure cubes, not merely recognise a stated total. Recognition-only or tap-to-reveal formats can demonstrate the method but do not themselves elicit the independent counting that reveals how a learner handles hidden and edge cubes.

Observe the method, not just the final number: how a learner counts (by layers versus face-counting), whether they account for hidden cubes, and whether they avoid double-counting is visible only while they do the task.
Diagram-only counting depends on the drawing clearly implying the cubes hidden from view; pair it with real cubes so learners can check inferences about what is hidden.

Interactive supports such as a layer-highlight tool, a hidden-cube reveal, a layer-grouping counter that flags double-counts, and a cm³/in³ unit selector are optional aids that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
Correct cubic-unit notation is part of the skill and should be required, but a unit error alone (correct count, wrong unit) signals re-teaching notation, not the counting procedure.

startingActivity.title: Build the prism layer by layer
learnerActions: Set a box to 4 × 3 × 5 and watch the base layer tile in as 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes, which cover a base area of 12 cm²; name this base area B.
Stack that identical 12-cube layer upward 5 times to fill the box, tracking the readout as it builds '12 × 5 = 60 cm³' alongside '4 × 3 × 5'.
Change the height from 5 to 10 and predict, then check, what happens to the number of layers and the total volume.
Switch to a tank skin and relate the same count to how much water fills the container.
Re-express the result as B × h and say in words: 'one base layer, repeated so many times high.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying the three edge lengths counts cubes because l × w is one layer and h is how many identical layers there are; V = l × w × h is the same idea as V = base area × height.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base layer (l×w) iterated h times
V = l × w × h and V = B × h
Labelled cuboid
Real containers (box, tank)
commonMisconceptions: Uses V = l×w×h rotely with no sense of layers (Strategy D), so cannot adapt to B×h or explain why it works.
Adds the edge lengths (l+w+h) instead of multiplying, or multiplies only two of the three dimensions.
Confuses volume with surface area, or records cm² instead of cm³.
constraints: Derive V = l × w × h from the layer structure (l × w cubes in the base layer, covering l × w cm², repeated h times = B × h) so the formula is understood, not memorised.

A static labelled image or a recognition/compute task can present or check the idea but does not by itself elicit the learner building and explaining the layer structure; pair it with manipulation (physical cubes or an interactive build).

Physical unit cubes and a screen model offer different experiences of the same cube-packing derivation; learners should connect the cube-packing to the multiplication, in line with the standard's packing-with-unit-cubes method.
Watch that all three dimensions are multiplied (not added) and that none of the three is left out; distinguish volume (cm³, filling) from surface area (cm², covering).
Record volumes in the correct cubic unit (cm³ or m³) and estimate before calculating in real-context problems.

startingActivity.title: Pull the step-solid apart (exploded decomposition)
learnerActions: Meet a step-shaped or L-shaped block with most edge lengths labelled and one or two left to deduce.
Draw a cut line to split the solid into two (or more) cuboids, then separate the pieces into an exploded view so you can see each one whole.
Check that your pieces do not overlap — no cube belongs to two pieces and none of the solid is left out.

Find any missing edge from the labelled measurements (for example, subtract the known part from the overall length, add parts to get an overall length, or use a matching parallel edge), then write down each cuboid's l, w and h.
Compute each cuboid's volume with V = l × w × h, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³ here), and add them for the total.
Re-split the same block a different valid way and confirm you get the same total.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Volume is additive: a composite solid can be decomposed into non-overlapping cuboids, each cuboid's volume found by l × w × h, and the parts summed — and any valid non-overlapping split rebuilds the same total.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: L-shaped / step solid split into cuboids
Exploded decomposition diagram
Missing-dimension deduction from the whole
Sum of the part-volumes
commonMisconceptions: Chooses overlapping pieces and double-counts the shared region.
Mis-deduces a hidden dimension (uses an overall length for a part, or forgets to subtract).
Adds the part-volumes incorrectly, or omits one of the parts.
constraints: Pieces of the decomposition must be non-overlapping right rectangular prisms: each cube of the solid belongs to exactly one piece and none is omitted.

Missing dimensions must be deduced from the overall measurements (e.g. subtract a known part from the full length) before any volume is calculated — never take an unlabelled edge as a whole-figure measurement.
Keep consistent cubic units throughout and in the final total; cm³ is the usual unit here, with m³ appropriate for larger real-world objects — match the labelled measurements.

A static exploded diagram with tap-to-reveal part volumes and sum can show the method but allows no manipulation or re-splitting; treat it as a scaffold that demonstrates rather than one that elicits the learner's own decomposition.

Multiple-choice or fill-in items can assess the idea with overlap and missing-dimension answer choices, but recognition-only responses do not require the learner to independently construct a decomposition; pair them with at least one constructed split-and-sum.

This learning centres on spatial decomposition and calculation; a dialogue-only format does not by itself elicit the learner's spatial decomposition or the construction of the calculation, though explaining one's reasoning remains valuable alongside doing the method.

Physical interlocking or unit cubes are a standard concrete model for building and decomposing composite solids, and on-screen 3D models represent the same solid; neither medium is established by the cited standards as uniquely necessary or more effective.

Always ask both directions: read a value off a given chart AND add to or construct a chart (or table), so interpreting and constructing reinforce each other.

A static annotated pictogram (labelling key, symbol, category) is a useful vocabulary reference, but it does not let the learner construct a chart or apply a changing many-to-one key; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
Recognition-only items (e.g. 'how many?' multiple choice) can assess interpretation but do not by themselves elicit the construction/reversal direction; pair them with a draw/build step.
When using a half-symbol, choose a key value such that half is meaningful (e.g. a key of 2 gives a half-symbol = 1).

startingActivity.title: Build a bar graph from our data on gridded paper
learnerActions: Collect or use a given data set with up to four categories (e.g. favourite pets: cats 9, dogs 6, fish 4, birds 2)
On squared/gridded paper or a gridded canvas, draw one bar per category, shading one square per unit so each bar's height equals its count
Keep every bar the same width, rising from a common baseline (zero line), evenly spaced, and label both axes with a single-unit scale
Read a chosen bar's value back by tracking its top straight across to the scale number, and check it matches the original count
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Height means count: a bar's top read against the scale gives the number of items in that category. This only works if every bar starts from the shared zero baseline. Equal widths keep the bars fair to compare by eye, so that only height carries the count.

Picture graph with one symbol per unit, aligned in rows
Two bars aligned to show the difference for 'how many more'

commonMisconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value instead of the difference between the bars
Reads a bar's value off by one (counts gridlines instead of the value the top reaches, or bars not starting at zero)
Draws bars of unequal width, floating off the baseline, or unevenly spaced, so height no longer means count
Draws picture-graph symbols of different sizes or unaligned, so rows can't be compared by length
constraints: Use the child's own collected data where possible so each unit maps to one square/symbol and height visibly means count.
Insist on the grammar of a bar graph: equal-width bars, common baseline (zero), even spacing, labelled axes, single-unit scale.

A static labelled bar graph or tap-to-reveal annotation is a reference/scaffold only: it can name the parts but does not let the learner construct a graph or compute a comparison, so it cannot by itself evidence the construction skill.

Optional interactions (sliding bars together, shading the difference, dragging bar heights) are illustrative aids, not required mechanisms; the learner must still state the subtraction or count.

startingActivity.title: Build and read a tiled rectangle grid
learnerActions: Set the number of rows and the number of columns for a rectangle, and watch it fill with same-size squares that snap to a grid; if a partition leaves gaps or overlaps, notice it flagged and correct it so the squares are equal and aligned.
First count the squares one-by-one (slowly), then switch to a rows × columns view and watch the same rectangle resolve to its total instantly — e.g. 4 rows of 6 squares becoming 4×6 = 24.
Write the multiplication fact that matches the grid you built, and say how many squares are in each row and how many rows there are.
Add one more column (or one more row) and predict the new total before revealing it.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A rectangle tiled with equal squares is a rectangular array; its total comes from rows × columns, not from counting each square, and this square-count is what area will later measure.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned into a grid of equal unit squares
Rows × columns structure (the array within the grid)
Link to a multiplication fact for the total
Precursor to the area-by-counting-squares model
commonMisconceptions: Partitioning into unequal squares/pieces (not same-size units).
Leaving gaps or overlapping squares when tiling.
Counting every square one-by-one instead of using rows × columns.
Confusing the number of rows with the number of squares in a row.
Not connecting the grid count to a multiplication fact (treating it as pure counting).
constraints: Squares must be the same size and tile the rectangle with no gaps or overlaps — this equal-unit requirement is what makes the count structural and underpins area.

Do not force the rows × columns shortcut; the structural count is adopted with exposure. A child who partitions correctly but still counts one-by-one has a developmental gap, not an error to penalise.

A static labelled grid (tap-to-reveal rows, columns, total) is a useful reference but cannot let the child vary the grid or contrast counting versus structure, so use it alongside, not instead of, construction tasks.
Recognition/matching items check that the structure is understood but do not elicit independent construction of a partition; pair them with a hands-on partition task.
Keep this planar: volume and 3D packing are a separate later topic and are not part of this objective.

A paper/card rectangle has slight real thickness; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat figure when discussing the squares as area units, and talk about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical sheet.

activityReferences.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order
Predict then count the hidden features
Flat face versus curved surface
Faces as 2-D shapes and nets
Check and explain the counts

startingActivity.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order
learnerActions: Hold a real cube and turn it in your hands.
Count the faces first: colour or number each flat surface as you touch it, saying 'face' each time, until every face is marked. Record the total.
Then trace each edge with a finger, marking each traced edge (e.g. a gold line or sticker), saying 'edge' each time, until all are traced. Record the total.
Then dot each vertex (corner) with a sticker, saying 'vertex' each time. Record the total.
Recount starting from a different face to check your totals stay the same (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A face, an edge and a vertex are three different things; counting each property separately in a fixed order, and marking features as you go, keeps them distinct and makes sure nothing hidden is missed or double-counted.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Handleable solids (cube, cuboid, pyramid, sphere, cylinder, cone) counted by touch
Colour-a-face / trace-an-edge / dot-a-vertex marking system while counting
Nets that fold up into the solid, showing each face as a separate 2-D shape
A cube-vs-cylinder pair to contrast flat faces with a curved surface
commonMisconceptions: Blurs faces, edges and vertices under everyday words, calling edges 'sides' and vertices 'corners' so the three properties run together when counting.
Counts only the faces/edges/vertices that are visible, missing the hidden ones on the far side (gives a cube 3 faces, 9 edges or 4 corners).
Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' (e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces).
Treats the whole solid as if it were the 2-D shape of a face, not distinguishing the flat face from the 3-D object.
constraints: Tap-to-reveal or labelled-model activities that show a feature's name and definition on tap can teach vocabulary, but they display the answer rather than requiring the child to build the count or feel the flat-versus-curved distinction; use them to introduce terms, not to replace counting.

A flat-screen tally that colours each tapped face/edge/vertex can build the keep-them-distinct skill, but a flat screen makes it harder to reveal hidden features on the far side — a main source of miscounting; pair it with a solid the child can turn.

A rotatable on-screen 3-D model lets a child turn the solid to catch hidden features and can toggle to a cylinder for the curved-surface convention; it is one good way to surface the hidden-feature error, but real solids in the hand should confirm what the screen shows, and the on-screen model should be understood as a model of the solid, not the solid itself.
Scored recall questions check whether a child remembers counts; they do not on their own build the counting strategy or the property distinction, so use them as an end-check.
Always state explicitly which convention you are using for describing curved solids, because schemes differ.

Paper nets and card cutouts have a slight real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat faces, which have no thickness; use them to represent faces but keep attention on the flat 2-D shape represented rather than on picking up or handling the card as a definition of the shape.
Recognising or recalling counts is not the same as producing a reliable count by handling and tracking features; expect production, not only recognition.

activityReferences.title: Predict then fold: does this arrangement close into a cube?
Anchor a base and track where every square lands
Make it fail, then make a new one
Extend the reasoning to other solids

startingActivity.title: Predict then fold: does this arrangement close into a cube?
learnerActions: Look at a flat arrangement of six squares and, before folding, commit to a prediction: 'will this fold into a closed cube?' and say WHY.

Fold the arrangement (physical card/Polydron cut-outs, or by folding a paper net) to check the prediction — treating the card as a stand-in for the ideal flat net and asking about the cube it would form, not about the card as an object.
Start with the familiar cross/T net, then meet an unfamiliar 'staircase' zig-zag (2-2-2) net and predict it before folding.
Fold the staircase and observe that it ALSO closes into a cube, with every face covered once and no face left open (allowing for slight gaps from card thickness).
Try a 2-by-3 block of six squares: predict, fold, and watch squares overlap onto the same face while other cube faces are left uncovered.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Whether a net closes into a cube is decided by the ARRANGEMENT of the squares, not merely by having six of them. Unfamiliar nets can be valid and prototype-looking blocks can fail.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Physical fold-up nets (card, Polydron) folded and unfolded from the solid
The eleven cube nets chart; the T/cross prototype set beside non-standard nets
Base-face plus a 'line of four squares' composite
Face-to-face mapping diagram linking each net shape to a solid face
commonMisconceptions: Only the familiar T/cross net makes a cube (prototype-as-only-net; Mariotti 1989) — other valid nets are rejected and near-prototypes trusted.
Any arrangement with the right number of faces folds up — attends to face count, not arrangement.
Cannot predict the fold direction of an L-shape, so mis-assigns which faces meet — a face is thought 'stuck in the corner' or two squares that should be opposite are left adjacent.
constraints: Suitable for ages roughly 8–11 (upper Key Stage 2 geometry).
The predict-then-fold step is load-bearing: a prediction must be committed to and justified BEFORE folding, not after. Omitting the prediction reduces the task to observation.

Physical card/Polydron cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held, but they stand in for ideal flat (zero-thickness) faces; frame questions around the mathematical net and the cube it would fold into, not around whether the physical card can be picked up.

The 'line of four squares' composite applies to nets that contain such a line (e.g. the cross/1-4-1); it is not present in every valid net (e.g. the 2-2-2 staircase), where the general strategy is to track each square's destination from the base.

A static labelled net (each square tagged to the cube face it becomes, optionally with lift-the-flap or tap-to-highlight mappings) is a useful reference and reinforces face-to-face mapping, but it cannot be folded, so on its own it cannot provide the predict-then-fold experience.

A flat 2-D fold animation (drag squares, press fold, with overlap/missing-face flags) supports prediction and immediate close/fail feedback, but a flat animation can under-represent the spatial depth of the fold; pair it with physical folding or a rotatable model where possible.

A rotatable 3-D fold (watch faces swing up around a base, rotate the closing solid, see which squares become opposite) and hands-on physical card/Polydron both make the spatial fold concrete; they offer different experiences and either can carry the core mental action. Supporting non-standard nets on screen or in card lets 'only the T-net works' be disproved directly.

A 'which of these fold into a cube?' selection question is a useful CHECK after folding work; include a valid non-prototype net and an invalid six-square block as options. Recognition-only selection does not by itself elicit the folding reasoning or the production of a new net — pair it with asking the child to name opposite faces or draw a new valid net.
Spoken explanation of a prediction is a valuable prompt but is not a substitute for the spatial folding itself.

startingActivity.title: Measuring lenses: watch which one wins change
learnerActions: Place a tall thin bottle and a short wide jar side by side.
Apply a length comparison (e.g. a ruler lens or measuring them against each other): name the taller as the winner — 'taller'.
Apply a weight comparison (e.g. a balance that tips to the heavier): name which is heavier.

Apply a capacity comparison: fill the tall bottle to the top and pour it into the wide jar; if the jar takes it all with room to spare it holds more. Choose containers where the pour really shows this, and let the actual result stand.
Say aloud which object wins for each attribute, using the matching comparative word.
Notice that the same two objects can win on different attributes, so there is no single answer to 'which is bigger?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: There is no single 'bigger': each object has a height, a weight, and a capacity, and these are different questions with different answers. When which object wins changes per attribute, 'bigger' dissolves into separate, nameable attributes.

keyRepresentations: One object shown with three separate 'measuring lenses' — a length lens, a weight lens (balance), a capacity lens (fill) — each answering a different question about the same object
Two contrasting objects (tall+thin vs short+wide) where the winner changes depending on which attribute is chosen
Comparative word banks paired to each attribute: long/short, tall/short, heavy/light, full/empty, more/less
A balance scale and a pouring/filling demonstration to make weight and capacity felt as attributes distinct from how big something looks
commonMisconceptions: Undifferentiated 'bigger': treats length, height, area, weight and capacity as one global size, so the 'biggest-looking' object is assumed to be the longest AND heaviest AND to hold the most
Height–capacity conflation: a taller container is assumed to hold more, regardless of width
Size–weight conflation: a bigger object is assumed to be heavier
Absolute rather than comparative use of attribute words: labels each object 'tall' or 'big' but cannot say one is taller than another (treats 'tall' as a category, not a relation)
Recognises only a single attribute of an object ('how big it is') rather than seeing that one object has several measurable attributes
constraints: Sorting/matching and multiple-choice ('which attribute does this word measure?') can assess and reinforce recognition of attribute names; they do not, by themselves, let the child observe which object wins change across attributes or construct attribute language in a live comparison — pair them with hands-on comparison and pouring.
Tap-to-reveal of an object's attributes shows one-object-many-attributes but does not dynamically change which object wins a comparison; use it alongside a comparison activity.

Absolute vs comparative language is developmental: provide many graded side-by-side comparisons and let comparative relations emerge; do not drill comparative vocabulary in isolation or mark absolute answers wrong.

Capacity outcomes depend on the actual containers: a wide jar holding more than a tall bottle must be verified by filling and pouring, not assumed, and must NOT be described as 'the one that overflows first holds more' (the first to overflow actually holds less). Choose containers where the pour genuinely demonstrates the point, and let the real result stand.

Counterexample outcomes (big ball lighter than small stone; tall glass vs wide bowl) depend on the specific objects chosen; pick objects that reliably produce the intended contrast and confirm by weighing or pouring rather than asserting.

startingActivity.title: Measuring station: choose the tool and the unit
learnerActions: Set out a mixed set of objects one at a time — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if available, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler/tape, a kitchen scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer all available.
For each object, first say out loud what KIND of measurement this is: how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?
Pick the matching instrument, then choose the standard unit (m or cm, kg or g, litres or ml, °C).
Measure to the nearest mark and state the amount with its unit.

Try a deliberate mismatch — measure the pencil in metres — and notice the number is useless (to the nearest metre a pencil rounds to '0 m'); then switch to centimetres and get a clean reading (a real pencil is usually somewhere between about 10 cm and 19 cm, depending on how much it has been sharpened).
Try reaching for the ruler to measure the jug of juice and notice it cannot give a capacity reading at all.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: You first decide what kind of quantity you are measuring so the unit family and tool fit, then choose a unit grain that gives a sensible, readable number.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A measuring station: ruler/tape, kitchen scale, measuring jug, thermometer, with unit dials m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, °C
Benchmark objects for each unit (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1 litre bottle)

commonMisconceptions: Uses a unit or tool from the wrong attribute — e.g. reaches for a ruler to find 'how much water', or gives grams for a length.
Picks the wrong grain — measures a pencil in metres ('0 m') or a room laboriously in centimetres — not choosing to the nearest appropriate unit.
Happily reports a non-standard count ('6 cubes') when a standard measurement is asked for, not seeing why standard units matter.
Reads the instrument carelessly — doesn't measure to the nearest mark, mis-reads the jug's meniscus or the scale.
constraints: Introduce standard units once the need for them is understood; heavy early use of many varied non-standard units, before the purpose of measurement is grasped, can interfere with understanding why standard units are needed.
Sorting and targeted-question checks verify the judgement of which unit to use but do not rehearse the physical act of measuring; pair them with hands-on measuring.
A reference card reminds learners of benchmarks but cannot let them make and test a choice; it is a scaffold, not the core activity.
Assessment is best done by watching the learner choose the tool and unit across a mixed set of objects, not by asking them to recite rules.
An interactive live-recompute station is one way to make a bad grain visibly awkward; real instruments and objects achieve the same learning and should not be treated as replaceable by a screen only.

Choosing units is primarily a categorical/attribute judgement; a spatial 3D setting may offer little specific additional leverage for it, and in-role dialogue can discuss but not itself rehearse the watched act of picking a tool — these are observations about fit, not claims that any medium is necessary or impossible.

startingActivity.title: Tile and count an L-shaped garden
learnerActions: Cover an L-shaped figure's whole interior with unit squares so there are no gaps and no overlaps, including the awkward squares inside the notch of the L.
Count the covering squares systematically — row by row, or by splitting the L into two rectangles and counting each — marking each square as you count it so none is missed or double-counted.
State the result in square units, e.g. '18 square cm' or in square metres, not just a bare number.
Repeat with a plain rectangle and then compare two shapes side by side, deciding which covers more by comparing their counts.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares that cover the inside of a shape — notches and all — and is about the surface inside, not the fence or distance running around the edge.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Square-centimetre tiles covering a book cover
L-shaped and irregular figures on squared paper
A shape decomposed into rectangles for systematic counting
A count recorded with its square unit (e.g. '18 square cm')
commonMisconceptions: Counts the squares around the boundary (perimeter) instead of the squares covering the interior.
Leaves gaps or overlaps, or counts unsystematically so squares are missed or double-counted (especially on L-shapes).
Counts every partly-covered square at the edge as a whole square, overestimating.
Gives the count as a bare number without the square unit.
constraints: Count every square that covers the inside of the outline, with no gaps or overlaps — including the squares along the edge, which are part of the area. Do not count only the border squares, and do not count squares outside the outline. The distance around the outline (perimeter, measured in unit lengths) is a different kind of quantity from an area count.
Count systematically (row by row, or by decomposing an L-shape into rectangles) so each square is counted exactly once.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m, etc.); a bare number is an incomplete answer.

Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat edge part-squares informally (e.g. pairing two halves) and do NOT drill a part-square formula yet — part-square figures are for discussion, not scored counts.
Real tiles and squared-paper diagrams each support learning differently — tiles ground the physical covering, diagrams abstract it; neither is claimed as universally necessary.
A revealed static figure is a reference/scaffold: it shows the result but does not let the child practise the covering and counting, so it should not replace hands-on tiling.
A count-the-squares check verifies understanding and can catch edge-counting, but does not by itself build the systematic covering skill.

startingActivity.title: Build the array and watch the multiplication grow
learnerActions: Set up a rectangle 4 rows tall and 6 squares wide, adding one complete row of six unit squares at a time.
As each row is added, count on by six: 6, 12, 18, 24, and notice the running total jump by six each time.
Alongside the growing grid, build the matching statement '4 × 6' and connect it to 'four rows of six'.
Rotate the rectangle so it becomes 6 rows of 4; check that the total is still 24, showing 4 × 6 = 6 × 4.
Say in your own words why you do NOT have to count all 24 squares — each new row simply adds another six.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The multiplication IS the array: one factor is how many squares are in a row and the other is how many rows, so rows × squares-in-a-row gives the same total as counting every tile. Rotation preserves area, which is why 4×6 = 6×4.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A rectangle tiled with unit squares showing rows and columns
A 4×6 array with '6 in each row, 4 rows' annotated and 4×6 = 24
Row-strips (cut-outs) repeated to fill the rectangle

commonMisconceptions: Adds the side lengths (4 + 6 = 10) instead of multiplying — confusing area with perimeter.
Cannot structure the array — counts squares one by one with no sense of rows × columns, so never reaches the multiplication.
Multiplies the sides as a rote rule but cannot explain why it equals the tile count.
Miscounts rows or columns, especially when the grid is only partly drawn.
constraints: Multiplication for area must grow out of the array: one side is squares-in-a-row, the other is number-of-rows. Do not introduce length×width as a rote rule before the child can structure rows and columns.
Keep the figure planar. Avoid moving to 3D blocks here, which can blur rectangular area with volume; area is a covering of flat unit squares.
Tile in complete rows and columns with no gaps or overlaps. Partly-drawn grids cause miscounts; complete the grid before counting.
Always use square units for area and distinguish them from the linear units used for the border/perimeter.

A static labelled array (e.g. '6 in each row, 4 rows, 4×6 = 24') is a useful reference, but on its own it does not let a child build rows or rotate to feel commutativity; pair it with hands-on tiling or construction.

A conversation or verbal explanation can discuss the array and check understanding, but does not by itself get the child to construct, tile and count the rows; pair any discussion with hands-on tiling or array construction.
Items that only ask the child to select or fill in an answer can check the link but do not by themselves build the array sense; include construction, tiling and explanation.
For a child who cannot yet see rows and columns, prioritise spatial-structuring practice (row-strips, drawing rows/columns, skip-counting) over imposing the formula.

startingActivity.title: Grid playground: reshape a rectangle and watch area and perimeter move apart
learnerActions: On cm² paper (physical squared paper or an on-screen grid), draw or drag the corners of a rectangle and, as it changes shape, keep two counts — tallied by hand on paper or shown live on screen: the squares filling the inside (area, in cm²) and the units traced around the outline (perimeter, in cm).
Compare a 6×4 rectangle (24 cm², 20 cm) with other shapes you make, saying aloud which count is 'squares covering it' (area) and which is 'steps around it' (perimeter).
Switch to a 'missing side' task: with the area fixed at 48 cm² and the length given as 8 cm, find the width (6 cm); then try area 48 m² with length 8 m → width 6 m.
Switch to an 'irregular blob/pond' task: shade whole squares and part-squares on the grid and combine them to estimate the blob's area, stating that it is an estimate.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Area and perimeter are different quantities with different units: area counts the unit squares covering a surface (cm²); perimeter measures the distance around the edge (cm). One can stay the same while the other changes as a shape is reshaped.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter — uses one formula for the other, or gives the distance around when asked for the covered surface.
Overgeneralises 'area = length × breadth' and reports the answer in linear units (cm) instead of square units (cm²).
When estimating irregular area, counts only whole squares and ignores part-squares (or counts every touched square as a whole).
constraints: Label every answer with correct units: area in square units (cm², m²), perimeter in linear units (cm, m).

Treat irregular-area counting as an estimate; agree one explicit rule for part-squares — either count a part-square as one if it is at least half and ignore smaller parts, or pair part-squares that together make about one whole — and apply it consistently.
The tap-to-reveal reference supports recall of the formulae and units but cannot show area and perimeter changing as a shape is reshaped; use it alongside, not instead of, grid manipulation.

Keep the formulae anchored to meaning (array of unit squares for area, distance around for perimeter) so they are not learned purely instrumentally; avoid overgeneralising l × w to non-rectangular shapes.

Live counters, dragging corners and a slider estimate are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; physical squared paper, tiles and finger-tracing achieve the same purpose and neither is mandatory.

activityReferences.title: Cut it, re-lay it: equal amount beats equal look
Sort the partitions: quarters or not?
Which is the bigger share: a third or a quarter?

startingActivity.title: Cut it, re-lay it: equal amount beats equal look
learnerActions: Partition a square into four parts where the pieces look different — e.g. one long thin strip plus some oddly-shaped bits — but each covers the same amount.
Before checking, predict: is the long thin piece the same amount of the square as a fat corner piece? Say why.

Check equality physically: cut the long strip and lay it over the fat piece to see it rearranges exactly onto it. For pieces whose edges follow a faint underlying grid you can also count the unit squares each covers; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement rather than counting, since squares get split.
Decide whether all four pieces are quarters and give the reason (each is the same AMOUNT, one of four equal parts).

Now quarter the SAME shape in a completely different way (e.g. three equally spaced vertical cuts giving four equal strips, then a 2x2 grid, then two diagonals) and argue each piece is still a quarter.

Partition a circle into three equal parts (120-degree slices) and explain how you could check the three parts really are equal (overlay one onto another — they are congruent — or compare the area each covers).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A quarter means each part is the same amount (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts — the pieces may look different as long as each covers the same amount; and the same shape can be partitioned into the same fraction in many valid ways.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned several ways into the same fraction (multiple valid cuts)
Circle partitioned into thirds (120° shares)
Equal-area different-shape pieces that rearrange onto one another
Faint unit-square grid under a shape for checking equal area
commonMisconceptions: Equal shares must look the same / be congruent — rejects equal-area different-shape pieces as 'not fair'
Any N pieces count as Nths regardless of size (ignores the equal-parts requirement)
A shape can only be partitioned into a fraction one 'proper' way
Judges share size by one dimension (length) rather than area
Thinks halving repeatedly is the only way to make parts, so thirds feel impossible
constraints: Equal shares must be equal in AMOUNT (area); they need not be congruent or look the same.
Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not sufficient — unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters.
Move beyond halving to thirds so children cannot rely on repeated halving; a circle into three (120-degree shares) is a good non-halving case.

Compare share sizes (e.g. a third vs a quarter) only for identical wholes; this scopes the comparison to represented portions. As numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.

Counting unit squares is a valid equal-area check only where piece edges follow the grid; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement, since grid squares get split. Overlay alone proves equality only for congruent pieces; for equal-area pieces of different shape, cut and recompose (or count unit squares if their edges follow the grid).

Sorting/categorisation tasks are recognition: they may check and sharpen the equal-parts criterion but do not let a child physically prove equality by rearranging, so use them alongside hands-on cutting and overlaying, not instead of it.
Physical paper/card cutouts have slight thickness and model the ideal flat figure being partitioned; the lesson is about the 2D area partition they represent, for which thickness is irrelevant.

An on-screen faint unit grid that tints pieces green when areas match is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete, not a required mechanism — cutting and rearranging pieces works too, and is needed for differently shaped pieces whose edges do not follow the grid.
Static galleries of correct/incorrect partitions can serve as a reference but do not let the child test equality by rearranging pieces; pair them with a hands-on check.
A third spatial dimension is not needed for partitioning 2D shapes; keep the work planar unless there is a specific reason otherwise.

activityReferences.title: Build the fraction, build the name
Label the fraction's jobs
Classify and match for fluency

startingActivity.title: Build the fraction, build the name
learnerActions: Cut a bar into M equal parts (for example set it to 4) and shade N of them (for example 3), then write the symbol that matches: the parts taken on top, the equal parts in one whole on the bottom.
As you shade, say the fraction as one spoken quantity ('three-quarters'), not 'three, four'.
Label each number to its job: the numerator is 'the 3 parts we took' and the denominator is 'the 4 equal parts in one whole'.

Now push the numerator past the denominator (shade 5 parts when the whole holds 4): the shading overflows into a second whole. Record that this is called an improper fraction (5/4) and write its mixed twin beside it (1 1/4).

Sort every fraction you build into four trays: unit (numerator 1 and denominator more than 1, like 1/4), proper-but-not-unit (numerator more than 1 but less than the denominator, like 3/4), improper (numerator as big as or bigger than the denominator, like 5/4 or 4/4; 1/1 also goes here because it equals one whole), and mixed (like 1 1/4). A unit fraction like 1/4 is a special kind of proper fraction, so sort each card into its most specific tray.

Shade 2/4 of a bar, then slide that shaded length to overlay 1/2 of a bar of the same length (the same whole): notice the symbols differ but the shaded length is identical, so they name the same amount.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Fraction notation names one number. The bottom number tells how many equal parts one whole is cut into; the top counts how many we have. Pushing the numerator past the denominator shows 5/4 is a real number greater than one (equal to 1 1/4), and overlaying 2/4 on 1/2 shows different symbols can name the same quantity.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar/area model with the symbol written alongside and each number labelled to its job
Number line locating the fraction as a single point (a fraction is a number)
Fraction wall showing unit vs non-unit and proper vs improper
Word-symbol-picture triple card (three-quarters / 3/4 / shaded bar)
commonMisconceptions: Reads 3/4 as two separate whole numbers ('three, four') rather than one quantity
Writes the fraction upside down — swaps numerator and denominator
Believes an improper fraction like 5/4 or 4/3 'isn't a real number / can't exist'
Mixes the vocabulary — calls the bottom number the numerator
Thinks 2/4 and 1/2 must be different amounts because the numbers differ
constraints: Always anchor the vocabulary to a model (bar, circle or number line); do not teach numerator/denominator as memorised top/bottom labels.
Deliberately include improper and mixed forms (5/4, 1 1/4) so children learn the notation can name amounts greater than one; do not leave them believing 'you can't have 5/4'.
Say fractions as single spoken quantities ('three-quarters') so the symbol is heard as one number, never 'three, four'.

When sorting into unit / proper / improper / mixed, make clear that a unit fraction is a special proper fraction (sort it as unit) so the categories are not treated as if a fraction like 1/4 belonged in two trays.

The labelled-reference activity supports naming and reading only; it cannot let a child build improper/mixed forms or manipulate equivalence, so it is a scaffold, not a replacement for generating notation.

Classification, matching and fill-in tasks check fluency and recognition; a sort or match does not itself elicit independent construction of the single-number idea, so follow them with building and explaining.

A spoken quiz or dialogue can check naming, but it does not by itself elicit the writing and shading that produce the notation; pair any dialogue with building rather than treating talk as a substitute.

startingActivity.title: Fraction-of-a-set bench: share into equal groups, then take some
learnerActions: Put out 12 counters as the whole. To find 1/3, share ALL 12 into 3 equal groups (one group per hoop) and take one group - record '1/3 of 12 = 4'.
To find 3/4, share all 12 into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take THREE of the four groups - record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Say aloud 'the bottom number is how many equal groups; the top number is how many groups I take' as you act it out.

Check a non-dividing case: with a different set of items that does not share evenly (for example 10 counters into 3 groups), notice the leftover. It means the groups cannot all be equal with whole items, so that fraction of the set cannot be found exactly with whole counters (1/3 of 10 is not 3).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The denominator sets how many EQUAL groups/parts to make; the numerator says how many of those to take - so 3/4 is three quarters, not one piece, and the same fraction describes both a set and a shape.

commonMisconceptions: Reading the denominator as the group SIZE, not the number of groups (1/3 of 12 -> makes groups of 3)
Treating a non-unit fraction like a unit fraction - taking only ONE part for 3/4

constraints: Fractions require EQUAL parts/groups; share the whole into denominator-many equal parts before taking any.
For a set, share into denominator-many equal GROUPS (not groups of that size), then take numerator-many groups.
Keep the whole explicit and fixed throughout a task.
Non-unit fractions (2/4, 3/4) are repeated unit fractions - take numerator-many parts, not one.

A reference poster or labelled image is reference-only: tapping to highlight parts-taken versus total-parts can support naming but does not have the child do the sharing, so it is a scaffold, not a replacement for partition-and-select practice.
Recognition and matching tasks assess and consolidate naming/writing but do not on their own require the learner to construct the partition; pair them with hands-on sharing.
When a set does not divide evenly, address any leftover explicitly rather than ignoring it.

When the whole is an amount of stuff (e.g. food or material), fair sharing makes the AMOUNT equal; equal COUNT only guarantees this for identical items, so distinguish count from amount when items differ in size. startingActivity.title: Build fourths: three cuts, not four marks
learnerActions: Start with a bare line labelled only 0 and 1 — the 0–1 segment is the unit.

To make 'fourths', first try the common mistake: drop FOUR equally spaced marks inside the 0–1 segment. Notice this cuts the unit into FIVE equal parts, each one a fifth (1/5) — the far interior mark sits at 4/5. So you have actually made fifths, not fourths: a sign something has gone wrong.
Correct to THREE interior marks so the unit is cut into exactly four equal parts (quarters); the marks land at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).
State the rule in your own words: b equal parts need b−1 interior marks.
Place 3/4 by jumping the quarter-length three times from 0, landing one quarter-length short of 1.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Four equal parts require three interior cuts (b equal parts need b−1 interior marks); a/b is measured as a LENGTH from 0 (a jumps of 1/b), not as a count of tick marks. Drawing four equally spaced interior marks cuts the unit into five equal parts (fifths), so calling them fourths mislabels the pieces — making the tick-counting error visible so the child can correct it.

Both interpret (read a shown point) and produce (place on a blank line) are required; recognition alone does not elicit the independent partitioning and placement that demonstrate understanding.

A number line is one-dimensional; the unit-interval idea lives on a single line, so added dimensions are not needed for this particular objective (this is a scope note, not a claim that other media cannot teach).
Children aged ~8–9 (KS2 Years 3–4) are the intended audience; keep lines and partitions simple (halves through tenths).

startingActivity.title: Split each part of a fixed bar (2/3 becomes 4/6)
learnerActions: Shade two of three equal parts of a bar to show 2/3.
Split every third into two equal pieces by drawing a line through each part; count that four of six parts are now shaded and write 4/6.
Describe what happened to the length of shaded strip: it did not grow or shrink, there are just more lines.
Keep splitting to generate the family: split each part into three for 6/9, into four for 8/12; each time check the shaded strip stays the same length.

Test changing only one number: on an identical bar change only the bottom number (2/3 to 2/6) or only the top number (2/3 to 3/3) and shade it; check that the shaded amount changes, so changing just one part does NOT make an equivalent fraction.
Try the trap: add one to the top and one to the bottom (2/3 to 3/4) and shade 3/4 of an identical bar; compare the shaded length with the original 2/3.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Splitting each part (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) makes more, smaller pieces that cover exactly the same amount; for fractions like 2/3, changing only one of the two numbers, or adding one to each, shifts the amount, so neither is a way to make an equivalent fraction.

keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / stacked equal-length bars (canonical equivalence reference)
A single bar re-partitioned by splitting each part (2/3 → 4/6)
Number line with dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) showing the same point
Area model (identical rectangles shaded to the same amount)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — 4/6 judged more than 2/3 'because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces'
Different numbers must mean different amounts (denies equivalence)
Makes 'equivalents' by ADDING the same number to top and bottom (2/3 → 3/4)
Compares shaded amounts across different-sized wholes
Thinks changing only the numerator or only the denominator keeps the value
constraints: When comparing represented portions (shaded areas or bar lengths), always use identical-sized wholes; comparing shaded amounts across different-sized wholes invalidates the equivalence judgement. As numbers on a number line, equivalent fractions remain comparable and coincide at one point.
Teach the multiplicative structure (splitting each part, multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) with diagrams BEFORE introducing any 'times top and bottom' rule.

Both numerator and denominator must be multiplied by the same number: for fractions less than one, such as 2/3, adding one to each (2/3 to 3/4) or changing only one of the two numbers shifts the shaded amount and does not make an equivalent fraction. (Adding one to each keeps the amount the same only when the fraction is a whole, e.g. 3/3 to 4/4, so it is not a valid rule.)
Matching, sorting and fill-in-the-blank tasks consolidate and check classification/completion but do not on their own build the underlying structure; use them after diagram-based construction.
A fraction wall shows which fractions align but does not itself demonstrate the split-each-part mechanism; pair it with active splitting.
Suitable for ages 7-8 (small denominators); the goal is recognising and showing equivalence with diagrams, not symbolic manipulation in isolation.

activityReferences.title: Split a tenth into ten hundredths
Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary and place them on a line
Predict and compare: which is bigger, a tenth or a hundredth?

startingActivity.title: Split a tenth into ten hundredths
learnerActions: Start with a strip that is one whole, already partitioned into ten equal tenths.
Take a single tenth and cut (or subdivide) it into ten equal pieces; name one piece 'a hundredth' and write 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100.

Work out how many of these small pieces would fill the whole strip: each of the ten tenths holds ten hundredths, so 10 × 10 = 100. Connect this to 'a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts of the whole'.
Count aloud in hundredths across the tenth boundary — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and pause at 10 hundredths to say it is also 1 tenth.
Lay one hundredth directly beside one tenth and describe how much smaller the hundredth is.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Hundredths come from dividing a tenth again by ten; ten hundredths rebuild one tenth and 100 hundredths make one whole. A hundredth is smaller than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10, because the same whole is split into more equal parts.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred grid (whole = 1, column = 1/10, small square = 1/100)
Length / number line from 0 to 1/10 subdivided into 10 hundredths
A tenth-strip physically cut into ten hundredth-pieces (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100)
Place-value nesting diagram: whole → tenths → hundredths, each ten-for-one
Counting sequence in hundredths crossing 10/100 = 1/10
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias on the denominator: believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 is bigger than 10'.
Not coordinating the nesting — treating 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as different, unrelated amounts.
Believing hundredths can only be made by cutting the whole into 100 at once, not by subdividing tenths (missing the recursive ×10 structure).
Losing count across the tenth boundary (after 9 hundredths, not seeing 10 hundredths = 1 tenth).
Thinking 'hundredths' refers to the large number 100 rather than to tiny parts of a whole.
constraints: A 10×10 hundred grid and a length/number-line model are complementary and are recommended together (whole grid/strip = 1, one column or row = 1/10, one small square or gap = 1/100); pairing the two models is the original's preferred approach, though a single well-chosen model can also support the learning.
Derive hundredths by subdividing a tenth, not by cutting the whole into 100 pieces in one go, so the recursive ten-in-one structure is felt.

Whole-number bias is the central obstacle and must be addressed, not merely stated; directly comparing exactly one tenth against exactly one hundredth is the strongly recommended means (the original's named approach), though it is one effective technique rather than the only possible one.

Paper or card strips have real thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal flat fractional length; a screen model shows the idealised zero-thickness version. Either can support this learning; neither is required.

Recognition or ordering tasks (e.g. picking which is bigger from options, filling '10 hundredths = __ tenth') check outcomes but do not by themselves build the nesting insight; use them alongside subdivision work, not as a substitute for the child performing the split.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a live counter that steps in hundredths and snaps to the 1/10 tick with a flipping '10 hundredths = 1 tenth' label; a size-compare mode dropping one hundredth beside one tenth; zooming between 0 and 1/10 to place several hundredths; a tappable column revealing '1 tenth = 10 hundredths'. These are illustrative, not mandatory.
