startingActivity.title: One quantity, three names — fill and watch them move together
learnerActions: Fill a hundred square (or slide a bar) to show a chosen amount, e.g. drag to fill fifty squares.
Read the linked panel as it updates in lockstep: 50/100, 0.5, 50%, with a marker halfway along a 0%–100% number line.
Say the decimal aloud in place-value language ('five tenths, one half, fifty per cent'); use a 'read it' option to hear the correct reading.
Fill nine squares and confirm the panel reads 9/100, 0.09, 9% and voices the place-value name 'nine hundredths' alongside the digit reading 'zero point zero nine'.
Switch to context skins (a '9% off' price tag, a jug 0.5 full) and state the same fact as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
When finding part of an amount, practise saying and writing 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80') rather than '9% = £37.80'; equivalences such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' are still correct.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction, a decimal and a percentage are not three separate topics but one quantity wearing three names; the correct place-value reading and the 'per cent = out of 100' meaning are visible in the same moment the learner acts.

keyRepresentations: Four-way display: shaded hundred square + fraction (n/100) + decimal + point on a 0%–100% number line
0–1 / 0%–100% double number line linking the three forms
Place-value chart for reading decimals aloud (ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths)
Real-context cards (50% off, jug 0.5 full, 3/4 of a pizza) matched across notations
Matching sets of fraction–decimal–percentage cards for one value
commonMisconceptions: Reading decimals as digit strings ('point oh nine', 'point seven') instead of place-value names ('nine hundredths', 'seven tenths').
Treating fraction, decimal and percentage as different, unrelated things rather than three names for one value.
Misusing percentage notation — writing '10% = 42' instead of '10% of 420 = 42'.
Reading the percentage number as the whole ('50% means 50') rather than as parts per hundred.
Confusing per cent (out of 100) with a plain count.
constraints: Insist that learners can give the place-value reading of decimals: 0.09 is 'nine hundredths', 0.7 is 'seven tenths'. Digit readings such as 'zero point zero nine' or 'point seven' are conventional and not wrong, but they do not show place value, so always ask for the place-value name as well.

When finding a percentage of an amount, always write 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80'), never '9% = £37.80', including in worked feedback; per cent means parts per hundred of a base, and 100% is the whole. Equivalences between forms, such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' or '50% = 0.5 = 1/2', are correct and should be encouraged.
Treat the three forms as names for one value, not as separate topics; show them together on a shaded hundred square and/or a 0%–100% number line.
Introduce 'terminating decimal' and 'convert' as working vocabulary during the act of converting, attached to actions rather than defined in isolation.
Matching, multiple-choice and sorting tasks check correct usage but do not by themselves build the linked-representation habit; use them alongside an activity where the learner drives the change.
A fixed reference display shows one value at a time and cannot be re-driven by the learner; pair it with manipulable work across many values.
The target is USE in context, not reciting definitions; judge success by how a learner reads, writes and moves between forms with real quantities.

startingActivity.title: Stretch-and-shrink bar: predict before you scale
learnerActions: Look at a 7-unit bar placed beside a faint marker of the original length 7.
Before anything moves, predict out loud or in writing whether scaling by a chosen multiplier will make the bar longer, shorter, or the same, and say WHY.
Set the multiplier to 3/4 and watch the bar contract to sit short of 7 (3/4 × 7 = 5.25).
Set the multiplier to 5/3 and watch the bar stretch past 7 (5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67).
Set the multiplier to 4/4 and watch the bar hold exactly at 7, re-partitioned to show it is still the same length.
Sweep the multiplier dial slowly across 1 and notice the exact point where the bar flips from shrinking to growing.
State the rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is more than 1.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: For a positive quantity scaled by a positive multiplier, the product is larger than, equal to, or smaller than the quantity exactly according to whether the multiplier is greater than, equal to, or less than 1 — the number 1 is the pivot, not whether the multiplier is written as a fraction.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line / elastic band stretched (×>1) or compressed (×<1) relative to the original length
Photo or shape enlargement/reduction by a scale factor
Double number line pairing a quantity with its scaled image
× n/n = ×1 shown as re-partitioning without changing length (equivalence link)
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes the number bigger' (and division always smaller) — predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7 (Fischbein's primitive intuitive model; named explicitly in the IES guide).
Over-corrects to 'any fraction makes it smaller' — predicts 5/3 × 7 < 7 because the multiplier is written as a fraction, ignoring that 5/3 > 1.
Thinks multiplying by n/n changes the value (because 'you multiplied'), not recognising n/n = 1.
constraints: Target age roughly 10–11 (Year 5 / Grade 5); conceptual objective, not a computation drill.

Insist on prediction and reasoning BEFORE any calculation — the reason is the diagnostic part. A learner can guess 'less than 7' without understanding; require 'because 3/4 is less than 1, so it's part of 7'.
Always pair a multiplier >1 (e.g. 5/3) with one <1 (e.g. 2/5 or 3/4) so learners must track size relative to 1 rather than applying a blanket 'fractions shrink' rule.
Sorting and multiple-choice items assess direction and can bait errors, but they ask for selection; include tasks where the learner constructs a reason, a counterexample, or a corrected rule.
A static before/after image can show one enlargement and one reduction but does not let the learner vary the multiplier across 1; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main concept-building task.
Keep concrete numbers correct: 3/4 × 7 = 5.25 (short of 7), 5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67 (past 7), 2/5 × 7 = 2.8 (short of 7), 4/4 × 7 = 7.

A zero-thickness on-screen bar or elastic is an idealised model of magnitude/length; physical strips, elastic bands, or photos are approximations with their own properties (slight thickness, stretch limits) — use either to make resizing felt, without claiming one is required or superior.
Compare fractions here as numbers/multipliers against 1; do not teach any 'denominator rule flips' idea — the direction of change comes from the multiplier's size relative to 1.

startingActivity.title: Build the tape diagram: draw, find one block, read off
learnerActions: Given '£20 shared in the ratio 3:2', build two bars — 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks — keeping every block the same width.
Place a brace spanning all 5 blocks and label it with the total, £20.
Find the value of one block by dividing the total by the number of blocks: £20 ÷ 5 = £4.
Fill every block with £4, then read off the two shares: 3 × £4 = £12 and 2 × £4 = £8; check they add back to £20.
Toggle the same ratio between part-to-part twin bars (3 and 2) and a part-to-whole single bar of 5, and say which layout the question needs.
Repeat independently for a new problem: share £18 in the ratio 5:1 — six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.
Re-read one of your diagrams as a proportion: 'what fraction of the money is the shaded bar?' (e.g. 3 out of 5).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each block is an equal unit standing for the same amount; dividing the whole by the number of blocks gives one block's value, and from that single fact every share and proportion can be read straight off the picture without a memorised rule.

keyRepresentations: Part-to-part twin bars (e.g. 3 equal blocks : 2 equal blocks) with a brace showing the total
Part-to-whole single bar split into the total number of parts, one section shaded
Cubes/counters as the concrete precursor to drawn blocks
Ratio table and double number line as complementary models to contrast
One labelled block annotated with its value (the pivot of the three-move routine)
commonMisconceptions: Draws blocks of unequal size, so the model no longer represents equal units
Sets up part-to-whole when the problem is part-to-part (draws a bar of 3 for a 3:2 ratio and treats the 2 as part of it), or vice versa
Jumps to arithmetic without finding the value of one block, so the diagram is decorative rather than a solving tool
Maps the wrong quantity to the wrong bar, or forgets which bar is which after drawing
constraints: Every block in the bars must be the same size and stand for the same amount; the model breaks if blocks are drawn unequal.
Distinguish part-to-part (two separate bars, e.g. 3 and 2) from part-to-whole (one bar of 5, or a whole split), and choose the layout the question needs.
Always draw the diagram before calculating so problem structure is made visible rather than guessed from key words.
Label the diagram fully — the total (a brace over the whole), the known value and the '?' — so it carries the problem's information.
Make 'find the value of one block' the pivot: a diagram that is drawn but never used to find one block's value is decorative, not a solving tool.
Reading a prepared model (tap-to-reveal, worked example) is a scaffold toward constructing one; it does not by itself require the learner to build a model for a new problem.
Matching and multiple-choice items assess recognition; independent construction requires the learner to draw a correct model for a new ratio.
The bar model is planar; a flat layout keeps the equal-unit comparison clear. Added depth is not needed for this representation (this is a scope note, not a claim about 3D teaching generally).

startingActivity.title: Drag-to-sort (or hands-on sort) with self-counting groups
learnerActions: Face a jumble of coloured shapes and three labelled groups/bins (physical trays or an on-screen mat).
Before starting, say aloud the single attribute: 'we are sorting by COLOUR.'
Move each shape into its matching group until every shape is placed and none is left over.

Watch or build each group as a line with one object per equal-sized space (or a stack of same-size counters standing for the objects) so groups can be compared fairly, and keep a running count of each group.
Read off which group has the most and which has the fewest by comparing the counts.
Then re-sort the SAME set a different way (by size): tip everything out, relabel the groups, and sort again, noticing the counts change.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Sorting means applying one consistent rule to classify every object, and 'most/fewest' is read from the counts once the groups are arranged for fair comparison. The same fixed data can also be grouped in more than one way — how you sort is a choice.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Sorting hoops / bins or trays, one per category
Objects lined up one-to-one in rows (an emerging bar graph)
A simple two- or three-row count record (category name + count)
Real class data the child helped generate (favourite colour, shape cards)
commonMisconceptions: Shifts the sorting criterion partway (starts by colour, drifts to size), producing mixed groups
Judges 'most' by the space a group takes up rather than its count (a spread-out group of big objects looks like 'more')
Miscounts a group by losing track when objects are scattered (insecure cardinality)
Thinks each object can go in more than one pile, or leaves objects unsorted
constraints: Keep one sorting attribute fixed within a single sort; name it aloud before starting so groups don't drift into mixed criteria.

Arrange groups as lines with one object per equal-sized space (e.g. a grid mat), or as stacks of same-size counters or blocks, so 'most/fewest' is read from count, not from the space a group happens to fill — large or spread-out objects can look like 'more' while being fewer, and stacks of different-sized shapes cannot be fairly compared by height.
Every object must be classified into exactly one non-overlapping group; none left unsorted and none in two piles.
Secure cardinality supports this skill: if a child loses track counting a scattered group, that is a counting lapse to steady (slide each aside / line them up), not a sorting error to reteach.

Assess by watching the child sort and count (the doing), not by asking them to describe sorting: observe whether they hold one rule, sort exhaustively, count with cardinality, and read most/fewest from counts. Recognising an answer in a multiple-choice check is not the same as independently sorting and counting.
A tap-to-reveal of an already-sorted set with counts can serve as reference, but it does not let the child perform the sorting, which is the skill; use it only as a scaffold, not the main task.

An open conversation or a 3D handling task is not required for this flat, single-attribute classification; a multiple-choice 'which has most?' may check the read-off, but recognising the answer does not elicit independent sorting and counting.

startingActivity.title: Survey organiser: from response cards to a table that answers the question
learnerActions: Start from a real question the class cares about, e.g. 'which of these three snacks is most popular?' or 'which of these three fruits does our class like best?'
Take a shuffled stack of class response cards and sort each card into one of 2-3 categories, building a tally as you go
Write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list
Check that the row counts add up to the number of cards you started with (e.g. '7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards')
Order the categories from most to fewest so the category with the biggest count rises to the top (if two categories have the same biggest count, say that they are tied rather than naming one winner)
Read the table back aloud to state which category answers the question

Test the table as a live record: if two more children chose one fruit, update that count, check that the new total is 2 more than before (e.g. 18 instead of 16), and see whether the ordered answer changes
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An organised table is a tool that ANSWERS a question, not just a store of numbers: once ordered, the record visibly shows the most popular category, the totals should reconcile with the whole set, and updating a count updates the answer.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Simple frequency table / list (category name + count)

Sorted objects or cards arranged in rows as the concrete source

commonMisconceptions: Records counts that don't line up with their categories (rows misaligned in the table)
Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table treated as decoration)

Forces every item into the given categories (or invents overlaps) when some items fit none
constraints: Begin from a genuine statistical question so the organised data has a purpose to answer; always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration

nodes.title: 提出统计问题
nodes.description: Distinguish a statistical question — one that anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, so its answer must account for that variability (even when it is reported as a single summary value such as a mean or median) — from a question answered by a single fixed fact; for a statistical question, identify the population (who or what is being asked about), the attribute being investigated, and the variation expected in the answers
learningGoals: Sort questions such as 'How tall am I?', 'How tall are the pupils in my class?', 'How many days are in March?' and 'How many hours of sleep do 12-year-olds usually get?' into statistical and non-statistical, explaining each choice by whether the answers are expected to vary

For a given statistical question, name the population and the attribute being measured, describe the variation they expect (e.g. 'sleep times will differ from person to person, perhaps from 7 to 11 hours'), and explain that a good answer must account for that variability in the data — even a single-number summary such as 'a typical 12-year-old sleeps about 9 hours' stands for many differing values, unlike the one fixed answer to 'How many days are in March?'

Explain why a question about a group can still be non-statistical (e.g. 'How many pupils are in my class?' has one fixed answer), and rewrite a non-statistical question as a statistical one (e.g. 'How long is my journey to school?' becomes 'How long are journeys to school for pupils in my year?')
nodes.originalAssessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} whether 'How many pets does our family have?' and 'How many pets do children in your class have?' are the same kind of question, can they explain that the second one has lots of different answers — so you'd need to collect data from many people — while the first has just one answer?

startingActivity.title: Label the chart and sort the data
learnerActions: Finish a half-built bar chart by placing the right term onto each part: the title, each axis label, the scale (the equal number steps up the side), the category names along the bottom, and the frequency (the count shown by the height of each bar on the value axis).
Say each term aloud as you place it — 'this is the scale', 'these are the category names', 'this axis shows the frequency' — so you are wielding the word, not just matching it.
Sort real variables into 'discrete (counted)' or 'continuous (measured)': e.g. 'number of pets', 'goals scored' versus 'how tall', 'time taken', 'temperature'.
For each variable, apply the test: 'Could there be a value in between?' — someone can be 125-and-a-half cm tall (continuous) but cannot have two-and-a-half pets (discrete).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Data vocabulary is mastered by using it correctly in a real chart and a real sorting task — height is continuous because a value can fall in between, even when it is written as a whole number.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A chart the child annotates: title, both axis labels, an even scale, category names
Contrast-pair cards (discrete/continuous; tally/frequency)
A sorting mat for variables: counted vs measured
Tally chart feeding a frequency table (marks → count)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses discrete and continuous — e.g. thinks height is discrete because it's written as a whole number, or that 'continuous' just means 'a lot of data'
Uses 'frequency' for the category name, or conflates the tally marks with the frequency total
Muddles 'label' and 'scale' — calls the category names the scale, or numbers an axis in uneven steps yet still calls it a scale
Calls every display a 'bar chart' or 'graph', not matching the term to the representation
constraints: Teach each term at the point it is needed inside a real data activity, not as an up-front word list.
Recognition and tap-to-reveal glossary tasks support recall but do not, by themselves, elicit independent construction; pair them with building and labelling a chart and sorting real variables.
The contrast-pair glossary is a scaffold: it displays comparisons but does not require the child to use the term, so confirm mastery through active labelling and sorting with feedback.

Matching, categorisation and fill-the-blank items can check correct use (e.g. a discrete/continuous sort with a 'whole-number-written' trap, a tally-versus-frequency match), but keep them as checks alongside the hands-on build rather than the main teaching.

A real survey/chart with actual categories, an even scale and variables to sort is the core for this LANGUAGE objective; picture-only or definition-reciting versions are weaker for eliciting correct use because the vocabulary is learned by wielding it.

startingActivity.title: Flip the scale: watch the same bars change value
learnerActions: Draw bars for a small data set on squared paper where 'each square = 1'.
Then change the key to 'each square = 5' and re-read every bar: say what each bar now means (e.g. a 4-square bar is now 20, not 4).
State out loud: 'The height on its own doesn't tell me the value — I only know the value once I read it through the scale.'
Optional with an interactive scaled-graph builder: use a scale selector (each square = 2/5/10) that re-labels the axis live, so the same drawn bars instantly re-map to new values.
Choose a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) for a given data set so the largest value fits, mark the axis in equally spaced intervals, and explain why that scale works.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A bar's or symbol's size maps to a value only via the scale; changing the scale re-maps every value, and a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) makes the largest value fit with equal intervals.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Scaled bar graph on squared paper (each square = 2/5/10)
Scaled pictogram with a stated key and part-symbols
Frequency table as the source, with the scale chosen from the largest value
Two bars aligned for a difference, or stacked for a sum
commonMisconceptions: Ignores the scale and reads each square/symbol as one unit (or just counts symbols)
Cannot read an intermediate value — rounds a mid-interval bar to a gridline or ignores a part-symbol
Collapses a two-step problem to one step (reads a value but doesn't combine, or does the wrong operation)
Constructs a scaled axis with unequal intervals, so positions no longer map to values
constraints: Always read the key/scale first, before reading any value ('each square stands for 5').

Learners should both READ and CONSTRUCT scaled graphs; recognition-only or tap-to-reveal items that show a key and values can check reading but do not themselves elicit the independent scale choice or multi-step solving that construction and open problems require.
A static scaled graph with a tappable key can serve as a reference, but it cannot let the learner change the scale or solve multi-step problems; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
Multiple-choice two-step items should include a 'one-step' wrong option (just the top value) so collapsing to one step is detectable; such items check reading/solving but do not require construction.
Half-symbols and bar tops between gridlines must be included so intermediate reading is practised, not avoided.

When a half-symbol or mid-interval value is used with learners, choose a key/scale that yields an exact value (e.g. an even key so a half-symbol is a whole number), or state the half value explicitly (2½, 12½) rather than rounding to a nearby whole number.

startingActivity.title: The Chance-master's bag: say it, then watch it happen
learnerActions: Look into a bag you can see holds mostly red counters (e.g. 7 red and 3 blue) with the composition visible.
Before any draw, say in words how likely a red draw is and WHY, grounding the reason in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than wanting red.

When you declare red 'certain', watch the game-master take out and show a blue counter (picked on purpose, or by drawing until one appears, because a single random draw will usually be red), then repair your word: was red certain, or only likely? Explain the difference.

Answer the opposite trap: the game-master suggests 'landing on 7 with this ordinary 1–6 die is only very unlikely, isn't it?' — decide whether 7 is very unlikely (rare but possible) or impossible (cannot happen at all), and say why.
Describe a green draw ('there are no green counters'), and a 'red or blue' draw ('only those two colours exist'), choosing and justifying a word for each.
Reject vague answers: if you say '50-50', be ready for 'but there are 7 red and 3 blue — is that even?' and recount to decide.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each likelihood word corresponds to how many of each outcome there are; 'likely' is not a guarantee and 'impossible' (cannot happen at all) is stronger than 'very unlikely' (rare but possible). 'Even chance' requires equal numbers, not merely two possible outcomes.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Likelihood line / probability word-scale strip (impossible ↔ certain)
Bags of coloured counters with visible, countable composition
Spinners with equal vs unequal sections
Everyday-event cards to sort and order
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'even chance' as meaning 'any situation with two possible outcomes' (e.g. calling a 1-red / 5-blue draw 'even chance' because there are two colours)
Collapsing the graded words to guarantees — 'likely' taken to mean it will definitely happen, 'unlikely' that it definitely won't
Confusing 'impossible' (cannot happen, probability 0) with 'very unlikely' (rare but possible) — e.g. calling a rare draw 'impossible'
Judging likelihood by personal preference or wishful thinking rather than by how many of each outcome there are
constraints: The objective is correct USE and justification of the five words in context; activities must make the child produce and justify the vocabulary, not merely select it.
Justifications must be grounded in the composition (how many of each outcome), not in personal preference or wishful thinking.

Reserve 'certain' and 'impossible' for the true endpoints (all favourable / zero favourable) and use the graded middle for everything else; do not let 'likely' become a guarantee or 'unlikely' become 'impossible'.

Keep 'impossible' (cannot happen at all, e.g. 7 on a 1–6 die or a green draw when none are present) distinct from 'very unlikely' (rare but possible); never present a strictly impossible outcome as a graded-middle case.

Use unequal compositions early (e.g. 7 red/3 blue, a spinner with one big section) so 'even chance' is not over-generalised to any two-outcome case; when comparing two represented outcomes, 'even chance' requires equal numbers.

Sorting/sequencing and the tap-to-reveal scene are recognition or reference scaffolds: they can assess classification or model reasoning but do not on their own elicit the child's independent, justified use of the words — pair them with spoken/written reasons or follow with open dialogue.
The live strip's slider/recolouring and suggested-word zone are optional illustrative interactions, not required mechanisms; the child must still voice the word themselves.

A spatial/3D environment is not required for this vocabulary-focused objective, which centres on producing and justifying words rather than spatial reasoning; the source judged it to add little over a flat scale and dialogue, but treat this as a scoped, untested design judgement, not a universal claim that 3D media add nothing.

activityReferences.title: Predict, flip, tally: run and read a coin experiment
Watch the proportion settle: scale up the number of trials
The coin has no memory: confront recency thinking
Interpretation check: does a small sample prove bias?

startingActivity.title: Predict, flip, tally: run and read a coin experiment
learnerActions: Before flipping, predict the expected number of heads in 20 flips (about 10) and write it down.
Set up a tally chart with one row per outcome (heads, tails).
Flip the coin 20 times, marking exactly one tally per flip AS it happens — not reconstructing from memory afterward.
Total the marks and check the total equals the number of flips (20).
Describe what you notice: was it about half? Exactly ten? How close to your prediction?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fair device produces outcomes clustered near the expected split but not exactly matching it; disciplined one-tally-per-trial recording is part of the procedure, and the total must reconcile with the number of trials.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Tally chart / frequency table (one row per outcome)
Coins, dice, and bags of counters as trial-generators
Bar or block chart of observed frequencies against the expected line
Prediction-vs-result comparison
commonMisconceptions: Expecting the experiment to match the theoretical split exactly, and concluding the device is biased when it does not (law of small numbers)
Recency thinking — predicting the next trial from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, so tails is due', or 'heads is on a streak')
Recording carelessly — backfilling tallies or losing count so the total does not match the number of trials
Treating the result of a small experiment as the true probability rather than an estimate
constraints: The child must actually perform and tally the experiment; a recognition-only or reading-a-completed-tally task does not elicit the independent conducting-and-recording skill the topic requires.
Enforce one-tally-per-trial recording as the trial happens, not reconstruction from memory; total the marks against the number of trials so a mismatch is caught.
Have children predict the expected outcome before running, so the prediction-versus-result comparison is theirs to make.

Distinguish an execution lapse (careless recording, miscounting) from a conceptual error (expecting an exact match, recency thinking) — support the recording habit for the former, confront the belief for the latter.
A completed-tally interpretation check supports reasoning about bias and independence but is a supplement; it does not replace conducting the experiment.

Physical tossing (coin/die) and on-screen simulators offer different experiences — tactile realism versus the ability to scale rapidly to hundreds of trials; recording and comparing frequencies is not a spatial task, so neither is universally required. Treat the choice as a trade-off, not a ranking.
A small experiment yields an estimate of the probability, not the true probability; make this explicit to avoid treating a 20-trial result as definitive.
Live-tally, running proportion bar, 'run 20 vs run 500' contrast, and manual single-trial mode are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tooling.
After any run, each flip of a fair coin stays 50-50 and heads is exactly as likely as tails next — never present one outcome as 'most likely' following a streak.

startingActivity.title: Build a fair three-colour spinner and test it by sampling
learnerActions: Try to divide a spinner into three colours (red, blue, green) so that each colour is equally likely to be landed on.
Spin the spinner many times (e.g. 100 times) and keep a tally of how often each colour comes up.

If one colour comes up clearly more often over many spins, examine the spinner: is one wedge bigger than the others? (Small differences in the tally can happen by chance even on a fair spinner.) Adjust the boundaries until the three wedges are the same size, checking the sizes directly, then spin and tally again.
State in your own words what makes the three colours equally likely — the equal AREA of each section, not the fact that there are three colours.
Then build the opposite: a cube with 1 red face and 5 blue faces (six equal faces), or a spinner split into six equal sections with 1 red and 5 blue; predict and then tally the long-run result.
Compare your prediction with the tally and explain why two colours did NOT give a 50-50 result.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Equal chance depends on each outcome region being the same size (or the same number of equal ways), not on how many different outcomes there are; sampling many times reveals equal-area regions producing roughly equal frequencies and unequal regions producing a lopsided tally.

commonMisconceptions: Assuming that because there are two (or three) possible outcomes, they must be equally likely — counting the number of outcome types rather than their sizes
Equiprobability bias — believing any chance situation gives all outcomes an equal chance because the result is 'random/luck'

constraints: Target the crux: equal chance is decided by the SIZE/number of each outcome region, not by how many different outcomes there are.

A static tap-to-reveal comparison can present the definition but cannot let the child test a wrong judgement by sampling; treat it as a scaffold, not the main mechanism.

Sampling (spinning many times and tallying) is what reveals that equal-area regions give roughly equal frequencies and imbalance gives a lopsided tally; keep this as the empirical check, noting small samples vary.

Optional interaction examples (dragging spinner-section boundaries, adding/removing counters in a bag, a 'spin many times' tally, highlighting equal vs unequal area) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.

activityReferences.title: Choose your start: count on from the larger addend

Is a square a kind of rectangle?

startingActivity.title: Choose your start: count on from the larger addend
learnerActions: For 3 + 9, first count on starting from 3 — draw or hop all nine moves across a number line and watch it crawl from 3 to 12.
Now start from 9 instead and count on three — land on 12 in just three hops.
Say what is the same (both reach 12) and what is different (far fewer hops when you start from the larger number).
Answer: why is swapping the order allowed here? Connect to 'the order you add in doesn't change the total.'
Try the same choice for 2 + 8 and 8 + 2: decide which number to start from and explain your choice before you count.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Starting the count-on from the larger addend reaches the same total with far less work, and this is allowed because addition can be done in any order (commutativity).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line for count-on-from-larger (comparing hop counts)
Place-value / arrow cards and a tens-and-ones column machine
Venn-style overlapping shape hoops (four sides; four right angles)
Base-ten blocks showing +10 as one added ten-rod
commonMisconceptions: Always counts on from the first number written, not the larger, because order is treated as fixed
Adds 10 by counting in ones or by changing the ones digit (47+10 = 48) rather than seeing the tens digit change
Believes a square is not a rectangle because they look different / have different names (prototype and mutually-exclusive categories)
Applies commutativity to subtraction (34-10 handled like 10-34)
constraints: Count-on efficiency should be felt by actually comparing the number of hops for the two starting choices; simply being told 'start from the bigger' performs the move without building the reason.

A scored check or single multiple-choice answer can confirm which start is quicker or which digit changes, but it hides whether the child reasoned structurally or guessed; use it only after the hands-on work and follow with a 'why' question.

Annotated or tap-to-reveal reference pictures (shape hoops, labelled digits) are useful as a reference but do not let the child test the count-on choice or predict a column; they are a scaffold, not the place the strategy is built.
Reordering to count on from the larger addend is justified only for addition; do not let the child extend it to subtraction (12 − 4 is not 4 − 12).
Adding ten changes only the tens digit for two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds; keep examples within that range unless deliberately extending.

Paper/card shape cutouts and base-ten rods are thin physical approximations of ideal figures; direct the child's attention to the mathematical properties (sides, right angles, one whole ten) they represent, not to the physical object.

startingActivity.title: Balance beam: build both sides and watch it level
learnerActions: Set an expression on the left pan and another on the right (for example 5+2 on the left, 6+1 on the right) using identical cubes on a physical pan balance (5 cubes and 2 cubes on one side, 6 cubes and 1 cube on the other), or number/operation tiles on an on-screen balance that weighs each side by its value.
Predict whether the beam will tip or settle level, and say why, before releasing it.
Watch whether the beam tips or settles level: with identical cubes (or an on-screen balance that weighs by value), it sits level only when both sides share the same value.
Try a case where the sides look different but balance: put 8 on the left and 5+3 on the right and observe that the beam still sits level.
Try a missing-number challenge: add to one pan to level the beam, e.g. make 8+3 balance 9+□ (the blank is 2, since both sides then make 11).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The equals sign is the pivot/balance point: two sides are equal when they share the same value, regardless of how each side looks or which side 'the answer' is on. '=' is not a direction to compute leftward.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Pan balance / balance beam with equal masses or cubes on each side
Number balance (bucket balance) where hanging weights on numbered pegs balance
Part-whole bar with the same total shown two ways
Double ten-frame showing both expressions holding equal counts
Equation cards in varied layouts with a true/false sorting mat
commonMisconceptions: Reading '=' as 'work out the answer' / 'the total goes here' (operator misconception) — so 8 = 5+3 looks 'backwards' or wrong.
Rejecting bare identities like 8 = 8 as 'not a sum' or incomplete.
In a+b = c+□, writing the running total of the left side into the box (e.g. 8+4 = 12+□ → box = 12 or 12+? = to next), the classic Falkner/Carpenter error.
Believing there can only be one number after the '='.
Thinking both sides must LOOK identical rather than share a value.
constraints: Read '=' aloud consistently as 'is the same value as' / 'balances', never as 'makes' or 'gives you'.
Present answer-left, operations-both-sides and identity forms early so children do not fix on left-to-right computing.
Prioritise true/false judging and relational (compensation) reasoning over always calculating both sides, but still ensure learners can construct and complete equations, not only recognise them.

A fixed balance picture and recognition-only true/false items do not require the learner to construct equations or feel the beam respond to their own expressions; use them as scaffolds alongside hands-on or constructive tasks.

Checkpoints: age 6 — judges 4+1 = 5 and 5 = 4+1 true, 4+1 = 6 false; age 7 — judges 5+2 = 6+1 true without fully computing, using compensation; age 7+ — fills a missing number to balance each side (8+3 = 9+□) and explains using 'the same as'.
Address the running-total error directly: in a + b = □ + c the blank is 'what makes this side the same value as the other', solved by balancing, not by writing the left-hand total.

startingActivity.title: Balance the unknown with counters
learnerActions: Set out an equation with a box, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, on a two-pan balance or bar model where one side already shows 5.
Add or remove counters in the box until both sides match: too few and the box side is too light, too many and it tips down.
State the value that makes both sides balance (for 5 = □ − 3 the box must hold 8, because □ − 3 has to equal 5).
Repeat with the unknown in every position: 8 + ? = 11, □ + 6 = 12, 6 + 6 = □.
Check each solved equation by putting the found number back in and confirming both sides match.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The box holds whatever value makes the two sides equal; '=' means balance, so an answer-on-left form like 5 = □ − 3 is not 'backwards' — it is the same balancing task. One balancing method works for every position.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole diagram with the unknown segment shaded
Pan balance with an unknown mass on one side
Empty number line for count-on / inverse jumps
Fact-family triangle to pick the needed operation
Equation cards with the box in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Adding the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position (8 + ? = 11 → 19).
Reading answer-left forms as backwards (5 = □ − 3 → writes 2, i.e. 5 − 3).
Always subtracting or always adding by keyword rather than by the unknown's role.
Not checking the solution by putting it back into the equation.
Treating '=' as 'work out the total' so a box before '=' is confusing.
constraints: Systematically vary the unknown's position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Introduce non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to counter the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
Read '=' as 'both sides balance', not 'work out the total'; a box before '=' is legitimate.
Insist on checking by substituting the found value back into the equation.

Fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice practice (e.g. choosing the inverse calculation that solves □ + 9 = 14, with '2' as a wrong option for 5 = □ − 3) is useful for spaced retrieval and checking fluency, but recognition/selection does not itself require the child to construct and reason through the balancing move, so pair it with constructed solving.
Worked static diagrams anchor the position→operation mapping but do not themselves provide practice with feedback; follow them with fresh items to solve.
Trial-and-error can produce correct answers but does not build the intended inverse-method fluency; prompt the inverse once accuracy is secure.
Keep the wrong-answer value '2' (from 5 − 3) only as an incorrect option; the correct answer to 5 = □ − 3 is 8.

activityReferences.title: Build the bar from the story, then write the sentence
True/false and balance: '=' means 'the same as'
Explain-why with a study partner
Read the links both ways (worked example / warm-up)

startingActivity.title: Build the bar from the story, then write the sentence
learnerActions: Read a story such as: '6 red apples, and some green apples, 10 apples altogether.'
Build a part-whole bar: first decide and label which quantity is the WHOLE, then place the known part, then mark the missing part with '?'.
Notice the classic error — putting 6 and 10 side by side as two parts — and correct it by recognising that 10 is the whole, 6 is a part, and the green apples are the missing part.
Write a matching number sentence (6 + ? = 10) and then write at least one other correct form for the same bar (e.g. 10 − 6 = ?).
Say aloud what each number in the sentence stands for in the story.

For a separate 'how many more' story with its own numbers (e.g. 'Tom has 5 stickers and Mia has 8 stickers — how many more does Mia have?'), build a COMPARISON bar instead, lining up the two amounts to show the difference, and write a matching sentence.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A part-whole bar shows the structure of a situation — which quantity is the whole and which are the parts — so you must identify the whole before deciding what to add, and one bar can be matched by several correct sentences (adding or subtracting). A comparison bar is a different representation that suits 'how many more' situations by lining up two amounts to show the difference between them.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Part-whole bar model (whole on top, parts beneath; unknown marked with ?)
Comparison bars for 'how many more' situations
Number sentence with the unknown in varied positions (□ + 5 = 12, 7 + □ = 6 + 4)
True/false number sentences as a relational-equality routine
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' as 'work out the answer' (operational), so accepts or writes left-to-right computes like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 → 12 regardless of the structure
Grabs the two numbers in a story and adds them without asking which is the whole and which is a part
Ignores 'altogether'/total language when deciding what to combine
Can produce a matching sentence but cannot say what each number represents in the story
constraints: The bar model must be used to expose structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits), not as a procedure for getting the answer.

Provide comparison bars as a distinct representation for 'how many more' (difference) situations alongside the part-whole bar, and give the comparison story its own numbers/context so a value is not simultaneously treated as a whole in one task and a compared quantity in another.

Build the relational equals sign explicitly with true/false sentences and open sentences with the unknown in varied positions; telling children '= means the same as' is reported as insufficient on its own.
Require the learner to say what each number represents and to defend structural judgements with a reason; producing a correct sentence without explanation is a partial outcome to be drawn out.
Accept several structurally faithful sentences for one situation (e.g. 6 + □ = 10 and 10 − 6 = □); do not mark only one form correct.

Recognition-only formats (e.g. multiple-choice 'which sentence matches?') can check recognition but do not require constructing a sentence from structure or explaining the connection, and can be satisfied by the compute-left-to-right habit; use them only as warm-ups, not as the main assessment.

A tap-to-reveal static triple is a scaffold/worked example: it cannot let the learner build the mapping or respond to an operational-equals error, so it should not replace construction and explanation.

Optional interactive mechanisms (a draggable bar builder that flags a part exceeding the labelled whole; a balance/seesaw that tips until both sides are equal) are illustrative ways to make structure and relational equality felt — they are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.

activityReferences.title: The 'convince me' partner
Build an explanation you can test
Model a complete because-chain (scaffold)
Critique items: real reason or just saying it's right? (complement)

startingActivity.title: The 'convince me' partner
learnerActions: Pose the child a within-20 calculation (e.g. 8 + 5) and ask them to explain HOW they worked it out.
Then ask 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'.
When the child stalls or only asserts ('I just know', 'I reckon it's right'), hand over a sentence stem: 'Start with because…' and prompt for the missing link.
Have the child upgrade a confident hunch into a chain, e.g. 'because 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10, so 10 and 3 more is 13'.
Ask the child to show the same calculation a different way and check whether it also gives the answer ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?').
Present a worked example containing a slip (e.g. a number bond that doesn't actually make ten) and ask 'Is this right? How can you tell?' — pushing for WHICH step is wrong and WHY.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A confident answer is not the same as a justification; a reason that works can be built by linking steps with 'because' and 'so', and an alternative method that agrees is supporting evidence that backs up the reason, though it does not replace explaining why.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Drawings and number sentences as the medium of explanation
Alternative-method check (two routes to the same answer)
Sentence stems with connectives (because / so / therefore)
True-or-false equation judgements
The explain → convince → justify steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Confident assertion ('I reckon it's right') offered as justification, with an incomplete or incoherent chain (convincing mistaken for justifying)
Describing the method but stopping short of saying WHY it gives the right answer unless heavily prompted
Spotting that a worked example is wrong but being unable to explain the flaw
Treating 'justify' as 'do the sum again' rather than giving a reason
constraints: Target the gap between convincing and justifying: confident-but-vague is a normal developmental rung, NOT wrong reasoning — hand over connectives and ask for the missing link rather than marking it wrong.
Do not accept 'do the sum again' or 'because it's right' as justification; the target is a reason WHY the method gives the right answer.
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of explanation at this age.
Modelled/tap-to-reveal justified examples are scaffolds: the child sees a chain but does not build one, so always follow with independent construction.

Selected-response critique items assess recognition of flaws and reasons, not the child's own construction of a justification; use them to complement, not replace, dialogue and building tasks. Recognising a good reason does not by itself elicit producing one.
Error-finding should require naming the faulty step AND why it is faulty, anchored on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?), not just flagging that the answer looks off.
Alternative-method agreement is used here as a form of justification ('two routes, same answer') — frame it as supporting the reason, not as a substitute for explaining why the method works.

activityReferences.title: Convince the friendly skeptic
Build and test an argument workspace
Spot and explain the faulty step

startingActivity.title: Convince the friendly skeptic
learnerActions: State a general claim, e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number', and offer an example such as 4 + 6 = 10
Respond to a partner (an adult or a role-play) who cheerfully agrees each example is even but keeps asking: 'Can you give me another? And another?'
Face the key question: 'I believe every pair you've tried — but even numbers go on forever, so you could never check them all. How do you KNOW there isn't one pair that breaks it?'
Reach for a reason that covers all cases at once, e.g. 'every even number is made of pairs with none left over, so two of them still make complete pairs, so the total is even'
Then take a FALSE statement from the partner (e.g. 'adding two numbers always gives an even number') and topple it with a single counter-example such as 2 + 3 = 5
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When there are endlessly many cases, as with even numbers, no pile of examples can establish a claim for every case, but a structural reason can — and a single counter-example is enough to disprove a general ('always') statement even though many examples cannot prove one.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Generic/visual proof (even number as pairs; place-value columns)
Counter-example as a disproof tool
Multi-step because/therefore chain
Worked examples containing deliberate errors
The justify → prove steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Empirical proof scheme — treating a few confirming examples as proof that a general statement is always true
Convincing-not-justifying — a confident argument with missing steps, close to but not yet a complete chain
Identifying an error only as 'the answer is different' rather than naming the faulty step and why
Not realising that one counter-example is enough to disprove a general statement
constraints: Accept examples as legitimate illustration and a starting point; explicitly name that a few examples do not prove a general claim. This empirical-to-structural shift is a known developmental milestone and is hard and slow — treat it as development, not as a failing to be corrected sharply.

Distinguish 'convincing' from 'justifying': a confident multi-step argument with a missing link is close to proof. Don't dismiss it — ask 'what's the missing step between here and here?' and offer because/therefore stems to complete the chain.

Keep always/sometimes/never logic precise: a single counter-example disproves an 'always' claim and a single confirming case disproves a 'never' claim, but a genuine 'sometimes' classification requires both a case where the statement holds and a case where it fails.

Tap-to-reveal / worked-example companions model a general argument or flaw but do not require the child to construct the argument; use them to illustrate, then move to tasks where the child builds and states the reasoning.

Always/sometimes/never items, 'is this a proof or just examples?' items, and spot-the-error items probe critique and discrimination well, but a recognition-only response cannot show a child independently constructing a general argument; use these to complement, not replace, construction tasks.
When critiquing the flawed worked example, keep the focus on naming the faulty step and the place-value rule; do not reteach the addition procedure itself.
The error-spotting task assumes the child can already perform columnar addition with regrouping; if that prerequisite is shaky, address it separately rather than inside the justification task.

activityReferences.title: Match the two rows and find the leftover
Count both groups and compare
The conservation trap: longer isn't always more

startingActivity.title: Match the two rows and find the leftover
learnerActions: Set up two rows of objects and pair each object in the top row with one in the bottom row (draw a connecting line, or drag a string from each to its partner).
When one or more objects are left with no partner, say that row has MORE (and the other row has FEWER); when every object is paired, say the rows are EQUAL.

As an alternative, build the two groups as towers of identical cubes stood side by side (taller tower = more, same height = equal), or, using only identical objects of the same weight, use a balance/see-saw image to show two equal groups level each other.
Read off a full sentence about the two groups you built, using the frame '__ is more than __' or '__ is equal to __' with your own counts.
Use a 'make it fair' action: add or take away one object until every object pairs up and both rows read EQUAL.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Pairing objects one-to-one shows which group has more (a leftover) or whether they are equal (a clean pairing) — a strategy that works even before counting is secure.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two rows lined up for one-to-one matching (connect-the-pairs; the leftover).
Two ten-frames side by side (empty cells show the gap).
Cube towers stood next to each other (taller = more; same height = equal).
A balance / see-saw image for 'equal to'.
commonMisconceptions: Length/spacing = number: judging the longer or more spread-out row as 'more' regardless of count (the classic conservation error).
Using 'bigger' / 'taller' loosely instead of comparing quantity; confusing 'fewer' with 'smaller objects'.
Comparing by which row 'ends further along' rather than by matching or counting.
Believing two groups can't be equal if the objects look different or are arranged differently.
constraints: Keep groups to no more than ten objects, consistent with K.CC.6.

A static labelled 'more/fewer/equal' picture can serve as a reference but does not let the child match, count, or rearrange to resolve a comparison; it is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for the child doing the matching.

Multiple-choice 'which has more?' items and categorising pairs into more/fewer/equal can check whether a child can pick the right comparison, but do not themselves require the child to construct the matching or justify it.
A fairness conversation ('who has more sweets — is that fair?') can frame the task and motivate the vocabulary; it does not itself settle the comparison, which is resolved by matching or counting.
Use identical objects when first teaching 'fewer' so children do not confuse 'more items' with 'bigger items'.

Expectations by stage: younger children match two small groups and say which has more/fewer or if equal; others compare groups to ten by counting both; the most secure are not fooled when the larger group is bunched shorter than a spread-out smaller group and justify by matching or counting.

activityReferences.title: Count, scatter, re-ask: the total that stays put
Give me exactly N (count-out task)
Start counting from three (parroting trap)
Count from the other end (order-irrelevance)
Subitising small sets as wholes
Predict-then-check: will bunching change how many? (assessment companion)

startingActivity.title: Count, scatter, re-ask: the total that stays put
learnerActions: Count a small set of objects aloud (start with 5, e.g. five toy ducks or cars) and say the total: '…four, five — five altogether!'
Place or keep visible a total badge/numeral card showing the count beside the set.
Now move the same objects around: bunch them in a corner, spread them out in a ring or long line — without adding or removing any.

Before recounting, say how many there are now and explain why (if the total card is still showing, ask why the card still matches the set, so the answer is reasoned rather than simply read off the card).
Check by recounting together only if needed, and notice the total is the same.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Moving objects around cannot change how many there are; the total is a fixed property of the set, so you do not need to recount after rearranging.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten-frame / five-frame (the filled frame shows the total as a stable whole).
Dot / dice / domino patterns for subitising (cardinality without counting).
The 'count → cover it → how many?' routine (forces recall of the total, not a recount).
A numeral card placed beside a counted set (numeral ↔ quantity).
commonMisconceptions: Recounting when asked 'how many?' — treating the count as a performance rather than something that yields a total (the diagnostic error).
Last-word parroting without meaning — repeating the final word said even when the count started at the wrong number (Bermejo: counts 5 from 'three', answers 'seven').
Believing rearranging or spreading out a set changes how many there are (pre-conservation; length/spacing mistaken for quantity).
Thinking the last number names only the last OBJECT, not the whole set.
constraints: Target standards: EYFS 'Number' ELG (deep understanding of number to 10); CCSS-M K.CC.4b and K.CC.4 ('connect counting to cardinality'); NC Year 1 '1 more/1 less' and the language 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least' presuppose cardinality.
A child who RECOUNTS when asked 'how many?' after a completed count may not yet have grasped cardinality — this is a key diagnostic sign, best confirmed with give-N and other probes.

Progression checkpoints: Tier A (4–5) answers 'how many?' with the last word without recounting and gives-N for N≤5; Tier B (5–6) knows rearranging a counted set of ≤10 does not change the total without recounting; Tier C (6) sees the total is unchanged when counted from a different start/order and is not fooled by spreading out (early conservation).
Order-irrelevance and conservation develop late; build them through experience and do not mark a child wrong for predicting a different total before they have discovered otherwise.

A static labelled scene ('5 counted, 5 altogether') can serve as a reference but cannot by itself animate the rearrange-and-recheck that demonstrates invariance; use it alongside hands-on rearrangement.

Multiple-choice or slider-style response formats ('how many altogether?', 'same or different total?', give-N via slider) can serve as an assessment companion; recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent count-out production that most strongly evidences cardinality.
A screen 'persistent total badge' or live recolouring/dragging is one optional way to make invariance visible; physical objects a child can move by hand serve the same purpose and are equally valid.
Keep sets small to preserve focus on the small-set quantity; avoid cluttered or busy displays that distract from the quantity itself.

activityReferences.title: One more, one less in lockstep

startingActivity.title: One more, one less in lockstep
learnerActions: Build a tower with cubes (or fill a ten-frame one cell at a time) and say the count as you go.
Before adding, predict: 'If I add one more cube, what number will it be?' Then add exactly one cube and check that the count moves to the next word.
Add one cube and say the next number in the same beat, so that 'the next number' means 'one more thing'.
Now remove one cube and say the number that is one less, naming it as the mirror move of adding one.
On a number track, hop a marker (or a frog along lily-pads) exactly one place right for 'one more' and one place left for 'one less'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each successive counting number is a quantity exactly one larger than the previous one, and one back is exactly one smaller; +1 and −1 are a single step in opposite directions on the same track.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number track / number line (steps of one; right = more, left = less).
Cube tower / staircase (each step one taller).
Ten-frame filled one cell at a time.
'One more / one less' arrow cards or a +1/−1 machine.
commonMisconceptions: Recounting from 1 to find 'one more' instead of counting-on (successor not yet linked to cardinality).
Knowing 'one more' but not 'one less' — the backward direction lags because the string is learned forward only.
Treating 'one more' as merely 'the next word I say' rather than a quantity one larger (fails when the count starts wrong).
Not realising every step is exactly one — thinking numbers grow by an inconsistent amount.
constraints: Teach 'one more' and 'one less' together as inverse moves on the same model (steps right/left on a number track), not as two unrelated facts.
Do not force counting-on before it emerges: count-from-one dependence is developmental and matures with practice, not a deficit to drill.
Treat the predecessor ('one less') as developing separately from the successor; practise it as its own game rather than assuming backward is automatically as easy as forward.

A static staircase or labelled track supports reference and retrieval but does not itself let the child enact the add-one step or feel the quantity change; pair it with enacting the step, whether on physical objects or an interactive number track.

Fill-in and 'what comes next' prompts are useful retrieval and checking companions but assess recall of the successor; recognising an answer is not the same as enacting the quantity change, so pair them with enacting the +1/−1 step (adding or removing one, on objects or an interactive track).
Concrete objects (cubes, counters, marbles in a box) and screen/number-track models offer different experiences; either can support the step — do not present one as the only possible medium.

startingActivity.title: Feed the squirrel: tap-count a scattered pile
learnerActions: Count a small pile of objects (e.g. 7 acorns to feed a squirrel) by touching each one exactly once, saying one number word with each touch.
Move or tap each counted object into a 'counted' pile/basket so it is clearly separated from the not-yet-counted objects.
Deliberately rush once and double-tap an object; notice the spoken total becomes wrong (e.g. you say 'eight' even though the basket still holds only 7 acorns).
Tidy the scattered objects into a line and recount, touching each once, so it is easier to get a total you can trust.
When the line count gives the right answer, say aloud why: each object got one word and none was counted twice.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The rule 'one word per object, and keep track of what you've already counted' is the very difference between a wrong count and a right one; the counted/uncounted split can be made visible and must be maintained.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Moveable counters + a 'counted' pile / sorting tray (the partition made physical).
Five-frame and ten-frame (structured slots enforce one object per cell).
Fingers — a built-in one-to-one manipulative.
A counting track / row of boxes where each object sits in exactly one box.
Number names spoken in rhythm with points (the aural–motor pairing).
commonMisconceptions: Coordination errors: saying words faster than pointing (or vice versa) → skips or double-counts as the word and the touch drift out of sync.
No tracking strategy on scattered sets → recounting some objects and missing others (the counted/uncounted partition never forms).
Believing pointing without saying (or saying without pointing) still 'counts' — the pairing IS the principle.
Confusing one-to-one correspondence with merely reciting the number-word sequence (stable order): a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' yet not tag objects one-to-one.
constraints: Start with small sets (≤5) of moveable, tangible objects, then build to ≤10–20 and finally scattered sets to 20.
Insist on synchrony: one point/touch = one number word; slow the count so tag and word land together, since rushing causes the classic skip/double-count coordination errors.
Progress arrangements deliberately: line → array/circle → scattered. Scattered sets are hardest because there is no natural start or track.
Distinguish one-to-one correspondence from merely reciting the number-word sequence: a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' without tagging objects one-to-one.

A static labelled set (each object pre-tagged 1..n) can serve as a reference showing a completed correct count, but it does not let the child perform the one-tap-one-word act, so use it as a reference/scaffold alongside the child counting, not as a substitute.

A multiple-choice or matching task ('how many?' / 'did they count correctly?' / match each object to one numeral) can check recognition and verify whether a count was correct, but does not itself elicit the child's physical one-touch-one-word performance; use it as a retrieval and verification companion alongside, not instead of, the child performing the count.

Point/say coordination lag is a developmental stage, not a misunderstanding — do not drill or verbally correct; slow the pace and have the child physically move each object, which tends to self-correct with the move-it scaffold.
Error-monitoring of others' counts develops later than performing one's own count; a child may reject a wrong total yet be unable to locate the double-counted object.

This is a foundational enabling skill: the statutory Year 1 goal 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' (National Curriculum in England) assumes accurate object counting but is not itself a line stating one-to-one correspondence.

startingActivity.title: Five shown four ways, driven from any face
learnerActions: Set a small number (to 20) and see it at once as counters, a dotty picture (or tally/ten-frame), a point on a number line, and the numeral card.
Add or remove one counter and watch the picture gain or lose a dot, the number-line marker move one step, and the numeral change to match.
Drive the change from a DIFFERENT face: slide the number-line marker, or add a tally, and watch the other three faces re-form to match.
Say aloud 'these all show ___' each time, naming the quantity after a change.
Switch the number line between numbered-track mode (discrete squares) and continuous-line mode, and between a marked line and a blank one.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A quantity has many faces — blocks, dots, a spot on the line, a symbol — and when the amount changes, every face must change to match, because they all show the same amount in different clothing.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Counters / cubes / fingers (concrete).
Dots, tally marks, ten-frame (pictorial).
Number track (numbered squares) → number line (marked → blank).
The numeral card (abstract) linked to all of the above.
commonMisconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate task rather than the same quantity in different clothes.
Number-line errors: starting at 1 not 0, or counting the marks/gaps incorrectly; treating the line as a picture rather than a measured, ordered scale (the early 'number-line-as-picture' seed).
Drawing an inexact picture or miscounting tallies so the pictorial doesn't match the quantity.
Believing the numeral is 'the real number' and objects/pictures are not (or vice versa).
constraints: Keep all faces (objects, picture, number line, numeral) side by side and always tie each back to the quantity ('these all show five') so representations don't become disconnected rituals.
Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before a continuous line, and a marked line before a blank one; the number line is the hardest, measured, ordered representation.
Use varied pictorial forms (dots, tallies, ten-frames) so the child abstracts 'fiveness' from the arrangement rather than memorising one picture.

Recognition-only tasks (tap-to-reveal, 'which shows 5?' matching) assess and name but do not by themselves show the child can independently construct or translate a quantity; pair them with build/draw/place work.

Tier the demand: 4–5 shows a number ≤10 with objects/fingers and draws a matching picture; 5–6 locates on a marked 0–20 line and matches object/picture/numeral; 6 moves fluently among all four and explains they are the same amount.

A static reference image cannot itself let the child create or translate a quantity, so use it as a companion rather than the main teaching activity — this is a scope note about that specific scaffold's affordance, not a claim that static images cannot teach.

startingActivity.title: Organise and count a scattered set
learnerActions: Start with a small scattered pile (up to 10) of moveable counters or buttons spread randomly.
Count them by moving each counted item aside into a 'counted' tray (or sliding it along a consistent path) so counted and uncounted are clearly separated.
Say how many there are altogether, then recount and check you get the same number.
Repeat with a larger scattered set of up to 20 counters (a harder extension), choosing your own tracking path.
Match a numeral card to the final count.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A chaotic scatter becomes reliably countable by imposing order — moving each item as you count it so nothing is skipped or counted twice — and the last number you say is how many there are, no matter how the objects are arranged.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten-frames (one full + a partial for teens).
Moveable counters + a 'counted' tray.
Sets shown in line / array / circle / scattered (a deliberate arrangement ladder).
A numeral card matched to the counted set.
commonMisconceptions: Losing track on scattered sets → skips or double-counts (no tracking strategy).
Recounting when asked 'how many?' (cardinality not secure) or miscounting across the teens.
Treating teen numbers as unanalysable words rather than 'ten and some ones'.
Believing a rearranged set has a different total (conservation).
constraints: The core objective is an enacted count: the child must physically tag, track, and count out objects. Recognition-only tasks (choosing 'how many?' from options, judging a shown count) can assess or supplement but do not by themselves elicit the independent counting and give-N that is the point.
A labelled, already-counted set can serve as a reference example but cannot enact the count or the give-N task; use it only as a scaffold.
Give-N (count out exactly N) is a stronger check of cardinality than 'how many?' — include it, not just set-reporting.
Scattered-set tracking is a developing habit: if a child loses track, model a strategy (move each item aside) rather than reteaching counting as though the concept is absent.
Keep objects moveable and connect each count to the spoken total ('altogether') and the written numeral.

If an on-screen version is used, features like tap-to-count lockout (a counted item cannot be tapped again), a 'tidy into a line/ten-frame' helper, a drag-out give-N mode, and a persistent total badge can make the mechanism concrete — these are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms, and should not replace hands-on counting with physical objects.

activityReferences.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
Spotting the pattern on a multiples chart
Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things
Fluency practice: fill, continue, match

startingActivity.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
learnerActions: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples shaded (pattern by column/diagonal).
Number line with equal jumps (the jump = the step size).
Equal groups / arrays of 2, 5, 10 (the bridge to multiplication).
Fingers (5s/10s), tally marks (5s), coins (5s/10s).
commonMisconceptions: Reciting the multiples as a chant with no sense that each step is +one group — so it doesn't transfer to multiplication.
Thinking the multiples are the ONLY numbers that 'exist', or that skip counting removes the in-between numbers (7 isn't 'skipped away').
Only able to start from 0 — can't skip-count from a different multiple or backwards.
Confusing 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', or losing the pattern at decade boundaries (5s: '…45, 50, 55').
constraints: Teach skip counting as adding one equal group each step (repeated addition), not as a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Count from different starting multiples (not only 0) and in both directions, so the skill is flexible rather than a fixed rote song.

A pre-marked multiples chart and fill/continue practice items are references and recognition checks; they show or test the pattern but do not require the learner to independently construct each step, so pair them with tasks where the learner generates and explains steps.

Reverting to counting the in-between numbers by ones, and difficulty starting from a non-zero multiple, are developmental stages that improve with practice — do not mark them as errors; scaffold with equal jumps and hundred-square patterns.
Do not imply that only the multiples 'exist' or that in-between numbers are removed; the full number sequence is still present, we just land on every 2nd/5th/10th number.
Watch decade boundaries in 5s (…45, 50, 55) where the pattern is easily lost.

activityReferences.title: Predict across the decade boundary on a hundred square
Start anywhere and keep going
Daily rhythmic oral counting and take-turns buddy counting
Fill the gap and fix the sequence (retrieval practice)

startingActivity.title: Predict across the decade boundary on a hundred square
learnerActions: Point to a chosen starting cell on a hundred square (e.g. 67) and count on aloud, moving a pointer or marker cell by cell: '68, 69…'
As you approach a decade boundary, pause and predict the next number BEFORE saying it ('after 69 comes…?') and check whether the tens goes up by one ten (to 70) rather than inventing 'sixty-ten'.
Trace down a single column and say the numbers aloud to notice the ones digit stays the same while the tens digit climbs.
Repeat for the rehearsed seams: 28, 29, 30 and 38, 39, 40, until each bridge is automatic.
Then run the marker the other way to count backward across a boundary (e.g. 41, 40, 39…).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 100 numbers are not 100 separate things to memorise: the ones digits cycle through 0–9 again and again (on a 1–100 square each row runs from 1 to 10, e.g. 31–40; on a 0–99 square from 0 to 9, e.g. 40–49). So once you know the repeating ones pattern, the decade words and the irregular teens, and can cross cleanly into the next ten, most of the sequence becomes predictable.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Hundred square (rows of ten; a column shares a ones digit).
Number track / number line 0–100.
Counting songs, rhymes and choral chant (the aural sequence).
A pointer/marker moving along the track as the class counts.
commonMisconceptions: Decade-boundary stalls: '…28, 29, twenty-ten' or jumping to the wrong decade — the ones-cycle-to-next-ten transition isn't secured.
Irregular teens: 'eleventeen', or mapping teen words to the wrong quantity; hearing 'thirteen' as 30.
Counting forward from one but not backward or from a mid-point — the sequence is stored as a single forward chant.
Confusing rote reciting with meaningful counting — chanting numbers with nothing attached and assuming that IS counting.
constraints: Reciting the number sequence is not the same as counting objects; keep both and name which is being done so chanting with nothing attached is not mistaken for enumeration.

Backward counting and starting mid-sequence are genuinely harder than forward-from-one and develop later; restarting at 1 or halting backward counting are developmental stages to practise, not errors to penalise.
Recognition or multiple-choice items check remembered numbers but do not elicit independent oral production of the sequence; include spoken recite tasks so the learner constructs the sequence aloud.
A hundred square makes the ones-cycle and decade structure visible, which supports prediction, but it does not by itself build oral fluency — pair it with daily spoken counting.
A static hundred square works as a reference chart (tap/point → number) but cannot itself drive a start-anywhere or backward count; the adult or learner must direct that movement.
Build the ordered list at least as long as needed before expecting accurate object counting over that range (you cannot count seven items if the names stop at six).
Distinguish 'thirteen' from 'thirty' and similar teen/decade pairs explicitly, as they are easily confused by sound.
The cited NC standard is 'to and across 100'; a little counting past 100 is within that standard, not off-objective, even though the short title says 'to 100'.
