activityReferences.title: The diagonal reveal: shading 3s on a hundred square
Number-line 3-jumps and groups of three
Counting back and entering mid-sequence
Retrieval and oral fluency

startingActivity.title: The diagonal reveal: shading 3s on a hundred square
learnerActions: Step forward in 3s from 0 (3, 6, 9, 12…), shading or marking each multiple on a hundred square as you say it.
Notice that, unlike the vertical columns 5s and 10s make, the multiples of 3 march down the grid as repeating parallel diagonal lines (a diagonal pattern).
Use the diagonal pattern to predict the next multiple before you reach it, then check.
Play 'spot the multiple of 3' by pointing to multiples anywhere on the grid, not only counting up from 0.
Pay special attention to crossing each decade (…18, 21… and …27, 30…) so the +3 step is not lost across the ten.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiples of 3 are patterned, not random — the diagonal pattern lets you predict the next multiple and recognise multiples anywhere, countering the feeling that '3s have no pattern'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples of 3 shaded (diagonal stripes).
Number line with equal 3-jumps.
Arrays / groups of three (bridge to the 3× table and thirds).
Backward-count track from 30.
commonMisconceptions: Feeling 3s have 'no pattern' because they don't form neat columns (they form diagonals).
Reciting 3s as isolated rote with no link to groups of three or the 3× table.
Being able to count forward but not backward in 3s.
Losing the step when crossing a decade (…18, 21…) — miscounting the +3 across the ten.
constraints: Quick-recall questions and recognising/choosing the next multiple check and build fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent counting or the pattern insight; pair them with counting aloud and with the visible diagonal pattern.
Oral partner counting supports fluency and backward practice but does not show the diagonal pattern; combine it with a seen hundred square or number line.
Do not drill for speed when a child sub-counts intervals by ones — treat it as developmental and make the +3 step visible; fluency grows with exposure.
Treat backward counting and mid-sequence continuation as distinct skills to be practised, not as automatically following from forward counting.
The diagonal on the hundred square is a flat 2D pattern; it needs to be seen, but added depth/3D is not required to teach it.

activityReferences.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square
Concrete why: add a ten-rod with base-ten blocks
Say-it and spot-the-slip practice
Explain the pattern out loud

startingActivity.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square
learnerActions: Start on a non-multiple, e.g. 27, on a hundred square.
Make a +10 move by dropping straight DOWN one row: 27 → 37 → 47 → 57, saying each number aloud.
Each step of this 27 → 57 run, point to the ones digit (the 7) and say 'the ones stay the same'; point to the tens digit and say 'the tens go up by one' (true while you stay inside a hundred).
Reverse it: make −10 moves by going straight UP one row: 83 → 73 → 63 → 53, saying what stays (the ones) and what changes (the tens).
Watch for drifting sideways — keep the move strictly vertical so you stay in the same ones-digit column.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten never touches the ones digit; it is the same single downward (or upward) step on the hundred square whatever number you start from. '+10' is not 'add a zero' — it is 'one row down'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Hundred square (vertical move = ±10; ones digit fixed down a column).
Base-ten blocks / Dienes (add or remove a ten-rod).
Place-value chart (tens column changes, ones column unchanged).
Number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start.
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit too (e.g. 27 → 38) — not isolating the +10 to the tens.
Only able to add 10 to multiples of 10 (can't start from 7 or 23).
Treating +10 as 'just add a 0' — which fails for non-round numbers (27 ≠ 270).
Losing the column on the hundred square (drifting sideways instead of straight down).
constraints: Always practise from NON-multiples (7, 23, 83…), not just 10, 20, 30 — multiples can be done by chanting decade names without the place-value insight.
Include backward (−10) as well as forward counting; backward from a two-digit number additionally tests subtraction of ten.

State the robust invariant to children: the ones digit always stays the same. The tens digit normally goes up (or down) by one, but at a hundred boundary it rolls over: forwards (96 → 106) it goes from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears; backwards (106 → 96) it goes from 0 to 9 and the hundred goes. The ones digit is unchanged either way.
A hundred-square counter or screen model shows the move but is a representation; pair it with base-ten blocks for the concrete 'why' when a learner only mimics the grid.
Error-spotting and 'which digit is wrong' tasks check recognition; also require the learner to produce sequences and explanations independently.
Do not teach '+10 means add a 0' — adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10 (27+10 = 37, not 270; 20+10 = 30, not 200).
Keep the move strictly vertical on the hundred square; drifting sideways reverts to counting in ones.

activityReferences.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials
Annotated thousand-square and place-value reference
Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks
Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)

startingActivity.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
learnerActions: Set a start number — round (e.g. 240) or ragged (e.g. 315, 268) — and choose a step of +5, +10 or +100.
Before tapping, predict aloud the next number and say which digit you think will change.

Tap the step and watch three linked views move together: a thousand grid lights the landed number, a number line draws one equal jump, and place-value columns (H-T-U, with a Th column that appears when you reach 1000) roll the digit or digits that change.
Stop deliberately at 190 and predict 'what comes next in 10s?', then tap +10 and watch ten tens-rods trade for one hundred-flat while the hundreds digit rolls 1→2 and the tens resets to 0.
Repeat the boundary move by counting in 5s up to 995→1000 and describe, in your own words, which columns carried.

Switch to a '10 more / 100 more instantly' challenge: state the answer without counting on by ones, then tap to check which digit rolled (just one digit unless the step crosses a hundred or thousand boundary, e.g. 195 → 205).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding 10 rolls the tens digit and adding 100 rolls the hundreds digit; if no boundary is crossed, the other digits stay the same. When a hundred/thousand boundary is crossed (e.g. 190 → 200), the next place up also changes because of regrouping (ten of one place trading for one of the next), not a mysterious jump.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Scalable number line marked to 1,000 with equal jumps (jumps of 10 and of 100) to show constant step size and boundary crossings
Thousand grid / linked hundred squares where each skip count lights a column or diagonal, exposing the 5s, 10s and 100s patterns
Base-ten blocks (unit cubes, tens rods, hundreds flats) with regrouping — ten rods trade for one flat at the hundred boundary
Place-value columns (H T U) with digit-rollers so a step by 10 or 100 visibly advances one column and carries into the next
commonMisconceptions: Hundred-boundary stall — reaching 190 the child says '191, 192…' or '100-ten', not knowing 200 comes next; the decade/hundred bridge is the classic breakdown point.
'+10 means add a zero' / '+100 means add two zeros' — over-generalised from round numbers, so 268+10 becomes 2680 or 26810.
Treating the count as a longer rote chant and losing track of which digit changes, so skip-counting from a non-round start collapses.
Confusing tens and hundreds steps (counting 240, 250, 260 when asked to skip in 100s) because the difference between which column moves is not yet secure.
Losing the ones digit when skip-counting by 10s or 100s from a ragged start (315→320 instead of 325) because the child re-rounds to a decade.
constraints: The annotated thousand-square and place-value reference is a scaffold: it shows patterns and names columns but does not itself enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so pair it with a manipulable counter or base-ten materials.

Checking/diagnostic tasks are primarily for verifying the pattern and catching misconceptions; their feedback can also prompt reteaching, but they are best placed after the constructive activities rather than being the sole means of building the place-value insight.
Spoken partner practice rehearses the sequence orally but does not by itself make the digit-rolling visible; keep it alongside visual/concrete work.

Base-ten cutouts and rods are physical approximations of the ideal place-value idea: use the trade of ten rods for one flat to represent regrouping, and connect the concrete piece to the spoken digit and the written column.
Practise backward counting across boundaries as its own skill rather than assuming it transfers automatically from forward fluency.
When crossing a boundary during a ragged-start count, keep the ones/tens that should stay fixed in view so the learner does not re-round to a decade.

activityReferences.title: The doubling chain: stacked number lines for 2s, 4s and 8s
From skip count to equal groups and arrays
Counting in 50s and 100s with money and the hundred square
Oral fluency and self-check with a counting partner

startingActivity.title: The doubling chain: stacked number lines for 2s, 4s and 8s
learnerActions: Lay out (or display) three aligned number lines starting at 0: one marked in 2s, one in 4s, one in 8s, with the same spacing so matching numbers sit directly above one another.
Step along the 8s line one jump at a time. For each 8-jump, mark the two 4-jumps directly beneath it, and the four 2-jumps beneath those.
Say aloud as you go: 'one jump of 8 is the same distance as two jumps of 4, which is four jumps of 2.'
Count the 4s aloud (0, 4, 8, 12, 16…) and ring every other number starting from 0 — notice the circled numbers are exactly the 8s count (0, 8, 16…).
Count backwards in 8s from 96, checking each step against the 4s line.
Repeat from a non-zero start once the forward count is secure (e.g. count on in 4s from 24).
Link the new counts back to the 2s, 5s and 10s you already know, so 4s/8s/50s/100s join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 8s are doubled 4s and 4s are doubled 2s; a slip in one count can be repaired using the other, because the step sizes nest inside each other.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Stacked/aligned number lines (2s, 4s, 8s) showing the doubling of jump size
Equal groups and arrays (groups of 4, groups of 8) linking the count to repeated addition and multiplication
Hundred square with each multiple shaded to reveal the pattern (4s, 8s columns/diagonals; 50s and 100s down the rows)
Coins and a money line (50p, £1) anchoring the 50s count in half-hundreds
commonMisconceptions: Treating 4s and 8s as unrelated rote lists and never noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a slip in one count cannot be repaired from the other.
Adding the wrong step (drifting into 2s when counting 4s, or 5s when counting 50s) because the step size isn't held steady.
Miscounting 50s as 'fifties are like fives with a zero' and producing 50, 100, 150, 250 — losing a step or mis-pairing to hundreds.
Not connecting the skip count to groups, so the child can chant 4, 8, 12 but cannot say how many groups of four make 12 — the count stays verbal and never becomes multiplicative.
Boundary slips crossing hundreds while counting in 50s or 100s (150→200, 950→1000) when the hundreds digit must roll.
constraints: Counting in 4s and 8s is best built from the doubling relationship, not taught as separate rote chants, so learners can repair one count from the other.
Every skip count should be tied to equal groups/arrays so the count becomes multiplicative, not merely verbal.
Do not drill for speed when a learner is sub-counting; connect to the known related count and let fluency grow through repeated jumps and retrieval.

Sequence, fill-in-the-blank and matching exercises can check these counts but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — use them to check mastery after the relationship has been taught; a sort/match verifies classification without eliciting an explanation of why 8s are doubled 4s.

A pre-shaded pattern reference (static or tap-to-reveal) supports pattern spotting and the equal-groups link but does not let the learner drive the count or see the doubling animate; treat it as a reference, not the primary build.

Interactive overlays (advancing lines, ghosted smaller jumps, live shading) and physical coins are optional concrete aids to make the mechanism visible; they are means, not required mechanisms — aligned paper strips and real coins work too.
A standard 1–100 hundred square displays the 4s/8s patterns; use a number line or track for 50s and 100s up to 1000.

activityReferences.title: Step the count and watch the pattern form (pattern explorer)
Hundred-square reference with reveal-on-tap structure
Check counts and table links
Oral rehearsal partner for the weak 7s

startingActivity.title: Step the count and watch the pattern form (pattern explorer)
learnerActions: Pick a count (6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, or 1,000s) and step it one jump at a time, saying each multiple aloud.

Step0,9,18,…,90. From9 to90, treat9 as09 if comparing tens and ones: the tens digit rises by1, the ones falls by1, and the digit sum is9. Then inspect99: its digits sum to18, so the earlier pattern does not continue unchanged.
For the 6s, show each 6-jump as two 3-jumps (the jump 0→6 is 3+3, and the jump 6→12 is a further 3+3), so each multiple of 6 is reached by pairs of 3-jumps.
For the 7s, build each step as a 5-jump plus a 2-jump (7 = 5 + 2) and rebuild any forgotten term that way.
For25s, partition a100-unit bar or collection into four equal25-unit parts, then continue25,50,75,100,125,150. A quarter-hour clock uses15-minute steps to60, so do not use it to label25-unit steps.
For the 1,000s, step along a number line that continues through 0 into negatives, and find 1,000 more or 1,000 less of a given number.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Use patterns within a stated range:9 through90 have digit sum9, while99 has digit sum18; each6-jump is two3-jumps;7-jumps can be5+2; four25-unit parts make100; and1,000-unit steps continue through zero.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Hundred square with the 9s shaded to reveal the diagonal and the digit-sum-9 pattern (and 6s to show doubled 3s)
Aligned number lines pairing 3s with 6s (doubling) and 5s+2s composing 7s
Equal groups / arrays for 6, 7, 9 linking each count to its multiplication table
Money and clock models for 25s (four quarters = 100, quarter-hours) and an extended number line through 0 for 1,000s and negatives
commonMisconceptions: Counting in 7s (and 6s/9s) as pure rote with no structural anchor, so a single slip cannot be repaired and the count derails.
Missing the 9s pattern and treating each step as '+10 then −1' incorrectly, e.g. writing 9, 18, 27, 37 by adding 10 and forgetting the −1.
Confusing adjacent tables (drifting between 6s and 8s, or 7s and 9s) because the steps feel similar and no pattern flags the error.
Mishandling 25s past 100 (25, 50, 75, 100, 125 becoming …100, 105) by reverting to a smaller or rounder step at the hundred.
Counting in 1,000s but stalling or reversing sign incorrectly when crossing 0 into negatives (…1000, 0, then '1000' again instead of −1000).
constraints: Use number structure: pair3-jumps for6, compose5+2 for7, partition100 into four25-unit parts, and continue1,000-unit steps through zero. Scope the9s tens-up/ones-down and digit-sum9 pattern to9 through90;99 has digit sum18.
Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern; interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into ×6, ×7 and ×9, not a parallel skill.

A fixed/reference hundred square can reveal and confirm patterns but cannot let the learner generate the count or watch the digit pattern update step by step; use it as a reference, not the sole teaching vehicle.
Short check questions verify counts and table links but do not by themselves build the pattern insight; pair them with activities where the learner generates the count.
Do not respond to sub-counting by ones with more chanting alone; build fluency through retrieval — derive from known facts, use number-line jumps, and keep practice short and daily.
For the 1,000s crossing 0, the sign flips exactly once (…1000, 0, −1000, −2000); avoid repeating a positive term after 0.

The digit-sum9 check used here applies to9 through90, with9 written as09 for a tens/ones comparison. It does not apply unchanged to99; do not reject a correct multiple of9 just because its digits sum to18.

activityReferences.title: Single-column counting on a place-value chart
Crossing the boundary: the roll-over cascade
Spot the step and predict the next terms

startingActivity.title: Single-column counting on a place-value chart
learnerActions: Choose a step that is a power of ten (10; 100; 1,000; 10,000; or 100,000) and a direction (forwards or backwards).
Starting from a given number such as 462,000, count on in 10,000s aloud: 462,000 → 472,000 → 482,000 → 492,000, each time saying which single column changed.
On a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) or with place-value counters, add or remove ONE counter in the chosen column per step and read the whole number.

Say the count structurally too, keeping the unchanged places fixed: '46 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 47 ten-thousands and 2 thousand, 48 ten-thousands and 2 thousand...' so only the ten-thousands count ticks while the 2,000 stays put.
Repeat for a different power of ten (e.g. count back in 100,000s from 800,000: 700,000 → 600,000 → 500,000) and name the column that now ticks.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Counting in a power of ten means repeatedly nudging a SINGLE place-value column up or down while every other digit stays frozen, as long as no boundary is crossed; the chosen step decides which column ticks. (When a column rolls over, e.g. 492,000 → 502,000, a neighbouring column changes too. This is covered in the boundary activity.)
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (step ticks one column)
0-1,000,000 number line with power-of-ten hops
Sequence strips (predict next terms)
Place-value counters (add/remove one 10,000 etc.)
Digit-stepper display showing the changing digit
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong column for the chosen step.
Boundary errors when a column rolls over (990,000 + 10,000).
Losing track of direction (counting back but incrementing).
Reverting to counting in ones for large steps.
Not generalising the pattern across different powers of 10.
constraints: Reading a count on a static annotated chart or choosing the next term from fixed options can serve as a reference or check, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent counting and roll-over handling that is the objective; learners should generate the counts themselves aloud, in writing, or by acting on a chart/counters.
Keep the step size constant within any one count; mixing step sizes mid-count is a separate, harder task and should be flagged, not assumed.
Always state the direction (forwards/backwards) explicitly so decreasing counts are not accidentally incremented.
Boundary crossings (e.g. 492,000 → 502,000; 990,000 → 1,000,000) are the key difficulty and must be practised deliberately, not left to chance.

Interactive examples (a step selector with one highlighted column that ticks, an animated carry cascade, a number-line toggle of equal power-of-ten hops, a hidden-term prediction mode) are optional ways to make the single-column mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and equivalent work can be done with a paper chart, counters, and spoken counting.

startingActivity.title: Anchor the numeral to its amount, then compare on a number line
learnerActions: Take two numeral cards, for example 4 and 7, and place each on a number line marked 1–10.
Beside each numeral build or reveal its quantity — a little tower of cubes, counters, or a filled ten-frame — so the amount behind the symbol is visible.
Say which is further along the line when you count, and therefore which is greater and which is less.
State the comparison out loud in BOTH directions: '7 is greater than 4 AND 4 is less than 7.'
Repeat with pairs that include an equal pair (for example 5 and 5) so you meet all three outcomes.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A written numeral names an amount; you compare the amounts, and the number line settles it because the numeral further right is greater. Equality is a possible result, so comparison has three outcomes (>, <, =).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line / number track (position encodes size).
Two ten-frames or sets, one per numeral (the quantity behind the symbol).
The <, >, = symbols shown opening toward the larger set.
A balance image for '='.
commonMisconceptions: Comparing the numerals as marks (which looks bigger / is written larger) rather than by value.
Using <, > by mnemonic with no meaning → placing the symbol backwards.
Assuming a later-learned or longer-to-say numeral is automatically bigger; confusing 'greater' with physical size.
Forgetting '=' is a possible result (assuming one number must be bigger).
constraints: Always anchor each numeral to a quantity (set, ten-frame, or number-line point) before comparing; never teach a bare-symbol trick.

Introduce >, < only after the quantity meaning is secure, and present them as a sign opening toward the larger number rather than as a meaning-free 'hungry alligator' mnemonic, which is a known trap that produces backward signs.
Always include equal pairs so learners experience three outcomes (>, <, =) and do not assume one number must be bigger.
Distinguish a numeral's value from its appearance on the page: a boldly or largely printed digit is not automatically greater.
A static number line with two numerals marked is a useful reference but does not let the learner test and place a sign themselves; use it as a scaffold, not the whole activity.

Recognition-only tasks (choosing from given options) can give useful practice but do not by themselves require the learner to orient and place the sign independently; include at least some tasks where the learner places or writes the sign.

A learner who still builds or counts sets for each numeral is at a developmental stage where the numeral-to-amount link is forming; this is a prerequisite still bridging, not a comparison error to be penalised — reconnect to the prerequisite on linking numerals to their magnitude (counting / number-line position).

startingActivity.title: Word–numeral–quantity triple match
learnerActions: Hear or read a number word such as 'thirteen'.
Place or drag that word card onto its numeral (13).
Place it onto a ten-frame or set showing one full ten plus three.
Match across the number words one–twenty (with 0–20 available as reference), including a playful pairs/memory game over the words.
Also work the reverse direction: given a numeral or a quantity, find and say the matching word.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The number word carries meaning: it names a specific numeral AND a specific quantity, so the word must be read for meaning, not just decoded as text.

keyRepresentations: Triple-match cards: numeral (13) ↔ word (thirteen) ↔ ten-frame/quantity.

commonMisconceptions: Reading a number word as text without linking it to a quantity or numeral.
Spelling confusions: four/for, eight, nine→'nighn', and the many silent/irregular letters.
Teen/decade word muddles by sound: 'thirteen' vs 'thirty', 'fifteen' vs 'fifty'.

constraints: Reading/recognition and matching tasks support consolidation but do not by themselves elicit independent spelling; include writing/production of the words to cover the full objective.

activityReferences.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
Minimal-pair contrast: -teen versus -ty
Fluency check: read, write, place, order

startingActivity.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken two-digit number (e.g. 'sixty-eight') and write or point to its numeral.
Place the numeral in its position on a 100-square (state whether it is a 1–100 or a 0–99 layout), then check whether it lands where that number belongs.
Build a number from tens-and-ones cards: compose 42 by taking the '40' card and placing the '2' over its zero, so the tens and ones are explicitly separated.
Work across decade boundaries: continue 28, 29, __ and 78, 79, __ , writing each numeral (30 and 80).
Do both directions: say-it → write it; show it → read it aloud; point-to-it on the grid.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 0–100 is one regular system, not a hundred separate facts: moving down a column the tens digit goes up while the ones digit stays the same, and moving along a row the ones digit changes. On a 0–99 square each row shares one tens digit. On a 1–100 square the decade number (10, 20, … 100) ends each row, so it is the one cell in its row with a different tens digit. Either way, each numeral means 'this far along', not just two loose digits.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 100-square and Gattegno tens-and-ones chart exposing the regular two-digit pattern.
0–100 bead string / number line linking each numeral to a position/quantity.
Place-value / arrow (Dienes) cards building 42 as 40 and 2 to reinforce which digit is which.
Decade-boundary number tracks (25–35, 75–85) for the tricky crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Transposing spoken two-digit numbers (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — confusing the ones-first teens with the tens-first pattern of the rest.
Decade-boundary errors when counting/writing (after 29 saying/writing 'twenty-ten', or 39→50).
Reading a two-digit numeral as two separate digits ('four, two' for 42) rather than as forty-two.
Miswriting the 'ty' decades (writing 70 as 17, confusing seventy/seventeen).
Omitting or misplacing 0 in decade numbers (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400).
constraints: Secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing and rote counting to 100 are prerequisites before extending to 100.

This is procedural numeral fluency, not full place-value reasoning (two-digit composition/decomposition is a separate topic); keep representations tied to quantity/position but do not assume full place-value understanding.
Writing teen numbers in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen') is a normal developmental transcription stage that matures with place value; do not drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly.

A static tappable 100-square is a useful reference and can present a numeral and its word, but it cannot by itself rehearse the productive skills of writing from dictation or free reading; use it as a scaffold alongside writing/speaking practice.
Recognition-only (multiple-choice) responses confirm reading but do not elicit independent numeral writing; include actual writing-from-dictation for the production half of the skill.
Decade numbers keep the 0 as a ones-place holder (40, not 4 or 400); treat zero omission/misplacement as its own error alongside transposition and -teen/-ty confusion.

Teens are written tens-first (13, 14) just like all two-digit numerals; only the SPOKEN order of teens differs, so teach the spoken/written order distinction rather than implying teens are written ones-first.

Position-lighting, grid cells, card-dragging and spoken prompts are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms; the same work can be done on paper, with a bead string, or with spoken dictation.

startingActivity.title: Numeral studio: trace, build the quantity, self-correct
learnerActions: Trace a numeral along a guided stroke-order path (start dot and directional arrows) on a whiteboard, in sand, by sky-writing, or on a coded surface that models stroke order.
As the numeral is formed, build or watch a ten-frame fill to that many (using a second ten-frame for 11–20), so the symbol is felt as a quantity rather than a squiggle.
Flip the task: tap/lay out a set of counters, then write or select the numeral that names how many.
Switch frequently between the modes — numeral card → make the set; set → write the numeral; hear it → write it — so reading, writing and representing stay linked.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A numeral is a symbol FOR a quantity, written and read, not a decoration; the three modes (spoken word, quantity, written symbol) are one connected idea.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten-frame(s) beside the numeral (a full ten + extras for teens) linking symbol to a structured quantity.
Numeral formation cards with directional arrows / stroke-order guides for handwriting.
Number track / 0–20 washing-line pairing each numeral with its position and a matching set.
Numeral ↔ objects ↔ spoken-word matching cards (three-way correspondence).
commonMisconceptions: Digit reversals (2, 3, 5, 7, 9 written mirror-image) — a formation issue needing direct correction.
Teen transposition from speech: writing 'thirteen' as 31, 'fourteen' as 41 (hearing the ones first).
Reading a numeral without connecting it to a quantity (naming '7' but unable to make seven).
Confusing visually similar numerals (6/9, 2/5, 7/1) or omitting/misreading 0.
Treating a two-digit teen numeral as two separate single digits (reading 15 as 'one, five').
constraints: Numeral writing (actual formation of each digit) is half the objective — matching, multiple-choice and tap-to-reveal reference activities test or support recognition but do not themselves require numeral formation and must not fully replace writing.
Always keep the numeral tied to a quantity (ten-frame, fingers, counters) so 0–20 are symbols for amounts, not decorations; grounds in cardinality (a prerequisite).
Treat digit reversals (commonly 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9) as a handwriting/formation issue needing stroke-order cues, not as a number error.
Treat teen transposition (41 for 'fourteen') as a normal developmental transcription stage; keep modelling the ten-and-ones structure rather than drilling or repeatedly marking it wrong.
Include 0 deliberately as 'none' and as a written symbol, since many children can count but hesitate to read or write zero.
A tap-to-hear numeral chart or number track is a useful reference but cannot capture the child forming numerals; use it as support alongside writing practice.

Stroke-order paths, reversal-blocking pens, live ten-frame fills and drag-to-match are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory, and paper, sand, whiteboards and counters with adult feedback can serve the same goals.

activityReferences.title: Make a ten and the leftovers
Compose and decompose, both ways
The numeral shows what the word hides

startingActivity.title: Make a ten and the leftovers
learnerActions: Count out loose counters for a teen number such as 14.
Fill a ten-frame by placing counters one at a time until the frame holds ten.
Once ten are grouped, treat the full frame (or a ten-bead bar / Dienes ten-rod) as ONE 'ten' unit; put the remaining counters in a second frame.
Say the result aloud: 'one ten and four ones'.
Repeat with 13, 16, 17, 19, each time grouping exactly ten and naming the leftovers.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A teen number is not a heap of single ones — ten of them bundle into one 'ten' unit, and the rest are the extra ones. This bundling (unitising) is the seed of all place value.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Double ten-frame: one full (the ten) + one partly filled (the ones) showing 10 + n.
Ten-bead bar / bead string with the first ten a distinct colour, then extra beads.
Dienes ten-rod + unit cubes composing a teen number.
Part-whole model / equation (14 = 10 + 4) linking the structure to symbols.
Numeral with the tens digit and ones digit colour-linked to the ten-group and the extra ones.
commonMisconceptions: Seeing a teen number as a heap of individual ones, with no 'ten' unit (no place-value structure yet).
Reading the numeral literally as two ones ('one, four' for 14) rather than 'one ten and four'.
Teen word transposition (thirteen → 31) from the ones-first naming.
Thinking 'eleven' and 'twelve' are unrelated to ten because the words give no clue.
Miscounting the ten (treating the ten-rod as one object = 1, so 14 becomes 5) — unitising confusion.
constraints: Make the TEN something the child can see and handle as a single unit — a filled ten-frame, a ten-bead bar, or a Dienes ten-rod — so a teen is 'one ten and some ones' rather than many separate ones.

Fill-in-the-blank, matching teen numerals to ten-and-ones pictures, and multiple-choice ('which shows one ten and three ones?') can check whether the structure is understood, but recognition responses do not elicit the physical bundling that builds the unitising insight; use them to verify, not to teach it.

A fixed labelled double-ten-frame image (tap to reveal 'one ten', 'and four ones', and link digits to groups) is a useful anchor, but because it is not manipulable it cannot provide the act of bundling ten ones into a ten; pair it with hands-on grouping.

A dialogue or character prompt can ask the child to explain how many tens and ones are in a teen number (e.g. fifteen) and probe the naming trap, which may elicit or check an explanation of the structure; on its own it does not provide the physical bundling/handling, so pair it with hands-on grouping.
Watch for unitising confusion: a child may count the ten-rod as '1' and get 14 → 5. Re-ground by unbundling to ten single ones and recounting.

Optional interactive supports can make the mechanism concrete: dragging loose ones so the tenth one closes a frame into a single 'ten' bar, extras spilling into a second frame, the numeral assembling with its '1' visibly tied to the ten-bar and '4' to the extras, a decompose mode that bursts the ten-bar back into ten ones while recording 14 = 10 + 4, and a 'name vs structure' panel that plays 'thirteen' beside 10 + 3. These are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.

Matching provided words to numerals checks recognition; independent spelling requires a response in which the word is not supplied. A free-writing or open fill-in task can elicit that production, especially when the learner also explains its quantity.

A static decade-word chart with tap-to-hear audio is a useful reference wall but does not rehearse active spelling/production or sound-alike discrimination; treat it as support, not the main practice.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.

startingActivity.title: Count on from any number across 100 (interactive grid and line)

activityReferences.title: The 100-square vertical jump
Add or remove one ten-rod

startingActivity.title: The 100-square vertical jump
learnerActions: Point to a starting number on a 100-square (for example 56).

On a 100-square numbered from the top (1-10 in the top row), to find 10 more, move straight DOWN exactly one row, staying in the same column; to find 10 less, move straight UP one row in the same column. (On a bottom-up 100-square the directions are reversed. Check which way the numbers grow on your grid.)
Say the new number aloud (56 → 66 for 10 more, 56 → 46 for 10 less).
Repeat the +10 jump several times to trace a straight vertical stripe down the grid: 56 → 66 → 76 → 86.
Each time, name the ones digit and the tens digit and state what changed: 'the ones stayed 6, the tens went up by one.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten is always the same move — straight down or up one row — and the ones digit never moves because only a whole ten is added or removed.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 100-square (vertical moves = ±10) — the canonical model
Base-ten tens-rods and ones-cubes (add/remove one rod)
0-100 number line with hops of 10
Place-value chart showing only the tens digit changing
Gattegno chart (change the tens-row selection, keep the ones)
commonMisconceptions: Counting on in ones (56, 57, 58…66) instead of jumping a ten — no place-value shortcut.
Changing the ones digit as well, or changing the wrong digit (56 → 57 for '10 more').
Confusing 10 more with 1 more.
Miscounting on the 100-square by moving diagonally or the wrong direction.
Struggling at decade boundaries because the pattern is memorised without understanding the tens digit's role.
constraints: Move from concrete models (100-square, rods) to the mental generalisation fairly quickly, and demand the explanation ('the ones stay the same, the tens go up/down by one'), not just the answer.

A static annotated 100-square is a useful reference for the pattern, but it does not let the child perform the jump and watch the ones hold still; use it alongside, not instead of, an activity where the child makes the move.

Scored/timed practice consolidates recall but assesses output; it is best used AFTER the place-value concept is built, and it does not on its own reveal whether the child is counting or jumping — watch the method during practice.
Multiple-choice/recognition items can spot wrong-digit errors but do not elicit independent construction of the answer or the explanation; include production items too.
Keep practice within the two-digit range where only the tens digit changes by one; 90→100 introduces a hundreds digit and is an extension case, not a routine item for this objective.
Rehearse decade crossings (e.g. 10 less than 40 = 30) deliberately, since a pattern memorised without understanding often breaks down there.
Distinguish '1 more / 1 less' explicitly from '10 more / 10 less'; confusing 10 more with 1 more is a common error.

startingActivity.title: Base-ten exchange: bundle and break a ten
learnerActions: Gather ten loose single cubes and join them into one tens-rod that is visibly ten cubes long.
Reverse the move: break (or separate) one tens-rod back into ten loose ones.
Watch or track a running count of the total cubes before and after each swap, and confirm it does not change.
Toggle/say the name for the very same pile two ways: 'ten ones' and 'one ten'.
Respond to challenges such as 'make one ten' and 'break a ten into ten ones, then give me 3 of them — how many loose ones are left?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: One ten and ten ones are the same quantity, named and organised two ways; bundling or unbundling changes the arrangement, not the amount, and the ten is itself a countable unit.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten single cubes physically snapping into one tens-rod (and the reverse).
Ten-bead bar / bead string where the ten is one strung unit of ten beads.
Exchange mat: 'ones' column and 'tens' column with a swap action (10 ones ↔ 1 ten).
Ten-frame filled completely = 'one ten' label.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a tens-rod is 'one' (counting bundles as single objects), so 3 rods = 3 rather than 30 — the core unitising error.
Believing the ten and the ten ones are different amounts (not conserving quantity across the exchange).
Being unable to reverse the bundling (can make a ten from ones but not break a ten back into ones).
Treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten.
Confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.
constraints: Use proportional materials where the ten is visibly made of ten (a rod ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar, a filled ten-frame) before introducing pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the tenness is seen not asserted.
Make the exchange genuinely two-way: bundling ten ones into a ten AND breaking a ten back into ten ones; reversing the bundle is the move needed later for borrowing in subtraction.
Name the unit deliberately as 'one ten' and contrast counting 'ten ones' versus 'one ten' for the same pile.
The reveal image and the recognition quiz are scaffolds/checks: they anchor or test the equivalence but do not let the child perform the conserving exchange that builds unitising.

Checkpoint tiers: (A, age 6) group 10 single cubes into one rod and say why; (B, 6–7) explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten; (C, age 7) exchange 10 ones for one tens block and back fluently and use it in a simple problem.

Watch for the core errors: counting a rod as 'one' (so 3 rods = 3), non-conservation across the swap, inability to reverse the bundling, treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten, and confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.

startingActivity.title: Comparison bench: build, see, and place the symbol
learnerActions: Build or show two two-digit numbers in two forms at once: base-ten block piles and dots/markers on a shared 0-100 number line.

Decide which is greater by looking at the quantity/position first (more tens rods and more blocks in total, further right on the line), then say it aloud: e.g. 'forty-three is greater than thirty-four'.
Place the correct symbol (<, >, or =) into the gap between the two numbers.
Read the completed statement both ways: 34 < 43 ('thirty-four is less than forty-three') and 43 > 34 ('forty-three is greater than thirty-four').
State the rule used: compare the tens first; the number with more tens is greater, and if the tens are equal, compare the ones.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 'Greater' and 'less' name a real difference in quantity/position, and the symbol records that relation — the same fact can be read from either end.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two sets of base-ten blocks placed side by side (more tens = taller/greater)
0-100 number line where the number further right is greater
Tens|ones place-value chart aligning two numbers column by column
The <, >, = symbols with the 'points to the smaller / opens to the larger' orientation, grounded in quantity
Ordered track or 'washing line' for pegging a set of numbers smallest to largest
commonMisconceptions: Using the crocodile/Pac-Man mouth as a rote trick with no sense of which number is actually bigger, so the symbol is placed by guess.
Comparing by digit count of the numeral or by the ONES first (34 vs 38: choosing by 4 vs 8 alone is fine here, but 52 vs 48 wrongly judged by 2 vs 8) — ignoring the leading (tens) digit.
Reversing the symbol — knowing which is bigger but writing > where < belongs.
Thinking = can only sit between identical-looking expressions, not that it asserts equal value.
For same-tens pairs, defaulting to 'they're the same' because the tens match, instead of moving to the ones.
constraints: Establish the meaning of each symbol with quantities/positions before pushing for speed; 'the open mouth eats the bigger number' is only a memory crutch and must be grounded in 'greater than / less than' with real quantities.
Treat recognition and drill tasks (choosing or filling a symbol) as consolidation/check; they verify the skill but do not by themselves build quantity sense or independent reasoning.

A single fixed illustration can anchor the tens-then-ones rule with one worked pair, but on its own it cannot let the child compare varied pairs or order a set, which is where the skill is practised; use it as an anchor, not the main activity.
Keep symbol orientation (open side to the larger number) as a separate check from the greater/less reasoning, so a correct comparison written with a reversed symbol is diagnosed accurately.
Base-ten blocks and the drawn number line are physical representations with slight thickness; they stand for the abstract numerical values being compared, not the values themselves.

startingActivity.title: Problem playground: partition, operate, recombine
learnerActions: Take a problem such as 34 + 20 and split 34 into a 30-part and a 4-part (using base-ten blocks, a part-whole 'cherry' diagram, or drawing).
Add the 20 onto the tens part only, saying aloud 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50'.
Recombine the parts: 50 + 4 = 54, and state the full chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54.
Try a 'mystery number' / work-backwards problem such as '__ + 10 = 45': cover or guess the start number and test candidate values on a number line until the equation holds.
Repeat with fresh problems (e.g. 34 + 30, 56 + 20) so the strategy — not one answer — is what transfers.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A number bond you already own (like 3 + 2) can do the heavy lifting on tens, so an unfamiliar calculation can be derived by partitioning and recruiting a known fact rather than counted out from one.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram splitting a number into tens and ones
Base-ten blocks for partition–operate–recombine
Empty/marked number line for jumps of tens and ones
Bar model for missing-number and comparison problems
Fact-family / derived-fact chains (3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54)
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a counting-in-ones or column method instead of using place-value structure, because the number-fact link was never made.
Applying a known bond but forgetting the unit — saying 30 + 20 = 5 (using 3+2 but dropping the tens).
Unable to work backwards — treating 'think of a number' problems as if they can only be solved forwards.
Partitioning incorrectly under a problem's wording (mis-splitting 34 as 3 + 4 rather than 30 + 4).
Focusing on getting an answer without checking it fits the problem, so an unreasonable result goes unquestioned.
constraints: Keep the work strategy-based (partition–operate–recombine), not column-algorithm based, at this stage.
Always name the unit: a known bond like 3 + 2 scales to 30 + 20 = 50 only because these are tens; dropping the unit (saying 5) is the error to catch.
Partition correctly: 34 = 30 + 4, not 3 + 4 — the leading digit stands for tens.

Recognition/selection-only items (choosing which partition, spotting a trap answer) assess application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or spoken justification; pair them with building, writing, or explaining.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines, bar models) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
Insist on justification ('which fact? how did you split it?') so the META goal is assessed, not just the final answer.
A single static worked example cannot pose or respond to new problems; use it as an anchor alongside generative practice.

activityReferences.title: Many faces of the same number
Estimate on a benchmarked number line
About how many? — estimating set size

startingActivity.title: Many faces of the same number
learnerActions: Pick a number (e.g. 247) and build it several ways: a set or base-ten blocks (2 hundreds flats, 4 tens rods, 7 ones cubes), the numeral 247, the expanded form 200 + 40 + 7, and words.
Place that same number as a point on a number line.
Change one representation and update all the others to match so they always show the same quantity (e.g. add one tens rod to make 257, then fix the numeral, the expanded form and the line point).
Say aloud why these are all the 'same number wearing different clothes'.
Match a mixed set of base-ten pictures to their numerals and to the matching words.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A single number can appear as a set, base-ten blocks, a point on a number line, a numeral, expanded form or words, and you can translate between them because they all encode the same quantity.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line (marked, then empty with benchmarks) for position, order and estimation of magnitude.
Base-ten blocks (hundreds flats, tens rods, ones cubes) for the same number.
Place-value chart / arrow cards and expanded form (247 = 200 + 40 + 7).
A 'same number, many faces' board linking set ↔ blocks ↔ line ↔ numeral ↔ words.
commonMisconceptions: Treating the representations as unrelated (can build 34 with blocks but can't place it on a line).
Placing numbers on a line by counting marks only, ignoring proportional spacing (47 put just past 0, or bunched near a benchmark).
Believing estimation is 'wrong maths' — wanting to count exactly instead of judging 'about how many/where'.
Misusing an empty number line by assuming equal gaps where none are marked, or ignoring the scale.
Reading base-ten blocks by counting every cube rather than using the tens/hundreds units.
constraints: A tap-to-reveal poster or a static 'same number five ways' display is a useful reference for the links between representations, but on its own it does not give placement or estimation practice; pair it with actual line placement and 'about how many' tasks.

A slider or matching quiz (place a number on a line, match blocks to numeral, choose an estimate for a flashed set) is suitable for checking representational links and estimation, but recognition/selection responses do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of a number across forms — include tasks where the child builds and translates representations.
Keep base-ten work tied to place value: children should read rods and flats as tens and hundreds, not count every unit cube.

Number lines used for placement and estimation must show their endpoints (e.g. 0–100 or 0–1000) and be drawn to a uniform scale, so equal distances stand for equal differences even where no interior marks are drawn; children should check whether the line runs to 100 or 1000. Open 'empty' number lines used for jottings are not drawn to scale, so do not use them for proportional estimation.

Early number-line estimates are commonly uneven: small numbers are spread too far apart and larger numbers are crowded together toward the upper end. Treat this as developmental and respond with benchmark practice, not by marking placements wrong.

activityReferences.title: Building decades with tens rods and a visible zero
Decade reference chart — tap, reveal, and lift the flap
Consolidation: sequence, match, and justify the zero
'Convince me the zero matters' discussion

startingActivity.title: Building decades with tens rods and a visible zero
learnerActions: Set up a tens|ones chart (drawn or physical) with two columns.
Add tens rods one at a time into the tens column, placing no unit cubes; after each rod, say the count aloud: 'ten, twenty, thirty …' and write the numeral (10, 20, 30).
Each time, write a 0 in the ones column so the empty ones place is seen, not left blank.
Build 30 with three rods and say '30 is 3 tens and 0 ones'; build 50 with five rods and say '50 is 5 tens and 0 ones'.
Rebuild 30 with three rods, then add a single loose ones cube and read what you have: 30 becomes 31. Describe what the 0 was doing before you added the cube.
Optionally mark each decade on a 0-100 number line or bead string so the spoken word, the tens count, and the position all line up.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A decade is a whole number of tens with the ones column filled by zero; the 0 is a place-holder that keeps the tens digit in the tens place and marks that there are no ones. Decades are not a separate kind of number — they are the ones-is-zero case of tens-and-ones.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Tens rods alone in the tens column with a visible 0 in the ones column
Bead string / number track marked in tens for skip-counting
0-100 number line with decade stops highlighted
Tens|ones place-value chart showing 'n tens, 0 ones'
Gattegno/place-value chart row of decades (10, 20 … 90) linking each to n×10
commonMisconceptions: Treating the 0 in a decade as meaningless ('nothing there') rather than as a place-holder marking zero ones.
Reading the tens digit as its face value — saying 30 is 'three' rather than 'three tens/thirty'.
Decade-word confusion — mixing thirteen with thirty, fifteen with fifty, because the '-teen' and '-ty' endings sound alike.
Believing decades are a separate kind of number unrelated to ordinary two-digit numbers, rather than the ones-is-zero case of tens-and-ones.
Miscounting the rods and losing track that each rod is worth ten, not one, when skip-counting.
constraints: Keep the ones column empty of cubes when building decades, but always write the 0 so the empty ones place is seen, not omitted — this is the seed of the place-holder idea.
Tie the build to skip-counting in tens so 'thirty', 'three tens', and the third stop on the number line line up as the same thing.
Always contrast a decade with an adjacent non-decade (40 vs 43; 30 vs 31) so the 0 means 'no ones', not 'nothing'.
Each rod is worth ten, not one; watch for miscounting that loses track of the ten-value during skip-counting.
When extending the place-holder idea to larger numbers (e.g. 300), state the digit's actual place (hundreds) rather than carrying 'tens place' across every example.

The reference chart and the sequence/match/justify practice consolidate or check the pattern but do not have the child build the underlying grouping on their own; precede them with hands-on rod building.
Recognition and matching tasks check the pattern but do not require the child to construct the grouping independently; include building and verbal explanation for that.
Discussion can surface and articulate the reasoning; for this build-and-see insight it is proposed as a follow-up to manipulating rods rather than as a substitute for building.

activityReferences.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
Many ways to show the same number
Convince me the 4 means forty
Check and sort by place value

startingActivity.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
learnerActions: Set out a two-column mat labelled 'tens' on the left and 'ones' on the right.
Drop loose cubes one at a time into the ones column; each time you reach ten loose cubes, bundle those ten into a single labelled 'ten' (a rod) and move it to the tens column.
Build 47 by placing four bundled tens in the tens column and seven loose ones in the ones column.
Say aloud 'four tens and seven ones', then write the numeral 47 and the expanded form 47 = 40 + 7.
Break one of the four tens back into ten loose ones and re-count: show the pile is still 47 but now reads as 30 + 17.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The '4' in 47 is not 'four' — it is four whole bundles of ten (40). Position gives the digit its value, and the same quantity can be split in more than one way without changing how much there is.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (tens rods + unit cubes) — the canonical proportional model where a ten is physically ten ones
Two-column tens|ones place-value chart with bundled tens and loose ones placed in position
Expanded-form / part-whole (cherry) diagram: 47 splits into 40 and 7
Bead strings and ten-frames grouped into complete tens plus extras
Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7) that physically overlap to build 47, making expanded form tangible
commonMisconceptions: Reading the tens digit as its face value — treating the 4 in 47 as 'four' rather than 'forty/four tens'.
Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.
Losing the unit when there are zero ones — thinking a decade like 40 has 'no place value in the ones' rather than 4 tens and 0 ones.
constraints: Always build a two-digit number concretely first (bundled tens + loose ones), then connect it to the numeral and expanded form; never leave a digit floating free of a quantity.
Read digits by unit aloud — 'four tens', 'seven ones' — not 'four, seven'; naming the unit prevents the digits-as-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) only once standard partitioning (47 = 40 + 7) is secure.
A fixed labelled picture of 47-with-blocks is a useful reference anchor but shows one number only and does not let the child perform the bundling; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on grouping.
Recognition and fill-in-the-blank checks can confirm the idea is held and classify answers but do not on their own build the unitising insight; use them for consolidation and diagnosis.

The reasoning/convince-me prompt is proposed as a short follow-up after concrete work; grouping quantities may help young children reach this insight more reliably than discussion alone, but this comparison is not established by the provided sources.

A dynamic model where ten cubes snap into one rod (and a rod breaks back into ten) is one way to make bundling visible; physical bundles, bead strings, ten-frames, part-whole (cherry) diagrams, and overlapping arrow/place-value cards are equally valid concrete and pictorial routes.

activityReferences.title: Pair-them-up frame
Predict then check with real counters
Counting in 2s and the last-digit rule

startingActivity.title: Pair-them-up frame
learnerActions: Choose a number of counters (start up to 10, then up to 20) and drop them into a two-row frame so they arrange into pairs.
Look at the result: if one counter is left with no partner the number is ODD; if every counter is matched the number is EVEN.
Use a slider or counter to add one and remove one, watching whether the lone counter appears or disappears each time.
Say out loud what changes each step: adding one either strands a single counter (makes it odd) or creates a new pair (makes it even).
Use an 'equal addends' strip to write each even number as n + n (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A number is even when its objects pair with none left over and odd when exactly one is left over; because adding one either completes a pair or strands a single, odd and even alternate, and every even number is a double (n + n).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Objects arranged in two rows / pairs (leftover = odd)
Ten-frame (pairs in columns; a lone counter shows odd)
Number track coloured by odd/even (alternating pattern)
Counting-in-2s hops on a number line
Doubles facts (n + n) linked to even numbers
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about being 'big/small' or arbitrary, not about pairing.
Confusing odd/even with the count of digits or with multiples of other numbers.
Believing 0 is odd, or being unsure whether 0/2 are even.
Memorising the last-digit rule with no grasp of why (can't justify).
Miscounting pairs and so misclassifying near-boundary numbers.
constraints: Anchor the concept in the pairing action first; introduce the last-digit shortcut only after the pairing meaning is secure and have children justify it: every ten splits into 5 pairs with none left over, so only the ones can leave a leftover.
'Even' means pairs with none left over — equal pairing. Splitting a number into any two groups (e.g. 13 as 7 and 6) does not make it even; the groups must be equal.
0 is even (nothing is left unpaired); address the 'zero is odd' claim explicitly rather than leaving it ambiguous.
Decouple parity from size: deliberately show small odd numbers and large even numbers so children do not infer parity from magnitude.

A sorting/categorising or multiple-choice task (sort into odd/even bins, fill 8 = __ + __, choose and explain) is suitable for consolidation once the pairing meaning is built; such a task can check or reinforce classification but does not by itself elicit the independent pairing construction and explanation.

A static paired-vs-leftover illustration with tap-to-reveal is a useful reference, but it cannot be manipulated by the child; the alternation insight is stronger when the learner changes the count and watches the parity flip.
Use two-column / ten-frame arrangements so 'paired vs one sticking out' is visually obvious; these can be physical counters or an on-screen model.

Fluency practice with boundary items

startingActivity.title: Digit stepper: watch one column respond
learnerActions: Start with a three-digit number shown in an H|T|O place-value chart (e.g. 638).
Predict which digit will change before pressing +100, then press it and check: only the hundreds digit ticks up (638\u2192738) while tens and ones stay fixed.
Repeat with +10, -10, -100 on several numbers, each time saying aloud which column changes and which stay the same.
Contrast +10 and +100 side by side on the same starting number to track that they act on different columns.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding/subtracting 10 acts on the tens column and adding/subtracting 100 acts on the hundreds column; when no column rolls over (as with 638), the other digits hold still. This is a place-value jump, not counting on in ones. Boundary cases such as 190 + 10 come in the next activity.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (change one row = change one digit)
H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 10 or one 100)
0-1000 number line with ±10 and ±100 hops
100-square generalisation / number grid
Base-ten flats/rods for the concrete +100 / +10 move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding 100 but stepping the tens).
Failing at boundaries — 190 + 10 giving '1100' or '190' unchanged instead of 200.
Counting on in ones instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 10 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, so mishandling the carry when a column rolls over.
constraints: Fill-in and multiple-choice practice consolidates and checks fluency but should follow conceptual work with a chart, counters, or number line; recognition-only responses do not by themselves build the place-value reasoning or the explanation of which digit changes.

A static annotated chart can serve as a reference for which digit +10/+100 changes, but learners need to carry out the transformation (physically, with counters, or interactively) to experience the roll-over; treat a fixed image as a reference scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Always require learners to explain which digit changes and why, so the method stays place-value based rather than counting on in ones.

Interactive highlights, locked digits, animated carries, number-line toggles, timed rounds, and sliders are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same insight can be reached with base-ten counters, a Gattegno/place-value chart, or a paper number line.

Tier the work: emerging learners find 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing using a chart; secure learners do it mentally for any number to 1000 and name the changing digit; extending learners handle genuine roll-over boundaries (190+10, 950+100) and explain the exchange.

Bundle physical materials: ten tens into one hundred
Match and complete the three views of 100

startingActivity.title: Fuse ten tens into one hundred on an exchange bench
learnerActions: First re-bundle ten single ones into one ten-rod as a familiar recap, naming what happened: 'ten ones make one ten'.
Gather ten ten-rods into a staging tray; as the tenth rod lands, watch the ten rods merge into a single 10×10 hundred-flat.
Say aloud the pattern that connects the two moves: 'ten of the last unit always makes one of the next'.
Use a 'three views' toggle to flip the same hundred between 100 loose cubes, 10 rods, and 1 flat, while a counter stays steady at 100.
Look at a dimmed 'next level' shelf showing ten flats waiting to become a thousand-cube, and predict what comes next.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 100 is literally ten tens (and a hundred ones); each new place is ten of the one before, so place value is a self-similar ×10 pattern that keeps going.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base-ten hundred-flat (10×10) vs ten tens-rods vs 100 unit-cubes — three views of 100
Hundred-square (10×10 grid) showing ten rows of ten
Gattegno / place-value chart adding the hundreds column
Bundled straws: ten bundles-of-ten wrapped into one bundle-of-hundred
0-1000 number line with hundred markers
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 100 is 'ten' with zeros, not literally ten tens or a hundred ones.
Failing to see the repeating ×10 structure — treating hundreds as an unrelated new idea.
Confusing a hundred-flat with a ten-rod (not tracking which unit is which).
Believing 100 ones and 10 tens are different amounts rather than the same quantity re-unitised.
Counting the little squares one-by-one instead of trusting the unit (no unitising).
constraints: The fuse/split construction should come before matching or fill-in tasks: recognition and completion check equivalence but do not elicit the independent act of unitising.

A static side-by-side reference (flat beside ten rods and 100 cubes with tap-to-reveal equivalences) is a useful anchor for the three views but does not let the child perform the fuse/split; use it to support, not replace, the hands-on move.

Paper, card, straw bundles and base-ten blocks have real (slight) thickness; a 2D screen flat is an idealised picture of the hundred-flat. Treat both as representations of the same quantity and name which unit each piece stands for.
Keep the 'next level' shelf (ten flats → thousand-cube) as an optional teaser to show the pattern is open-ended; do not require mastery of 1000 at this stage.

Diagnostic: show ten tens-sticks and ask what the bundled block is called, how many single ones it is, and how the child knows — the reason reveals ten-tens structure versus rote counting. Discriminating follow-up probes: 'How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens, and how could you be sure without counting them all?'; 'If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?'; 'Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?'

activityReferences.title: Scan the places left-to-right with two aligned builds
Consolidation: choose the symbol, order a set, make it true
Annotated worked reference for the scan
Convince-me: rebut a wrong comparison

startingActivity.title: Scan the places left-to-right with two aligned builds
learnerActions: Build or view two numbers (e.g. 352 and 358) as aligned base-ten builds or counters in H | T | O columns.
Place a >, =, or < card between them, with the open side facing the larger number.
Work left to right: decide at the hundreds first; only if the hundreds tie, move to the tens; only if the tens tie, move to the ones. Stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Say aloud which place settled the decision and why.
Repeat with trap pairs: same-hundreds (352 vs 358), digit-swap (352 vs 325), and mixed-length (99 vs 100).
Then order a set of 4-5 numbers smallest to largest and place numbers on a 0-1000 number line.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When the numbers are lined up by place, the comparison is always decided at the first (highest) place where the two numbers differ; move down to the next place only on a tie. A bigger ones digit does not by itself make a number larger. A whole number with more digits (and no leading zeros) is larger because it reaches a higher place, as when 100 has a hundred and 99 does not.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Aligned base-ten builds / place-value counters in H|T|O columns
0-1000 number line for magnitude placement
>, =, < symbols (open side to the larger)
Place-value comparison chart scanning left-to-right
Ordered card rails (smallest→largest)
commonMisconceptions: Comparing ones or the biggest single digit instead of hundreds first (358 > 372 because 8 > 2).
'More digits = bigger' misapplied, or failing 99 vs 100 by digit count reasoning done wrongly.
Not descending to the next column when the hundreds tie.
Reversing the symbol or binding it to page order.
Ignoring internal zeros when comparing (305 vs 350).
constraints: UK DfE National Curriculum, Year 3: 'compare and order numbers up to 1000'. US CCSS-M 2.NBT.4: compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens and ones digits using >, =, <.

Include same-hundreds pairs (352/358), digit-swap traps (352/325) and mixed-length comparisons (99/100) so learners cannot order by eyeballing or by the ones digit. For mixed-length pairs, link the extra digit to the higher place it represents.
Progress from single pairs to ordering a set to number-line placement to connect comparison with magnitude.
Right-align numbers by place before comparing; include internal-zero cases (305 vs 350).
A static annotated reference models the procedure but does not substitute for practice across many varied pairs; use it as a scaffold.

Scorable item formats (choose-the-symbol, order-the-set, fill-the-blank, number-line slider) are well suited to consolidation and checking; they exercise the procedure and do not by themselves scaffold the initial left-to-right scan.
The 'convince-me' dialogue targets justification; because the skill is procedural, keep it paired with hands-on comparison practice rather than using it alone.

startingActivity.title: Place-value problem workbench: re-unitise to answer
learnerActions: Read a problem card such as 'How many tens are in 340?'
Build 340 with place-value pieces (three hundred-flats, four tens-rods) or arrow cards.
Exchange each hundred-flat for ten tens-rods on an exchange pad and watch 340 reassemble as 34 tens-rods, then read off the answer: 34 tens.
Repeat for another number (e.g. how many tens in 350? how many hundreds in 680?) and say which decomposition you used.
Name the strategy you used each time ('I re-unitised the hundreds into tens').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The same number can be re-unitised into equivalent decompositions; you pick the view that answers the question, and you can check by rebuilding the original number.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Part-whole and bar models for problem structure
Place-value counters and H|T|O chart
Money (pounds/tens of pence/pence) as a place-value context
0-1000 number line for jump/benchmark reasoning
Arrow cards for flexible partitioning
commonMisconceptions: Only seeing canonical partition (340 = 300 + 40) and missing '34 tens'.
Counting in ones instead of using place-value structure.
Mishandling internal zeros in problem numbers (407).
Inverse-blindness on missing-digit/missing-number clues.
Not mapping money/measure contexts onto place-value columns.
constraints: Target the actual objective — flexible re-unitising and problem solving — not routine recall of 'hundreds, tens, ones'.

Recognition-only items (multiple choice, matching) assess and consolidate but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation that are the goal; pair them with construction and spoken reasoning.
A worked example is a reference, not varied problem practice; it cannot replace the child working new problems.
Keep money/measure mappings honest: pounds / 10p / 1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones, and the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p) must be handled explicitly.
Honour placeholders: a clue like '4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones' must build 407, not 47.

Physical base-ten pieces, arrow cards and screen models all make re-unitising visible; none is uniquely necessary. On-screen live recolouring/exchange is an optional way to show the move, not a requirement.
The evidence expects the child to explain the strategy, so build explanation into every activity.

Where a 'how many hundreds/tens' question does not re-unitise to a whole count (e.g. 680 as hundreds gives 6 hundreds and 8 tens over), treat the remainder honestly rather than forcing a clean single number.

startingActivity.title: Three-pane number translator (build, type, name)
learnerActions: Work with three linked views of one number side by side: a numeral display, a word-tile builder, and an expanded-form strip, with a base-ten build (flats/rods/cubes) shown beneath.

Change any one view and watch the others and the blocks rebuild: assemble the word-tiles 'three hundred and forty-two' and confirm 342 appears alongside 300 + 40 + 2 and three flats, four rods, two cubes.
Translate deliberately in BOTH directions: read a shown numeral and build its words; and start from spoken/word form and write the numeral.
Sequence difficulty: start with no-zero numbers (342), then one internal zero (306), then a trailing zero (340).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Numeral, words and expanded form are three views of ONE number; expanded form reveals each digit's place value, and the empty column shows why a placeholder zero must be written (306, not 36 or 3006).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The three registers side by side: numeral | words | expanded form
Place-value chart / arrow cards linking words to columns
Base-ten build under each register as the anchor
Number-word cards (hundred, and, -ty, teen) for constructing names
0-1000 number line for locating the number named
commonMisconceptions: Writing what you hear literally: 'three hundred and six' → 3006 or 30006.
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (340 written as 34; 306 as 36).
Mis-ordering words vs digits, or omitting the hundreds word.
Confusing teen and -ty words within the tens part (forty vs fourteen).
Treating expanded form as separate numbers (300, 40, 2) rather than a partition of one number.
constraints: Always tie the three registers to a base-ten build so translation stays anchored to meaning rather than word order.
Deliberately sequence no-zero → one internal zero → trailing zero (342 → 306 → 340) to isolate the hard cases.
Expanded form must partition ONE number into place values (300 + 40 + 2), not be treated as three separate numbers; the tens digit must be expanded by place value (30, not 3).
A fixed reference image consolidates the correspondence but does not by itself elicit two-way reading/writing production; use it alongside, not instead of, tasks where the child writes and reads.
Oral read-it-back is light practice; it does not reliably capture a child's written numeral, so pair it with a writing task.

This is a notation/language task with no spatial dimension; a 3D spatial build is not expected to add a relevant affordance here, so it is not prioritised (this is a scoping judgement, not a claim that 3D cannot teach).

startingActivity.title: Hundreds-only builder with live numeral and placeholder zeros
learnerActions: Build 100, 200, 300 … 900 using only hundred-flats placed in the hundreds (H) column of a place-value chart, leaving the tens (T) and ones (O) columns visibly empty.
Watch or write the numeral as each flat is added (100 → 200 → 300) and note that two zeros appear because the T and O columns hold nothing.
Add a single tens-rod to the empty tens column of 300 and observe the numeral change to 310, then remove it to return to 300.
Say aloud what each digit means, e.g. '300 is 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones', and read the whole number as 'three hundred'.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: The two zeros in a multiple of 100 are not padding: they record that the tens and ones places are empty. When something is actually placed in the tens column, the zero is replaced, which shows the zero was holding a real place.

startingActivity.title: H|T|O exchange bench: build, name, expand
learnerActions: Set up three labelled columns: Hundreds | Tens | Ones.
Build 362 by placing 3 hundred-flats, 6 ten-rods and 2 ones-cubes into the matching columns.
Say the number name aloud ('three hundred and sixty-two') and write the expanded form 300 + 60 + 2.
Now empty the tens column (remove all 6 rods) and read the new number: 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones = 302. State what the 0 in the tens place means.
Work in reverse: 'Build seven hundred and six.' Leave the tens column empty and write 706, 700 + 0 + 6.
Build and contrast 76, 706 and 760 side by side; say how the columns differ.
Partition the same number more than one way, e.g. 362 = 300 + 60 + 2, 362 = 300 + 62, 362 = 340 + 22, 362 = 250 + 112.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each column shows how many hundreds, tens or ones a digit counts, so a digit's value depends on its place; a 0 marks an empty place that still must be held, which is why 706 (7 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones) is not 76.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base-ten flats/rods/cubes in an H|T|O place-value chart
Place-value counters (100, 10, 1) in labelled columns
Arrow / place-value cards (300 + 60 + 2 → 362)
Part-whole model partitioning the whole into H, T, O
0-1000 number line and Gattegno chart (hundreds/tens/ones rows)
commonMisconceptions: Concatenation: writing 300 + 60 + 2 as 30062, or reading digits separately.
Mishandling internal zeros — writing 'seven hundred and six' as 76 or 7006.
Assigning the wrong place value (thinking the 3 in 362 means 3, not 300).
Losing the placeholder: dropping the 0 in 706 or 350.
Transposition of the spoken order vs written columns in larger numbers.
constraints: Keep concrete build, number name and expanded form in lockstep for every number so the three views stay connected.
Give heavy, explicit attention to internal and trailing zeros (706, 350, 300) — this is where three-digit place value commonly breaks down.
Recognition and matching items check structure but do not elicit independent construction; include build and partition tasks where the learner produces the number and states digit values.
The static labelled anchor is a reference scaffold: it cannot let a learner build arbitrary numbers or watch the placeholder emerge, so pair it with active building.
Dialogue is a supplement for eliciting a learner's reasoning; it does not itself produce the physical build, so place it to follow hands-on building.

Flat paper/card items such as overlay cards have slight thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal notation; a screen bench with a live readout is one option, not a requirement, and physical materials can carry the activity equally.
Extend the two-digit model deliberately so the hundreds place is seen as the same idea, not a brand-new rule.

Additional source representations — place-value counters (100/10/1) in labelled columns, a 0–1000 number line, a part-whole model, and a Gattegno chart — may support the same place-value structure and can substitute for or supplement the flats/rods/cubes and arrow cards; the alternative non-canonical partition 362 = 340 + 22 is another valid flexibility example.
