startingActivity.title: Digit-stepper: which column responds to +1000?
learnerActions: Start from a four-digit number such as 4,562 shown in a place-value chart or on a number line.
Press +1000 (and −1000) and observe which digit moves: the thousands digit ticks 4→5 for +1000 (giving 5,562) or 4→3 for −1000 (giving 3,562) while hundreds, tens and ones stay locked.
Before each press, predict the result and name the digit that will change; then check against what moves.
Compare +10, +100 and +1000 side by side on the same starting number, saying which column each operation drives.
Use a 0–10,000 number-line view to see ±1000 as equal hops along the line.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 1000 normally changes only the thousands digit, extending the same place-value logic that governs +10 and +100.

Convince-me: rebut the big-digit claim

startingActivity.title: Place-aligned comparison bench
learnerActions: Take two numbers (including different lengths like 987 and 1,024) and write or place them so the digits stack by place value, right-justified into a place-value chart.
Starting at the highest place, compare column by column; mark each tied place and move down one place only when the current place is equal.
Place a > or < symbol between the numbers based on the first place that differs, and say which place decided it; use = only if every place ties.
Work the trap pairs: 4,562 vs 4,526 (same thousands and hundreds), 4,050 vs 4,005 (multi-zero), and 987 vs 1,024 (mixed length).
Then order a set of 5 numbers from smallest to largest using real data such as city populations, justifying each neighbouring comparison by place value.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Once two numbers are lined up by place, the larger number is decided at the first (highest) place where they differ, not by which number has a big digit somewhere. On a tie you keep going down to the next place; if every place ties, the numbers are equal. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, the number with more digits is always larger, because it reaches a higher place.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Aligned numerals / place-value charts stacked by place
0-10,000+ number line for magnitude
>, =, < symbols (open to larger)
Ordered card rails (smallest→largest)
Real-context data (populations, distances) as numbers to order
commonMisconceptions: Comparing by number of digits incorrectly, or by the largest single digit.
Not descending to the next place on a tie (declaring equal too early).
Mishandling multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005).
Aligning numbers to the left instead of by place value (mixed lengths).
Reversing the symbol or binding it to reading order.
constraints: Right-align by place value, not to the left; left-alignment causes mixed-length errors such as judging 987 larger than 1,024.
On a tie at any place, descend to the next lower place rather than declaring the numbers equal; only if every place, including the ones, ties are the numbers equal.
Treat zeros as place-holders that must be compared in their column (4,050 vs 4,005 is decided in the tens).

Recognition-only formats (choosing a symbol from options) consolidate and assess but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the aligned comparison or state the deciding place; include tasks where the learner lines up numbers and justifies the order.
A worked/annotated scan is a reference scaffold, not varied practice; learners still need to compare and order fresh numbers themselves.

Interactive auto-alignment, animated scans, and live 'order the set' checking are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same learning is achievable with aligned numerals on paper and a drawn number line.

startingActivity.title: Linked-representations estimator on a 0-10,000 line
learnerActions: Work with four synced views of one number: numeral, expanded form, place-value counters (Th|H|T|O), and a draggable marker on a 0-10,000 number line.
Change any one view (e.g. add/remove counters) and watch the others, including the marker's position on the line, update to match.
Play an estimation round: a target such as 6,300 appears; drag the marker to where you think it sits, then compare with the revealed true position and your error.

Use landmark hints — find 5,000 (halfway) first, then 2,500 and 7,500 — and decide where the number falls: ask yourself 'is 6,300 past halfway? is it yet past three-quarters?' and justify your answer before checking.
Optionally use a bar/strip model alongside the line to reason about proportion (e.g. shade roughly 6,300 out of a 10,000 strip) and relate the shaded length to where the marker should sit.
As you improve, work on lines where tick marks are removed so placement must come from proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Say aloud what you found first on the line and why the number lands where it does (e.g. '6,300 is past the middle but not yet at three-quarters, about halfway between 5,000 and 7,500').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The same number can be expressed as a numeral, expanded form, and counters, and these all correspond to one proportional position on the number line; magnitude is a distance anchored by landmarks, not the leading digit alone.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 0-10,000 number line with benchmark landmarks (the magnitude spine)
Place-value counters and Th|H|T|O chart
Expanded form and numeral (with comma)
Base-ten thousand/hundred/ten/one pieces
Bar/strip model for proportional estimation on the line
commonMisconceptions: Placing numbers by leading digit only (putting 4,900 and 4,100 at the same spot).
Treating the number line as evenly-spaced counting rather than proportional magnitude.
Ignoring landmarks and guessing position.
Confusing representations (reading expanded form as separate numbers).
Mis-scaling: putting 5,000 not at the halfway point of 0-10,000.
constraints: Treat numeral, expanded form, counters/base-ten, and the number-line point as interchangeable views of one number and practise translating in all directions, not just one way.

Use the 0-10,000 line as the magnitude spine with benchmark landmarks (5,000 halfway, 2,500/7,500 quarters, thousands); progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning rather than counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.

The tap-to-reveal poster and selection/slider quick-checks are scaffolds and samples: they show or test correspondences but do not require the learner to construct or estimate independently; include construction and line-placement tasks for that.

Address common errors directly: placing by leading digit only, treating the line as even counting rather than proportional magnitude, ignoring landmarks, reading expanded form as separate numbers, and mis-scaling (5,000 not at the halfway point).

Linked live-recompute panels, draggable markers, fading tick marks, landmark hints, and a bar/strip model for proportional estimation are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tools; the learning goal is learner action and benchmark reasoning on the line, achievable on paper too.

startingActivity.title: Build and recompose in the Th|H|T|O bench
learnerActions: Extend the familiar H|T|O column bench to Th|H|T|O and assemble a number such as 3,452 using thousand-cubes, hundred-flats, ten-rods and ones.
Drag ten hundred-flats into a tray and watch them fuse into one thousand-cube, saying aloud 'ten hundreds make one thousand' — the same unitising move one column up.
Keep three things in view at once as you build: the blocks, the numeral with its comma (3,452), and the expanded form 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2.
Use arrow (place-value) cards to lay out 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2, then slide them together so they overlap into the single numeral 3,452, linking the expanded form to the compact numeral.
Place the finished number on a 0-10,000 number line to check its rough magnitude, noticing how the comma/grouping helps you read size at a glance.

Swap two digits in your built number — for example exchange the 4 and the 5 in 3,452 to make 3,542 — and compare both on the bench and on the number line to see that moving a digit into a different column changes its value and the whole number's size.
Empty one column at a time (3,452 → 3,402 → 3,002) and describe what happens to the numeral and the expanded form.

In a reverse mode, listen to or read a spoken number such as 'three thousand and six' and build it; leave the hundreds AND tens columns empty so two bold placeholder 0s appear and the numeral resolves to 3,006 (not 36 or 3,600).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is set by its column, not by the digit itself — so swapping digits between columns changes the number; thousands repeat the ×10 pattern (ten hundreds = one thousand); and empty columns must still be written as 0 so magnitude and the comma are correct.

startingActivity.title: Periods-based number translator to a million
learnerActions: Build a six-column place-value chart split by a comma into a thousands period and a ones period (e.g. 403 | 072), and add a millions column when showing 1,000,000, which needs seven digits.

Enter or read a number and keep three linked forms in sync: the grouped numeral (403,072), the number name ('four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two') and expanded form (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2).
Read the number by chunks, one period at a time, rather than reciting single digits.

activityReferences.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart
How many times greater? Counting the place-shifts
Division and multiplication sentences as the place-value step

startingActivity.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns for ones, tens, hundreds, thousands (and more).
Place a single digit — say a 3 — in the hundreds column so it is worth 300.

Move that same 3 one column to the LEFT and state its new value (3,000). Say what happened to the value and by how much: it became ten TIMES as much, not 'ten more'. (For whole numbers the written numeral also gains a zero, but that is a by-product — the reason is the ×10 in value.)
Move the 3 back to the RIGHT (÷10): from 3,000, one column right returns it to 300, and a further column right makes it 30.
Write the matching sentence each time, e.g. 300 × 10 = 3,000 and 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Shifting a digit one place left multiplies its value by 10 and one place right divides it by 10; place value is multiplicative between adjacent columns, not merely 'adding a zero'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Gattegno place-value chart (rows scale ×10 down each column)
Place-value chart with a digit sliding between columns
Base-ten pieces showing ten-of-one-unit = one-of-next
Multiplication/division sentences (×10, ÷10) between places
Arrow-card / expanded form as the additive counterpart
commonMisconceptions: Seeing place value only additively and missing the ×10 relationship between places.
Thinking the 3 in 3,000 is '10 more' than in 300 rather than 10 times.
Confusing 'ten times' with 'add a zero' as a meaningless trick (fails for decimals later).
Miscounting the factor across non-adjacent places (×10 vs ×100).
Not connecting 700÷70=10 to the adjacent-place relationship.
constraints: Hold the additive (partition) view and the multiplicative (×10 between places) view together: 3,452 is 3,000+400+50+2 AND each place is ten times the next. Do not drop the partition view.

Avoid teaching 'add a zero' as the rule; name the underlying ×10 relationship so the idea still works when extended to decimals (÷10 into tenths). For whole numbers the written zero is a by-product, not the explanation.
A static or paper place-value chart is a valid reference and teaching tool; an interactive sliding chart may make the live recompute more vivid but is not the only way to teach this relationship.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. '700 ÷ 70 = __', 'which is ten times 400?') are useful for consolidation and assessment but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and explain the place-shift reasoning; pair them with tasks that ask for the factor AND its justification.
When comparing non-adjacent places, require the number of place-shifts to be counted (one shift ×10, two shifts ×100); do not let any gap be treated as a single ×10.
Distinguish the digit's face value (3 in both 300 and 3,000) from its place value (300 vs 3,000) whenever learners say the numbers are 'the same'.

startingActivity.title: Build the largest number: a digit-constraint puzzle
learnerActions: Take the task: 'Make the LARGEST six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.'
Arrange digit choices into a six-column place-value chart (hundred-thousands down to ones) and write the value they build.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: Magnitude is controlled by the highest-value places, so maximising a number means front-loading the biggest digits into the leftmost columns while respecting the digit-sum constraint.

startingActivity.title: Large-number problem workspace: pick the right tool
learnerActions: Load a scenario with mixed demands, e.g. three ocean trenches at -8,376 m, -9,052 m and -7,921 m plus a country's population of 8,274,500 needed for a news headline.

For the headline, round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and state the result (8,000,000); name the single digit that decided the rounding (the hundred-thousands digit, 2) and explain why the digits after it do not change the decision.

Order the three trench depths from deepest to shallowest, placing each on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level, and justify ordering by position (more negative = lower = deeper), not by comparing the digits while ignoring the minus sign.

Estimate a combined attendance for three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000, then compute the exact total and state whether your rounded estimate came out over or under, explaining how you can tell.
Say back in context which figure each situation needs: a rounded headline for the population, exact negatives for ranking the trenches.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The same set of numbers can demand different place-value tools — rounding for a headline, exact negatives for a ranking — and estimating first tells you whether the exact answer is believable.

activityReferences.title: Sweep the exponent on a place-value chart
Reference ladder of powers of ten
Defend it against the 'add zeros' rule

startingActivity.title: Sweep the exponent on a place-value chart
learnerActions: Place a number — e.g. 3.4 — on a place-value chart with the decimal point marked in a fixed position.

Set a power of ten (10¹, then 10², then 10³) and, for each, slide every digit left by the number shown in the exponent; the column count is the total shift from 3.4 and equals the exponent: 3.4 → 34 (10¹, one column) → 340 (10², two columns) → 3400 (10³, three columns), keeping the point pinned.
Alongside, write the power in expanded form (10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000) and tally its zeros.
State in words: 'The exponent tells me how many columns the digits jump.'
Repeat with division by powers of ten (shifting digits the other way, e.g. 3.4 ÷ 10 = 0.34) and with a whole number like 7 (7 × 10 = 70) to compare where zeros appear.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The exponent equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift, so 'powers of ten' and 'place-value shift' are the same idea. For a decimal like 3.4, multiplying by 10 does not append a zero (3.4 × 10 = 34, not 3.40); any zeros appearing in larger products such as 340 or 3400 are placeholders filling emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original number — so the 'add-a-zero' rule is not the real pattern.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with digits sliding N columns for ×10^N (point fixed)
Expanded factor strings: 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with zeros tallied
Exponent stepper linking 10¹, 10², 10³ to 10, 100, 1000 and their zero counts
Arrow cards showing 3.4 → 34 → 340 with '×10' per hop
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplying by a power of 10 just adds zeros' — fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 ≠ 3.400)
Reading 10³ as 10×3 = 30 (confusing exponent with a factor)
Believing the decimal point moves rather than the digits
Miscounting the shift — shifting by the base (10) rather than the exponent (3)
Assuming the exponent equals the number of digits in the result rather than factors of ten
constraints: Define an exponent as the number of factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count of the power of ten is a consequence, and the 'add that many zeros' rule works only for whole-number products and breaks for decimals.

Distinguish appended zeros from placeholder zeros: multiplying a decimal does not append zeros after its decimal point to the original digits, but placeholder zeros may legitimately fill emptied whole-number columns (e.g. 340, 3400, 2560). Do not tell a learner 'no zeros appear' when the displayed product contains them.
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed; avoid teaching 'move the decimal point' as the primary idea, though it can be mentioned as an equivalent description.
Include division by powers of ten alongside multiplication so the shift is seen as bidirectional.
The reference ladder is a static anchor: on its own it does not show the digit shift as an action, so pair it with the moving chart.
Selected-response consolidation checks the pattern but does not elicit the learner's own explanation; keep a task that requires constructing a justification.
Live recolouring/highlighting, digit sliding, a mobile exponent dial, zero tallies and a divide toggle are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as required mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Slide the same digit across the places
learnerActions: Work on a place-value chart with columns from millions down to thousandths and a fixed decimal point.
Take a single digit, for example a 4, and place it in the tenths column so it reads 0.4.
Move the same 4 one column to the left to read 4, then 40, then 400, then 4000; each move, say aloud 'ten times as much' and write the ×10 relationship.

Before moving right, split one tenth into ten equal parts and check that each part is one hundredth (and one hundredth into ten parts gives thousandths). Then move the same 4 one column to the right from 0.4 to 0.04 to 0.004; each move, say aloud 'one tenth of' and write the ÷10 relationship.
Park the same 4 three columns apart (for example 4000 and 4, or 4 and 0.004 — each three steps, so ×1000) and state how many times larger one is than the other.
Finish the sentence: '0.4 is ten times 0.04; 0.04 is one tenth of 0.4.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A digit's worth changes multiplicatively (×10 each step left, ÷10 each step right) according to its place; the decimal point stays fixed while the digit moves, and the same self-similar rule runs through the decimal point.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (digit slides between columns, value scales ×10 or ÷10)
Place-value chart spanning millions to thousandths with the decimal point fixed and digits mobile
Arrow/relationship cards labelling adjacent columns '×10 →' and '← ÷10'
Base-ten / Dienes extended to decimal flats-longs-units where the 'one' can be reassigned
commonMisconceptions: Believing 'moving a place left just adds a zero' — a rule that breaks for decimals (0.4 → 4, not 0.40)
Treating the decimal point as moving rather than the DIGITS moving relative to a fixed point
Thinking the gap between places is additive (0.4 is '0.36 more than' 0.04) rather than multiplicative (ten times)
Assuming longer decimals are always larger, ignoring place value (0.004 seen as bigger than 0.4)
Losing the self-similar structure at the decimal point — seeing tenths as unrelated to ones
constraints: Present whole-number and decimal place value as ONE continuous ×10/÷10 chain running through the decimal point, not two separate systems.
Require multiplicative language ('ten times', 'one tenth of'); do not accept 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation of the relationship.

Recognition-only tasks (for example choosing from multiple options or filling a blank) can consolidate and assess the rule but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own justification; include tasks where the learner states and defends the relationship.

A static annotated chart with reveal cards is a useful reference, but it tells rather than lets the learner perform the slide; treat it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the learner moving a digit and reading the recomputed value.
Partitioning (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) should be established concretely before abstracting to the divide-by-ten rule.

startingActivity.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart
learnerActions: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths
Thousandths grid (10×10×10 nesting) or 1000-cube partition of the unit

'Shorter decimal is larger' (over-correcting to 'fewer digits = closer to whole')
Reading 0.062 as 'point zero sixty-two' and losing the thousandths meaning
Treating the decimal part as a whole number after the point (comparing 372 vs 38)
Misplacing digits in expanded form — attaching 1/10 to the hundredths digit
constraints: Read decimals with place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the place meaning stays audible.
Equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) when comparing; this exposes 'longer-is-larger' as false without changing value.
Watch for over-correction to 'shorter-is-larger' (fewer digits = closer to the whole); length alone decides nothing — only the first differing place does.
5.062 is not 5.62: keep placeholder zeros when a spoken place name requires the final digit to sit further right.

A static labelled number with revealed place values anchors reading and expanded form but cannot carry out the padding/alignment that resolves comparisons; use it alongside the comparison activity, not instead of it.

Grid shading, column-highlight tools and a number line to hundredths/thousandths are illustrative, complementary supports for the comparison mechanism, not required equipment; the reasoning can also be carried out on paper by writing values to equal length.

startingActivity.title: Period builder with live three-way echo
learnerActions: Set each digit onto a place-value chart labelled Millions | Thousands | Ones, grouped into three-digit periods.

As each digit is placed, watch the number appear three ways at once: the comma-grouped numeral (e.g. 7,045,200), the words read period by period ('seven million, forty-five thousand, two hundred'), and the expanded form.

Deliberately build numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (e.g. set the hundred-thousands place — the leading digit of the thousands period — to 0, as in 7,045,200) and observe how the words panel skips the empty place without dropping the period boundary.
State aloud, for a chosen digit, its full place value (e.g. 'the 7 is worth seven million').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The comma/period grouping — not the raw digit count — is what lets you read a large number aloud; each nonzero three-digit period is read as a number then given its period name (the ones period has no spoken name, and a period that is all zeros, as in 7,000,200, is skipped entirely), and an internal zero silently holds a column without being spoken.

Order standard-form numbers by scale

startingActivity.title: Dial-the-exponent place-value converter
learnerActions: Set up two linked views: an ordinary number shown on a place-value chart, and an A × 10ⁿ expression you can change.

Starting with A = 4.5 and n = 0, increase n and watch the digits slide LEFT into higher place-value columns (equivalently, the decimal point moves right) one column per unit of n until 4.5 becomes 4,500,000 (4.5 × 10⁶); describe what each change of n does to the place value.

Now set A = 3.2 and n = −4; watch the digits slide RIGHT four columns into smaller place values (equivalently, the decimal point moves left four places) to give 0.00032, and state in words why the result is small but still positive.

Deliberately type an expression like 34 × 10⁵ and notice it is flagged as not in standard form; renormalise it yourself to 3.4 × 10⁶ by adjusting A and n together, then check the ordinary number is unchanged.
Record a short rule: 'n is how many places the point moves — right for positive n, left for negative n — and n never makes the number negative.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Standard form is the ×10/÷10 place-value shift turned into notation: the exponent counts and directs how many columns the digits move, and a negative exponent makes a number small, not negative.

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with the point shifting n places for ×10ⁿ

commonMisconceptions: Leaving A outside 1 ≤ A < 10 (writing 34 × 10⁵ or 0.34 × 10⁷)
Miscounting the exponent — using the number of zeros incorrectly, or wrong sign for small numbers
Moving the digits the wrong direction for negative exponents (3.2×10⁻⁴ written as 32000)
Comparing by mantissa first and ignoring the exponent's dominance
Thinking a negative exponent makes the number negative rather than small/positive
constraints: Enforce 1 ≤ A < 10; use non-examples such as 34 × 10⁶ and 0.5 × 10³ to make the normalisation rule explicit.
Teach positive n (large numbers) and negative n (small positive numbers) together so the sign of the exponent carries meaning.
A fixed scale poster or illustration motivates and displays values but cannot perform conversions or enforce normalisation; use it alongside, not instead of, active conversion practice.

Recognition-only or single-answer selection consolidates fluency but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify conversions; include tasks where learners produce the conversion and check it.
Keep the sign of the number distinct from the sign of the exponent throughout: a negative exponent never makes a number negative.
Scope the exponent-first comparison rule to positive, normalised values (1 ≤ A < 10).

activityReferences.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
Consolidation across places with targeted traps
Rounding-hill reference image (scaffold)

startingActivity.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
learnerActions: Place or drag the target number (e.g. 4,367) as a marker on a number line between its two bounding multiples — 4,300 and 4,400 when rounding to the nearest 100 — with the midpoint 4,350 clearly flagged.
See that 4,367 sits PAST the midpoint, so it is nearer to 4,400; watch the marker snap to 4,400 (an arc or snap animation makes the 'nearer multiple' choice visible rather than recited).

Drag the marker back and forth across the midpoint and watch the rounded result flip at 4,350: whole numbers below 4,350 (e.g. 4,349) round down to 4,300, while 4,350 itself and anything above round up to 4,400. This shows that the midpoint is the tipping point, and that the half-rounds-up convention decides the exact-halfway case.
Use a target-place selector (10/100/1000) that rescales the line and changes the bounding multiples, so you feel how the target place chooses which multiples bound the number.
Work a cascade case: round 4,970 to the nearest 100 and watch the roll up to 5,000 — the hundreds carry over (49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000).
After the line meaning is built, name the 'decider' digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to — and connect it to which side of the midpoint you are on.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Rounding means choosing the nearer multiple of the target place; the midpoint is the tipping point, and the 'look at the next digit' rule is just a quick way of telling whether the number is below halfway (decider 0-4, round down) or at or past halfway (decider 5-9, round up, with exactly halfway going up by the agreed convention).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with the two bounding multiples and midpoint (the canonical model)
Place-value chart to identify the rounding digit and the decider digit
'Rounding hill'/rollercoaster midpoint image
0-10,000 line for rounding to 1000
Estimation contexts (sensible approximations)
commonMisconceptions: Rounding by the wrong digit or to the wrong place (ignoring which place is the target).
Always rounding down (truncating) or always up.
Chained/successive rounding (rounding the ones then tens then…) instead of one decision.
Mishandling the halfway case or the cascade (4,970 to nearest 100 → 4,900 not 5,000).
Treating rounding as a rule with no sense of 'nearer to', so unable to check reasonableness.
constraints: Teach rounding as a number-line nearness decision FIRST; only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint, so it is understood rather than memorised.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).

Deliberately teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade/carry cases (e.g. 4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100); state the convention explicitly since 'half rounds up' is a chosen convention, not a mathematical necessity.
The rounded value must be a multiple of the target place: all digits after the rounding place become zero.
Avoid chained/successive rounding (rounding ones, then tens, then hundreds); rounding to a target place is a single decision from the original number.

The static hill/poster is a reference scaffold; its limit is that it shows rather than requires the learner's own nearness decision. A fill/multiple-choice format consolidates and checks but does not by itself require the learner to construct the number-line justification.
When assessing, watch the working (which digit decides and what happens to trailing digits), not only the final number, to reveal which rule the child is running.

The decider digit for a target place is the digit one place to the RIGHT of it (for 4,367 to nearest 100 the decider is the tens digit 6, not the hundreds digit 3, the ones digit 7, or the thousands digit 4).
Carry arithmetic must match the actual number: 4,970 → 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; 1,970 → 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.

startingActivity.title: Scaled rounding bench: drag across the midpoint
learnerActions: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000: place it on a number line between the bounding multiples 450,000 and 460,000, with the midpoint 455,000 flagged.
Decide which multiple it is nearer and state the rounded value (460,000); check it against the midpoint.
Change the target place to nearest 100,000 so the line rescales to the bounding multiples 400,000 and 500,000 (midpoint 450,000), and round 456,782 again (it is past the midpoint, so 500,000).
After each decision, write out the rounded number and confirm every digit after the rounding place is now zero.
Explain which single digit you used to decide (the one immediately to the right of the rounding place) and why the rest are irrelevant.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Rounding a large number is the same nearness decision scaled up: the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples and the midpoint, the one decider digit settles the decision, and all trailing digits become zeros.

keyRepresentations: Number line with large bounding multiples and midpoint
Place-value chart marking the rounding digit and decider digit
0-1,000,000 line rescaled per target place
Estimation contexts (populations, budgets)
'Rounding hill' midpoint image scaled up
commonMisconceptions: Looking at the wrong decider digit or rounding to the wrong place.
Successive/chained rounding across places instead of one decision.
Truncating (always down) or always up.
Cascade errors (950,500 to nearest 100,000 mishandled).
Losing place value in the unchanged trailing digits (they become zeros).
constraints: Keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning; the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Use only the single decider digit immediately to the right of the rounding place; the remaining digits are irrelevant to the decision and become zeros.
Make one rounding decision per task; do not round step-by-step across successive places (chained rounding is an error).
State and apply a halfway convention explicitly (conventionally round up) and name it when at an exact midpoint.
Rounding direction depends on the decider digit relative to the midpoint; do not always round down (truncate) or always round up.

A static scaled 'rounding hill' or poster is a useful reference but does not itself require the learner to act on the decision; pair it with a task where the learner makes and justifies the rounding decision.
Selected-response items (multiple choice, matching) check recognition; to elicit the procedure, also require the learner to construct or explain the rounding decision.

Number-line nearness is a one-dimensional model, so a flat line with bounding multiples and a midpoint is sufficient and no 3D representation is needed for this objective; this is a scoped sufficiency note, not a claim that other media cannot teach it.

activityReferences.title: Bounds explorer on a number line
Writing and checking error intervals
Estimate by rounding and judge over/under

startingActivity.title: Bounds explorer on a number line
learnerActions: Enter a rounded value and its rounding unit (e.g. 12 to the nearest cm).
Mark on a number line a closed point at the lower bound (11.5) and an open point at the upper bound (12.5), labelling the interval 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5.
Place a 'true measurement' marker anywhere inside the bracket and check it stays within the half-unit each side.
Drag the true marker to the open upper end and reason about what happens: 12.5 would round up to 13, so it is excluded from this interval.
Change the rounding unit to 'nearest 10' and redraw the bracket at ±5; try 'nearest 0.1' and redraw at ±0.05.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A single rounded number really stands for an interval one rounding unit wide, with half a unit on EACH side; the upper bound is the excluded (open) end of the bracket because exactly halfway rounds up to the next value.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with the rounded value central and the half-unit interval bracketed (open/closed ends)
Bound-bracket diagram: lower bound ●──rounded value──○ upper bound
Half-unit strip showing ±0.5 of the rounding unit
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with exact values and over/under flags
commonMisconceptions: Treating a rounded measurement as exact (12 cm means exactly 12)
Using ± a whole unit rather than half a unit for the bounds
Getting the inclusive/exclusive symbols the wrong way round at the bounds
Assuming the upper bound is the rounded value itself (12.5 rounded to 12 but writing x ≤ 12)
Forgetting to halve the LAST place unit (nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05)
constraints: The half-unit applies to the LAST place of the rounding unit: nearest unit → ±0.5, nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05.
Use the convention lower bound included (≤) and upper bound excluded (<); keep the strict/inclusive symbols distinct at each end.

A static labelled bracket diagram (e.g. 11.5 ●─ 12 ──○ 12.5 with the convention annotated) can illustrate one case, but on its own does not let the learner test the top-end exclusion or vary the rounding unit — use it as an illustration, not the main investigation.

Fill-in / multiple-choice prompts can consolidate and check stating bounds and intervals, but do not by themselves build the spatial interval concept; recognising a correct interval is not the same as producing one.

A mentor question such as 'the sign says 12 cm to the nearest cm — what is the smallest and largest it could truly be?' can productively challenge the belief that 12 is exact, as a complement to manipulating the interval.

Estimation requires actually rounding to a convenient figure (ideally one significant figure) and comparing with the exact value; when the two factors round in opposite directions, do not assert a single over/under direction from the rounding alone — compare with the exact value.

startingActivity.title: Build-a-numeral bench with a contrast challenge
learnerActions: Place or drag symbol tiles (I, V, X, L, C) into a row and read the value aloud as you build, e.g. XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17.
When you write 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII, notice it is flagged and rewrite it the valid subtractive way (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1).
Convert both directions: given 44, build XLIV; given XLIV, read it as 40 + 4.

Take the contrast challenge: write 88 (LXXXVIII) and notice how many repeated symbols it needs; then try a very large number like 3,000 and see how unwieldy it becomes — within the taught symbols you would need a huge string of C's, and the usual Roman form MMM uses M, a symbol beyond those you are taught; then try to write zero and find there is NO symbol at all — each shown beside the compact base-ten numeral.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Roman numerals combine fixed symbol values by adding (and sometimes subtracting the smaller-before-larger pair); because they have no place value and no zero placeholder, numbers with many repeats become unwieldy, very large numbers become enormous strings or need symbols beyond the basic set, and zero cannot be written at all — which is exactly why position-carries-value and a placeholder zero are powerful inventions.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Roman symbol→value reference (I,V,X,L,C)
Additive decomposition (XVII = 10+5+1+1) vs subtractive (IX = 10−1)
Side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic conversion chart
Real artefacts: clock faces, monument dates, book chapters
Place-value chart as the contrast (what Roman lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Pure additive thinking, writing 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII instead of IV/IX.
Inventing invalid subtractive forms (IL for 49 instead of XLIX).
Misordering symbols or ignoring the subtractive-position rule.
Thinking Roman numerals have a zero or place value.
Reading a subtractive pair additively (IX as 11).
constraints: The deeper objective is conceptual appreciation of place value and zero by contrast, not just symbol decoding; the contrast must be run explicitly (try to write a long numeral, a very large number, and zero in Roman).

Recognition and matching tasks consolidate and check the skill but do not by themselves elicit an independent spoken or written explanation of why our system differs; include a construct-an-explanation prompt.
A static chart or annotated image teaches symbol values and make-up but cannot be manipulated to compute values live or stage the balloon/zero contrast; treat it as a reference scaffold.

Valid subtractive forms are IV, IX, XL, XC; when writing, treat IIII and VIIII as non-standard (use IV and IX), noting that IIII is a traditional variant still seen on many clock faces, and reject invalid forms such as IL (for 49, use XLIX).
Roman numerals genuinely have no zero symbol and no positional place value — present this as the real system contrast, not as a claim about any particular teaching medium being uniquely necessary.

This topic teaches symbols I to C only; large numbers (e.g. 3,000) should be used to show how numerals become unwieldy within the taught set and that conventional large-number symbols such as M lie beyond those taught — not presented as part of the required symbol set, and not framed as literally 'running out' of symbols.

startingActivity.title: Build and decode years with a symbol-tile decoder
learnerActions: Assemble a year from symbol tiles including D and M, or read a given year such as MCMXCIX.
Split the year into coloured groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and state each group's value (1000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 1999).
Convert both directions: read a Roman year into Hindu-Arabic, and write a modern year (e.g. 2024 → MMXXIV) in Roman.
Try an illegal shortcut such as IC for 99, see it flagged, and correct it to XCIX.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A long, intimidating Roman year is really a chain of familiar subtractive/additive groups; each group reads independently, and only certain subtractive pairs are valid.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Extended symbol→value chart (I,V,X,L,C,D,M)

commonMisconceptions: Invalid subtractive forms at scale (IC/IM for 99/999 instead of XCIX/CMXCIX).
Reading chained subtractive groups additively (misreading MCMXCIX).
Confusing D and M values or omitting a group.
Pure-additive over-long strings (writing 900 as DCCCC not CM).
Thinking Roman numerals gained a zero/place value.
constraints: Restrict subtractive pairs to the valid conventions: I before V/X, X before L/C, C before D/M; reject over-applied subtraction such as IC or IM, and use IV (not IIII) for 4 in standard writing, while noting that many clock faces traditionally show IIII as an accepted variant.

A static annotated artefact (monument date, clock face) is a useful reference and reading task but does not by itself exercise writing/producing Roman numerals; pair it with construction or two-way conversion for the full objective.

Matching and multiple-choice checks consolidate and assess reading, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a year; include tasks where the learner writes the Roman form themselves.
Keep genuinely dated examples (real years) rather than only abstract numerals so the 'recognise years' objective is met.
Interaction examples (colour grouping, live value readout, invalid-form flagging) are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms, and their efficacy relative to other media is untested.

The midpoint x.5 and the round-up convention

startingActivity.title: Which whole is it nearest? Placing decimals on a number line
learnerActions: Draw or use a number line from 3 to 4 with each tenth marked, and plot 3.7 on it.
Ask aloud: is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4, and roughly how much nearer? Measure or count the gaps (0.3 to 4, 0.7 to 3).
Plot 3.2 on the same line and decide which whole it is nearer, explaining from the position (0.2 to 3, 0.8 to 4).
Mark the halfway point 3.5 and say what is special about it.
Repeat with a fresh set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 2.8, 5.1, 7.4), stating each result and why.

Finally state the rule in your own words as a consequence of distance: 'look at the tenths — if it is in the lower half it rounds down, in the upper half it rounds up, and the exact midpoint follows the agreed convention.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Rounding is a nearness judgement on a line: the whole you round to is the one the number is closer to. The tenths digit is a shortcut that reports which half of the interval you are in, not an arbitrary 'chop or bump' instruction.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line 3–4 with 3.7 plotted and 3.5 marked as halfway
Bead string / hundred square segment between two wholes
A 'rounding hill' where a ball rolls to the nearer whole
Place-value chart
commonMisconceptions: Truncates — drops the decimal and always rounds down (3.7 → 3)
Always rounds up when any decimal part is present (3.2 → 4)
Thinks the exact midpoint 3.5 rounds down, or is unsure what to do with it
Confuses rounding with changing the digit (3.7 → 3.10 / 4.0 muddle)
constraints: Teach 'nearest' on a number line FIRST; introduce the 'round up at 5' rule only afterwards and only for the exact midpoint, framed as an agreed convention, not a distance fact.
Do not teach 'if there is anything after the point, go up' — that wrongly sends 3.2 to 4. The tenths digit indicates which half of the interval the number is in.
Distinguish rounding from truncating explicitly: 3.7 rounds to 4; it is not chopped to 3.
Avoid muddling rounding with changing digits (e.g. 3.7 becoming 3.10 or a stray 4.0 confusion); the result is a whole number.

When illustrating error patterns, attach each error to a number where it actually produces a wrong answer: truncation errs on 3.7 (gives 3), always-up errs on 3.2 (gives 4). Do not present the always-up answer (4) as a 'wrong move' for 3.7, whose correct answer is 4.

A static labelled number line with tap-to-reveal can display one rounding as a reference aid, but it does not let a learner test many cases or feel why the midpoint is special, so it is a scaffold rather than the main teaching tool.
Selecting a rounded answer from options checks the outcome but does not by itself elicit the distance justification; pair any selection task with a spoken or written 'why'.
A number line captures nearness in one dimension; added depth or 3D representation is not needed here, though it is not claimed to be harmful.

activityReferences.title: Zoomable number line: one-step rounding and the visible carry
Identify the deciding digit on a place-value chart
Checkable rounding and estimation questions

startingActivity.title: Zoomable number line: one-step rounding and the visible carry
learnerActions: Plot 3.47 on a number line showing whole numbers 3 and 4; mark the 3.5 midpoint and judge that 3.47 sits just below it, so it is nearer 3.

Deliberately try the tempting wrong path: round 3.47 to 3.5 first, then watch 3.5 round up to 4 — the WRONG whole. Compare side by side with going straight from 3.47 (tenths digit 4, below half) which gives 3.
Zoom the line to tenths and round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).

Switch to a 12.9–13.0 view and round 12.95 to one decimal place; notice it sits exactly halfway, so by the usual rule (a deciding 5 rounds up) it snaps to 13.0, and watch the whole-number digit tick from 12 to 13 as the carry ripples in.

Use an estimation view to round 4.83 and 2.17 each to the nearest whole and add (5 + 2 = 7); then compare with the true sum (7.00) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal — here rounding 4.83 up and 2.17 down cancel, so the estimate equals the true total.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Round in ONE step from the original number; to the nearest whole only the tenths digit decides, so 3.47 → 3. The boundary carry (12.95 → 13.0) is a real event where a rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole, not a rule failure.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line zoomed to the target precision (wholes; then tenths)
Place-value chart marking the target place and the deciding digit
Estimation on a number line for sums like 4.83 + 2.17
Boundary number line 12.9–13.0 for the carry case
commonMisconceptions: Double rounding: 3.47 → 3.5 → 4 to the nearest whole
Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (or a chain of digits) when rounding to a whole
Drops the boundary carry: 12.95 → 12.10 or 12.9 instead of 13.0
Omits the trailing zero / place: writes 13 when 1dp is asked, or truncates
constraints: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value.
Keep the target place value: rounding to 1dp requires the trailing place (write 13.0, not 13).
The static annotated number line and place-value chart are reference/scaffold aids: they can label the deciding digit for one case but do not demonstrate precision-switching or the carry dynamically.

The set of checkable questions checks answers and surfaces misconceptions via distractors; this format does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line shows, so pair it with the number-line work rather than treating it as the sole route to the nearness concept.
For the estimation example 4.83 + 2.17, the estimate (7) equals the true sum (7.00); do not require learners to pick 'above' or 'below' — accept 'exactly equal'.
Prerequisite reteach for double rounding and wrong-deciding-digit errors is flagged to an earlier place-value micro-topic in the source assessment.

activityReferences.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart
Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry
Rounding to estimate a calculation

startingActivity.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
learnerActions: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with the two rounding candidates and a marked midpoint
Place-value chart to isolate the rounding place and the deciding next digit
'Rounding hill/valley' visual (nearer candidate is downhill) for the midpoint decision
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with the exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Rounding digit-by-digit / double rounding (3.4567 → 3.457 → 3.46 → 3.5) instead of one decision at the target place
'Always round 5 down' or inconsistent treatment of the exact-midpoint case
Truncating (chopping) rather than rounding (3.48 → 3.4 to 1 dp)
Forgetting the round-up cascade across a 9 (3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, not 3.79 or 3.710)
Dropping the trailing zero that records the rounded place (writing 3.8 for 3.80 to 2 dp when the place must be shown)
constraints: Multiple-choice, slider, and fill-in response formats can consolidate and check rounding outcomes (e.g. a truncation distractor of 3.4 for 3.48), but recognising a correct rounded value does not by itself show the learner is reasoning from the midpoint; pair outcome checks with working that reveals the method.
A static annotated number line illustrates a single rounding case but does not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or experience a boundary cascade; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Dialogue prompts (e.g. 'you rounded 3.4567 to 3.46 — walk me through why, not digit by digit') can surface double-rounding and truncation errors; the nearness decision can also be made where the number is placed and compared spatially.
Round in one decision at the target place; do not round digit-by-digit (double rounding) and do not truncate.
Treat the exact midpoint and above as rounding up to the higher candidate; avoid 'always round 5 down'.
Preserve trailing/placeholder zeros that record the required place (2.40, not 2.4; 10.0, not 10).

Reverse build: reconstruct the numeral from given values (placeholder zeros)

startingActivity.title: Reveal each digit's value (digit × place-unit)
learnerActions: Write or display a number to three decimal places, e.g. 4.378, above a place-value chart with columns labelled Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths and units 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000.
For each digit, say and write its value as digit × place-unit: the 7 is 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths = 0.07; the 8 is 8 × 1/1000 = 8 thousandths = 0.008.
State explicitly how adjacent places relate: the hundredths place is one tenth of the tenths place (÷10 moving right, ×10 moving left).

Within a single number containing two identical digits in adjacent decimal columns, e.g. 2.335 (2 ones, 3 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths), compare the two 3s and explain why their values differ (3 tenths = 0.3 versus 3 hundredths = 0.03) even though the digit is the same.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is its face value times the unit of the column it sits in; adjacent decimal places differ by a factor of ten, not by addition, so the same digit can mean very different amounts.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths with unit labels 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000
Digit-value cards: '7 → 7 hundredths → 0.07'
Thousandths grid showing each place as ten of the next-smaller
Reverse-build slots (digit-into-place) with a live numeral readout
commonMisconceptions: Naming the place but giving the wrong value (the 7 is 'in the hundredths' but stated as '7' or '0.7')
Reading the decimal part as one whole number (378) rather than digit-by-place values
Confusing tenths and hundredths (off-by-one place), especially with a leading zero
Dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing (writing 4.73 for 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths)
Believing adjacent places differ additively rather than by a factor of ten
constraints: Learners must state each digit's value as digit × place-unit (e.g. '7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100 = 0.07'), not only name the place.
Include the reverse reconstruction task; naming values forward alone can hide the placeholder-zero error, so reconstruction from values is needed to prove two-way understanding.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. 'value of the 3 in 2.635', 'reconstruct 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths = ___') can consolidate and check understanding but do not themselves build the place-unit link; pair them with construction and explanation.

A fixed labelled diagram with revealed per-digit values is a strong reference for the reveal step but cannot host the reverse-build that tests placeholder zeros, so it is a partial scaffold for this objective.

Optional interactive affordances (tap-to-reveal, drag value tiles into columns, live numeral readout, ÷10/×10 arrows) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; equivalent learning is possible with a paper chart and spoken reasoning.

When contrasting identical digits, use a number where the repeated digit appears in genuinely different places and state the correct factor between those places (adjacent columns = ten times; non-adjacent columns differ by a larger power of ten).
Checkpoint tiers: age-10 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?'; explain 'the relationship between adjacent decimal places'; write 'the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths'.

startingActivity.title: Highlight the significant figures, round once, rebuild the size
learnerActions: Take a number such as 34,750 and decide to round it to 2 significant figures.
Mark the counted significant digits (the 3 and the 4), confirming you start at the first non-zero digit.

Identify the single deciding digit immediately after the last required place (the 7) and place the number on a number line between its two candidate rounded values (34,000 and 35,000) and their midpoint (34,500); decide the round-up in one step.
Reassemble the answer as 35,000, writing in the placeholder zeros that keep the number in the thousands — do NOT stop at 35.

Now take 0.004982 and round to 2 significant figures: cross out the leading zeros as 'not significant', count the 4 and 9, apply the deciding digit (8) so 49 rounds up to 50, and write 0.0050 — keeping the front zeros for magnitude and the trailing zero for precision.
Repeat 0.004982 rounded to 2 decimal places (= 0.00) and place both answers side by side to see that dp and sf give genuinely different results.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit; zeros can be placeholders that hold a number's size or trailing zeros that record precision, so they cannot simply be dropped. Rounding is one nearness decision based on the next digit, after which place value must be restored.

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart marking the rounding place and the deciding next digit
Number line with the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint
Significant-figure highlighter (first non-zero digit onward)
Side-by-side dp-vs-sf comparison of the same number
commonMisconceptions: Counting leading zeros as significant (0.0049 seen as 4 sig figs)
Dropping the placeholder zeros after rounding to sig figs (35,000 written as 35)
Confusing decimal places with significant figures
Truncating instead of rounding, or double-rounding through intermediate digits
Losing the trailing zero that records the rounded precision (2.90 written as 2.9 when 2 dp is required)
constraints: Teach significant-figure identification before rounding to sf: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit, leading zeros never count, and placeholder/trailing zeros hold magnitude and record precision.
Treat rounding as a single nearness/midpoint decision using only the digit immediately after the required place; avoid digit-by-digit chain rounding, which can make the answer drift.
Always restore place value with zeros after rounding large numbers to sf (35,000 not 35; 47,000 not 47) and keep trailing zeros that record precision (2.90, 0.0050).
Contrast dp and sf on the same number so learners see the rules diverge, especially on leading zeros and large magnitudes.
Closed-response/quick-check items check outcomes and do not, on their own, build significant-figure identification; use them to consolidate after construction work, not instead of it.
A single static worked example illustrates one case but cannot cover arbitrary numbers or let a learner test the dp-vs-sf divergence interactively; use it as a reference, not the whole task.

startingActivity.title: Build the jump: make each arrow's length equal the amount
learnerActions: Start at 38 on a number line and add a forward jump of 20, then a forward jump of 7, landing on 58 then 65 (showing 38 + 27 = 65).
Notice and state that the +20 jump is drawn visibly longer than the +7 jump because the LENGTH of the jump is the amount.
Build 52 − 24 yourself using backward (leftward) jumps, e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30, landing on 28.
Label each jump with its size and label the start and end points.
Both interpret a diagram you are given and construct one for a new calculation.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Distance on the line equals the amount: a jump represents 'add/subtract this much', not the point it lands on. Addition moves forward and subtraction moves backward, and partitioning a jump mirrors the mental place-value strategy.

startingActivity.title: Operate a directed number line: fire and flip the arrow
learnerActions: Enter 4 + (-7): start a marker at 4 and draw/trace an arrow 7 units LEFT, landing on -3 — state that the negative sign IS the leftward direction and the 7 is how far.
Enter 1 - (-3): show that the arrow subtraction would send LEFT instead FLIPS to point RIGHT, landing on 4; compare with adding 3 (1 + 3 = 4) and confirm you land in the same place.
Say in words why the arrow reversed: removing a -3 (e.g. clearing a debt of 3) is the same as adding 3.

Replay both journeys vertically on a thermometer/lift mode: for 4 + (-7), count aloud straight down through zero (4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3); for 1 - (-3), count up from 1 (2, 3, 4) and notice that this journey stays above zero.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Signed addition and the direction-reversal of subtracting a negative become visible: 'two minuses make a plus' is a direction reversal you can see, not a spell to recall. Numbers do not stop at zero.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning zero (arrows for direction and length)
Vertical thermometer / floors of a building / sea level

commonMisconceptions: Orders negatives by magnitude - thinks -7 > -3 because 7 > 3
Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation ('two minuses', reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7 arbitrarily)
Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so cannot count or move through zero
Thinks subtracting always makes smaller and adding always makes bigger (fails for negatives)
Treats 'subtract a negative' as more negative rather than as reversing direction
constraints: Anchor every idea on a number line/thermometer/floors/balance where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'.
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas; counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives.
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative moves in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction (right/up on the chosen axis).
Explicitly distinguish the subtraction operation from the negative sign using colour, gesture, or brackets, e.g. 4 + (-7).
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating it as a rule.
A fixed reference poster/line supports reading sign, magnitude and zero-in-context but does not animate a learner-chosen operation; use it to complement, not replace, learner production of arrows.

startingActivity.title: Build and test a number-line inequality
learnerActions: Choose an inequality symbol (<, ≤, >, ≥) and a boundary value, then draw the matching number line: decide whether the boundary circle is open or closed and which way the arrow points.
Test several sample values by asking of each, 'does this value satisfy the inequality?', and mark those that satisfy it (e.g. in one colour) and those that do not (another colour).

Switch the symbol from ≥ to > (or ≤ to <) on the same boundary and observe what changes: the boundary circle hollows, and a value sitting exactly on the boundary flips from satisfying to not satisfying.
Deliberately draw the arrow the wrong way, then test values along it to see that a whole stretch of the line fails the check — confirming direction matters.
Read a given diagram (e.g. a filled circle at −2 with a right-pointing arrow) back into symbols and words.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Inclusion is not an arbitrary drawing convention: whether the circle is filled depends on whether the boundary value itself is a solution. The arrow/segment represents the whole set of satisfying values, and its direction is fixed by what the symbol means.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with open vs closed circle at the boundary plus an arrow for the solution set

commonMisconceptions: Confuses strict (<, >) with inclusive (≤, ≥): uses the wrong circle style (open for ≥, filled for <).
Shades or points the arrow the wrong way (reads the symbol direction backwards).
Treats the solution as a single boundary value (x < 5 means x = 4) rather than a whole set.
Worded-boundary error: renders 'at least 12' as x > 12 (strict) instead of x ≥ 12.
constraints: A static reference card mapping symbols to circle style and arrow direction supports recall but does not rehearse building, translating or reading inequalities independently; pair it with construction tasks.

Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items can check the representation (e.g. 'open or closed circle for x ≥ 3?', 'at least 12 → x __ 12') but recognition-style responses do not elicit independent construction of a diagram or translation; include tasks where the learner draws the number line and states the inequality themselves.
This content lives on a one-dimensional number line, so a three-dimensional representation carries no extra spatial payload for it; a 2D line with circle, arrow and test values is sufficient.
The negative-multiplier direction-reversal rule is a KS4 extension; keep the KS3 focus on the representation and translation.
Keep the solution-as-set idea explicit: an inequality's answer is every value in the range, contrasted with an equation's single value.

startingActivity.title: Pick the tool, work the problem, justify the fit
learnerActions: Solve 34 + 28 using a palette of tools: cubes/base-ten, a number line, a hundred square, a ruler.
If you reach for single cubes, build and count 62 in ones — notice it is slow and easy to miscount. (Base-ten rods group the tens, so they avoid most of this counting.)
On the number line, jump 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 in two jumps.
On the hundred square (numbered with 1 at the top), add the 20 by moving two rows down to 54, then add 8 by moving forward eight squares (crossing into the next row) to reach 62.
After solving, answer: 'Why did that tool help?' and 'When would cubes actually be the better choice?'

Then tackle a measuring task: 'How long is the ribbon?' (a ruler fits, the number line does not) and 'How tall is the door?' (a metre stick fits better than a short ruler). Explain why the tool follows the problem's purpose AND the size of the object.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The right tool follows the PURPOSE of the problem and the size of the numbers or object, not habit: a representation that carries the tens (number line, hundred square) spares you counting ones, while a length problem needs a measuring tool matched to the object's size. Cubes remain a good fit for small numbers — this is a fit judgement, not a ranking of tools as 'babyish' or 'proper'.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: Below-zero numbers are a genuine continuation of the counting sequence, not a separate set; the line extends left/below zero, and counting down keeps going in the same direction past zero. A static thermometer or number-line poster is a useful reference and can support counting, but cannot itself be dragged or stepped; pair it with active ordering/counting on a line rather than relying on it alone.
Conversation/context framing (e.g. a polar scientist) can motivate and give extra ordering practice, but should not be the sole route to the ordering concept.
US note: formal integers are Grade 6 (CCSS-M 6.NS.5-6); for this age treat the work as pre-integer number-line and temperature intuition.
When counting across zero, guard against skipping 0 or bouncing (1, 0, 1); ensure zero is named as a step and the sequence continues below it.

activityReferences.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line

startingActivity.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line
learnerActions: Set a starting value in a real context, e.g. the temperature is −4°C, marked on a vertical thermometer or horizontal number line.
Apply a change, e.g. 'it rises by 7 degrees', and move a marker one step at a time, saying each value aloud: −4 → −3 → −2 → −1 → 0, then 1 → 2 → 3.
Deliberately split the count into two parts: how many steps up to reach zero (4), then how many steps beyond zero (3), and record the landing value (3°C).
Count backwards through zero as well: start at 3 and step down in ones — 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 — saying what comes after 0, so you can move both forwards and backwards across zero.

Switch the SAME line into a different context — sea-level depth or a bank balance — keep the start and change equivalent, and notice the number behaves identically even though it means something different.
State in words where you crossed zero and why the total rise is 7 even though you land on 3.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is found by counting the gap along the line through zero — so many steps up to zero, then so many more beyond — not by a sign rule; you can count both forwards and backwards across zero, and negatives in different contexts behave the same positionally.

keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning negatives and positives
Vertical thermometer / sea-level scale
Number line 'gap counting' for intervals across zero
Real contexts: temperature change, floors/lifts, bank balance
Ordering strip mixing negatives and positives
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−4 > −1).
Counting the interval across zero wrongly (forgetting the zero step or double-counting it).
Treating a negative as just its digit (ignoring sign).
Believing you 'can't go below zero'.
Applying whole-number intuitions (bigger digit = bigger) to negatives.
constraints: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful rather than abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap through zero on the line, not by memorised sign rules; make the zero crossing explicit (e.g. −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more).
Support counting both forwards and backwards through zero, including stepping down below zero into the negatives.
Keep to counting and intervals in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years (US formalises integers in Grade 6; this is the pre-formal contextual foundation).

Ordering and placing tasks (ordering a set, placing on a line, fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice) can assess placement, ordering and simple cross-zero intervals, including the magnitude trap, but selection/recognition responses do not by themselves show the learner can count through zero and construct the reasoning aloud — pair them with the learner explaining their method.

A static thermometer or context poster is a useful reference and can introduce negative readings, but it cannot let the learner step through a changing value; use it as a scaffold alongside an activity where the learner actually counts the gap.
The 1D number line/scale is the natural representation for this topic; a 3D model is not needed here (this is a representation preference for this content, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing).
The role-play/spoken extension is optional and supplementary; do not treat it as a replacement for working on the number line.

startingActivity.title: Measure distance from zero on a draggable number line
learnerActions: Drag a point along a number line and watch a glowing arc from 0 to the point report its length as |x|, which is positive on either side of zero and is 0 only when the point is at zero.
Park the point at −5, then flip on a mirror toggle so the reflection at +5 lays down an identical arc — observe |−5| = |5| = 5.

Read a twin read-out that shows the signed value beside its absolute value; move the point to −9 then to −2 and notice the arc for −9 is LONGER even though −9 sits further LEFT (is the smaller number).
Drag the point across zero and watch the |x| read-out shrink to 0 and climb again — distance tracks how far from zero, never which side.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Absolute value is a distance (a length) from zero: it is never negative, two symmetric points share one absolute value, and 'further from zero' is a different question from 'greater number'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with a distance arc from 0 to the point (length = |x|)
Mirror/fold about zero showing −a and a mapping to the same distance
Context strips (debt size, depth) where magnitude is the salient quantity
Paired statement cards contrasting order (<, >) with absolute value (|·|)
commonMisconceptions: Believing |x| just 'removes the minus sign' as a symbol trick rather than measuring distance (fails for expressions like |x−3|)
Thinking the number with the greater absolute value is automatically the greater number (−9 > −2)
Assuming absolute value can be negative
Conflating 'larger debt/depth' (magnitude) with 'larger number' (order)
Treating |−5| and −5 as interchangeable
constraints: Define |x| strictly as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0); avoid teaching it as 'remove the minus sign', which hides the meaning and fails for expressions like |x−3|.
Always pair order and magnitude explicitly (e.g. −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|) so learners do not assume greater absolute value means greater number.
Distinguish |−5| from −5: they are not interchangeable.
Recognition/matching/true-false items consolidate and check classification but do not elicit independent construction; use them after the number-line meaning is built, not as the primary teaching.
The static annotated line is a scaffold that lacks live movement across zero; if used alone, add tasks where learners trace the distance changing on both sides of zero.
A 3D representation was judged to add little because absolute value is a one-dimensional distance; this is a design judgement for this topic, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.

startingActivity.title: Power/root workbench on arrays
learnerActions: Set a base and exponent: pick base 3, exponent 2, and watch a 3×3 square fill in reading area = 9; raise the exponent (e.g. to 4) and see a factor string assemble, 3×3×3×3 = 81 (that is 3⁴).
Switch to root mode: given an area of 49, resize a square until it fits exactly — side 7 — and record √49 = 7.
Given an area of 20, try to square off a whole-number side; observe that no whole side fits, the exact label √20 stays pinned, and a decimal read-out ticks 4.47…, 4.472… without ever landing.
State in your own words why √20 is the exact value while the decimal is only ever an approximation.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A power is repeated multiplication (not base × exponent); a root is the inverse that recovers the side/edge; and for non-perfect roots the surd is the exact value while the decimal only approximates it, never catching up.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Square array (area) for n² and cube stack (volume) for n³
Inverse-pair diagrams: 7 → (square) 49 → (root) 7
Power-sequence tables (2¹–2¹⁰, 3¹–3⁵) as landmarks
Number line contrasting the exact surd √2 with its decimal approximation region
commonMisconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 and n³ as n×3 (multiplying by the exponent instead of repeated multiplication)
Believing a rounded decimal equals the root (1.414 = √2) rather than approximating it
Assuming every number has a 'nice' exact root, or that √ always yields a whole number
Confusing square and cube (or their roots), especially in volume/area contexts
Mishandling powers in BIDMAS — evaluating left-to-right rather than powers before ×/÷
constraints: Define powers as repeated multiplication with square→area and cube→volume made concrete before abstracting to notation.
Present roots explicitly as the inverse of powers (√ undoes squaring, ∛ undoes cubing), starting on perfect squares and perfect cubes.
Draw the exact-vs-approximate line sharply: √2 is the precise value; 1.414 is a rounded approximation that never equals it.
Apply BIDMAS so a power binds to its base before +, −, ×, ÷ (3 + 2² = 7, not 25).
The reference wall and the recognition/fill-in items are fluency aids and do not elicit the repeated-multiplication or inverse-root actions on their own.
The 3D cube build covers only the cube case; squares, higher powers and the exact/approximate idea need the array and surd activities.

Physical cube and card/array models have slight real thickness and are approximations of the idealised geometric figures; treat on-screen arrays as models of the number relationship, not as the figures themselves.

activityReferences.title: Decimal-signature classifier: repetition, not length, decides
Squeeze another number in: density of the line
Dialogue: why √2 cannot be a fraction
