startingActivity.title: Decimal-signature classifier: repetition, not length, decides
learnerActions: For each, write out or stream the decimal expansion and decide whether it TERMINATES or REPEATS. For √2 and π, note that a finite list of digits can never show that a decimal does NEITHER: some rationals have very long repeating blocks (1/97 repeats only after 96 digits). We know √2 and π are irrational because it has been proved, so their decimals never terminate or repeat.
Mark the repeating block when there is one (e.g. box the 3 in 0.3̅, or the 142857 in 1/7) and write the equivalent fraction.
State a rule in your own words for deciding rational vs irrational, then test it against √9 = 3 and 0.333…
Keep √2 and π written exactly as symbols, noting that 1.414… and 3.14… are only approximations.
Locate √2 and π approximately on a number line (e.g. √2 just past 1.4, between 1 and 2; π between 3 and 4) using their decimal approximations, while keeping the exact symbol pinned alongside.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A number is rational exactly when it can be written as a ratio of two integers — which shows up as a terminating OR repeating decimal. The deciding feature is whether the digits settle into a repeat, not how many digits there are: 0.333… is endless yet rational (=1/3). √2 is proved to be irrational, so its expansion never repeats. Checking a finite number of digits could never establish that on its own.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Zoomable number line demonstrating density (always another number between two)
Decimal-expansion classifier: terminating / repeating (rational) vs non-terminating-non-repeating (irrational)
Set nesting diagram: integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals filling the gaps
Fraction ↔ decimal conversions showing why some terminate and some repeat
commonMisconceptions: Believing any number with infinitely many decimals is irrational (0.333… is rational)
Thinking √2 or π 'equal' their rounded decimals (1.414, 3.14)
Assuming there is a 'next' number after a given one, or a smallest gap on the line
Confusing 'irrational' with 'very large' or 'undefined' rather than non-repeating-non-terminating
Thinking there are finitely many numbers between two close decimals like 0.12 and 0.13
constraints: Keep irrationals in exact symbolic form (√2, π); treat 1.414… and 3.14… as approximations, never as equal to the exact value.
The decision test is repetition/terminability (equivalently, expressibility as a ratio of integers), NOT how long or 'messy' the decimal looks — 0.333… is rational.
The root symbol does not determine irrationality: √9 = 3 is rational while √2 is irrational; evaluate the value.
A static nested-sets diagram is a reference scaffold: it anchors vocabulary and structure but does not demonstrate density or dynamically classify expansions, so it should accompany active tasks.
Selected-response/sorting tasks are consolidators that follow concept-building; pair them with required justifications so they elicit reasoning rather than recognition alone.

Tier the challenge: age-13 checkpoint 'Is 0.75 rational? Give its fraction'; mid 'Explain why √2 is irrational, not just that it has lots of decimals'; stretch 'Name a number between 0.12 and 0.13, then argue there are infinitely many.'

startingActivity.title: Story-modelling with counters and a mat
learnerActions: Listen to or look at a short situation, e.g. 'There are 6 apples on the tree; the wind blows 2 down.'
Take 6 apple counters and place them on a mat to match the start of the story.
Act out what happens — move the 2 fallen apples to the ground, or cross them out on a drawing.
Count what is left on the tree and say the answer aloud (4).
Retell the story in your own words and point to each quantity (the 6, the 2, what's left) in your model.
Repeat with a joining story, e.g. 'Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now?', adding counters to match and reading off the total (7).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: You don't need a rule to decide 'add' or 'subtract' — you build what actually happened in the story with objects, and the answer is simply what you can then see and count.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes acted on to match the story
Children's drawings/jottings (dots, crossing-out) of the situation
Part-part-whole model mapping story quantities to parts and whole
Simple bar/tape model for compare problems ('how many more')
Five-frame/ten-frame to organise the objects being combined or removed
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching ('altogether'→add, 'left'→subtract) instead of modelling the situation, which fails on compare and change/start-unknown problems.
Modelling only result-unknown structures and being stuck when the unknown is the change or the start.
Grabbing the two numbers in the problem and combining them regardless of what the story describes.
Miscounting the objects when acting out, or not matching the drawing to the actual quantities in the story.
For compare problems, adding the two amounts instead of finding the difference.
constraints: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: 'altogether'/'left'/'more' must not become fixed triggers for + or −, because they fail on compare, change-unknown and start-unknown problems.
Keep totals within 10 so counting is manageable; start with result-unknown and introduce missing-number and compare forms only once simple modelling is secure.
Systematically vary problem structure (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare) and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown), not just the numbers.

A fixed single-story illustration (tap to count, reveal the answer) can anchor one problem's modelling but cannot let the child model varied structures or make their own drawing; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole skill.

Picture-based multiple-choice items can check whether a child recognises/applies the right operation, but a scored recognition format does not itself elicit the child building a model and can be answered by keyword-matching; if used, pair each item with a picture and avoid phrasing answerable by keyword alone.
Use consistent representations (counters/cubes, part-part-whole, bar/tape, five-/ten-frame) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.

Interactive affordances are optional illustrations, not requirements: e.g. dragging objects onto a mat, crossing out, a part-whole/bar frame to organise quantities, narrated scenes, auto-varying the problem type. These make the mechanism concrete but need not all be present.

startingActivity.title: Combining mat: push two groups into one whole
learnerActions: Drop three counters into one framed region (a basket or ten-frame) and two counters into a second framed region beside it.
Count each part aloud: 'three red here, two blue here.'
Physically sweep both piles together into a single large 'altogether' region.
Count the whole merged set and say how many there are altogether.
Say the matching sentence aloud: 'three and two more — that's five altogether.' (Leave the written 3 + 2 = 5 for the later, separate symbol topic.)
Switch modes: in ADD-TO, add objects to one existing group one at a time ('3... then 2 more arrive'); in PUT-TOGETHER, start with two ready-made parts and merge them at once.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Two separate groups the child made become ONE group with a single count — addition felt as a physical join, not a recited fact. 'Altogether' names the whole combined set, however it was built.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two groups of physical objects (counters, cubes, toys) that are literally pushed together
Ten-frame(s) filling up as objects are added
Part-part-whole (part-whole 'cherry') model showing two parts joining into a whole
Fingers and five-frames for small totals

commonMisconceptions: Recounting the whole from 1 every time and never trusting the total — a cardinality gap surfacing inside addition.
Thinking addition always means 'a group gets bigger by things arriving' (add-to only), so static put-together and part-part-whole situations aren't recognised as addition.
Believing the total is 'the last number you say' regardless of combining, i.e. reciting rather than combining quantities.
Losing track when combining by miscounting the join (double-counting an object or skipping one).
Assuming the bigger group must be said/written first, an early seed of not seeing addition as flexible (commutativity comes later).
constraints: Keep numbers within 5-10 and keep the joining action visible before introducing the + symbol; the written symbol is a later, separate topic.
Build on secure cardinality (last-number-said = how many). If the child cannot trust the count of the whole, that prerequisite needs attention before counting-on is expected.
Counting-all from one is an expected early developmental stage — encourage but do not force 'counting on', and do not mark counting-all as wrong.
Picture-only scenes and lift-the-flap totals are scaffolds for the 'altogether' label; they do not let the child perform the combining and should not be the only experience.

A scored multiple-choice/linear check may test recognition of a combined total but does not itself elicit the child's physical combining or spoken explanation, and such assessment is developmentally weak at ages 4-6; keep any such check to picture-based items with very small numbers and never as the main activity.

On-screen 3D manipulation (rotating or positioning virtual 3D objects) adds handling cost for pre-readers without a clear conceptual gain here (combining small groups has little spatial payoff), so flat on-screen objects/scenes and real physical counters are preferred for this topic; this is a scoped judgement, not a claim that 3D never helps.
Teach both add-to and put-together explicitly so children recognise static part-part-whole situations as addition too.

startingActivity.title: Linked windows onto one calculation
learnerActions: Place counters onto a mat to show a given sum such as 3 + 2.
Watch linked representations update together: a ten-frame fills, a dot-drawing sketches itself, and the number sentence 3 + 2 = 5 assembles alongside the counters.
Tap the '2' in the number sentence and see exactly two counters, two dots, and two ten-frame cells light up at once across every pane.
Try a 'cover a window' challenge: predict what the drawing will look like before it is revealed, then check.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The objects, drawing, ten-frame and number sentence are not separate exercises — they are the same quantity shown different ways; and I can begin to carry the picture in my head.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes and fingers (concrete)
Ten-frames and five-frames as structured object layouts
Part-part-whole ('cherry') diagram
Children's own drawings/jottings (dots, marks, crossing-out for removal)
Mental images and the spoken number sentence as the bridge to symbols
commonMisconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate, unrelated task and not seeing that the objects, drawing and number sentence all show the SAME calculation.
Drawing elaborate pictures that obscure quantity (detailed apples instead of countable dots), losing the mathematical point.
Staying dependent on concrete objects and not progressing toward drawings/mental images, so efficiency never develops.
Mis-mapping between representations — e.g. drawing the total when the story described only one part.
Using a drawing as decoration after getting an answer another way, rather than as a tool to find or explain the answer.
constraints: The core skill is MAPPING between representations, not mastering any single one — always link them explicitly ('point to the 3 in the cubes, now in your drawing').

Matching or recognition-style tasks assess recognition of correspondence but do not elicit the independent construction of a child's own representations; keep them as a supporting check, not the main activity.

Dialogue prompts ('show me another way') work best alongside a drawing or object tool, since much of the re-representation work here is manual/visual; talk can still prompt and explain re-representation.
Tap-to-highlight, live-updating linked panes, and the hide-a-pane challenge are optional illustrative mechanisms to make the correspondence concrete — not mandatory features.
Value children's own jottings while nudging toward quick countable marks (dots) over elaborate pictures, so quantity stays in focus.
Aim to progress concrete → pictorial → mental image → symbolic so representations become efficient mental tools rather than permanent crutches; do not leave children dependent on objects.

Paper/cubes and an on-screen canvas offer different experiences; neither is required, and a fixed worked example can still anchor the parallel-representations idea even though it cannot be manipulated.

activityReferences.title: Take-away mat: remove and read what's left
Difference mode: 'how many more?' as subtraction

startingActivity.title: Take-away mat: remove and read what's left
learnerActions: Start with 5 biscuits on a plate; physically remove (drag/take) 2 into a bin.
Watch or track the remaining count fall as you remove: 5 → 4 → 3.
Say and, if ready, assemble the statement '5 − 2 = 3'.
Point to which biscuits are the answer — the ones still on the plate, not the ones taken.
Narrate the action then the result: '5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The starting group splits into 'gone' and 'left', and the answer to a take-away is what remains — subtraction felt as a physical removal, with 'how many left' attached to the remaining quantity.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A group of physical objects with some physically removed/covered (take-away)
Ten-frame with counters removed, remainder visible
Part-part-whole model: whole splits into part-taken and part-left
Two rows of objects lined up for 'how many more' comparison (difference)
Act-out story scenes and drawings with a crossing-out to show removal
commonMisconceptions: Equating subtraction ONLY with 'take away', so comparison ('how many more') and missing-part problems aren't recognised as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.
Trying to 'take away' the larger from the smaller in a comparison and getting confused, or reversing to keep it 'takeable'.
Recounting the whole rather than the remainder, or counting the removed objects instead of what's left.
Believing subtraction always makes a number 'small' and being surprised that 8 − 1 is still large.
Reading 7 − 3 left-to-right as an instruction with no sense that it asks 'how many remain', so missing-number forms feel impossible.
constraints: Keep quantities within 5-10 and use objects the child can physically remove.

Do not stop at 'take away': deliberately introduce comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings. The evidence base identifies that if only 'take away' is taught, children tend to stop recognising comparison and missing-part problems as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.

A still take-from picture (crossed-out/bite scene with tap-to-reveal) anchors the take-away meaning but does not let the child perform the removal or explore comparison/missing-part meanings; treat it as a scaffold, not the sole teacher.

Talk-only prompts lean on still-forming language at this age; pair any 'how many are left?' conversation with real objects rather than using it alone. This does not mean talk cannot support reasoning.
Do not insist on counting-back or mark slow recounting of the remainder as wrong; counting-back matures later. Removing objects and recounting the remainder is acceptable.

Scored, linear picture quizzes are developmentally weak for ages 4-6; a small picture item may check recognition of 'how many left' but does not itself elicit the child's own physical removal, so keep any such item minor and not the primary route for building the concept.

Watch for 'subtraction always makes a number small': show that taking away leaves fewer than the start but not necessarily a small amount (e.g. 8 − 1 = 7, still a lot), so the child isn't surprised by it.

startingActivity.title: Drive a ten-frame and number-line calculator
learnerActions: Build the first number on a double ten-frame (two ten-frames, since one frame holds only 10) (e.g. place eight counters on the first frame for 8+7).

Add or subtract the second number by moving counters, and for bridging cases split the second number to fill the frame to ten first (slide two counters over to complete ten, leaving five, to reach 15).
Show the same calculation as a jump on a 0-20 number line.
Write the matching number sentence alongside the action (e.g. 8 + 7 = 15).
Repeat with a non-bridging case (14 + 5) and a take-away (17 − 3).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Within-20 sums and differences can be found by using bonds and making ten, not by counting all in ones; bridging reorganises the quantity around ten.

keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / rekenrek for within-20 sums and bridging
Empty number line for jumps (including a 0 jump that stays put)

commonMisconceptions: Assuming +0 or −0 must change the number (giving 5+0=6 or 5−0=4).
Counting all/counting on in ones across the ten boundary instead of making ten.
Errors at the teen boundary (miscounting when crossing 10).
Ignoring the operation and just combining the two numbers seen.
Reversing subtraction to keep the larger number first without noticing the meaning changes.
constraints: Keep calculations within the 0-20 range, including the teen boundary (crossing ten).
Use bonds and making-ten rather than counting all; the procedural work should reinforce the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete attention — it is where zero's identity role is established and a common misconception lives.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect them to the child's own representations to keep meaning attached.
A fixed worked example can anchor the ideas but cannot supply the varied, re-drivable practice the procedure needs; use it as an anchor, not the main vehicle.

A practice set drills and assesses the procedure but does not by itself build the making-ten strategy; discussion surfaces reasoning but is not calculation practice. The hands-on calculation is the proposed primary vehicle for building the strategy here, with efficacy stated as proposed rather than proven.

Tiered expectations: at age 5, non-bridging cases via a fast strategy; age 5-6, bridging cases and correct +0/−0; age 6, fluent within-20 calculation with an explanation of why ±0 leaves the number unchanged.

Distinguish subtraction meaning when ordering: 17 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 17; do not reorder subtraction to keep the larger number first without noting the meaning changes (and 3 − 17 lies outside the Y1 within-20 range).

startingActivity.title: Story-to-bar-model builder
learnerActions: Listen to or read a one-step problem with numbers to 20, e.g. 'I had some sweets, ate 9, and 7 are left.'
Drag the quantities you know into a bar or part-whole frame — for this story, split a whole into a '9 eaten' part and a '7 left' part.
Mark where the unknown sits in the model (here the WHOLE — the number you started with — is the mystery).
Act on the model to find the unknown — combine the two parts to fill the whole (7 + 9 = 16), or count on along a number line.
Repeat with problems that rotate the unknown through result, change and start positions, and with pure missing-number equations like 7 = ? − 9.
Write the equation that matches your model, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after the = sign).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A problem where the unknown is the START or the CHANGE, not the answer, is not impossible: the bar model shows exactly where the mystery sits. If the unknown is the whole, combining the known parts finds it. If the unknown is a part, taking the known part away from the whole (or counting on from it) finds it. Children learn to model any structure rather than hope a keyword tells them what to do.

startingActivity.title: Sentence builder linked to a balance
learnerActions: Push two groups of counters together on a work surface and record what happened with a sentence strip, placing a '+' between the groups; take some counters away and use a '−' instead.

Build the sentence 3 + 2 = 5 and check the two sides balance (a two-pan balance loaded with identical counters or cubes, so that weight goes up with count, or a balance image/animation that only levels when both sides have the same value).
Now build 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 and notice the sides STILL balance — discuss why this is allowed even though no single 'answer' sits after the =.
Try true/false sentences (e.g. 5 = 3 + 2 (true), 4 + 1 = 3 + 2 (true, both equal 5), 3 + 2 = 2 + 1 (false)) and predict whether the balance will level or tip before testing.
Keep the referent objects (counters / ten-frame / part-whole model) visible beside the sentence throughout.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The symbols record actions the child already does (+ = combining, − = taking away) and = means 'the same value on both sides', not 'write the answer here' — so numbers may legitimately appear on either side.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The three symbol cards +, −, = alongside the concrete action each records
Number sentences built from digit + symbol cards under a concrete model
Ten-frame / part-whole model paired with its matching equation
A simple two-pan balance image for = as 'same value on both sides'
True/false sentence cards for interrogating the = meaning
commonMisconceptions: Reading = as 'the answer comes next' (an operator/'makes') rather than 'is the same as', so 5 = 3 + 2 or 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 look wrong.
Confusing + and − by shape/name, especially when reading quickly, or ignoring the symbol and just combining whatever numbers appear.
Writing sentences with the operation and answer in the wrong order, or omitting the = sign.
Treating the number sentence as a left-to-right instruction to 'do something' with no sense that it states a relationship.
Believing something must always be written after the = (rejecting 7 = 3 + 4 or missing-number forms).
constraints: Present = relationally from the first lessons and in varied positions (5 = 3 + 2, 3 + 2 = 2 + 3, 4 + 1 = 3 + 2); never only 'sum then answer', which teaches = as 'write the answer here'.
Keep referent quantities (objects/ten-frame/part-whole model) visible beside sentences so symbols stay tied to meaning.
The reference wall is a scaffold: it anchors meaning but cannot let the child build or test sentences, so pair it with generative tasks.
Selected-response and true/false items assess and reinforce recognition but do not elicit independent construction of a sentence; use them after building/writing, not instead of it.
Mirror-writing or reversed digits/symbols at ages 5-6 are a normal early-writing developmental stage, not a maths misconception; model correct orientation rather than drilling it as an error.
Read sentences aloud in full mathematical language ('plus', 'minus/subtract', 'equals / is the same as') so notation and vocabulary co-develop.
The deeper true/false relational understanding of = is a later dependent objective; at this stage aim for accepting non-canonical forms and simple true/false judgements, not full equation reasoning.
Ensure any sentence used to 'balance' has genuinely equal sides (e.g. 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 both equal 5) and any 'false' example has unequal sides (e.g. 4 + 1 = 2 + 2).

startingActivity.title: Ten-frame 'make ten' practice
learnerActions: Look at a ten-frame holding some counters (e.g. 7 counters, so 3 cells are empty).

Add (drag, tap, or place physical counters) the missing counters to fill the frame to 10, then check.

commonMisconceptions: Counting on from the given number every time rather than recalling the bond, so speed never develops.
Knowing 7 + 3 = 10 but not the related 10 − 7 = 3 (bond not held as a fact family).
Confusing bonds to 10 with bonds to other totals when the ten-frame isn't present.

constraints: Aim for recall grounded in the ten-frame image, not isolated rote drill divorced from meaning.
Recognition and matching formats check familiarity but do not require independent construction; include items where the child must say or write the complement unprompted.
A fixed reference display of the full set is useful for looking up a partner but does not provide the repeated retrieval needed for recall; pair it with active practice.
Oral quick-fire alone cannot efficiently deliver the many fast repetitions automaticity requires; use it as a check and warm-up alongside visual/written practice.
Physical counters, bead strings and the rekenrek are concrete supports; the goal is to fade the structure so the child answers from the remembered image or known fact.

startingActivity.title: Part-whole bench: slide the divider, keep the whole
learnerActions: Place a fixed whole of counters (e.g. 5) into a single frame, then move a divider across so the counters fall into two parts.
Slide the divider to a new spot and read the two parts aloud (e.g. 1 and 4; then 2 and 3).
Record each split as an equation (5 = 1 + 4, 5 = 2 + 3, …) next to a drawing of the two groups.
Keep a running list of pairs found and check whether every pair has been discovered.
In a 'make 10' mode, fix the whole at 10 and find pairs that make ten.
Flip a found pair to subtraction: having built 5 = 2 + 3, state that 5 − 2 = 3.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A number is not one fixed pair but a whole family of pairs; the parts trade while the total is conserved, and each known pair also tells a missing-part subtraction fact.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Part-part-whole ('cherry'/bar) model with a fixed whole and two changeable parts
Ten-frame showing a number split by colour into two parts
Bead string or two-colour counters partitioned into two groups
A systematic list/table of all pairs for a number (0+5, 1+4, …) with equations
Rekenrek (arithmetic rack) for showing splits of 5 and 10
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a number has only ONE decomposition (e.g. 5 is 'just' 4 and 1) and not seeing it as a family of pairs.
Losing the whole — changing a part but not compensating the other, so the total drifts (5 becomes 2+4).
Missing pairs or double-counting when not working systematically, so 'all the ways' is never securely established.
Treating 2+3 and 3+2 as entirely unrelated rather than the same pair reordered.
Not connecting decomposition to subtraction — failing to see that if 5 = 2 + 3 then 5 − 2 = 3.
constraints: Primary goal is flexible, systematic generation of multiple pairs with a conserved whole; a child producing only one split or changing the total has not yet met the objective.

Recognition and fill-in tasks (multi-select, slider, matching) consolidate and diagnose bond facts but do not by themselves elicit independent generation of decompositions; use them after construction, not as a substitute for it.

A static anchor diagram presents pairs ready-made; it is a display/anchor and is proposed to follow hands-on or interactive generation so the child feels the whole conserved rather than only reading pairs off.

Guided talk prompts can support searching but do not themselves provide the physical trading or visual comparison, since the generating and comparing is still largely manual and visual at this age; pair them with a manipulative rather than relying on talk alone.

Checkpoints: Tier A (age 4) find at least two different pairs for a given number with objects; Tier B (age 5) find several pairs up to 10 and record as equations; Tier C (age 5-6) work systematically to find ALL pairs and explain the whole stays the same while parts change.

Address known misconceptions: a number having only one decomposition; losing the whole when re-splitting; missing/double-counting pairs when unsystematic; treating 2+3 and 3+2 as unrelated; and failing to connect 5 = 2 + 3 to 5 − 2 = 3.
Treat reversals (1+4 vs 4+1) as the same pair reordered; introduce commutativity only gently, not as a formal rule.
The distractor pair in recognition tasks should over- or under-shoot the target whole (e.g. off by one); never present it as a correct way to make the target.

startingActivity.title: Quick-flash fact practice from a dot pattern
learnerActions: A five-frame, dice or domino pattern (e.g. four dots) appears briefly, then the child says or taps the answer to a fact tied to it (e.g. 4 + 1, or 5 − 1 from the same image).
Keep answering a short daily set of items in a few minutes, mixing addition and subtraction.
When a fact is answered quickly and correctly, show the image more briefly next time; when the child hesitates or errs, re-show the pattern longer and talk through what they see.
Include zero cases such as 4 + 0 and 3 − 3 in the mix.

commonMisconceptions: Counting from 1 on fingers for every fact, never moving to recall — fluency stalls.
Equating fluency with speed and rushing, producing errors, or freezing under time pressure.
Knowing additions but not the related subtractions within 5.
Uncertainty with 0 (thinking 3 + 0 must change the number).
Over-reliance on one strategy (always counting on) rather than recognising known facts.
constraints: Fluency means accuracy + efficiency + flexibility (choosing a good strategy), not speed alone; avoid making timed drill the primary mechanism, as time pressure can induce maths anxiety without improving learning.
Do not ban or penalise finger-counting from one — it is a normal developmental stage that, for many children, gives way to recall with regular short subitising and retrieval practice.
Build recall FROM subitising and part-whole understanding, not rote drill, so facts are meaningful; keep the quantity image attached until recall is secure.
Always interleave subtraction with addition and include the +0/-0 case so the small-fact set is complete and connected.

A static dot/five-frame reference aids recognition but cannot by itself drive repeated retrieval; oral quick-fire struggles to deliver enough varied fast reps, so each works best alongside frequent short practice.
A recognition-only check (multiple-choice) confirms what is recalled but does not by itself build automaticity; use it periodically, not as the daily engine.

startingActivity.title: Fact-family machine: one relationship, four facts
learnerActions: Set a whole of 13 with two parts, 8 and 5, in a part-whole triangle (whole at the top, parts in the lower corners).
Read the four facts that the relationship generates: 8+5=13, 5+8=13, 13−8=5, 13−5=8. Say each one aloud.

Change a part (e.g. make the parts 7 and 6 with whole 13) and watch all four equations rewrite, so you see the same structure holds for every bond (for a double such as 6+6=12, the four forms reduce to two different facts: 6+6=12 and 12−6=6).

Use a 'cover a corner' mode: hide one number and say the missing one. Then set a new, clearly labelled whole (e.g. whole 16 with parts 7 and 9) and practise missing-number forms such as 7 = 16 − ? and 16 − ? = 9.
Practise shaky family members again in short interleaved rounds until the four facts come quickly from recall or near-instant derivation.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: One relationship among three numbers IS four facts: learning 8+5 gives you 13−5 and 13−8 for free, so subtraction is derived from addition rather than memorised as a separate list.

Recognition-only or fixed-item practice can check facts and support relational understanding but does not by itself build the many spaced repetitions recall requires; interleave and space the practice.

startingActivity.title: Make ten by moving counters on a double ten-frame
learnerActions: Set out 8 counters in the first ten-frame (two cells empty) and 6 in the second to add 8 + 6.
Move 2 counters from the 6 across to fill the first frame to 10, and notice the 6 has broken into 2 and 4.
Read the result as 10 + 4 = 14, and say aloud which part you moved and why.
Record the same move on an empty number line as a jump of +2 to reach 10, then +4 to reach 14.
Repeat with other bridging facts (e.g. 7+5, 9+6), each time completing the first ten first.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Making ten is a MOVE: reorganising an awkward fact around the friendly ten (8+6 becomes 10+4) shows WHY the strategy works, not just that it gives 14.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two ten-frames showing one filled to 10 and the extra spilling into the second
Rekenrek for shifting beads to make ten
Empty number line with a jump to 10 then beyond
Part-whole model decomposing the second addend (6 = 2 + 4)
Bead string of 20 partitioned at the ten
commonMisconceptions: Counting on/back in ones across ten instead of using ten as a landmark (slow and error-prone at the boundary).
Splitting the wrong addend or splitting it wrongly when making ten (e.g. taking 4 not 2 from the 6 to fill an 8).
For subtraction, decomposing incorrectly across ten (13−4 done as 13−4 in ones with a boundary error).
Not connecting making-ten to known bonds to 10, so the strategy feels arbitrary.
Applying making-ten rigidly even when a known fact or near-double would be quicker.
constraints: Assess the METHOD, not just the answer: a correct 14 reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate making-ten. Watch how the child reaches the answer.
Reaching ten first requires splitting the correct number: for 8 + 6 only 2 (not 4) crosses to the 8, matching the first frame's two empty cells.
In subtraction bridging, both parts of the decomposed amount must be SUBTRACTED (13 − 3 then − 1 = 9); subtracting to ten and then adding the remainder gives the wrong answer 11.
Fill-in-the-step and recognition tasks check recorded steps but do not elicit the hands-on reorganisation; use them after children have performed the move with counters.
A static worked example of a bridging split anchors the strategy but does not let a child perform the move on varied facts; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Counters, paper ten-frames, bead strings and number lines are all suitable concrete media; an on-screen draggable version is one option, not a requirement.

startingActivity.title: Adaptive fluency practice with fading ten-frame support
learnerActions: Answer within-10 facts presented one after another (e.g. 6 + 4, 7 + 2, 9 − 4, 10 − 6), aiming to say the answer without counting.
Start with a faint ten-frame (or rekenrek image) behind each fact; as the child answers quickly, let the visual fade so they move from 'seeing' to recalling.
When a child stalls on a harder fact like 4 + 5, surface a strategy hint that shows the near-double (4 + 4 and one more) so they reconstruct rather than freeze.
Use a fact-family mode that surfaces the related subtraction for each bond (6 + 4 = 10 alongside 10 − 4 = 6, 10 − 6 = 4).
Interleave fact types (doubles, bonds, near-doubles, +/−1) so the child discriminates between similar facts (7 + 2 vs 7 + 3) rather than pattern-guesses.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A hard fact becomes easy when the child sees the double or bond inside it; isolated answers become a connected, flexible web of facts, including the subtraction partners — real fluency, not brittle speed.

commonMisconceptions: Persisting with count-all/count-on for every fact instead of using derived facts or recall.
Mastering additions but not the related subtractions within 10.
Treating fluency as pure speed, leading to errors under pressure or anxiety.
Not recognising doubles/near-doubles as a shortcut (computing 6+7 from scratch).
Confusing similar facts (7+2 vs 7+3) when practice isn't interleaved.
constraints: Fluency means efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone; avoid long timed tests that cause errors or anxiety and use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval instead.
Do not penalise counting under time pressure; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and derived-fact reasoning so automaticity develops naturally.
Include all subtraction facts within 10 and link them to their addition partners (fact families); mastering additions alone is incomplete.
Interleave fact types so children discriminate between similar facts rather than pattern-guess.
A static strategy anchor and an oral quick-fire are recognition/warm-up scaffolds; they do not by themselves deliver the repeated varied retrieval needed for automaticity.
Visual supports (ten-frame, rekenrek) should be faded as recall strengthens, not relied on permanently.

startingActivity.title: Personal fact grid: track recall vs counting, little and often
learnerActions: Keep a grid of single-digit sums where each cell is a fact the child is practising (e.g. the row/column for crossing-ten sums like 8+7, 6+9).
Mark a fact as secure once it is recalled instantly (roughly within 3 seconds, no counting), and as 'still counting' when the child has to count on or pause.
Return frequently and briefly to the 'still counting' facts, mixed in with secure ones, rather than drilling one fact many times in a row.

When a fact slips, rebuild it aloud with a strategy — near-double (6+9 → 'double 6 is 12, plus 3 more is 15') or make-ten (8+7 → '8+2 is 10, then 5 more is 15') — then try it again cold a little later.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Automaticity is the fluent endpoint of understanding: instant recall for most facts, with a strategy to reconstruct any that momentarily slip, so recall stays connected to reasoning rather than brittle.

keyRepresentations: Addition fact grid (sums of two one-digit numbers) for tracking coverage
Fact-family triangles linking each sum to its two subtractions
Doubles/near-doubles and make-ten visuals as fallback strategies

Derived-fact chains (8+5=13 → 18+5, 80+50) showing the payoff
commonMisconceptions: Still counting on/back for facts that should be recalled, indicating incomplete automaticity.
Knowing sums but not the related subtractions (fact family incomplete).
Speed-without-accuracy under timed pressure, or anxiety suppressing recall.
Treating memorised facts as disconnected from strategies, so a forgotten fact can't be reconstructed.
Failing to use known facts to derive related facts to 100 (recomputing 18+5 from scratch).
constraints: Automaticity should be the fluent endpoint of strategy understanding, not rote memorisation that bypasses reasoning; keep a reconstructable strategy (make-ten, near-doubles) available for slips.
Keep practice low-stakes; avoid high-pressure timed testing as the main vehicle, which can suppress recall through anxiety.
Include all subtraction facts as members of fact families, not just additions.
A static fact grid or strategy card is a reference scaffold and does not by itself drive the retrieval practice needed for recall.

A speeded quiz is close to the target behaviour but is less adaptive and diagnostic than interleaved practice that targets each child's shaky facts; use it to monitor which specific facts are non-automatic and target those.

Optional interface features (live green/amber heatmap, one-tap strategy hints, subtraction rounds, derive-to-100 bonus) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same practice works on paper or orally.

Focus practice on the facts that are still shaky (often crossing-ten sums); secure within-10 facts do not need repeated drilling, though they can be mixed in occasionally to keep practice interleaved and maintain them.
Treat the ~3-second recall benchmark as a guide to automaticity, not a pressure threshold to be enforced under anxiety.

startingActivity.title: Drag a pair to make ten on the ten-frame
learnerActions: Start with three movable number tiles above a ten-frame, e.g. 5, 7 and 3.
Scan the three tiles and decide which two you would add first: a pair that makes exactly ten, or, if there is no such pair, a double.
Drag two tiles together; if they make ten the frame fills completely and leaves a simpler 'ten and a bit' (here 5 + 10).
Deliberately try a less useful pairing first (e.g. 5 + 7 = 12) and notice the frame does not land on a clean ten, then find the better pair — it still gives a correct total, just by a slower route.
Repeat with triples that reward a make-ten pair, and with at least one triple that rewards a double instead.
Add the remaining third tile on last and read the running total.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Spotting the pair that makes ten (or a double) first turns an awkward three-number sum into an easier one: a make-ten pair leaves 'ten and a bit', and a double gives a known fact to add on to. The written order is not fixed, you are free to reorder, and any ordering still gives the same total.

startingActivity.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back
learnerActions: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.

startingActivity.title: Same bond, bigger units: scaling 6+4 to 60+40
learnerActions: Complete 6+4 on a ten-frame by sliding four counters in to fill all ten; confirm this is a known, secure bond making 10.
Switch the counters to tens: let each counter become a ten-rod (or restate each counter as 'one ten') so the same full frame now reads 100.
Say aloud what changed: 'six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100' — the gesture and picture are identical, only the unit changed.
Repeat the tens-scaling with another known bond: 5+5=10 → 50+50=100 (five tens plus five tens is ten tens).
Separately, derive 35+5 by using the ones bond 5+5=10: 30 + (5+5) = 40, so here the 5 is added as five ones, not scaled to tens.
Deliberately contrast 35+5=40 with 35+50=85: in 35+50 you are adding five tens, not five ones, so the answers differ.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Deriving a decade fact like 60+40 is scaling a known bond, not memorising a new fact: six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100. A different move is using a bond inside a larger number — 35+5 uses the ones bond 5+5=10 to give 40. Which unit you add (ones vs tens) decides the result, so 35+5=40 and 35+50=85 are different.

A tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a reference scaffold for the inverse relationship; it does not exercise retrieval speed or the scaling derivation, so pair it with practice and the two-scale model.
A fill-in or choice retrieval format can check the derive insight and give recall practice, but a single check does not build automaticity; genuine fluency needs repeated spaced practice over time.

startingActivity.title: Grouping bench: choose which pair to combine first
learnerActions: Set out three equal-status objects or number tiles for a triple such as 2, 8, 5 (counters, cubes, or draggable tiles).
Choose any two to combine first; merge them into a single running sum, then bring in the third.
Try the same triple a second way (e.g. combine 8+5 first) and compare the final total.
State out loud which pair you combined first and why that choice made the calculation easier.
Repeat with a triple that rewards a make-ten pair (e.g. 2+8+5, where 2+8=10 then 10+5=15) and one that rewards adding a double first (e.g. 4+4+7, where 4+4=8 then 8+7=15).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: You may choose which pair to combine first; a smart choice (make a ten, or add a double) makes the sum easier while the total stays identical because the three amounts themselves never change.

keyRepresentations: Three counter groups / cube towers that can be pushed into different pairs before merging
Bracket notation over three addends, (a+b)+c vs a+(b+c), with the first-combined pair highlighted
Ten-frame showing a make-ten pair filling first, then the remainder added
Bar/part-whole model with three parts and one conserved whole bar

commonMisconceptions: Believing the total changes if you add in a different grouping (failing to conserve the whole).
Conflating associativity with commutativity — thinking they are the same 'any order' rule.
Over-generalising to subtraction, e.g. assuming (10−3)−2 = 10−(3−2).
Losing track of an addend when regrouping (dropping or double-counting the third number).
Thinking brackets are just decoration rather than an instruction about what to combine first.
constraints: Teach as a licence to regroup for convenience (look for a ten, add a double first), not as an abstract named law; children need not use the formal term 'associative'.

Distinguish associativity (which pair we combine FIRST) from commutativity (which order numbers come in); learners frequently conflate them, so address them explicitly. Note that combining two numbers that are not next to each other first (e.g. 4 and 6 in 4+7+6, or 2 and 5 in 2+8+5) uses both properties together.
Do NOT extend the grouping rule to subtraction: (10−3)−2 = 5 does not equal 10−(3−2) = 9. Use this contrast to probe, not as a rule to apply.
Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities stay the same; only which pair is combined first differs. Guard against dropping or double-counting an addend during regrouping.

Closed matching/true-false items and the fixed side-by-side anchor are consolidation and reference scaffolds; they do not let a learner freely explore alternative groupings and should follow, not replace, hands-on choice. This is an observable limit of those formats, not a claim that only manipulation can teach the concept.

The optional interactive touches (a total bar pinned at a fixed value while intermediate sums recompute, a make-ten pair glowing, tiles fusing on drag) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Do and undo it on a number line (with a fact-family triangle)
learnerActions: Start at 15 on a number line and make a forward jump of +7, landing on 22.
Before reversing, predict out loud where a backward jump of 7 will land and why.
Make the backward jump of −7 and confirm you return exactly to 15.
Say in your own words why the subtraction lands back on the start: it is the same jump run in reverse.
Fill in a fact-family triangle with the whole (22) and the two parts (15 and 7), then write all four facts: 15 + 7 = 22, 7 + 15 = 22, 22 − 7 = 15, 22 − 15 = 7.
Check a subtraction by adding the parts back: verify 22 − 7 = 15 by computing 15 + 7.

(Optional) Show the same reversing with another model: a balance that returns to its start after you add then subtract the same amount, or Cuisenaire rods laid as 15 + 7 and then the whole with one part removed.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Subtraction reverses addition over the SAME three numbers, so taking one part from the whole returns the other part; one sum gives four related facts and a built-in way to check.

keyRepresentations: Fact-family / part-whole triangle (one whole, two parts, four facts)
Bar model with the whole and two parts, read as add or subtract

Cuisenaire rods showing a+b and the reverse whole−a
commonMisconceptions: Treating the four fact-family facts as unrelated things to memorise separately.
Believing subtraction facts can also be reversed freely (10 − 6 = 6 − 10), over-extending the 'undo' idea.
Checking a sum by repeating the SAME operation rather than using the inverse.
Solving □ + 9 = 14 by adding 9 and 14, not recognising subtraction as the inverse move.
Thinking 'undoing' requires a different, brand-new procedure rather than the operation they already know.
constraints: Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation so the learner sees one relationship, not four isolated facts.
Make 'check by the inverse' a routine habit after calculating, in line with the objective, rather than an optional afterthought.

Distinguish the whole from the parts explicitly: subtractions take a part from the whole (22 − 7, 22 − 15); a part minus a part (15 − 7) is NOT one of this fact family's four facts (15 − 7 = 8 is a valid operation but a different problem).
Emphasise that subtraction does not reverse 'freely' — order matters, so do not over-extend the undo idea to 15 − 7 = 22.

A fixed/static fact-family picture with tappable corners can anchor the four facts and the checking idea, but it does not let the learner perform the reversing action; it can support rather than stand in for do-and-undo work.

Recognition and matching tasks can check recall of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, but recognition alone does not elicit independent production or the felt experience of reversing; pair them with reversing and explanation work rather than relying on them alone, without mandating a particular medium or strict ordering.

startingActivity.title: Bridge the decade on a number line with a base-ten mat
learnerActions: Work 36 + 7 by first jumping from 36 to the next decade (40), then completing the jump with the remaining ones (to 43).
On a base-ten mat, watch four loose ones combine with the existing ones to make a whole new ten-stick as the jump reaches 40, so the tens digit change has a visible cause.
Switch to subtraction mode for 52 − 4: jump back to the decade first (52 − 2 = 50), then take the remaining 2 to reach 48.
Mix in non-bridging items such as 43 + 5 and decide for each item whether the ones cross a decade before choosing to bridge.

Optionally view the same bridging in another representation: a ten-frame filling up to a complete ten of ones, or a hundred square where you move along a row and drop to the next row as you cross the decade, so the new ten is seen forming in more than one way.
State out loud which decade you bridge through and why the tens digit does or does not change.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When adding makes the ones fill up to a whole ten, a new ten is formed and the tens digit increases by one; when subtracting takes away more ones than there are, a ten is broken into ones and the tens digit decreases by one (52 − 4 = 48). Partitioning the ones to reach the decade makes this regrouping explicit for both addition and subtraction.

constraints: Ground the strategy in base-ten blocks and the number line (with ten-frames or a hundred square as alternative representations) so the new ten is seen forming (and un-forming when subtracting) before expecting mental calculation.
Always mix bridging and non-bridging items (e.g. 43 + 5) so children learn to bridge only when the ones cross a decade and do not over-apply the strategy.
A fixed practice sequence consolidates fluency but does not provide live regrouping feedback; use it after hands-on manipulative work.
A static worked image anchors what bridging looks like but does not rehearse the count; it is a reference, not a substitute for doing the procedure.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 6) adds ones without crossing a ten and with blocks when crossing; Tier B (age 7) bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade; Tier C (age 7+) explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping) as children progress.

activityReferences.title: Talk with a 'prove-it' partner who never accepts a bare rule
Show the whole is conserved: partition with materials, compensate on a number line
Annotate a worked strategy with the reason for each step
Spot the flawed reasoning / pick the valid justification

startingActivity.title: Talk with a 'prove-it' partner who never accepts a bare rule
learnerActions: Solve 46 + 37 by adding tens and ones separately (40 + 30 = 70, 6 + 7 = 13, 70 + 13 = 83), then say the answer aloud.

When your partner (teacher, peer, or an in-role character) asks 'but why doesn't breaking 46 into 40 and 6 lose anything?', explain in your own words why splitting and recombining keeps the same total.
Try splitting 37 a different way — e.g. 35 + 2 instead of 30 + 7 — and explain whether the method still works and why, to show the reasoning transfers to a new split.
Solve 46 + 99 by adding 100 and then adjusting; when asked 'why take one BACK rather than add one?', explain how much too much 100 is compared with 99 and why the surplus must be removed.
Respond to a counterexample your partner offers (e.g. a friend who split 46 into 40 + 6 but only added the 40 and forgot the 6) and say whether that mistake means splitting itself is unreliable.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A remembered procedure becomes an owned explanation: the number IS its tens and ones, so like parts can be added and recombined without loss, and this holds whichever way you split; adding 100 for 99 adds exactly one too many, so you subtract one to land on adding exactly 99.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (whole conserved under partitioning)
Number line (compensation: overshoot then step back)
Part-whole diagram (the number as tens + ones)
Worked strategy with each step annotated by its reason
Bar model (equivalent transformations preserve the total)
commonMisconceptions: Restating the procedure or citing authority ('the teacher said') instead of giving a reason
Doubting that splitting/reordering preserves the total (fearing something is lost when a number is broken up)
Compensation direction error: adding 100 for 99 then adding 1 (not seeing 100 is one too many)
Explaining WHAT was done but not WHY it is valid
constraints: The goal is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers; do not score the discussion right/wrong — surface reasoning for discussion.

Manipulatives, number lines, bar models and annotated strategies seed and model the explanation but do not themselves make the child articulate WHY — pair them with an explicit request for the child's reason.
Justification can be produced in speech or in writing; the dialogic routine is well-suited to eliciting it but is not the only valid medium.

Selection tasks (choose the valid justification, spot the flaw) assess and probe recognition; recognising a correct justification does not elicit independent construction of one, so follow them with the child explaining in their own words.
Compensation direction must be tracked quantitatively: 100 is one MORE than 99, so adding 100 adds exactly one too many and one must be subtracted; watch for the error of adding 1.
The compensation direction error (adding 1 instead of subtracting) should appear only as a flaw to be identified, never presented as a valid option.

Prerequisites to revisit if reasoning is shaky: three-digit place value / composition of number (if the child doubts splitting preserves the total), and the compensation strategy itself (if the compensation logic is absent).
Subtraction is not commutative even though addition is — do not let 'any order works' be over-generalised to subtraction.

activityReferences.title: Add and remove tens while the ones stay put
Fluency practice: one-step add/subtract tens
Explain and predict the invariant digit

startingActivity.title: Add and remove tens while the ones stay put
learnerActions: Start with a base-ten representation of 45: four ten-sticks and five single ones, with the numeral 45 shown alongside.
Before acting, predict the answer to 45 + 30 and say which digit you think will change.
Add three more ten-sticks one at a time for +30, saying the running total aloud: 45 → 55 → 65 → 75, and notice that the five single ones never move.
Switch to subtraction: start from 82 (eight ten-sticks, two ones) and remove four ten-sticks for 82 − 40, reaching 42, with the two ones untouched.

Repeat the same moves on a hundred square numbered with 1 at the top: for +30 move three rows straight down (45 → 55 → 65 → 75); for −40 move four rows straight up (82 → 72 → 62 → 52 → 42), watching that the ones column stays the same.
Immediately afterwards do 45 + 3 with single ones to feel the difference: now the ones pile changes and the tens stay the same.

Optionally, show the same tens move on other representations of place value — an empty number line with jumps of ten, a Gattegno place-value chart where the tens row slides while the ones stay, or arrow cards that separate the tens and ones — to reinforce that only the tens change.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting a multiple of ten moves only the tens; the ones digit is invariant. Adding ones is a different move that changes the ones instead.

Hundred square with vertical jumps
Empty number line with jumps of ten

Arrow cards separating tens and ones
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit as well as the tens when adding tens.
Adding the tens digit to the ones (45 + 30 → 48 or 75... e.g. treating 30 as 3 ones).
Miscounting the number of tens jumps.
Confusing add-tens with add-ones procedures.
For subtraction, borrowing into the ones unnecessarily.
constraints: Build from an existing '10 more/10 less' skill: adding 30 is three jumps of ten, so the ones stay fixed and, when the total stays below 100, the tens digit goes up by three.

Include a contrast with adding ones (e.g. 45 + 3) so learners do not merge the add-tens and add-ones procedures; this contrast is strongly recommended and is the basis of the diagnostic discrimination between the two moves.

A static highlighted hundred square can anchor the idea but does not let the learner practise the move; treat it as an anchor, not the main activity.
Live digit updates, dragging ten-sticks, and vertical hundred-square jumps are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete but are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms.

activityReferences.title: Exchange on a place-value mat: compose and decompose a ten
Subtraction as finding a difference on a number line
Annotated worked example and targeted consolidation

startingActivity.title: Exchange on a place-value mat: compose and decompose a ten
learnerActions: Set out 34 + 27 on a place-value mat using base-ten blocks (or draggable on-screen tens and ones).

Pile the ones together to find there are eleven; because that is ten or more, perform a 'make a ten' action that swaps ten loose ones for one ten-rod moved into the tens column, leaving one loose one, then read the answer as 61 (not 511, not 51).
Set out 63 − 28; find there are not enough ones to give eight, so take a ten-rod and break it into ten loose ones, so 63 is now 50 and 13.
Hand over eight ones (13−8=5) and subtract the tens (50−20=30) to reach 35.
Record each physical step as a matching jotting: 30+20=50, 4+7=11, exchange → 61; and 63 = 50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30 → 35.
Say aloud why 34+27 cannot be 511 ('ten ones is the same as one ten, so the extra ten joins the tens').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Composing a ten (addition) and decomposing a ten (subtraction) are the same exchange run in opposite directions; 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are fair swaps between ones and tens, not separate digit tricks.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks with a place-value mat (compose/decompose a ten)
Number line (jumps for adding; count-up for difference)
Part-whole / partitioning jottings (30+20 and 4+7)
Bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction)
Hundred square
commonMisconceptions: Failing to compose the ten: adding tens (50) and ones (11) and writing them side by side (511) or keeping 51
Smaller-from-larger subtraction: 63−28 done as 8−3 in the ones, answer 45
Counting every unit and losing the ten-structure (not treating a ten-rod as one ten)
Misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat
constraints: Build the skill from repeated hands-on exchange with base-ten blocks and a place-value mat before any formal column method; introduce 'carrying'/'borrowing' only as names for the exchange already performed.
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action; do not jump straight to abstract digit manipulation.
A static annotated worked example or tap-to-reveal reference can show the steps but does not let the child perform the regroup; use it as reference alongside, not instead of, hands-on exchange.

A set of items that includes the common wrong answers 511/51 and 45 can consolidate and expose errors, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the exchange; pair with the learner performing and recording the swap.
When describing whether an exchange is needed (e.g. 34+25 vs 34+27), check the ones sum directly — exchange is needed only when the ones reach ten or more (4+5=9 needs none; 4+7=11 does).
Treat a ten-rod being recounted as ten separate ones as a developmental stage in unitising, not an error to drill away; keep reading it both ways aloud.

The place-value mat is essentially planar (tens and ones, place value), so these activities do not propose a third dimension or spoken-only delivery as the main medium for the exchange insight; this is a design preference, not evidence that 3D or dialogue cannot teach it, and talk is still used so the child can explain their strategy.

A bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction) and a hundred square remain available as further optional representations and should not be presented as replacements for the base-ten exchange work.

startingActivity.title: Watch a ten compose when you cross the boundary
learnerActions: Start with 46 shown on a bead string or in a base-ten workspace
Add single ones one at a time, saying the running total aloud (47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53)

When the added one makes ten loose ones, see that they complete a ten (on a bead string, the next block of ten beads is filled; with base-ten blocks, swap the ten ones for a ten-rod), so the count goes 49, then 50, then on to 53
Re-tell what happened: 'I added 4 to reach 50, then 3 more to make 53', and link it to the partition 7 = 4 + 3
Repeat for 53 + 9 (bridge to 60 by adding 7, then +2)
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Bridging a ten is not an arbitrary rule: the extra ten is physically composed from ten ones, and the make-ten partition (7 = 4 + 3) is the same move used within 20 applied at 46.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bead string / 100-bead frame (bridging a ten made visible)
Base-ten blocks (tens rods and ones)
Number line with jumps (partition the added amount into a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Part-whole model (partition the addend, e.g. 7 = 4 + 3)
Hundred square (move along for ones, down for tens)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a multiple of ten as ones: 38+40 done as 38+4=42
Not bridging the ten: 46+7 done as 6+7=13, keeping the 3 and losing the extra ten (answer 43), or concatenating to 413
Adding the added amount to the wrong part (ones added to the tens digit)
Persisting with count-all/count-on-in-ones instead of using place value
constraints: Teach as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm.
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging.

Fill-the-blank and multiple-choice items rehearse, check and consolidate the strategy and suit practice after the insight is built; they do not let the child enact the ten-crossing regroup by hand, so pair them with the hands-on activity (and the part-whole scaffold) rather than using them to first build the strategy.
A labelled or tap-to-reveal part-whole picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup; it is a scaffold to pair with hands-on bridging, not a replacement.
Do not ban counting-on in ones or penalise slowness; it is a valid developmental strategy that matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the efficient jump alongside the child's count.

Optional interactive supports (dragging ones that compose a ten at the boundary, a running count, sliding ten-rods onto the tens, a toggle mirroring the action as a number-line jump and jotting) make the mechanism concrete but are examples, not required mechanisms; equivalent physical bead strings and base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.

startingActivity.title: Build the story as a bar model (money two-step)
learnerActions: Take the problem 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p — how much now?' and draw a bar to represent the starting 35p.
Cut 12p off the bar for the spending, and label the segment that is left — write 35−12=23 and mark 23p as the intermediate result.
Add a 5p bar for 'then found 5p' and compute the final total: 23+5=28p. Label the answer with its unit.
Repeat with a lengths story, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm — how long is left?', drawing and labelling the bar and giving the answer in cm (45−18=27cm).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Drawing the situation turns a confusing word problem into visible parts; seeing the middle number (23p) appear is what stops a child from stopping after step one, and labelling keeps the units correct.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model (comparison, part-whole, two-step)
Part-whole diagram
Number line (count-on for change/difference)
Coins / ruler as concrete context for money and measures
Jottings vs mental — an anchor chart of when to use each
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy: picking the operation from words ('left'→subtract, 'altogether'→add) rather than the situation — breaks on multi-step and compare problems
Doing only the first step of a two-step problem and stopping
Losing or misusing the intermediate result
Ignoring units, or mixing units in measures/money problems
Defaulting to a written method when a mental one is far quicker (or vice versa)
constraints: Represent the situation first (bar model or part-whole) before choosing numbers or method — structure before calculation.
For two-step problems, make the intermediate result explicit ('how much after spending, before finding?') so the child does not stop after step one.
Attend to units and context in money and measures (p, cm) so answers are labelled and sensible.
Use problem vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) so the operation is drawn from the situation, not from keywords.

Checking an operation choice with a multiple-choice or matching question can diagnose keyword or method-choice errors, but recognising the right operation does not by itself show the child can construct and track a model; pair any such check with building and solving.
A static worked bar model with tap-to-reveal labels is a useful reference for structure but does not let the child model a new problem, so it is a scaffold, not the main task.
Spoken discussion can elicit structure well but does not provide the manipulable diagram or practice volume on its own.

activityReferences.title: Removing whole tens from a tens-only mat
Contrasting 70 − 3 with 70 − 30
Linking the known fact on a reference chart

startingActivity.title: Removing whole tens from a tens-only mat
learnerActions: Lay out seven ten-rods (or ten-sticks/strips of ten) to represent 70.
For 70 − 30, physically remove three whole rods and say the running count aloud: 70 → 60 → 50 → 40.
Name what is left as 'four tens, which is 40', pointing at the four rods rather than counting individual cubes.
Say the matching single-digit fact: 'seven tens minus three tens is four tens, just like 7 − 3 = 4.'
Repeat for 80 − 50 (eight rods, remove five, leaving three = 30) and 90 − 60 (nine rods, remove six, leaving three = 30), each time removing whole rods and stating the answer in tens.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Subtracting multiples of ten is the same subtraction as the known single-digit fact, spoken in units of ten; the zero in the answer is a real placeholder showing zero ones, which keeps the 4 in the tens place. It is not decoration.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten-rods / base-ten tens (remove whole rods)
Bead string in tens or 100-bead frame
Number line with jumps of ten
Hundred square (move up in tens)
Place-value chart showing the tens column
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the ten-unit: subtracting 7−3=4 and answering 4 instead of 40
Treating the zero as a spelling trick ('add a zero') with no unit meaning
Counting back in ones (70,69,68…) and losing track
Confusing 70−3 with 70−30 because the unit isn't tracked
constraints: The reference chart and reveal-style layouts are consolidation scaffolds: they link 7−3 to 70−30 but do not let the child remove tens and watch the count change, so they do not by themselves build the unitising action.

Practice sequences and choice items rehearse the strategy and can surface errors such as the dropped ten-unit, so they are well suited to consolidation and checking, and are less likely than hands-on removal to first establish the unitising idea.
Chanting supports the count-sequence; on its own it does not establish why the answer is four tens.

Paper strips, rods, or card tens have slight physical thickness and are approximations of abstract tens; keep attention on 'each piece is worth ten', and an idealised on-screen counter is a model of the tens count, not the tens themselves.
Do not forbid or mark wrong a child who counts back in ones — it is a valid strategy that matures; model the ten-jump alongside it.
Keep the 'subtract the tens digits, keeping the ten-unit' shortcut scoped to decade−decade subtraction; it is not a general rule for cases needing regrouping.

activityReferences.title: Carry and exchange with counters beside the columns
Bridge from expanded partial sums to the compact column
Spot the error in a worked column
Explain your steps aloud

startingActivity.title: Carry and exchange with counters beside the columns
learnerActions: Set out 347 + 185 in columns on squared paper or a headed H-T-O grid, ones under ones.

Add the ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write the 2 in the ones column and the carried 1 above the tens; alongside, exchange ten of the 12 one-counters for a single ten-counter and place it in the tens column, so the written '1' and the real ten move together.
Add the tens: 4 + 8 + 1 = 13. Write 3, carry 1 hundred, and exchange ten of the 13 ten-counters for a single hundred-counter, placing it in the hundreds column.
Add the hundreds: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5, giving 532.

Now set out 502 − 276. To take 6 from 2 in the ones you need more ones, but the tens column is 0: first break one hundred into ten tens (502 becomes 400 + 90 + 12 after the cascade), then break a ten into ten ones.
Estimate first by rounding (≈ 350 + 200 = 550, or 300 + 200 = 500, for the addition; ≈ 500 − 280 = 220 for the subtraction) and check the subtraction by adding 226 + 276 back to 502.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A carried or exchanged digit is a real ten or hundred moving between columns, not a meaningless mark; across a zero you must decompose a hundred into tens before you can get a ten, then a ten into ones.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Column grid / squared paper with H-T-O headings
Place-value counters alongside the algorithm
Expanded written method (partial sums) as the stepping stone
Base-ten blocks for the exchange step
Number line / estimation for the check
commonMisconceptions: Place-value misalignment: writing digits ragged so ones and tens are added together
Smaller-from-larger: subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column regardless of position (83−25→62 pattern, now at three digits)
Carry omitted or mis-placed: forgetting to add the carried ten/hundred to the next column
Borrow-across-zero errors when the adjacent column is 0 (502−276)
constraints: Introduce the compact algorithm only after children can compose and decompose numbers concretely.
Keep base-ten blocks or place-value counters available alongside the written method during the transition, especially for exchange.
Teach subtraction exchange as decomposition ('take a ten, make ten ones'), not a memorised 'borrow', and rehearse across-zero cases.
Always estimate first by rounding and verify with the inverse operation; any close rounded estimate (not an inflated one) serves the sanity-check.
Insist on place-value alignment using a column grid or squared paper so ones sit under ones.
Error-spotting and repeated drill rehearse and check accuracy but do not on their own build the place-value understanding; pair them with meaning-focused work.
Explain-aloud discussion is a supplement for reasoning; it cannot replace sufficient aligned written practice.
A worked annotated example is useful reference but cannot catch a child's own alignment slips; have the child produce calculations too.

activityReferences.title: Snap the pairs that make a tidy number
Partition into tens and ones, and compose the tens carefully
Explain and defend the smartest grouping

startingActivity.title: Snap the pairs that make a tidy number
learnerActions: Take four addends to add, e.g. 15, 8, 25, and 12, arranged as cards that can be physically moved (paper cards, counters on a tray, or draggable on-screen tiles).
Before adding anything, scan the four numbers and decide which two, placed together, would make a multiple of ten.
Pair 15 with 25 to make 40, and 8 with 12 to make 20, then add the two round numbers: 40 + 20 = 60.
Repeat with 24, 17, 6, 13 (24+6=30 and 17+13=30, giving 60) and say aloud which pair you spotted first and why.
Try one example by adding strictly left-to-right, then again by pairing first, and compare how much easier the paired route felt.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Because addition can be done in any order and grouping, reordering to make pairs that total a multiple of ten turns a fearsome four-number sum into an easy sum of round numbers. The properties of operations are a lever, not an abstraction.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / bead strings (spotting pairs that make ten)
Draggable number cards (reorder addends to pair)
Part-whole / column jottings (tens together, ones together)
Number line (cumulative jumps)
Base-ten blocks (composing several tens)
commonMisconceptions: Adding strictly left-to-right and missing pairs that make ten (not using commutativity to simplify)
Losing track when combining many ones, or forgetting to compose more than one ten (ones sum to 23, only one ten carried)
Believing the addends must be added in the given order (no reordering allowed)
Miscounting during a long running total
constraints: Prerequisite: pairing numbers to make ten (as in adding three one-digit numbers) and exchanging ten ones for a ten; revisit these if a child insists order is fixed or loses a composed ten.

Recognition-style tasks (matching pairs that make ten, choosing the smartest first step, filling blanks in running totals) rehearse and check the strategy and can catch left-to-right grinding, but because they do not require the child to reorder the addends themselves they do not on their own elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first; pair them with tasks where the child reorders the addends.
A static worked example with the pairs ringed is useful reference but does not let the child try reordering; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
Manipulatives (ten-frames, bead strings, base-ten blocks) should make 'making a ten' and composing several tens visible before moving to numbers alone.
Keep sums engineered so tidy pairs exist when teaching the strategy, but also include a sum with no neat pair so the child learns the fallback of partitioning into tens and ones.

activityReferences.title: Double exchange on a place-value mat: 256 + 167
Cascade across a zero: 402 − 137
Annotated worked example: reveal each exchange step

startingActivity.title: Double exchange on a place-value mat: 256 + 167
learnerActions: Lay out 256 and 167 with base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) on a H-T-O mat.
Combine the ones: 6+7=13. Exchange ten ones for one ten and move that ten into the tens column (leave 3 ones).
Combine the tens: 5+6+1(carried)=12 tens. Exchange ten tens for one hundred and move it into the hundreds column (leave 2 tens).
Combine the hundreds: 2+1+1(carried)=4. Read the result: 423.
Record the matching written steps beside the blocks — first in an expanded layout, then in compact columns — so each written mark names a physical exchange.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Carrying across two columns is the same exchange move repeated at a second boundary: ten ones become one ten, and ten tens become one hundred.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones, ten-rods, hundred-flats) on a place-value mat
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
Part-whole / partitioning drawings (256 = 200+50+6)
Number line for count-up subtraction across hundreds
Expanded written layout bridging to compact columns
commonMisconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction across any column (e.g. ones done as larger-minus-smaller)
Failing to compose a hundred: ten or more tens left in the tens place (170+80 recorded with 15 in the tens column)
Borrow-across-zero errors: decomposing when the adjacent column is 0 (402−137) done incorrectly
Treating each column independently with no exchange, so carried/borrowed units vanish
constraints: Work concrete→pictorial→written for the SAME calculation so the written recording mirrors the physical exchange.
Make both boundaries explicit in both directions: ten ones↔one ten and ten tens↔one hundred.
Deliberately include across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137); do not treat it as an afterthought.
A step-revealing worked example is a reference scaffold: it shows exchange steps but does not let the child perform the double regroup, so pair it with hands-on work.
Practice items consolidate and diagnose errors but rehearse rather than build the exchange insight; use them after concrete and pictorial work, not instead of it.
Place-value counters or base-ten blocks on a labelled H-T-O mat should be arranged so an exchanged unit physically moves one column, and the written record should name that move.

startingActivity.title: Same calculation, two tools: feel which method fits the numbers
learnerActions: Take 71 − 68 and first work it on a base-ten column workspace: there are not enough ones, so decompose a ten, cross out, and carry through the several steps of the borrow.
Now work the same 71 − 68 on a number line: count up from 68 to 71 and see the difference is just three.
Place the three-hop count-up beside the multi-step borrow and say which was quicker and why.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: The efficient method depends on the numbers: when the numbers are close, counting up the difference beats a columnar borrow; regrouping must be composed or decomposed deliberately so the extra ten is never silently dropped.

learnerActions: Start with 345 on a place-value chart and add 40 mentally: before calculating, predict which digits will change and which will stay the same.
Confirm that only the tens change (4 tens + 4 tens = 8 tens), giving 385, with the hundreds (3) and ones (5) unchanged.

activityReferences.title: Cascade the thousand: borrow across two zeros with base-ten quantities
Align and compose: mixed-length columnar addition and subtraction
