startingActivity.title: Cascade the thousand: borrow across two zeros with base-ten quantities
learnerActions: Set up 4002 - 1367 in place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers, aligning from the ones column on the right.
Build 4002 physically (or on a screen model): four thousand-blocks and two ones, with empty hundreds and tens.
Try to subtract 7 ones from 2 ones; notice there is nothing in the hundreds or tens to exchange from, so the exchange must come from the thousands.

Exchange one thousand-block into ten hundred-blocks, then one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones — watching the single thousand ripple down through the two empty columns until the ones column holds 12.
Record each changed digit in the written algorithm in step with the blocks (4002 becomes 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) and finish the subtraction to reach 2635.
Round both numbers to make an estimate (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600). Ideally do this before the exact working in the steps above. Then compare the estimate with the exact answer 2635.
Check with the inverse: confirm 2635 + 1367 = 4002.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Borrowing across zero is not a special rule: when an adjacent column is empty you continue the exchange one column further left, and a single thousand can cascade down through the zeros to free up ones. The written digits are a record of quantities actually regrouped.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers
Base-ten blocks including the thousand cube (exchange made physical)
Part-whole bar model
Empty number line for the rounding estimate
commonMisconceptions: Borrow-across-zero failure — cannot decompose when the adjacent column is 0 (4002-1367)
Smaller-from-larger bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position
Misaligns digits when the two numbers have different lengths (right-aligning wrongly, or lining up under the wrong column)
Fails to compose — leaves a two-digit result in a column instead of carrying
Treats checking as redoing the sum rather than estimating or using the inverse
constraints: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit throughout — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — so the algorithm does not become a symbol-pushing trick.
Deliberately include at least one across-zero subtraction (e.g. 4002-1367): it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case.
Use place-value column headers or grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (e.g. 878 under the right-hand end of 3456), anchoring from the ones column on the right.
Estimate first by rounding so a place-value slip is caught, and check every answer with the inverse operation.

A fill-in-the-column or reveal-the-exchange practice format can assess and rehearse the carried/borrowed digits and the rounded estimate, but it cannot verify a child's handwritten column ALIGNMENT, so include some set-it-out-on-paper work where the child chooses the layout.

A tap-to-reveal worked-example reference can show the ten-for-one exchange behind each carry/borrow mark, but it does not let the child perform the exchange, so it supplements rather than replaces active regrouping.

Screen-based base-ten models and physical blocks offer different experiences; either can make the exchange visible, and neither is required over the other. Physical cubes have thickness and can be handled; a screen model is an idealised representation of the same grouped quantities.

startingActivity.title: Two-track strategy bench: match the method to the numbers
learnerActions: Meet a problem such as 300-298. Before computing, glance at the numbers and predict which method will be quickest.
Solve it two ways side by side: an empty-number-line track (count up from 298 to 300) and a column-algorithm track (set up and exchange across the zero). Time or step-count both.
Compare: on 300-298 the number line jumps the gap in one hop of 2 while the column track is still exchanging across the zero (and may trip over it).
Now try 456+287 the same way and compare: no obvious shortcut stands out for these numbers, so the column algorithm is a sensible, efficient choice here.

Add a check step using the inverse, with this activity's own numbers: for 300-298, add your answer (2) back to 298 and confirm you reach 300; for 456+287 (=743), subtract one addend from the total to recover the other.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Fluency means matching the method to the numbers, not grinding one algorithm; close numbers favour counting up, near-multiples favour compensation, and messy numbers favour the column algorithm.

startingActivity.title: Plan-then-compute with a multi-bar model
learnerActions: Before calculating, lay out the whole problem as a bar model: for the bottle problem, draw Week 1 (12,450) and Week 2 (8,372) as combining bars, then set that combined bar against the 25,000 target bar with the shortfall shown as an unknown gap.
Label every step and name each intermediate result explicitly (e.g. write '20,822 = two-week total, NOT the answer').
State an up-front estimate of the final answer (e.g. 'about 25,000 - 21,000 = roughly 4,000 more').
Choose a method for each step by looking at the numbers: count up for 25,000 - 20,822; use a column method for an awkward sum like 12,450 + 8,372.
Answer the actual question asked (how many MORE are needed = the gap, 4,178) and check it against your estimate and the story.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A multi-step problem is not finished until the final question is answered; the structure of the situation, modelled before computing, determines which operations and in what order, while the numbers determine the best method per step.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Multi-bar model (running total / comparison)

commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy - picks operations from words rather than the situation
Drops a step - solves two of three steps and stops
Offers an intermediate quantity as the final answer
Uses a written method where counting-up is far quicker (25,000 - 20,822), or vice versa
Does not estimate, so a missing step or wrong magnitude goes unnoticed
constraints: Situation-modelling, not keyword-spotting, is the crux; design tasks so operations follow the story, not surface words.
Learners must name intermediate results explicitly and answer the actual question; a running total (e.g. 20,822) is not the answer to 'how many more'.
Method choice is per step and driven by the numbers: counting up for near-value subtractions (25,000 - 20,822), column methods for awkward sums; do not mandate one method throughout.
An up-front estimate and an end reasonableness check are required so dropped steps or magnitude errors surface.

Recognition/selection tasks (sequencing, choosing a method from options) check discrimination but do not elicit independent construction of a plan; include at least one task where the learner builds and carries out a fresh plan.

A worked example and an interactive annotated example are scaffolds that reveal structure but do not by themselves require the learner to plan a new problem; a fixed worked example can still teach even though it cannot be manipulated.

The 'answer slot rejects the intermediate' idea is one optional interaction that makes the final-step requirement concrete; it is not the only way to teach this and should not be presented as the only effective mechanism.

activityReferences.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
Adding three numbers of up to five digits: when the carry is more than one
Worked-example reference and estimate-then-check routine

startingActivity.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
learnerActions: Set out 500,000 − 234,178 in columns aligned by place value, from the ones on the right.
Before computing, estimate by rounding (about 500,000 − 234,000 = 266,000) and note the expected size of the answer.

At the ones there is nothing to take 8 from, and every column to the left is 0; work the exchange by taking one hundred-thousand and walking it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 as a ten is passed along, until the ones finally hold 10.
Complete the subtraction to get 265,822.
Check with the inverse: 265,822 + 234,178 should return 500,000, and compare to your estimate (~266,000).
Optionally model the same subtraction as counting up on an empty number line — jump from 234,178 up to 500,000 and total the jumps — as an independent alternative that should also give 265,822.
Optionally repeat with an easier round-number case such as 500,000 − 234,000 and discuss why that borrow is simpler.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A single exchange can cascade through a row of zeros — each zero becomes a 9 as the ten is passed along, and the ones finally hold 10 — so a wall of zeros is not a dead end.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with headers to hundred-thousands
Base-ten / place-value counters for the exchange rationale
Empty number line for the estimate and for counting-up subtraction
Part-whole bar for multi-addend structure
commonMisconceptions: Extended borrow-across-zero fails — cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros (500,000 - 234,178)
Smaller-from-larger bug persists at larger scale
Misaligns digits when numbers have different lengths
When a column totals 20+ (three addends), carries only 1 instead of 2
Checks by redoing rather than estimating or using the inverse
constraints: This is a doing-on-paper procedural skill: the child must actually set out and compute the algorithm, not only recognise or describe correct steps.
Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety.

Deliberately include at least one subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero) and at least one three-or-more-addend sum whose column genuinely totals 20 or more (so a carry of 2 actually occurs).
Use place-value headers or squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers of different lengths stay aligned from the ones on the right.
A fill-in-the-blank or slider-based quiz can check carried/borrowed digits and estimates but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so observe paper setup directly.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a static scaffold exercising recognition; it supports but does not replace independent construction on paper.

Base-ten counters, an empty number line, and on-screen place-value models offer different experiences of the exchange; any can make the cascade or the structure concrete, and none is strictly required.
Checking must use estimation or the inverse operation (or an independent counting-up method), not a re-run of the same calculation.

activityReferences.title: Scaling bench: a small fact with zeros bolted on
Counting up from a round number
Choosing a strategy to fit the numbers
Explain your mental shortcut

startingActivity.title: Scaling bench: a small fact with zeros bolted on
learnerActions: State a known small fact first, e.g. 6 + 4 = 10, then scale it up a place-value row at a time: 60 + 40 = 100, 600 + 400 = 1,000, 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000, saying aloud how many zeros the answer gains.
Repeat the scaling with a fact that bridges, e.g. 45 + 8 = 53, to reach 450 + 80 = 530 and 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000; say the unit explicitly ('45 thousand plus 8 thousand is 53 thousand').

Check each scaled answer keeps '53' as its non-zero digits and changes only in magnitude, matching the size of the numbers being added (530 is 53 tens; 53,000 is 53 thousands); flag an answer that loses that digit pattern (e.g. 125,000) or that keeps the digits but lands at the wrong magnitude (e.g. 5,300 instead of 53,000) as a scaling slip, not a new sum.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A 'big' calculation is often a small fact the learner already owns, with place value shifting the whole fact up predictably; the zeros are bookkeeping, not extra arithmetic.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Empty number line (counting up, bridging)
Place-value chart / Gattegno chart (scaling a fact by ×10)
Part-whole partitioning diagram
Known-fact 'family' cards scaled up
commonMisconceptions: Fails to scale a bond correctly - misplaces zeros (45,000 + 8,000 given as 125,000 or 5,300)
Tries to visualise the full column algorithm mentally and loses track of the exchanges
Subtracts from a round number by decomposing in the head instead of counting up, and errs
Treats +/- of large numbers as fundamentally harder rather than the same facts scaled
Ignores an efficient strategy (counting up, compensation) and grinds digit by digit
constraints: These are mental strategies: the aim is flexible place-value reasoning, not reproducing the written column algorithm in the head.
Jottings such as an empty number line should support the mental method, not replace it with full written working.

Sorting tasks and fill-in-the-blank recall can rehearse and check scaled facts and strategy classification, but recognising or categorising a strategy is not the same as independently constructing and carrying out the calculation; keep the main work learner-generated and spoken/explained.

A reference poster or tappable fact-family display is useful as a lookup, but on its own it does not require the learner to perform the scaling or the counting up; use it alongside active calculation.

A linked place-value chart that slides a fact up a row while the answer gains zeros, and a number line showing counting-up hops that total the answer, are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are optional supports, not required apparatus.
Do not ban or time-pressure a child who still counts on in ones for parts of a calculation; this matures as derived-fact fluency grows. Keep modelling place-value jumps and let the counting recede.

Defend your plan and tool choices
Sequence, method, and spot the impossible answer
Walk through an annotated worked example

startingActivity.title: Charity accounts mission planner
learnerActions: Read a real multi-step problem, e.g. 'A charity had 3,450,000 pounds. In March it spent 1,280,000 pounds and received donations of 2,000,000 pounds. In April its costs were 675,450.75 pounds. How much does it have at the end of April?'
Before computing, model the whole problem with a running-total bar and mark every event as a signed change on the bar.

Build a running estimate first: estimate each step's expected result as well as the final total (about 3.45m - 1.28m + 2m - 0.68m is roughly 3.5m, with intermediate ballparks of about 2.17m then 4.17m along the way).
For each step, choose mental, written, or calculator, carry out the computation, and write one sentence saying WHY that method fits those numbers.
After any calculator or written step, compare that result's order of magnitude against your estimate for that same quantity before accepting it.
Re-read the original question and give the end-of-April balance (3,494,549.25 pounds), interpreted back in context, not an intermediate total.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A calculator does not free you from thinking: the estimate is what tells you whether to trust the display, and the final answer must answer the question asked, not report a running total.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Multi-bar / running-total model
Step-and-method planner (step | operation | method | why)
Estimate strip for the reasonableness check
Real contexts: populations, money, distances, measures (decimals)
commonMisconceptions: Offers an intermediate quantity as the final answer, or drops a step
Word-spots operations rather than modelling the situation
Over-relies on the calculator (keys in steps doable mentally) or refuses it for genuinely awkward computation
Trusts the calculator display without an estimate, so a keying/place-value error goes unnoticed
Loses track of the decimal point or a period (thousands/millions) in large or decimal numbers
constraints: Numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals (e.g. pounds-and-pence) must appear so the magnitude stakes of a keying/place-value slip are real.
Problems must be modelled from the situation, not solved by word-spotting operations from keywords.
The estimate should be built before or alongside computing, not after, and as a running/per-quantity estimate so it can actually gate each calculator/written result.

Recognition and ordering tasks assess understanding but do not elicit independent construction of the plan and computation; include at least one task where the learner builds and justifies the whole solution.

The worked-example walkthrough is a scaffold: it displays structure but does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan and method choices; pair it with a task where the learner constructs and justifies the whole solution.
Interactive magnitude-warning gates, running bars, and live checks are optional illustrative mechanisms; the same learning works on paper with a planner grid and estimate strip.
Method fit is a reasoned choice about the numbers, not a fixed rule; do not teach 'always use a calculator' or 'never use a calculator'.

activityReferences.title: Decimal exchange bench: aligning by the point and trading ten-for-one
Confronting 'longer-is-larger' with ragged decimals
Explain why the points must line up

startingActivity.title: Decimal exchange bench: aligning by the point and trading ten-for-one
learnerActions: Set up 3.4 + 2.78 in place-value columns with the decimal point fixed in a central column; notice that 3.4 has an empty hundredths slot (to the right of the 4, above the 8), and add the placeholder zero so it becomes 3.40 with tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths.

Compute 3.45 + 2.78: the hundredths total 13, so fuse ten hundredth-pieces into a single tenth-piece and carry it one column left — exactly the ones-to-tens carry already known. Record the answer 6.23.
Solve 5.03 − 2.67 by decomposing: exchange one whole into ten tenths and one tenth into ten hundredths so you can take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths; record 2.36.
Before each calculation, estimate roughly (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) and use the estimate to check the point is in the right place afterward.
Re-scale base-ten blocks so a flat = 1, a rod = 0.1, and a small cube = 0.01, and physically trade ten small cubes for one rod to mirror ten-ones-make-a-ten.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Decimals are not a new arithmetic: the point just marks where the columns keep going, and the ten-for-one exchange across every boundary (hundredths→tenths, tenths→ones) is unchanged from whole numbers. You must line up tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths because you can only add like to like.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with a fixed, aligned decimal point (Th... O . tenths hundredths)
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01)
Number line for counting up (5.03 - 2.67)
Money and metric-measure contexts (pounds.pence, metres.cm)
commonMisconceptions: Aligns the digits by the right edge instead of by the decimal point (3.4 + 2.78 set up wrongly)
Treats the digits after the point as a separate whole number ('longer decimal is bigger', so mis-orders/mis-sets)
Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer
Fails to borrow across the tenths, especially with a zero (5.03 - 2.67)
Thinks appending or dropping a trailing zero changes the value
constraints: The computation is a doing skill: learners must actually set up, regroup, and compute, not merely recognise correct setups. Fill-in-the-blank or slider-estimate items can assess column setup, regrouped digits, and estimates, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the algorithm.

Always include at least one ragged-decimal item (e.g. 3.4 + 2.78) and one borrow-across-a-zero item (e.g. 5.03 − 2.67); clean equal-length items alone confirm only the basic algorithm and hide the decimal-specific hazards.

When checking 'longer-is-larger', include at least one comparison where the longer decimal is the smaller value (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); a comparison where the longer decimal is also larger (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.45) does not discriminate the misconception on its own.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (tap the point to reveal 'tenths under tenths'; tap the carry to reveal ten hundredths = one tenth) is useful as fixed reference, but a fixed example cannot be re-set by the learner, so pair it with hands-on setup and computation.
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01) are an approximation: the physical pieces have thickness and the scaling is a convention, so keep the mapping (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, cube = 0.01) explicit.
Money (pounds.pence) and metric-measure (metres.cm) contexts are helpful, but watch that the two-place convention of money does not reinforce 'always two digits after the point'.

activityReferences.title: Sensible or silly? Judge before you compute
Check by adding back: the inverse as an independent test
How do you KNOW it's right? Reasoning discussion
Rounding to a fair ballpark

startingActivity.title: Sensible or silly? Judge before you compute
learnerActions: Look at a calculation paired with a proposed answer, e.g. 412 + 389 = 121, and decide quickly whether it is 'sensible' or 'silly' BEFORE working out the exact answer
Say aloud the rounded ballpark you used: '400-and-something plus about 390 is roughly 800, so 121 can't be right'
Judge a batch of items, some with reasonable answers (e.g. 801) and some deliberately wrong, flagging the silly ones
Record your estimate and the exact answer side by side in two columns, so you can compare the ballpark against the worked result
Only after committing to your judgement, work out or reveal the exact answer and see whether your estimate caught the nonsense
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A rounded ballpark, formed before calculating, is enough to catch a wildly wrong answer — so estimation is a genuine check, not busywork or a guess made after the fact.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line / rounding scale (which ten or hundred is it nearest?)
Bar model showing the inverse (whole minus part returns the other part)
'Sensible or silly?' answer cards to judge
Estimate-then-exact two-column jotting
Fact-family triangle (linking + and − for the inverse check)
commonMisconceptions: Treating estimation as pointless — 'you can't know until you do the real sum'
Estimating AFTER calculating, bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation)
'Checking' by repeating the identical operation (which reproduces the same error) instead of using the inverse
Rounding erratically so the estimate isn't a fair ballpark
constraints: Estimation must come BEFORE calculating to function as a genuine check; estimating afterwards invites bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation).

The inverse check must be understood as an independent re-derivation; repeating the identical operation is a weak check because it can easily repeat the original error (especially a misunderstanding of the method), even though it sometimes catches a careless slip.

An estimate bounds how big an answer should be and catches gross errors, but does NOT prove exactness — an answer close to the estimate can still be slightly wrong. Do not teach 'close to the estimate = correct'.
Treat the reasoning probes as discussion to surface thinking, not as scored right/wrong items; what matters is the quality of the epistemic reasoning.
A static rounding scale, bar model or fact-family triangle is a useful reference but does not by itself exercise the judging habit — pair reference tools with active judging and checking.

A timed 'buzz silly before the answer reveals' format is an optional motivational scaffold (short time pressure forces rounding over computing); it is not required, and the core objective is the estimate-first reasoning, which can also be done untimed on paper or aloud.

activityReferences.title: The estimate as a lie-detector: prove an answer wrong without redoing it
Honest precision: choosing the right level of accuracy for the purpose
Convince the sceptic (spoken reasoning)
Quick checks: spot the impossible answer and sort by needed precision

startingActivity.title: The estimate as a lie-detector: prove an answer wrong without redoing it
learnerActions: Take a completed sum with its answer, e.g. 47,832 + 23,156 = 3,988.
Round each number to a useful grain (nearest 1,000: about 48,000 and about 23,000) WITHOUT recomputing the exact sum.
Add the rounded numbers to get a ballpark of about 71,000.
State whether the given answer is possible: 3,988 is nowhere near 71,000, so it must be wrong - perhaps a place-value, alignment or copying slip; the estimate shows that it is wrong, not why.
Decide, for a stated context, whether a nearest-100 or a nearest-1,000 estimate is the better grain, and justify which keeps enough discrimination to be a useful check.
Repeat with other answers, including one that is close to the estimate (e.g. 70,988) and judge whether 'close' is enough to trust.
Explain, in your own words, why this check catches the error faster than redoing the full algorithm.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An estimate is an independent order-of-magnitude check: it can PROVE an answer impossible in seconds without ever doing the exact calculation. An estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival exact answer.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line showing the estimate as a bracket/ballpark around the true value
Rounded-vs-exact comparison ('about 71,000' beside 70,988)
Context cards (crowd / money / distance) ranking needed precision
Order-of-magnitude 'gauge' (is the answer in the right zone?)
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a good estimate should EQUAL the exact answer (so treats the small difference as an error)
Checks by recomputing exactly rather than estimating - defeating the purpose
Believes more accuracy is always better; cannot see when rounding is appropriate
Rounds to an unhelpful level (too coarse to discriminate, or too fine to be an estimate)
Treats the estimate itself as the required answer
constraints: Estimation must be taught as a CHECK performed independently of the exact method - never by repeating the exact calculation, which can easily repeat the same error (especially a misunderstanding of the method) and so may not catch it.

Round to a level that keeps useful discrimination (e.g. nearest 1,000 for five-digit sums, not nearest 10,000); choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 is itself a reasoned, context-dependent decision.
An estimate is a deliberate ballpark; being near the exact answer is correct, not an error. 'Close to the estimate' rules out large errors but does not guarantee the exact answer is right.
Accuracy is a decision justified by purpose and audience, not 'more digits = better'; both spurious precision and over-coarse rounding are wrong for their context.

Recognition/selection tasks confirm a choice but do not by themselves show the learner can independently generate an estimate or justify a precision level - pair them with spoken or written reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a gauge, dial, number-line bracket, or tap-to-reveal poster are aids to make the mechanism visible; the objective is the learner's own judgement, so fade them as learners articulate the reasoning unaided.
Treat estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as one connected habit; a learner who performs each in isolation but cannot link them has only a partial grasp.
Context-dependent precision claims (e.g. whether '50,000' is too rough) depend on the specific purpose and must be reasoned per case, not applied as a fixed rule.

startingActivity.title: Build the bar model, then write the equation (start-unknown focus)
learnerActions: Read a start-unknown story such as: 'Some children were on the bus. 15 got off. Now there are 28. How many were there at the start?'
Build a bar model: place the known parts (15 and 28) and leave the start as a labelled empty segment — decide whether the unknown is a part or the whole
Recognise that here the START is the whole, so the empty bar is found by adding the known parts 15 and 28
Write a matching equation using a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 28 + 15 = □ (equivalently □ − 15 = 28), so the picture and equation agree
Compute and check the equation and diagram tell the same story
For a two-step story, build a labelled intermediate bar and name that middle amount before doing the second step
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The structure of the situation — not a cue word — determines the operation. 'Got off' suggests subtraction to a keyword solver, but when the start is the unknown whole and the two parts are known, you add. Seeing the diagram contradict the cue word is the moment modelling beats keyword-hunting.

Talk me through your plan: justify each step and method

startingActivity.title: Model the structure before you compute (bar-model planner)
learnerActions: Before writing any calculation, draw or build a bar model of the whole story showing which quantities are known and which are unknown.
Work the trap problem: 'Sam has 340 stickers. That is 85 more than Kim. How many stickers do they have altogether?' First decide who has MORE — Sam or Kim.
Notice that the 'altogether' total cannot be found yet because Kim is unknown; find Kim first by 340 - 85 = 255, then add 340 + 255 = 595.

Then work the aggregation problem: 'A shop has 415 apples. In the morning it sells 168. In the afternoon a delivery brings 230 more. How many are there now?' Model it, then compute 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477.
Name the intermediate quantity out loud (e.g. '247 is the apples after the morning, not the final answer').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The operation comes from the structure of the situation, not from a keyword. 'More than' can require subtraction (to find the smaller unknown quantity) before any adding, and a two-step problem has an intermediate value that is not the final answer.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

One-step-only — solves the first step and offers the intermediate quantity as the final answer
Wrong order of steps, or choosing operations from the numbers present rather than the story
Uses a written method where a mental one is efficient, or vice versa
Does not notice an implausible answer
constraints: The learning target is situation structure and method choice, not arithmetic fluency alone; the arithmetic should be within reach so attention stays on planning.
Do not teach keyword rules ('altogether means add', 'more than means add', 'left means subtract'); these are the misconception this topic targets.
A static annotated worked problem can illustrate the two-step structure but does not let a learner plan or model a new problem — treat it as an exposition scaffold, not the main task.
Selection/ordering items are recognition tasks and do not by themselves elicit an independently constructed plan or model; use them alongside construction and justification, not instead of them.

A tool that physically blocks keyword-adding (e.g. a total bar that will not close until the unknown part is found) is an optional mechanism to make the dependency visible; a drawn bar model on paper serves the same purpose.
The intermediate quantity must be named and distinguished from the final answer so it is not reported as the solution.

The reasonableness check must use expected magnitude for the specific story; do not teach that 'more than the starting amount' is automatically implausible, since in the apple problem the correct answer (477) is legitimately more than the 415 start because the 230 delivery outweighs the 168 sale (net +62).

startingActivity.title: Share-and-group the same pile
learnerActions: Take 12 counters and 3 plates (or hoops). Deal counters out one at a time — 'one for this plate, one for this plate, one for this plate' — until the pile is gone, then count how many each plate got (4).
On the SAME 12 counters, now scoop them into groups of 3, setting each group aside until none remain, then count how many groups you made (4).
Say the matching division sentence for both actions: 12÷3=4. Notice the same answer arrived from two completely different actions — sharing among 3, and making groups of 3.
Try a total that will not share evenly (e.g. 13 counters among 3 plates): deal fairly until you cannot give everyone one more (4 each), and name the leftover (1 left over).

Optional with an interactive counters tool: toggle between a SHARE mode (choose number of plates, tap 'deal', watch counters distribute one at a time) and a GROUP mode (choose a group size, lasso groups); flip modes on the identical pile to see the same equation form on screen.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Division has two meanings — equal shares and equal groups — and the same numbers can be pictured both ways, giving the same answer; this is the twin meaning children most often miss.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Equal-sharing model — dealing counters one-at-a-time into plates/hoops (partitive)
Equal-grouping model — scooping a set into groups of a fixed size (quotitive)
Arrays and equal groups linking division to its inverse multiplication
Bar model (whole split into equal parts) and number line (equal jumps back for grouping/repeated subtraction)
commonMisconceptions: Believing division only means sharing-out (partitive), so a 'how many groups of 3?' problem is not recognised as division at all.
Treating sharing and grouping as different operations rather than two meanings of the same ÷ — not seeing they give the same answer.
Thinking division is commutative: that 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same (they are not).
Confusing which number is shared and which is the number of groups/size of group (dividend vs divisor) when moving to symbols.
Assuming every sharing must come out exactly and being thrown by leftovers, or sharing unequally and still calling it 'fair'.
constraints: Keep totals small, concrete, and initially remainder-free so the core idea is secure before leftovers complicate it.

Teach BOTH structures deliberately: sharing meets the fairness intuition first, but grouping must be explicitly taught because children default to sharing and grouping is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
Treat leftovers gently at this age: name 'there's one left over' and move on; do not reteach remainders as a misunderstanding — remainder work comes later.
Start fully concrete (dealing and scooping actions) before introducing symbols; the physical act carries the meaning.
Sorting/matching and fill-in-the-answer tasks can check classification but do not themselves elicit the physical dealing/scooping — use them after hands-on sharing and grouping, not instead of it.
A talking character or puppet cannot let the child manipulate quantity, so keep dialogue as a supplement to concrete dealing.

Watch for the dividend/divisor confusion as symbols appear: be clear which number is the total being shared and which is the number of groups or the size of each group; division is not commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12).

startingActivity.title: Build and read an array
learnerActions: Lay out counters (or draw dots) in equal rows and columns to make an array, e.g. 3 rows of 4.
Say aloud exactly what you made: '3 rows of 4' — then also read it as columns: '4 columns of 3'.
Find the total WITHOUT counting every object: skip-count each row, '4, 8, 12'.
Write the multiplication the array shows: 3 × 4 = 12.
Try building another array to order as an extension, e.g. 'Show me 2 × 5 as an array', and state its total.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An array has a regular row/column structure, so you can find the total by using the rows rather than counting every object one by one.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The rectangular array of counters/dots (rows × columns)
The array rotated 90° to show commutativity
Fact-family link: one array → two × facts + two ÷ facts
The array as precursor to the area model / grid method for written multiplication
commonMisconceptions: Confusing rows with columns and so mis-describing the array (though the total is the same, the language matters for later).
Counting every object one-by-one instead of using the row/column structure (missing the point of the array).
Not seeing that a rotated array has the same total — treating 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts.
Building arrays with unequal rows (ragged rectangles) — breaking the equal-groups structure.
Not recognising the array as a division picture as well as a multiplication one.
constraints: Keep rows and columns equal and aligned in a rectangle; ragged arrangements break the equal-groups structure the array depends on.

Learners should construct and build arrays (from counters, drawing, or a drag-to-set builder), not only recognise or match pre-made ones — recognition/matching tasks check array-reading but do not elicit independent construction.
Keep the rows/columns aligned as a rectangle so the transition to the area model and grid/expanded written methods stays continuous.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 5) make a 2×3 array and count the total; Tier B (5–6) write the multiplication for an array and rotate it; Tier C (6) from one array write two multiplications and a division.

A static labelled array (e.g. a fixed on-screen image) is a useful reference and can show the fact family, but the learner cannot resize or rebuild it, and a fixed screen image cannot be rotated. Pair it with building/rotating work when the commutativity-by-rotation insight is the aim.

An array is a flat 2D rectangular arrangement; distinguish the grid from any physical counters used to build it. A 3D rendering is not required for this 2D objective and adds handling cost — this is a design judgement for this task, not a claim that 3D provides no learning value in general.

startingActivity.title: Equal-groups builder: watch groups, sentence and number line move together
learnerActions: Set a group size, e.g. 4.

Add groups one at a time. With each group added, watch three things update together: a new '+4' joins a running repeated-addition sentence (4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4), a jump advances along a number line (4→8→12), and a total counter climbs.

Notice where each number-line jump lands (4, 8, 12) and say these numbers as counting in fours; also try a group size of 2, 5 or 10 and compare where the jumps land with the skip counting you already know.
Use a collapse control to fold '4+4+4' into '3 groups of 4', then expand it back.
Try adding an unequal group (e.g. a group of 3 among the fours) and see it flagged as 'not equal groups yet'; fix it so all groups match.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: '3 groups of 4', '4+4+4', and 'counting in fours three times' are three views of one and the same thing, and the groups must be equal for it to be multiplication.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Equal groups of concrete objects ('3 groups of 4')
Number line with equal jumps (linking to skip counting)
Repeated-addition number sentence (4 + 4 + 4)
Arrays (rows of equal size) as the bridge to the × symbol
commonMisconceptions: Adding groups that are not equal and still calling it multiplication — losing the 'equal groups' defining property.
Reading 3 × 4 as 3 + 4 (confusing multiplication with a single addition).
Counting the number of groups when asked for the total, or vice versa — muddling the two roles.

Believing multiplication is ONLY repeated addition (a seed of later trouble with fractions/decimals/scaling) — at this age fine, but teachers should model equal-groups language, not 'times means add lots'.
Miscounting the total by losing track of which groups have been counted (no systematic skip count).
constraints: Groups must always be EQUAL; adding unequal groups and calling it multiplication is the defining error to prevent.
Keep the two numbers in 'a groups of b' distinct: how many groups vs how many in each group. Do not let '3 groups of 4' blur into '4 groups of 3' even before commutativity is formalised.
Do not read 3 × 4 as 3 + 4; multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups, not a single addition of the two numbers.

Repeated addition is the entry model for this age, not the full meaning of multiplication; avoid 'times just means add lots'. Scaling and continuous quantities come later. Model equal-groups language instead.
Matching/sequencing/fill-in tasks check the connection but do not by themselves have the child construct and vary equal groups; keep hands-on building central.
A static picture or tap-to-reveal caption can introduce equal groups but does not let the child vary the number of groups; treat it as an introduction or scaffold, not the main concept-builder.
Interaction examples (live sentence growth, number-line jumps, collapse control, unequal-group flag) are illustrative options, not mandatory mechanisms.

Use commutativity to get facts for free

startingActivity.title: Predict then rotate the array to prove 3×4 = 4×3
learnerActions: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 counters (or dots) and count the total: 12.
Before you turn the array, predict whether the total will change if you turn it, and give your reason.
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3 — do not add or remove any counters.
Count again and confirm the total is still 12; record 3×4 = 4×3.
Repeat with another pair you choose (e.g. 2×5 and 5×2) and state the matching fact.
Explain in your own words WHY the total cannot change when you turn the array.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The same set of objects, read in two directions, gives the same product, so multiplication can be done in either order — this is predicted and then seen by rotating, not merely stated as a rule.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The array rotated 90° (the proof of commutativity)
The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry
Counters showing 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (the non-commutative counterexample)
Paired context pictures (3 groups of 4 vs 4 groups of 3)
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising commutativity to division and subtraction (thinking 12÷3 = 3÷12, or 8−3 = 3−8).
Believing 3×4 and 4×3 are different facts needing separate memorisation.
Accepting commutativity as a stated rule without being able to justify it (no array reasoning).
Confusing 'same product' with 'same situation' — not seeing that different stories can share an answer.
Applying commutativity correctly to × but then assuming order never matters in any calculation.
constraints: Prove commutativity by action (rotating the array) rather than stating it as a rule; a static paired image or captioned diagram is a useful reference but cannot itself let the learner perform the rotation or test the division counterexample.
Always teach the division (and subtraction) boundary alongside commutativity so learners do not over-generalise 'order doesn't matter'.
True/false, matching and sort tasks check whether the learner holds the property and its boundary, but do not by themselves elicit the structural proof-by-rotation; pair them with hands-on building.

The dialogue/character task is a supplement: the actual disproof should be done by sharing quantities, not by bare assertion alone — a worked counterexample is valid reasoning; an unsupported 'no' is not.
Distinguish 'same product' from 'same situation': commutativity gives the same total, not the same story.
A learner who gets both facts right numerically but justifies only by 'I worked them both out' has not yet reached the structural insight; prompt for the array reason.
Commutativity nearly halves (not exactly halves) the facts to learn, because facts on the diagonal of the multiplication square (e.g. 3×3) have no separate partner.

startingActivity.title: Problem playground: model the story, then solve
learnerActions: Read a contextual equal-groups or sharing story (e.g. '5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many altogether?').
First decide: is this a multiplication story (combining equal groups) or a division story (splitting into equal parts — by sharing or by grouping)? State your choice before solving.
Choose how to model it: build an array, lay equal jumps on a number line, write it as repeated addition, or use a known fact.
Solve and check that your model actually matches the story (equal groups, the right group size and number of groups).

Repeat with a sharing story (e.g. 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children'), a grouping story (e.g. '15 sweets are put into bags of 3 — how many bags?') and an array task (e.g. 'Draw an array for 4 × 3').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A word problem's structure (equal groups, array, or sharing/grouping) determines which operation and representation fit; meaning should drive the method rather than grabbing the numbers and operating blindly.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Arrays (structure of equal-groups/array problems)
Repeated addition and number-line jumps
Bar model (representing the problem structure)
Known multiplication/division facts applied to context
commonMisconceptions: Counting every object in ones instead of using groups or a known fact — not progressing in efficiency.
Not recognising which operation a word problem needs (multiplication vs division; sharing vs grouping).
Modelling with unequal groups and still treating it as multiplication.
Grabbing the numbers and operating without representing the problem's structure first.
Muddling the roles of the numbers (number of groups vs group size) when setting up the calculation.
constraints: Include both multiplication and division stories, and both division structures (sharing and grouping), so problem-recognition is practised — not just computation.
Represent the problem's structure (array, bar model, or number line) before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting; keep any demonstrated fact within the facts the child actually knows.
Let children choose the representation rather than prescribing one method.
Matching/multiple-choice sorting rehearses and checks problem-recognition but does not by itself teach how to construct a model; pair it with hands-on modelling.

A fixed illustrated worked example (tap-to-reveal array and fact) can show one case but cannot provide the varied, decision-rich practice of choosing and applying a method; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
These problems are modelled with flat arrays, bars and number lines; a 3D presentation is not expected to add conceptual value for this topic — a design judgement here, not a general rule.
Keep the bar model/array as a tool for the structure of the word problem, not as decoration added after the answer.

startingActivity.title: Pairing machine: pair the counters and spot the leftover
learnerActions: Choose a quantity of counters (start with numbers to 10, then extend to 20).
Pair the counters up into twos — physically with real counters, or by tapping a 'pair up' control if using a screen model.
Optionally lay the counters on a ten-frame to see full pairs versus one lonely counter.
Decide: if every counter has a partner, the number is EVEN; if exactly one counter is left on its own, the number is ODD.
Test number after number and watch the result build on a hundred square (even numbers shaded) so the alternating-column / ends-in-0,2,4,6,8 pattern appears.
Use a '2×n' / two-equal-rows view to see each even number as two equal groups, linking it to the 2s table.
Test 0: zero counters, zero left over — so 0 is even.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Even means everything pairs up with none left over (two equal groups / 2×n); odd means exactly one is left unpaired. The ones-digit rule and the 2s table both come from this pairing structure, not from an arbitrary ending.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Pairing counters into twos (leftover = odd)
Two equal rows / the 2s array (even = two equal groups)
Ten-frame (full pairs vs one lonely counter)
Hundred square with even numbers shaded (alternating columns)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about a number's SIZE rather than divisibility by 2.
Forgetting that 0 is even.
Judging by the first (leading) digit instead of the ones digit.
Believing a number could be both odd and even, or neither.
Not connecting even numbers to the 2s table / '2×n' — treating the ending rule as unrelated to multiplication.
constraints: Define odd/even by pairing (or making two equal rows) first; introduce the ones-digit rule as something derived from the pairing pattern, not as a bare fact to memorise.
Insist that the two groups be EQUAL and match one-to-one: splitting 7 into 3 and 4 does not make it even. Line the piles up so the unpaired counter is visible.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero counters, none left over) and that odd/even is independent of a number's size.
A paired-vs-leftover picture is an introduction/support: it cannot be run across many numbers by the learner, so pair it with hands-on testing.

A sorting/choice check can teach and check classification but may be answered by the digit rhyme alone; use it after the pairing meaning is secure, and include a show-or-explain step to confirm understanding.
Do not accept the last-digit rule as proof of understanding — ask the learner to show the pairing and explain why one is left over.
Recognition or labelling tasks do not by themselves show that a learner can construct and justify the pairing; include predict-and-explain or show-with-counters tasks.

startingActivity.title: Build-and-balance: linking pictures, symbol sentences and equal value
learnerActions: Make an array (for example 3 rows of 4 counters) and write the multiplication sentence that matches it: 3 × 4 = 12.
Share a set of counters into equal groups (for example 12 counters shared into 3 groups of 4) and write the matching division sentence: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Go the other direction too: given a sentence like 2 × 5 = 10, build the array or grouping picture that matches it.

Place expressions on each side of a two-pan balance and check whether it sits level: show 12 as 12 identical cubes on the LEFT pan and 3 × 4 as 3 groups of 4 of the same cubes on the right (or use a screen balance), and check that the beam sits level.
Using the same identical cubes, try 3 × 4 against 2 × 6 (it should balance) and 3 × 4 against 3 + 4 (it should tip), and say in words why each result makes sense.
Say each symbol aloud as you work: × as 'times / groups of', ÷ as 'divided by', = as 'is the same value as'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each symbol records a meaning and a picture, and = means 'the two sides have the same value' — not 'the answer comes next'. A true equation can be written with the product on the left (12 = 3×4) or with an expression on each side (3×4 = 2×6).

keyRepresentations: Number sentences mapping symbols to arrays/groups
Balance / pan-scale model for the equals sign (relational meaning)
Story ↔ array ↔ symbol translation triples
Symbol reference (×, ÷, = with spoken names and meanings)
commonMisconceptions: Reading = as 'the answer is / write the result here' (operational) rather than 'is the same value as' (relational) — the single most damaging notation error, blocking later algebra.
Rejecting true sentences like 12 = 3×4 or 3×4 = 2×6 because 'the sum isn't on the right'.
Confusing × with + (treating 3×4 as 3+4).
Writing division in the wrong order (since ÷ is not commutative, 12÷3 and 3÷12 are different).
Reading a symbol sentence with no attached meaning — manipulating symbols without knowing what they represent.
constraints: The relational meaning of = ('is the same value as') is the load-bearing idea; never let = be presented or read as 'the answer comes next'. Deliberately include equations with the product on the left (12 = 3×4) and with an expression on each side (3×4 = 2×6).
Keep division order explicit: ÷ is not commutative, so 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 are different; the first number is the whole being divided.
Explicitly contrast × with + (3 × 4 is three groups of four = 12, not 3 + 4 = 7) to prevent symbol confusion.
A symbol-reference display supports recall and self-checking but does not exercise the balance or translation; use it alongside the build-and-balance work, not instead of it.
True/false and fill-in-symbol items check reading and judging, but children must also PRODUCE a sentence for a picture; recognition-only tasks do not show independent construction.

A flat/planar treatment suits this abstract notation; no claim is made that any one medium is required — paper, counters and a screen model can each serve. A physical pan balance and a screen balance offer different experiences of the same sameness idea.

Interaction examples such as auto-forming pictures, typing a sentence to build a picture, dragging expressions onto pans, and a live tipping beam are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.

startingActivity.title: Equal-groups builder: set the groups and the group size
learnerActions: Choose how many groups and how many in each group (for example, 5 groups of 7), then place that many counters into each hoop.
Watch an array of rows × columns assemble beside the hoops and a running repeated-addition sum (7+7+7+7+7) build underneath, all three reading the same total.
Collapse the long sum into the product by writing it as 5 × 7, and read it aloud as 'five groups of seven'.
Deliberately drag one extra counter into a single hoop so the groups become unequal, and notice the arrangement can no longer be written as a single product until all groups match again.
Vary the two quantities and say, each time, which number is the number of groups and which is the size of each group.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A product is equal groups counted efficiently: the total recomputes as you change how many groups and how many per group, and the groups must be equal for a single multiplication to describe them. Repeated addition and the product are two forms of the same quantity.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Equal groups (counters in hoops / bags of sweets) — the primary meaning of a product
Rectangular array (rows × columns) — makes the total structured and countable, and previews commutativity and area
Number line with equal-sized hops — links × to skip counting and to scaling
Bar model / repeated-addition strip — 5 equal bars of 7 bridging + to ×
commonMisconceptions: Reading 5 × 7 as '5 and 7' or adding the factors (5+7=12) rather than seeing groups.
Confusing which factor is the number of groups vs the group size, then drawing 7 groups of 5 for '5 groups of 7' — harmless for the product but a sign the structure isn't understood.
Believing the groups need not be equal — counting any collection as multiplication.
Thinking × always makes a 'much bigger' number and being surprised by ×1 or (later) ×0 and fractional factors.
Treating × as an unrelated new operation rather than a shorthand for repeated equal addition.
constraints: Adopt one convention for reading the factors (first = number of groups, second = group size), but show that the total is the same either way as a bridge to commutativity; do not treat a right total with swapped factors as a product error.

Groups must be equal for a situation to be written as a single product; unequal collections as given (e.g. 3+5+4) cannot be described by one product and should be used as explicit non-examples, while acknowledging that regrouping the counters into equal groups (e.g. 3 groups of 4) creates a new equal-groups situation.

Reference diagrams and recognition/matching/sorting tasks check or anchor vocabulary and classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction or explanation, so pair them with activities where the child builds groups and writes the expression.
Spoken-explanation activities are a supplement: keep a visible array or collection alongside so the total and structure are shown, not only described.
Keep repeated addition visible next to the product at each step so × is experienced as a compression of equal addition, not a separate memorised fact.
Avoid implying × always makes a 'much bigger' number; this prepares for later ×1, ×0 and fractional factors without surprise.

startingActivity.title: Share-and-group the same pile
learnerActions: Start with one pile of 56 counters.
First, SHARE: deal the counters one at a time, round-robin, into 8 plates until the pile is empty. Count how many landed on each plate (7).
Then, GROUP: from a fresh pile of 56, repeatedly scoop a group of 8 counters into a bag until the pile is empty. Count how many bags you made (7).
Write 56 ÷ 8 = 7 beside BOTH actions, then say aloud what the 7 means in each: '7 on each plate' versus '7 bags'.

Repeat both actions with 58 counters. When sharing, deal only full rounds (one to every plate) and stop when there are too few left to give all 8 plates one more. When grouping, stop when fewer than 8 counters remain. Notice the 2 leftover counters that cannot complete another round of equal shares or another group of 8. These are the remainder (58 ÷ 8 = 7 r2).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: One division expression encodes two different questions. Doing both actions on the same quantity shows that 56 ÷ 8 lands on 7 either way, yet the 7 means 'number in each share' when sharing and 'number of groups' when grouping. Leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group are a remainder.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Sharing model — dealing counters one-by-one into a fixed number of plates (partitive: answer = per plate)
Grouping model — repeatedly taking a fixed group size until the pile is gone (quotitive: answer = number of groups)
Array / rows×columns — shows ÷ as the inverse of × (56 in 8 rows → 7 per row)
Number line — equal backward hops of 8 from 56 to 0 (grouping) counts the number of jumps
commonMisconceptions: Believing division has only one meaning (sharing), so grouping/quotitive word problems are misread or mis-drawn.
Thinking division is commutative — that 56÷8 and 8÷56 are the same — by analogy with ×.
Sharing unequally or forgetting shares must be equal.
Believing the answer must always be smaller and being confused by remainders or by dividing a smaller by a larger number.
Divorcing ÷ from × and treating it as a standalone symbol rather than the inverse operation.
constraints: Teach both structures deliberately and by name — partitive/sharing ('how many in each?') and quotitive/grouping ('how many groups?') — using the SAME numbers so one expression models two actions.
Keep division tied to multiplication (56 ÷ 8 relates to 8 × ? = 56, and arrays show the inverse relationship) so it is not learned as an isolated procedure.
Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract: physically share/group, then draw/array/number-line, then write the expression, keeping the action visible.
Division is NOT commutative: 56 ÷ 8 and 8 ÷ 56 are different. Address this explicitly, including using a correctly reversed-story distractor (e.g. 6 ÷ 24 as the reversal of 24 ÷ 6).

Sorting, matching, and multiple-choice tasks verify and reveal understanding (including recognition-only responses) but do not by themselves have the learner independently perform the sharing and grouping actions; use them after hands-on work.
A fixed two-panel diagram anchors vocabulary but cannot be manipulated to let the learner discover the equivalence; pair it with hands-on actions.
Introduce remainders informally through the same actions (leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group) before any written method.
Shares must be equal; guard against sharing unequally and against the belief that a quotient must always be smaller or that one cannot divide a smaller number by a larger one.

startingActivity.title: Scaling machine with a 'why' window
learnerActions: Start from 3×4 = 12, then produce 3×40 and 3×400 by scaling up by ten each step
For each step, explain WHY the product gets ten times bigger using place value (40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift one place left) rather than saying 'add a zero'
Predict 3×4000 and state whether the same reason guarantees it will work, then check
Now test the idea going the OTHER way: 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so is 3×0.4 a tenth of 12? Work it out and explain why the place value, not an added zero, decides this
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The product scales by ten BECAUSE place value shifts the digits one column, so the pattern must keep working (including for 3×4000). Reasoning from place value (not just appending zeros) also handles decimal cases like 3×0.4 = 1.2 — here 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12, with the digits shifting one column right. The add-a-zero shortcut cannot explain this, and it gives wrong answers for decimals (1.2 × 10 is 12, not 1.20).

Notices a pattern but treats it as coincidence, unable to say why it must hold or whether it always will

Recognition/selection questions can check whether a generalisation exists but do not elicit the child's own construction or justification; always pair them with a 'why does it work?' step and treat them as a supplement to construct-and-test work.

A static annotated scaling chain or fraction wall can show and explain the pattern, but cannot let the child generate and test new cases; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the place where testing happens.

Discussion on its own supplies no concrete case or model for the child to test a generalisation against; pair any talk with numbers, a place-value chart, a fraction model, or an array so claims can be checked.

startingActivity.title: Shade the table: derive the 5s from the 10s
learnerActions: On a multiplication grid or hundred square, shade the 10s column (10, 20, 30, 40, 50…) and read them as place-value facts: 10×3 = 3 tens = 30.

Beside it, shade the 5s (5, 10, 15, 20, 25…) and line each 5s value up against the matching 10s value. On a multiplication grid this is the 5s column; on a hundred square the 5s fill two columns, the numbers ending in 5 and those ending in 0.
Notice and say aloud that each 5s value sits exactly halfway to the 10s value: 5×4 = 20 is half of 10×4 = 40.

Shade the 2s (on a multiplication grid, the 2s column; on a hundred square, every column ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8) and state that the answers in the 2s table are even numbers, and that 2×n is the double of n.
Pick one fact per table and write it as a derivation: '10×6 = 60, so 5×6 = 30 (half), and 2×6 = 12 (double of 6).'
Optionally, show the same facts as equal jumps on a number line (counting in 2s, 5s or 10s) to connect the shaded columns back to the skip-counting the child already knows.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The 2, 5 and 10 tables are a connected web, not three separate lists: 10s come from place value, 5s are half the matching 10s, 2s are doubles — so any fact can be rebuilt if forgotten.

commonMisconceptions: Being able to chant the table from the start but not recall a fact out of order — mistaking the chant for fluency.
Knowing the multiplication fact but not the corresponding division fact.
Treating 5×4 and 4×5 as separate facts to memorise (not using commutativity).

A fixed poster or static grid is a good pattern reference but cannot run out-of-order recall practice or generate arrays on demand; combine it with spoken or interactive mixed-fact practice.
Out-of-order, mixed × and ÷ recall is the target; a chant that only works from the beginning of the table is not yet fluency.

startingActivity.title: Sum the rows: build the equal-addend equation from an array
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 array (3 rows, 4 dots in each row) and point to one row to establish that it holds 4 dots.
Add the array one row at a time, saying and writing the running total: 4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4 = 12 — one addend per row.
After writing 4+4+4=12, write the matching multiplication 3×4=12 and say which number tells how many rows and which tells how many are in each row.
Read the same array by columns instead and write it as 3+3+3+3 (four 3s), noticing you get 12 again.
Now try a ragged arrangement where one row has 4 and another has 5; attempt to write a single equal-addend equation and explain why it will not form.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each equal row of an array is one equal addend, so adding the rows gives the total; the multiplication fact is just the shorthand for adding equal rows, and this only works when the rows are equal.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangular array read row-by-row (each row = one equal addend)
Repeated-addition equation (4 + 4 + 4 = 12)
Paired addition/multiplication (4+4+4 ↔ 3×4)
Ragged (unequal-row) non-example for contrast
commonMisconceptions: Adding UNEQUAL groups and still writing it as a single multiplication (missing the equal-addends requirement).
Counting every object individually rather than adding equal rows.
Confusing the number of rows with the number in each row when writing the equation.
Not connecting the repeated-addition equation to the multiplication (seeing them as separate).
Miscounting by losing track of which rows have been added (no systematic row-by-row approach).
constraints: Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable (counters, dots, or drawn grids) so rows and columns stay clear and countable.
Emphasise throughout that the addends must be EQUAL; always contrast the array with a ragged, unequal-row arrangement that is NOT a multiplication situation.

Matching/fill-in tasks assess recognition and completion; they do not on their own elicit independent construction of an array or equation, so include at least one task where the child builds an array from an equation or assembles the equation from scratch.

A static labelled array (tap- or lift-to-reveal addends and the × fact) is a useful reference and shows the bridge, but does not let the child build the sum row by row or test the equal-addends requirement dynamically; treat it as a scaffold, not a replacement for building.
Do not push the repeated-addition shortcut on a child who still needs to count every object to trust it; let repeated addition earn trust through several verified examples.

If optional on-screen interaction is used (tapping a row to drop its value into a running equation, a 'fold'/combine action collapsing 4+4+4 into 3×4, a rotate control to read by columns, a ragged-array mode), these are illustrative mechanisms to make the bridge visible, not required tooling.

activityReferences.title: The doubling chain: 2s → 4s → 8s
One fact gives four: multiplication and division fact families
Out-of-order recall and targeting the sticky facts

startingActivity.title: The doubling chain: 2s → 4s → 8s
learnerActions: Pick a 2s fact such as 3×2=6 and build it as an array (3 rows of 2).
Double the array to make 3×4=12, then double again to make 3×8=24, saying aloud 'double the 2s gives the 4s; double the 4s gives the 8s'.
Repeat the chain for several facts (e.g. 7×2=14 → 7×4=28 → 7×8=56), each time predicting the next fact before doubling.
When an 8s fact is forgotten, recover it by finding the matching 4s fact and doubling it (e.g. forgot 3×8 → find 3×4=12 → double → 24).

Shade the 3s, 4s and 8s on a hundred square (or read their rows on a multiplication square): on the hundred square, notice that the multiples of 3 make diagonal stripes, and on either grid notice that the 8s multiples are every other 4s multiple.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The 8s table, usually the hardest, is 'just double the 4s, which are double the 2s'. Facts are a connected, patterned web, not three isolated lists, so a forgotten fact can be rebuilt.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / times-table grid (patterns and commutative symmetry)
Doubling-chain number lines (2s → 4s → 8s, each jump doubling)
Arrays for each fact and its fact family
Hundred square with 3s, 4s, 8s shaded (diagonal / doubled-column patterns)
commonMisconceptions: Chanting a table but being unable to recall a fact out of order or its division fact.
Learning 4s and 8s as unrelated lists and not noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a forgotten 8s fact can't be repaired.
Treating a×b and b×a as separate facts (not using commutativity).
Confusing adjacent tables (3s with 4s, 4s with 8s) because the steps feel similar.
Doubling errors when deriving 8s from 4s (adding instead of doubling, or doubling the wrong term).
constraints: The learning target is recalled facts: timed/mixed recall exercises check fluency but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — pair them with array building and the doubling chain.

A static multiplication-square or hundred-square poster is a strong reference and pattern-shower but cannot run out-of-order recall or animate the doubling; use it as a support alongside active practice.

Oral quiz-partner drill offers rehearsal and can verbally prompt the 'double the 4s' repair on an 8s miss, but talking alone does not display an array doubling in size; pair it with a visual array where you want the relationship seen.
Division facts must be rehearsed to the same security as multiplication; left implicit they tend to lag.
When using paper arrays or counters, remember they approximate the abstract fact; the point is the number relationship, not the physical objects themselves.

Interactive aids that recolour the grid, pop an array on tapping a cell, or animate an array doubling in size are helpful optional ways to make the mechanism visible — they are examples, not requirements.

startingActivity.title: Adaptive mixed-fact retrieval with a structural rescue
learnerActions: Answer short, mixed sets of multiplication and division facts (within 12×12) quickly, with × and ÷ interleaved rather than tested table-by-table.
Say aloud any fact you had to work out rather than instantly recall, so slow facts are surfaced.
When you stall on a fact, rebuild it from structure instead of guessing: picture or draw the array (e.g. 7 rows of 8), or use a derivation chain (9×7 = 10×7 − 7 = 70 − 7 = 63).
Over repeated short sessions, concentrate practice on your own small set of sticky facts (commonly 6×7, 7×8, 7×9, 8×6 and the 12s) mixed among easier wins.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A forgotten fact can always be rebuilt from structure, so recall is a connected web rather than a list of brittle isolated strings; targeted spaced practice shrinks your personal 'hard core'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / hundred grid — the whole fact space, revealing symmetry (commutativity) and patterns
Array / area model — the structure that lets a forgotten fact be rederived
Fact-family triangle — binds each × fact to its two ÷ facts
Derivation chains (double 2→4→8; 10-group-minus-one for 9s) — facts as a connected web, not isolated items
commonMisconceptions: Treating tables as meaningless rote strings, so a forgotten fact cannot be rebuilt and errors are undetectable.
Learning × facts but not the matching ÷ facts, leaving division recall weak.
Systematic slips on the 'hard core' (6×7, 7×8, 7×9, 8×6, 12×) and 0/1 special cases.
Miscounting when skip-counting up from the start instead of recalling (a sign of non-fluency).
Confusing adjacent facts (7×8 vs 6×8) without a structural check to catch it.
constraints: Fluency is fast, accurate, effortless recall PLUS flexible derivation — not rote parroting divorced from meaning; miscounting by skip-counting up from the start is a sign of non-fluency, not recall.
Teach every × fact together with its ÷ partner so division fluency is built in, not bolted on.
Prefer short, frequent, spaced, interleaved retrieval over long massed drills; keep timing low-stakes to avoid maths anxiety.
Track and target each child's specific unknown facts rather than re-drilling the whole table; the hard core is a small set.
A multiplication square is a reference/pattern tool: it anchors structure and commutativity but supports memorisation indirectly, so pair it with active retrieval practice.
A timed quiz checks and consolidates fluency and pinpoints weak facts; on its own it does not adapt to the child or supply a structural rescue when they stall.
Watch the special cases of 0 and 1 and the notorious cluster (6×7, 7×8, 7×9, 8×6, 8×9, 12×) and 7×8 vs 6×8 confusions; a structural check (array/derivation) helps catch these.
The 9s digit-sum pattern: 9×1 is 9, for 9×2 to 9×10 the two digits add to 9, and the digital root remains 9 for larger multiples; present it with that scope.

CCSS-M 3.OA.7 expects fluent multiplication and division within 100 and, by the end of Grade 3, knowing from memory all products of two one-digit numbers (up to 9×9); recall of all facts to 12×12, including the 11s and 12s, is an England National Curriculum (Year 4) expectation.

startingActivity.title: Derive-it: rebuild hard facts from known ones
learnerActions: Face a mixed stream of × and ÷ questions within 100.
When you stall on a fact, use a named derivation strategy rather than counting up: for 9×7, start from 10×7=70 and subtract one group of 7 to get 63; for 6×8, split into 5×8+8 = 48.
Take a round of 'derive-it' challenge facts chosen so they are best cracked by transforming a fact you already know (rather than counting up), and state the known fact you started from.
For division questions, flip to the multiplication fact family (e.g. for 54÷6 ask 'what times 6 makes 54?' → 9).
Say or write which strategy you used after each hard fact.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Once a few anchor facts are secure (such as ×2, ×5 and ×10), unknown facts within 100 can be reached from facts you already own, so fluency is a connected web of strategies rather than a wall of isolated things to memorise.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Derivation chains and 'fact from a fact' diagrams (10×7−7 → 9×7; double 2→4→8)
Array/area model — justifies the partitioning strategy (6×8 = 5×8 + 1×8)
Fact-family triangle — the inverse as a fluency strategy
Multiplication square — to locate a known neighbour to derive from
commonMisconceptions: Equating fluency with speed alone, leading to guessing under time pressure instead of using a reliable strategy.
Being able to recite a table in order but unable to answer a fact out of sequence or its ÷ partner.
Not using the inverse, so division facts lag behind multiplication.
Failing to derive — stuck facts stay stuck because the child has no strategy to rebuild them.
Not transferring facts into multi-step calculations (knows 7×8 in isolation but not inside a written method).
constraints: Keep timing low-stakes to protect against maths anxiety while still building speed; emphasise a correct efficient method over raw speed alone, and do not equate slow-but-correct with wrong.
A fixed, non-adaptive fact check chiefly measures fluency; pair it with explicit strategy teaching rather than using it as the only route to fluency.
A reference grid or overlay shows strategies but does not drill fluent retrieval; always follow look-ups with unaided practice.

Conversation can build strategy selection and metacognition, but its slower pacing limits rapid repeated retrieval, so on its own it is not suited to building the quick retrieval that supports the efficiency side of fluency (which is efficiency, accuracy and flexibility, not speed alone).
Interleave × and ÷ so the inverse is practised as a retrieval strategy; division facts lag when only multiplication is drilled.
Apply facts inside multi-step calculations and word problems so fluency transfers beyond isolated recall.
Interaction examples (array peeling a column, splitting into 5×8+8, one-tap division flip) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and optional, not mandatory mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Shade, fold and decompose the multiplication square
learnerActions: Shade a chosen times-table on a multiplication square (e.g. shade every multiple of 5) and describe what you notice about the digits — for 5s, every product ends in 0 or 5.
Fold or reflect the grid across its main diagonal so a cell like 7×8 lands exactly on 8×7; observe that every cell matches its mirror.
State WHY the table is symmetric: because 7×8 and 8×7 are the same product (commutativity).
Pick a 4×n cell and split it into two equal addends (2n + 2n) to show why 4×n is always even.
Use a 'predict the next' prompt: extend a shaded pattern one or two steps, say what you expect, then check against the grid.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern can be explained from the structure of the operation itself — the table's symmetry is a consequence (and a picture) of commutativity, and 'always even' follows from decomposing into equal addends — so maths patterns are consequences of properties, not coincidences.

commonMisconceptions: Describing a pattern but 'explaining' it by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking.
Missing that the multiplication table is symmetric (not linking it to commutativity).
Thinking a pattern is coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.

constraints: Always demand a structural/property-based reason, not a restatement — ask 'why does that happen?' and accept only a cause (symmetry → commutativity; 4×n even → doubling/distributive; 5s → half of 10).

Multiple-choice or matching tasks verify whether a child can recognise a correct explanation; they do not elicit the child's own independently constructed reasoning, so pair them with tasks that require stating the reason.

A static DIGITAL tap-to-reveal multiplication square anchors and showcases patterns well but does not let the child fold or decompose cells on the same surface; supply physical folding of a paper square, hand-drawing, or an interactive fold/split tool so the child builds the explanation rather than only reading it. (A printed paper square, unlike a fixed digital image, can itself be folded along the diagonal.)
Paper/card cutouts of the square have real thickness and can be folded physically; a screen 'fold' is an idealised model of the same reflection — both represent the diagonal symmetry.
Guard against over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking, and against treating a pattern as coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.
