startingActivity.title: Fact-family array: grow the eights until you reach 32
learnerActions: Face the question '32 ÷ 8 = ?' alongside a grid showing 8 rows whose columns are hidden behind a shutter.
Instead of dividing, add columns of 8 one at a time, tracking the running total: 8, 16, 24, 32.
Stop when the total reaches 32 and count how many columns you added (4).
Reveal the full array and read off all four related facts together: 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Say aloud what you just did: 'I found 32÷8 by asking how many 8s make 32.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Division answers the question 'how many of this factor fit into the whole?' — it is multiplication with a missing factor, and the same array simultaneously shows the multiplication and its inverse division.

keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle (the 8/4/32 trio generating all four ×÷ statements)
Array/rectangle with one side unknown — division as finding the missing dimension

commonMisconceptions: Seeing ÷ and × as unrelated, so learning division facts from scratch instead of deriving them from known products.
Writing the fact family wrongly by treating ÷ as commutative (32÷4 and 4÷32 as the same).
Getting the missing-factor direction confused (solving 8×?=32 as 8×32).

constraints: The rewrite-and-match-and-check format mainly verifies and consolidates; it does not elicit construction of the array model or show the missing dimension, so use it after hands-on work, not as the first exposure.
The static triangle anchors the four facts but does not let learners vary the trio and watch the inverse hold across many cases — pair it with the variable array.
Dialogue prompts support the verbal missing-factor habit but should accompany, not replace, manipulation of the array and triangle.

Division is not commutative: the whole (e.g. 32) must be the number being divided, so guard against the commutativity error 4÷32; also guard against 32÷32, which reuses one number and is not part of the 8/4/32 family.
The slider/shutter and tap-to-reveal are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; the same learning can be done with counters, drawn arrays, and paper triangles.
Keep the missing-factor direction explicit: 8×?=32 is solved by finding the factor (4), not by computing 8×32 (=256) or by adding to reach 32.

activityReferences.title: Rectangle hunt: build every rectangle of a number
Factor pairs as a mental-calculation tool
Prove the list is complete (systematic-search reasoning)
Check and sort: factors, pairs, and multiples

startingActivity.title: Rectangle hunt: build every rectangle of a number
learnerActions: Take 24 counters (or squared paper, tiles, or dots) and arrange them into complete, gap-free rectangles, recording the dimensions of each as a factor pair.
Work systematically: ask 'does 1 fit? does 2 fit? does 3 fit?...' in order, logging each rectangle you can make (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6).
After making 3×8, try to make 8×3 and observe it is the SAME rectangle turned a quarter-turn — record it as one pair already found, not a new one.
Keep going (5 does not fit; 6 gives 6×4, the same rectangle as 4×6) and notice that no NEW rectangles appear once the two sides meet in the middle; explain why you can stop there.
Repeat with 23 counters and discover only a single 1×23 line forms — a whole number greater than 1 that makes only a single 1×n line is prime.
Draw a 'factor rainbow': arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 to show each pair and completeness.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Factors are the possible side-lengths of all rectangles a number can form; commutativity collapses 3×8 and 8×3 into one pair; a systematic search can stop where the factors meet in the middle because every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one; and a whole number greater than 1 that makes only the 1×n rectangle is prime.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array for each factor pair — factors as side lengths of all rectangles of that number
Systematic factor-pair list (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6) with the 'meet in the middle' stopping point
Factor 'rainbow' arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 — shows commutativity and completeness
×÷ fact family — factor-finding as division
commonMisconceptions: Listing 3×8 and 8×3 as different pairs (not applying commutativity), inflating the count.
Missing factor pairs by searching unsystematically, especially the middle ones.
Confusing factors with multiples (factors go INTO the number; multiples are in its times table).
Forgetting 1 and the number itself are always a factor pair.
Not knowing when to stop — continuing past the square root and re-finding pairs in reverse.
constraints: Count a factor pair once: 3×8 and 8×3 are the same unordered pair. The common error of listing them separately (giving 24 '8 pairs') must be corrected in teaching, not presented as a valid option.

Checking/sorting tasks verify understanding and check classification; they do not by themselves build the rectangle intuition or let a learner discover the meeting-in-the-middle point, so they are well placed after hands-on exploration (not a universal requirement).

A static factor-rainbow diagram is a useful reference and can show completeness and commutativity, but it does not let the learner search for pairs or discover the meeting-in-the-middle point themselves.

Physical counters, tiles, or dots have slight thickness and stand in for the ideal flat rectangle; treat the arrangement as a representation of the number's structure where side-lengths = factors and the total count = the number — this legitimately bridges to arrays and area, so preserve (do not deny) the array/area interpretation.
Factor pairs are planar (two factors, rectangles). A three-factor/volume (cuboid) treatment belongs to a different topic and should not be introduced here.
Always include the 1×n pair; every number has 1 and itself as a factor pair.
The 'one rectangle = prime' observation applies only to whole numbers greater than 1; 1 forms only 1×1 but is not prime.

startingActivity.title: Reorder three factors to find the easy pair
learnerActions: Work out 2 × 7 × 5 in your head, saying aloud which two numbers you multiply first and why.
Try pairing 2 and 5 first to make 10, then multiply by 7 to get 70; compare this with going left to right (2 × 7 = 14, then × 5 = 70).
Check that different orders give the same total: is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Explain why you are allowed to reorder.
Repeat with 2 × 9 × 5 and 4 × 3 × 5, each time scanning for a pair that makes a ten or a known fact first.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Reordering factors is always allowed (commutativity/associativity) and the total stays the same — but some orderings turn a fiddly three-number product into a single known fact, so it pays to look for the friendly pair before calculating.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Equal-groups images for the identity/zero cases (1 group of n; n groups of 1; 0 groups)
Rearrangeable factor tiles for three-number products (regroup to make a ten)
Place-value counters for × multiples of ten
Number line / known-fact chains for derived facts
commonMisconceptions: Thinking ×0 gives the other number, or ×1 doubles/changes it, when treated as rote rules.
Believing multiplication always makes a number bigger (so ×1 or later × a fraction surprises).
Not reordering three factors, so multiplying left-to-right the hard way.
Confusing ÷1 with ÷0 or thinking ÷1 halves.
Miscounting place value in 40×6 (getting 24 instead of 240).
constraints: Keep ÷0 out of scope; if a learner raises it, explain meaningfully that you cannot share 8 among zero groups, and no number of groups of 0 ever makes 8 — so 8 ÷ 0 is undefined — rather than giving a number.
Teach ×0, ×1 and ÷1 through the equal-groups meaning so they are understood, not memorised; rules learned by rote without meaning can leave learners prone to the ×0 = n and ×1 = 0 confusions.
Multiplication does not always make a number larger: ×1 leaves it unchanged and ×0 gives 0. Expect and address this surprise rather than letting 'multiplying makes it bigger' stand.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the right answer, filling a blank) verify results and can prompt justification, but do not by themselves elicit independent mental strategy construction; pair them with learners computing and explaining their own method.

Tap-to-reveal panels and draggable factor tiles are optional scaffolds that make invariance and group meaning concrete; they illustrate the mechanism and are not required for the learning, and a fixed worked example can still teach the same meaning.
The additive identity (adding 0) and multiplicative zero (×0) behave differently; contrast them explicitly so learners do not carry over 'adding 0 leaves it unchanged' to multiplication.

startingActivity.title: Scaling a known fact by ten with place-value counters
learnerActions: Build the known fact 7×3 as an array of 21 single counters (or draw them).
Replace each single counter with a rod of ten, stating aloud 'now there are 21 tens'.
Regroup the 21 tens: exchange ten tens for one hundred, repeat, ending with 2 hundreds and 1 ten.
Record the result on a place-value chart (hundreds | tens | ones) and read it as 210.
Say the full reasoning chain: '7×3 = 21, so 7×30 = 21 tens = 210, because 30 is 3 tens.'
Repeat for 5×60 (5×6 = 30, so 5×60 = 30 tens = 300) and 3×40 (3×4 = 12, so 3×40 = 12 tens = 120), each time naming the known single-digit fact first.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 is multiplying by the single-digit fact and then by ten; the extra zero in the product is the result of every digit shifting one place left as the amount becomes ten times larger, not a zero 'stuck on the end'.

activityReferences.title: Property playground: rotate, split, regroup on one array
Split-area anchor for the distributive fact
Consolidate and sort: valid forms and the division trap

startingActivity.title: Property playground: rotate, split, regroup on one array
learnerActions: On an array/area canvas, meet an 'ugly' fact like 8×7. Drag a divider through the 7 to carve the array into 8×5 and 8×2; watch the two sub-rectangles light up as 40 and 16 and combine to 56.
Rotate the same array 90° and confirm the total does not change (8×7 = 7×8) — commutativity as 'same array, two orientations, same total'.
For three factors (2×3×5), toggle or drag the bracket between (2×3)×5 and 2×(3×5), and confirm the total holds — associativity as regrouping into an easier pair (6×5 or 2×15).

Switch to a division mode: swap the two numbers in a ÷ calculation (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 becomes 8÷32, which is less than 1) and see that the answer changes, then say in your own words why division is not commutative (32÷8 is not 8÷32).
Choose your own split for a new ugly fact (e.g. 8×9 = 8×5 + 8×4) and check the partial products add to the whole (40 + 32 = 72).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: In multiplication, reordering, regrouping and splitting change how a calculation is written without changing its total; a hard multiplication fact can be cut into two friendly facts and reassembled. This 'cut-the-hard-one-into-two-easy-ones' move is the distributive property, and it is the same move that formal written multiplication later makes compact. Division and subtraction are not commutative or associative, so swapping or regrouping their numbers can change the answer.

commonMisconceptions: Overgeneralising commutativity/associativity to division (32÷8 = 8×32; (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)).
Applying the distributive split incorrectly — e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 (forgetting to multiply the second part) or splitting the wrong factor.

Not seeing that the area model IS the distributive law, so written multiplication later feels disconnected.
Thinking reordering changes the answer, or conversely that any reordering is always allowed.
constraints: Teach these as strategies for efficient calculation, not as formal named laws to memorise; CCSS-M notes pupils need not know the property names.
Make explicit that division is NOT commutative or associative, and that subtraction is not either; use counterexamples so learners do not overgeneralise.
Guard against the additive-split error (8×7 = 8×5 + 2): both parts must be multiplied by the shared factor (8×5 + 8×2).

The static split-area anchor and the sort/fill tasks check and consolidate property use, but a fixed diagram cannot vary the split or regrouping across many cases; manipulable exploration across varied cases can let learners meet the invariance across many instances, so pair the static anchor and check tasks with it.
Recognition and fill-in tasks assess property use; they do not themselves elicit the learner independently choosing and justifying a strategy, which the dialogue and open splits target.
Three-factor associativity can suggest a cuboid, but that belongs to volume; keep properties-as-strategies work in planar arrays/area to avoid added manipulation cost and off-topic meaning.

startingActivity.title: Cover-and-solve with a fact-family triangle
learnerActions: Work with one trio of linked numbers, e.g. 6, 7 and 42 arranged on a fact-family triangle (42 at the top as the product; 6 and 7 at the bottom as the factors).
Cover one of the three numbers and decide: to find THIS number, do I multiply or divide? State your choice aloud before revealing.
Now cover a DIFFERENT number of the same trio and decide again. Notice when the operation flips: cover 42 (acting as product or dividend) → multiply 6×7; cover a factor like 7 → divide 42÷6.
Write the matching equation for each covered case: 6×?=42, ?×6=42, 42÷?=6, and ?÷6=7. Confirm the single trio solves them all.
Say in your own words: 'What I do — times or divide — is decided by WHERE the gap is, not by the numbers.'
If a bar model or balance view is available, use it to see which quantity (whole or part) is missing and recolour/update it as you solve.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The operation needed to find an unknown is determined by its position in the equation (missing factor → divide; missing dividend/product → multiply), and one fact family generates every related missing-number equation.

keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle — cover-a-number to choose the operation
Bar model — whole/part structure showing which quantity is missing
Balance/scale image — the relational equals sign
Inverse-rewrite chains (8×?=48 → 48÷8=?)
commonMisconceptions: Applying the same operation regardless of the unknown's position (e.g. always dividing), so a missing dividend is wrong.
Reading '=' operationally ('do something to get the answer') rather than as balance, mishandling 5 = ?÷3.
Treating division as commutative when rewriting (?÷5=9 → ?=5÷9).
Guess-and-check without using the inverse, which is slow and error-prone.
Not checking the answer back in the original equation.
constraints: Include unknowns in EVERY position (factor, product, dividend, divisor, quotient), not just missing products.
Always require checking by substituting the found value back into the original equation.
Emphasise the relational meaning of '=' (both sides balance), not 'the answer comes next', to prevent misreading reversed equations like 5=?÷3.
Division is not commutative: ?÷5=9 rearranges to ?=9×5, never 5÷9 or 9÷5. Correct this error directly rather than leaving it uncorrected.

A fill-in-the-blank or multiple-choice format is well suited to assessing across positions but, being fixed, tests the strategy more than it elicits the position-dependent reasoning; pair it with manipulable or verbalised work for teaching.
A static tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a clean strategy anchor but does not let the learner try many cases with feedback; use it alongside active practice.

Optional supports such as a bar model, a balance view, live recolouring of the missing quantity, or a hidden-card triangle make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Scaling studio: watch the known fact grow
learnerActions: Take 40×60 and name the known fact hiding inside it (4×6=24).
Place 24 on a place-value chart and scale it by ×100, watching the digits slide two columns to the left to make 2400 — because a ten times a ten makes a hundred, and both numbers contributed a ten.
Explain in units: '4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400', so the answer has two zeros, not one.
Try the same scaling move on a division: link 360÷9 to the known fact 36÷9=4, then scale by ×10 to get 40.
Contrast with a tricky case where a naive 'add a zero' rule would mislead (e.g. a decimal such as 0.4×60, which is 24, not 240) to feel why scaling by place value is the reliable idea.
Optionally use a live place-value chart where the digits visibly shift columns, rather than zeros simply appearing, to make the scaling felt.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying/dividing by tens and hundreds scales a known fact by place value; tens×tens makes hundreds, so the number of zeros follows from the place-value reasoning, not from a memorised 'append a zero' rule.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Known-fact-scaled-by-place-value chains (4×6 → 40×60 = 2400)

commonMisconceptions: 'Appending zeros' without place-value understanding, misfiring on decimals or miscounting zeros (40×60 as 240 or 24000).
Partitioning incorrectly (7×15 = 7×10 + 5, dropping the second multiplication).
Not using the inverse/related facts for division, computing from scratch.
Fixating on one strategy rather than choosing the most efficient.
Losing a place value in ÷ scaling (360÷9 as 4 rather than 40).
constraints: Keep ×÷ by tens/hundreds grounded as place-value scaling of a known fact, not 'append zeros' — the latter can lead to miscounted zeros (e.g. when the known fact already ends in zero, as in 50×40 = 2000) and fails on decimals.

startingActivity.title: Splitting a rectangle: area model for 13×4
learnerActions: Draw or view a rectangle 13 units wide and 4 units tall and cut it with a vertical line at the boundary between the tens and the ones, so it becomes a 10×4 piece and a 3×4 piece.
Work out the product for each piece (10×4 = 40 and 3×4 = 12) and write the number inside each region.
Add the two partial products to find the whole area: 40 + 12 = 52.

Line the grid up next to the expanded written form (40 + 12), saying which partial product matches which region of the grid. Then look at the compact column layout and explain how the 12 from 3×4 becomes 2 ones and a carried ten, which joins the 4 tens from 10×4 to make the 5 tens in 52.
Repeat with 23×4: split into 20×4 = 80 and 3×4 = 12, then combine to 92.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A two-digit × one-digit product is the sum of the partial products from each place-value part; the '10' in 13 contributes 10×4 = 40 (not 1×4), because you must multiply the whole value of the tens, not just its digit.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area model / grid method (distributive law made visible)
Partitioning into tens and ones
Arrays scaled up to the area model
Expanded then compact written layout
commonMisconceptions: Place-value error: treating the tens digit as ones (13×4 done as 1×4 + 3×4).
Forgetting to combine ALL partial products (computing 10×4 and 3×4 but not adding them).
Multiplying digit-by-digit without regard to their place value.
Not connecting the grid/area model to the numbers (seeing it as a separate trick).
Losing the link between the mental partition and the written record, so the written method becomes meaningless steps.
constraints: Known table facts are prerequisites: 10×4 and 3×4 (and similar) must be secure before combining them, and division work relies on known multiplication facts — reteach the relevant facts if they are shaky.

Progress in order — mental partitioning, then recorded grid, then expanded, then compact written form — keeping the link between stages explicit so children can fall back to meaning rather than memorising disconnected steps.
Keep place-value names attached throughout ('2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80') to pre-empt the error of multiplying bare digits.

A fixed, labelled diagram can show and teach the correspondence between grid and written method; being able to move the split line and watch partial products recompute is an added affordance for building the distributive insight interactively, not a claim that a static image cannot teach this.

Matching and fill-in checks can confirm whether the method and its pitfalls are grasped, but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the full method from scratch; pair them with building and explaining activities.

An area model is planar; use squared paper, cut-out rectangles, or a screen grid as convenient — none is uniquely necessary, and a paper cutout (which has slight real thickness) approximates the idealised flat area model well enough that this does not affect the mathematics.

startingActivity.title: Method bridge: area model beside the columns
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding a factor, e.g. for 234×5 use ≈200×5=1000 (or ≈50×6=300 for 47×6), and write the estimate down before calculating.
Draw an area/grid model splitting a factor by place value: for 234×5 make three sub-rectangles 200×5, 30×5 and 4×5; for 47×6 make 40×6 and 7×6.
Set out the same calculation in a short-multiplication column layout right next to the area model.

Work each partial product in the columns in lockstep with the matching sub-rectangle. For 234×5: 5×4=20 → write 0 in the ones and regroup 2 tens; 5×3=15, +2=17 → write 7 in the tens, regroup 1 hundred; 5×2=10, +1=11 → write 1 in the hundreds and 1 in the thousands, giving 1170.
Say aloud what each carried digit means, e.g. 'the little 2 is 2 regrouped tens'.
Add the area sub-products (1000+150+20=1170) and check they equal the columnar answer exactly.
Compare the finished answer against your estimate; if it is off by a factor of ten, look for a misaligned column.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The carried digits are the area model regrouped and folded into columns — multiply the digit first, THEN add the carry, keeping one digit per column.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area/grid model (partition each factor by place value) — the conceptual home of short multiplication
Place-value columns with counters — makes carrying = regrouping visible
The compact columnar layout with the carry digit recorded
Estimation on a number line / rounding — to bound the answer
commonMisconceptions: Treating carrying as a meaningless ritual and misplacing or forgetting the carried digit.
Multiplying only the ones and 'adding' the tens digit rather than multiplying it (place-value error): 47×6 giving 42+... wrong.
Aligning digits incorrectly or dropping a place, producing answers off by a factor of 10.
Not connecting the compact method to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.
Skipping estimation, so a wildly wrong magnitude goes unnoticed.
constraints: Build the algorithm from the area/grid model (47×6 = 40×6 + 7×6) before compressing to columns; do not teach column carrying as disconnected digit-manipulation.
Always require an estimate before calculating (round a factor) to set expected magnitude and help catch place-value slips.
Multiply the digit first, THEN add the carried number; do not add the carry before multiplying.
Only one digit per column; the regrouped ten/hundred travels one place left.
The written method assumes automatic recall of the relevant table facts; if single-digit products are slow or wrong, shore those up separately.
Recognition and fill-in items consolidate and assess but do not, on their own, elicit a learner independently setting out and carrying a full calculation — pair them with full worked practice.
Worked examples and annotated references anchor the structure but do not give feedback on the learner's own fresh calculation.

startingActivity.title: Bridge the area model to the written method (34 × 27)
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding both factors: 34 × 27 ≈ 30 × 30 = 900, and keep this estimate in view as you work.
Draw an area model for 34 × 27 and partition it into four labelled sub-rectangles: 30×20, 30×7, 4×20, 4×7.
Alongside, set up the long-multiplication layout and compute the first partial product 34 × 7 = 238 (which is the 30×7 and 4×7 tiles: 210 + 28).
Compute the second partial product 34 × 20 = 680, writing a 0 in the ones place FIRST because this whole row is ×20, i.e. tens (this is the 30×20 and 4×20 tiles: 600 + 80).
Add the two partial products: 238 + 680 = 918, and confirm it matches the sum of all four area tiles (600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918).
Check the result against your estimate of 900 — are they close?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The second partial-product row is shifted and carries a placeholder zero because it is ×20 (tens), not ×2; the four area sub-rectangles are exactly the same quantities as the two written partial products broken apart, so the algorithm and the area model are two views of the same calculation.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area/grid model with four sub-rectangles (the home of the partial products)
Expanded partial-products layout bridging grid to compact form
Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the second partial product (treating ×20 as ×2).
Multiplying only by the ones digit of the two-digit multiplier and forgetting the tens.
Carrying errors across several columns, or adding carries into the wrong place.
Misaligning partial products when adding them.
Not connecting the algorithm to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.
constraints: Recognition and fill-in/spot-the-error tasks consolidate the procedure but do not elicit the child independently constructing an area model and mapping it to the written method; use them after, not instead of, the bridging construction work.

Annotated static worked examples (area model above, written method below, tap to reveal each partial product's region) are useful reference scaffolds, but a fixed example cannot give feedback on a child's own fresh calculation or their own placeholder-zero error — pair them with tasks the child computes.

Spoken dialogue alone lacks a shared visible written layout, so it cannot display aligned columns or reliably catch column-placement errors in this spatial, multi-step procedure; keep a written/drawn layout at the centre rather than relying on talk alone (this is a layout-affordance limit, not a claim that dialogue can never support the procedure).

The area model is a conceptual scaffold for place value; the goal is eventual fluent compact long multiplication with the area link available for self-diagnosis, not permanent dependence on drawing grids.
Treat carrying/alignment slips as performance errors (re-estimate and recheck the flagged column) rather than reteaching the whole method.

startingActivity.title: Sliding digits on a place-value chart
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with labelled columns from hundreds down to thousandths (… H  T  O • t  h  th) and a fixed decimal point.
Place 3.45 in the columns, then multiply by 100: slide every digit TWO columns to the LEFT so the 3, 4 and 5 become 345. Note that nothing was appended — the digits moved.
Now test the tempting 'just add two zeros' shortcut on 3.45 and compare: it gives 3.4500, which is wrong. Discuss why the shortcut fails for decimals.
Divide 72 by 1000: slide every digit THREE columns to the RIGHT, and fill each empty column it crosses with a placeholder zero, giving 0.072 (including the leading 0).
Compute 6 × 10 by sliding one place left (giving 60), and connect the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 (×1000 → 3 places).
Optionally switch the chart to a metric mode so the same kind of shift is reread as a conversion: metres → centimetres is ×100 (two places left) and centimetres → millimetres is ×10 (one place left).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten changes what each digit is worth, so the digits shift the matching number of place-value columns; the decimal point does not move, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart with sliding digits (point fixed)
Arrow/shift diagram showing 1/2/3 places for 10/100/1000
Decimal place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Metric conversion tables as an application
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero' rule misapplied to decimals (3.45×100 wrongly written as 3.4500).
'Move the decimal point' causing confusion about direction or number of places.
Shifting the wrong number of places for the power of ten.
Forgetting to fill empty places with zeros as placeholders when needed (e.g. 72÷1000 = 0.072).
Thinking dividing always makes the digits smaller in value without understanding the place shift.
constraints: Teach the operation as a digit shift across place-value columns (left for ×, right for ÷), not as 'add a zero' or 'move the decimal point': 'add a zero' gives wrong answers for decimals, and 'move the decimal point', although it gives the same numerical result, hides the change in place value and is easily misapplied to whole numbers and placeholder zeros.
Always fill empty columns crossed by a shift with placeholder zeros, including leading zeros (e.g. 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072).
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through dividing by 10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful before relying on them.
Link the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and, later, to exponent notation.

Reference charts and multiple-choice / fill-in items consolidate, check and diagnose whether digit-shift reasoning transfers, but do not themselves provide the sliding manipulation; pair them with active manipulation rather than treating them as sufficient alone.

A manipulable sliding chart, a static annotated chart, a dialogue, and consolidation items each serve a different observable purpose; none is inherently sufficient alone, and no claim is established here that only one medium can teach this.

startingActivity.title: Share the columns: short division with place-value counters
learnerActions: Lay out 4932 as place-value counters: 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones.

Share each column left to right into 6 equal groups, starting with the thousands (4 thousands won't make a group of 6, so that place gives 0 — exchange the 4 thousands for 40 hundreds and carry them on).

When a column won't share evenly, exchange each leftover counter for ten counters of the next-lower place and add them to that column (e.g. a spare hundred becomes ten tens that join the tens column).
Record the quotient digit for each place above the bus-stop layout as you go, and write the carried amount beside the next digit.
When the divisor won't go into a place at all, write 0 in the quotient for that place and carry the whole amount onward — do not skip the place.
Finish with 4932 ÷ 6 = 822 and note there is no remainder here; then repeat with a dividend that leaves a remainder.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The 'carried remainder' of the written short-division method is the same idea as regrouping/exchanging place-value counters: a leftover in one column is worth ten of the next place down. Every place of the dividend produces a quotient digit, including a 0 when the divisor won't go.

keyRepresentations: Short-division ('bus stop') layout with carried remainders
Place-value counters/columns — exchanging the remainder into the next place
Array/area with an unknown dimension — division as inverse of ×
Number line / bar model for remainder interpretation in context
commonMisconceptions: Mishandling the remainder carry — not moving it to the next place or adding it wrongly.
Interpreting the remainder wrongly for the context (rounding down when you must round up, e.g. minibuses).
Dropping a place when the digit is smaller than the divisor (not writing the 0 and carrying).
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.
Treating short division as digit-manipulation divorced from place value/sharing meaning.
constraints: Short division must be grounded in place-value exchange: present 'carrying the remainder' as regrouping a leftover into ten of the next-lower place, not as an isolated digit trick.
Every digit of the dividend must yield a quotient digit, including writing 0 (and carrying the whole amount) when the divisor won't go into a place — explicitly teach this 'won't go' case.

Interpret the remainder according to the context (round up, round down, keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal); the same calculation can give different correct answers in different stories, so demonstrate all three readings on ONE division.
Always check with the inverse (quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend) and against an estimate; estimates should round to friendly numbers without deflating the divisor.

Multiple-choice or spot-the-error items can assess procedure and interpretation (e.g. '52 children, minibuses of 9 — how many buses?'), but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit the learner independently running their own division or exchanging counters; pair them with learner-produced working.
Discussion-only activities may support remainder interpretation but do not themselves rehearse the written layout, so combine them with worked division.
Place-value counters (physical or on-screen) are an approximation that makes exchange concrete; the written bus-stop layout is the target notation the learner must ultimately produce.

startingActivity.title: Method-chooser: the same division, two ways
learnerActions: Solve 3648÷16 using short division ('bus stop' layout), using a list of multiples of 16 (16, 32, 48, 160, 1600, …) to support the multiply-subtract step at each place.
Solve the SAME calculation 3648÷16 using long division, writing out each multiply-subtract step.
Compare the two side by side and state which was quicker for THIS divisor and why.
Now try a divisor many learners find awkward, e.g. 4080÷17, by short division; notice whether and where holding multiples of 17 mentally becomes error-prone.
Solve 4080÷17 again by long division and compare how reliable each felt.
State a rule of thumb in your own words: when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold, short division is efficient; when they are hard, long division is safer.
Estimate first (e.g. 3600÷16 ≈ 225) and check the final answer by multiplying the quotient back (228×16 = 3648?).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Whether short or long division is the better tool depends on how friendly the divisor is, not on habit — and you can experience this trade-off by doing the same calculation both ways. Both methods are legitimate; the skill is choosing and justifying.

startingActivity.title: Step-by-step long multiplication with an estimate check
learnerActions: Before calculating, estimate 2463×37 by rounding both factors: 2500×40 = 100000, and write this down as the expected ballpark.
Work 2463×37 by long multiplication, writing the ×ones row (2463×7 = 17241) and the ×tens row underneath.
When starting the ×tens row, write the placeholder zero in the ones column first, then multiply by 3 tens to get 73890.
Add the two rows: 17241 + 73890 = 91131, keeping the columns aligned.
Compare the final answer with your estimate of ~100000 — 91131 is in the right ballpark, so the magnitude is plausible.
At each step, check that any carry is jotted above the correct column and added into the next multiplication.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each partial-product row multiplies the whole of 2463 by a part of 37 (by 7 ones, then by 30), and the rows are added to recombine the parts. The placeholder zero is there because the second row is really ×30, not ×3. The estimate bounds the answer's size, so a lost zero shows up as a clearly wrong magnitude. A carry slip usually changes only one or two digits and can still look plausible, so it has to be caught by checking the working itself.

startingActivity.title: Slide the digits across a place-value chart
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns from thousands down to ten-thousandths, with the decimal point marked fixed at the ones boundary (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths ten-thousandths); the extra low columns are needed because 45.2 ÷ 1000 lands a digit in the ten-thousandths place.
Write 3.456 into the chart using digit cards, then multiply by 100: slide EVERY digit two columns to the LEFT in one move, keeping the point pinned in place, to land on 345.6.

Now take 45.2 and divide by 1000: slide every digit three columns to the RIGHT (the tenths digit travels into the ten-thousandths column), and write a placeholder 0 into each emptied column that is written (ones and tenths) to get 0.0452.
Say aloud for each step: 'the digits moved ___ places ___ because I multiplied/divided by ___', linking the number of places to the power of ten.
Try a target challenge: starting from 3.456, work out which single operation reaches 345.6, and which reaches 0.3456.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten moves every digit a fixed number of place-value columns while the decimal point stays put; the number of columns equals the number of zeros in the power of ten, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with sliding digit cards spanning thousands to thousandths and the decimal point fixed at the ones boundary.
Left/right shift arrows annotated with the power of ten (×10 = 1 left, ×100 = 2 left, ÷1000 = 3 right).
Gattegno chart (rows of ×10 scaling) to show a digit jumping between rows as it is multiplied/divided by powers of ten.
Zoom / 'ten-times' number line to reinforce that ×10 makes the whole quantity ten times as large, not merely longer to write.
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero when you multiply by 10' — wrong for decimals (2.5 × 10 ≠ 2.50) and a source of place-value damage.
'Move the decimal point' — leads to moving the point the wrong way or mispositioning it; the point is fixed, the digits move.
Omitting placeholder zeros when dividing (45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 or .0452 rather than 0.0452).
Confusing the DIRECTION: multiplying making the number smaller (shifting right) or dividing making it larger.
Shifting only one digit or the wrong number of places, especially for ×/÷1000 (three places).
constraints: Explicitly teach 'digits move, the point stays' and avoid 'add a zero' because it gives wrong results for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40). Do not lead with 'move the decimal point': it gives the same answers, but it hides the place-value reason, and the point is better treated as a fixed marker of the ones place.

Placeholder zeros must be confronted directly: when division empties columns, a 0 must hold each written vacated place (0.0452 has zeros in the ones — by convention — and tenths), and answers like 0.452 or .0452 should not pass unaddressed.
Match the number of places shifted to the power of ten (×/÷10 = one place, ×/÷100 = two, ×/÷1000 = three) and keep direction correct (× shifts left/bigger, ÷ shifts right/smaller).
Provide a chart with enough low columns for the task: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 needs a ten-thousandths column, so the chart should extend beyond thousandths for the division example.
Recognition and fill-in tasks check fluency but do not by themselves build the shift image; pair them with enacted chart work.

Discussion/dialogue activities can surface and challenge misconceptions and can accompany the enacted chart work; they need not be treated as the only route, but the curriculum concept here centres on the learner performing the digit shift.

Paper or card digit cards used on a chart have slight physical thickness and are approximations of the abstract place-value idea; an on-screen chart with sliding digits is a model of the same relationship — both are legitimate ways to enact the shift.

startingActivity.title: Multi-step problem workbench: plan, carry, interpret
learnerActions: Read a genuinely two-step problem where step 1's result feeds step 2 — e.g. 'A trip needs 52 children transported in minibuses holding 9; each minibus costs £20. What is the total cost?' (first find the number of minibuses, then multiply by the cost). Note: the pencil problem 'packs of 6 pencils for £1.50 each — how much do 5 packs cost?' is solved in a single step (5 × £1.50 = £7.50; the pack size 6 is not needed), so use it for operation-choice practice, not for carrying an intermediate result.
Lay out a bar model for step 1, record the intermediate result, then build a second bar model for step 2 on top of that result rather than restarting.
Write an equation that matches the plan, using a letter such as n for the unknown.
Before computing a final figure, state an estimate of what a reasonable answer looks like.
Compute, then check: does the answer match your estimate, and does the inverse operation confirm it?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A multi-step problem is solved by planning a sequence of operations and carrying the output of one step into the next; the equals sign expresses relationships, and an up-front estimate plus an inverse check catch magnitude and step errors.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model — planning and structuring multi-step problems
Equation with a letter for the unknown (n) — abstracting the plan
Number line / rounding — estimation and reasonableness check
Context frames for remainder interpretation (buses, bags, sharing)
commonMisconceptions: Doing only one step of a multi-step problem, or losing the intermediate result.
Interpreting the remainder wrongly for the context (rounding down the minibus count).
Key-word guessing the operation instead of reasoning from structure.
Not checking reasonableness, so magnitude/step errors go unnoticed.
Writing an equation that doesn't match the problem, or misusing '=' operationally across multiple steps.
constraints: Use multi-step problems where step 1's output is genuinely needed for step 2, so learners practise holding and carrying intermediate results — the core difficulty of the objective. The single-step pencil/cost problem does not serve this purpose and should be used only for operation-choice practice.
Require a real-world answer to remainder problems (whole minibuses, whole teams, or a justified fraction/decimal); a bare 'r7' is not an acceptable final answer.
Do not teach a fixed remainder rule ('always round up' or 'always drop'); the treatment must be driven by the specific context.
Require an estimate up front and a reasonableness/inverse check at the end, not only a computed number.

Recognition and matching tasks (quiz-style) can check operation choice, equation-matching and estimation and can be used during teaching, but they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a plan or bar model.
Discussion and worked-exemplar activities support reasoning and provide models but do not substitute for the learner independently building bar models and equations on new problems.

Optional interactive supports — a bar-model builder that carries the intermediate result forward, a context-interpreter where the learner sets round up / drop / keep / fraction to match the story (e.g. dragging in a 6th bus to seat the stranded 7 children), an equation strip for placing a letter for the unknown, and an estimate meter that flags unreasonable answers (e.g. an answer of '5 r7' or '5.8 minibuses', or a total cost far from the estimate) — make the mechanism concrete but are illustrative, not required.

startingActivity.title: Long-division workbench with a multiples menu (4752÷13)
learnerActions: Set up 4752 ÷ 13 in the long-division layout.
Before dividing, build a side menu of multiples of 13 (13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117) to consult when estimating each quotient digit.

At each step, use the menu to decide how many 13s fit (e.g. 'how many 13s in 47?' → 3 because 39 ≤ 47 < 52), write that quotient digit above the correct column, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

If the working number after bringing down is ever smaller than 13, write a 0 in the quotient for that place and bring down the next digit. This does not happen in 4752 ÷ 13 (the working numbers are 47, 85 and 72), so practise it on an example such as 3913 ÷ 13 = 301.
Finish with the remainder 7, then reframe it three ways: as the fraction 7/13 (remainder over divisor), as a decimal continuation (≈365.54), and rounded to suit a context.
Check the whole answer by computing 365×13 + 7 and confirming it equals 4752.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Long division by a 2-digit divisor is a repeating estimate–multiply–subtract–bring-down cycle; a multiples menu replaces the recalled facts you no longer have, and the same single division can yield several correct answers depending on how the remainder is interpreted.

Chunking / partial-quotients layout (repeated subtraction of multiples)

Place-value errors in the quotient (dropping a place when the divisor doesn't fit).
Mishandling the remainder — wrong fraction denominator, or wrong rounding direction for the context.
Bring-down/subtraction slips propagating through the calculation.
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.
constraints: Fraction, decimal, and rounded interpretations of the remainder must all be practised, not just a whole-number remainder; the context determines which is appropriate.
Chunking/partial-quotients is a legitimate method and transparent bridge, not just a crutch to discard; keep it available alongside the compact algorithm.
A multiples menu is a scaffold for estimation; the goal is for the child eventually to estimate quotient digits reliably, including writing a 0 when the divisor doesn't fit a brought-down value.

A tap-to-reveal worked example or multiple-choice item can serve as a reference or assessment, but recognition/reveal formats do not by themselves elicit the child's own estimation and self-correction cycle; include construction where the child does the dividing.

startingActivity.title: Round it right: scenarios where the rounding move has consequences
learnerActions: Compute a problem that yields a raw decimal, e.g. 80 people needing 15-seat buses: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.33 (to 2 d.p.).
Choose a rounding move — round to the nearest whole, round down, or round up — and, where relevant, to which place.
Play out or describe the result of your choice in the situation: rounding to the nearest whole (5 buses) seats only 75 and leaves 5 people stranded at the kerb; rounding up to 6 buses seats everyone.
State in words why context (needing to carry everyone), not the deciding digit, forces rounding up here: the deciding digit (the 3 in 5.33) would round down to 5, yet the situation needs 6.
Repeat with a 'round down' context, e.g. 'How many complete 50 cm lengths can be cut from 3.4 m?' 340 ÷ 50 = 6.8 → 6 complete lengths, not 7, even though 6.8 is nearer to 7.
Repeat with a 'nearest' context where the plain rule does apply, e.g. 'round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place' → 7.8.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The context — what the answer is used for — decides whether you round up, down, or to the nearest, and this can override the mechanical nearest-value rule.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with the answer marked between the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint, to justify nearest-value rounding.
Context decision card: the problem, the raw answer, and a choice of round up / down / nearest with the reason.
Place-value view highlighting the digit being rounded and the deciding digit to its right.
Real-world icons (coins to the penny, containers that must be whole) anchoring why context overrides the plain rule.
commonMisconceptions: Applying the nearest-value rule when context demands rounding up ('need 3.2 buses' → answering 3 instead of 4) or down ('how many whole boxes fill' → rounding up wrongly).
Rounding at intermediate steps and accumulating error into the final answer.
Rounding to the wrong place, or using the wrong deciding digit (looking two places along).
Giving impossible precision for the context (money to 3dp, a count of people as a decimal).
Truncating (chopping digits) instead of rounding, e.g. 3.68 to 1dp given as 3.6.
constraints: A sorting/categorisation or multiple-choice format can rehearse and check which rounding move fits, but on its own it does not require the learner to carry out the full compute-then-interpret problem or explain the reasoning — pair it with worked problems and justification.
A static number-line reference supports the rounding mechanic but does not let learners play out contextual consequences; use it alongside scenario and discussion work.
Treat animated scenario outcomes as one way to make consequences visible; the same insight can come from drawing, acting out, or discussing what happens to the extra people/units.
Distinguish arithmetic slips from rounding misconceptions: if the rounding logic is right but the division is wrong, have the child recompute and re-round rather than reteaching rounding.

Choose scenario numbers so the intended teaching point is genuine: to show context overriding the plain rule, a 'round up' context needs a fractional part below .5 (e.g. 5.33 → 6 needed), and a 'round down' context needs a fractional part of .5 or more (e.g. 6.8 → 6 complete lengths); otherwise the rule and the context agree and no override is demonstrated.

activityReferences.title: Factors-and-multiples explorer (three linked modes)

Is it prime? Decide and justify the stopping point

startingActivity.title: Factors-and-multiples explorer (three linked modes)
learnerActions: Factor mode: for a chosen number N (e.g. 36), form every possible rectangle (array) of N counters and log each pair of side-lengths as a factor pair on a factor rainbow — e.g. (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6).
Explain how you know you have found them all: pairs are logged from the outside in, and once you reach the square root the pairs repeat, so the set is complete.

Multiple mode: set one number line to skip-count in 7 and read off the first five multiples (7,14,21,28,35); then set two adjustable number lines to skip-count in 6 and 8, watch where the hops coincide, and record the first THREE common multiples (24, 48, 72) — the first collision is at 24.

Common mode: set two numbers (e.g. 24 and 36), pour each factor list into a two-set Venn diagram, slide the shared factors into the overlap, and identify the largest shared factor (12) as the highest common factor; then repeat with 36 and 48 (shared factors 1,2,3,4,6,12, highest common factor 12).
State in words what 'common' means here: a factor or multiple shared by BOTH numbers — the intersection of the two sets.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 'Common' literally means the overlap of two sets; completeness of a factor list comes from systematic pairing around the square root; and the first common multiple is the first place two skip-counts collide. Factors are finite and divide into a number (rectangle side-lengths), while multiples are infinite times-table hops.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — factors as side lengths (factor rainbow for completeness)
Number line / multiplication-grid rows — multiples as skip-count hops
Two-set overlap / Venn diagram — common factors and common multiples
Factor and multiple lists side by side to spot the intersection
commonMisconceptions: Confusing factors with multiples (factor of 12 vs multiple of 12).
Missing factor pairs through unsystematic searching, especially middle ones and the number itself/1.
Thinking there is a 'largest multiple' or a 'smallest factor other than 1' confusion.
Treating 'common' loosely rather than as shared between BOTH numbers.
Forgetting 1 is a common factor of every pair, or that the numbers themselves are factors.
constraints: Target age 9–11; coverage: all factor pairs for numbers 1–100, common factors and common multiples of two numbers, and using these to solve problems, with prime/composite as a related discrimination.
Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each) and stop near the square root, using commutativity to confirm the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Treat 'common' strictly as shared between BOTH numbers (the intersection of two sets), not loosely.
Remember 1 is a common factor of every pair, the number itself is a factor, and there is no 'largest multiple'.
Define prime as exactly two distinct factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.

Ground work in problems (arranging rows, coinciding events, sharing into equal groups), not just listing, and link explicitly to simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), and later HCF/LCM and ratio.

The static rainbow/Venn and the quiz are scaffolds and checks: they let a learner read off or recognise answers but do not themselves require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers. Use them after, or alongside, active construction.

The interactive examples (dragging counters into rectangles, adjustable number lines whose hops light up on coincidence, factor lists pouring into a Venn with the largest shared factor highlighted) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper factor rainbows, two written multiple lists, and a hand-drawn Venn.

startingActivity.title: Re-factoring: turn an ugly product into a friendly one
learnerActions: Face a product such as 24×25 and, before calculating, ask: which factors could pair up to make a round number?
Split one factor and re-group: pull a 4 out of 24 (so 24 = 6×4) and pair it with 25 to make 4×25 = 100, leaving 6×100 = 600.
Confirm the total is unchanged by the rearrangement — only the grouping changed, not the value (associativity).
Try the same move on 16×25 (= 4×(4×25) = 4×100 = 400) and other products with a friendly hidden factor.
State in words why the shortcut works and when it does NOT help (if no factor pairs to a round number).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fearsome-looking product often never needs a written algorithm: spotting a friendly factor pair (like 4×25 = 100) and using associativity collapses it to a one-step mental calculation. Rearranging factors leaves the total unchanged.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Factor rainbow / factor pairs — the re-factoring toolkit
Divisibility-rule checklist — reasoning about multiples
Array/area re-partition — showing 24×25 as 6×(4×25)
Squares/cubes list — search space for sum/target puzzles
commonMisconceptions: Grinding the standard algorithm instead of spotting a factor-pair shortcut.
Misapplying divisibility rules (e.g. thinking any even number is a multiple of 6).
Re-factoring incorrectly (breaking associativity: 24×25 ≠ 24×4×25).
Confusing factors, multiples, squares and cubes when selecting a tool.
Not justifying membership/answers, so errors go unchecked.
constraints: Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks (e.g. 'is 156 a multiple of 6?' with justification options, 'the smartest way to compute 16×25', 'two squares summing to 100') are useful for checking divisibility judgements and strategy choice, especially with distractors built from the mis-applied-rule and wrong-re-factor errors; but recognition-only responses check rather than elicit the learner's own re-grouping, so pair them with tasks where the learner constructs the re-grouping themselves.

A worked gallery of shortcut exemplars (e.g. revealing the 6×(4×25) re-group) and a divisibility-rule reference card are helpful references, but the skill requires applying structure to NEW problems, which fixed exemplars alone do not demand.

A Socratic 'is there a cleverer way than the algorithm?' dialogue can build the strategic habit and prompt justification; the re-factoring step may be clearer when learners can physically rearrange the factors themselves, though this comparative benefit is untested here.
When re-grouping a product, a factor must be split before it is moved: 24×25 = (6×4)×25 = 6×(4×25). Writing 24×4×25 changes the value and is wrong.
Require justification and checking, not just an answer, so errors (such as a miscalculated digit sum) are caught; distinguish a strategy error from an arithmetic slip and respond accordingly.

Interactive re-grouping (e.g. dragging a factor to form a round number, or a panel showing instant pass/fail against each divisibility rule) is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required mechanism.

startingActivity.title: Rectangle-building: when is only 1×n possible?
learnerActions: Take a number and try to arrange that many counters (or squares on grid paper) into complete rectangles with more than one row and more than one column (a single line, 1×n, does not count as another rectangle).
For 51, find that a 3×17 rectangle can be built, so 51 has factors other than 1 and itself — it is composite.

For 97, try rows of 2, 3, 5 and 7 — the primes up to its square root (just under 10), since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested — and find that only a single 1×97 line forms, so 97 is prime.
Try the number 1: it forms only a single 1×1 square — one factor — so it fits neither the prime nor the composite group.
Record each verdict with its factor pair as justification (e.g. '51 = 3×17, composite'; '97, only 1×97, prime').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A prime number can only be made into the 1×n rectangle (exactly two factors); a composite makes at least one other rectangle; and 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only a single factor.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair)
Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square — crossing out multiples leaves the primes

Divisibility-rule checks up to the square root
commonMisconceptions: Believing 1 is prime (it has only one factor — it is neither).
Thinking all odd numbers are prime (9, 15, 21, 51 are composite) or that 2 isn't prime because it's even.
Classifying by 'feel' without checking factors/divisibility.
Checking divisibility inefficiently (testing all numbers, not just primes to the square root).
Confusing 'prime factor' with 'factor' — not every factor is prime.
constraints: A pre-made, tap-to-reveal hundred square and definition card are useful as a reference and primes-to-19 memory aid, but do not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or run the sieve themselves; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on building.

Multiple-choice or categorisation tasks (prime / composite / neither, 'is 51 prime?') verify recognition and recall but do not by themselves build the rectangle/sieve intuition; pair recognition with construction and justification.
Always require a factor justification ('51 = 3×17 so composite'), not just a prime/composite label.
Distinguish 'factor' from 'prime factor': not every factor is prime.
The definition is exact and fragile — a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor and is neither; 2 is prime despite being even.

activityReferences.title: Growing squares: why 7² is not 7×2
Building a cube: what 'cubed' really means
Reading and recalling the notation

startingActivity.title: Growing squares: why 7² is not 7×2
learnerActions: Build or draw an n×n square array for a chosen n and count the total cells, writing it as n².
Start small and step n up: 1 (1 cell), 2 (a 2×2 of 4), 3 (a 3×3 of 9), 4 (a 4×4 of 16). Write each as 1², 2², 3², 4².
Build a 7×7 square (49 cells) and, beside it, a separate 7×2 rectangle (14 cells); compare the two by eye — note that 7² = 49 is far larger than 7×2 = 14.
Say out loud what the little 2 means: 'how many 7s are multiplied together', i.e. 7×7, NOT 'multiply 7 by 2'.
Notice how much is added each time n grows by one: the totals jump 1, 4, 9, 16, and the gaps are 3, 5, 7 — successive odd numbers.
Plot each square number onto the diagonal of a multiplication table (where the row number equals the column number) and see that square numbers are the products of a number with itself.

Optionally notice that a square number has an odd number of factors — e.g. 9 has factors 1, 3, 9 (three of them) — because its square root is a repeated factor that pairs with itself instead of a different partner.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: n² means an n×n square array (its area), not n×2. The notation is a picture of a square, and square numbers are the products of equal factors that lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: n×n square array — area meaning of n²
n×n×n cube of unit cubes — volume meaning of n³
Multiplication-table diagonal — the square numbers
Notation cards linking 7² = 7×7 = 49 and 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64
commonMisconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 (7²=14) and n³ as n×3 (4³=12).
Confusing squared and cubed, or the notation ²/³.
Thinking of square/cube numbers as arbitrary lists rather than areas/volumes.
Believing squaring always makes a much bigger number without the geometric picture (surprised by 1²=1).
Not recognising square numbers as products of a number with itself (table diagonal).
constraints: Tie ² and ³ to geometric meaning: n² as an n×n square's area, n³ as an n×n×n cube's volume, so the names and notation make sense rather than being arbitrary labels.
Directly confront the exponent-as-multiplier error by showing 7² (a 7×7 array of 49) alongside 7×2 (14), and 4³ (64) rather than 4×3 (12).
Distinguish squared from cubed by number of equal factors (two vs three) and by shape (flat area vs solid volume).

Recognition/recall practice (matching, fill-in, multiple choice) tests and consolidates but does not by itself build the area/volume meaning — use it after or alongside construction, not instead of it.
Include 1² = 1 so learners see squaring does not always make a much larger number.

Expectations by stage: at age 9, read/write ² and ³ and compute small cases as repeated equal multiplication; by age 9–10, list the first ten squares and explain 7² as a 7×7 square; by age 10, explain why n² ≠ n×2, connect squares to the multiplication-table diagonal, and cubes to volume.

Physical unit cubes and build-it screen models offer different experiences; either can make 'cubed' spatial. A flat drawing can still show and teach the square meaning even though it cannot be dragged to vary n.

activityReferences.title: Prime factory: build the tree, discover uniqueness
Venn organiser for HCF and LCM
Reference anchor: reveal the index form and the Venn result

Socratic challenge: why is factorisation unique and why 1 isn't prime

startingActivity.title: Prime factory: build the tree, discover uniqueness
learnerActions: Take a number such as 360 and repeatedly split it into a factor pair (e.g. 4 × 90), then keep splitting each branch until every leaf is a prime.
Collect the prime leaves and write them in index form: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
Now build 360 a second time starting from a different first split (e.g. 8 × 45 instead of 4 × 90). Record the prime leaves again.
Lay the two sets of prime leaves side by side and check: the trees branched differently, but the collected primes are identical (2³ × 3² × 5 both times).
Check each tree for composite leaves left unsplit (e.g. a 4 or a 9 that should become 2×2 or 3×3) and finish splitting them.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime 'fingerprint': the order and shape of the splits do not change which primes (and how many of each) you end up with. Composite leaves must be fully broken down before the factorisation is complete.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Factor tree branching a number down to its prime leaves, then collected into index form.
Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors: intersection → HCF, union (whole diagram) → LCM.
Index-notation product (360 = 2³ × 3² × 5) as the number's unique 'prime fingerprint'.
Prime-factor tiles/counters that can be regrouped to show different trees yield the same multiset of primes.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a number can have different prime factorisations depending on how the tree is drawn (missing the uniqueness property).
Treating 1 as prime, or including 1 in a factorisation.
Confusing HCF with LCM (taking the largest common multiple or smallest common factor), or muddling which is 'highest' vs 'lowest'.
Taking the highest index for HCF / lowest for LCM (rule reversed).
Stopping a factor tree at composite leaves (e.g. leaving 4 or 6 unfactored) so the factorisation isn't fully prime.
constraints: 1 is neither prime nor composite and never appears in a prime factorisation; primes are the multiplicative 'atoms'.
A factor tree is only finished when every leaf is prime — composite leaves (4, 6, 9, …) must be split further.
HCF takes the LOWEST power of each shared prime; LCM takes the HIGHEST power of each prime present. These are different selections and are easy to reverse — guard against the swap explicitly.

A common factor is built only from primes BOTH numbers share; a prime appearing in just one number cannot be part of it. Where two numbers share all their primes (e.g. 24 and 36), the only error to guard is taking too high a power, not an unshared prime.
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers holds for a pair; use it as a check, not as a definition.

Reveal-on-tap worked trees/Venns are reference anchors: they show the format and region logic but cannot be re-split or re-grouped, so they do not by themselves demonstrate uniqueness — pair them with learner-built trees.
Consolidation checks test results (recognition/recall) and do not elicit independent construction of the decomposition or the uniqueness reasoning.

Index notation should be connected to prior powers/indices work, and HCF/LCM grounded in motivating problems (sharing into equal groups for HCF; repeating events and fraction denominators for LCM) so the concepts have purpose.

Optional live/drag interactions (dragging shared prime tiles into a Venn overlap, auto-collecting leaves into index form) are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms, and their effectiveness relative to static anchors is not established.

startingActivity.title: Build the distributive law with a lettered area rectangle
learnerActions: Draw or display a rectangle that is 3 tall and (n+5) wide.
Split the width into an n-part and a 5-part, making two strips: a 3-by-n strip and a 3-by-5 strip.
Label the strips 3n and 15 (because 3×5=15) and write the whole area as 3(n+5)=3n+15.
Deliberately try the tempting wrong answer 3n+5 by multiplying only the n-strip, then look for what area is left unaccounted for.
Identify the missing 3×5 block as the reason 3n+5 is wrong, and state why the 3 must act on BOTH terms.
Check with a number: let n=2, so 3×(2+5)=21, 3n+15=21, but 3n+5=11.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Distribution multiplies every term inside the bracket, not just the first; the area of the whole rectangle equals the sum of the two strips, so 3(n+5)=3n+15 is built, not memorised.

commonMisconceptions: Distributes over the first term only: 3(n+5) = 3n+5 (multiplier not applied to the second term)
Treats the letter as an object or label ('n is a name') rather than a number, or conjoins 3n+5 into 8n

constraints: A multiple-choice or true/false check using the 3(n+5)=3n+5 wrong-answer option and hierarchy items can surface and check classification errors, but a correct selection can mask shaky reasoning; always pair it with a 'why' justification step, since recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own construction or explanation.

A tap-to-reveal poster or pre-built annotated split is a reference scaffold only: it does not let the learner produce the wrong 3n+5 split and see the missing block, so it should supplement, not replace, learner-constructed partitioning.

Dialogue alone provides no written symbols or diagram for the learner to partition; structural reading of expressions is better supported when the symbols and a structure-revealing representation (such as the area model) are visible to act on — an affordance observation, not a claim that dialogue can never contribute.

The optional interactive version (a lettered area-model splitter where dragging a divider cleaves the rectangle into a labelled 3n strip and a 3×5 strip, plus a linked hierarchy tree that highlights inherited properties on selection) is one proposed way that may make the mechanism concrete (efficacy untested), not a required medium; paper rectangles and a drawn hierarchy can achieve the same reasoning.

Any physical rectangles or cut shapes used are representations of the ideal mathematical region or figure, not the figure itself; the reasoning concerns the mathematical shape represented, and physical thickness is not a criterion in this 2-D work.
Keep n explicitly as a number that varies, not as an object or label, so unlike terms (3n and 5) are not conjoined.

activityReferences.title: Two paths, two answers: feeling why we need a rule
Same tier, left to right
See the structure before you compute
Brackets override the default order
Why is this right? A questioning discussion

startingActivity.title: Two paths, two answers: feeling why we need a rule
learnerActions: Meet a live multi-operation string such as 8 + 2 × 5 and decide which operation to resolve next by selecting it.
Follow the path when you choose '+' first: watch 8 + 2 become 10, then × 5 become 50.
Place a second copy of the same string beside it and resolve it the agreed way: 2 × 5 = 10 first, then + 8 = 18.
Compare the two: identical symbols, two different answers — then state in your own words why an agreed order is needed.
Try other ambiguous strings and predict both the 'reading-order' answer and the conventional answer before resolving.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The order of operations is an agreed convention that removes genuine ambiguity: the same symbols can yield different values unless everyone resolves them the same way, with multiplication/division taken before addition/subtraction.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A tiered 'staircase' or ladder diagram: Brackets on the top step, Orders next, ×÷ on one shared step, +− on the bottom shared step — visually encoding that same-step operations are equal and read left→right.
Colour-coded expression annotation (circle brackets, underline ×÷, box +−) applied to the live expression before evaluation.
Step-by-step rewrite chains where the expression shrinks one line at a time (12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 → 4 + 8 → 12), each line showing exactly one tier resolved.
Number line / equal-groups callback for WHY 8 + 2 × 5 = 18: the 2 × 5 is one chunk of ten added to 8, not (8+2) copied five times.
commonMisconceptions: Strict left-to-right computation ignoring precedence: reading 8 + 2 × 5 as 50 because they add first.
Treating the acronym literally: doing Division before Multiplication (or Addition before Subtraction) because D/A come first in BODMAS, e.g. 12 ÷ 2 × 3 wrongly done as 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
Believing multiplication ALWAYS beats division rather than sharing a tier resolved left→right.
Ignoring or mis-scoping brackets — evaluating outside a bracket first, or dropping the bracket once opened.
Thinking the convention is a deep mathematical truth rather than an agreed notation choice, which blocks understanding of why brackets can override it.
constraints: Motivate the need for the rule first by collecting the conflicting answers (18 and 50) before naming it, so learners feel the ambiguity the convention resolves.

Teach ×÷ as one equal-rank tier and +− as one equal-rank tier, always swept left→right; explicitly rehearse counterexamples (e.g. 12 ÷ 2 × 3 = 18, where doing the × first wrongly gives 2) so the acronym's letter order does not cement 'division before multiplication' (BODMAS), 'multiplication before division' (PEMDAS) or 'addition before subtraction' (both).
Frame the order as an agreed convention for removing ambiguity, not because multiplication is 'stronger' or gives bigger answers; brackets are the legitimate override.

A static reference staircase or chart anchors the hierarchy well but does not let the learner evaluate a live expression or feel the left→right sweep; use it alongside active evaluation, not instead of it.

Recognition-only or outcome-only checks (e.g. picking the first operation, or a final-value answer) can confirm the result but do not by themselves require the learner to state or justify the order; pair them with tasks that ask for the sequence and the reasoning.
This is a flat symbolic/notational concept with no spatial dimension, so a 3D/spatial setting is unlikely to add value for it; keep attention on the structure of the expression.

startingActivity.title: Expression builder with a live structure mirror
learnerActions: Hear or read an instruction such as 'add 18932 and 921, then make it three times as big' and assemble it from number, operator and BRACKET tiles — e.g. 3 × (18932 + 921).

As you wrap (18932 + 921) and prefix × 3, watch a bar-model alongside show one inner bar for the sum and then three copies of that bar stacked, so 'three times as large' appears as literal repeated length — with no total ever calculated.

Switch to a compare mode: two near-identical expressions sit side by side; drag the brackets from around one sub-part to another and watch the bars re-shape, noticing whether and how the comparison changes.

State which expression is larger, giving no numerical value; for a pair like 3 × (18932 + 921) and 18932 + 921, name the FACTOR ('three times'), but for look-alike pairs such as 3 × (18932 + 921) and 3 × 18932 + 921, explain the difference from structure, since there is no simple factor.
Deliberately use very large or awkward numbers so computing is unappealing and you reason from the ×3 structure alone.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Structure — where the brackets sit and what the multiplier scopes over — determines meaning and relative size; you can read 'three times as large' directly from the form without computing.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model showing an inner quantity (a + b) and an outer bar three copies long, so 3 × (a + b) is literally three of the inner bars — 'three times as large' made visual without numbers.
Two-column translation table: verbal instruction | matching expression, built up so brackets appear exactly where 'first' is spoken.
Expression 'family' cards that look alike (5×(n+3), 5×n+3, 5×n×3) sorted by what they mean, to foreground structure.
A 'relative size' comparison strip: two expressions placed side by side with a factor arrow ('×3') linking one to the other, no values shown.
commonMisconceptions: Compulsively evaluating — rushing to a number instead of describing structure, which defeats the purpose and often introduces arithmetic error.
Omitting brackets when order matters, writing 8 + 7 × 2 for 'add then double' (which the order-of-operations convention reads as 8 + 14).
Reading 3 × (18932 + 921) as '3 times 18932, plus 921' — mis-scoping the multiplier over the bracket.
Assuming two expressions with the same numbers must be equal regardless of brackets/structure (5×(n+3) vs 5×n+3).
Confusing 'three times as large' (multiplicative, ×3) with 'three more than' (additive, +3) when narrating an expression.
constraints: Keep WRITING an expression separate from EVALUATING it — make 'don't work it out' an explicit, repeated instruction, since the whole skill is reading structure; reward a good interpretation over a computed number.

Use deliberately large or awkward numbers (e.g. 18932 + 921) so computing is unappealing and the relative-size answer is visible from the × 3 alone; where the structure shows a factor, give relative-size answers as that factor ('3×'), never as a computed total.
Depend on brackets-as-grouping: 'add then multiply' MUST be written with brackets to be faithful, because the order-of-operations convention reads 8 + 7 × 2 as 8 + 14.
Contrast expressions that look alike but scale differently (5 × (n + 3) vs 5 × n + 3) to show structure, not digits, decides meaning; this seeds early algebraic reasoning.
Matching/selection checks verify interpretation but do not elicit independent construction of an expression — include tasks where the learner builds or writes the expression themselves.

The annotated static expression is an anchor/reading scaffold: it cannot let the learner re-shape or build expressions, so it should not be the only activity (this is a format limit, not a claim that other media add nothing).
A bar model showing relative length illustrates 'three times as large' without numbers; treat it as a representation of the structure, not a computed total.
