startingActivity.title: Three marks make fourths: partition and place on an interactive line
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line, set a 'cut this unit into ___ parts' control to 4 and watch exactly THREE marks drop in, splitting the line into four equal segments.
Say aloud how many marks made four parts (three, not four), and colour each of the four segments, counting SEGMENTS rather than marks.
Drop a bead on the third mark; if the line reports a fraction, check it announces '3/4' and explain why that point is 3/4.

Extend the line from 0-to-1 to 0-to-4, keeping each whole-number unit the same length (or redraw it that way), and notice the 3/4 bead stays three-quarters of the way from 0 to the first '1', nowhere near the '3'.
On a second track below, lined up with the same 0 and 1 and labelled in tenths, slide a 1/2 bead until it lands exactly on 5/10, and state that the two labels name the same point.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction 1/b comes from cutting one unit into b equal segments (needing b−1 interior marks), and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th segment. The unit stays 'one whole' even when the line gets longer, so 3/4 lives between 0 and 1, not between 3 and 4. Equivalent fractions are the same point under different labels.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line partitioned into equal segments (the core model)
Minimally-labelled landmark line (0, 1/2, 1)
Dual-labelled line (two fractional-unit sequences) for equivalence
Fraction strip laid alongside the line to link area-model and length-model
commonMisconceptions: Treats the number line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treats the whole line as the unit — e.g. locates 3/4 three-quarters of the way across a 0-to-5 line
Sees a fraction only as part of a shape, not as a single number that has a place on a line
Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3
constraints: Hold the unit (the 0-to-1 distance) visible and fixed so children do not treat the whole line as the unit; test transfer on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line, not only on a pre-segmented 0-to-1 line.
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE interior marks; generalise that 1/n needs n−1 interior marks. Insist on counting segments, not tick marks.

A fixed labelled reference line can teach and be used while teaching, but on its own it does not require the child to construct segments or re-place a point on a longer line; combine reference-reading with active partitioning and placement.

Fraction strips and paper cutouts have real slight thickness and only approximate the ideal flat model; use them to bridge area and length, and treat any on-screen line as a model of the idealised (zero-thickness) number line.

When comparing unit fractions such as 1/8 and 1/3, keep the SAME whole and compare how one segment's length changes as the denominator changes; describe this as 'more parts means smaller parts', never as a denominator rule that 'flips'.

Placing and comparing points is a construct-and-check task: recognition-only or matching responses can check placement but do not by themselves elicit the child independently partitioning a unit and justifying a location. Include at least one task where the child makes the marks and states the reasoning.

Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, snapping/announcing bead, length toggle, tenths track) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required equipment; the same learning can be done on paper with careful partitioning.

startingActivity.title: Same point on the line: 0.3 and 3/10
learnerActions: Mark where 0.3 goes on a number line from 0 to 1, then mark where 3/10 goes, and say whether they land on the same point.
Explain in your own words why both are 'three tenths of the way from 0 to 1' — the same magnitude shown two ways.
Place 0.35 and 0.5 on the line and explain which is bigger and why (0.35 is less than 0.5), checking against a tenths/hundredths grid.
Apply the same reasoning to a fresh pair, e.g. 0.27 and 27/100: place both on the line and explain the equivalence.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A decimal and its equivalent fraction are the same number — the same position/magnitude on the line — so notation (decimal vs fraction) is not identity; magnitude is.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line carrying fractions and decimals at shared points (equivalence as one position)
Area model / array for multiplication linked to the written method
Bar model for sharing/division and for multiplication structure
Hundredths grid linking a decimal to its fraction
commonMisconceptions: Treats a decimal and its fraction as different kinds of number that can't share a point (0.3 ≠ 3/10 'because one's a decimal')
Applies whole-number thinking to decimals (0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5'; reads 0.3 as 'three')
Reads the area/bar model as a separate procedure from the written method, unable to say how they show the same calculation
Counts parts of a diagram without seeing that numerator and denominator name a single quantity
constraints: Require construction and explanation, not just recognition: the child should build diagrams, place values on lines, write equations, and say what each number means. A matching-type warm-up ('which decimal equals 3/10?') can activate prior knowledge but does not show the child can construct a translation or explain shared structure.

A static side-by-side of story, diagram, area model, and equation with tap-to-reveal links can illustrate connections and serve as a worked example, but it does not let the child build or vary the representations themselves; use it as a scaffold, then move to child-generated work.
Evocative illustrations cannot be trusted for exact decimal/fraction positions — placements on a number line need accurate, marked or verifiable scales.

Optional interactive supports (if available) can make the 'same structure, different view' idea concrete: linked panels where dropping 0.3 on a line snaps 3/10 to the same tick, or an area-model↔written-method splitter where dragging the 20+3 split recolours both the rectangle regions and the partial products together. These are helpful examples, not required mechanisms; the same goals can be met with paper, a drawn number line, and spoken explanation.
When comparing decimals, hold the comparison honest: 0.35 vs 0.5 is about magnitude (0.35 < 0.5), not about which digit string looks bigger — route placement through the value.
4×23 = 92: the partial products are 4×20=80 and 4×3=12, summing to 92. Keep these exact values in any example; '60' is not a valid partial product here.

startingActivity.title: One quantity, three costumes: the linked hundredths grid
learnerActions: Shade 35 of 100 squares on a hundredths grid and read off the three labels that name the same shaded region: 35/100, 0.35 and 35%.
Change the shading to a different amount (e.g. 8 squares) and state the fraction, decimal and percentage, explaining why all three must still match the shaded area.
Place the same quantity at a single point on one number line that carries fractions above and decimals/percentages below.
Answer the direct challenge: 'Is 0.35 the same as 35%, or is one bigger?' and justify using the shaded area and the per-hundred meaning, not '35 is bigger than nought-point-something'.
Say aloud what the % symbol means ('parts per hundred') and what the quantity is 35% OF.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 0.35, 35/100 and 35% were never three numbers to convert between; they are one magnitude shown three ways, and 'per cent' means parts per hundred.

commonMisconceptions: Treats 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as three different things rather than one magnitude shown three ways
Does not hold 'per cent = parts per hundred', so reads 35% as the number 35 (or a decimal with no meaning)
Grabs both readings off a line graph and adds them instead of asking which quantity and which operation the situation needs
Reads a bar/area model as a separate procedure from the multiplication equation it represents
constraints: Show all three notations on ONE representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so equivalence is seen as the same magnitude, not three conversion rules.
Ground percentage in 'parts per hundred' using the grid before introducing any conversion rule, so 35% is a quantity rather than a bare number.
At every step insist on 'what does each number represent?' and translate in every direction.

A static annotated grid or labelled bar model can illustrate equivalence but does not let the child vary the amount or interactively respond to the percentage misconception; treat it as a worked example / scaffold, not the full activity.

Match-the-equivalent exercises test recognition and can reward rote conversion; recognition alone does not elicit independent construction or explanation, so use them only as a warm-up, not as evidence the child can construct the translation or explain the shared magnitude.
The reasoning/argument dialogue is for eliciting explanation and should not be scored.

activityReferences.title: Many forms, one line
Zoom in — is there a smallest place?
Value of a digit at any scale
Which is smaller, and why

startingActivity.title: Many forms, one line
learnerActions: Draw a single number line and place each of these numbers on it: −3/4, 0.6, −2, and 1.25. Then, on a separate zoomed-out view using an appropriate scale, mark a large integer such as 4,700,000, noting that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs both views.
For each number, say in words where it sits relative to zero and to the nearest whole-number landmarks (e.g. '1.25 is a quarter of the way from 1 to 2').
Place 3/4 and 0.75 separately, then check that both land on exactly the same point; write one sentence explaining why they must coincide.

Write all the numbers in order from smallest to largest, treating 3/4 and 0.75 as one point, and justify the order using position on the line, not the digits (−2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 3/4 = 0.75 < 1.25 < 4,700,000).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions all belong to one number line governed by a single ×10/÷10 structure; each names a single point and equivalent forms name the same point. On a standard (left-to-right) line, size is read as position (leftmost is smallest) across every type, even when very large and very small values must be shown at different scales.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Single number line hosting integers, decimals, negatives and fractions together
Place-value chart extended arbitrarily far left and right of the decimal point
Zoomable number line to locate decimals/fractions between integers
Form-conversion cards (fraction ↔ decimal) feeding points onto the line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking place value 'runs out' at a largest place (millions) or smallest place (thousandths)
Treating whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions as living on separate scales rather than one line
Placing negatives as if their magnitude sets their order (−3/4 to the left of −2)
Assuming a fraction and its decimal (3/4 and 0.75) are different points rather than the same point
Comparing mixed forms by surface features (digit count) rather than converting to a common form
constraints: Learners should construct placements and justifications themselves; multiple-choice or slider checks can consolidate the unified-line idea afterwards, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent placing, converting and justifying that evidences full understanding.

When comparing mixed forms, convert to a common representation (decimal or common denominator) or locate each between integer landmarks before ordering; do not compare by surface features such as digit count. Fractions remain comparable numbers; the common-reference requirement is about positioning represented portions consistently.

A static, annotated line showing several forms on one axis can illustrate the unification and is a useful scaffold, but it cannot be re-scaled by the learner, so pair it with hands-on subdividing/zooming when demonstrating that the structure is unbounded and that more numbers always fit between landmarks.

Treat large integers and sub-unit decimals at appropriate separate scales when a single drawn line cannot show both; the point is that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs each, so the unification is conceptual even when two views are used.
The number system here is one-dimensional, so a single line is the correct representation; avoid adding extra spatial dimensions that would misrepresent ordering.

'Leftmost is smallest' assumes the conventional left-to-right orientation of the number line; use that standard orientation and make it explicit rather than treating it as an intrinsic property of the numbers.

Consolidate the symbol conventions with true/false and ordering checks

startingActivity.title: Drop mixed-form numbers onto one number line and choose the symbol between neighbours
learnerActions: Take a set of mixed cards — 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, −0.75, 7/10, −2, −1.5, 1/2 — and place each at its correct position on a shared number line.
Use a 'show as decimal' conversion (e.g. 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) to check cross-form values before placing them.
Notice that 0.75 and 3/4 land on the IDENTICAL point and coincide there.
Between each adjacent pair of placed cards, select a symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and justify the choice.
Confirm that between the two coincident cards the strict symbols < and > (and ≠) are false; = is the most precise choice, and the inclusive ≤ and ≥ are also true because they allow equality.
Deliberately test the surprise case: see that −0.8 sits LEFT of −0.75, so −0.8 is smaller, even though 0.8 > 0.75 for positives — defeating the 'bigger magnitude wins' instinct for negatives.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Position on the number line (left = less) is a single rule that orders integers, decimals, fractions, positives and negatives uniformly; equal values coincide, so < and > cannot hold between them, while = (and the inclusive ≤, ≥) are true.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line as the arbiter of order (left → right = least → greatest)
Common-form conversion (3/4 → 0.75) to compare across representations
Symbol cards =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ placed between two values
Sorting track / ordering slots that snap items into line positions
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−5 placed as greater than −2)
Comparing fractions and decimals by surface features instead of converting to a common form
Confusing < and > direction (the 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic misapplied)
Treating ≤/≥ as identical to </> and missing the equality case
Assuming a longer decimal or larger denominator is automatically larger/smaller
constraints: Order by POSITION on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule rather than sign-specific tricks.
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line.
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤), making the equality case explicit.

Deliberately bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error two ways: with negatives (−5 vs −2, where the larger-magnitude number is smaller; and −0.8 vs −0.75, where −0.8 < −0.75) and with unequal-length positive decimals (0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal is larger) so the misconception is confronted directly rather than accidentally confirmed.
Recognition/selection items (true/false, matching) check convention use but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering; use the hands-on positional sort for that.

A static labelled line with forms placed and symbols shown can illustrate a completed ordering but does not let the learner perform the sort or select symbols with feedback; it is a worked-example scaffold, not the full task.

Position-order for this objective is represented along a single line (one dimension), so a third spatial dimension is not needed here; this is a scoped observation about representing order, not a general claim that 3D 'adds nothing'.

activityReferences.title: Overlay check: proving 1/2 = 2/4 by covering
Equal sharing: deriving equivalent fractions
Finding a fraction of a quantity by equal sharing

startingActivity.title: Overlay check: proving 1/2 = 2/4 by covering
learnerActions: Take two identical chocolate bars (or paper strips of the same length). Cut one into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces.
Before moving anything, predict and say aloud: are 2 pieces from the four-piece bar MORE, LESS, or the SAME as 1 piece from the two-piece bar? Give your reason.
Place the two quarter-pieces exactly on top of the one half-piece and check whether they cover it with nothing left over and no overlap.
Write the result as a fraction sentence: 1/2 = 2/4, and say in words 'the same amount, cut into a different number of parts'.
Find at least one more name for the same amount (for example cut another identical bar into 6 and check that 3/6 also covers one half).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Two quarters cover exactly one half, so 2/4 and 1/2 name the same amount even though 2/4 uses bigger numbers. A fraction has many names for one value. The prediction step surfaces the 'bigger numbers = more' intuition so the overlay can confront it directly.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two identical bars, one halved and one quartered, with two quarters overlaid on one half
A fraction wall aligning 1/2 with 2/4
A set of 6 shared into two equal groups (1/2 of 6 = 3)
Number line with 1/2 and 2/4 landing on the same point
commonMisconceptions: 2/4 is more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger (whole-number bias)
Two fractions written with different numbers cannot name the same amount (no concept of equivalence)
Errors computing a unit fraction of a quantity (1/2 of 6) by not sharing equally
constraints: Use identical-sized wholes (same-length bars or strips) when demonstrating equivalence by overlay; different-sized wholes let the child escape with 'it depends on the bar' and break the comparison. This common-whole requirement applies to comparing the represented portions; as numbers, 1/2 and 2/4 remain comparable (indeed equal).
Every whole must be cut into EQUAL parts before counting or sharing; unequal parts invalidate both the fraction-of-a-quantity work and the overlay.

Matching and multiple-choice tasks assess recognition of equivalent pairs; they do not elicit independent construction or explanation, so include tasks where the child builds a model and states why in words.

A printed fraction wall or equivalence poster is a useful reference but is fixed: the child cannot test the overlay on it. Pair reference images with an activity where the child actually cuts and overlays pieces.
Keep the prediction step before the check: recording the child's reason first is what makes the whole-number bias visible and the overturning meaningful.

When a quantity does not share cleanly into the number of groups named by a denominator (e.g. sharing 6 whole counters into four equal groups), route the task through an equivalent unit fraction (2/4 of 6 via 1/2 of 6) rather than forcing fractional counters.

startingActivity.title: Share the set into equal groups, then take some
learnerActions: Start with 12 counters and the request 'show me 1/4'. Set the denominator to 4 and form four group-rings (or draw four rings/circles on paper).
Deal the 12 counters out one at a time so each ring holds an equal share — 3 each. If any group is unequal, keep dealing until they match.
Take one group for 1/4: say and record '1/4 of 12 = 3'.
For 3/4, light up / shade / move three of the four groups and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9; record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Change the set size: re-share 8 counters into four equal groups and see each group is now 2, so 1/4 of 8 = 2. Compare with 1/4 of 12 = 3.
State in words why 1/4 means making 4 equal groups rather than just taking 4 counters.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The whole is the whole SET; the denominator counts the equal groups to make and the numerator counts the groups to take. The same fraction names a different quantity when the set changes, so a fraction is a relationship, not a fixed number of objects.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Counters shared into equal groups (12 → four groups of 3)
Array / grouping diagram
Bar model of the set partitioned into b parts with a shaded
Double number line (objects ↔ fraction of the set)
commonMisconceptions: Takes the denominator as the answer: 1/4 of 12 is '4' because the fraction has a 4
For a non-unit fraction, finds 1/4 (=3) and stops, giving 3 for 3/4 instead of 9
Names a coloured set part-to-part (3 coloured, 9 not → 3/9) instead of part-to-whole (3/12)
Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator
constraints: Choose set sizes that divide evenly by the denominator so sharing yields equal whole-number groups (e.g. 12 and 8 for quarters); keep denominators small as required for this age.

A static grouped-set picture with tap-to-reveal (e.g. 'one group = 1/4 = 3 counters') can serve as a reference aid, but it does not let the child do the sharing or vary the set size, so it is a scaffold rather than the main activity.

Recognition-only or selection items can check the result without requiring the child to construct the groups or explain the reasoning: a '1/4 of 12' item with answer options such as 3, 4 and 48 surfaces the denominator-as-count error (4) and a multiply slip (48), while a separate 'what fraction is coloured?' item offering 3/12 versus 3/9 surfaces the part-to-part naming error.

Keep the focus on visually dividing the set into equal parts; avoid phrasing that treats the answer as a fact to recall ('eight strawberries, so a quarter is two') rather than the result of equal sharing.
Encourage reading fraction names ('one-quarter', 'three twelfths') rather than 'one-over-four', which can feed the digit-as-count error.

activityReferences.title: Stamp the unit-fraction jumps and cross the whole

startingActivity.title: Stamp the unit-fraction jumps and cross the whole
learnerActions: Work on a number line marked 0 to 2 with whole-number anchors at 1 and 2.
Add one 1/4 jump at a time starting from 0, saying each landing aloud: 'one quarter, two quarters, three quarters'.
Keep a running record that shows BOTH the count (number of copies) and the value n/4, alongside a growing equation 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 ...
On the fourth jump, notice the marker lands exactly on 1 and the tally reads 4/4; then deliberately keep going — tap again to step to 5/4, past the whole, still a definite point on the line.
Continue to the seventh jump, landing exactly on 1 3/4, with the equation showing seven 1/4's and the side note 7/4 = 1/4 × 7.

Switch the unit to 1/3 and repeat while keeping the whole-number anchors 1 and 2 fixed, counting up to six jumps (6/3 = 2) on this 0–2 line. To continue to seven jumps (7/3 = 2 1/3), extend the line past 2 first. Each jump is now larger: three third-jumps reach the same point 1 that four quarter-jumps reached.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction a/b is just a count of equal units 1/b; nothing forces the count to stop at the whole, so improper fractions like 7/4 are ordinary points on the line. The denominator names the size of the unit you are counting.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with equal 1/b jumps from 0, continuing past 1 (0, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4=1, 5/4, 6/4, 7/4)
Fraction strips / identical unit tiles laid end to end (seven 1/4-tiles making 7/4)
Repeated-addition equation 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4
Bar model spanning more than one whole to show 7/4 as one whole plus three more quarters (1 3/4)
Skip-counting sequence in unit-fraction language ('one-fifth, two-fifths, three-fifths...')
commonMisconceptions: Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so an improper fraction like 7/4 'isn't a real/proper number' or must be an error.
Adding denominators when joining unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 rather than 2/4.
Whole-number bias in placing improper fractions: reading 7/4 as near 7 (or treating the 7 as the dominant number) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
Losing the unit: writing 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 but unable to say the denominator stays 5 because each part is the same size 1/5.
Thinking the number line 'stops' at 1 for fractions, so not continuing the jumps past the whole.
constraints: Use the number line as the primary model with equal 1/b jumps from 0, extending past 1 so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting; this representation is recommended by the cited guide.
Speak the count aloud ('one fifth, two fifths, three fifths') so the iteration is audible and the numerator is heard as the number of copies.
Deliberately cross the whole (4/4 = 1, then 5/4, 6/4, 7/4) rather than stopping at 1.

Keep the denominator fixed while counting copies of a unit. If the denominator changes, keep the whole-number anchors fixed and change the jump size: thirds reach1 in three jumps, quarters in four jumps.
When a task uses values beyond a whole (e.g. ordering up to 9/4 = 2 1/4), draw the line long enough to contain them rather than clipping to 0–2.
A pre-built reveal or worked illustration conveys the decomposition but does not have the learner iterate themselves; pair it with learner construction when possible.
Unit tiles and fraction strips are physical approximations of the ideal equal jumps; keep each tile the same size to represent equal units.

A quiz or fill-in check can verify the outcome (expressing a/b as a sum, placing an improper fraction), but recognition or selection alone may not elicit the learner's own construction of the sum or placement; use such checks alongside tasks where the learner builds and justifies, not as the sole learning surface.

startingActivity.title: Place a fraction on a number line as a length
learnerActions: Given a number line that runs 0 to 4, decide where 3/4 belongs before marking it.

If you first place it between 3 and 4, judge how far that point is from 0 — it stretches past 3, far too long for 'three quarters' (an interactive tool can light up this length, but you can equally read the distance on a fixed, accurately drawn line).
Drag or redraw 3/4 back between 0 and 1, partition that first unit into four equal parts, and mark three of those steps from 0.
State the single amount that point names in one sentence (e.g. 'three of four equal parts of one whole, which is less than 1').
Use a whole-number/fraction view to contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits.
Extend: place 5/4 and explain how a fraction can be more than 1.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction is a single number with a magnitude — a length/position from 0 — not a numerator and a denominator parked side by side as two whole numbers.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line (fractions as lengths/positions; whole numbers labelled as fractions; equivalent fractions stacked above/below)
Bar/strip diagram for fractions and multi-step money/measurement problems
Part-whole and comparison bar models with an unknown

commonMisconceptions: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, reading numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers
Counts tick marks or parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity
Partitions with the wrong number of marks (four hash marks for fourths) or treats the whole line as the unit
Keeps the operational equals-sign habit in multi-step money/measurement sentences and drops units off the numbers
constraints: Reading/placing a correct point on a number line, or selecting a correct equation, is recognition; it does not by itself show the child can CONSTRUCT the translation or explain magnitude/structure. Pair any recognition warm-up (e.g. 'which point is 3/4?') with a construction-and-explanation task.

Illustrations and diagrams that are evocative rather than measured cannot be trusted for precise fraction positions; use tools or drawings where the partition is exact when the point itself is the learning target.

Unmarked number lines and 'what one quantity is this?' questioning are the intended scaffold against counting-without-understanding; if a line is pre-marked, the child may count ticks and bypass the concept.
Area/strip manipulatives remain useful but carry a known risk of children counting parts without seeing a single quantity — pair them with magnitude language and the number line.

Keep units on every number in money/measurement work and confirm units match (m vs cm), converting to a common unit BEFORE combining; the objective includes referent- and unit-faithful equations, not just a numeric answer.

The linked/tap-to-reveal worked example is a scaffold: it shows correspondences but does not require the child to place a fraction, partition a line, or confront the misconception, so it should lead into construction tasks.

Dialogue with a literal reader

startingActivity.title: Maths proofreader's bench: fix the almost-right statements
learnerActions: Work through a set of statements that are almost right and repair each one: '£3.5' (a price), '35' (a length), 'the top number is the denominator', and '7 + 5 = 12 + 3'.

Submit each statement first as it is written — the sloppy version — to a reader that acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation, then submit the repaired version and compare what the reader does with each. For example, when the two-decimal-place convention is dropped, a reader could misread '£3.5' as three pounds and five pence (£3.05) and short-change the customer; writing '£3.50' removes that ambiguity.

Repair the price to '£3.50', add 'cm' to the 35, and rewrite the fraction sentence as 'the top number is the numerator', checking it against a fraction bar where the numerator counts the shaded parts.
Decide whether '7 + 5 = 12 + 3' is true, and state why the equals sign means 'is the same as' rather than 'here comes the answer'.
Proofread each finished statement by asking 'could someone misunderstand this?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork; a dropped unit, a missing decimal place, or a swapped term can change the meaning a reader takes from it, so following shared conventions is an act of communication, not a nitpick.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Measurement answers written with units (35 cm, 2 kg, 500 ml)
Money notation to two decimal places (£3.50)
Fraction written with numerator and denominator labelled
Comparison and equation notation (>, <, =)
Fraction bars / number line linking symbol to quantity
commonMisconceptions: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for 35 cm (CCSS)
Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or mixes symbols as '£3.50p'
Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — calls the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' rather than denominator
Uses 'equivalent' loosely for any related fractions rather than only equal-value ones
constraints: Precision tasks should have the child produce or repair notation (write/say the corrected statement), not merely recognise a correct label; a static labelled example or reference card can support but cannot accept the child's input to host the production/repair practice.
Recognition-only or spot-the-error items screen for slips efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the child's reasoning about why a convention matters — use open prompts for that.

Keep fraction vocabulary tied to roles: numerator counts the parts we have (top); denominator names how many make the whole (bottom); 'equivalent' applies only to fractions of equal value, not to any related fractions.
Money in pounds is written with £ and two decimal places, and money in pence is written with p and no decimal point (e.g. '£3.50' or '350p'); never use both symbols ('£3.50', not '£3.5' or '£3.50p').
A fraction bar or number line that links the symbol to the quantity helps keep the term attached to its meaning; this is a representation choice, not a required mechanism.

In strict decimal '£3.5' equals '£3.50'; the till/character device illustrates how dropping the two-decimal-place convention invites a reader's MISREADING (e.g. as £3.05), and must not be stated as £3.5 literally equalling £3.05.

activityReferences.title: Convince the skeptic without a picture
Find the broken step in a long multiplication
Tear and rearrange: from evidence to a reason why ALL triangles have angles summing to 180 degrees
Counter-examples and the asymmetry of proof

startingActivity.title: Convince the skeptic without a picture
learnerActions: State a claim, e.g. 3/4 > 2/3, and offer your first justification however you like (a drawing is fine to start).

When challenged ('your drawing looks close - how do I know you didn't just draw it that way? Convince me without the picture'), reach for a general reason: convert to a common denominator - 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, and 9/12 > 8/12.
State explicitly why this reason settles it for ANY representation, not just your drawing.
Respond to repeated pressing ('but ALWAYS?') and refuse to let 'I tried it and it worked' count as proof.
Try the same argument on a fresh pair, e.g. 5/8 versus 2/3, to test whether your method generalises (work out the common-denominator comparison rather than guessing).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A confirming example or a careful drawing can persuade, but a reason that holds independent of any picture is what actually settles a general claim.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Common-denominator conversion (3/4=9/12, 2/3=8/12) as the engine of a size argument
Column/grid long-multiplication layout for locating a misaligned partial product
Tear-and-rearrange triangle (three corners meeting on a straight line) as a visual proof of the 180° angle sum
A because/therefore chain frame connecting givens to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: Treating a confirming example (or a careful drawing) as a proof of the general claim
Comparing fractions by whichever has the bigger numerator or bigger denominator rather than by a common referent
Critiquing by answer-agreement — 'the total's wrong' — without locating the misaligned step or explaining the place-value error
Believing the tear-and-arrange result is a lucky fact of that one triangle rather than a general property
constraints: Do not accept a correct verdict (e.g. agreeing 3/4 > 2/3) as evidence of reasoning; a child can be right for the wrong reason via a single-component comparison rule. The discriminating act is explaining WHY examples don't settle it and producing the general reason.

Fixed-answer or 'spot the misaligned step' recognition tasks can serve as a warm-up but do not elicit a constructed general justification or a flaw explained in the child's own words; a score on such a task is not evidence of the reasoning practice, and recognition formats can inadvertently reward the confirming-example habit. Recognition alone does not elicit production.

Annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons with tap-to-reveal explanations can seed critique talk but do not themselves respond to a child's over-reliance on examples or capture a constructed chain; use them to launch discussion, not as the assessment.

A single confirming example or drawing is a starting point for talk, not a proof; always push toward a reason that holds independent of the representation. Fractions remain comparable as numbers; the common-whole caveat applies only to comparing represented portions within a drawing.
Separate two distinct causes of wrong fraction comparisons: a faulty comparison rule (reteach comparison) versus a reasoning-articulation gap (scaffold and scribe); treat them differently.

Paper-corner tear-and-arrange uses physical cutouts as an imprecise, concrete approximation of idealised angles; a draggable on-screen triangle is a model of the same relationship. Both offer repeated examples that make the pattern vivid, but neither proves the general claim by itself, and neither is universally required.

Optional interaction examples (draggable triangle re-forming the straight line, nudging partial products in/out of column alignment, linked fraction/angle/multiplication tools) are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory features. Comparative claims that one medium uniquely teaches, or that another 'cannot', are not established by the sources.

startingActivity.title: Build the bar, build the equation, balance it
learnerActions: Take the word problem: 'I think of a number, multiply by 4, add 27, and get 87.'
Draw a bar model: four equal unknown parts plus a 27-block, all equal in length to an 87-bar.
Write the matching equation 4x + 27 = 87 beneath, and point to where the x, the +27 and the 87 each appear in the bar.

Treat the equation as a balance with two equal sides. Try removing 27 from only one side and say what would go wrong; then remove 27 from BOTH sides (leaving 4x = 60) and explain why the two sides stay equal.
State in your own words why '=' lets you do the same thing to both sides, and finish solving (4x = 60, so x = 15).

If a dynamic model is available, size an unknown bar and watch the equation assemble; in a balance-beam mode, removing weight (such as the 27) from only one pan tips the beam, so removing it from both becomes a felt necessity, and the 27 vanishing on both sides at once mirrors the equation step.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A bar model and an algebraic equation are the same structure in two forms; the equals sign is a promise that both sides are the same amount, which is exactly why you may apply the same operation to both sides.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model with a labelled unknown mapped to an algebraic equation
Algebraic equation (e.g. 4x + 27 = 87) read relationally as a balance
Coordinate grid plotting ordered pairs from a table
Pie chart / fraction / percentage showing one proportion of a whole
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' in an equation as 'work out the left-hand side' (operational), so cannot justify doing the same operation to both sides
Treats a bar model and an algebraic equation as unrelated — can draw one but not see it as the other's structure
Treats a pie chart, fraction and percentage as different things rather than one proportion of the whole
Reverses coordinates or reads a point's value without connecting it to the quantity the axis represents
constraints: The equation should be CONSTRUCTED and the both-sides step JUSTIFIED by the learner; recognition-only tasks (e.g. 'which equation matches the bar?') can check a match but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the translation or the relational explanation, so use them only as a warm-up.

A static, tap-to-reveal set linking story, bar, equation and chart can illustrate the connections but cannot let the learner operate on a balance or plot points; treat it as a worked-example scaffold, not the productive activity.

When describing the balance, the required move is to keep the two sides equal (do the same to both); do not let a learner finish having only chanted 'move it over, change the sign' without the balance reason.
For the coordinate work, require the situational meaning of axes and coordinates before any relationship is read, to prevent number-reading without interpretation.

Dynamic recolouring, balance-beam tipping, draggable bars and linked updating displays are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not mandatory, and the reasoning can also be done on paper.

startingActivity.title: Order unit fractions under one shared whole
learnerActions: Take fraction cards 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and arrange them from largest to smallest.

Represent each card as a bar the same length as a single common '1 whole' bar, split into that many equal parts with one part shaded, and line the bars up beneath that '1 whole' so the shaded pieces can be compared by length.
State and check the order: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest, confirming 1/5 is the shortest and 1/2 the longest.
Explain out loud why 1/2 is bigger than 1/5 by pointing at the piece lengths against the same whole.

keyRepresentations: Aligned equal-length bars for unit fractions (a fraction wall column)

commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — orders unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 (bigger denominator judged bigger)
Over-correction — after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses same-denominator fractions too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5)
Compares numerators and denominators independently rather than as one quantity
Cannot place the fractions consistently on a number line to check the order
Ignores that the whole must be the same when comparing
constraints: When comparing fractions with bars or area representations, the represented whole must be the same; aligned bars and number-line placements only work when they share one unit. As numbers, fractions still have comparable magnitudes (e.g. by position on a shared number line).
A static fraction wall or reference image lets children read off comparisons but does not let them enact the ordering, so use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on ordering.
Recognition or multiple-choice practice checks whether the order is correct but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify the ordering; pair it with explanation.

Keep the two cases explicitly connected: unit-fraction comparison varies the denominator (numerator fixed at 1), while same-denominator comparison varies the numerator (denominator fixed) — explain that they compare different quantities, which is why 'bigger bottom = smaller' must not be over-generalised to same-denominator sets. This is not a single rule flipping.
Fraction comparison here uses lengths of bars and positions on a number line (or areas of equal wholes); for this objective a third spatial dimension adds no comparative information.

startingActivity.title: Solve it WITH a mentor who never gives the method
learnerActions: Work through a mixed bag of fraction word problems with a partner or in-role mentor (a teacher, another child, or a Socratic tutor character) who reads each problem aloud.
Before doing any arithmetic, say out loud what KIND of problem this is — find-a-fraction-of, compare/order, equivalence, or add/subtract — and HOW you can tell from the situation.
Talk through a plan (what will you do first, and why) before calculating.

When the mentor deliberately offers a tempting key word ('it says altogether, so we add?'), decide whether that word really fits the situation or whether the problem is actually about something else (e.g. finding 1/4 of a set).
After getting an answer, check it makes sense ('could 3/4 of 12 be more than 12?') every single time.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Recognising what a problem is really asking — and checking whether an answer is plausible — is the skill, not the arithmetic. The habit becomes owned when the child hears themselves catch a key-word trap and reason from the situation's structure instead.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar / strip models to represent the quantities and relationships in a word problem before choosing an operation
A visible problem-solving frame (understand → plan → do → check) the child fills in
Double number line for fraction-of and comparison problems
Recording that separates the CHOICE of strategy from its execution (e.g. 'this is a fraction-of problem because...')
commonMisconceptions: Key-word matching: latches onto a surface word ('altogether', 'left') and applies the associated operation regardless of the problem's meaning
Applies the most recently taught procedure to every problem regardless of what it asks
Calculates without a plan and never checks whether the answer is plausible
Cannot start a problem unless the operation is explicitly stated ('but it doesn't tell me to divide')
constraints: This is a META objective: the goal is the disposition and habits of a strategic problem-solver (sense-making, monitoring, plausibility-checking), not mastery of a single procedure. Children must already be able to find a fraction of a set, compare/order fractions, work with equivalence, and add/subtract fractions; if a child cannot find a fraction of a set at all, revisit that prerequisite before this work.
Keep problems MIXED across the four fraction ideas and vary surface features; a single-type set lets children pattern-match and defeats the recognition objective.
Deliberately include key words that point the wrong way ('altogether' in a fraction-of problem) so key-word matching can be surfaced and challenged rather than rewarded.

Insist on a plausibility / looking-back check every time (for a proper fraction of a positive quantity the answer is smaller than the whole, e.g. 'a fraction less than one whole, such as 3/4, of 20 can't be more than 20').

Recognition-only or multiple-choice responses measure the OUTCOME of strategy selection but do not by themselves elicit the independent planning, justification, and self-monitoring that the objective targets; pair them with open 'how did you know?' reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a fixed solving frame or a sort-tag-model workspace structure the thinking but constrain openness; fade them so the child eventually imposes structure unprompted on novel, multi-step problems.
When a child cannot begin because no operation is stated, scaffold sense-making (draw the situation) rather than supplying the operation.

Static tap-to-reveal pictures and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits for THIS metacognitive objective because strategic problem-solving is generative and dialogic and has no spatial content to manipulate; this is a scope judgement for this objective, not a universal claim that such media cannot teach.

startingActivity.title: Lock the numerator, grow the denominator: watch the parts shrink
learnerActions: Set up two bars (strips, drawn area models, or an interactive tool) pinned to the SAME whole.
Set both bars to 3/4 to start (numerator 3 and denominator 4 on each), so the two shaded amounts are identical.
On the first bar, raise the denominator from 4 to 8 so it shows 3/8; keep the second at 3/4.
Describe what happens to each part as the bottom number grows from 4 to 8, then state which shaded amount is larger.
Write the correct symbol between them (3/8 __ 3/4) with the sign opening toward the larger amount.
Say aloud: 'Same number of parts (3), but each eighth is smaller than each fourth, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When the numerator is held fixed, a larger denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller parts, so the fraction gets SMALLER, not bigger. The digits '8 > 4' do not mean '3/8 > 3/4'.

keyRepresentations: Aligned fraction strips / bars on one whole
Single 0–1 number line
Same-whole area models
Equal-sharing scenario (more sharers = smaller share)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — a larger denominator means a larger fraction (1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3; 3/8 > 3/4 by comparing denominators) (IES)
Comparing across different wholes (3/4 of a small bar vs 1/2 of a large bar)
Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers
Over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' so blindly it mis-fires on same-denominator pairs
constraints: When comparing by shaded models/pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole; a picture drawn on a different-sized whole can mislead. (As numbers, fractions such as 3/4 and 3/8 remain comparable regardless of any drawing.)
Reason about the SIZE and COUNT of parts, never the digits alone (e.g. 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth').
Read > and < as opening toward the larger amount; = means the two amounts are equal.

The same-numerator and same-denominator cases are DIFFERENT comparisons: with a shared denominator compare numerators (more same-size parts is more); with a shared numerator compare part sizes (larger denominator = smaller parts). Do not let a learner apply 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a same-denominator pair.
The fraction wall is a recall aid only; it cannot let the learner vary the denominator or test a comparison, so it should not replace the modelling/building activities.
Recognition and sorting tasks consolidate and check classification but do not on their own elicit independent construction of a model and a justification.
This microtopic targets same-numerator and same-denominator comparisons for age 8–9; general comparison of fractions with different numerators AND denominators is beyond this scope.

Physical fraction strips and card models have slight real thickness and are approximations of ideal equal parts; treat any paper or on-screen model as a model of the same-whole comparison, not the ideal figure itself.

startingActivity.title: Strategy workbench: common denominator OR benchmark
learnerActions: Take a pair such as 3/8 versus 5/12. Choose the common-denominator path: re-partition both bars (on paper or with a model) to the same fine grid — twenty-fourths — so 3/8 becomes 9/24 and 5/12 becomes 10/24, then compare the numerators 9 versus 10.

Take a pair such as 5/8 versus 3/7. Choose the benchmark path: place each on a number line marked 0, 1/2, 1. Decide which side of 1/2 each sits on (5/8 is more than 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 is less than 1/2 because 3 is less than half of 7).
Switch into an ordering task: drag or write three or more fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/5, 7/10) onto a line or into order, choosing whichever strategy fits the numbers.
State, for each comparison, which strategy you chose and why it suited those particular numbers.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Renaming two fractions to the same denominator makes them directly comparable (the comparison collapses to comparing numerators), and the 1/2 benchmark settles many comparisons at a glance without full computation. Choosing the strategy to fit the numbers is part of the skill.

keyRepresentations: Common denominator via equivalent-fraction renaming
Number line marked 0, 1/2, 1 (benchmark lane)
Dual-labelled number line for different denominators
Ratio table / times-tables for the common multiple
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone (3/8 vs 5/12 → '5 > 3 so 5/12 is bigger', or '12 > 8 so smaller') (IES)
Comparing without a common denominator (cross-adding, or comparing tops and bottoms separately)
Renaming only one fraction, or using a non-common multiple
Benchmark misapplied — e.g. judging 3/7 > 1/2
constraints: Learners must reach fractions with DIFFERENT numerators and denominators; same-denominator or same-numerator pairs alone are stepping stones, not the full objective.
Both strategies should be available: benchmark reasoning when fractions straddle 1/2 or sit near 0 or 1, and common denominators when fractions are close together or benchmarks do not separate them.

A benchmark/reference number line with fractions pre-placed is a recall and placement scaffold; it does not re-partition fractions or carry out an ordering, so it must be combined with active renaming and ordering work.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice, sorting, fill-in) check application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a full ordering with justification; include a task where the learner produces the ordering and its reasoning.
Always require justification with a visual model and explicitly guard against whole-number bias (ordering by numerator or denominator alone).
Verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence and ensure both fractions reach the same common multiple.

Comparing a fixed numerator (as in same-numerator pairs) with a fixed denominator varies different quantities; there is no 'denominator rule that flips', so explain each comparison by magnitude rather than a sign-flip rule.

Live re-partitioning of bars to a shared grid and drag-to-order on a line are example interaction mechanisms that make the strategies concrete; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms — the same work can be done with drawn bars and written orderings.

Interpret this content for approximately ages 9–10; in the England curriculum Year 5 pupils compare and order fractions whose denominators are all multiples of the same number, and Year 6 extends this to comparing and ordering fractions more generally, including fractions greater than 1 (source marked unverified).

startingActivity.title: Place and order fractions on a number line, measuring each gap to 1
learnerActions: Place the set 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 onto a number line running from 0 past 2.
For each fraction, mark or measure the distance from the fraction to the '1' mark (its gap to a whole): 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12.
State the order smallest to largest (3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12) and explain the link: the BIGGEST gap to 1 means the SMALLEST fraction, so 3/4 is smallest and 11/12 (hugging 1) is largest.
Place 7/5 and 4/3 on the same line and notice both land PAST 1; convert each to a mixed number (7/5 = 1 2/5) to confirm position.
Rewrite 7/5 and 4/3 over a common denominator (21/15 vs 20/15) and compare the numerators to decide which is larger.
Compare the counter-pair 2/3 and 2/5: which is larger, and why does the same number of larger-denominator pieces come to less?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Fraction size is one quantity located on the number line, not two independent whole numbers. For a near-whole set the fraction closest to 1 is largest; fractions greater than 1 sit past 1; and a common denominator turns any comparison into a single numerator comparison.

startingActivity.title: Re-partition a bar to build equivalent fractions
learnerActions: Start with a bar showing 1/3: one of three equal parts shaded.
Split each part into 2 and recount: the bar now shows 2/6, but the shaded LENGTH is unchanged.
Write the numeric move alongside the picture: ×2 on the top and ×2 on the bottom, 1/3 = 2/6.
Repeat splitting each part into 3 and into 4 to generate 3/9 and 4/12, each time checking the shaded length stays the same.
Deliberately test 'add 1 to each' (1/3 → 2/4): redraw 2/4 and compare its shaded length to 1/3 — it is longer, so the amount changed.
Build a simplify version: group the parts of 4/8 into equal groups and divide both counts by the common factor to reach 1/2, checking the shaded amount is unchanged.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same whole number greater than 1, or dividing both by a common factor greater than 1, re-partitions the SAME amount into more (or fewer) equal parts, so the value is preserved; adding the same non-zero number to both changes the amount (except for a fraction equal to one whole, such as 2/2 → 3/3).

startingActivity.title: Rename the same amount: fix the shaded length, change the labels
learnerActions: Shade 2/3 of a bar (or mark 2/3 as a point on a number line) and keep that shaded length physically fixed — e.g. with a strip of coloured paper laid over the bar.
Subdivide every third into 2 equal pieces, then 3, then 4, and each time count the total pieces and the shaded pieces.
Record the sequence of names for the SAME shaded length: 2/3 → 4/6 → 6/9 → 8/12, and alongside each write the equation ×2, ×3, ×4 applied to both numerator and denominator.
State in your own words why the shaded amount never moved: each part was re-cut into more, smaller pieces, so both counts grew together while the whole and the shaded magnitude stayed the same.

Now test the additive move: change 2/3 by adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 3/4. Shade 3/4 on an identical bar and lay it against the 2/3 strip. Observe that 3/4 reaches further — it is a different, larger amount.
Explain the difference out loud: multiplying re-cuts the same whole; adding a constant to each part does not re-cut anything, so here (and for any fraction not equal to 1) it lands on a new amount.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying numerator and denominator by a whole number n (n ≥ 1) re-partitions the same whole into finer equal parts, renaming a fixed magnitude; adding the same number to each is not re-partitioning and changes the amount (unless the fraction equals 1). Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1.

keyRepresentations: Area model re-partitioned (each part → n parts)

commonMisconceptions: Additive equivalence — adding the same number to top and bottom keeps it equal (IES whole-number thinking)
Whole-number bias — (n×a)/(n×b) 'must be bigger' because the numbers are bigger (4/6 > 2/3)
Multiplying only one part
Believing the value must change because 'you did something to it'
constraints: A reference display of ×n families (tap 2/3 → 4/6, 6/9, 8/12 with ×n annotations) aids recall but does not let the learner enact the magnitude-preserving re-partition; use it as a support, not the main teaching move.

Recognition/selection tasks (choose which fraction equals 3/5; match ×n pairs; fill in 3/10 = ?/100) are useful for testing the rule and surfacing the additive distractor, but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own re-partition explanation — pair them with a construction or spoken justification.

When using paper strips or cutouts, treat them as approximations of ideal flat regions (real paper has slight thickness); the point is the preserved shaded magnitude, so keep the shaded length physically fixed when comparing names.
Correct the 'multiply only one part' error at the model: both numerator and denominator must change together because every part is re-cut; changing one alone is not equivalence.

A live, draggable subdivision slider with a linked ×n equation and a colour change on the additive move is one way to make the mechanism visible; it is an optional interaction example, not a requirement — the same insight can be reached with paper strips and a number line. Comparative efficacy between these media is not established by the sources.

activityReferences.title: Un-grouping a bar: 18/24 back to simplest form

startingActivity.title: Un-grouping a bar: 18/24 back to simplest form
learnerActions: Start with a bar partitioned into 24 cells with 18 shaded, labelled 18/24.
Choose a number to 'group by' (a divisor) and merge the cells into equal groups of that size, watching the fraction label recompute (e.g. grouping in sixes gives 4 fat groups with 3 shaded → 3/4).

Observe that for each valid grouping of the original 24-cell bar the shaded LENGTH does not move while the label takes an equivalent form (grouping by 2 → 9/12, by 3 → 6/8, by 6 → 3/4) — the quantity is unchanged, only the cut is coarser.
Deliberately try a divisor that is NOT a common factor (e.g. 5): notice the cells will not group evenly and leftovers remain, so that divisor is rejected.
Keep going until no grouping beyond 1 is possible, then state the simplest form and name the HCF (6) that would have reached it in one step.
Also try the valid repeated route (÷2 then ÷3) and confirm it lands on the same 3/4.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Dividing both parts by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger equal pieces, leaving the value (length) unchanged; simplest form is reached only when no common factor above 1 remains.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / bar model where equivalent fractions align to identical length (6/8 sits exactly over 3/4)
Area model / grid that can be re-partitioned by merging small cells into larger groups (24 cells shaded 18, re-grouped into 4 columns of which 3 are shaded → 3/4)
Factor pairs and HCF listing beside the fraction (18 = 2×3×3, 24 = 2×2×2×3, common = 2×3 = 6)
Number line showing 18/24 and 3/4 landing on the identical point
Common-multiple ladder for the common-denominator task (thirds and eighths both re-cut into 24ths)
commonMisconceptions: Simplifying by SUBTRACTING a common amount from numerator and denominator (6/8 → 4/6 by taking 2 from each) instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
Stopping before simplest form: dividing 18/24 by 2 to get 9/12 and calling it done, not checking for a remaining common factor.
Operating on only one part — dividing the numerator but not the denominator (or renaming only the denominator when finding a common denominator).
Believing simplifying changes the fraction's value ('3/4 is bigger than 6/8 because 4 is fewer pieces') rather than renaming the same quantity.
When finding a common denominator, changing the denominators to match but forgetting to scale the numerators correspondingly.
constraints: Build simplifying on the equivalence principle learners met in Year 5 (a/b = (n×a)/(n×b)); do not teach it as an isolated rule.
Make the number theory explicit: divide by a common factor (efficiently the HCF) to simplify; use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM) for a common denominator.
Always ask 'can you go further?' — distinguish 'an equivalent simpler fraction' from 'simplest form'. Stopping at 9/12 is unfinished, not wrong.
Accept repeated division by any common factor (e.g. ÷2 then ÷2 where both divide evenly, or ÷2 then ÷3 for 18/24) as valid; the concept, not the HCF shortcut, is the target.
Simplifying compares and regroups the SAME fraction; no denominator rule 'flips' — dividing both parts by a shared factor is a single consistent operation.

A static tap-to-reveal worked example (e.g. tap to show factor pairs of 18 and 24, highlight the HCF, reveal ÷6 on both parts) can serve as a reference card but does not let the learner try divisors or feel the regrouping; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on work.
Recognition/short-answer items assess the output (simplest form, common denominator) but do not by themselves elicit the regrouping insight; pair them with construction on a model.
Scale BOTH parts by the same factor: dividing only the numerator, or changing denominators without scaling numerators, changes the quantity.

startingActivity.title: Sequence machine: force the jump to a far term
learnerActions: Look at a sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and notice the constant difference of 4.
Try to reach the 20th term by extending term-by-term and feel how slow and error-prone this gets.
Make a table pairing position (n) with term so the relationship becomes visible.
State a position-to-term rule (e.g. term = 4×position + 1) and use it to jump straight to the 20th term (81).
Check the rule against a known early term (does it give the 3rd term correctly?) before trusting it.
Then be asked for the 100th term, where listing is clearly impractical, so the general rule proves its worth.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A position-to-term rule lets you reach any term in one step, which counting-on cannot do efficiently; a rule is only trustworthy once checked against a known term.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Percentage bar / double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%)
Sequence tables pairing position (n) with term to expose the position-to-term rule
Equivalent-fraction and factor models for ×25 = ×100 ÷4

commonMisconceptions: Predicts the 20th term by extending term-by-term (or drawing all terms) instead of a position-to-term rule
Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and cannot jump to a far term efficiently
Treats each percentage as a separate conversion rather than building from 10% and 5%

constraints: A static percentage bar or sequence table can display the relationship but cannot force the far-term jump or test a learner's stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the task that elicits independent generalisation.

Recognition-only formats (picking the correct method or the 20th term from options) can test the general method, but should be paired with a 'why/how' step so they elicit justification rather than guessing; on their own they do not require the learner to construct and verify a rule.
Include a term-by-term distractor (one that gives only the next term) when testing sequences, to catch recursive-only thinking.
Verification against a known term should be required, not optional: a rule stated from a few cases is not yet trusted.

Percentages and linear sequences are numeric relationships; manipulable numbers, tables, ratio tables or bars support the work. 3D representation is not needed here, though this is a judgement about this content, not a universal claim.

Open discussion without a concrete referent gives the learner nothing to manipulate or test; pair any discussion with an actual sequence, number or percentage to reason about (as the probing activity does).

startingActivity.title: Collect the tenths back into one whole
learnerActions: Start with a single whole bar or strip and partition it into ten equal segments.
Collect the segments one at a time while counting aloud: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths … up to ten-tenths.
At the tenth count, reassemble the ten segments end-to-end against the original whole and check that they match exactly, labelling the result '10/10 = 1 whole'.
Lay a piece covering exactly five tenths over one half of the whole and confirm that 5/10 = 1/2, so a single tenth is plainly far smaller than a half.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Ten equal tenths put back together remake exactly one whole, so 10/10 = 1 (not 'ten'), and each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole — far smaller than a half.

keyRepresentations: Whole strip partitioned into ten equal tenths (recomposes to one whole)
0-to-1 number line marked in tenths
Sharing model: three wholes shared among ten to show 3/10 = 3÷10

commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — reads ten-tenths as 'ten', or thinks a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'
Larger denominator = larger part (a tenth 'bigger than a half because 10 > 2')
Accepts any ten pieces as tenths, ignoring that the parts must be equal
Sees no connection between 3/10 and 3÷10 ('3 ÷ 10 can't be done, 3 is smaller than 10')
Thinks a tenth of a large whole and a tenth of a small whole are the same size
constraints: Keep the whole visible throughout, and keep it the same size except when deliberately comparing tenths of different-sized wholes, so that a tenth is always understood relative to its own whole.
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole; any ten pieces are not tenths unless they are the same size.
Deliberately pause counting at 10/10 and reassemble to one whole, rather than letting the count slide into 'ten'.

Placing, naming, matching, and fill-in tasks (e.g. on a number line) check and consolidate understanding but do not by themselves build the recompose-to-one-whole insight; use them after the hands-on partitioning and sharing work.

A static labelled tenths strip can show the facts (this is 3/10; these ten make one whole; 5/10 = one half) but cannot itself enact the moment ten tenths fuse back into one whole; pair it with a recomposition the learner performs.

Partitioning and recomposing a visible whole provides the concrete experience of ten tenths reforming one whole; spoken discussion can support the reasoning about why a tenth is small but does not itself supply that partitioning and recomposition, so include the hands-on work rather than relying on discussion to provide it.

activityReferences.title: Order decimals on a number line and a length bar
Align place-value columns and read every digit by its name

startingActivity.title: Order decimals on a number line and a length bar
learnerActions: Take three cards — 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 — and place each on a number line ticked every 0.1 with minor ticks every 0.01, smallest to largest.
Say aloud why 0.54 lands furthest right and 0.39 nearest the start, naming the tenths: 'five tenths beats four tenths beats three tenths'.
View each number also as a growing length bar so the relative sizes are visually clear (0.54 is the longest bar).
Then place 3.72 and 3.27 on a 3–4 number line, first checking the whole-number parts tie at 3, then deciding on the tenths (7 vs 2).
State the order and justify by comparing the highest differing place first.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Decimal size can be read as position on a line: ordering is decided by the highest place at which the digits differ, read left to right, not by the raw digit string or the rightmost digit.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line marked in hundredths (0–1, and 3–4 for the 3.72/3.27 pair)
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
LAB / linear arithmetic (length) blocks
10×10 hundredths grid for area backup
commonMisconceptions: Reads the decimal part as a whole number ('72 > 27') — lands the right answer here but is a fragile, non-place-value strategy
Compares from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding
Ignores or misreads the whole-number part when it is present
constraints: Keep all practised and scored comparisons the same length (up to two decimal places) within this topic; teaching the ordering of unequal-length / ragged decimals, which reveal longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger, belongs to the next topic. Two exceptions are allowed: appending a trailing zero to show equivalence (writing 0.6 as 0.60 so 0.6 = 0.60) as an equal-value demonstration, and a single brief, unscored verbal transfer probe (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) used only to show that the read-it-as-a-whole-number trick breaks.

Equal-length comparisons are a weak diagnostic on their own: a correct place-value strategy and a read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the same answer, so always elicit the reasoning, not just the ordering.
A static number line with tap-to-reveal place values is useful as a reference card, but ordering should remain an active decision the child makes, not a result they read off.

Prefer a number line and a length (linear) model for showing relative size; a 10×10 hundredths grid can serve as an area backup. Depth/volume models are not needed for this one-dimensional size idea (a design preference, not a proven ranking of media).
Watch for the specific error of comparing from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding, and for ignoring or misreading a present whole-number part.
Optional interaction examples (drag-and-snap cards, a colour-the-winner cue, a growing length bar, slider placement, tap-to-reveal place values) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.

startingActivity.title: Build 3/10 + 4/100 on a hundredths grid
learnerActions: Take a blank 10×10 hundredths grid where each full column of ten small squares represents one tenth.
Shade 3/10 by filling three whole columns, then count the small squares covered to confirm it is 30 hundredths.
Add 4/100 by shading four more single squares.
Count all the shaded small squares and report the total as hundredths (34/100), then, when ready, write it as a decimal (0.34).
Deliberately try shading just three lone single squares for 3/10 first, notice that this is only 3/100, then correct it to three full columns.

Optionally model the same amounts with base-ten blocks, where the flat is one whole, a rod is one tenth, and a small cube is one hundredth, to see the same ×10 relationship in a different manipulative.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Three tenths covers the same shaded area as thirty hundredths, so tenths must be converted to hundredths before they can be added to hundredths.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundredths grid (column = tenth, square = hundredth)
Place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns
Number line 0–1 marked in hundredths
Base-ten flat/rod (rod = tenth of the flat, small cube = hundredth)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across both denominators: 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110 (adds tops and bottoms)
Treats 3/10 as 3 hundredths, shading three single squares, and reports 7/100
Thinks the denominators can be added because 'they are close', ignoring that the pieces are different sizes
constraints: Convert before combining: shade tenths as whole columns, then extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares — do not add until the pieces are the same size.
Never add denominators; 3/10 + 4/100 is not 7/110, and 3/10 is not 3/100. These are the two priority errors to surface and correct, not merely caveat.
A static labelled grid or tap-to-reveal image is a reference scaffold: it can show 7/10 = 70/100 but is not manipulable, so it supports rather than replaces active grid or base-ten work.

Paper or card grid cutouts have slight thickness and can be handled; a drawn or on-screen grid is a flat model of the same quantity — in every case the question is about the fractional amount represented, not the physical object.
Response-selection and sorting tasks can prompt reasoning during teaching but, used alone, check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction of the conversion.

An optional live-tally/snap-counting grid makes the recomputation visible but is one way to realise the activity, not a required mechanism; the same learning works with a drawn grid, base-ten blocks, or spoken counting.

activityReferences.title: Two-way converter checked against a grid and a number line
Contrast sets that drill the placeholder
Annotated place-value chart as a reference (scaffold)

startingActivity.title: Two-way converter checked against a grid and a number line
learnerActions: Enter a decimal (e.g. 0.62) and write the matching fraction; confirm against a 10×10 hundredths grid that shades 62 squares and a number-line marker that lands just past halfway.
Enter a fraction (e.g. 3/10) and write the matching decimal (0.3); confirm by shading 3 of the ten columns and placing the point on the line.
Do the hard placeholder case: for 9/100, if you write 0.9 the grid floods with ninety squares — far more than nine — so the mismatch is obvious; correct it to 0.09 so exactly nine squares glow.
Run rapid two-way rounds (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) across a deliberate set of placeholder and ragged cases: 0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100.
Read each decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths', 'seven hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The placeholder zero is not a rule to memorise but something you can see: for 9/100 the zero keeps the nine out of the tenths place. The denominator is determined by the final decimal place, and every symbolic answer can be checked against a shaded quantity and a position on the line.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside the fraction
10×10 hundredths grid shaded to match the decimal and the fraction
Number line for locating 0.3, 0.4, 0.62
Contrasting sets {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07} to drill the placeholder
Bidirectional conversion cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other)
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero: writing 9/100 as 0.9, or reading 0.07 as 7/10.
Adding an unneeded zero: writing 3/10 as 0.03 by over-applying 'hundredths = two places'.
Using one denominator for every decimal: writing 0.4 as 4/100 regardless of the number of places.
Reversing digits or reading position wrong: 0.62 → 6/2 or 26/100.
Placing decimals on the number line by whole-number reasoning rather than by tenths/hundredths.
constraints: Practise both directions (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) from the start; a learner may be fluent one way but not the other.
Deliberately include placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases (0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100): easy items can be answered correctly by digit-copying and so do not reveal understanding.
Correct answers: 0.62 = 62/100; 0.07 = 7/100; 0.4 = 4/10 (equivalently 40/100); 3/10 = 0.3; 9/100 = 0.09; 0.03 = 3/100; 0.4 sits at four tenths, just below halfway on a 0–1 line.
Check every conversion against a quantity (shaded grid) and a position (number line) to catch place-value errors such as 0.62 → 6/2 (dropping the place value) or 0.62 → 26/100 (reversing digits).
The annotated chart is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for repeated production with feedback.
Fixed worked examples can still teach the method; they simply cannot be manipulated, so pair them with learner-generated items.

A scored check can be used during teaching to surface errors, but on its own it measures the skill more than it builds it; use its placeholder distractors (e.g. 0.9 for 9/100, 7/10 for 0.07) diagnostically.
