activityReferences.title: Column workbench: aligning and padding to thousandths
Make 1: complements to a whole at three decimal places

startingActivity.title: Column workbench: aligning and padding to thousandths
learnerActions: Set out the subtraction 1.5 − 0.375 in place-value columns (ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths) aligned on the decimal point — the measuring context is a 1.5-litre bottle from which 0.375 l is poured out, finding how much is left.
Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500 by writing zeros in the empty hundredths and thousandths columns before subtracting.
Carry out the subtraction, borrowing just as with whole numbers (from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths), to reach 1.125 l remaining.
Add the three ragged measurements 1.2 m + 0.567 m + 2.233 m by first aligning on the point and padding every number to the same length (1.2 = 1.200), then summing each column to get 4.000 m.
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) and check the answer's size against the estimate.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 1.5 and 1.500 are the same number, but writing the padding zeros makes the hundredths and thousandths columns available so the digits line up and the borrow can ripple from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value columns to thousandths, aligned on the point
Number line zoomed to thousandths
Bar / complement model for 'make 1'
Measuring contexts (litres, metres) for the quantities
commonMisconceptions: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point (1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199)
Treats the decimal tail as a separate whole number ('longer is larger')
Forgets to pad and borrow across the point (1.5 − 0.375)
Complement-to-1 errors: completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the required 3 d.p. (0.4 + 0.6)
constraints: Use ragged-length decimals (different numbers of decimal places) in practice, not only tidy same-length items: equal-length items can let faulty right-justify or 'longer is larger' rules pass undetected.

A static aligned-columns picture or tap-to-reveal reference can illustrate one calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems; reserve it for modelling or review and require learners to lay out and compute fresh problems themselves.

Multiple-choice or fill-in checks can diagnose misalignment and complement errors but assess recognition of a final value; independent construction requires learners to set out the columns, pad, and carry/borrow themselves.
Insist complements be written to the required three decimal places (reject 0.4 + 0.6 for a 3-d.p. task even though it sums to 1).

When writing distractors for 1.5 − 0.375, the correct answer is 1.125; plausible error-based distractors include 1.275 (subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing) and 1.225 (borrowing without reducing the tenths digit from 5 to 4). Include 1.125 once as the correct option, and make sure no distractor equals it.

activityReferences.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias
Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero
Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths

startingActivity.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
learnerActions: Start with a number line showing just 0.34 and 0.35, with nothing marked between them, and predict aloud roughly where 0.345 should go.
Zoom into the gap between 0.34 and 0.35 and divide it into ten equal steps; name what each single step is worth (one thousandth, a tenth of the gap between two hundredths).
Count the steps and place 0.345 exactly on the fifth mark (the midpoint of the gap), then state why: it is 5 thousandths past 0.34.
Repeat the zoom-and-split for another thousandth, e.g. place 0.347, so the subdivision becomes a repeatable action, not a one-off.
Extend the action one level further: split a single thousandth into ten equal parts and name each tinier piece a ten-thousandth, illustrating that the ÷10 subdivision can always be repeated again.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A thousandth is a tenth of the gap between two hundredths; the number line never 'runs out' — you can always subdivide one more time by ten to locate a finer value (a tenth of a thousandth is a ten-thousandth).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart: ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths
Number line with zoom between two hundredths, split into ten thousandths
Recursive subdivision model (whole → tenth → hundredth → thousandth, ten-for-one each step)
Comparison pair 0.05 vs 0.005 to break whole-number bias
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: a thousandth taken as bigger than a hundredth or tenth 'because 1000 > 100'.
Placeholder error: writing 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025), not 0.025.
Miscoordinating the nesting: saying 10 thousandths = 1 tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Treating the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.025 is read as 'twenty-five' and mis-sized.
Thinking the number line 'runs out' at hundredths, so not subdividing further to place a thousandth.
constraints: Target age roughly 9–10 (Year 5): recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents.
Build thousandths by subdivision and zooming as actions the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt, not merely asserted.

A reference chart or diagram with tappable nesting facts and a notation flap can communicate the structure as a reference, but on its own it does not let the child perform the subdivision or the zoom; use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on subdivision.

Checkable question formats with distractors assess outcomes and can diagnose errors (whole-number bias, placeholder) but do not by themselves elicit the construction of the nesting; use them to check and route, not as the sole means of teaching the insight.
Always use placeholder cases (25/1000 = 0.025) and comparison cases (0.05 vs 0.005) because faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items.
Address whole-number bias directly by making 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller' visible, rather than by rule assertion.
Treat any physical paper split as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition: real card has slight thickness and only approximates the mathematical subdivision.

startingActivity.title: Order ragged decimals against a length model
learnerActions: Before using any model, predict the order of ragged decimals from smallest to largest and say why, e.g. for 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5.
Represent each decimal as a bar or length drawn to a common scale (for example a Linear Arithmetic Block / bar model), then check your predicted order against the lengths.

State the correct order (0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5) and justify it in place-value language: 0.312 and 0.38 both have 3 tenths, so they are smaller than 0.4 (4 tenths) and 0.5 (5 tenths); among the 3-tenths numbers, 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths).

Also compare the counterexample ragged pairs 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11, and 0.45 vs 0.405: predict first, then check each against the length model and in place-value words. These pairs deliberately trip both faulty rules — for example 0.45 vs 0.405 tempts longer-is-larger (405 looks bigger than 45), yet 0.45 (4 tenths 5 hundredths) is larger than 0.405 (4 tenths 0 hundredths 5 thousandths); and on the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 set a shorter-is-larger learner can still land the right order.
Locate the decimals on a number line and, where helpful, zoom between 0.3 and 0.4 to see 0.38 and 0.312 separated in the hundredths.
Compare 0.7 with 0.70 (optionally using an annex-zero toggle or shading) and explain why trailing zeros do not change the value.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The decimal with more digits is not automatically larger, and the one with fewer digits is not automatically larger either; size is decided by the highest place where the digits differ. A length/number-line model shows that more digits need not mean more length (0.38 is shorter than 0.4, but 0.87 is longer than 0.4). Annexing trailing zeros gives decimals the same number of decimal places without changing their value.

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with decimals aligned on the point
Number line (with zoom) for locating and comparing ragged decimals
Linear Arithmetic Blocks / length model where size = length
10×10 hundredths grids shaded for each decimal to compare area
Side-by-side correct vs incorrect comparison cards for discussion
commonMisconceptions: Longer-is-larger: judging the decimal with more digits as larger (0.45 > 0.5, 0.311 > 0.4), treating the tail as a whole number.
Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 0.4 > 0.87 because 0.4 is read as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87 ('sharing among fewer gives more').
Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 0.4 > 0.87 from the over-applied partial truth that a tenth is bigger than a hundredth.
Believing annexing a zero changes value (0.7 ≠ 0.70).
Comparing digit-by-digit from the right, or comparing the fractional parts as isolated whole numbers regardless of place.
constraints: Use ragged decimals deliberately (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11, 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.45 vs 0.405); same-length pairs let both faulty rules pass undetected and should not be the only practice.
On the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 ordering set a shorter-is-larger learner can still reach the right order, so include at least one pair (such as 0.4 vs 0.87) that directly exposes shorter-is-larger.
Teach 'annexing zeros is value-preserving' (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute for place-value reasoning.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method; rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and can mask the misconception.

A length model or number line (where size is shown by length) is the recommended visual here; the source synthesis prefers length over volume/3D models for this topic. This is a stated preference for showing decimal magnitude, not a universal claim that other media cannot teach.

A static aligned chart or single shaded grid is a reference/scaffold: it may support reading or checking a comparison but does not by itself provide the repeated ragged-case practice with feedback that builds the comparison skill.

Multiple-choice/ordering/true-false questions with distractors built from longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger can diagnose which faulty rule a child uses, but recognising the right option does not by itself build place-value insight; pair any quizzing with construction and justification.
Scope: Year 5 expectation is to read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places; extend from hundredths to thousandths deliberately.

startingActivity.title: Watch a fraction become a decimal: 3 ÷ 8
learnerActions: Before dividing, predict: will 3/8 be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why (3 shared among 8 people is less than one whole).
Carry out the division 3.000 ÷ 8 step by step, keeping the decimal point and trailing zeros, to reach 0.375.
Compare the result against your prediction. If you predicted more than 1, check whether you divided 3 by 8 or 8 by 3.
Try a case that never stops: carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... keep repeating, and note it does NOT equal 0.3.
Round only when told to (e.g. 1/3 ≈ 0.333 to three decimal places), and explain why the division never terminates.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The fraction bar means 'divide the numerator by the denominator'; 3/8 is 3 ÷ 8, and some divisions (like 1 ÷ 3) produce recurring, non-terminating decimals.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Long/short division laid out for 3 ÷ 8 (with the decimal point and trailing zeros) to show a fraction becoming a decimal
A triple-labelled bar or hundred-grid showing the same shaded quantity named as fraction, decimal and percentage at once
A number line from 0 to 1 with fractions, decimals and percentages all plotted, so order is visible spatially
A double number line / equivalence table of the landmark fractions and their decimal & percentage partners
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the division: reads 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3 (divides the larger by the smaller out of habit), giving 2.67 instead of 0.375.
Compares mixed forms by surface digits — thinks 1/3 is largest of {30%, 1/3, 0.35} because '3 is a big number' or because the numbers look bigger, without converting to a common form.
Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 (or 0.33) and terminating, not recognising the recurring decimal.
Believes every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal, so is thrown when a division doesn't stop.
constraints: A tap-to-reveal triple-labelled bar of landmark equivalents consolidates recall but does not let the learner choose and carry out a division or order an arbitrary mixed set, so it builds memory rather than the flexible conversion at the heart of this topic — pair it with active division and ordering work.

Recognition and matching checks (e.g. pairing 1/5↔0.2↔20%, or ordering a given set) can confirm the target skill but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct a conversion; include tasks where the learner carries out 3 ÷ 8 and explains their ordering.
1/3 does not equal 0.3 or exactly 0.33: it is the recurring 0.333..., so it is slightly larger than 30%. Round only when instructed, and treat 33.3% as a rounded value too.
Read 3/8 as 3 ÷ 8 (numerator ÷ denominator), not 8 ÷ 3; the reversed division giving 2.67 is a misconception to correct, never a valid answer.

Interactive panels (a digit-by-digit division display, a draggable 0-1 ordering line, a convert-to-common-form toggle) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and the same tasks can be done on paper.

startingActivity.title: Scale to a power of ten — does it land?
learnerActions: Take 1/8 and try to turn it into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths: find the multiplier (×125) that makes the denominator 1000, giving 125/1000 = 0.125; confirm it 'lands' exactly.
Now try 1/3 the same way: aim for 10, 100, 1000… and find that no power of ten works; carry out the division 1 ÷ 3 and watch the 3s continue (0.333…), a recurring decimal that never stops.
Write each denominator as a product of primes side by side: 8 = 2×2×2; 6 = 2×3; 3 = 3. Mark which denominators are built only from 2s and 5s.
State the rule you discover in your own words, then test it on 1/20, 1/40 (should terminate) and 1/6, 1/7 (should recur), factorising each denominator first.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator is built only from the primes 2 and/or 5 — because those are the primes of ten, so the denominator can be scaled to a power of ten. Any other prime factor forces a recurring decimal.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Prime-factor trees of denominators
Short division for fraction→decimal
FDP triple number line / equivalence cards
Hundredths and thousandths grids
commonMisconceptions: Reads 0.375 as 375/100 (denominator doesn't match the last place value)
Inverts the division, computing 8 ÷ 3 instead of 3 ÷ 8
Believes every fraction terminates, or truncates a recurring decimal (1/3 = 0.3) and treats it as exact
Decides whether a decimal terminates from the numerator or 'how neat it looks' rather than the denominator's prime factors
constraints: Recurring decimals must be shown genuinely recurring (1/3 = 0.333…); do not truncate (0.3 or 0.33) and call it exact. Rounding a recurring decimal to a set number of places is an approximation introduced for Year 6, not the exact value.
The 2-and-5 rule applies only to the denominator IN LOWEST TERMS; simplify first and ignore the numerator when judging termination.

Matching is recognition-and-recall practice, a sort checks classification of denominators, and a fill-in chain asks the learner to produce values; on their own these task types do not require the learner to carry out a full conversion in both directions and articulate the reason, so pair them with at least one activity where the learner constructs and explains a full conversion and a termination prediction (as the fill-in-and-explain and predict-and-justify steps do).

A tap-to-reveal equivalence card (fraction → decimal → percentage with denominator prime factors) is a useful reference aid but cannot let a learner test the terminate/recur boundary themselves; use it alongside, not instead of, the scaling/conversion work.
Fraction-as-division must be the direction numerator ÷ denominator (3 ÷ 8), not denominator ÷ numerator.

startingActivity.title: Factor-pair regrouping run beside the column method
learnerActions: Work out 25×16 without the column algorithm, splitting 16 into 4×4, then pairing one 4 with 25 to make 100, so the product collapses to 100×4 = 400 in two moves
Carry out the column method for 25×16 as well, and compare how many steps each route took
State the 'hinge' that made the shortcut work (25×4 = 100) and explain why spotting it saved effort
Try the same thinking on 50×16 and 25×24: regroup each to a friendly round number (50×2×8 = 100×8 = 800; 25×4×6 = 100×6 = 600) and show the route
Test a non-example, 23×16: try to find a neat factor pair to a hundred and explain why 25×16 is 'luckier'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A hard-looking multiplication can dissolve when you spot a factor pair that builds a friendly round number (here 25×4 = 100); recognising WHAT makes a shortcut available is the skill, not just reaching the answer.

keyRepresentations: Factor trees and factor-pair regrouping (16 = 4×4; 25×4 = 100)
Triple representation of FDP (bar, number line, and 0.75 / 3⁄₄ / 75% cards)

commonMisconceptions: Runs the standard column algorithm for 25×16 without looking for factor pairs that make it a mental step
Converts laboriously every time instead of recognising 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as the same number
Measures a missing angle with a protractor rather than deducing it from an angle fact
Picks the fraction/decimal/percentage form by habit rather than by which is efficient for the task
constraints: Reference cards, FDP match tasks and static angle-fact posters consolidate recall but do not let the child test alternative routes or feel the efficiency difference; pair them with problems that require choosing a method and explaining the choice.

Scored matching or 'which route is quickest?' items can check the structural choice but can mask whether efficiency was actually reasoned; always ask the child to say why, so recognition is not mistaken for independent construction.

The 25×4 = 100 factor-pair shortcut is specific: it works because 25 is a factor of 100 and 16 splits to supply the needed 4. State this condition and include non-examples (e.g. 23×16) so the move is not over-generalised as a universal trick.
The best FDP form is numbers-dependent (3/4 suits £80, 1/8 suits 12.5% of £80); do not teach a single 'always use' form.

Factor regrouping, FDP equivalence and these angle facts live in number lines, arrays and 2D diagrams; a 3D model is not needed here, though this reflects the topic's flat content rather than a general rule about 3D.

Open discussion alone gives the child no numbers, bars or diagrams to regroup or manipulate; these activities need those representations present, which does not imply dialogue cannot support the reasoning.

startingActivity.title: Stamp quarters past the whole and watch wholes form
learnerActions: On a number line marked in quarters, add one quarter at a time, counting aloud: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
At the 4th quarter, group the four quarters into one whole unit; do the same again at the 8th quarter.
Keep going to the 11th quarter and read off what you have: two whole units with three quarters sitting past them, so 11/4 = 2¾.
Now work the other way for 3⅖: break each of the 3 wholes into fifths (one whole = 5 fifths, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths), then add the 2 extra fifths to get 17/5.
Keep the denominator unchanged throughout, and say the running total in both forms as you go.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The improper form and the mixed form mark the SAME point: every b copies of 1/b fuse into one whole, and each whole breaks back into b pieces. This is why you multiply 3 × 5 (each whole is 5 fifths) and then add the 2, not add the whole to the numerator.

keyRepresentations: Number line with unit-fraction jumps continuing past 1 whole

commonMisconceptions: Mixed→improper adds the whole to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3+2)/5 = 5/5
Multiplies but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes (e.g. 11/4 → 3¾)
Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' and must always be written as a mixed number
Changes the denominator during conversion
constraints: Keep the denominator unchanged during conversion — only the grouping of equal-sized pieces changes.
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, then add 2), not as a bare '× then add' trick, so the first product is understood as counting pieces.
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not errors that must always be rewritten as mixed numbers.

The labelled static-bar activity is a scaffold: it can show and name the wholes inside an improper fraction but does not require the learner to enact the reversible grouping, so pair it with hands-on or line-based conversion.

Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks using the distractors 5/5, 15/5 and 32/5 can surface misconceptions, but watching the learner's working (grouping pieces vs. manipulating digits) is what discriminates understanding from a half-remembered rule; a recognition-only response does not by itself show independent construction.

startingActivity.title: Same two fractions, four operations
learnerActions: Fix two operands, e.g. 3/4 and 2/3, and work all four operations on this same pair, writing out each method.
For addition and subtraction, recut both to a common denominator (9/12 and 8/12) before combining: 3/4 + 2/3 = 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12.
For multiplication, multiply across without a common denominator: 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 — notice a common denominator is NOT needed here.
State out loud or in writing when a common denominator is required and when it is not, and say why (addition combines same-size parts; multiplication scales).
Before each calculation, estimate: should 3/4 + 2/3 be more or less than 1? Check your exact answer agrees.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Whether a common denominator is needed is a structural feature of the OPERATION, not a ritual applied to every fraction calculation: addition/subtraction combine same-size parts (need a common denominator) while multiplication/division scale (do not, in the standard methods).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A comparison table of +, −, ×, ÷ applied to the same two fractions, exposing which needs a common denominator
Number line for signed-integer addition/subtraction
Improper-fraction rewrites for × and ÷ of mixed numbers
Estimation with benchmarks / whole-number bounds
commonMisconceptions: Applies the wrong algorithm for the operation — finds a common denominator to multiply, or multiplies across to add
Leaves the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeks a common denominator in multiplication/division
Sign errors with negatives (e.g. −5 + 3 treated as −(5+3), or confusing −×− with −+−)
Multiplies or divides mixed numbers without first converting to improper fractions (distributes incompletely)
constraints: Scored multiple-choice or sorting tasks (e.g. 'which method does this need?', sorting calculations into needs/does-not-need a common denominator, matching a wrong worked example to its error) may efficiently check which method a pupil selects and surface algorithm confusion, but recognition of a method is not the same as producing one: such tasks do not themselves require a pupil to construct and justify a full written method, so pair them with pupils writing out and explaining their own working.

A static comparison chart of the four operations on one pair (tap-to-reveal each worked method, lift-the-flap 'why does × not need a common denominator?') supports the contrast but cannot let a pupil test method-selection on new operands; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Always require an estimate before each calculation to catch mis-applied algorithms and sign errors.
Watch and discuss the written method, not just the final answer, since the imported procedure is where the confusion shows.

A tutor-style 'which method and why?' dialogue can press past 'because that's the rule' and surface a pupil's reasoning, but the computation and the signed/mixed manipulations need a visual or symbolic working surface alongside it.

startingActivity.title: Locked-unit bar combiner (fixed-denominator model)
learnerActions: Work with a bar already partitioned into a fixed unit, e.g. fifths, with the label 'fifths' shown on the bar.
Combine 2/5 and another 2/5 by placing the pieces onto the bar; watch a running count read '4/5' as each piece is read aloud as 'one fifth'.

Test the answer '4/10' by laying four tenth-sized pieces next to the 4/5 you built. Notice that they cover only as much as two fifths, which is less than the four fifths on the bar, so 4/10 is the wrong amount. The pieces you are counting are all fifths.
Switch to subtraction on an eighths bar and remove pieces: start with 6/8 and take away 3/8, reading off 3/8 left.
Try adding one 2/5 too many and watch it run past the end of the bar, foreshadowing sums beyond one whole.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When denominators are the same, you are counting same-size pieces, so only the count (numerator) changes and the unit (denominator) stays fixed.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Fraction strip / bar partitioned into the fixed unit (sevenths, eighths) where pieces are combined or removed
Number line marked in the unit fraction, counting on/back in that unit
Discrete 'like objects' framing (each piece = one unit fraction) to make combining feel like counting
Paper folded/cut into equal parts (NFER's cut-a-strip-into-sevenths)
commonMisconceptions: Adds (or subtracts) the denominators as well as the numerators: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/10, misapplying whole-number addition (IES; ~10% of lower-achieving Y6 on an easy same-denominator item, NFER).
Drops the unit and answers a bare whole number: 6/8 − 3/8 = 3, operating only on the numerators as if the denominator weren't there.
Treats the denominator as a quantity to be operated on rather than the name of the unit being counted.
constraints: Keep to same denominators with results within one whole first; establish which of a pair is bigger before adding.
Confront the add-across error (2/5 + 2/5 ≠ 4/10) and the dropped-unit error (6/8 − 3/8 ≠ 3) early and directly, using models where the denominator cannot change.
Do subtraction alongside addition as separating the same units, keeping the unit fraction fixed; don't assess only one operation, which lets a learner pass on a lucky case.

A static tap-to-reveal strip (labelling numerator vs denominator, showing one worked sum) can serve as a reference anchor but does not let the learner combine pieces themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main doing.
Scored quiz items elicit recognition or a final answer, not independent construction of the combining, so pair them with construction on a model.
Paper/card pieces have real thickness and are an approximation of ideal flat equal parts; a screen bar is an idealised model — both are usable, neither is uniquely necessary.
Compare fractions by holding the common unit (denominator) fixed and counting the numerators; the denominator is a fixed label of the unit, not a quantity that is operated on or 'flipped'.

activityReferences.title: Spilling into the next whole: an adding model across two bars
Counting on past one whole on a number line
Check and explain: improper and mixed forms

startingActivity.title: Spilling into the next whole: an adding model across two bars
learnerActions: Set up two identical bars side by side, each partitioned into the SAME fixed unit (e.g. eighths), with the denominator kept locked so only the count of pieces changes.
Add 7/8 + 3/8 by placing eighth-pieces: fill the first bar with eight eighths, then let the remaining two eighths land in the second bar.
When a full set of denominator-many pieces (eight eighths) completes the first bar, group that full set into a single 'one whole' tile, so the child watches the whole form from the count.
Read the quantity both ways on the same shaded amount: as an improper fraction 10/8 and as a mixed number 1 2/8.
Repeat with 3/5 + 4/5: count fifths past 5/5 and re-group 7/5 as 1 2/5.

Do subtraction too: a within-whole case (5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6) where like units are simply separated, and a genuine crossing-the-whole case from a mixed/improper start that requires re-grouping a whole back into unit fractions (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5 = 6/5 − 3/5 = 3/5), treating both as separating like units.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction can exceed one whole; when the running count of unit fractions reaches the denominator those pieces re-group into one whole, which is how an improper fraction becomes a mixed number — seen, not memorised. Subtraction reverses the same re-grouping when a whole must be broken back into unit fractions.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two (or more) partitioned whole-bars side by side, pieces spilling from one into the next
Number line extending past 1, counting on in the unit fraction (fifths past 5/5)
Ten-frame-style grouping where a full set of denominator-many pieces fuses into one whole
Improper↔mixed toggle on the same shaded quantity (10/8 ↔ 1 2/8)
commonMisconceptions: Adds the denominators as well: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10 (add-across; on harder items this error spreads into middle-achieving pupils, NFER).
Believes a fraction cannot exceed one whole, so forces the result — stops at 5/5 = 1, or flips 7/5 to 5/7 — rather than accepting an improper fraction.
Miscounts the re-grouping when converting improper to mixed (e.g. 7/5 = 2 2/5 or 1 3/5), losing track of how many wholes the denominator makes.
constraints: Keep the denominator locked in all models so the unit stays fixed; this is what makes the add-across error visible as a change of unit.

A single static worked example can display one crossing-the-whole case and an improper↔mixed pair as an anchor, but it does not let the child perform the re-grouping; use it only as a reference alongside an activity where the child acts.

Matching and multiple-choice items consolidate and check, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction; include tasks where the child writes and explains both forms themselves.

Introduce the numeric improper↔mixed conversion rule only after the child has done the re-grouping on a model; the model-before-rule ordering is the intended sequence, not a claim that a rule-first approach can never work.

Include subtraction that crosses the whole (from mixed/improper starts) as well as within-whole subtraction, since the objective covers both; crossing-the-whole subtraction must actually start from or pass one whole (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5), unlike 5/6 − 2/6 which stays within one whole.

Answer options that 'cap at one whole' or flip the improper fraction are useful bait for the can't-exceed-one belief, but ensure the correct answer and feedback explicitly validate the improper fraction as a real number.

activityReferences.title: Trade a whole for unit fractions: make the borrow and carry physical
The improper-fraction fallback, side by side
Estimate first to police the answer

startingActivity.title: Trade a whole for unit fractions: make the borrow and carry physical
learnerActions: Work the subtraction 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 using whole tiles and fraction tiles that are locked to sixths so you cannot change the denominator.
Try to take away 5 sixths when you only have 2 — notice you are stuck. Break one whole tile into 6 sixths (the borrow), so you now have 8 sixths, and finish: 8/6 − 5/6 = 3/6, leaving 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Work the addition 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 the same way: gather the fifths, and when 5 fifths collect, fuse them into a fresh whole tile, giving 4 2/5.

Optionally model the same two problems on a number line: jump the whole numbers first, then the fraction parts, and watch a jump cross a whole boundary — the same regroup seen as a different representation.
Write each exchange as a number sentence: 4 = 3 + 6/6, and 7/5 = 1 + 2/5.
Say aloud whether the carry and the borrow are the same exchange running in opposite directions.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Borrowing is not a mysterious digit-move: it is literally trading one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6), and carrying is the reverse — fusing a whole-worth of unit fractions back into one whole. The denominator stays fixed because fifths only join with fifths.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line: jump the whole numbers, then the fraction parts, crossing whole boundaries
Bar model with whole tiles plus fraction tiles; a whole tile that shatters into b unit-fractions for the borrow, or b fraction tiles that fuse into a whole
The regroup written as 4 = 3 + 6/6 (or the improper rewrite 26/6)
Improper-fraction form beside the mixed form for comparison
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the fraction parts (3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10), applying whole-number addition to numerator and denominator
Subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never borrows (4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5|=3)
Leaves an improper fraction part in the answer (3 7/5) instead of regrouping to 4 2/5
Miscounts when converting mixed to improper (2 3/5 → 10/5 then forgets the +3/5, or writes 5/5)
constraints: Lock the denominator as a fixed unit so fifths add to fifths; this blocks the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits.
Always check whether fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup so answers are proper mixed numbers (7/5 → 1 2/5).

Worked-example or revealable-step formats support meaning but do not let the learner trigger the exchange on their own numbers — treat them as scaffolds and follow with independent construction on fresh problems.

Recognition and matching tasks (mixed-to-improper, choosing the right answer) can check understanding but do not elicit the learner's own step-by-step regrouping; include tasks where the learner shows every step.
Teach both methods; do not present the improper route as the only correct one — the separate-parts route is where the borrow and carry become meaningful.

activityReferences.title: Align the strips: cut thirds into sixths to make a common unit
Equivalence-and-combine practice that surfaces common errors
Read a worked conversion, then perform your own

startingActivity.title: Align the strips: cut thirds into sixths to make a common unit
learnerActions: Try to combine 1/3 and 1/6 using a thirds strip and a sixths strip laid together; notice the pieces are different sizes and do not line up as they are.
Cut each third-piece in half so each single third becomes TWO sixth-pieces; watch the label change 1/3 → 2/6 as the one piece splits into two and the numerator ticks 1→2.
Now that every piece is a sixth, combine: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6.
Simplify 3/6 to 1/2 and check on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length.

Repeat the same cut-to-match process for 3/4 − 1/8 (recut quarters into eighths, giving 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8) and 2/5 + 3/10 (recut fifths into tenths, giving 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10), simplifying where possible.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When you add by counting parts, thirds and sixths must be made the same size first; cutting each third in two makes it two sixths (so the numerator doubles exactly as the denominator doubles), and only then do both fractions share one common unit and combine by counting like parts.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two fraction strips with related partitions (thirds and sixths) overlaid so one must be re-partitioned to match
Number line where thirds are subdivided into sixths to align the two fractions
Fraction circles/area model showing 1/3 recut into 2/6 to give a common denominator (IES Fig 6)
Equivalence chain 1/3 = 2/6 shown as cutting each third in two (numerator doubles with denominator)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9, combining numerators and denominators (NFER's 3/9-type error).
Renames the denominator without scaling the numerator: converts 1/3 to 1/6 and gets 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 — 'just inserts the larger denominator' (IES).
Forgets to simplify the result (leaves 3/6 rather than 1/2), or doesn't recognise the answer can be reduced.
constraints: Establish the NEED for a common unit before any rule, using a representation that makes different-sized parts obvious (thirds and sixths cannot be counted together as they are).
Renaming must scale BOTH numerator and denominator together (1/3 → 2/6, not 1/6); the commonest slip is changing only the denominator.
Use estimation to judge reasonableness (1/3 + 1/6 must be more than 1/3, so 2/9 cannot be right).
Always simplify the result and check it against the model (3/6 → 1/2); connect back to counting like units once denominators match.

Prefer representations that hold the unit (the whole) constant — fraction strips, number lines, fraction circles. Dot paper has been noted (IES) as reinforcing adding without a common denominator, so avoid it for this objective.

Multiple-choice and fill-in items are useful for diagnosing and practising, but a recognition response does not by itself show the learner can independently perform the re-partition and combine; include a task where they carry out the conversion.

If paper fraction strips or circles are used as physical manipulatives, keep the represented whole constant and explicit each time pieces are cut, so the mathematical fraction — not the physical object — is what is combined; the slight thickness of real card is a negligible approximation of the ideal flat region it stands for.

Scope this to RELATED denominators (one a multiple of the other) so exactly one fraction is renamed; fully unlike denominators are a later step. Here the fractions are quantities being combined, so the common-unit requirement is about representing both portions on one whole — it is not a comparison of unit fractions.

Act out pouring and joining with a locked-unit model
Study then classify the two story structures

startingActivity.title: Model the story before you compute
learnerActions: Read: 'A jug holds 3/4 of a litre of juice; 2/4 of a litre is poured out — how much is left?' Draw a bar showing 3/4, shade the 2/4 poured away, and read the remaining 1/4 off your picture.
Read: 'Two ribbons are 2 3/8 inches and 1 5/8 inches long — what is their total length?' Draw the two ribbons laid end to end on a bar marked in eighths.
Before writing any symbols, say aloud whether the story is a 'take away' or a 'combine', and name which quantity is removed or joined.
Write the matching equation, keeping the denominator fixed (quarters stay quarters, eighths stay eighths): 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4; 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 4.
When the fraction parts reach 8/8, regroup that whole into the whole-number count so the total reads 4 inches, not 3 8/8.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The story tells you the operation; a picture drawn first makes join-versus-separate visible, and holding the denominator as a fixed unit means combining 3/8 and 5/8 gives 8/8 = one whole, never 8/16.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model of the jug (part poured out shaded) or the ribbons laid end to end
Number line for combining/removing lengths
Story ↔ equation ↔ picture triple
Regroup of a fraction sum crossing a whole (8/8 = 1)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across denominators when combining (2 3/8 + 1 5/8 → 3 8/16)
Chooses the wrong operation — adds when the story separates, or vice versa
Leaves a crossing sum unregrouped (3 8/8 rather than 4)
Misreads which quantity is removed or kept in the context
constraints: All fractions in a problem must refer to the same whole and share a like denominator; these tasks do not cover unlike-denominator addition.
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit: combining 3/8 and 5/8 gives 8/8 = 1 whole, never 8/16. The denominator names the piece size and does not change when like fractions are joined.
Regroup any crossing sum: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 4; 3 8/8 has the same value but has not been regrouped, so write the final answer as 4.

Sorting, matching and multiple-choice tasks assess operation-choice but do not elicit independent drawing/modelling of a new story; use construction tasks (draw the model, write and solve the equation) to build that skill.
A tap-to-reveal worked pair illustrates the two structures but does not let a learner model a fresh story — treat it as a scaffold, then move to learner-constructed models.

An interactive locked-unit model, a hand-drawn bar/number line, and an in-role conversation can each support the reading/modelling in different ways; none is uniquely necessary, so do not require a particular medium.

activityReferences.title: Slice one bar many ways
Mixed number as one count of like parts
Check and sort candidate decompositions
Explain, don't just compute, subtraction as separating

startingActivity.title: Slice one bar many ways
learnerActions: Start with a bar whose total length represents 5/6 of a whole, marked off into five equal sixths (each one-sixth of the whole) against a fixed ruler so its length cannot change.
Group the sixths one way (e.g. 1 and 4) and write the matching sum of sixths underneath: 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6.
Regroup the SAME bar differently (2 and 3; then 1, 1 and 3) and write each new sum: 2/6 + 3/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 3/6.
Line up all the sums you have written against the single unchanged bar and say aloud: 'all of these are 5/6'.
Repeat the whole process with a fresh fraction you have not seen (e.g. 7/8) to produce at least two distinct decompositions.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A fraction is not one fixed break-up: any grouping of its unit parts that uses the same denominator and the same total count measures the same quantity. Addition joins those parts and subtraction separates them, while the unit stays fixed.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Fraction bar that can be sliced into groups in multiple ways, total length fixed
Number line showing a fraction reached by different combinations of unit-fraction jumps
Part-part-whole / bar model linking a fraction to its decompositions
Mixed-number bar showing whole sets of the unit plus the extra part (2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8)
commonMisconceptions: Alters denominators when decomposing (a reverse add-across): writes 5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6, so the parts don't actually total 5/6.
Believes a fraction has only one 'correct' break-up (3/8 must be 1/8+1/8+1/8) and cannot produce a different valid decomposition.
Treats a mixed number's whole and fraction parts as disconnected numbers, unable to express 2 1/8 as a single count of eighths (17/8).
constraints: Keep the denominator (the unit) fixed throughout every join, separate, and decomposition; this is the non-negotiable idea that blocks the reverse add-across.
Always demand MORE THAN ONE decomposition of the same fraction; a single memorised split does not demonstrate flexibility.

The reverse add-across (5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3) is a genuine error, not an acceptable alternative answer: its parts sum to 5/3, not 5/6, and are not measured in sixths. Never present it as valid; use it only as a checked-and-rejected trap.
2 wholes of eighths are 16/8, not 2/8; ensure the whole part is recounted in the shared unit before converting (2 1/8 = 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8).

Selecting or recognising a correct decomposition is a check on reasoning and does not by itself show independent construction; pair recognition tasks with the learner producing their own decompositions.
Static worked examples can show a couple of decompositions for reference but cannot let the child generate new groupings, which is the actual skill; treat them as support, not the main activity.
Justify each decomposition against a model where the total measure is invariant (fixed-length bar or number line), so different sums are seen to share one measure.

Narrow medium affordances (not universal laws): discussion alone can support explaining a decomposition but does not itself let a child perform the slicing and grouping; and because this content is planar part-whole reasoning, a 3D/spatial model adds no dimension the task needs. Neither observation means any medium 'cannot teach' — explaining aloud is retained as part of several activities.

activityReferences.title: Shared-grid combiner: rename both fractions, then combine
Mixed-number subtraction with a regroup across the whole
Explain and check with a model

startingActivity.title: Shared-grid combiner: rename both fractions, then combine
learnerActions: Set up 2/3 + 5/4 on two strips or two number lines, one gridded in thirds and one in quarters, and notice they will not combine while the units differ.
Choose a shared unit (a common multiple of 3 and 4) and re-grid both strips into twelfths, re-tiling each fraction: 2/3 becomes 8/12 and 5/4 becomes 15/12.

State explicitly that cutting each third into four pieces turns 2/3 into 8/12 — the top is multiplied by the same factor as the bottom — and check the same for 5/4 (each quarter cut into three, so 5/4 = 15/12) before combining.
Combine the re-tiled pieces to get 23/12 and regroup into the mixed number 1 11/12.

Before computing, estimate: 5/4 is already more than 1, so adding a positive 2/3 makes the sum more than 1 (indeed more than 1.5). That already rules out answers like 7/7 = 1; the true sum lands just below 2 (23/12, just under 24/12).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Unlike fractions can only be combined once BOTH are rewritten over the same unit; each numerator scales by the same factor as its own denominator, and estimation gates whether a result is even possible.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two strips/number lines re-gridded to a common denominator (thirds and quarters → twelfths)
Area/fraction-circle model showing both fractions recut to the shared unit
Mixed-number bars showing a whole tile broken into the common unit to enable borrowing (1 whole → 20/20)
Improper-fraction conversion as an alternative route (3 1/4 = 13/4) laid beside the mixed form
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7, combining numerators and denominators.
Finds a common denominator but scales only one (or neither) numerator, or uses a wrong common denominator (2/3 = 2/12).

In mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of position (does 12/20 − 5/20), never regrouping across the whole when the minuend's fraction part is smaller.
constraints: Target age approximately 10–11 (Year 6); learners should already be able to generate equivalent fractions and convert between mixed and improper forms, since these are the enabling moves for the regroup.
A common multiple of the denominators gives the shared unit; the product always works and the least common multiple is sometimes tidier — do not teach that one specific denominator is required.
Both numerators must scale with their own denominators; the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling errors appear, so check both equivalences before combining.
Keep the unit constant within any representation and avoid manipulatives that let learners combine pieces without first establishing a common denominator.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-blank items (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4 with 7/7 as a distractor, or a mixed subtraction with the no-borrow answer as a distractor) can diagnose add-across, partial-scaling, and no-borrow errors, but recognising a correct option does not demonstrate independent construction of the renaming and regrouping; use alongside tasks where the learner carries out the full procedure.
A fully worked static picture can anchor one conversion or borrow but does not let the learner perform the re-gridding themselves; use it as a reference rather than the main activity.
Teach both the borrow-a-whole and convert-to-improper routes and let learners choose; the improper route is often cleaner precisely when a borrow would be needed.
Estimation benchmarks must be stated correctly: 2/3 + 5/4 is more than 1 (5/4 alone exceeds 1) and lands just below 2 (23/12); do not state it exceeds 2.

activityReferences.title: Jump-counter number line for n × a/b
Build from repeated addition before stating the rule
Targeted practice that baits the multiply-denominator error

startingActivity.title: Jump-counter number line for n × a/b
learnerActions: Set the jump size to 3/8 and dial the number of jumps to 4; watch four identical hops march along the line and land on 12/8.
Re-group the landing point into a mixed number: 12/8 = 1 4/8 (= 1 1/2).

Keep the jump size fixed and change only how many jumps there are for n × 1/4 with n = 3, 5, 8, each time reading off the total count of quarters and converting past-one results to mixed or whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4; 8 × 1/4 = 8/4 = 2).
Switch to a mixed-number mode: lay three whole 2 1/3 bars end to end so every part is tripled, and read that three 2s and three thirds make 6 + 3/3 = 7.
Say aloud what changed and what stayed the same after each build: the unit (the eighth, the third) never changed, only how many of them there were.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Because the unit part stays the same size, multiplying by a whole number only multiplies the COUNT of parts: n × a/b = (n×a)/b, with the denominator unchanged. A mixed number × whole requires multiplying every part.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated equal jumps of the unit/non-unit fraction
Fraction bars showing n copies of a/b combined
Repeated-addition equation aligned with the (n×a)/b rule
Improper↔mixed conversion of the product (6/5 = 1 1/5)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too: 4 × 3/8 = 12/32, applying the whole number to both parts instead of just the count of unit fractions.
Incompletely distributes over a mixed number: 2 1/3 × 3 = 6 1/3, multiplying the whole but forgetting the fraction part.
Confuses the operation with addition (adds 4 + 3/8) or cannot see 5 × 1/4 as five quarters.
constraints: A static worked example (e.g. tapping 5/4 to reveal five quarter-pieces) can anchor the idea but does not let the learner build and vary the jumps; use it as a reference, not the main construction activity.

Multiple-choice and fill-in items elicit recognition and computation and can bait the denominator error, but do not by themselves require independent construction of the repeated-addition model or spoken justification; pair them with build-and-explain work.
Keep the unit (denominator) genuinely fixed in any model so the learner changes only the count; the pedagogical point is lost if the part size appears to change.
For mixed numbers, ensure the model or working shows EVERY part multiplied; only tripling the whole part reproduces the incomplete-distribution error.

activityReferences.title: Build the area and watch the tiles appear
Read a tiled diagram and justify each number

startingActivity.title: Build the area and watch the tiles appear
learnerActions: Start from one whole unit square. Partition it in two directions — cut it into 3 columns one way and 4 rows the other way — to model 2/3 × 3/4.
Count the small tiles that appear in the whole unit square (3 across × 4 down = 12) and name the value of ONE tile: 1/12 of the unit square.
Shade the 2-by-3 corner block (2 of the 3 columns, 3 of the 4 rows) and count the shaded tiles: 2×3 = 6, so 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2.
Compare the shaded rectangle against the whole unit square and confirm it is exactly half of it — an area smaller than either side length (because each side is less than 1).
Say aloud which number in the picture gives the denominator (3×4 = 12 tiles per unit) and which gives the numerator (2×3 = 6 shaded tiles).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Cutting the unit square in two directions redefines the unit into b×d equal tiles (so denominators multiply) and the shaded a×c block gives the numerator — this is why (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, and why the product can be smaller than both sides when both sides are less than 1.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two-way partitioned unit square (area model) with a×c tiles shaded out of b×d
Single unit-fraction tile labelled 1/(b×d) as the counting unit
Grid extended across several unit squares for mixed-number sides
Side-by-side diagram and equation (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd with the tiles that justify each factor
commonMisconceptions: Reads the tile as 1/(b+d) — e.g. 1/7 for a 3-by-4 partition — adding the partitions instead of multiplying (area treated additively)
Confuses area with perimeter — measures the boundary of the shaded rectangle rather than counting interior tiles
Partitions in only one direction, so the two-dimensional tile is never formed and denominators are not multiplied
Loses the unit square: counts shaded tiles as a whole number (6) rather than 6 of 12 of ONE unit
Believes area must be larger than the sides, so distrusts an area (1/2) smaller than either side length
constraints: Keep the unit square explicit and labelled throughout — losing track of what '1' is is the commonest failure.

A static or tappable tiled diagram supports reading (naming the tile, identifying the multiplication) but cannot host the produce half; pair it with an actual drawing task where the learner chooses both cuts.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice on tile value, shading on a pre-partitioned grid) can check specific points — e.g. distinguishing 1/12 from 1/7 — but do not require the learner to construct or explain the representation, and cannot verify a freely produced diagram. Use them as checks, not as the main task.

Rectangular area here is a planar (flat) idea; a thin cutout or screen grid only approximates the represented ideal unit square (ideal figures have zero thickness, while real paper or card has slight thickness). Avoid 3D/volume renderings, which can misframe the unit-square idea being taught.
Start each build from the whole unit square and partition in TWO directions; a one-direction cut never forms the two-dimensional tile and does not multiply the denominators.

Interpreting and producing a tiled diagram is visual-spatial work; talk alone cannot display the two-way partition or capture the learner's drawing, though discussion can support the reasoning alongside the diagram.
The 'product is smaller than either side' intuition applies only when both side lengths are less than 1; do not state it unconditionally, since the mixed-number extension (1 1/2 × 2/3 = 1) breaks it.

activityReferences.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
Contrast multiplication with the addition rule
Compute and simplify (practice and self-check)

startingActivity.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
learnerActions: Shade 4/5 of a unit square with vertical stripes.
Shade 2/3 of the square with horizontal stripes, over the same region.
Watch the square rule itself into a 3×5 grid of fifteenths; count the crosshatched overlap (8 tiles) and read the product as 8/15.
Repeat for 3/4 × 2/3: see the overlap as 6 tiles out of 12, then use a simplify step to collapse 6/12 to 1/2 on the same picture.
Say each product in words using 'of': '2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths.'

Fold in a whole-number case: model 2/3 × 4 (as 2/3 × 4/1) using four unit squares, splitting each into thirds and shading 2/3 of each (equivalently, splitting the 4 wholes into 3 equal parts and taking 2), and read off 8 thirds = 8/3 = 2 2/3; optionally show the same on a number line, jumping 2/3 four times to land on 8/3.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multiplying two proper fractions means taking a part of a part; the crosshatched overlap sits plainly INSIDE both striped regions, so the product is smaller than either proper factor, and the b×d grid gives the denominator automatically (no common denominator needed). The whole-number case is different: 2/3 × 4 is four copies of 2/3, so 8/3 is larger than 2/3.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area model: unit square partitioned b×d, one fraction shaded each way, product = overlapping tiles
'Fraction of a fraction' bar: take c/d of the whole, then a/b of that piece
Number line for the fraction × whole case
Equation (a×c)/(b×d) aligned with the shaded grid count
commonMisconceptions: Leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3), over-generalising the common-denominator rule from addition to multiplication (IES).
Seeks a common denominator before multiplying, importing the addition procedure unnecessarily.
Believes the product must be bigger than the factors, so distrusts a smaller answer.
Computes the product but leaves it unsimplified (6/12 rather than 1/2).
constraints: Read every product as 'of' first (2/3 × 4/5 = two-thirds OF four-fifths) and model it before computing symbolically.
Explicitly contrast with addition: multiplication multiplies straight across and needs no common denominator; raise this whenever a learner tries to find one.
Always put products in simplest form, and where possible simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers (8/3 = 2 2/3).
The practice items check fluency and bait known errors; they do not by themselves build the 'part of a part' meaning, so pair them with the area-model construction rather than substitute for it.

A static finished picture (e.g. tapping to reveal 8/15 on a pre-shaded square) can serve as a reference anchor, but it does not let the learner build the shading or vary the factors, which is where the understanding forms — use it as a supplement, not the main activity.
The area model is planar; a flat grid is the natural representation here and a 3D rendering is not needed for this objective.

The claim 'product is smaller than either factor' is scoped to two nonzero proper fractions; when a proper fraction multiplies a whole number greater than 1, the product (e.g. 2/3 × 4 = 8/3) is smaller than the whole number but larger than the proper fraction factor.

startingActivity.title: Recipe scaler with a four-region area model
learnerActions: Take a recipe needing 2 1/3 cups of flour and a goal of 1 1/2 batches, and first estimate by scaling (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) before doing any exact computation.
Draw or build a rectangle 2 1/3 wide and 1 1/2 tall to represent the product.
Tile the rectangle into its four regions: the 2×1 block, the 2×1/2 strip, the 1/3×1 strip, and the 1/3×1/2 corner; label each region's value (2, 1, 1/3, 1/6) and add them to get 3 1/2 cups.
Alongside, rewrite both mixed numbers as improper fractions and compute 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2, checking it matches the area total.
Check the exact answer (3 1/2 cups) against your earlier scaling estimate of about 3.5 cups.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Mixed × mixed produces four partial products; the shortcut of only multiplying wholes and fractions omits the two large cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), so the answer 2 1/6 is far too small. Converting to improper fractions or counting all four regions gives the complete product, and a scaling estimate confirms direction and magnitude.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area model of mixed × mixed with four partial-product regions
Improper-fraction rewrite of both mixed numbers
Recipe/scaling bar showing the ingredient stretched by the batch factor
Estimation with rounded decimals or whole numbers
commonMisconceptions: Incomplete distribution: multiplies whole × whole and fraction × fraction, omitting the cross terms (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 1/6)
Multiplies without converting mixed to improper, mishandling the parts
Leaves the denominator unchanged / seeks a common denominator (importing add/subtract habits into ×)
Skips the reasonableness check, so an implausible product goes unnoticed
constraints: Target age 10–11; procedural real-world fraction and mixed-number multiplication.
Convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying, OR lay out all four partial products in an area model; do not multiply whole×whole and fraction×fraction and add.
This is multiplication: both denominators multiply and no common denominator is required — do not import addition/subtraction habits.

Require a scaling estimate before computing and check the exact answer against it; include at least one less-than-one (shrinking) factor so learners meet a case where the product is smaller than the original.

The static diagram and the recognition/matching items are scaffolds or checks: they support interpretation but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a new product or catch their own live omission.
The area model is a 2D representation of the product (cups × batches), not a physical area: cups of flour are actually a volume measure, but a 3D volume model is unnecessary and could mislead here.
Interactive touches (flashing uncounted regions, estimate slider, tappable regions) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory.
The '3' option is an explicitly-wrong distractor only; do not present it or 2 1/6 as a valid answer, and do not assert a certified origin for the '3' error beyond plausible rounding/omission.

startingActivity.title: Operator machine: set an amount, set an operator, watch it partition
learnerActions: Enter an amount shown as a whole bar or hundred-grid (e.g. 200).

Work one example at a time, each with its own entered amount: with 200 in the bar apply the fraction 3/4; then re-enter 60 and apply the percentage 20% — watch the same machine partition into equal parts and shade the taken portion each time.
Read the equation printed beside each partition: 3/4 × 200 = 150; and separately 20% = 20/100 = 0.2, so 0.2 × 60 = 12.
Move the operator above 1 (e.g. 150% of 200 = 300, or 5/4 of 200 = 250) and below 1, and describe in words whether the result grew or shrank from the starting amount and why.

Second stage — a shop: start from a £45 price, apply '20% off' so 20% of £45 = £9 is shaded (a double number line pairing £0–£45 with 0–100% can show where 20% sits), then subtract to reach the £36 paid; state the two separate moves — find 20% OF the price, THEN take it away.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 'Of' is one action — partition the whole into equal parts, then take a copies — whether it wears a fraction hat or a percent hat. Whether the result is bigger or smaller than you started is decided by the operator's size, not by multiplication 'always enlarging'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model of the whole amount partitioned into b equal parts, a of them shaded
Hundred-grid / percentage bar for percentage-of
Double number line pairing the amount with 0-100% for percentage-of
The operator equation a/b × q, written beside the partition it summarises
commonMisconceptions: Finds the unit fraction and stops (200÷4 = 50 offered as '3/4 of 200'), forgetting to take a copies
Converts the percentage wrongly — 25% treated as ÷25 or ×25, or 20% as 0.02 / 2.0
Believes 'of'/multiplication must enlarge, so distrusts a correct smaller answer
Adds/subtracts the percentage directly to the amount instead of operating (20% of 60 read as 60+20 or 60-20)
constraints: Build from the known unit-fraction case before compressing: make the two-step structure (÷denominator to find the unit part, then ×numerator to take a copies) explicit for non-unit fractions.
Convert percentages deliberately (20% = 20/100 = 0.2) so percentage-of reuses the identical operator rather than becoming a separate rule.
Deliberately contrast an operator below 1 (shrinks) with one above 1 (grows, e.g. 150% of, 5/4 of) so learners do not glue 'multiply' to 'gets bigger'.

Keep each operator example's amount explicit so the printed equation matches the amount actually set (e.g. 3/4 of 200, 20% of 60, 20% of £45) — do not silently change the amount between a stated setup and its result.
Use realistic multi-step contexts (discount, VAT, tips, recipe portions) and require judging the answer's reasonableness.

The staged worked bar is a scaffold: it makes structure inspectable but the learner cannot vary the operator, so it must not be the only format — pair it with activity where the learner sets the operator and with production tasks.
The scored check assesses and diagnoses fluency; it does not by itself build the operator meaning and should follow, not replace, the constructive work.
Recognition/multiple-choice responses do not elicit independent construction; include tasks where the learner computes and shows method, not only selects an answer.
Discount tasks require two distinct moves — find the percentage OF the amount, then subtract — and both should be stated separately.

startingActivity.title: Slide the digits right on a place-value chart
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns labelled hundreds, tens, ones, then a decimal point, then tenths and hundredths.
Place digit cards for 37 (3 in tens, 7 in ones) and predict what dividing by 10 will do.
Divide by 10 by sliding each digit card one column to the RIGHT: the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 moves from ones to tenths, giving 3.7. Notice the decimal point itself does not move.
Read the result back by place value: '3 ones and 7 tenths'.
Now place a single digit card for 4 in the ones column and divide by 100 by sliding it two columns right, so the 4 lands in hundredths.
Notice the tenths column is now empty and write a 0 to hold that place, giving 0.04. Say why, without the 0, you would wrongly read 0.4.

Optionally model the same shrink with another representation — base-ten blocks with exchange (letting a flat be one whole so a rod is a tenth of a flat and a small cube a hundredth), a Gattegno tenths/hundredths chart, or a number line — to see the quantity becoming ten or a hundred times smaller.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 (or 100) shifts every digit one (or two) places right and makes it ten (or a hundred) times smaller; a placeholder zero is needed whenever a column between the point and a digit is left empty.

commonMisconceptions: Applies 'move the decimal point' by rote and gets the magnitude wrong (37 ÷ 10 → 0.37 or 370)
Omits the placeholder zero: 4 ÷ 100 → 0.4
Over-generalises 'divide by 10 = take a zero off', which fails on numbers without a trailing zero
constraints: Teach digits-shift-right with the decimal point staying fixed; do not teach 'add/remove a zero' as a rule, since it fails for any number without a trailing zero (e.g. 37 ÷ 10), and do not teach 'move the decimal point' as the main rule, since it gives the same result but hides why each digit's value changes and can lead to errors when a placeholder zero is needed (e.g. 4 ÷ 100).
Always make the placeholder zero explicit: 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04, not 0.4; require learners to say why the tenths place needs a 0.
Have learners read results by place value ('3 ones and 7 tenths'), not as a bare digit string, so magnitude is checked.
A static chart labels landing places but does not perform the movement; use it as a reference beside activities where the learner actually slides the digits.
Recognition/selection questions check whether a result is correct but do not by themselves elicit the learner independently constructing the movement; pair them with hands-on chart work.

Alternative representations (base-ten blocks with exchange, Gattegno chart, number line) are optional supports, not requirements; when using base-ten blocks, fix which block is the whole so a rod reads as a tenth.

startingActivity.title: How many fit? Predict then count on a length bar
learnerActions: Take a 4-unit strip/bar and a stack of 1/5 tiles (ribbon lengths or number-line jumps work equally well).
BEFORE placing any tile, write down a prediction of how many 1/5 tiles will fit, and a one-sentence reason.
Lay the 1/5 tiles end-to-end across the bar, counting as you go: 5 fill the first whole, 10 the second, and so on until you reach 20.
Compare the count (20) with your prediction, and discuss why the answer is bigger than 4.
Repeat with a different piece size (e.g. 1/2 gives 8, 1/10 gives 40) and describe how the size of the piece drives the count.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When the piece is small, many copies fit, so dividing a positive whole number by a fraction between 0 and 1 produces a count larger than the dividend. The quotient is something you can physically count, not a trick.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number line partitioned into fifths with jumps counted across 0–4
Ribbon/tape model: unit-fraction lengths laid end-to-end inside the whole (IES Fig 8 style)
Array of unit-fraction pieces filling the dividend
The inverse equation 20 × 1/5 = 4 written beside the count
commonMisconceptions: Quotient must be smaller than the dividend, so 4 ÷ 1/5 'can't' be 20 (whole-number over-generalisation that division shrinks)
Divides by the denominator instead: 4 ÷ 1/5 read as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 (treats the unit fraction as its denominator)
Confuses with multiplication: computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 (imports the more-familiar operation)
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers rather than 1/5 as one quantity
constraints: Lead with the 'how many fit' measurement question on a length model; the quotient should be something the child physically counts, not a rule they apply.
Confront 'division makes smaller' directly: predict first, then fit pieces and see the count exceed the dividend, then discuss why (small divisor → many copies).
Always tie back to the inverse check (20 × 1/5 = 4); do not teach an invert-and-multiply rule without this meaning.

A static number-line image showing 4 wholes cut into fifths with 20 countable segments supports the meaning well, but does not let the learner vary the divisor to test the pattern; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the misconception but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and explanation; pair them with activities that require counting and justifying.

Optional interactive supports (e.g. dragging 1/5 tiles into a bar with a running counter, a divisor dial that swaps 1/4, 1/3, 1/10 and shows the count change, an inverse panel animating 20 fifths fusing into 4 wholes, a contrast switch to the partition case 1/3 ÷ 4) make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
Keep the model one-dimensional ('how many lengths fit'); adding 3D depth risks implying volume and is not needed for this concept, though this is a design judgement, not a proven limitation.
Distinguish 4 ÷ 1/5 (how many fifths in four) from both 4 ÷ 5 (dividing by the denominator) and 4 × 1/5 (four fifths); model the contrasts explicitly.

startingActivity.title: Share a third four ways on a bar
learnerActions: Start with a whole bar that has one-third shaded.
Apply a '÷4' cut to the shaded third so it splits into 4 equal parts.

Re-rule the WHOLE bar the same way: if your cuts run along the bar (crossing the third-lines), extend them across the whole bar; if they run across the bar like the third-lines, cut each of the other two thirds into 4 equal parts too. Count: the whole is now ruled into 12 equal parts.
Read off one little shaded piece and name it: it is one-twelfth, not a smaller third.
Say out loud where 12 comes from: 3 original parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12.
Gather 4 of the twelfths back together to remake the original third, confirming 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
Optionally repeat on a number line: split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 equal sub-segments and see each is 1/12 of the whole 0–1 line.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Sharing one-third among 4 cuts the whole into twelfths because the second cut (into 4) multiplies the first partition (into 3): 3 × 4 = 12. The answer is smaller than 1/3, and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely — this is the picture, not a memorised rule.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area/bar model: a shaded 1/3 sub-divided into 4, with the whole re-ruled into 12
Number line where the 0–1/3 segment is split into 4 sub-segments of 1/12
The double-partition grid (3 × 4) tying the 12 to the two cuts
Inverse equation 1/12 × 4 = 1/3 beside the picture
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalises the just-learned 'dividing by fractions makes bigger' and inverts: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/3 × 4 = 4/3 (confuses partition with measurement division)
Gets 1/12 by a rule but cannot say why the pieces are twelfths — thinks they are still thirds
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, dividing the wrong part (e.g. 1 ÷ 4 over 3)
Adds the whole number to the denominator: 1/3 ÷ 4 → 1/7
constraints: A multiple-choice or recognition item confirms the result (1/12) but does not show the learner can independently construct the partition or explain why the pieces are twelfths; pair any recognition item with drawing the split and stating the inverse.

A static or fixed bar figure can teach the partition meaning if it is read and explained, but it does not let the learner vary the sharer to generalise; include at least one case the learner partitions themselves (e.g. 1/6 ÷ 3).

The partition can also be shown on a number line (split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 sub-segments of 1/12), a representation named in the research alongside area models; offer it as an additional representation, not a replacement for the bar.

Interactive splitting (dragging a '÷4' cutter, cut lines auto-extending across the whole, auto-labelling 1/12, an inverse panel reassembling the pieces, a contrast switch to 4 ÷ 1/5) is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required mechanism.
Partitioning a fraction of a bar is a planar task; a 3D treatment is not needed here and could invite a volume misreading — kept as a noted limitation, not a claim that 3D can never help.
Always ground the answer in meaning: require the learner to state whether the result is smaller than the original fraction and why, not just produce the numeral.

startingActivity.title: Build the model, then write the equation
learnerActions: Read a word problem, e.g. 'How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups?'
Decide whether the story is sharing an amount out among groups (partition) or finding how many portions fit inside an amount (measurement).
Choose and build the matching model on a bar or number line: either share one bar among N people, or fill a 2-cup bar with 1/3-cup portions and count them.
Write the matching division equation (2 ÷ 1/3 = 6) once the picture matches the words.
Lay the story, the picture, and the equation side by side so the three represent the same situation.

If a digital modeller is available, dragging the story onto a bar so the equation and answer recompute live lets pupils see a mismatched picture when they pick the wrong structure — this is one helpful interaction, not a required one.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The story tells you which division it is: sharing an amount out among more than one group gives each less than the whole, while asking how many sub-one-unit portions fit inside an amount gives more than you started with — and the picture either matches the words or it visibly does not.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model of the amount being shared (partition) or filled with portions (measurement)
Number line for 'how many 1/3s fit in 2'
Story ↔ equation ↔ picture triple laid side by side
Inverse check written under the answer
commonMisconceptions: Picks the wrong operation — multiplies, or divides in the wrong order (2 ÷ 1/3 done as 1/3 ÷ 2)
Reverses dividend and divisor — computes 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 for '3 share 1/2 lb' instead of 1/2 ÷ 3
Expects the quotient to be smaller in a measurement problem, so distrusts '6 servings' being more than 2
Sets up the numbers but cannot tell which quantity is being split, so the model does not match the story
constraints: Matching stories to expressions and multiple-choice 'which calculation solves this?' check the choice only; classifying stories into 'sharing' vs 'how many fit' usefully targets the core difficulty (reading the structure, a source-endorsed move) but on its own does not elicit building the matching model and writing the equation. Pair classification with pupil-built models and pupil-written equations rather than treat selection alone as the whole learning.
Story invention must be produced by the pupil (constructing/writing a context), not selected from options, to reveal whether the measurement structure is owned.

A static worked pair of stories with reveal-the-setup flaps can illustrate the two structures but does not let a pupil attempt and test their own setup on a new story; treat it as a scaffold or reference.
When counting portions physically (measuring cups, cut ribbons), these are concrete approximations of the bar/number-line model; keep the link to the written equation explicit.

Contexts here are quantity and length sharing, which model naturally on a bar or number line; three-dimensional representations are not needed for these particular contexts (this is a scope note, not a claim that 3D could never help elsewhere).
