startingActivity.title: Placing probabilities on the 0-to-1 measure line
learnerActions: Work with a 0-to-1 line marked with the fixed landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain).
Place a probability of 0.7 and a probability of 1/4 at their correct positions, and read off the same point shown three ways as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
For each placement, state which landmark the event sits near and justify its position ('0.7 is above even chance, so toward the certain end').
Place a set of everyday-event cards on the scale and justify each position in words.
Test the bounds: try to place a marker beyond the certain end or below the impossible end and state why no probability can go there.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A probability is one point on a bounded measure line; the same value can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage, and nothing can lie below 0 or above 1.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 measure line with impossible / even chance / certain landmarks
Fraction = decimal = percentage triple labels on the line
Fair vs biased devices (equal spinner vs loaded spinner vs drawing pin)
Everyday-event cards placed and justified on the scale
commonMisconceptions: Equiprobability bias — assuming n possible outcomes means each has probability 1/n even when they are not equally likely (biased spinner)
Believing a probability can exceed 1 or be stated as a raw count of outcomes
Comparing probabilities written in different notations by their surface digits without converting
Assuming every probability can be CALCULATED from symmetry, with no notion that some must be estimated from data
constraints: Equal probabilities (P = favourable/total, or '1/n each') are only valid for genuinely equal sections/outcomes; do not apply symmetry to biased devices.

For asymmetric or biased devices where no value is stated (loaded spinner of unknown bias, bent coin, drawing pin) the probability cannot be got by symmetry and must be estimated from repeated data; where a bias value is stated/given (e.g. red = 70%), use the stated value directly. Any estimate from a finite number of trials is approximate and scatters around the true value.
No probability is below 0 or above 1, and a probability is never a raw count of outcomes — unlike a general fraction of a quantity, it cannot exceed 1.
Compare probabilities by converting to a common notation (or to line positions); do not compare by surface digits.

A draggable marker, live tri-notation readout, bias/fair switch and repeated-trial sampler are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; a static labelled scale with tap-to-reveal notations is a valid reference but cannot flag a mis-placement on its own.
Recognition/ordering items can be used while teaching, but used alone they do not elicit the learner's own construction and reasoning; pair them with explain-why prompts.

startingActivity.title: Build the Venn and expose the double-count
learnerActions: Use 30 student tokens (physical or on-screen) and a two-circle Venn (A = football, B = cricket) inside a universal rectangle, with the facts: 18 like football, 14 like cricket, 6 like both.

Try the instinctive approach first: allocate 18 to the football circle and 14 to the cricket circle without using the overlap. Those two counts sum to 32 (18 + 14), yet only 30 students exist — on screen a counter reads 32, while with physical tokens you run out before finishing the cricket circle. Either outcome shows that some students are being counted twice — here, the 6 'both' students. Note that the excess of 2 (32 − 30) is not the size of the overlap, because 4 students like neither sport.
Move the 6 'both' students into the overlap region, then adjust so each circle's own-only region reads 12 (18 − 6) and 8 (14 − 6).
Place the 4 left-over students in the 'neither' region inside the rectangle, and check the regions total 30.
State the union count by adding the distinct regions once: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26.
Shade and state in words what each region means for A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Elements in both sets are counted twice if you compute |A| + |B|; filling the intersection first and subtracting it from each total gives the correct circle-only regions, and the 'neither' region must be included so everything totals the population.

Writing each set's full total inside its circle without subtracting the overlap, so the diagram over-counts
Placing elements in the intersection that belong to only one set
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the regions don't total the whole population
constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract it from each set total so the circle-only regions are correct.
Count the union as |A unionB|=|A|+|B|-|A intersectionB|. Subtract the overlap once; if it is zero, direct addition is valid. In this example the union is18+14-6=26.
Always account for the 'neither' region inside the universal-set rectangle; the regions must total the whole population (30 here).
Tap-to-reveal and read-only diagrams teach layout and notation but do not let the learner build a diagram or test a miscount; use them as scaffolds alongside hands-on construction.
Choice/classification steps drill enumeration and the double-count trap but do not elicit free shading or independent diagram construction; pair them with a build/shade task.
Socratic dialogue can surface overlap and 'neither' errors, but learners should still do the placement and counting themselves.
The '32' (18 + 14) and '38' (football-only 18 + overlap 6 + cricket-only 14) figures are learner error patterns only and must never be offered as valid counts; the correct union is 26.

startingActivity.title: The two-dice grid: why totals are not equally likely
learnerActions: On paper or a 6×6 grid, write the total in every one of the 36 cells for (first die, second die), keeping the two dice as an ordered pair so 3+4 and 4+3 are separate cells.
Shade all cells where the total is 7 and count them (6 cells: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1), then shade cells where the total is 2 (1 cell: 1+1).
State P(total = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(total = 2) = 1/36.
Explain in a sentence why P(7) is NOT 1/11, referring to the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The 36 ordered (die1, die2) outcomes are equally likely; the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT, because different totals arise from different numbers of ordered outcomes.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Sample-space grid / two-way table (e.g. 6×6 for two dice)
Systematic ordered listing of outcomes
Probability tree with values on branches; multiply along, add across
Reduced-denominator second branches for dependent events
commonMisconceptions: Assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treating the eleven totals of two dice as each 1/11 (equiprobability bias)
Ignoring order when listing — counting 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, undercounting the sample space
Adding probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplying AND/OR)
Reusing the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event
constraints: Sample spaces must be built on genuinely equally-likely outcomes; for two dice that means the 36 ordered (die1, die2) pairs, not the eleven totals.
Order must be respected when listing: (3,4) and (4,3) are distinct outcomes; ignoring order undercounts the sample space.
For dependent (without-replacement) events, every second-level branch must be recomputed from the reduced contents; first-event probabilities cannot be reused.
The OR (add-across) rule applies only to separate, mutually exclusive complete paths; the AND (multiply-along) rule applies within a single path.
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.

Short-answer, fill-in and tap-to-reveal items can reinforce and self-check the rules, but do not require a learner to independently construct a complete fresh sample space; pair them with construction tasks.

Tap-to-reveal grids/trees and a replace/don't-replace toggle are optional supports to make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and should be used after the learner has reasoned, not instead of reasoning.
Rolling physical or 3D dice can add realism and generate data, but the counting and branch arithmetic are carried by the grid and tree; feed any physical results back into the grid/tree.

activityReferences.title: Build a two-circle Venn from student data, then shade and read probabilities
Generate the full outcome set, then sort it into the diagram

startingActivity.title: Build a two-circle Venn from student data, then shade and read probabilities
learnerActions: Place 30 student tokens into a two-circle Venn (football / cricket) inside a rectangle; fill the intersection first (likes both), then the 'only' crescents (by subtracting the overlap from each set total when only totals are given), then the 'neither' region outside both circles — e.g. 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither.
Check that all regions sum to 30 before reading anything off.
Name each region in words BEFORE writing notation: 'likes both' = A∩B, 'football only' = A only, 'likes either' = A∪B, 'neither' outside both.
Shade 'likes cricket but NOT football' (the cricket-only crescent, 8 students) and write its probability as 8/30 = 4/15 over the total of 30.
Shade A∪B and find its COUNT two ways: by adding region counts (12 + 6 + 8 = 26), and by checking 18 + 14 − 6 = 26 to see why the overlap is subtracted; the probability is then 26/30.
Switch to a conditional: 'among the cricket-lovers, what fraction also like football?' — identify the new denominator (14, all who like cricket) and compute 6/14.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The overlap counts once, so the union COUNT is A + B − A∩B; and the denominator is the whole universal set unless a question conditions on a restricted subset, in which case the denominator shrinks to that subset.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two-circle Venn diagram inside a labelled rectangle (universal set)
Three-circle Venn diagram for three-set problems (seven internal regions)
Intersection-first fill order: overlap, then 'only' regions by subtraction, then 'neither'
Two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions
commonMisconceptions: Confusing intersection and union — shading 'in either' when asked for 'in both', or vice versa
Double-counting the overlap — adding the two circle totals for A∪B without subtracting A∩B
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the diagram's regions do not sum to the universal-set total
Using a circle total (or the whole universal set) as the denominator for a probability that is actually conditional on a restricted subset
constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract to get the 'only' regions, then place 'neither' inside the rectangle but outside both circles — and check all regions sum to the universal-set total.

When one member of the universal set is chosen at random (each equally likely), compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; restrict the denominator only when the question conditions on a subset.
Keep probabilities and counts distinct: a union COUNT may exceed 1 (e.g. 26), but the probability is that count over the total (26/30) and always lies between 0 and 1.

Recognition and sorting tasks (tap-to-reveal, matching, categorization, multiple choice) assess and build vocabulary but do not elicit independent construction of a diagram from raw data or an independently chosen denominator; keep a genuine construct-from-description task in the sequence.
A completed/pre-authored Venn is a scaffold: it teaches what each region means but cannot test whether the learner can build a diagram or choose the correct denominator on a new case.

Interactive features (drag tokens into regions, tap-to-shade with live set-notation and probability recompute, a conditional mode that greys out the rest and switches the denominator, a flag when the union overlap is selected twice) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not required.
A two-way table is a valid alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions; do not treat the circle layout as the only representation.
Three-circle Venn diagrams (seven internal regions) extend the same logic for three-set problems.

startingActivity.title: Catch every triangle (varied-case shape hunt)
learnerActions: Look at a field of many shapes that mixes tidy triangles with long-thin, tilted and point-down triangles, plus near-miss non-examples such as a figure with one curved side and three lines that do not quite close.
Tap/pick out every triangle you can find, including the ones that look unusual.
After choosing, say for one of the unusual ones WHY it is a triangle (e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up').
Say why a near-miss is NOT a triangle (its side is curved, or it isn't closed).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Sameness of a shape lives in its features — three straight sides and a closed figure — not in its size, proportions, or which way it points. A long, thin, upside-down triangle belongs to the same family as the tidy one.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A set of varied exemplars of one shape (many sizes/orientations/proportions) displayed together
Example / non-example pairs ('is it or not?')
Feature cues: 'closed', 'straight sides', counting the sides and corners
Shape sort / shape hunt (find all the triangles in the room)
commonMisconceptions: Judges a shape only against a visual prototype: accepts the equilateral, horizontal-based triangle but rejects long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down triangles (non-prototypical TYPES are hardest — about half of children miss isosceles and right triangles).
Treats ORIENTATION as if it defines the shape: a square rotated 45° is called a 'diamond' not a square; a triangle without a horizontal base is rejected.
Names by overall resemblance to an object (a 'roof', a 'mountain') rather than by counting straight sides and corners.
Uses 'diamond' for a rotated square, rhombus or kite — there is no 2-D shape called a diamond.
constraints: The learning target is deciding-and-justifying on new, varied cases; a static display showing one shape in many guises (e.g. a wall-card where tapping a fat/thin/tilted/upside-down triangle reveals 'three straight sides — still a triangle') is a useful reference and scaffold but does not rehearse the act of deciding on fresh figures.
Recognition-only responses (tapping or sorting without a stated reason) do not show whether the child reasons from features; always pair the choice with 'how do you know?'
Include non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start — these are exactly the figures children wrongly reject, so leaving them until 'later' hides the misconception.
Accept informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge but model and expect precise terms ('three straight sides', 'closed', 'corners').
Keep any drawn or on-screen figures clear enough that straightness and closure are unambiguous; illustrations are evocative, not exact.

Paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held and turned; they are thin models of the flat (ideal, zero-thickness) shape. Use them as approximations and ask the child about the shape REPRESENTED by the outline (its sides and corners), not about the physical card.
'Diamond' should not be used as a 2-D shape name for a rotated square, rhombus or kite; name the actual shape.

activityReferences.title: Build a triangle from counted components
Draw a rectangle (and a non-canonical one)
Build a cube frame: from one square to a solid

startingActivity.title: Build a triangle from counted components
learnerActions: Name the attributes aloud first: 'a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners, so I need 3 sticks and 3 balls.'
Count out exactly 3 sticks and 3 clay balls before joining anything.
Join the sticks at the balls into a CLOSED loop so every corner meets.
Check the finished model against a real triangle.
Then make a different triangle — a long thin one — so the build is driven by the attributes, not one remembered picture.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A shape's attributes tell you which parts to gather and how to join them; a triangle must be a closed figure of 3 straight sides meeting at 3 corners, and many different triangles satisfy that.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Sticks/straws (edges) and clay balls/connectors (vertices) for building frames
Geoboard and dotted paper for constructing straight-sided closed figures
A real triangle/cube to compare the built model against
One square face raised into a cube frame to show the 2-D→ 3-D step
commonMisconceptions: Uses the wrong number of components — grabs 4 sticks for a triangle, or the wrong count of straws/connectors for a cube — not matching parts to the shape's attributes.
Leaves the figure OPEN or makes wobbly/curved sides, so the corners don't join into a closed shape.
Builds a cube flat as a single square or a laid-out cross, not raising it into a closed 3-D frame.
Draws only the prototypical wide, horizontal rectangle (or rounds the corners) and cannot draw a tall or tilted one.
constraints: Building and drawing are active production tasks: the learner must assemble components or draw the figure, not just recognise or tap a finished picture.
Closure is a required outcome, not a stylistic preference: an open figure (an unjoined V, a rectangle with a gap) does not yet count as the shape.

Checking whether a drawing is closed, with four straight sides and four square corners, can confirm the rectangle task, but it does not let a child build a frame or verify edge/vertex counts — use it only as a complement to hands-on building.

Physical sticks-and-balls and clay are central; an optional on-screen snap-together builder (with a live edge/vertex/face tally that only 'sets' when the frame closes, and an open shape that refuses to set) can make closure and counting feel concrete, but is a complement to real materials, not a replacement. Treat both the screen frame and the physical frame as models of the mathematical solid — real sticks and balls have slight thickness, while the ideal cube's edges and vertices are thicknessless.
The cube step (2-D face raised into a 3-D solid) is the hardest to coordinate and benefits most from genuine 3-D handling; a flat picture or 2-D-only tool makes this step harder to feel.
A real triangle and a real cube should be available to compare the built models against.

startingActivity.title: Two triangles become one rectangle
learnerActions: Take two identical right triangles (physical cut-outs and/or an on-screen pair beside a rectangle outline).
Before moving them, answer the prompt 'What ONE shape do you think these will make?'
Arrange them to fill a rectangle outline, turning one triangle (if both start facing the same way, about 180°) so the corners and edges meet with no gaps or overlaps.
Rearrange the same two triangles to make a LARGER triangle by joining matching legs; unless the triangles are isosceles right triangles, you will need to flip one over, not just turn it.
Say aloud what single shape you have made each time: 'I put two triangles together and made one rectangle.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Two separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity (part–whole); the same two pieces can compose into different wholes depending on how they are turned, flipped and joined.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks with outlined puzzles (e.g. a hexagon to fill) grading to open puzzles
Two identical right triangles to combine into a rectangle or a larger triangle
Tangrams for composing pictures and larger shapes
Rotate/flip actions to seat a piece by matching its corner to the gap
commonMisconceptions: Places shapes separately or by pure trial and error, not anticipating that pieces will combine into a new shape.
Matches side LENGTHS but not ANGLES, so pieces leave gaps/overlaps or a corner won't fit the space (e.g. a square's right angle in a rhombus gap).
Cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it must be rotated off a horizontal base, and doesn't turn it to fit.
Sees the result as still 'two triangles' rather than one new rectangle — misses the part-whole identity of the composite.
constraints: This is a 2-D planar composition task; 3-D composing is a separate, later topic and depth is not used here.

A fixed quiz can check a single known combination but, being fixed, cannot provide the free rotate-and-fit composing or the graded outlined-to-open progression where most of the learning happens; use it only as an occasional spot-check, not the main activity.

On-screen snapping, seam-fade, and angle-flash cues are optional supports that make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and children should still experience physical blocks and cut-outs they can turn and glue.

Trial-and-error placement without anticipation is a normal trajectory level (Picture Maker), not an error to drill or mark wrong; respond by offering puzzles about one level up and prompting 'what will fit here?'.
Teach roughly one trajectory level above the child's current level; pitching too far ahead can cause frustration.
Recognition-only responses (e.g. tapping a correct picture) do not elicit the independent construction this objective requires.
Physical cut-outs and blocks approximate ideal flat figures; treat them as representing the mathematical 2-D shapes composed, not as objects defined by being pickable or by their slight thickness.

startingActivity.title: Fold test: does each half land on the other?
learnerActions: Cut out a paper/card rectangle (a non-square one).
Fold it along the vertical line down the middle: check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Now fold the same rectangle corner-to-corner along the diagonal and watch what happens to the corners.
Say out loud for each fold whether it is a line of symmetry and why.
Repeat the fold test on other cut-out shapes (square, triangle), hunting for every fold where the halves coincide.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is a fold where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (coincide), not just a line that makes two pieces the same size. The diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but a corner overhangs when folded — so congruence is not enough.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Paper/card shape cut-outs for folding along a candidate line
A small mirror (or Mira) placed on the line to check the reflection
Pegboard/dot-paper symmetric-pattern completion (draw the missing mirror half)
Side-by-side square vs non-square rectangle for comparing side-count and number of symmetry lines
commonMisconceptions: Thinks any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry, without checking the halves coincide.
Thinks any line that cuts a shape into two equal/congruent parts is a line of symmetry — e.g. accepts the diagonal of a rectangle because it makes two identical triangles.
Judges 'the halves are the same' by eye/size rather than by folding or mirroring to see if they actually land on each other.
Confuses the vertical line of symmetry with 'any line through the centre' and does not realise a shape can have several (or no) lines of symmetry.
constraints: Line symmetry of a 2-D shape is planar; keep the work flat (folding, mirrors, dot-paper) — adding depth/3-D is not needed for this concept and can distract from the flat fold.

Watching pre-drawn lines of symmetry or tap-to-reveal mirror highlights can show correct examples, but a watch-only display does not let the child test their OWN candidate line or resolve the diagonal misconception through their own folding; treat such displays as a scaffold and still have the child perform a fold or mirror test.

Multiple-choice ('which line is a line of symmetry?') and draw-the-line tasks can check the skill but do not themselves perform the fold, so they do not let the child feel whether the halves coincide; use them to assess, not as the primary teaching of the crux.

Paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness; treat them as a good physical approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape. If an on-screen fold/reflection tool is used, note it models the same zero-thickness reflection.

Recognition-only responses (picking a line from options) do not require the learner to construct or verify the fold themselves; include folding, mirroring, or completing a mirror half for independent construction.
The diagnostic non-example must be a NON-SQUARE rectangle: a square's diagonal IS a line of symmetry, so using a square would break the congruence-vs-coincidence contrast.

startingActivity.title: Fill the outline with the right pieces
learnerActions: Give the child flat shape pieces (for example, pattern blocks, tangram pieces, or cut-out triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, half-circles and quarter-circles) and an outline puzzle card that those pieces can cover exactly. Standard pattern blocks and tangrams do not include half-circles or quarter-circles, and tangrams have no trapezoid, so add cut-out pieces for any shapes the set lacks.
As they work, ask them to say which shape they are using and why.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Will this piece fit this gap? How do you know?' — encouraging a prediction from the gap's edges and corners.
When a piece doesn't fit, have them compare the gap's edge length and corner angle to the piece, then choose one that matches.
Let them use turns and flips to make a piece fit, naming what they did ('I flipped it so the slanted edge lines up').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A piece can be chosen in advance by matching its side length and angle to the gap, rather than by trying pieces at random until one happens to fit.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks and tangram pieces
Outline puzzle cards of increasing difficulty
Two triangles composing a square or larger triangle; half-circles composing a circle
Angle-and-side-length matching between a gap and a piece
commonMisconceptions: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the new shape (an expected early trajectory level, not a fault).
Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so pieces do not fit the gap.
Sees the composite as one whole and cannot decompose it into the simpler shapes it is made from.
constraints: The core skill is a manipulative, spatial act: children must physically (or on-screen) fit, turn, and flip pieces into outlines. Recognition-only tasks (matching a composite to its parts, naming shapes) check understanding but do not elicit the independent act of composing.
A static composite with a tap/reveal of its decomposition is a reference and naming aid; it cannot exercise choosing and fitting pieces.
This is a planar concept; it needs a flat working surface (physical blocks or a 2-D screen). A 3-D rendering is not needed and can distract from the flat composition being learned.
Spoken prediction ('which piece will fit?') is valuable for eliciting anticipation but should accompany actual placement, not replace it.
Trial-and-error assembly with no advance plan is an expected early trajectory LEVEL, not a fault to be marked wrong; respond by offering a puzzle one step ahead and fading support.

Engineer puzzles to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line at a time) and pitch one level beyond the child's current level; the cited study reports this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (effect size .55).
For the 'two triangles make a square' example, use congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles; two equilateral pattern-block triangles form a rhombus, not a square.

startingActivity.title: Triangle studio: what can change, what cannot
learnerActions: Drag the three corners of a triangle to stretch it into different types (long-thin, right, obtuse) and tilt it to any angle, checking after each change whether it is still a triangle and saying why (if the three corners are dragged into one straight line, it flattens and is no longer a triangle).
Use size and colour controls to make the triangle big, small, and recoloured, and confirm the label 'triangle' stays the same because three straight sides and closure have not changed.

Break the shape on purpose: bend one side into a curve, or drag a corner apart so the outline no longer closes, and watch the label flip to 'not a triangle' with the non-straight side or the open gap highlighted.
State in your own words which attributes can be 'thrown around' with no effect (colour, size, orientation) and which changes end it (for example a curved side or an open corner).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Size, colour and orientation can swing wildly while a shape keeps its identity, but the instant a side curves or a corner opens it stops being a triangle — this makes defining versus non-defining attributes directly visible.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 'Must-have versus doesn't-matter' attribute contrast
Example / near-miss non-example sets (curved side; not closed)
The same shape rotated and resized to show invariance
Tracing each side and checking 'straight' and 'closed'
commonMisconceptions: Treats ORIENTATION as defining (an 'imposed attribute'): a rotated square is a 'diamond'; a triangle 'must' have a horizontal base — about 15% of children reject even a prototypical triangle once it is rotated.
Treats shape type as defined by its image/prototype: only 'regular' triangles or brick-like rectangles count; long-thin, right and obtuse triangles are rejected.
Thinks size or colour can change a shape's identity (a very big or a red triangle is 'a different shape').
Accepts a near-miss non-example (a curved-sided or unclosed 'triangle') because it resembles the prototype — ignoring 'straight' and 'closed'.
constraints: Target age 6–7; conceptual geometry about 2-D attributes. Avoid introducing a third dimension/solids for this planar objective, since it adds load and can mislead toward solids.

Treat classification choices (triangle / not a triangle, square / diamond) as scaffolds: the stated reason, not the yes/no, is the real evidence, because a correct choice can come from the prototype alone.
Static reference panels and sorts support but cannot by themselves rehearse deciding on new borderline cases; include tasks where the child decides and justifies fresh figures.
Make non-prototypical and rotated cases the main event (long-thin, right, obtuse, point-down triangles; tilted squares), because these are where imposed attributes get mistaken for defining ones.
Choose near-miss non-examples deliberately: three sides but one curved, or three straight lines that don't quite close, so the defining feature is isolated.

Physical cut-outs and stick builds have real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat shape; ask about the mathematical shape represented, and distinguish the cut-out from the shape it represents.
Interaction examples (draggable vertices, colour/size controls, a label that flips with the broken feature highlighted) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not mandatory mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Build a cube frame from straws and connectors
learnerActions: Before building, predict and count how many edges (straws) and vertices (connectors) a cube needs, and state the target: 12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces.
Build the cube frame, snapping straws (edges) onto connectors (balls of clay or plastic joints for vertices).

Check that every straw is the same length and that the corners are square (right angles, not leaning), because equal straws alone can still give a squashed frame with diamond-shaped faces; then compare the finished frame against a real cube-shaped solid.
Point to and count the edges, vertices and faces on the completed frame to confirm the structure.
Try building a cuboid with edges of different lengths as a contrast and describe how it differs from the cube (not all edges equal, so some faces are rectangles that are not squares).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A cube is defined by its structure — 12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces — and building it requires coordinating that structure rather than approximating a box shape.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Straws-and-connectors (or clay balls and sticks) for building edge/vertex frames
A real solid to grab and rotate through many orientations
Dotted paper / geoboard for accurate 2-D drawing
Nets that fold into the solid, linking 2-D faces to the 3-D shape
commonMisconceptions: Does not recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — calls a rotated or point-down pyramid 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or with the wrong number of sides.
Treats a shape's name as tied to its usual position, so turning it seems to change what it is.
constraints: The curriculum requires making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so children should build frames and turn real solids, not only watch or tap.

Recognition tasks (multiple-choice 'which is the same shape rotated?', or picking a drawn path) can check outcomes but do not let a child build a frame or freely rotate a solid, so they must not replace construction and manipulation.

On-screen builders and spinners are useful complements but approximate true 3-D construction and free rotation in a flat projection; pair them with real straws, clay/connectors and a wooden solid where possible.

Paper and card cut-outs and straw frames have real thickness; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal mathematical solid (whose faces have zero thickness), and treat any zero-thickness screen model as a model of the solid it represents.

Name shapes by invariant properties (for 2-D: closure, number of straight sides and, where relevant, angles such as a rectangle's right angles; for 3-D: faces/edges/vertices and how they meet), not by a single remembered picture or usual position.

startingActivity.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count
learnerActions: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Geoboard / pegboard and dotted paper for constructing polygons to a target side-count
Mixed shape sets containing regular, irregular, tilted and near-miss examples plus non-examples
Side/vertex tally marks made while counting
Side-by-side regular vs irregular pentagon/hexagon to show both satisfy the attribute
commonMisconceptions: Draws or accepts only the prototypical regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example and misses irregular or rotated members of a class.
Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying (draws six sides when asked for five; loses track counting an irregular shape).
Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
Judges class membership by the name/look ('that's not a quadrilateral, it's a diamond') rather than by counting the sides.
constraints: Tasks must require active drawing/construction and selection, not tap-to-reveal recognition: a static labelled picture can show examples but does not itself let the learner build or choose, and active production and selection are where the prototype misconception can surface.
Mixed 'find them all' sets must include irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples; a set of only regular shapes cannot discriminate attribute-use from picture-matching.

Any 'draw a pentagon' response format should be paired with a side-count check (counting/marking by the learner or an adult), since free drawing alone does not reliably verify the exact number of straight sides.

A fixed single-answer format under-rewards the many-different-valid-answers goal; whatever format is used, multiple distinct correct shapes (including irregular ones) must be treated as equally valid.

A live side-counter, closure check, and visible acceptance of any valid shape (e.g. a highlight on a correct irregular pentagon, a pulse on a missed tilted quadrilateral) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete, but are optional illustrations, not required technology.

activityReferences.title: Fold-and-match test with a drawn candidate line
Movable mirror line on a geoboard or with a mirror
Sort shapes by number of lines of symmetry

startingActivity.title: Fold-and-match test with a drawn candidate line
learnerActions: Start with a cut-out or on-screen rectangle. Draw where you think each fold line (line of symmetry) should be, and say why before testing.
Fold (or let a screen model fold) one half across each drawn line and check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Deliberately try a diagonal corner-to-corner: fold along it and watch the far corners — they miss each other, so it is NOT a line of symmetry.
Confirm the vertical and horizontal lines through the side midpoints: these fold to an exact match, so the rectangle has 2 lines, not 4.
Tilt or rotate the shape (e.g. 30-40 degrees) and re-check the same lines are still there without turning the page upright.
Progress to non-regular polygons and a few asymmetric shapes (answer: 0 lines), testing every candidate line by folding.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is whatever survives the fold-and-match test, not whatever a count-the-sides rule predicts; symmetry is a structural property of the shape independent of its orientation.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Fold test — physically folding a cut-out shape so halves coincide (the definition made concrete)
Geoboard with an elastic band as a movable mirror line
Mira/mirror placed on a candidate line to see if the reflection completes the shape
Rectangle-versus-square comparison showing 2 lines vs 4
Carroll/Venn sorting by number of lines of symmetry
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — so a rectangle is given 4 lines instead of 2 (over-generalised from regular shapes).
Treating a diagonal of a rectangle (or other non-square) as a line of symmetry, when folding along it shows the halves do not match.
Only recognising a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in tilted or rotated shapes.
Thinking every shape must have at least one line of symmetry (not recognising asymmetric shapes).
constraints: Define a line of symmetry operationally: fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly. Teach checking by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding — but note careless cutting distorts the result, so a near-miss may be a cutting artefact.
Actively confront the 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation with many NON-regular shapes; do not rely only on regular shapes, which breed the misconception.

Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample (2 real lines vs 2 falsely assumed diagonals) and contrast with equilateral triangle (3), square (4) and regular hexagon (6) to show the side-count rule holds for regular shapes only.
Present shapes in varied orientations (tilted and rotated), judging symmetry by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and can be imperfectly cut; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat shape whose exact halves coincide, and reason about the mathematical shape it represents rather than the physical card.
Recognition and multiple-choice items assess the concept but do not, by themselves, generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce; pair them with hands-on or learner-proposed folding.

A tappable-line reveal shows fixed, pre-drawn lines; it illustrates the idea but does not let a child test their own candidate line, so use it as support alongside active folding, not as a replacement.
This is planar (line/reflective) symmetry of 2-D shapes; keep away from 3-D planes of symmetry and depth, which are a different topic.

startingActivity.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?
learnerActions: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Property checklist / definition card for each category (right-angle marks, equal-side tick marks, parallel arrows)
Nested Venn diagram: quadrilaterals ⊃ rectangles ⊃ squares, with rhombuses overlapping so square sits in the intersection
A 'stretchy' square that can be pulled into an oblong rectangle or squashed to a rhombus, showing square as the special case where both hold
Set-square and ruler to physically verify right angles and equal sides
commonMisconceptions: A square is not a rectangle — they are two different, separate kinds of shape (exclusive/partition thinking)
A rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square cannot be one (oblong prototype; the unequal-sides attribute is wrongly treated as defining)
A shape can only belong to one category, so it cannot be a rectangle AND a square at the same time
A square turned 45° is a 'diamond', not a square (orientation bound to the prototype)
constraints: Target concept is property-based classification and class inclusion, not shape naming; always require justification by defining properties, not a bare yes/no.

A scored sort/multiple-choice can assess whether a child accepts the inclusion (e.g. 'Is a square a rectangle?' with distractor 'No, they are different shapes') but does not by itself let the child feel a square pass the tests; use it to check, not to build, the insight.

A static tap-to-reveal Venn or hierarchy is a useful summary/reference showing where a square sits, but because nothing recomputes the child cannot TEST a shape's membership; best used after hands-on testing rather than as the primary route.

Distinguish an ideal zero-thickness plane figure from physical card/cutouts, which have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat cutouts as approximations of the represented flat shape and ask about the mathematical shape represented, not whether the physical card can be picked up. Quadrilateral classification is a planar, 2D property idea, so a third spatial dimension is not needed here (a limit of relevance, not evidence that any one medium is superior).
Treat the one-box (class-inclusion) stage as developmental: give more nested-set and everyday-inclusion experience rather than drilling the fact.
Set-square/ruler verification and recolouring/ticking checklists are optional supports to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.

activityReferences.title: Sort the tray: test every figure before you bin it
Draw it, don't just spot it
Sorting grids for mixed properties

startingActivity.title: Sort the tray: test every figure before you bin it
learnerActions: Lay out a mixed tray of shapes and lines including a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths tilted off horizontal, a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges, a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical, a rectangle, and a non-right triangle.

For each pair of sides, test for parallel: slide a ruler along one side keeping it touching, and check whether the gap to the opposite side stays the same, measuring straight across (at right angles to the lines) at two or more places, including near both ends where the lines lie alongside each other, or extend both lines to see whether they would meet.
For each corner you suspect is a right angle, drop a set-square or the square corner of a card into the corner and check whether it fits exactly against both sides.

Record each figure by property, testing the two properties independently: does it have a pair of parallel sides? does it have a right angle / is it a right triangle? A figure may pass BOTH tests (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), just one, or neither — note what each check shows rather than forcing it into a single exclusive box, and only decide after the check, not after a glance.

Say out loud, for at least three figures, which check you used and what it showed (for example: 'I slid the ruler and the gap never changed, so these sides are parallel even though one line is longer' or 'the rectangle passed both — parallel sides and a right-angle corner').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A property, not the look of a figure, decides the category: a tilted, unequal-length pair is just as parallel as a tidy horizontal pair, and a rotated triangle is still a right triangle if a corner tests at 90 degrees. Properties are independent, so a figure can have both (a rectangle), one, or neither. The question shifts from 'does it look like the book example?' to 'does it pass the test?'
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Set-square or the square corner of a card as a right-angle checker; a ruler slid between two lines to test constant distance
Carroll and Venn sorting grids with criteria ('has parallel sides', 'has a right angle', regular/irregular)
A dynamic pair of lines whose length and orientation vary while the parallel/perpendicular relation is held or broken
Sets of triangles varied by orientation and side length — some right-angled, some not
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the vocabulary — mixes up 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by always-equal-length textbook examples)
Only recognises parallel/perpendicular when the lines are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Fails to recognise a right triangle when it is rotated or looks scalene (right-angle-legs prototype)
constraints: The classification skill is a doing-and-checking action: learners must physically test figures (slide/extend a ruler, apply a set-square or square card corner), not only name or recognise properties.

Include figures that defeat eyeballing — a tilted pair of parallel lines of unequal length, a slowly-converging near-parallel pair, and a right triangle rotated off the horizontal-and-vertical-legs position — because obvious upright examples let learners guess by appearance.

Treat the two properties as independent and test each on its own: a figure such as a rectangle can have both parallel sides and right angles, so do not force figures into a single exclusive bin — record each property separately or use a two-way grid.

Tasks that only ask learners to select or drag pre-made figures into categories test the classification outcome but do not require the learner to perform the ruler/set-square check, which is the actual skill; pair any such recognition task with hands-on checking or construction.
A reference poster or card supports vocabulary but does not let the learner verify an individual figure; treat it as a summary aid after hands-on work, not as the main activity.
Spoken discussion can rehearse the vocabulary and reasoning but does not itself perform the manual test; use talk to accompany checking rather than replace it.
This objective concerns parallel and perpendicular relations within flat 2-D figures; parallel/perpendicular in three dimensions is a later, distinct idea and is not required here.

The ruler, set-square and square card corner are physical approximations with real thickness; use them as practical checking tools, and keep the focus on the relation they reveal (constant gap, 90 degree corner) rather than on the tool itself.

startingActivity.title: The two-key lock: checking both conditions on a changing shape
learnerActions: Work with an adjustable polygon (3–8 sides) that can be reshaped, with two visible condition indicators overhead — 'all sides equal' and 'all angles equal' — and a 'REGULAR' badge that lights only when BOTH indicators are green.
Start with a square: confirm both indicators are green and the badge reads REGULAR.

Skew the square so it leans into a rhombus — the tool keeps all four sides equal — and watch the sides stay equal (green) while the angles become unequal (red), so the badge drops to IRREGULAR even though every side is still the same length.

Straighten the rhombus back into a square, then stretch it along one direction into a long rectangle: watch the angles stay as four right angles (green) while the sides are no longer all equal (red) — still IRREGULAR.

Take named shapes from a gallery (rhombus, oblong rectangle, square, regular pentagon, irregular pentagon) and place each onto the checker, predicting first whether it will be regular and which condition (if any) it fails.
Attempt a 'make it regular' challenge that only succeeds when both conditions hold at once.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Regularity is a conjunction: equal sides alone, or equal angles alone, is not enough — the badge is a two-key lock, and only a shape that turns both keys (the square among quadrilaterals) is regular.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A two-column check applied to each shape: sides equal? (tick/cross) | angles equal? (tick/cross)
A regular pentagon/hexagon/equilateral triangle beside their irregular counterparts (an irregular pentagon, a rhombus, an oblong rectangle)
Sorting / Carroll cards: 'regular polygon', 'irregular polygon', 'equal sides but not equal angles', 'at least one right angle' (NCETM)
The rhombus (sides tick, angles cross) and the rectangle (angles tick, sides cross) flanking the square (both tick)
commonMisconceptions: Regular = equal sides only — ignores the equal-angles condition, so a rhombus is wrongly called regular
Regular = equal angles only — so a non-square rectangle is wrongly called regular
'Regular' means an ordinary/symmetrical/tidy-looking shape and 'irregular' means an odd or random-looking one (everyday-language interference)
Assumes a polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides — over-generalised from only ever seeing regular examples (NCETM)
constraints: Regularity requires checking BOTH conditions together: equal sides AND equal angles. A shape failing either is irregular — do not let 'all sides equal' alone stand as the test.
Use the rhombus (sides only) and the non-square rectangle (angles only) as the discriminating cases, flanking the square (both), so the single-criterion habit is broken from both directions.
Include many-sided and non-standard-orientation examples, and do not present only regular shapes, so 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype.
Explicitly separate the mathematical meaning of regular/irregular from the everyday meaning (tidy vs odd-looking); appearance must not decide classification.
Keep tool manipulations geometrically coherent: a rhombus demonstration must hold all four sides equal (a shear/skew) rather than imply a single-corner drag that would change side lengths.
A reveal/reference chart is a summary scaffold: it does not recompute when a learner changes a shape, so it cannot replace activities where the learner tests shapes they alter.

Sorting or multiple-choice items can check the rule but do not require the learner to construct a counterexample; include production tasks (drawing/labelling a shape that passes one test and fails the other) for full mastery.

Regularity is a planar property of sides and angles; adding a third spatial dimension is not needed to teach it. This is a scope note, not a claim that any representation is incapable of teaching the concept.
Dialogue can surface the single-criterion error and is a useful accompaniment to hands-on checking and sorting of shapes; its efficacy relative to those activities is untested.

startingActivity.title: Construct a triangle from a base and two base angles (ASA-style)
learnerActions: Rule a base exactly 7 cm long, placing the ruler's zero mark (not its physical end) on the starting point, then mark and join.
At the left endpoint, before reading, decide: is the 40° angle smaller or bigger than a square corner (right angle)? Use that estimate to pick which of the two protractor scale numbers to read.
Place the protractor with its centre hole on the vertex dot and its zero-line exactly along the base, count up from the 0 on the arm laid along the base, mark 40°, and rule the ray.
Repeat at the right endpoint to set a 65° angle and rule the second ray so the two rays meet.

Check the triangle against the specification: re-measure the 40° and 65° angles and the 7 cm base, then measure the third angle, which should be about 75° (the angles of a triangle add up to 180°). If an angle is out by more than about 2°, or the two rays spread apart and never meet (a sign that a supplement such as 140° was drawn), find where the placement or scale error crept in.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The two scales of a dual-scale protractor offer supplementary numbers (e.g. 40 and 140); your own estimate of whether the angle is bigger or smaller than a right angle is what picks the correct one. Careful placement and measuring from zero are what make the figure match its specification. (A base with an angle set at each of its two ends is an angle-side-angle construction.)

keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule (is it more or less than 90°?) to disambiguate the two scales
Single-scale or numberless protractor for the placement-learning phase
The 'centre-on-vertex, zero-on-line' placement diagram
Base-then-angles construction sequence for a triangle (SAS-style)
Side-and-turn model for constructing regular polygons
commonMisconceptions: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing the supplement (e.g. 60° instead of 120°)
Places the protractor's centre off the vertex or its zero-line off the side, so every angle is a few degrees out or the ray does not start at the vertex
Measures length from the physical end of the ruler rather than the zero mark, adding the end-margin to each length
Treats a 'nearly closing' triangle as correct rather than a signal of accumulated error
Draws sides to look right rather than to the measured length, or turns an inconsistent amount at each corner of a regular polygon
constraints: This is a hands-on motor-and-procedure skill: it must be practised with real ruler-and-protractor construction on paper (as the Y6 programme requires). Recognition-only checks (which scale, spot the misplacement) support reasoning but do not elicit the actual drawing accuracy that is the target skill.
A labelled picture or reference card can display the placement routine but cannot by itself build the placement-and-scale judgement; treat it as a reminder, not the main teacher.

A draggable on-screen ruler and protractor is an optional scaffold for the judgement (scale choice, placement, closure check) and should be paired with real tools so the physical motor skill develops alongside; it is not a substitute for drawing on paper.
Accept an accuracy tolerance of roughly ±2° and ±2 mm for a successful construction at this age.

The estimate-first rule ('bigger or smaller than a right angle?') resolves the supplement ambiguity only when the target angle is not itself close to 90°; for angles near a right angle, placement and careful reading carry more of the load.

A triangle built from a base plus an angle at each of its ends is an angle-side-angle (ASA) construction; a triangle built from two sides and the angle between them is side-angle-side (SAS). Name the construction accurately rather than conflating the two.

activityReferences.title: Build the shape by adding properties
Defend the asymmetry: which statement is true?

startingActivity.title: Build the shape by adding properties
learnerActions: Start with a general 'floppy' quadrilateral and switch on one property at a time: make opposite sides parallel, add right angles, make all sides equal.

Watch how the shape changes and where it belongs: making opposite sides parallel turns it into a parallelogram; adding right angles makes it a rectangle; instead making all sides equal makes it a rhombus; doing both makes it a square.

After each change, record in a property table which properties the shape now has (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals), noticing that these ticks accumulate as you go down each branch of the family tree.

Attempt the reverse challenge: try to make a rectangle that is NOT a parallelogram, and explain why you cannot — four right angles force each pair of opposite sides to be parallel (two sides that are both perpendicular to the same side are parallel), so every rectangle automatically meets the parallelogram definition.
Place the finished square, rhombus and rectangle onto a family-tree (hierarchy) diagram and into nested Venn sets, saying why the square sits inside BOTH the rhombus and rectangle regions.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A square inherits every property of the parallelogram, rhombus and rectangle because it is a special case of each; adding an extra constraint moves a shape DOWN the hierarchy, and the inheritance runs one way only — removing the extra property moves back up, but you cannot have a rectangle that is not also a parallelogram.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Quadrilateral hierarchy diagram (family tree) with quadrilateral ⊃ parallelogram ⊃ {rhombus, rectangle} ⊃ square
Nested Venn sets showing rhombus and rectangle overlapping, with square in the intersection
Property table: rows = shapes, columns = properties (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals) showing how ticks accumulate down the hierarchy
A parallelogram with adjustable angles and side lengths that becomes a rhombus, rectangle, or square as constraints are added
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'all squares are rectangles' as symmetric — concluding 'so all rectangles are squares' (or that both are equally true/false)
Reversing the subset direction — thinking a rectangle is a special square rather than a square a special rectangle
Exclusive/oblong prototype persisting from KS2: a 'real' rectangle must be longer than it is wide, so a square is not a rectangle at all
Not applying inheritance: agreeing a rhombus is a parallelogram in words, but not granting that it therefore has all parallelogram properties (e.g. opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisecting)
constraints: Build and defend the hierarchy from properties, not from appearance; the oblong/prototype view ('a rectangle must be longer than it is wide') must be directly confronted, not reinforced.

Classification, matching and true/false items check that the hierarchy is secure but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the inheritance insight; use them to confirm understanding alongside or after construction and reasoning work.

A tap-to-reveal hierarchy/property table is a useful reference once the idea is understood, but it does not let the learner add or remove constraints to feel a shape descend the hierarchy; pair it with construction activities.
Dialogue with a sceptic supports property-based justification; the structural subset relationships can be seen clearly in a diagram, nested sets or manipulative, so pair dialogue with those.

Optional interactive features (live constraint handles, animated descent down the tree, updating nested Venn sets, a ticking property table, tap-to-reveal nodes) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree can serve the same reasoning (a paper cut-out has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal flat quadrilateral it represents).
Keep class-inclusion attention one-directional: contrast 'all squares are rectangles' with 'all rectangles are squares' as genuinely different claims, not as a reversible rule.

Use 'equal diagonals' (true of rectangles and squares, not of general parallelograms or rhombuses) as the distinguishing property-table column so ticks genuinely accumulate; keep 'diagonals bisect each other' as a shared parallelogram property, not as an accumulating column.

startingActivity.title: Measure many circles and discover d = 2r
learnerActions: Draw several circles of clearly different sizes (small, medium, large).
For each circle, mark the centre, draw a radius from the centre to the edge and a diameter from edge to edge through the centre.
Measure the radius and the diameter of each circle and record them in a two-column table (radius | diameter).
Look across the table and describe the pattern you notice between the radius and the diameter.
State the relationship in your own words and as d = 2 × r.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Across every size of circle, the diameter is exactly twice the radius. Pupils' own measurements will come out close to double, allowing for small measuring errors, so they can see the pattern holding for themselves rather than memorising a rule.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A labelled circle: centre, radius, diameter, circumference
Radius vs diameter vs an off-centre chord, contrasted
A radius/diameter table across several circle sizes
String wrapped round a circle to show the circumference as a length
commonMisconceptions: Swaps radius and diameter, or substitutes a diameter where a radius is needed — the 'half/twice' error (NCTM).
Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or draws a radius/diameter that does not reach or pass through the centre.
Applies the conversion in the wrong direction (doubles when it should halve), or thinks the radius equals the diameter.
constraints: A static labelled diagram or reveal-on-tap reference states d = 2r but does not let pupils see it vary across sizes; pair it with hands-on drawing and measuring so the invariant is genuinely discovered.

A label/match/slider conversion check can verify vocabulary and the d = 2r computation but does not by itself build the defining-property understanding; use it as a check after the measuring and reasoning activities.
Recognition-only responses (matching terms to a standard diagram) do not elicit independent construction; require pupils to draw, measure, convert both ways, and justify.
Present diameters and radii in varied positions (including slanted and non-standard) so pupils do not over-rely on a horizontal prototype.
Always insist pupils state WHY (which line passes through the centre, whether they doubled or halved); the reason is what distinguishes understanding from a lucky guess.

startingActivity.title: Barrier game: describe a figure so a partner can draw it
learnerActions: Sit on one side of a barrier (screen, book, or divider) with a figure the partner cannot see: a tilted regular hexagon, a pair of parallel lines of clearly different lengths, and a perpendicular crossing

Describe the figure precisely enough that the unseen partner can reproduce it, naming which lines are parallel (∥ / arrows) and which are perpendicular (right-angle square), naming angles as ∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter, and calling the hexagon 'regular' because its sides AND angles are equal
Place or speak the notation marks the partner needs — parallel arrows, right-angle squares, ∠ABC labels, equal-length tick marks
Compare the partner's drawing with the original and discuss where it diverged
Swap roles and repeat with a new figure
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Precise words and marks make the drawing come out right while vague ones do not, so geometric language becomes a tool with consequences rather than a list to memorise.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Conventional notation set: AB, ∠ABC, AB ∥ CD, right-angle square, parallel arrows, equal-length tick marks
Barrier / describe-and-draw game (speaker uses terms, listener reconstructs)
Same shape shown in many orientations and as near-miss non-examples
Fold-lines and rotation overlays to demonstrate reflective and rotational symmetry
Regular vs irregular polygon pairs to force the equal-sides-AND-equal-angles criterion
commonMisconceptions: Prototype-driven naming: a shape is denied its name when tilted or non-standard (a 'slanted' square isn't called a square), even when the pupil knows the definition
Confusing or swapping 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', or believing parallel lines must be equal in length
Calling a polygon 'regular' when it has equal sides OR equal angles but not both (or just because it 'looks neat')
Writing ∠ABC with the vertex not in the middle, or naming an angle by a single letter where it is ambiguous
Using vague everyday words ('slanty line', 'pointy corner') instead of conventional terms and notation
constraints: The teaching goal is productive, property-based USE of terms and notation to describe, sketch and draw — not reciting definitions; assess by how pupils use terms in context, not by asking them to define words.

Always include tilted, scaled and non-example figures (e.g. a tilted regular hexagon, unequal-length parallel rails) so naming is forced onto defining properties; prototypical upright figures alone let prototype errors hide.

Reveal-on-tap interactive references and match/categorise tasks are scaffolds that check or expose receptive knowledge; they do not force the pupil to PRODUCE terms, so pair them with open labelling or describe-and-draw work.

Explicitly correct the 'parallel lines must be the same length' error and the swapping of parallel/perpendicular by regrounding each on its defining property (parallel: never meeting / constant distance; perpendicular: a square corner).

Tie 'regular' to BOTH equal sides AND equal angles; include counterexamples that satisfy only one condition (equal sides only, e.g. a non-square rhombus; equal angles only, e.g. a non-square rectangle).
Require three-letter angle naming (∠ABC with the vertex as the middle letter) whenever a point carries more than one angle, so the angle is unambiguous.

Paper/card cut-outs used for symmetry have real thickness and approximate the ideal plane figure; treat folds and rotations as evidence about the mathematical shape represented, and label any ideal zero-thickness screen model as a model.

A 3D environment is not needed for this planar vocabulary goal and adds cost without serving it; this is a scoped observation for this objective, not a universal rule that 3D adds nothing to geometry learning.

An in-role 'illustrator' conversation can elicit productive term use and let a partner probe misuse, but its reconstruction payload is essentially the barrier game; the persona adds little beyond the describe-and-draw task here (not a claim that dialogue cannot teach).

activityReferences.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge

startingActivity.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge
learnerActions: Take a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal or vertical), a pair of compasses and a straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor.
Open the compasses to MORE than half of PQ; discuss why an opening of half or less means the arcs only touch or never meet, and why an enormous opening just wastes space.
Place the compass point on P and sweep an arc above and below the segment; WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on Q and sweep again so the arcs cross at two points.
Rule the straight line through the two crossing points, leaving all construction arcs visible as evidence of method.
Explain why the line passes through the midpoint at 90°: the four equal radii form a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other.
Repeat on segments at several different orientations, not only horizontal/vertical ones.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from P and Q. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points, and the straight line through them is the perpendicular bisector; visible arcs make the method inspectable, though arcs alone do not prove they were placed correctly.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two equal-radius circles/arcs from the segment ends and the rhombus they define
The rhombus-around-a-diagonal image (segment as one diagonal; the construction produces the other)
Kite counter-example (unequal radii) showing perpendicular-but-not-bisecting diagonals
Isosceles triangle whose altitude bisects the base at right angles and bisects the apex angle
Dynamic-geometry compass/straightedge for concept-before-dexterity
commonMisconceptions: Changing the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus, so the line is perpendicular but does not pass through the midpoint
Drawing rather than constructing — using a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor/eye for the right angle — and leaving no construction marks
Opening the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs never intersect
Memorising the steps as an isolated routine with no link to the properties of circles and rhombuses
Treating the construction as valid only for horizontal/vertical segments (prototype-orientation bias)
constraints: Use compasses and an unmarked straight edge to locate the required points and lines from geometric properties, rather than by measuring. A ruler or protractor may check practical accuracy afterwards; such checks do not prove or replace the construction.
Require pupils to leave their construction arcs visible as evidence that the equidistance/rhombus property, not measurement, produced the result.
Keep the compass width unchanged between the two endpoints, and open it to more than half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below.
Present segments and angles at non-standard (diagonal, rotated) orientations, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes.

A dynamic-geometry compass is a concept-building scaffold: it may help pupils reason about equidistance and the rhombus-vs-kite distinction but does not develop the manual dexterity, which must be practised with real compasses afterwards.
Recognition/multiple-choice items assess the reasoning only; they do not evidence the pupil actually executing the construction, which is the performance target.

Treat tolerances such as ±2 mm / ±2° as accuracy targets for the manual skill, distinguishing a dexterity lapse (correct method, slipped arcs) from a conceptual error (unequal radii, measuring instead of constructing).

startingActivity.title: Place the object: follow spoken positional instructions
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken instruction naming an object, a landmark, and a relation, e.g. 'put the teddy behind the box'.
Move the named object into the correct relation to the landmark (for example drag it in a bedroom scene, or place a real toy with a real box and cup).
Try a short series that varies the relation: 'put the cup next to the teddy', 'put the pencil under the book'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A positional word is an instruction that tells you exactly where to put something relative to a named landmark.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Object–landmark–relation triples acted out with real toys and objects
The child's own body, with a right-hand sticker, for left and right
Everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — and simple picture scenes to describe
Barrier games: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for a partner to reproduce it
commonMisconceptions: Uses vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one') with a gesture instead of a positional word
Judges left/right from the child's own current facing and cannot adjust it for an object or person facing the other way
Cannot hold two relations at once — a thing that is above one object and below another is described with only one relation (egocentrism / dual relations)
Treats a position as belonging to the object ('the front') rather than as a relation to a named landmark and a viewpoint
constraints: The core objective is productive AND receptive USE: the child must both follow and give instructions. Recognition-only tasks (matching or categorising position words to pictures) can check recognition but do not by themselves elicit independent production, so they cannot alone demonstrate mastery of this language-in-context topic — use them, if at all, only as a recognition check.

Tapping a static picture scene to reveal position words is useful for exposure, but on its own it does not let the child produce instructions or receive manipulate-and-see feedback; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective. This is a scope limit, not a claim that static images cannot teach.

Do not mark vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one' with a point) as an error for 4-6 year olds: informal language normally precedes precise words. Recast and keep supplying positional language, expecting it to firm up over time.

Do not drill left/right for facing partners/turned objects as failure, and do not force two relations (above AND below) at once: both are developmentally hard and typically not mastered until early elementary school. Accept one relation and add the second in a recast.

A rotatable 3D scene could make frame-dependence (how behind/in front and left/right flip as you move around) felt, but that perspective-taking is the hard part not expected at 4-6 and exceeds the core naming goal; it is an optional enrichment, not required.

Always pair a position word with a named landmark. Move the object to new places to show that position is a relation to the landmark, not a fixed feature of the object. As light, optional enrichment, moving the viewer around a landmark with no front of its own (e.g. a plain box) can show that 'behind' depends on where you stand. For landmarks with their own front (a sofa, a person), 'behind' usually means the landmark's own back.

activityReferences.title: Clockwise, anti-clockwise and the right angle a quarter turn leaves
Give and follow a multi-step route that someone else can act on
