startingActivity.title: Clockwise, anti-clockwise and the right angle a quarter turn leaves
learnerActions: Watch a real clock's hands and name the direction they travel as 'clockwise'; then turn your own body a quarter turn clockwise (towards your right, the way the hands would go on a clock lying face-up on the floor and seen from above) and say where you now face.
Make a quarter turn clockwise and mark or point out the corner (angle) between where you started facing and where you finish facing; name it as a right angle.
Make the same quarter turn anti-clockwise and describe how the finishing facing differs.

On a clock face or turn dial, spin an arrow with a 'clockwise, quarter turn' control so it moves 90° and leaves a right-angle mark between start and finish; use 'anti-clockwise' to send it back the other way.
Make two quarter turns clockwise in a row and decide whether that equals one half turn, counting each quarter aloud.
Make a three-quarter turn clockwise, counting the quarters, and point out that three right angles have been passed.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A quarter turn always leaves a right angle between the start and finish arms, and clockwise versus anti-clockwise decides which way you turn — turning fuzzy words into exact instructions.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A clock face for clockwise and anti-clockwise
Body or floor-robot turns with start/finish facings, and the right-angle mark left by a quarter turn
Route maps and grids to describe and to follow with combined moves and turns
Two adjoining arms (the start and finish of a turn) showing the angle turned through
commonMisconceptions: Clockwise and anti-clockwise confused with each other or with left/right — a new convention on top of frame-dependent left/right
A quarter turn not connected to a right angle — the two treated as separate, unrelated facts
Turn amounts miscounted — a half or a quarter turn produced when a three-quarter turn is asked for
Egocentric direction-giving: routes given from the child's own viewpoint without accounting for the follower's facing
constraints: The goal is fluent, correct USE of the words in routes and turn descriptions, not reciting definitions.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors: frame-dependence is still developing at this age.
Egocentric direction-giving is developmentally expected, not a failure; surface it by having the follower act the route out literally rather than correcting abstractly.

Recognition/selection and matching tasks can check the vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit the child producing turns and followable routes, so the child must still construct turns and routes themselves.

A fixed picture or diagram can illustrate the quarter-turn/right-angle link but cannot be turned by the child; a manipulable dial or embodied turn supplies the dynamic experience. Neither claim is that a static image 'cannot teach' the idea.

Interactive controls (clockwise/anti-clockwise and quarter/half buttons, a stamped right-angle mark, a robot that hits a wall on a wrong move) are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms.
Rendering turns and routes in 3D is optional; the ideas are planar and do not require it.

activityReferences.title: Plot-and-complete on a numbered grid
Which coordinate completes the shape? — diagnostic choices
Reveal how a completed shape's coordinates relate

startingActivity.title: Plot-and-complete on a numbered grid
learnerActions: Plot a given point by finding the x-line first, travelling up to the y-line, and marking the intersection, counting from the origin against the numbered lines.
Plot (5,4) and then (4,5) and compare: show they land in different places to make the along-then-up order explicit.

Given three vertices of a genuine square, e.g. (1,1), (1,4) and (4,4) (whose fourth vertex is (4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides), STATE the fourth coordinate aloud before plotting it, then plot it and draw the sides; check all four side lengths are equal and all four corners are right angles so the figure is genuinely a square.
Check the completed figure is the intended polygon: right angles and matching opposite sides for a rectangle, right angles and four equal sides for a square.

Repeat with three vertices of a rectangle, e.g. (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) whose fourth vertex is (5,1), giving a 4-by-3 rectangle, so the shared-x / shared-y reasoning transfers and children see that unequal sides (4 and 3) make a rectangle, not a square.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A point's location is fixed by reading x (across) then y (up) from the origin, and the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines can be reasoned out because it shares one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y; 'looks right' is replaced by 'is right' when the drawn sides form the named shape, with right angles at every corner and matching side lengths — four equal sides for a square, equal opposite sides for a rectangle.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with origin, points plotted as line-intersections
Along-then-up plotting path from the origin to each point
Partly-drawn polygon with given vertices and one missing, to be completed
The missing vertex sharing one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y (rectangle/square)
Completed shape with all vertex coordinates labelled
commonMisconceptions: Reversal when plotting — going up before across, so the point lands in the mirror position (e.g. plots (5,4) at 4-across-5-up).
Completing a polygon by eye/appearance rather than reasoning from coordinates and shape properties, giving a wrong missing vertex.
Counting squares instead of numbered lines when plotting, producing off-by-one positions.
Joining vertices in the wrong order, producing a crossed or incorrect polygon even when the points are right.
constraints: Plot with along-then-up discipline: find the x-line, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection; count from the origin against the numbered lines, not by counting squares.

Completion must be reasoned from coordinates and shape properties (shared x and shared y of neighbours, for shapes whose sides run along the grid lines), not from appearance; verify side lengths and right angles — four equal sides with four right angles confirm a square, equal opposite sides with four right angles a rectangle.
Have children state the missing coordinate before plotting it so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the missing vertex, matching labels) are good for diagnosis but do not by themselves show the child independently plotting and drawing the sides to see the figure close; pair them with a produce-and-draw task.
A worked, labelled figure is a scaffold: it shows the relationship but cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so include a grid (interactive or paper) where the child plots and draws.
First-quadrant plotting and completing plane polygons is a 2D task; include the zero-coordinate/axis case, e.g. compare (3,0) and (0,3) as distinct points.

When a point set is named a square, confirm it actually has four equal sides; a set like (1,1),(1,4),(5,4),(5,1) has unequal sides (4 and 3) and is a rectangle, so use it as a rectangle example and reserve 'square' for equal-sided sets such as (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1).

activityReferences.title: Predict-then-slide on a coordinate grid
Describe the move between two positions
Tap-to-reveal before-and-after picture (scaffold)

startingActivity.title: Predict-then-slide on a coordinate grid
learnerActions: Set a translation such as '4 right and 2 up' on a first-quadrant grid containing a shape.
Before anything moves, predict and state (or type) the new coordinates of one named vertex — e.g. from (2,3) you should get (6,5).
Trigger the slide and watch every vertex glide by the same 4-across, 2-up while a coordinate readout ticks from the old to the new values.
Run a horizontal-only move (e.g. '3 right') and confirm the up-number (y) stays fixed while only the across-number changes.
Check two different vertices moved by identical amounts, confirming the shape did not turn, flip or resize.
Count the move in unit jumps from the start point, without counting the starting line itself as 'one'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A horizontal move changes only x and a vertical move only y; the whole shape shifts uniformly without changing size or orientation, and predicting from the (x+right, y+up) rule can be checked against the actual slide.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Coordinate grid showing a start point and its translated image with the slide arrow
Component decomposition: horizontal move (Δx) then vertical move (Δy)
Rule form: (x, y) → (x + right, y + up)
A shape and its translated copy, same size and orientation, every vertex shifted equally
Number-line counting of the move along each axis from the start position
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — swapping the right and up amounts (applying the horizontal shift to y and the vertical to x).
Changing the wrong coordinate — altering y for a move described as 'right', or changing both coordinates for a single-direction move.
Getting the direction sign wrong — moving left when 'right' is stated, or subtracting instead of adding.
Counting squares rather than numbered lines, giving an off-by-one image position.
Confusing the description of the MOVE with the destination coordinates (stating where it ends when asked how it moved, or vice versa).
constraints: Built on first-quadrant coordinate knowledge; learners should already read ordered pairs along-then-up before describing moves as coordinate changes.

Recognition/selection responses (multiple-choice, tap-to-reveal) can be used while teaching and for scoring, but they do not require the learner to independently construct a predicted coordinate or a worded description — keep genuine prediction and production in the sequence.

The tap-to-reveal picture is a scaffold: because the slide is fixed, the learner cannot set, carry out or predict their own move; progress to an interactive or hand-plotted grid so the rule is used, not just read.

Count moves as unit jumps from the start point: do not count the starting line as 'one'; the first jump lands on the next line. (When points sit on grid intersections, counting square widths crossed gives the same count.) This avoids off-by-one images.
Keep directions and signs explicit: right/up add, left/down subtract; state them when working opposite directions.
Translations here are planar left/right/up/down slides; a 3D setting adds complexity irrelevant to this objective rather than being inherently unteachable in other media.

activityReferences.title: Coordinate-journey grid: place the point and watch the path
Read the point: diagnose reversal and off-by-one
Labelled-grid reveal: seed the convention and the axis names

startingActivity.title: Coordinate-journey grid: place the point and watch the path
learnerActions: Given a target pair such as (4,2), place the point on a numbered first-quadrant grid.
Watch the tool trace the journey from the origin — along 4, then up 2 — and drop the marker where you placed it.
If you read 'up before across', notice your point lands at 2-across-4-up, a clearly different point (a different gridline crossing) from the target (4,2), with the along-then-up trail showing why.
Press a compare control to drop (2,4) and (4,2) side by side so you SEE they are two different points.
Count against the glowing numbered lines starting from the origin (0,0), not the squares between them.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The order of the pair fixes the point — reading up before across lands you somewhere else — and counting is read from the numbered lines starting at the origin, not by counting squares.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with the origin (0,0) marked
'Along the corridor, then up the stairs' journey from the origin (across before up)
Two contrasting points (2,4) vs (4,2) shown together to make order matter
The (x, y) ordered pair with axes labelled x (across) and y (up)
A shape plotted on the grid with each vertex's coordinates read off
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — putting the y-coordinate before the x (reading/plotting up before across), giving an incorrectly placed point (documented, NCETM).
Believing the order is arbitrary — treating (2,4) and (4,2) as the same location.
Counting squares/cells instead of reading the numbered grid lines, producing off-by-one positions.
Not anchoring to the origin — starting the count at 1 rather than 0, or from the wrong corner.
constraints: Scope is the first quadrant with a numbered grid for ages 8–9; whole-number coordinates read from the origin (0,0).

The static labelled-grid reveal seeds the convention and axis names but does not let a child test a placement or experience order mattering through their own action; use it alongside construction and reading tasks, not as the sole experience.
Reading/selected-response items diagnose and give practice but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a point; pair them with place-the-point work.
Build on Year 3/earlier position vocabulary (left/right, up/down, across) before introducing the formal (x, y) pair.
Counting must be anchored at the origin and read against the numbered lines, not the squares between them, to avoid off-by-one errors.

Interaction examples (path tracing, compare control, glowing numbered lines, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and should not be treated as mandatory mechanisms.

Reason across quadrants and name the quadrant from the signs

startingActivity.title: Plot it as a signed journey from the origin
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes, plot (−3,4): move LEFT 3 along the x-axis from the origin, then UP 4 along the y-axis, treating each sign as a direction.
Name the quadrant from its sign pattern: (−,+) is the second (top-left) quadrant.
Plot (2,−5) (two right, five down) and (−4,−1) (four left, one down), naming each quadrant from its two signs.

If a live tool is available, place the marker yourself and watch it replay the two signed moves; if you counted right for the −3 and landed in the (+,+) quadrant, notice the mismatch and re-plot reading the minus as 'left'.
Where offered, use a reflect-in-axis toggle to flip (−3,4)↔(3,4)↔(3,−4) and watch a single sign change hop the point across an axis.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A minus sign is a DIRECTION (left of, or below, the origin), not decoration on the digit; the quadrant is read directly from the pair of signs, and flipping one sign reflects the point across an axis.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the origin and both signed axes labelled
Counting stick / number line held horizontally and vertically to model signed movement along each axis
Thermometer or below-ground scale as a familiar signed vertical axis
Sign-pattern labels for the four quadrants: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−)
commonMisconceptions: Moving the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counting right for −3 or up for −5 — through weak grasp of order on a signed scale.
Putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, placing the point in the wrong quadrant.
Mis-ordering negatives (treating −5 as further out than −3 because 5>3), so points on a negative axis are misplaced.
Counting from '1' at the origin instead of '0', landing one square off.
constraints: The (across, then up/down) ordering convention carries over from the first quadrant; the genuinely new demand is reading the SIGNED scale on each axis, so secure directed-number sense is a prerequisite.
Recognition-only practice items confirm and diagnose but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the two signed movements; pair them with actual plotting where possible.

A static labelled four-quadrant grid can reveal a point's signed path and each quadrant's sign pattern on tap, which clarifies layout, but it does not let the child plot and self-check, which is where signed errors surface — treat it as a scaffold.
Keep to the 2D plane for this objective; introducing a third axis brings octants and z-values beyond this topic and would obscure the signed 2D reading.
Reflect-in-axis toggles, axis-lighting counts, and live replay are optional feedback examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory.
Always count MOVES from the origin (0), not the grid lines including it, to avoid the one-square-off error.

activityReferences.title: Along then up: the swapped-pair journey
Read it back: name the pair for a given point
Labelled grid reference (scaffold)
Navigator talk: give the pair before I move (alternative)

startingActivity.title: Along then up: the swapped-pair journey
learnerActions: On a numbered coordinate grid (first quadrant), first point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin. Then start at the origin (0,0) and plot (4,2): move 4 ALONG the x-axis first, then 2 UP, tracing the corridor-then-stairs path and marking the point where the lines cross.
Now plot (2,4) from the origin the same way (2 along, then 4 up) and mark that point too.
Compare: describe out loud where each marker landed and why the two points are in different places on the grid even though they use the same two numbers.
Write a sentence: 'The order matters because ___.'
Check your work: point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin again, and confirm that both journeys started at the origin (0,0).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The pair is an ordered address, not just two numbers: swapping the order sends you to a different place, and every reading starts from the origin and is read off the numbered lines.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines meeting at the origin, each labelled; the point reached by reading along then up
The 'corridor then stairs' / 'a-cross then up' journey traced from the origin to the point
(2,4) and (4,2) plotted together to show the order matters
A grid with numbered lines (not just squares) to read off directly
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — gives/reads the pair as (y, x): up before across (NCETM: 'putting the y-coordinate before the x')
Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point
Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
Loses the origin as the (0,0) start, or thinks the axes are just the borders of the grid rather than number lines
constraints: This microtopic is a first-quadrant, 2-D coordinate idea; a third axis is a much later topic and would distract from the ordered-pair convention here.

Recognition/matching items (which point is (3,5)?) check the convention but do not require the learner to construct the pair or watch the order change the point; pair them with plotting or spoken production.

A labelled reference grid is a consolidation scaffold: it is fixed, so the learner cannot themselves vary the order on it — use it after active work; this is a limitation of that one reference, not a claim that fixed images cannot teach.
Always read from the numbered lines and anchor at the origin (0,0); counting squares/gaps from a grid edge invites off-by-one errors.
If a learner cannot name x-axis/y-axis/origin at all, reteach that prerequisite (naming the axes and establishing the origin as (0,0)) before coordinate reading.

startingActivity.title: Plot a journey: the snail's progress
learnerActions: On a numbered first-quadrant grid, plot the ordered pairs (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) for a snail logging its distance each minute, marking each point at the intersection of the numbered gridlines
Narrate the route aloud while plotting: 'along the corridor to 3, then up the stairs to 6'
After plotting (3,6), answer 'what does this point tell us?' by completing the sentence 'after 3 minutes the snail had gone 6 centimetres'
Join the plotted points to see the journey line emerge
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A coordinate is not just a dot: it is a two-number route from the origin (x first, then y) and, on a data graph, a statement about a real situation.

keyRepresentations: First-quadrant coordinate grid with clearly numbered axes and a marked origin
'Corridor then stairs' / 'along then up' movement metaphor for the x-then-y order
Data table paired with its plotted graph (e.g. time in column 1, distance in column 2) so each row becomes a point
Journey/time-distance line built from plotted points, linking each dot to a moment in a story
commonMisconceptions: Reversing the coordinates — plotting (a,b) as if it were (b,a), going up before across
Counting the squares rather than the numbered gridlines, landing one place off
Assuming one square always equals one unit and ignoring an axis scaled in twos or fives
Treating a plotted point as just a dot, unable to say what its coordinates mean in the given scenario
constraints: Count along the numbered gridlines, not the squares between them, to pre-empt the off-by-one error; make explicit that the numbers label the lines, not the spaces
Rehearse the x-before-y convention as a fixed sequence of movements from the origin ('across, then up') before any data work, so the ordered pair is read as a route rather than two loose numbers
Introduce non-unit axis scales (twos, fives) only once the basic convention is secure
Children should both plot (mark the point from a pair) and read (state the pair from a point) in the same session — the two directions expose different errors

Keep each activity's real-data scenario internally consistent (same object and same distance unit throughout a single activity) so a coordinate reliably maps to one situation; where the object changes between activities, frame the new journey explicitly

Recognition-only or recall tasks (e.g. selecting the right pair from options) assess the plot/read skill but do not elicit the independent construction of plotting a point or an open explanation of what a coordinate means; include tasks that require actually placing points and stating meaning in a child's own words

A tap-to-reveal static grid can introduce the convention (e.g. tap a point to reveal 'across 4, up 7') but does not let the child perform a placement or receive feedback on their own plotting; treat it as a pre-teach scaffold, not practice of the skill
The skill is planar (two axes in a flat plane); a third dimension is not part of this objective

startingActivity.title: Build the butterfly's missing wing, point by point
learnerActions: Start from half a butterfly drawn on squared paper beside a clearly marked vertical mirror line.
For each key point of the given half (e.g. a wingtip), count the squares perpendicular from the mirror line to that point.
Count the SAME number of squares straight out on the far side, perpendicular to the mirror, and mark the partner point.
Repeat for every corner/key point, then join the partners in the SAME order as the original half.

Fold the paper along the mirror line (holding it up to the light if needed), or stand a mirror/Mira on the line and compare the reflection of the given half with your drawn half. Check that the two halves line up, allowing for small inaccuracies in drawing and folding.

Sliding a copy of the half across (translating) rather than reflecting, so the completed shape is not a true mirror image.

startingActivity.title: Name it: reconstruct the transformation that produced the image
learnerActions: On a grid showing a shape and its image already placed (produced by a rotation), work out which single transformation maps the first onto the second and reproduce it by setting the parameters yourself.
First try a reflection: flip the shape and compare handedness to the target — notice the 'sense' no longer matches (the target reads the same way round), so it cannot be a reflection.
Switch to rotation: choose a centre of rotation, set the angle of turn, and choose the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise) until your image lands exactly on the target.

State the full description aloud or in writing, e.g. 'rotation, 90° clockwise, about (2,1)', and check what each part controls: turning the same amount about a different centre makes the shape land somewhere else, and for a 90° turn, going the opposite direction lands it in a different place. (For a 180° turn, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, but still state the direction to keep the description complete.)
Confirm the image is congruent to the original (e.g. by tracing or matching vertices).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Checking sense is what distinguishes a rotation from a reflection, and a rotation is only fully specified by centre, size AND direction together. The centre and the angle always affect where the image lands. The direction matters for 90° turns, but a 180° turn lands in the same place either way.

keyRepresentations: Coordinate/squared grid showing object and image together
Mirror line with perpendicular 'joining lines' to corresponding vertices (reflection)
Centre-of-rotation marked, with an angle arc and a direction arrow (rotation)
Translation vector arrow (displacement) applied to every vertex
Tracing paper as the physical model for rotation and for congruence checks
commonMisconceptions: Calling a rotation a reflection (or vice versa) because sense/handedness is not checked.
Describing a rotation incompletely — giving the angle but omitting the centre and/or the direction.
When reflecting in a sloping mirror, keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror.
Reversing coordinates (up before across) when labelling where the image landed.
constraints: A complete rotation description requires all three parts — centre, size of turn, and direction; treat any missing part as incomplete.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language for reflection so methods generalise to sloping and offset mirror lines; use perpendicular-and-equidistant instead.
Label image coordinates consistently as (across, up) to guard against reversing the ordered pair.
Include non-standard cases (a turn that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching.
Discrete/recognition items (multiple choice, matching) check precision of stated description but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an image; pair them with producing tasks.
Tracing paper (pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction) is a useful physical model for rotation and for checking congruence; it is a supportive tool, not a required mechanism.

Interactive controls (mode buttons, draggable mirror line, pinnable centre with angle dial and CW/ACW toggle, live sense indicator and congruence overlay) are optional ways to make the descriptor-to-motion link concrete; the same learning can be done on paper.

These transformations are planar and are read from marks on a grid, so a third dimension is not needed to read a mirror line, vector or centre. A dialogue/persona format can discuss and prompt transformation work but does not itself present or manipulate the grid, so producing an image would still happen on the learner's own paper. These are scoping affordance notes, not claims that any medium is uniquely necessary, superior, or impossible.

startingActivity.title: Build a reflection vertex by vertex using the perpendicular-equidistant rule
learnerActions: Start with a scalene triangle on a squared grid and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right (choose scalene so a reversal of sense is visible).

For each vertex in turn, draw the line from the vertex to the mirror line that meets the mirror at a right angle (perpendicular to the mirror line); with this vertical mirror it runs along a horizontal grid line. Check the right angle rather than assuming it.
Count the squares from the vertex to the mirror along that perpendicular, then count the SAME number of squares beyond the mirror and mark the image vertex there.
Repeat for every vertex, then join the image vertices to complete the reflected shape.

Compare the vertex order: check that the image reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise order of corners becomes anticlockwise) — this reversed 'sense' is what makes it a true reflection rather than a slide.
State the coordinates of each image corner as (across, up), reading across first then up.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A reflection is produced point by point: every line joining an object vertex to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and the image vertex is the same distance beyond the mirror as the object is in front. Because this reverses the vertex order, the shape's sense flips — distinguishing a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.

keyRepresentations: Squared/coordinate grid with a vertical (then horizontal) mirror line
Perpendicular 'joining lines' from each object vertex to its image vertex, crossed at right angles by the mirror line
Tracing paper laid over object and image to demonstrate congruence
A translation vector shown as a 'staircase' arrow (e.g. 5 right then 2 up) applied identically to every vertex
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting by sliding the shape across the mirror unchanged, so its sense is not reversed (translate-instead-of-flip).
Placing the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often by miscounting or letting the shape touch the line.
Believing the shape changes size or becomes a 'different shape' once moved, rather than staying congruent.
Reversing the image coordinates (writing y before x) when reporting where the shape landed.
constraints: Use a scalene shape so the reversal of sense is visible; a symmetric shape can hide whether a learner reflected or merely slid.
Say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' rather than 'straight across/down', even for vertical or horizontal mirrors, so the rule generalises to sloping mirror lines later.
Report image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-before-y / y-before-x reversal.
When using tracing paper to check a reflection, the tracing must be turned OVER to overlay the image; the shape remains congruent and that flip is the reversed sense.

Discrete-item checks (choosing the correctly reflected image among a slid-across distractor and a not-equidistant distractor, filling in image coordinates, true/false on congruence) can diagnose the two misconceptions but, because nothing recomputes, they check rather than build the felt rule; use them alongside, not instead of, construction.

A pre-annotated worked diagram that reveals the perpendicular joining lines, the equal square-counts and the label 'congruent' can illustrate the rule but does not let a learner test their own placement, which is the core skill; treat it as a scaffold, not the assessment.

A live grid where dragging a vertex or the mirror line recomputes the image (with faint perpendicular joining lines, live square-counts that turn green when the two sides match, a sense badge that flips when the reflection is correct, a settable translation arrow applied to all vertices at once, and a ghost of the original for congruence) can make the invariants concrete; these interaction and feedback examples are optional ways to expose the mechanism, not mandatory.

Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figure; use it to demonstrate congruence of the represented mathematical shape while distinguishing that shape from the physical copy.

startingActivity.title: Predict, then reflect: watch the single coordinate flip
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid, start with a triangle plotted in the second quadrant and its vertices labelled with coordinates.
Before anything moves, choose 'reflect in the x-axis' and write down what you predict each vertex will become.
Run the reflection: watch each vertex move perpendicular to the x-axis (vertically, to the opposite side) while, in a coordinate table, only the y-value changes sign and x stays the same.
If a real mirror or Mira is available, stand it on the x-axis to check the image faces the opposite way and sits the same distance from the axis.
Now, starting from the SAME triangle, reflect in the y-axis instead and predict again: this time the shape flips sideways (perpendicular to the y-axis) and only x changes sign.
Compare the two results on the same vertex, e.g. (−4, 1) → (−4, −1) in the x-axis but (−4, 1) → (4, 1) in the y-axis.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape vertically, so the y-coordinate (vertical distance from the x-axis) negates and x is unchanged; reflecting in the y-axis flips it horizontally, so x negates and y is unchanged. The axis you reflect IN is the mirror and points move perpendicular to it.

keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the x- and y-axes as mirror lines
Coordinate mapping notation: translation (x, y) → (x+a, y+b); reflection in x-axis (x, y) → (x, −y); in y-axis (x, y) → (−x, y)
Real mirror / Mira placed on an axis to check the image, as a scaffold
Paired worked example showing the same vertex reflected in each axis to contrast which coordinate changes
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting in the x-axis but changing the sign of the WRONG coordinate (negating x instead of y), effectively reflecting in the other axis.
Reflecting by sliding/translating the shape rather than reflecting it, so the image is not reversed.
Getting the translation sign wrong — adding when the move is left or down instead of subtracting.
Reversing the coordinate pair (writing the y-value before the x-value) when stating image vertices.
constraints: Reflection and translation here are 2-D coordinate operations on the plane; a third dimension (z-values, planes of reflection) is not needed and distracts from the (x, y) sign rules.

Avoid 'straight across / straight down' as a generic rule; say points move perpendicular to the mirror axis so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (for the x-axis this motion happens to be vertical, for the y-axis horizontal).

Fully describe a rotation — centre, angle and direction
Translate and prove congruence

startingActivity.title: Reflect, then try to copy it with a rotation
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant coordinate grid, take a scalene, obviously-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) and reflect it in the line y=x, recording the image coordinates of each vertex (e.g. (1,4) maps to (4,1) — for y=x, swap the coordinates).

For each vertex not lying on the mirror line, draw the segment from the point to its image and check it meets the mirror line at a right angle, crossing at the midpoint — confirming the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of every such point→image segment (a vertex on y=x maps to itself, so it has no segment).
Note whether the shape's handedness has changed: for the reflection the 'F' should appear mirror-imaged.

Now try to land the ORIGINAL shape on top of your reflected image using a ROTATION instead: pin a centre, choose 90° clockwise, and compare. Observe that the rotated shape keeps its handedness and so cannot coincide with the flipped reflection.
State in your own words why reflection and rotation give different results here: one reverses sense (handedness), the other preserves it.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses sense while rotation and translation preserve it; this handedness test is what distinguishes a reflection from a rotation even when the image lands in a similar place. Reflecting in y=x swaps the x and y coordinates (reflection in y=−x swaps and negates them: (x,y)→(−y,−x)), not merely slides the shape across.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid showing object and image shapes
Tracing paper / transparent overlay for testing rotation (pin the centre and turn) and for checking congruence
Mirror line drawn as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment
A 'sense' / handedness marker — an L-shaped or scalene shape whose flip is visible at a glance
Column-vector notation for translations
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting in a diagonal mirror but keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane (overuse of H/V mirrors)
Confusing rotation and reflection because sense is never checked
Describing a rotation without its centre or direction, or assuming clockwise
Swapping x and y when reading or writing image coordinates (reversal) carried into the image
Thinking a rigid transformation can change the size of the shape
constraints: Every transformation must be described by its full data: translation = column vector; reflection = equation of the mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction. The one exception is a 180° rotation, where clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, so the direction may be left out. An under-described rotation should not be accepted as complete.

Include diagonal mirror lines (y=x, y=−x) and rotation centres away from the shape early, so pupils do not overfit to horizontal/vertical mirrors and vertex-centres. Note that the coordinate shortcut differs: y=x swaps coordinates while y=−x swaps and negates them ((x,y)→(−y,−x)), so each diagonal should be derived rather than assumed from a single rule.
Use a scalene, clearly-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) so that a reversed sense is visible at a glance; a symmetric shape would hide the flip.

Keep the work on the 2D coordinate grid used by the assessment. A 3D handling could dramatise chirality (a left hand cannot be rotated into a right hand) but adds a dimension the assessment does not use and complicates coordinate reading; reserve it for a later chirality extension rather than the core task.

The labelled-diagram and recognition/matching tasks are scaffolds for vocabulary and classification: recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent construction of performing and checking a transformation, so include actual performance (drawing images, setting mirror/centre/direction, measuring congruence).
Treat coordinate reversal (y before x) as a separate recording slip from the transformation itself; a transformation can be correct while the recorded coordinates are reversed.
Congruence should be checked (tracing-paper overlay or measuring corresponding sides and angles), not assumed; emphasise that rigid transformations cannot change size.

Interactive features such as live sense badges, springing perpendicular-bisector guides, a ghost overlay confirming congruence, pinning a rotation centre, and refusing to run a rotation until a centre and direction are set are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they illustrate the learning, they are not mandatory for teaching it.

activityReferences.title: Grow it by adding, then test whether it stays the same shape
Enlarge from a centre with ray lines

startingActivity.title: Grow it by adding, then test whether it stays the same shape
learnerActions: Start with a 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle and predict, in writing, whether making it '8 by 10 by adding 5 to each side' keeps it the same shape just bigger — say yes or no and WHY before checking
Divide each pair of corresponding sides and build a ratio table: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 beside 10÷5 = 2

Place the 3×5 rectangle on the 8×10 rectangle at a shared corner, with the 3 cm side along the 8 cm side and the 5 cm side along the 10 cm side. Extend the diagonal of the 3×5 that starts at the shared corner and observe whether it passes through the opposite corner of the 8×10 rectangle (it misses it)

Now compare the 3×5 against a 6×10 rectangle: check both ratios (6÷3=2 and 10÷5=2). Then, with the 3 cm side along the 6 cm side at a shared corner, extend the diagonal from that shared corner to see it pass through the opposite corner of the 6×10
State which rectangle is similar to the original and justify using a single shared scale factor
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding a constant to each side does not in general preserve shape (the only exception is when the sides being compared are equal, as in a square); similarity requires every pair of corresponding sides to reduce to the SAME multiplier. The 8×10 fails the ratio test; the 6×10 (×2) passes.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Centre of enlargement with ray lines through vertices (distances × scale factor)
Corresponding-sides ratio table (each pair reduced to the same scale factor)
Two overlaid shapes with corresponding angles marked equal and sides labelled with their ratio
Diagonal test: extending the diagonal of the original passes through the corner of a true enlargement but misses a fake (additive) one
commonMisconceptions: Additive reasoning: treats 'add the same amount to each side' as an enlargement (3×5 → 8×10 by +5), when similarity requires multiplying each side by a constant
Believes angles get bigger when a shape is enlarged (scales the angles along with the sides)
Uses a different multiplier for different sides, or checks the scale factor on only one pair of corresponding sides and assumes the rest match
Enlarges the shape but does not scale each vertex's distance from the centre of enlargement, so the image is the wrong size or position
constraints: Target the additive misconception explicitly: learners must compute corresponding-side ratios themselves and see the additive construction fail, not merely be told the rule.
Require the scale factor to be verified on EVERY pair of corresponding sides; one matching pair does not establish similarity.
Keep a genuinely similar contrast case available (e.g. 6×10, each side ×2) alongside the additive fake (8×10) so a correct 'not similar' verdict cannot come from a lucky guess.

A judgement/classification task assesses and reinforces the multiplicative test but does not by itself give the experience of distances scaling from a centre; pair it with hands-on or live enlargement.
A static reference card confirms the structure but cannot recompute as the scale factor changes; use it after construction, not instead of it.

Spoken or in-role framing can pose the additive trap, but whatever the medium the learner must themselves perform and see the corresponding-side computation; hearing a stated ratio is recognition, which does not by itself elicit that production.
Scaling solids (volume scale factor = SF³) is a later extension beyond this topic's 2D objective and should not be mixed in here.

startingActivity.title: Turn your whole body on the spot
learnerActions: Stand on a marked spot (hoop or footprints) with both feet staying put throughout the turn.
Mark your start facing (e.g. 'I'm facing the door'), then make a quarter turn to your right and name your new facing ('now the window').

Go back to your start facing (the door). Make a half turn and check you are facing the opposite way from the start; go back to the start facing, make a whole turn and check you are facing the same way as the start.

Go back to your start facing, then make a three-quarter turn to your right and check where you now face (three quarter-turns to the right from the start, the same facing as one quarter turn to the left).
Make two quarter turns in a row in the same direction (both to the right) and compare: is that the same as one half turn?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed point, felt in the body — not travelling. A quarter turn lands you on a new facing (about 90° from the start), a half turn faces you the opposite way, a three-quarter turn is three quarter-turns on, and a whole turn returns you to the same facing.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The child's own body turning on a spot, with start and finish facings marked by footprints
A programmable floor robot or a marked floor grid for building and walking routes
Quarter / half / three-quarter turn language tied to fixed landmarks to face
A simple route to follow and then to describe
commonMisconceptions: Confusing a turn (rotation on the spot) with moving forward — 'turning' by walking in a curve or stepping sideways
Under- or over-rotating: a 'quarter turn' that is a random amount because it is not referenced to a target facing
Left/right reversed, especially relative to the direction of travel or a facing partner (frame-dependence)
Treating half or quarter of a turn as unrelated to half or quarter of anything else — no sense of a fractional turn amount
constraints: This is a bodily performance skill: assess and teach by watching the child move and listening to the route, not by asking them to explain the procedure.

The child's own felt rotation about a fixed spot is where the idea lives; a screen or floor-robot game does not reproduce proprioceptive turning feedback and should be a companion to embodied movement, not a substitute.

Sequencing a route or picking the picture after a quarter turn can check the idea but does not itself elicit the physical rotation or route production — recognition-only tasks do not demonstrate the doing.

Left/right is frame-dependent and late-developing; expect residual reversal errors, especially after a change of facing or when facing a partner. Reinforce body-anchored left/right and keep exposure rather than drilling errors as failures.
A static picture cannot be turned, so it cannot by itself practise the rotation; use it only as a prompt alongside movement.
When a turn amount drifts, scaffold with a fixed target to turn TO rather than reteaching the concept — the under-/over-rotation is an execution gap, not necessarily a conceptual one.

activityReferences.title: Extend and rotate: what parallel really means
Anchor and separate the four words
Predict, observe, explain and a sorting check

startingActivity.title: Extend and rotate: what parallel really means
learnerActions: Start with two lines on screen or drawn on paper that look 'wonky' and are different lengths; predict aloud whether they will ever cross if extended, and say why before testing.

Extend both lines all the way to the edges (press an EXTEND button, or continue the lines with a ruler across a large sheet), observe whether they meet, and measure the gap between them at several places to see whether it stays the same.

Drag or draw a second pair that looks nearly parallel but leans enough to converge within the page or screen; extend them and watch them cross. Note that a very tiny lean might only cross beyond the edge, and the narrowing gap still shows the lines are not parallel.
Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal and confirm the relationship is kept when tilted.

Use a right-angle checker (the corner of a card, a set-square, or a detector that glows green) on a perpendicular crossing pair tilted to 45 degrees to confirm a right angle is still a right angle whichever way the corner faces.
Label real photos or scenes — railway tracks, ladder rungs, window frames, the letter H — as parallel or perpendicular, including tilted and unequal examples.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Parallel means staying the same distance apart and never meeting however far extended — not being flat and not being equal in length; and a right angle stays a right angle at any orientation.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Real-world referents: horizon/table (horizontal), wall/lamppost (vertical), railway tracks (parallel), window corner / plus-sign (perpendicular)
The corner of a card or a set-square as a right-angle checker for perpendicular
A ruler slid between two lines, or the lines extended, to test 'always the same distance / never meet'
Letters and shapes marked up — an H has parallel verticals and a perpendicular cross-bar; a rectangle's sides
commonMisconceptions: Confuses 'horizontal' and 'vertical' (which word is which)
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length
Thinks lines only count as parallel/perpendicular when they are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Confuses 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'
constraints: Perpendicular depends on the right-angle concept; learners need to recognise or check a right angle (card corner / set-square) first.

Recognition-only formats (sorting, matching, multiple choice) assess the outcome and do not elicit the independent prediction-and-justification that reveals a learner's underlying rule; use them alongside, not instead of, extend/predict tasks. This is a narrow affordance point, not a claim that sorts cannot support classification.

A static reference scene (tap tracks -> 'parallel'; tap a window corner -> 'perpendicular') is a useful poster but cannot be extended or re-tested, so it cannot run the never-meet check; use it as a reference after the interactive work.
Always include tilted and unequal-length examples; equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs alone reinforce the very misconceptions being targeted.

Interactive controls (extend button, drag/rotate, right-angle detector, photo gallery) are illustrative examples of making the test concrete, not mandatory tools; paper, ruler and card corner serve equally.

At this level these are planar page relations and extending to three dimensions is unnecessary here. A flat on-screen or paper diagram represents ideal lines, which have no thickness; the drawn marks are thin, finite approximations, and the 'extend forever / never meet' test reasons about the idealised lines.

startingActivity.title: Make and use a right-angle checker
learnerActions: Fold a piece of paper (or a paper circle) in half and in half again to make a right-angle tester with a crisp square corner.
Place the checker into real corners around the room and on shapes — a window frame, a book corner, a slice of pizza, an open pair of scissors.
For each corner, decide: does the checker fit flush (a right angle), or is the corner less open / more open than the checker?
Mark each confirmed right angle with a small square symbol.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: A right angle is one reusable unit of comparison; a corner is a right angle only if it fits the checker exactly, regardless of how it is turned or how long its arms are.

commonMisconceptions: A right angle must be 'upright' like a standard L; a rotated or mirrored one is not recognised as a right angle (orientation dependence)
A right angle drawn with long arms is 'bigger' or 'more than' one with short arms (the arm-length misconception carried over)
Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle — labelling corners by rough appearance rather than testing against the checker
Miscounting right angles in a turn — e.g. two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn returns you to the start
constraints: The right-angle concept is planar; turning in space or testing real 3D object corners can add interest but is not required to establish the benchmark idea.

Classification/counting questions (right / less / greater, order by openness, count right angles in a turn) can reliably assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the hands-on testing of fitting a checker or the physical composing of turns — pair any such assessment with hands-on testing and turning.

A static picture that reveals 'right angle / not' when corners are tapped can support recognition and the small-square notation, but does not let a child test corners or compose turns; treat it as a partial scaffold for one facet only.
Deliberately include rotated/mirrored and long-armed right angles in any task so the benchmark is not tied to a standard upright L or to arm length.
When children predict turns, have them state the result relative to a stated starting direction (e.g. 'facing the window') so the count of right angles is unambiguous.
Keep child-facing language to 'less open' / 'more open' than a right angle at this stage; introduce acute/obtuse only as later vocabulary, not within these Year 3 prompts.

activityReferences.title: Turn, then open: building angle as amount of turn
Change the arms, keep the opening: confronting the length rule
Walking the shape: a corner is a turn

Check and discriminate: same opening, different arms

startingActivity.title: Turn, then open: building angle as amount of turn
learnerActions: Physically turn your whole body a quarter turn, then a half turn; then do the same with an arm held out, describing each turn aloud.
Open a book, a pair of scissors, or a fan slowly and watch the angle between the parts grow while the two parts themselves stay exactly the same length.
Hold two hinged strips (geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker) pinned at one point; swing one strip open from a small opening to a large one and describe what is changing.
State in your own words what you actually had to do to 'make the angle bigger' (open the lines further apart / turn more).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An angle is the amount of turn or opening between two lines meeting at a point — something you grow by opening the lines apart, not by making the lines longer.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two hinged arms / geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker — the canonical dynamic model: open and close with arms of fixed length
The opening book, pair of scissors, or fan (opening grows, sides constant)
The child's own body turning (embodied quarter/half turn), then one arm held fixed while the other sweeps
Corners of familiar 2-D shapes with the angle arc marked at the vertex
commonMisconceptions: An angle is bigger when its arms/sides are longer — size judged by line length rather than opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. length-inconsistent trials near 0%)
An angle is 'the distance between the ends of the lines' — a gap between the tips rather than the opening
The whole-object assumption: 'angle' refers to the entire figure, so the amount-of-turn dimension is never separated out (van Hiele holistic processing)
A corner and a turn are unrelated ideas — the child fails to see a shape's corner as a turn, or a turn as producing a corner
constraints: Develop the dynamic turn/opening conception first, then bind it to the static corners children already see in shapes; the Year 3 aim is to recognise angles as a property of shape OR a description of a turn.

The key conceptual target is separating the SIZE of an angle (opening/turn) from the LENGTH of the lines that form it — activities must vary arm length against a fixed opening (and vice versa), not only present angles with equal arms.

A static reveal that merely labels corners as angles is a limited scaffold: it can name corners but does not let a child vary opening against length, which is where the concept forms. Pair any such display with manipulation.

Recognition or sorting tasks CHECK the discrimination but do not by themselves build the felt invariance of opening under changing arm length; use them after hands-on construction, require the learner's reason (not just the choice), and include both equal- and different-opening pairs so no response can be chosen by default.
Treat the whole-object framing ('angle' means the whole figure) as a normal developmental starting point to grow past over time, not a false belief to confront head-on.

A live hinge with a turn readout and a slider that stretches both arms while the arc/counter stay frozen is an optional interaction example that makes the opening-versus-length mechanism concrete; it is one way to realise the idea, not a required technology. Equivalent physical manipulatives (geo-strips, split-pin angle maker, scissors, book, fan) serve the same purpose.

Physical objects (scissors, books, fans, strips) approximate the mathematical idea: their arms are finite and have thickness, whereas a mathematical angle is the opening between two idealised lines; keep returning attention to the opening at the vertex rather than the ends.

startingActivity.title: Order the baited angles, then overlay to check
learnerActions: Receive four angles to drag into order from smallest to largest, where the smallest opening is deliberately drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms.
State out loud, before moving anything, which angle you think is biggest and why.
Overlay any two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned, so only the openings are compared.

Overlay the longest-armed angle on the shortest-armed one and watch the long-armed 'big-looking' angle's opening fall INSIDE the short-armed angle's opening, then compare the other pairs the same way and re-sort all four by opening.
Re-state the rule you now use to decide the order.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An angle's size is its opening, not the length of its arms, the distance between the tips, or the area enclosed. Overlaying vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned isolates the opening, so an angle with longer arms but a narrower opening is seen to be the smaller angle.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker as the dividing benchmark, and an 'openness' scale from nothing to a straight line with the right angle marked in the middle
A hinge / fan sweeping through acute → right → obtuse
Overlay (vertex-on-vertex) comparison for ordering by opening
Acute / right / obtuse angles picked out and colour-sorted within shapes
commonMisconceptions: Ordering angles by arm length or by the distance between the tips rather than by the opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. list side length, enclosed area and distance between the sides as the irrelevant properties children use)
Judging by the space or area enclosed between the arms rather than the opening
Naming by appearance rather than by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or the two names simply swapped
Naming before comparing: applying acute/obtuse labels without checking against the right angle
constraints: Anchor both names to the right angle: compare every angle to a right-angle checker before naming it. Acute = less open than a right angle; obtuse = more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared. Because the overlay compares the openings alone, differences in arm length, enclosed area and tip distance cannot drive the comparison.
Naming should follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition.

A static picture that reveals labels when tapped supports recognition and classification of clear cases, but it cannot carry out the overlay comparison or the dynamic sweep; treat it as a scaffold for classification only, not a replacement for the overlay work.

Classification and ordering practice (classifying angles as acute/right/obtuse, ordering them by size, and finding all of a type in a shape) is useful for assessment and practice, but recognising and ordering angles does not by itself build the overlay intuition for the length trap; pair it with hands-on overlay work.

If learners manipulate physical paper/card angle cutouts, note that cutouts have slight real thickness and can be held and overlaid, whereas the on-screen or ideal figure is a zero-thickness model of the mathematical angle; the comparison is about the represented angle, not the physical card.

activityReferences.title: Mark up a plain figure, then read a 'not to scale' one
Tap-to-reveal the mark key (reading scaffold)
Match and select: check interpretation and light production

startingActivity.title: Mark up a plain figure, then read a 'not to scale' one
learnerActions: Starting from a plain quadrilateral (a four-sided figure gives room to show two independent equal-side pairs without overlap), add a small square to the corner stated to be right-angled.

Add a single pair of tick marks to one pair of sides stated to be equal, and a double pair of ticks to a different, independent pair of equal sides — a four-sided figure is needed so the two pairs do not share a side.
Label a stated angle in three-letter notation by identifying its vertex: point to the vertex B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC, so the middle letter B names the angle ∠ABC.
Switch to reading: on a deliberately not-to-scale marked diagram where one side LOOKS longer but carries the matching tick, state which sides are equal from the marks, not the picture.
State aloud what each mark means as a relationship (e.g. 'these two sides are equal to each other', 'this angle is exactly 90°').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The marks, not the drawing, tell you the truth about a diagram, and the middle letter of three-letter notation is always the vertex.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The mark key: small square = 90°, single/double ticks = equal lengths, single/double arcs = equal angles, arrows = parallel
A triangle or quadrilateral fully marked up and read as a set of statements
∠ABC with B highlighted as the vertex and BA, BC as the arms
A deliberately 'not to scale' diagram whose marks override its look
commonMisconceptions: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at the first (or last) letter rather than the middle letter (the vertex)
Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value rather than 'equal to each other', or treats single and double ticks as equal to one another
Treats the marks as decoration and judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance (assumes it is drawn to scale)
Thinks the small square is just 'a corner' rather than exactly 90°, or misses that unmarked features are unknown
constraints: Cover BOTH directions: reading marked diagrams AND producing marks when drawing. A reading-only reveal tool is a scaffold and does not assess production; pair it with construction tasks.

Recognition and matching tasks check interpretation and light production but do not require constructing a complete marked diagram, so include a production task where the learner draws the square and adds matching ticks in pairs.
Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so learners practise trusting the marks over the picture.

Always add equal marks to every member of an equal group, so at least two sides are marked and never just one (e.g. both sides of an equal pair, or all three sides of an equilateral triangle); a stated right angle must carry a drawn square; unmarked features must be treated as unknown.

Reserve double ticks for a second, independent equal pair, and make clear single- and double-ticked sides are NOT equal to each other. Demonstrating two independent equal-side pairs needs a figure with at least four sides (a quadrilateral), not a triangle.

This notation is a convention of 2-D diagrams; a 3-D environment is not required for this objective. Paper-and-pencil marking is an acceptable medium for the production half alongside any interactive tool.

startingActivity.title: Sweep a ray and count degrees of turn
learnerActions: Grab a ray at the centre of a circle and sweep it round, watching a counter tick up one degree at a time as a thin wedge fills in behind the moving ray.
Notice the rim glow and snap at a quarter turn (90°), half turn (180°), three-quarter turn (270°) and full turn (360°).
Carry out the task 'turn through 45 degrees' and watch 45 little one-degree wedges stack up into half of a right angle.
Make the ray longer and check that the degree count does not change.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A degree is a tiny angle you can count: 90° literally means ninety one-degree turns, and measuring an angle is counting how many one-degree turns it makes — just like measuring length with a tiny unit. Stretching the arms longer leaves the count unchanged.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A circle of rotation partitioned into equal parts, with the one-degree wedge as the unit
The clock and compass: quarter (90°), half (180°), full (360°) turns
Pattern blocks meeting at a point (6 × 60° = 360°) for benchmark degrees
A circular 360° protractor or a rotating ray sweeping the circle
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a degree measures length, arc length, or the number of tick marks rather than an amount of turn
Sees 360 as arbitrary — no sense that it is the count of equal parts of a full turn — so 90°/180° aren't connected to quarter/half turns
Doesn't see a degree as itself a tiny angle that can be counted and added — treats the number as a label read off a tool
Believes the degree count changes if the arms are drawn longer (arm-length trap carried into measurement)
constraints: Build the degree as a fraction of a full turn and as a countable unit angle BEFORE introducing a protractor, or protractor use becomes a meaningless ritual.
Keep the arms as rays: the number of degrees does not depend on how long they are drawn — make this explicit, as arm length is a robust misconception.
Use circular (360°) protractors or a rotating ray before a straight ruler-like scale, so a degree reads as an amount of turn rather than a length.

A static diagram can explain the partitioned circle and label a one-degree wedge, but it cannot let a child iterate or rotate to feel the degree count accumulate; treat it as a support, not the main manipulation.
Matching/selection/fill-in response formats confirm recall and the definition but do not elicit the independent, felt construction of the unit count; use them to check, not to introduce, the idea.

Degree measure is a planar rotation, so a flat (2D) rotating model is sufficient for this objective; a spatial 3D treatment is not needed here (this is a scope statement for this objective, not a universal claim that 3D adds nothing).
A pattern-block or paper angle cutout has physical thickness and is an approximation of the ideal flat angle; treat the represented angle as the mathematical object.

Two angles overlaid vertex-on-vertex with adjustable arm lengths (to divorce size from arm length)
Parallel rails / road lines drawn at different lengths but constant separation
Corner-of-a-card or set-square as an orientation-free right-angle tester
A tilted trapezoid to mark parallel sides and right/acute/obtuse angles off-axis
commonMisconceptions: Angle size depends on arm length or the distance between the arms' endpoints — a wider-drawn angle with longer rays is judged 'bigger' (arm-length / whole-object bias)
'Angle is the distance between the ends of the lines' — treating the gap between endpoints as the measure
Parallel lines must be the same length, so a trapezoid's unequal parallel sides are rejected as not parallel
Right angles and perpendicular lines are only recognised in horizontal-vertical (upright) orientation and missed when the figure is tilted
A ray and a line segment are the same, or a 'line' stops at the drawn endpoints rather than extending
constraints: Teach vocabulary (point, line, line segment, ray, right/acute/obtuse, parallel, perpendicular) through drawing and marking, not memorised definitions.
Present right angles, perpendicular pairs and parallel pairs in tilted and rotated orientations, not only horizontal-vertical, to attack the upright-prototype habit.
A static labelled figure is a useful glossary and reference but cannot show the opening staying fixed as an arm is stretched; use it alongside, not instead of, drawing or live manipulation.

A fixed multiple-choice or sorting check can verify identification but does not by itself elicit independent construction and cannot deliver live 'arm length doesn't change the angle' feedback; use it as a check-up after hands-on work.
Lines, rays and angles are planar; for this drawing-and-marking topic a 3D model offers no distinct affordance over 2D drawing and manipulation, so it is not recommended here.
Score free-hand drawing leniently — judge whether the defining property was applied, not fine accuracy.
Mathematical lines and angle arms are idealised with no thickness; card corners, drawn lines and set-squares are physical approximations used to test the property.

startingActivity.title: Deduce the missing side: perimeter then area, from a not-to-scale rectangle
learnerActions: Work with a rectangle labelled '8 cm' on one side and 'perimeter = 28 cm', drawn deliberately almost square so measuring is useless; one side is a blank box.
Before calculating, mark the equal opposite sides (tick marks) and the four squared (90°) corners so the given 8 cm is seen on its opposite side too.
Reason the perimeter case aloud or in writing: two sides are 8; the four sides total 28; half the perimeter is 14; 14 - 8 = 6, so the missing side is 6 cm.
Switch to an area task: '48 cm², one side 8 cm' — divide 48 ÷ 8 = 6 to find the missing side, and note the inside is filled by a 6-by-8 region.
State the size of the fourth angle (90°) and justify it from the definition, not the picture.
Attach units throughout: cm for sides, cm² for area.
Transfer to a fresh rectangle with different numbers, choosing halve-then-subtract for perimeter and divide for area.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Missing facts about a rectangle are deduced from its properties and the given numbers, not read off the drawing; 'going round' (perimeter: halve, then subtract) and 'filling in' (area: divide) are different inverse operations that must be chosen by what the problem gives.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The rectangle with opposite sides tick-marked equal and all four corners squared (90°), given values labelled and the unknown as a box
P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w overlaid on the shape, with 'undo' arrows for the inverse step
A bar / part-whole model for perimeter showing l+w as half the perimeter
Deliberately not-to-scale rectangles where the marks and numbers override the look
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter, or their formulae/units — e.g. divides by a side when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area (Machaba: taught together, learned instrumentally)
Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter instead of from half of it
Reads unknown lengths or angles off the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing them from the properties and givens
Forgets that opposite sides are equal, so treats all four sides as unknown even after one is given, or doubts that the fourth angle is 90°
constraints: The task is reasoning and calculation with feedback, not measuring: diagrams should be marked as not to scale so lengths and angles come from stated properties and given numbers.
Keep perimeter and area (and their inverse operations and units) explicitly distinct; present both side by side so the child must choose the correct step rather than apply one method by default.
The reference/tap-to-reveal card is a recall scaffold only — it does not require the child to perform a deduction, so it should sit alongside active practice, not replace it.

Fixed-item practice (single-answer construction and multiple-choice) checks recognition and single-answer production and can present diagnostic wrong-answer options, but it does not let the child construct and visually confirm the inverse step; use it to complement constructive practice.
Boundary-trace and interior-tiling animations are optional confirmations of a correct answer, not the mechanism the child must use to reason.

Keep the work planar: length, area and perimeter of a rectangle are two-dimensional; adding a third dimension risks drifting toward surface area and volume, which is a different objective at this stage.
The perimeter inverse is halve-then-subtract (28 → 14 → 14 - 8 = 6); do not subtract the known side from the whole perimeter.

startingActivity.title: From many situations to one skeleton
learnerActions: Gather or look at pictures of angles in many different situations: an open door, clock hands, open scissors, a propped ramp, a bent straw, a bend in a road, and the corner of a shape.
For each one, mark where the two arms are and put a dot on the vertex (the meeting point), drawing an arc at the vertex to show the angle.
Strip each situation down to the SAME bare diagram — two rays meeting at a point with an arc — and lay these stripped diagrams side by side.
Say in your own words what the door, the clock and the scissors all share.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit second arm (the horizontal ground line) so the angle has both arms.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A door, a clock and a pair of scissors are all the same underlying thing — two arms meeting at a point — so an angle is that shared skeleton, not any one particular picture. Some situations (slopes, sightings) have one arm that must be drawn in.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two rays hinged at a vertex, with vertex and arms labelled and an arc marking the angle
A gallery of real situations (door, clock, scissors, ramp, road bend) each reduced to vertex + two arms
The clock face — hands as two rays from the centre — as a canonical everyday angle
A dynamic hinge showing the arms as extendable rays
commonMisconceptions: Holds separate, unconnected angle ideas for different contexts — a 'turn' and a 'corner' are treated as different things, with no single general concept
Judges or defines angle size by arm length or the distance between the arm-ends rather than the opening (persists even for doors and hinges)
Thinks the arms must be a fixed length, or that lengthening a ray changes the angle (arms are unbounded rays)
Only recognises an angle when both arms are drawn in a standard upright orientation — misses angles that are rotated or have an implicit arm (a slope)
constraints: Name the parts explicitly and consistently: the vertex (the meeting point) and the arms/rays, marking the angle with an arc at the vertex.
Stress that the arms are genuine rays that can be extended without changing the angle, to pre-empt the arm-length trap.
Always surface implicit arms: in a slope or a sighting ('how high is the tree'), one ray is the horizontal — draw it in.
Use at least one rotated angle and at least one non-angle (two lines that never meet) so recognition is not limited to the prototypical upright drawing.

Matching or multiple-choice tasks (e.g. identifying the vertex, matching situations to angle diagrams) can check recognition, but a recognition-only response does not by itself elicit the cross-context abstraction or the learner's spoken/written reason; include at least one task where the learner states why.
Paper cut-outs or physical hinges have slight thickness and are approximations; treat them as models of the ideal two-ray figure and keep attention on the vertex and opening rather than the material.

activityReferences.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
Scored estimation and classification practice
Benchmark-angle gallery with everyday referents
Add intermediate anchors to sharpen resolution

startingActivity.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
learnerActions: Look at an angle shown in a random orientation and, BEFORE any measuring, commit an estimate of its size in degrees (set a slider or type a number).
In ordering rounds, drag four angles into order from smallest to largest by eye before anything is measured.
Reveal the true measure and your error; when offered, fade in a faint benchmark 'ghost' (right-angle corner, or 180° straight line) over the angle to see how your estimate compared.
Meet angles whose ray (arm) lengths are varied at random so a wide angle sometimes has short arms — estimate by the opening, not the line length.
Meet reflex angles that swing past the straight line, and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller companion angle.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Any angle can be placed relative to a small set of benchmarks, and reflex angles (between 180° and 360°) are real angles estimated as 360° minus their companion — not the smaller angle on the other side.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Benchmark angles as mental anchors: 45°, 90° (right angle), 180° (straight), 270°, 360°
The right angle as the master reference ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner')
Reflex angle as 360° minus its companion angle (turn imagery)
Clock hands / opening door as dynamic referents for angle size
commonMisconceptions: Judges size by ray length rather than opening, so estimates a wide-but-short angle as smaller than a narrow-but-long one (arm-length carryover).
Has no reflex concept — sees a 270° reflex angle and reads/estimates the smaller 90° companion instead.
Anchors only to 90° and 180°, so estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines with poor resolution in between (e.g. calls everything obtuse '120°').
Treats 'estimate' as 'measure without care' and expects an exact answer rather than a reasoned approximate range.
constraints: Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; a large estimate-vs-measure gap signals that both should be rechecked (protractor placement and which scale was read, and the estimate itself), not that the estimate was worthless.
Reward closeness within a tolerance band, not exactness: an estimate is a reasoned approximate range, not a failed exact answer. An estimate of 120° when the protractor reads 128° is a good estimate.
A semicircular protractor reads only to 180°, so reflex angles must be reasoned as 360° minus the smaller companion angle; do not treat the smaller companion as the answer.

The benchmark gallery is a scaffold that anchors reference images; it may seed estimation but does not build the skill on its own, which requires repeated estimate-then-check trials. It is a useful precursor, not a universal requirement.

Classification and ordering response items check relative and absolute angle sense but, used alone, may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop; combine formats rather than claiming any one medium is required.
Vary ray length independently of opening deliberately: wide-but-short-armed angles are the key trap for the arm-length misconception and should be included on purpose.

45° is part of the target benchmark set; the resolution-sharpening activity only re-deploys it for learners who have anchored to 90°/180° alone, and does not imply 45° is an optional extra for everyone.
