startingActivity.title: Estimate-first measuring across orientations
learnerActions: Before touching the protractor, say aloud whether each angle is acute, right, or obtuse, and give a rough degree estimate against benchmarks (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°).
Place the protractor so the vertex sits exactly on the centre cross AND one ray lies exactly along the 0-line — check both before reading anything.

Read the OTHER ray on the scale that starts at 0 on the ray you lined up, and check that the number matches your acute/obtuse estimate, then state the measure (e.g. report a rotated angle as 47°, not its mirror value 133°).
Repeat with angles drawn in non-standard orientations: a ray pointing up, down, and diagonally — do not rotate the paper to force a ray horizontal.
When rays are drawn too short to reach the scale arc, extend a ray with a ruler first, then measure; confirm the measure is the same before and after extending.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The measure is the amount of opening between the rays, read once the tool is correctly placed; it does not depend on ray length or on any ray being horizontal. The correct scale is the one that starts at 0 on the aligned ray; the acute/obtuse estimate (checked against the 90° benchmark) is a quick check that the right scale was read. For angles very close to 90° both scales read about the same, so careful placement decides the read.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Protractor as a fixed fan of 180 one-degree unit angles laid over the angle (links directly to 'n one-degree angles = n degrees')
Full-circle 360° protractor (fraction-of-a-turn made visible) before the standard two-scale semicircular protractor
Benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) used as an estimation check on the read
The acute-vs-obtuse decision as the rule for choosing the inner vs outer scale
commonMisconceptions: Reads the wrong scale — lands on the mirror value (e.g. 133° instead of 47°) because the child reads whichever number the ray crosses without checking acute/obtuse.
Believes the protractor only works when a ray is horizontal ('standard position') and cannot measure a rotated angle.
Measures the length of the rays or the gap between their ends rather than the rotation between them (arm-length carryover).
Does not extend rays that fall short of the scale arc, then reads a smaller/ambiguous value or gives up.
constraints: Learners must perform the placement themselves (physical protractor and paper, or a draggable/rotatable on-screen tool): reading a value off a pre-placed protractor, choosing inner-vs-outer scale, or identifying a measure in multiple-choice form practises sub-skills but does not assess the placement performance that is the core objective.
A static labelled diagram can name the parts of a protractor but cannot let the child place it, choose a scale, or recompute a reading; use it only as a reference, not as the main practice.
Include non-standard orientations from the start; do not let rotating the paper become a crutch that masks whether the child can align the baseline to any ray.
Include at least one short-ray angle so extending rays (and the ray-length-is-irrelevant idea) is explicitly rehearsed.

Interactive examples (snap/glow feedback when vertex-on-centre and baseline-on-ray are both met, a scale that lights based on the acute/obtuse choice, a draw-mode that re-measures the drawn angle) make the mechanism concrete but are optional implementations, not required.
Accuracy expectation is reading/drawing to within about ±2°.

The semicircular scale only runs to 180°; reflex angles (e.g. 210°) cannot be read directly from it and need separate reasoning (measure the 150° non-reflex angle and subtract from 360°, or use a full-circle protractor).

activityReferences.title: Name the whole, then build and solve the equation
Part-whole bar model linking the symbol to the shared whole
Decompose and recombine a concrete angle
Not-to-scale diagram: reason from marked values, not appearance

startingActivity.title: Name the whole, then build and solve the equation
learnerActions: Look at each diagram and first decide and state the whole before any arithmetic: a straight line split by a ray is a half turn (180°); angles meeting at a point make a whole turn (360°); for a decomposed angle, either the whole is named and you find a missing part, or the parts are marked and you add them to find the whole.
For a straight line with one angle marked 65° and the other marked x, write the equation 65 + x = 180, then solve to get x = 115°.
For angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x, write 120 + 90 + x = 360, then solve to get x = 150°.
For a large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, write 35 + 40 = w with a symbol for the whole, then solve to get w = 75°.
After solving, check the answer back against the fixed whole (do all the parts add to 180° or 360°, or to the stated decomposition whole?).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An unknown angle is determined by the marked angles and the fixed whole, so it can be computed with an equation rather than measured. Choosing the correct whole (180° vs 360° vs a decomposition whole) is the first decision, not an afterthought.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Equation with a symbol for the unknown: 65 + x = 180, 120 + 90 + x = 360
Bar / part-whole model of the fixed whole (180° or 360°) with the unknown as a labelled segment
The straight line (180°) and the full point (360°) as the two 'wholes' to subtract from
Decomposition diagram: a large angle split into marked parts that sum to it
commonMisconceptions: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° at a point or 360° on a straight line because the configuration was not identified first.
Treats angle measure as non-additive — tries to measure the unknown on the diagram instead of computing it from the others.
Reads the diagram as if it were to scale — assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal (e.g. an isosceles-looking triangle), or measures the printed unknown, rather than using the marked values.
Arithmetic slip when subtracting from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 gives 45 instead of 35) — the angle reasoning is sound but the subtraction fails.
constraints: This is a procedural skill: learners must actually set up and solve their own equations across varied diagrams, not just watch a labelled worked example. A reveal-the-answer picture can illustrate a worked example but does not let the learner construct and solve, so it is only a scaffold toward independent solving.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. completing 65 + x = ___, or choosing whether to subtract from 180 or 360) give useful scorable practice and can be used during teaching, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves show independent equation setup; pair them with tasks where the learner writes the whole equation.

Always distinguish a reasoning error (wrong whole, treating measure as non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180 or 360) when giving feedback — they require different remediation.
Insist that the diagram supplies stated facts, not measurements; include at least one deliberately not-to-scale diagram so measuring or assuming look-alike angles are equal is caught.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (adding parts to find the whole, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
Physical angle cut-outs and strips are approximations with real thickness; use them to demonstrate additivity, but the represented angle is the idealised figure.

startingActivity.title: The shared-whole angle bench
learnerActions: Watch a ray that pivots on a straight line, with two angle wedges filling it; each wedge shows its degrees and a banner reads the running total, e.g. '110° + 70° = 180°'.
Drag the pivoting ray and notice that one wedge swells while the other yields, but the total never moves off 180°.
Say aloud the moment you realise you no longer need to measure the second angle: it is whatever is left of 180°.
Switch to a point version where three or four wedges share 360°, and drag to see the total stay locked at 360°.
Open a crossing-lines view: drag the lines and watch the vertically opposite pair stay equal as everything turns.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The whole (180° on a line, 360° at a point) is fixed, so the parts are constrained; a missing part is whatever is left of the whole, and vertically opposite angles are equal because each pair shares the same partner angle to make 180°.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Straight line as a half turn = 180°; full point as a whole turn = 360°
The fixed 'whole' shared out among parts (bar-like partition of 180° or 360°)
Right angle as the 90° quarter unit: two make a straight line, four make a point, three make 270°
Decompose-and-recombine diagram showing angle measure is additive
Vertically opposite pair derived from two straight-line sums
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two totals — uses 360° for angles on a straight line or 180° for angles at a point.
Angle measure treated as non-additive / not conserved — insists on measuring every angle separately and does not believe a missing angle is determined by the others.
Does not recognise a straight line as an angle of 180° (a straight/half-turn angle 'doesn't look like an angle'), so cannot apply the rule.
Thinks vertically opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180°) rather than equal, confusing them with the adjacent straight-line pair.
Assumes the parts must be equal (splits 180° as 90° + 90° by default) regardless of the given angle.
constraints: Ground both totals in turn (straight line = half turn = 180°, point = whole turn = 360°) rather than presenting the numbers as arbitrary facts to memorise.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from two straight-line sums sharing a partner angle, rather than asserting it as a separate memorised fact.

Recognition, sorting, and fill-in items consolidate applying the rules but do not elicit the independent reasoning that predicting a hidden part before revealing it requires; use them as practice, not as the sole check of understanding.
A static diagram can reveal and label the totals but cannot show the sum staying constant as the parts change, so the reasoning move stays told rather than discovered with it alone.
Always include cases where the two parts are unequal, so children do not infer that angles on a line must be 90° each.
Angles at a point and on a line are planar; a three-dimensional setting is not needed and can distract from the fixed-whole idea.

activityReferences.title: Torn corners make a straight line (deriving 180°)
Does the sum change when the triangle changes size?
Build the polygon sums by cutting into triangles

startingActivity.title: Torn corners make a straight line (deriving 180°)
learnerActions: Cut or tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them side by side so their vertices meet at a single point — observe that together they fill a straight line (180°), with no visible gap or overlap apart from small paper imperfections.

Alternatively derive the same result by using the longest side as the base: fold the top corner down so it touches the base at the foot of the height, then fold the other two corners in to meet it at that point — they again fill a straight line along the base.
Repeat either method with a differently-shaped triangle (e.g. a long thin one and a squat one) and confirm the three corners again fill a straight line.
On a drag-and-drop screen model, drag the three corner-wedges onto a straight line so they snap to fill 180°, with a banner reading the running sum.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The three interior angles of ANY triangle rearrange to lie on a straight line, so they sum to 180° — this is something you can see happen (by tearing or by folding the corners), not a number to recall.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Torn-corners demonstration: three triangle corners rearranged onto a straight line = 180°
Polygon partitioned into triangles: quadrilateral = 2 triangles (360°), n-gon = (n−2) triangles
Angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°
Regular polygon: total sum ÷ number of vertices = one interior angle (hexagon 720° ÷ 6 = 120°)
A stretchable triangle whose angle sum stays 180° as its size changes
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° rather than 180° (documented in diagnostic data), so subtracts from the wrong total.

Believes the angle sum (or a missing angle) depends on the triangle's SIZE — expects a bigger/longer triangle to have larger angles; contradicts the constant 180° sum (documented in children and adults).
Assumes a triangle is isosceles or equilateral because it looks that way on a not-to-scale diagram, so wrongly takes two angles as equal.
Knows '180° in a triangle' only as a disconnected fact and cannot extend it to a quadrilateral or polygon (does not partition into triangles).
For a regular polygon, reports the total angle sum as if it were a single interior angle (forgets to divide by the number of vertices).
constraints: '180° in a triangle' must be derived (e.g. torn corners on a straight line, or corners folded to the foot of the height on the longest side) and connected to the other polygon sums by partitioning into triangles — not taught as an isolated fact to memorise.
Scorable multiple-choice/number-entry practice rehearses and catches distractors but cannot by itself stage the size-invariance discovery; pair it with a manipulable or hands-on reshaping task.
Paper/card triangle cutouts have slight thickness and torn edges; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness plane figure. Label any screen model as an idealisation.

A static picture or table can seed the 180° fact and the angle-sum table but cannot let the learner reshape a triangle to experience the sum staying constant; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for manipulation.

'Not drawn to scale' problems require computing from marked angles only; do not infer equal angles from an isosceles-looking figure, and do not measure the drawing with a protractor to get the angles.
Separate genuine reasoning errors (wrong total, size-dependence, isosceles assumption) from mere arithmetic slips when interpreting a wrong answer.
Interior-angle sums here concern plane polygons; a 3D setting is not required and could be confused with solid angles.

startingActivity.title: Crossing-lines reasoner: watch the opposite pair stay equal
learnerActions: Work with two straight lines crossing at a point, with all four angles labelled.

Rotate one line and observe how all four angle values change together: each pair of vertically opposite angles grows and shrinks TOGETHER and stays equal, while each adjacent angle changes so that the two angles on each straight line always sum to 180°.
Set the crossing angle to several values and each time read off the opposite pair, confirming it matches the given angle exactly (not 180° minus it).

Deliberately predict what the angle opposite a 130° angle will be; set the crossing angle to 130° and check the opposite angle reads exactly 130° rather than 50°, then rotate and check the opposite angle keeps matching the changing angle.

Repeat with the whole figure tilted so neither line is horizontal or vertical, confirming the opposite pair is still identified as the two angles opposite each other across the vertex, sharing no arm.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: As an intersection turns, vertically opposite angles stay equal while each adjacent pair stays supplementary — these are two different claims about the same diagram, and 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not pointing up-and-down.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two straight lines crossing at a point, forming two pairs of equal opposite angles and two straight lines of supplementary angles
Hinged two-sticks / dynamic model where opposite angles stay equal as the crossing angle changes
'Given one angle, find the rest' diagram (e.g. 43° marked, three unknowns)
Angles-at-a-point (360°) and angles-on-a-line (180°) diagrams as the two 'wholes'
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line 180° rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180° minus the known angle instead of equal to it.
Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' to conclude all four angles at the intersection are equal, ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
Attaches 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation, so fails to recognise the opposite pair when the lines are tilted, or mislabels which angles are opposite.
Carries over the wrong whole — uses 180° for angles at a point (or 360° on a straight line).
constraints: Learners must JUSTIFY each angle with its named rule, not just state values; a correct number without reasoning does not demonstrate understanding.
Both relationships must appear on the SAME intersecting-lines diagram so children see they are different claims: opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary.
Vary orientation with tilted intersections so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not up-and-down.
Keep the two 'wholes' distinct: 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.
Prefer deriving 'vertically opposite angles are equal' from the straight-line rule over memorising it as a separate fact.
The static tap-to-reveal image is a vocabulary scaffold only: it shows fixed values and cannot display the equality holding as the angle changes.

Fill-in and sorting practice can score reasoning and target the characteristic error, but on their own present non-manipulable diagrams; pair them with a dynamic model so the invariance can be observed.

Vertically opposite angles are always equal; an adjacent angle equals the given one only in the special perpendicular (90°) case, where all four angles become 90° — do not let learners generalise all four angles to be equal otherwise.
OPTIONAL interactive features (draggable lines, live angle readouts, highlighting, tilt) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements.

activityReferences.title: Triangulate to build the angle sum

Regular or irregular: when may you divide by n?
Triangle angle sum: 180°, not 360°
Check and consolidate with mixed questions

startingActivity.title: Triangulate to build the angle sum
learnerActions: Start with a polygon whose number of sides you can change. Before calculating, predict: what do all its interior angles add to?
Split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one corner. Count the triangles: a pentagon gives 3, a hexagon gives 4.
Record the running total as (number of triangles)×180°: pentagon 3×180 = 540°, hexagon 4×180 = 720°.
State the general pattern in your own words: splitting from one corner, a convex n-sided polygon always makes n−2 triangles, so the interior sum is (n−2)×180°.
Add two more sides and confirm the sum GROWS with the number of sides — not with the polygon's size.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The interior-angle sum (n−2)×180° is a consequence of how many triangles the polygon decomposes into, and it depends on the number of sides, not the size.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Polygon partitioned into triangles from one vertex (n sides → n−2 triangles)
Torn-off triangle corners arranged on a straight line (demonstration of 180°)
A marker 'walking the perimeter', turning through 360° in total (exterior angles)
Interior and exterior angle pair at a vertex sitting on a straight line (sum 180°)
A regular polygon with equal angles beside an irregular one with the same sum but unequal angles
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a triangle's angles sum to 360°
Confusing interior and exterior angles
Dividing 360° (or the interior sum) by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assuming all its angles are equal
Believing a bigger polygon has a bigger angle sum (angle scales with size)
Reporting the interior-angle SUM as though it were one interior angle (forgetting to divide by n)
constraints: Division by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. Every regular polygon has equal angles, and regular polygons are the KS3 focus, but some irregular shapes do too: a non-square rectangle has four 90° angles (360÷4). For polygons with unequal angles, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum. Never present ÷n as giving each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal.

Two polygons with the same number of sides have the same interior-angle sum. Whether all the angles are equal (as in any regular polygon) affects only whether each angle equals sum÷n, not the sum itself.
Keep the two totals distinct: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
Tearing off triangle corners onto a straight line DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum; it is not a proof. Pupils should also meet the deductive argument.
The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not on the polygon's size; an enlarged copy of the same shape has the same angles.

When a convex polygon is split from one vertex, an n-sided polygon yields n−2 triangles (not n); diagonals are drawn only from the single chosen vertex, and the two sides meeting at that vertex do not each form a separate triangle base.
The perimeter-walk 'one full turn = 360°' model applies to convex (non-reflex) polygons, the intended KS3 case; the interior-sum (n−2)×180° and subtract-from-sum methods hold for any simple polygon.

Fixed diagrams (tap-to-reveal) can show one triangle split and label interior/exterior at a vertex but cannot let the child vary n or test the regular/irregular boundary; treat them as support, not as inferior in every respect.
Scored/recognition questions assess facts and distinctions but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own triangulation or open interior/exterior reasoning; pair them with construction work.
Polygon angle sums are planar; polyhedron angle defect is a different, later topic and is not needed here.

Optional interactive features (running sum as diagonals are drawn, perimeter-walk accumulator, regular/irregular toggle with ÷n button enabled only in regular mode) are illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tools and not evidence that the rules hold.

activityReferences.title: Morph a rectangle into a square and watch inclusion persist

startingActivity.title: Morph a rectangle into a square and watch inclusion persist
learnerActions: Start with a 'long' rectangle and list which names currently fit it: note that, of the names parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, only 'rectangle' and 'parallelogram' apply (it is also a quadrilateral).
Change the shape by moving its corners/sides until all four sides are equal, keeping the four right angles.
Observe that 'rhombus' and 'square' now apply too — while 'rectangle' never stopped applying.
Say in your own words why the square never stopped being a rectangle: it kept every rectangle property and simply gained the extra property of four equal sides.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A square is a special case of a rectangle (and of a rhombus): it satisfies every defining property of the more general class and adds more, so it belongs to both classes at once.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Dynamic quadrilateral with live name-tags (parallelogram/rectangle/rhombus/square) that light up as properties are met
Quadrilateral hierarchy Venn diagram / family tree
Fold-and-measure derivations of diagonal and symmetry properties
Circle with labelled radius, diameter and circumference and a circumference ÷ diameter ≈ 3.14 readout
Property tables comparing triangles/quadrilaterals for always/sometimes/never reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Partition/prototype classification: denying that a square is a rectangle (or a rhombus) because the shapes 'look different' or a rectangle 'must have two long and two short sides'
One-directional / non-transitive inclusion: accepting square ⊆ rhombus but not square ⊆ parallelogram, or thinking a rectangle cannot share square properties
Judging properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. assuming a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
Confusing radius and diameter, or believing π (circumference ÷ diameter) depends on the size of the circle
Treating each named shape as an isolated category with no overlapping membership
constraints: Build from hierarchical (inclusion) definitions and explicitly contrast them with partition definitions; a partition definition (e.g. 'a rectangle must have two long and two short sides') is the source of the core misconception and should be surfaced and corrected, not used.

Properties should be explored by construction, folding and measurement, then stated as checked for the shapes tested (within measuring accuracy) and, where possible, justified by reasoning from the definitions so they hold in general — avoid letting learners assert properties from appearance alone.

Paper/card cutouts have real thickness and are approximations of ideal zero-thickness plane figures; a flat screen is also a model. Distinguish the represented ideal shape from its physical or pictured representation.
Measurement of real circles yields ratios near 3.14 with small variation from measuring error; the invariance ('always a bit more than 3') is the learning point, not a perfectly identical decimal.

A static hierarchy/Venn reference is a useful support but cannot display a shape morphing while inclusion persists, and a fixed cutout cannot morph; pair either with a dynamic or adjustable model (or a deliberate compare-across-shapes activity) so inclusion is experienced, not only read.
Recognition-only response formats (picking the right option) do not by themselves elicit a learner's own justification; require them to state property-based reasoning in their own words.

When using always/sometimes/never, phrase items in singular form ('a rectangle is a square') so the verdict is well defined; a universally quantified statement is simply true or false, not 'sometimes'.

Optional interactive features — draggable corners, live name-tags that light up as properties are met, a diagonals overlay toggle, a resizable circle with a fixed C÷d readout — make the mechanism concrete when available, but are not mandatory; paper, string and construction tools serve the same objectives.

activityReferences.title: Chaining angle facts across a not-to-scale crossing
Hinged sticks: why opposite is equal and adjacent is supplementary
Introducing the vocabulary on a labelled crossing
Quick checks: spot the supplementary-for-opposite trap and match steps to reasons

startingActivity.title: Chaining angle facts across a not-to-scale crossing
learnerActions: Work from a not-to-scale diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, and a third ray splitting the opposite angle into two parts, one marked 40°.

(a) Find the three unmarked angles at the crossing. For each, write the exact fact you used (e.g. 'vertically opposite angles are equal', 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'). Then check that the four angles at the crossing total 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
(b) Find the remaining part of the split angle, carrying the already-found angle forward as a given.
(c) Two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130°; write an equation and solve it for x.

Before calculating, name which relationship applies: for an angle on a line or at a point, say the WHOLE (a straight line is a half-turn 180°, a point is a whole turn 360°) and take the unknown as the whole minus the known parts; but for a vertically opposite angle the unknown is simply EQUAL to its given partner, NOT whole-minus-parts.
Write each found angle onto the diagram so it becomes a visible given for the next step.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are deduced by combining named facts in a chain, where one result feeds the next; a vertically opposite angle is found by equality while line/point unknowns are found by subtracting from the whole, and the not-to-scale picture cannot be measured, so only the facts license the answer.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Crossing-lines ('hinged sticks') diagram for vertically-opposite versus adjacent angles
The whole as a fixed total shared among parts — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point
Not-to-scale multi-angle diagrams that force deduction over measurement
An equation written from the diagram (known + unknown = whole; or an opposite pair set equal)
commonMisconceptions: Treating vertically opposite angles as supplementary (subtracting from 180 to find the opposite angle)
Over-generalising that all four angles at a crossing are equal
Using the wrong whole — 360° where 180° applies, or vice versa
Measuring or reading the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing from facts
constraints: Diagrams must be presented NOT to scale so pupils cannot reliably measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts, and a reminder that the picture is not to scale is appropriate.
Every step must be justified with a named angle fact (e.g. 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not with F/Z/Z-angle mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises.

Name the WHOLE before calculating line/point unknowns (180° on a line, 360° at a point) and sanity-check against it; but do NOT apply whole-minus-parts to a vertically opposite angle — it is found by equality.
Hold the two crossing relationships apart explicitly: vertically opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary; do not let pupils apply 'subtract from 180' to an opposite pair.
Tap-to-reveal / static diagrams introduce vocabulary only; they cannot set a problem or check a chained deduction and must not be the sole activity for the multi-step skill.

Recognition and multiple-choice items assess isolated facts and the key trap; they do not elicit an independent multi-step chain with a stated reason at each step, which requires the construction task.

Live-recolouring, dragging rays and sliders are optional ways to make the equal/supplementary relationships visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and a physical hinged-stick model achieves the same demonstration.

The additive and equation-based steps rely on correct arithmetic: 180−130=50, 130−40=90, and 2x+10=130 ⇒ 2x=120 ⇒ x=60; check these when authoring items and do not offer wrong partial values as valid alternatives.

activityReferences.title: Translate the angle cluster along the transversal

startingActivity.title: Translate the angle cluster along the transversal
learnerActions: Draw (or use a prepared diagram of) two parallel lines crossed by a transversal, marking the parallels with matching arrows.
Trace the four-angle cluster at the upper crossing onto tracing paper, then slide the tracing straight down along the transversal until it lands on the lower crossing.

Observe that every angle in the slid copy lands on the matching angle at the lower crossing (as closely as tracing allows; in the ideal diagram the fit is exact). State which pairs this shows are equal: corresponding angles directly, and alternate angles by combining this with vertically opposite angles at the same crossing.
Now draw a second diagram where one line is deliberately NOT parallel to the other; trace and slide again, and record where the copy fails to fit and how the readings differ.
Write a one-sentence conclusion: equality of these angle pairs depends on the lines being parallel.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Corresponding angles are equal because one crossing's angle cluster can be translated along the transversal onto the other, which is a transformation, not a shape to recognise. Alternate angles are then equal because each one is vertically opposite a corresponding partner. These equalities break when the lines are not parallel.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Parallel lines + transversal with all eight angles, the two crossings' clusters colour-linked
Tracing-paper / translation-along-the-transversal overlay demonstrating equal angles
Colour-coded equal vs supplementary angle families
Off-set and rotated parallel-line diagrams (non-prototypical)
Angle-chase worked example with a reason justifying each step
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising 'angles on parallel lines are equal', so treating co-interior (supplementary) angles as equal
Confusing alternate and corresponding angles, and failing to identify them in non-standard diagrams
Relying on 'F'/'Z' mnemonics that give the answer without supporting reasoning
Not perceiving off-set lines (little overlap) as parallel, so not applying the angle rules
Applying parallel-line angle rules to lines that are not actually parallel
constraints: Pupils must produce full reasons, not just answers: 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal', not 'F angle'. 'F'/'Z' mnemonics give an answer without supporting the reasoning and should not stand in for a stated relationship.

Keep the equal family (corresponding, alternate) explicitly distinct from the supplementary family (co-interior); a single 'angles on parallel lines are equal' rule is a misconception to correct, not a shortcut to accept.

The angle rules apply only when the lines are genuinely parallel; require pupils to check the parallel marking before applying equalities, and do not apply the rules to unmarked or non-parallel lines.

A static labelled reference diagram (with tap-to-reveal partners and relationships) is a useful lookup aid but cannot animate the translation that justifies equality or let pupils un-parallel the lines; treat it as a scaffold, not the full lesson.

Tracing-paper cutouts have slight thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness lines and angles they represent; use them to demonstrate the translation while noting the idealisation.

Matching and multiple-choice items (e.g. sort pairs into 'equal' vs 'supplementary', find a missing angle, with a co-interior item offering a tempting but wrong '70° (equal)' option and a non-standard diagram) can probe the core over-generalisation and assess identification, but a recognition-only format does not by itself elicit the pupil's own constructed reasoning or the felt translation — pair it with tasks that require a written or spoken reason.
Multi-step angle-chasing depends on secure basic angle facts (straight line 180°, vertically opposite, angles at a point); shore these up first.

activityReferences.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine
Scale conversion as a multiplier, not an addition
Feeling the scale factor by zooming from plan to real room

startingActivity.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine
learnerActions: Construct a triangle from two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 55° between them: rule the first side from the ruler's zero, place the protractor with its centre on the endpoint vertex and zero-line along the side, set the 55° angle, measure and mark the second side, then rule the third side to close the triangle

Before reading the protractor, estimate first: 'Is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle (a square corner)?' Smaller, so choose the scale that gives a value under 90°, not the 125° on the other scale

Because you finish by joining the two free endpoints, an SAS triangle always closes, so closing does not show it is accurate. Instead, measure the third side and the other two angles and compare them with the expected values. For 6 cm, 8 cm and 55°, the third side should be about 6.7 cm and the other angles about 47° and 78°, and all three angles add up to 180°. A clear mismatch signals placement or measurement error: recheck the vertex placement, the zero-line and the scale you chose
Aim for accuracy to about the nearest degree and nearest millimetre
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Accurate construction depends on a disciplined sequence (base → included angle → side → join the endpoints) and on choosing the right scale on a dual-scale protractor by first estimating against a right angle. Joining the endpoints always closes an SAS triangle, so accuracy is checked by comparing the measured third side (about 6.7 cm) and remaining angles (about 47° and 78°) with the expected values, not by whether the triangle closes.

keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule to disambiguate the two scales (to nearest degree)
Base-then-included-angle-then-side SAS construction sequence
Scale statement 'real = drawn × scale factor' with a worked ratio (e.g. 1 cm : 2 m)
Scale plan / map with a stated scale for measuring and converting real lengths
Double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m (to make the multiplier visible)
commonMisconceptions: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference rather than multiplying by the scale factor — the classic additive-strategy error, most common in the ratio/proportion literature
Drops or muddles units in a scale conversion, or treats 'size' loosely (confusing length scale with area scale)
Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, measuring/drawing the supplement of the intended angle
Misplaces the protractor centre or zero-line, so measured angles are consistently a few degrees out
Accepts a nearly-closing constructed triangle as accurate rather than as evidence of accumulated placement/measurement error
constraints: Construction accuracy is a doing skill within the KS3 curriculum: it is built by actually ruling sides, placing a protractor, and measuring. A static diagram or tap-to-reveal picture can serve as a reference for the scale statement and protractor routine but does not itself elicit placement accuracy or the learner performing the multiplicative conversion.

Recognition-only items (choosing among options, naming the right scale) do not elicit independent construction of the triangle or independent assembly and explanation of the scale conversion; use them to consolidate, and assess the full skill through a performance task.
A zoom-from-plan-to-real-room experience is optional enrichment for intuition; the core conversion is numeric and should still be carried out and explained with units.
Keep units explicit throughout a conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area — length scale and area scale differ.

Interactive affordances (ghosted dual-scale numbers, a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, a live converter bar, a scale slider from 1:200 to 1:500, a green tick when the constructed triangle's measured third side and angles are within tolerance) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete. They are helpful options, not required, and the same learning is achievable with a physical ruler, protractor, paper, scale maps, ratio tables and double number lines.

activityReferences.title: Swing the non-included side: SSA's two triangles
Construct from conditions: when do data fix a triangle?

startingActivity.title: Swing the non-included side: SSA's two triangles
learnerActions: Set up a fixed 9 cm base line. At one end, mark a 40° angle, drawing the second arm of that angle as a long ray rising from the corner. Pin a 6 cm 'arm' at the FAR end of the base (so the 40° angle sits OPPOSITE the 6 cm side, not between the two sides).
BEFORE moving anything, predict in writing: how many triangles can you complete, and WHY?

Swing the 6 cm arm (physically, or draw a compass arc of radius 6 cm centred at the far end of the base) and mark every point where the arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle (the ray rising from the angled corner) — each crossing is a possible third vertex.
Count the crossing points and draw each complete triangle you find.

Reconfigure with the40-degree angle between the6cm and9cm sides. Fix both sides on the two rays and join their free endpoints; compare this lockedSAS construction with the freeSSA arc. Rotated or reflected copies are still congruent, not different-sized solutions.
State in your own words why moving the angle from 'opposite' to 'between' changes the number of triangles.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do NOT determine a unique triangle — the free side can swing to meet the other arm of the angle in up to two places. When the angle is INCLUDED between the two sides (SAS), the triangle is locked. 'Included' is the word that matters.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Dynamic triangle constructor / compass-and-ruler construction from given conditions
The 'swinging side' compass arc showing SSA's two intersection points
Side-by-side SAS (angle between) vs SSA (angle opposite) diagrams
Correspondence map △ABC ≅ △DEF with matched tick-marks and angle arcs
A one/none/many outcome table for given measurement sets
commonMisconceptions: Treating SSA as a valid criterion by conflating it with SAS — not checking whether the angle is included between the two sides
Believing AAA (equal angles) proves congruence, confusing congruence with similarity
Assuming any three given measurements determine a unique triangle
Mismatching corresponding parts — ignoring that the letter order in △ABC ≅ △DEF encodes the correspondence
Not realising AAS works (because the third angle is forced) while SSA does not
constraints: A static labelled panel of the cases and correspondence notation is a useful reference and vocabulary anchor, but a fixed image cannot let the learner swing the non-included side and see a second triangle appear; use it alongside, not instead of, construction.

Selected-response/matching items can check which criterion applies, the one/none/many judgement, and correspondence matching, and can use incorrect options that embody SSA-as-SAS and AAA-as-congruent errors — but recognition items do not elicit independent construction or the hands-on swinging experience, so pair them with hands-on construction.
For the SSA swinging-side task, require a stated REASON with the prediction; the reasoning (appealing to the non-included angle / swinging side) is the diagnostic part, not the bare count.
When demonstrating SSA, note that the swing can give zero, one, or two triangles depending on the measurements; the 6 cm/9 cm/40° setup is one specific case (two triangles), not a universal count.
In the swinging-side construction, the free arm meets the OTHER arm of the given angle (the ray from the angled vertex), not the base line itself; describe the crossing on that ray.

Distinguish congruence (same shape AND size) from similarity (same shape, possibly scaled) explicitly; AAA equal angles give similarity, which is a legitimate and useful relation, not merely a 'failed congruence'.
Paper/card strips and compass arcs are approximations of the ideal plane figure (real card has slight thickness); treat the drawn or physical triangle as a representation of the abstract triangle.

An optional interactive constructor can provide hinged rods, an angle setting, an arc/crossing counter and a correspondence readout. Ruler/protractor/compass work also permits constructing and comparing the triangles; no comparative learning-effectiveness claim is established here.

nodes.title: 哪些边长能组成三角形
nodes.description: Decide whether given side and angle conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle, and explain why, predicting with a freehand sketch and testing by construction (ruler and protractor, compasses, or dynamic geometry software): three sides give exactly one triangle when each pair of sides adds to more than the third, and none otherwise — if the two shorter sides add to less than the longest, the construction arcs do not meet, and if they add to exactly the longest (e.g. 3, 4 and 7), the arcs touch only on the base line, so the sides lie flat in a straight line rather than forming a triangle; three angles must add to 180° and then fix only the shape, not the size, so many triangles fit (none if the sum is not 180°); two sides with the included angle, or two angles with the included side, give exactly one triangle; and two sides with an angle that is not between them can give two, one or no triangles
learningGoals: Show that sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm make no triangle (the arcs do not meet) and that 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm make none either (the arcs touch on the base, giving a straight line), while 3 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm make exactly one
Explain that angles of 50°, 60° and 70° fit many triangles of different sizes, while angles of 100°, 50° and 40° fit none because they add to 190°
Sketch freehand, then construct, two different triangles with AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and angle A = 40°, and explain why making the 40° angle the one between the two sides gives only one triangle
nodes.originalAssessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to make a triangle from straws 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm long, could they predict that it can't be done and explain why — and say why 'angles of 50°, 60° and 70°' could describe lots of different-sized triangles?

activityReferences.title: Pour the squares: seeing a²+b²=c²
Circle the hypotenuse first, then choose add or subtract
Distance between two points as a hypotenuse

startingActivity.title: Pour the squares: seeing a²+b²=c²
learnerActions: Drag the two legs of a right-angled triangle and watch a square inflate on each of the three sides.
Watch the two smaller squares dissolve and tile, piece by piece, into the big square on the longest side, filling it exactly.
Read a live readout that updates to show a²+b²=c² as the legs change.
Optionally tap each square to reveal its area and confirm the two smaller areas sum to the largest.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The theorem is a relationship between the areas of the squares on the three sides: the two smaller squares together exactly fill the square on the hypotenuse, so a²+b² IS c² rather than a formula to memorise.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The three squares on the three sides — the two smaller squares' areas summing to the largest (area-dissection proof)
A right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse circled (opposite the right angle) before any numbers are used
Coordinate grid with the horizontal and vertical legs drawn between two points and the connecting segment as the hypotenuse
Side-by-side triangles where one shared length is a leg in one and a hypotenuse in the other
commonMisconceptions: Assumes the unknown side is always the hypotenuse, so always squares and ADDS — even when asked for a shorter side (the most common error; often triggered by triangle orientation)
Muddles a hypotenuse with a leg — judges by the number rather than by which side is opposite the right angle
When finding a shorter side, subtracts the wrong way around (leg² − hypotenuse² instead of hypotenuse² − leg²)
Forgets the final square root, reporting the squared value (e.g. 25 instead of 5)
For coordinate distance, adds the horizontal and vertical differences (3+4=7) or counts diagonal grid squares instead of forming a right triangle and applying the theorem
constraints: Pupils must identify the hypotenuse by position (opposite the right angle) before choosing an operation; do not let the activity accept the longest-looking side on the page or let the add/subtract choice precede this identification.
Vary triangle orientation deliberately, including right angles not at the bottom-left, so pupils do not default to 'the missing side is always c'.
Every calculation must end with a square root and a longest-side reasonableness check (a shorter side cannot exceed the hypotenuse), to catch the un-rooted value and add-when-should-subtract errors.

A static tap-to-reveal card can present the area-square proof and the two-part hypotenuse identity, but it cannot recompute as the triangle changes, so the add-vs-subtract decision stays told rather than practised — treat it as a summary scaffold, not the main task.

A recognition-only quiz (which side is the hypotenuse? add or subtract? fill the blank, plus a coordinate item with a 4+3=7 distractor) can reliably score the method-choice in fixed steps, but does not itself let the pupil see the leg-squares fill the hypotenuse square or construct the right triangle themselves.

A spoken/in-role character can pose problems verbally but does not itself render the area relationship or the coordinate legs the pupil must produce and see; keep the discriminating evidence as a computed length and a correctly identified hypotenuse.
3D space-diagonal work (√(a²+b²+c²)) is a later extension beyond this topic's add-vs-subtract objective; reserve it rather than including it here.

The ratio that refuses to change (similarity before the mnemonic)
Choose the ratio, then solve for a side or an angle

startingActivity.title: Labels that move with the reference angle
learnerActions: Mark the reference angle θ FIRST on a right-angled triangle, then label 'opposite' (across from θ) and 'adjacent' (next to θ, and NOT the hypotenuse) relative to it.
Label the hypotenuse as the side opposite the right angle — the longest side, which stays fixed.
Now mark the OTHER acute angle as θ on the same triangle and relabel: notice opposite and adjacent SWAP places while the hypotenuse stays put.
Repeat on a triangle drawn rotated out of standard orientation, labelling relative to θ rather than to the shape.
If a draggable θ marker is available, drag θ between the two acute vertices and watch the opposite/adjacent labels re-attach and swap live while the hypotenuse label stays fixed.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Opposite and adjacent are not glued to the shape; they depend on which angle you are working from. Only the hypotenuse is fixed by the right angle.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A right triangle with a movable reference-angle marker θ, and opposite/adjacent labels that re-attach as θ moves
The unit circle with the rotating radius, showing sinθ as the y-coordinate and cosθ as the x-coordinate
Nested similar right triangles showing opposite÷hypotenuse constant for a fixed angle (ratio invariance)
SOH-CAH-TOA presented as three side-pairs, each ratio highlighting exactly the two sides it uses
commonMisconceptions: Labels opposite and adjacent relative to the RIGHT angle instead of the reference angle θ, so every ratio is set up wrong
Relies on the SOHCAHTOA mnemonic without understanding, and cannot choose which ratio applies when given a particular pair of sides
Mislabels the sides when the triangle is drawn rotated or in a non-standard orientation
For an unknown side, cannot rearrange the ratio to isolate it (e.g. leaves the unknown in the denominator)
For an unknown angle, forgets to use the inverse function (uses sin instead of sin⁻¹) or reports the ratio value as if it were the angle
constraints: Mark the reference angle θ FIRST; always label opposite/adjacent relative to θ, never relative to the right angle. Only the hypotenuse is fixed (opposite the right angle, longest side).
Introduce ratio-invariance and similarity BEFORE the SOHCAHTOA mnemonic, so the ratio has meaning rather than being spelled.
Start in a standard orientation to keep the unit-circle link visible, then deliberately rotate triangles once the naming convention is secure.
Keep the two problem types explicitly distinct: unknown SIDE → rearrange the ratio; unknown ANGLE → apply the inverse function.
Apply reasonableness checks: a shorter side is never longer than the hypotenuse; an acute angle lies between 0° and 90°.

A tap-to-reveal / static labelled triangle can serve as a summary card (reveal opposite/adjacent relative to θ, reveal the hypotenuse as 'opposite the right angle, longest, unchanged', and name which two sides each ratio uses), but it cannot recompute, so the swap and the invariance remain told rather than shown — use it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the dynamic or constructive work.
Fixed-step/recognition items assess end states and do not require the learner to independently construct the labelled triangle or demonstrate the ratio staying constant.
Prerequisites to reteach when they surface: reliably identifying the hypotenuse (Pythagoras skill) and rearranging formulae (change of subject).

activityReferences.title: Handle, turn and name real solids
The circle-on-the-cylinder discovery
Beyond the prototype: find and vary
Feely-bag and flat-vs-solid sort (rehearsal and check)

startingActivity.title: Handle, turn and name real solids
learnerActions: Pick up, turn and feel each real solid (cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, cuboid, pyramid), saying what you notice.
Match each solid to its everyday twin: ball = sphere, tin/can = cylinder, cereal box = cuboid, party hat = cone, dice = cube.

Compare a solid object with a flat card that has a circle or a square drawn on it: notice the solid has bulk on every side (it is round all over, or has thickness all the way round), while the card pictures a flat shape. Sort them into 'flat shape' and 'solid' piles, putting a coin and a tin with the SOLIDS because they are solid all round (a round coin is a short cylinder). Note the approximation: a real card is not perfectly flat — it has slight thickness — but it stands for an ideal flat 2-D shape.
Describe each solid informally: does it have flat or curved surfaces? does it roll? how many corners?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A 3-D shape is a solid object with bulk on every side; it is distinct from a flat 2-D shape even when it looks round or square. A circle or square drawn on a card is just a picture of a flat shape, while a coin or ball is solid all round. Names should attach to properties, not just to one object.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Real solids to handle, each beside its everyday-object twin
'Can you pick it up?' flat-versus-solid sort (2-D card vs 3-D object)
Feely-bag / guess-by-touch, justifying from properties
Rolls / doesn't-roll and flat / curved surface cues
commonMisconceptions: Calls a solid by its flat 2-D name, or treats a solid object as a flat shape: a ball or coin is a 'circle', a box is a 'square' (the coin-is-2D error).
Recognises only the prototype (a party-hat cone, a dice-sized cube) and hesitates on unusual proportions such as a tall thin cuboid or a wide flat cylinder.
Names by the object rather than the shape ('it's a tin') without generalising to other cylinders.
Can point to or discriminate solids correctly yet know no defining property — perception without analysis.
constraints: Real, handled objects are central for this age: children should hold, turn and feel solids. Screen or 3-D-model rehearsal should sit alongside a basket of real objects, not replace it.
A flat screen or photo cannot convey handling and rotation; when used, keep property cues (rolls, bulk on every side, curved vs flat surface) explicit.

Recognition formats (matching, sorting, choose-the-answer) rehearse and check the solid/flat decision and classification but do not by themselves elicit independent handling and property analysis; use them to supplement hands-on work.
Accept informal language ('ball-shaped', 'tin-shaped') and model the formal name alongside it rather than rejecting the child's words.
A tap-to-reveal labelled scene is useful as a vocabulary reference but is static — it cannot let the child rotate a solid to see hidden faces, where the analysis lives.

Distinguish the solid from its flat face explicitly: a cylinder has circular faces but is not a circle; a round coin is a short cylinder, not a flat circle. Do not rely on 'can you pick it up?' as the definition of a solid — a flat card can also be picked up and has slight thickness; instead ask whether the object is solid with bulk on every side, and ask about the mathematical shape represented on a thin card rather than whether the physical card can be lifted. A pictured or modelled solid still represents a 3-D object even though the picture is flat.

Open in-role, pretend dialogue does not by itself elicit the hands-on handling, turning and rotation this naming task relies on at this age; spoken questioning can still draw out property talk, but it should accompany work with real solids rather than stand in for it.

startingActivity.title: Count by touching and marking every part
learnerActions: Hold a physical 2-D tile to count its sides and corners, or a flat-faced solid such as a cube or cuboid to count its corners and flat faces (curved solids like a sphere, cylinder or cone have curved surfaces rather than a full set of flat faces and corners, so describe those separately).
Count each side, corner or flat face by touching it and placing a sticker or pen mark on each one as it is counted, so none is double-counted or missed.
For a flat-faced solid (cube, cuboid), turn it over and count again from a different starting face to check the total stays the same.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A shape's number of sides/corners/flat faces is found by systematically counting all of them, including the ones round the back, not by guessing from the front view.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Handleable wooden/plastic 2-D shape tiles and 3-D solids (cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone)
Geoboards / pin-boards for making and counting the sides of a 2-D shape
Feely-bag: describe a solid by touch alone (forces attention to faces/edges/corners, not colour)
A 'peel-off' image of a solid whose faces lift away as separate 2-D shapes
commonMisconceptions: Judges a shape by its overall look or size rather than counting its sides/corners (the bigger-drawn shape 'has more').
Counts only the sides/corners/faces that are visible in a picture or facing them, missing the hidden ones.
Uses everyday words loosely — 'corner' and 'side' blur the difference between a solid's face, edge and vertex.
Treats a 3-D solid as if it were the 2-D shape of one of its faces (calls a cube 'a square').
constraints: Keep language informal at this age: 'corners' for vertices is acceptable; the mathematical work is attending to countable parts, not formal terminology.

Physical, handleable shapes that children touch, turn and mark are central; screen models are a complement that may expose hidden structure and peeling faces, not a substitute for handling real solids.

A static labelled image or a scored quiz can teach vocabulary or check counts, but neither elicits the independent counting, handling and discovery of hidden features that this topic targets; use them as support or end-checks, not as the main learning experience.
A feely-bag (describe a solid by touch alone) usefully forces attention to faces/edges/corners rather than colour, and geoboards let children make and count sides of a 2-D shape.
When comparing two shapes, compare one countable property at a time and vary size and orientation so children learn the property is independent of appearance.

Paper and card cutouts have real thickness and can be picked up, so 'can you pick it up?' does not reliably separate flat from solid; use cutouts as approximations for ideal flat faces and ask about the flat shape represented versus the solid it is a face of.
Use a genuinely cube-shaped object when naming something a cube, and a cuboid for a general box.

Confine systematic corner/flat-face counting to polyhedra such as cubes and cuboids; describe curved solids (sphere, cylinder, cone) by their curved surfaces — e.g. a sphere has no flat faces, edges or corners — rather than force-fitting them to a corner/face count.

startingActivity.title: Hold-and-turn sort with real solids and flat cut-outs
learnerActions: Gather a mixed set the child can handle: a ball, a cube-shaped box, a pyramid, a tin, a cone, beside a paper circle, square and triangle. The paper shapes can also be picked up and have a tiny thickness, so treat each as a stand-in for the ideal flat shape it represents.
Pick up and turn each object over in your hand. Ask: is it round or thick in every direction so it takes up space (solid), or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card (flat)?
Sort the set into two hoops or bins labelled 'flat' and 'solid'.
Include a cone and other less familiar or non-prototypical solids, not only balls and boxes.
Go on a 'shape hunt' around the room to find more solids (a tin, a ball, a box) and say why each takes up space in every direction.
Name the twin pairs aloud as you sort: circle/sphere, square/cube, and triangle/pyramid (a pyramid has triangle faces, though its base may be a square).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A flat shape has length and width but (ideally) no thickness, and a paper card stands in for it; a solid takes up space in every direction (length, width and height). 'Round like a circle' is not the same as flat — a ball is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere, not a circle. (For the adult: because a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness, 'can you pick it up?' is not the real test — ask whether the shape takes up space in every direction.)
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Real objects to handle: ball, cube/box, tin, cone beside paper circle, square, triangle
Twin-pair cards: circle–sphere, square–cube, triangle–pyramid
The 'draw it vs hold it' test
Flat/solid sorting hoops or bins
commonMisconceptions: Applies a flat (2-D) name to a solid object — calls a ball 'a circle', a cube 'a square', a cone 'a triangle' (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023; Nurnberger-Haag).
Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups the round ball with the round circle because both 'look round' (van Hiele visual level).
Confuses a drawing of a solid with the solid itself — treats a cube drawn on paper as 'solid' because of its name.
constraints: Handling is central here because it lets the child feel that a ball has depth every way while a cut-out is thin. Screen activities (spin-to-compare, drag-to-sort, tap-to-reveal label cards) are offered alongside handling real objects.

A drag-to-sort flat/solid game can give feedback, but every picture on a flat screen is itself flat — this risks reinforcing appearance-based sorting, so on its own it does not elicit physical handling of real objects.
A sort or multiple-choice check can verify or practise the classification but does not itself elicit physical handling or an explanation; use it as a post-check alongside handling real objects.
Conversation alone does not let a child physically handle a shape or see it take up space; use it to prompt the child to justify a sort rather than as the sole medium.
Everyday mislabelling (ball='circle', box='square') is the main obstacle; always acknowledge the child's accurate observation ('yes, round like a circle') before correcting to the solid name.

A paper cut-out is only an approximation of an ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape: it can be picked up and has a slight thickness. So the reliable discriminator is whether the shape takes up space in every direction, not whether it can be physically held — ask the child about the mathematical shape the thin card represents.

Distinguish the drawn solid from the real one: a cube drawn on a page is flat on that page even though its name is 'cube'; contrast the drawing (whose corners you cannot grasp) with a real cube that takes up space in every direction. When naming an example a cube, use a cube-shaped object, since a generic box need not be a cube.

startingActivity.title: Take a solid apart into its flat faces
learnerActions: Handle a real solid (a tin/cylinder, a cube, a square-based pyramid) and run a finger over its surfaces.
Unfold or 'pop up' a solid made from flat paper/card so its faces lie flat, then touch and count the separated faces.

Name each flattened face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) and rebuild the solid face by face. If a paper cylinder is unrolled, its curved side flattens into a rectangle, but on the cylinder that part is the curved surface, not a flat face.
State the link aloud: 'a cube is made of six squares', 'a cylinder has two circular faces and a curved surface'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A solid's flat faces are 2-D shapes; a solid with only flat faces (such as a cube or pyramid) is built from them, while a cylinder also has a curved surface. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether it is drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Pop-up / unfoldable solids whose faces flatten into 2-D shapes
Paint-stamp or trace-around prints of each face
A cube shown as six squares; a pyramid as triangles plus a square base; a cylinder as two circles plus a curved surface
Face-count charts (faces, edges, vertices)
commonMisconceptions: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'.
Cannot separate face from solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces (van Hiele visual level).
constraints: Use real 3-D solids and named flat faces; ensure the solid itself is correctly named, because a child who calls a cube 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find.
Use a cube-shaped object when naming a cube, and a square-based pyramid when describing triangular faces plus a square base, so the named example matches the shape.

Paper or card cutouts, printed marks, and pop-up nets have slight thickness and approximate ideal zero-thickness mathematical faces; a flattened paper face represents the 2-D shape of the solid's face. Ask children what mathematical shape it represents, not whether the paper can be picked up, and state this approximation within the activity.
A screen model where a face peels off is an idealised representation; label it as a model and pair it with handling real solids so children also feel flat versus curved surfaces.
Matching 2-D shapes to solids checks the outcome only; it does not by itself show the child understands decomposition — combine it with constructing, unfolding, or explaining.

A fixed labelled image where tapping a face reveals its 2-D shape can serve as a reference, but it does not let the child physically separate and count faces; use it as a scaffold, not the main activity.

A sort or recognition/matching task may teach or check classification but does not itself elicit the child's own explanation of how a solid is built from faces; include tasks where the child names, counts, and reassembles.

startingActivity.title: Build a rocket with real solids
learnerActions: Offer a set of real 3-D blocks: cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms, and a sphere.
Ask the child to build a rocket by combining shapes so that it stands up.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Which shape will fit on top before you place it? Where will it go and why does it fit?'
After building, ask the child to point to and name each shape used and say where it sits (e.g. 'a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

Try using the sphere as the base (or balancing the cone on its point) and let the child notice that it rolls or will not support more shapes, then choose a flat-faced solid — a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face — for the base.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A composite is made of named component solids combined on purpose; resting flat faces down keeps a structure stable, and you can plan which shape fits before placing it rather than only recognising the result afterwards.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Real 3-D blocks and construction manipulatives
Target-picture cards of composites (cone-on-cylinder rocket, cube tower, house)
The stack ('on') relationship; flat-faced base vs rolling curved base
Component-labelled composite diagrams
commonMisconceptions: Adds blocks unsystematically and only recognises what it 'looks like' after building — no advance plan (a normal early trajectory level, not a fault).
Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions.
Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so a cone or sphere used as a base makes the structure topple.
constraints: The core objective is composing with anticipation and describing a build by its component solids and their positions — this is a procedural curriculum goal that requires actual construction, with physical block-building as the core medium, not only recognising a finished shape.
Treat unsystematic stacking and post-hoc recognition as an expected early developmental level, not an error to drill or mark wrong; advance with one-step-ahead challenges.
Matching tasks and tap-to-name reference images support/check part-naming vocabulary (recognition) but do not themselves elicit independent construction, balancing, or advance planning.
Flat 2-D drag-and-combine can name parts but cannot convey which faces sit flat or how a tower balances; use it only as a naming scaffold.

Balance depends partly on resting flat faces down: a sphere (no flat face) rolls; a cone stands steadily base-down, but it topples if balanced on its point, rolls if laid on its side, and cannot hold a block on its apex; a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face is stable on its own, although a tower can still topple if pieces are placed off-centre or it gets too tall and narrow. Use this to explain why a flat-faced base is a good choice, not as a claim about any specific product.
A fixed labelled picture can still teach part-naming as a reference, but cannot be manipulated to practise stacking or anticipation.

startingActivity.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule
learnerActions: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes and 3-D solids plus everyday objects
Two sorting hoops / Carroll or Venn two-set frame labelled with an 'is / is not' criterion
Wipe-clean pen for marking faces/edges/vertices while counting
'Guess my rule' pre-sorted sets
commonMisconceptions: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or overall look — rather than a geometric property.
Groups shapes by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') and cannot state a single consistent rule, letting the rule drift mid-sort.
Miscounts sides, faces or vertices — losing track of where counting started — so shapes end up in the wrong group.
Can sort one way but cannot re-sort the same collection by a different property, or cannot infer the rule of a set sorted by someone else.
constraints: The skill is doing: placing shapes, testing a criterion, and re-sorting. A view-only tap-to-reveal illustration does not let the child perform or switch a sort, so it does not build the procedure on its own.

A fixed, scored categorization (sort by a GIVEN rule) can check sorting against a supplied criterion, but because the rule is provided it does not require the child to choose, articulate or switch the criterion; use it to check rather than to build the flexible re-sort.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Require a SECOND, different sort of the same collection plus a 'guess my rule' inference — these are what best separate property-based sorting from grouping by overall look.

Paper or card cut-outs and real solids have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat them as physical representations of the mathematical shapes, and ask children about the shape REPRESENTED, not whether the object can be picked up. A rotatable on-screen solid is a model that may supplement, not replace, handling where handling is available.

When naming a specific solid in an example, make sure it fits the property claimed (e.g. use a triangular prism/pyramid when illustrating 'has a triangular face', and only call a solid a cube when it is cube-shaped); do not assume a generic box is a cube.

An optional on-screen drag-into-two-loops sorter with a swappable rule tile and immediate feedback (a shape springing back with a red outline when it breaks the rule) can make the mechanism concrete; this is one possible interaction, not a required one, and its benefit over physical sorting is untested.

startingActivity.title: Fold real nets by hand: valid vs look-alike
learnerActions: Cut out and fold a real cube net from paper or card and check it closes with no gaps or overlaps
Fold a look-alike net that has the same six squares but in which two faces overlap or leave a gap, and observe that it refuses to close
Before folding each net, choose a base face and say aloud which face you think will land opposite it, then fold to check
Build a cube-shaped solid and a triangular prism from interlocking construction pieces (e.g. polydron), joining flat faces until the solid closes
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Having six squares is not enough — the arrangement must actually fold into a closed solid. Folding real nets makes the fold relationships concrete before pupils are asked to imagine them.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Foldable nets (cube, cuboid, triangular prism, square-based pyramid), physical and animated
Isometric drawings of the same solid in different orientations
Valid vs invalid look-alike nets (six squares that do / don't close)
'Choose a base, fold the rest up' anticipation sequence with the opposite-face highlighted
Interlocking construction pieces (e.g. polydron) for building from 2-D faces
commonMisconceptions: Judging the shape by the overall 'look' of the 2-D drawing rather than reasoning from faces/properties
Assuming any arrangement of six squares folds into a cube, without checking it closes without overlaps or gaps
Not anticipating which faces will meet or become opposite — no mental folding, just face-counting
Failing to recognise a solid drawn in a non-standard orientation (prototype/orientation bias)
Treating a flat net as a 2-D shape (its silhouette) rather than a foldable surface of a solid
constraints: Begin hands-on with real cut-and-fold nets and interlocking pieces so fold relationships are concrete before any mental folding is required

A static reference chart (tap a net to reveal its solid and highlight opposite faces) can support recall but does not let a pupil fold a net and watch it close or fail; treat it as a reference, not the main skill-building task

Matching/categorisation items (pick-the-valid-net, name-the-isometric-shape) can check recognition and are useful with look-alike distractors, but recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent mental folding and justification the objective targets; pair them with construction/prediction and a stated reason

Paper and card nets have a real slight thickness and are close approximations of the ideal zero-thickness mathematical surface; a screen folding model is likewise an idealised model — reason about the mathematical solid represented, distinguishing it from the flat picture or physical card

Interactive folding and wrap-onto-solid views are optional ways to make closure and face-adjacency observable; they are examples of the mechanism, not required tools, and should not replace hands-on folding
Include non-standard orientations and valid vs invalid six-square pairs deliberately, since prototype/orientation bias and 'any six squares' assumptions persist without targeted teaching
