startingActivity.title: Construct and fold the net of a triangular prism
learnerActions: Using card, a ruler and scissors, draw the net of a triangular prism: two congruent triangles and three rectangles of equal length, each rectangle as wide as the triangle side it joins.
Before cutting, predict and say which shape will be the bottom (base) and which two shapes will cap the ends.
Cut out the net, fold along the edges and tape it shut.
Point to the finished solid and count its faces, edges and vertices (target: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A valid net is more than the right set of faces — the faces must be arranged so they fold into a closed solid, and the structure of that solid (faces, edges, vertices) can be read off the built 3-D shape rather than the flat drawing.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Card or Polydron nets folded into solids
A tabbed net template that folds and tapes shut
The triangular-prism net: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles forming a band
Base-face-plus-composite layout (band of rectangles, then the two ends)
commonMisconceptions: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid.
Chooses the wrong face-set (e.g. all rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles for a prism).
Arranges the correct faces so the net cannot close; blames ragged cutting rather than the layout.
constraints: A static exploded or net diagram (even one tagged face-to-face, or where tapping a net face shows where it lands on the solid) is a useful planning reference but does not enact the fold-and-check procedure; use it to support planning, not as the build itself.
Matching or sequencing tasks that pair solids to nets and counts check recognition of nets and counts but do not elicit independent construction of a net; use them as a post-check.
Discussion can prompt a prediction for the child to justify, but talking does not itself elicit the physical construction and folding that is the target skill.
When cutting, folding or taping leaves ragged gaps, the fold-check becomes inconclusive — provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning rather than scissor control.
A flat 2-D interactive represents the 3-D fold and may under-sell it; confirm face/edge/vertex counts on a rotatable or physical solid.
Include assembly tabs so the model closes cleanly.

startingActivity.title: Predict, then slice: a cylinder gives more than a circle
learnerActions: Hold a play-doh or carrot cylinder and a plastic knife.
BEFORE cutting, predict AND justify the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle; write or say the reason.

Cut and compare the fresh cut face to your prediction (for a true cylinder a rectangle appears, not a circle; a real carrot that tapers gives a near-trapezium, an approximation to the ideal rectangle).
Make a second cut parallel to the circular ends and check that this one does give a circle.
State in your own words why the two cuts give different shapes.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so one solid yields many cross-sections depending on how it is sliced; a cylinder is only 'a circle' when sliced parallel to its base.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Sliced play-doh or food solids showing the fresh cut face
The cylinder's three cuts: circle (parallel), rectangle (perpendicular), ellipse (oblique)
A prism shown as its cross-section swept through a height
A face/edge/vertex tally taken from the solid in the round
commonMisconceptions: A solid has one fixed cross-section — a cylinder is 'always a circle' whatever the slice.
Confuses the cross-section with a pre-existing outer face, reporting a surface the solid already had.
Assumes a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D, so a slanted cut of a cylinder is judged a circle rather than an ellipse (over-applying 'the slice looks like the base').
Counts only the faces and edges visible in a 2-D drawing, missing hidden ones.
constraints: Hands-on cutting is the core method; the 3-D model, 2-D slider and labelled reference image are scaffolds or summaries, useful for illustration but not a replacement for predicting and cutting real solids.

A static or interactive picture can illustrate the three cuts but does not let the learner vary the slice themselves; a quiz that matches cuts to orientations or counts elements of pictured solids checks recognition only and does not itself elicit the independent prediction-and-justification that reveals the misconception.
Scaffold straight (orthogonal) cuts before slanted (oblique) ones; oblique cuts are harder and should not be the entry point.
Always require counting from the solid handled in the round (or a model that can be rotated), not from a single 2-D drawing, so hidden elements are included.

Paper or card cutouts and play-doh slices have real thickness; treat them as approximations to the ideal zero-thickness cross-section, and label any on-screen cut face as a model of that idealised surface. Ask about the mathematical surface represented, not whether the physical slice can be held.
Insist the cross-section is named as a NEW surface where the plane meets the solid, distinct from any pre-existing outer face.

startingActivity.title: Line up the ends, then compare (ribbons)
learnerActions: Look at two ribbons lying staggered on the table, with the SHORTER ribbon shifted so its right end pokes out past the longer ribbon's right end and the near ends left unaligned
Say which ribbon is longer and explain how you know
Either slide both ribbons to a common starting line, or (in a non-draggable image) draw a line to mark the common start, then compare the far ends again
Meet a 'mixed-up' puppet (e.g. Mr MixUp) who compares WITHOUT lining up the starting ends; catch and fix the puppet's mistake
Answer: 'Where does each ribbon START? Put your finger on the beginning of each one.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: To compare fairly, line up one end of each object at a common start; then the far ends show which is longer. Looking at the far ends tells you nothing reliable while the starting ends are not matched. The object that 'sticks out' at one end is not automatically the longer one.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two ribbons/pencils lined up against a common starting line, far ends compared
A 'mixed-up' puppet placing objects unaligned for the child to fix
Two towers, one raised on a book, prompting attention to a common base
Equal-length strips, one rotated vertical or bent into a curve, to confront non-conservation
commonMisconceptions: Judging by one endpoint — picks the object that 'sticks out farthest' at one end without aligning the starting ends
Ignoring the baseline for height — calls the tower whose top is higher 'taller' even though it stands on a book and has fewer blocks
Non-conservation — believes an object becomes longer when turned vertical, or that a ribbon becomes shorter when curved because its endpoints move closer
Using undifferentiated 'bigger' instead of the specific comparative word (longer/taller), signalling the length attribute is not yet differentiated
constraints: Pre-aligned comparisons (back-to-back, side-by-side at a common start) can be passed WITHOUT understanding, because the alignment is done for the child; include staggered pairs and a raised tower so the child must perform the alignment/baseline judgement.

A static picture or tap-to-reveal image can show aligned vs unaligned pairs and reveal the correct answer, but the child does not physically slide objects into alignment — the core action is demonstrated rather than done. Treat such images as a scaffold toward hands-on or draggable aligning.

A recognition-only selection task ('which is longer?') scores the alignment judgement but does not let the child perform the physical align action with live feedback — recognition alone does not elicit the aligning action; a draw-a-line-to-align step adds a construction element, though still short of free manipulation.
Non-conservation is developmental: do not mark it wrong or drill it. Provide repeated predict-then-check demonstrations and let conservation emerge with experience.
Keep this stage on fair DIRECT comparison with aligned ends; indirect-comparison bridges (e.g. using a string as a go-between) belong to a later stage.
Build precise comparative language (longer/shorter, taller/shorter) rather than the global 'bigger'.

Real objects have thickness and sit on surfaces; the alignment idea is about the endpoints/base. When using an on-screen model, treat it as a representation of the physical lining-up action, not a replacement for it where hands-on tools are expected.
Double/half language appears in the curriculum statement but is beyond simple direct comparison; introduce only when ready and do not conflate it with longer/shorter judgements.

startingActivity.title: Heft then balance: feel it, then confirm
learnerActions: Hold one object in each hand (heft) and say which feels heavier — try this with eyes shut so appearance can't guide the choice.

Pair a small heavy object (a metal weight or pebble) with a big light object (an empty plastic box or inflated balloon), checked beforehand on the balance so the small item really is heavier (a small pebble can be lighter than a large box). Predict which is heavier before touching.
Place both on a two-pan balance and watch which pan goes down; say 'the ____ is heavier than the ____' in a full sentence.
Repeat with several deliberately misleading pairs (e.g. big cushion vs small tin of beans), checked beforehand so the small item really is heavier, so that size is repeatedly the wrong guide.
Press gently on one pan with a hand to feel that pushing down harder on one side makes that pan go down, just as a heavier object does.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Weight is felt and measured, not seen — a small object can be heavier than a big one, and the balance settles cases your eyes cannot.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The two-pan balance (canonical model of comparison)
Hands as scales (hefting)
Deliberately mismatched pairs (small-heavy vs big-light)
commonMisconceptions: Bigger = heavier — judges mass by size or appearance
The taller/longer/fuller object is heavier (conflates mass with another attribute)
Misreads the balance — thinks the RAISED pan is the heavier side
Expects to order objects by weight just by looking
constraints: The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real objects in real hands: hefting a small heavy object and feeling it press down is the embodied experience intended to challenge 'bigger = heavier'. Screen and picture activities can point toward this but cannot supply the felt sense of weight (no haptics).

Deliberately include at least one small-heavy vs big-light pair, and ensure the chosen materials really do make the small item heavier — this mismatch is what makes size an unreliable guide; without it the activity can be solved by appearance alone.
Virtual-balance and balance-picture tasks are scaffolds for balance-reading and prediction; they do not assess or supply the felt sense of heft, so pair them with hands-on comparison.
Recognition-only picture tasks (choosing/matching) check interpretation but do not elicit the child's own physical comparison; do not rely on them as the only evidence of understanding.

startingActivity.title: Tile the length with identical cubes
learnerActions: Place a pencil or book in front of you and a tub of same-size cubes beside it.
Lay cube after cube along the pencil, end to end, from one end of the pencil.
Nudge the cubes so each one touches the next with no gaps and no overlaps.
Count the cubes and say the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes'.

startingActivity.intendedInsight: A length-count only means the length when identical units cover the object completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

keyRepresentations: Interlocking / unit cubes laid end to end along an object
Paper-clip chains as a non-standard unit
A child-made paper ruler with a single unit marked off repeatedly
Centimetre ruler

commonMisconceptions: Leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, treating measuring as 'placing things along' rather than covering the length.
Uses mixed-size units yet counts them as one total.
Counts the number of discrete objects (cardinality) rather than the length covered — e.g. a row of 6 short matches is called 'longer' than an equal row of 5 longer matches.
Begins counting the ruler at the numeral '1' instead of the zero/start.
constraints: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record before any ruler is introduced.

Recognition/selection items (spot-the-gap, how-many sliders) check understanding but do not by themselves build the hand-action of iterating and fixing a gappy row; use them as post-practice checks, not the main activity.

A static tap-to-reveal of a cube-row or ruler ('each cube = one length-unit', '0 starts here') can clarify the meaning of the marks as a reference, but a fixed image cannot be re-tiled by the child; pair it with hands-on or interactive iteration.

startingActivity.title: Balance it with identical units
learnerActions: Place a book (or other object) on one pan of a balance.

Add identical unit-weights (e.g. interlocking cubes) one at a time to the other pan until the beam levels, or is as near level as you can get; if one more cube tips it the other way, the object is between two counts.

Wait for the beam to settle before reading, then count the cubes and record the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes', or 'about 8 cubes' / 'between 8 and 9 cubes' if it never quite levels.
Before you start adding cubes, check every cube is the same size; set aside any odd-sized ones.
Before adding any cubes, estimate how many you expect; after measuring, compare your estimate with the measured count.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Mass can be quantified as a number of identical units that balance the object; the record is a number plus a unit, not just a number.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Balance with identical unit-weights on one pan
Dial / kitchen scale with graduations
The number-line-like scale of graduations
The record: '5 cubes' or '200 g'
commonMisconceptions: Uses non-identical units yet counts 'more units = heavier' (unit-size ignorance)
Reads a scale by counting marks rather than valuing intervals; misreads a pointer between graduations
Thinks the count itself is the mass regardless of which unit was used
Reads before the balance settles / uses a mix of unit sizes
constraints: Units must be identical when counting; mixing unit sizes breaks the count and must be caught before reading.
Wait for the balance beam to settle before reading — a tipping beam is not yet balanced.
Reading a scale means valuing the interval first, then counting intervals (spaces) to the pointer; read to the nearest graduation when the pointer is between marks.
Comparisons and ordering are only valid when the same unit is used throughout.

A short selected-response check (read-the-dial, fill in 'the book = ___ cubes', spot the 'more cubes must be heavier' error, order objects by reading) can check whether the ideas have landed, but it does not by itself provide the hands-on balancing and unit-swap experience; use it alongside, not instead of, actual measuring.

A static labelled dial with a reveal of 'each mark = 100 g' can support interval-reading practice, but it cannot show the live balancing or the count changing when the unit is swapped; reserve the dynamic unit-swap for a setting where the same object can be re-measured.
Estimate before measuring so the measured count can be compared against a prediction.
Standard-unit (g/kg) and symbol-comparison work reflects Year 2 expectations above the stated 5–6 age band; treat it as an extension built on the non-standard balancing foundation.

startingActivity.title: Measure, then place the symbol
learnerActions: Measure two objects in the same unit and write each measurement with its unit (e.g. a pencil case at 32 cm and a book at 45 cm).
Place >, <, or = between the two readings so the statement is true, then read it aloud ('45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres').
Check the symbol points its open side toward the larger amount.

Repeat with a mixed-unit pair, such as a 1 m ribbon and a 50 cm ribbon: before deciding, bring both to the same unit or line them up on one common ruler/scale, then record the true comparison (1 m > 50 cm).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number together with its unit; you must compare the actual amounts, not the bare digits. When units differ, convert to a shared unit first: 1 m equals 100 cm, which is more than 50 cm, so 1 m > 50 cm even though 1 is a smaller number than 50.

activityReferences.title: Carrying a length across a gap with a string
Building and extending a seriation staircase
Naming the transitive chain (check and consolidate)

startingActivity.title: Carrying a length across a gap with a string
learnerActions: Face two objects (e.g. two cube-towers, or a tall object by the door and a shelf across the room) that are clearly too far apart to bring together and line up.

Hold a fixed length of string against the first object, aligned at the same starting end, and note whether that object is taller or shorter than the string; keep the string's length unchanged for both comparisons (do not change it between the two objects).
Keeping the string uncut and unstretched, carry it across to the second object and see whether it overshoots the top or falls short.

Compare each object to the same string and state the conclusion, voicing the transitive chain — e.g. 'this one is taller than the string; that one is shorter than the string; so this one is taller than that one.'
Try a second far-apart pair to transfer the idea.

Optional screen version: drag a fixed length of string to one tower, then carry it to the other and watch whether it overshoots or falls short, so the transitive step is something the child performs rather than is told.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A string kept at one fixed length can be carried to a place where two objects cannot meet, letting you decide which is longer by comparing each to the same intermediary.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A set of three-plus ribbons or cube-towers arranged as an increasing 'staircase'
A length of string or paper strip used as an intermediary copy of a length
The seriation staircase image (each step the smallest increase in length)
commonMisconceptions: Compares only pairs and never chains the inference — insists on placing A directly against C instead of reasoning through the intermediary.
Orders by trial-and-error with no image of an increasing series, and cannot say where a new object should be inserted.
Does not keep the intermediary constant — stretches, re-cuts, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons.
Non-conservation: believes the string's length changed when it was bent or moved.
constraints: The learning objective is enactive: children must actually order objects and carry a constant intermediary, not only recognise or restate the rule. Recognition-only formats (choosing the taller from a worded prompt, tapping to reveal a chain) check or consolidate but do not elicit independent construction of the comparison.

A static staircase display can summarise and name the 'A>B>C so A>C' chain but does not let the child perform the ordering or the string comparison that carries the concept; use it as a reference, not the main activity.

The intermediary must be kept the SAME length throughout both comparisons — uncut, unstretched, aligned at the same starting end — or the comparison is invalid; this requirement is itself part of building conservation of length. Either approach is acceptable: a single fixed independent string compared to both objects, or a string set to one object's length then carried unchanged to the other; what is invalid is changing the string's length between the two comparisons.

Length comparison here is one-dimensional, so a flat staircase and a string are sufficient; a 3D spatial environment is not required for this objective (a scope note, not a claim that 3D can never aid any measurement learning).
Non-conservation of the intermediary and trial-and-error seriation are developmental stages, not errors to drill away; provide more experience rather than hard correction.

startingActivity.title: Measure a book with paper clips, filling the whole span
learnerActions: Lay identical paper clips along a book, starting flush at one end, so they continue end to end to the far end with no gaps and no overlaps
Run a finger along the book from the very start to the very end to check that the clips cover ALL of it

Report the length as the number of clips that span the book; if the last clip sticks out past the end or a small bit is left that is shorter than a clip, say 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips

startingActivity.intendedInsight: A length is the number of equal units that completely fill an object from end to end; gaps, overlaps, or a row that starts inset mean the count does not yet report the true length.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A book with same-size paper clips laid end to end along it, flush at the start, no gaps
A mixed-up puppet's row with visible gaps/overlaps for the child to correct
Two rows of equal total length — few long units vs many short units — to break 'more units = longer' (the matches task)
A home-made unit ruler built by iterating copies of a single unit
commonMisconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlaps between units but still counting them and reporting a length
Using different-sized units and treating the counts as comparable — concluding the object with MORE units is longer regardless of unit size
Not spanning the whole object — starting the first unit inset from the edge, or stopping before the far end, then counting
Counting the marks/junctions or endpoints rather than the units themselves, producing an off-by-one length
constraints: This skill is for roughly ages 6–7 (KS1 / first grade); the goal is non-standard units laid end to end, bridging toward rulers later, not yet fluent ruler reading.

The central evidence is the child actually laying units and counting; recognition-only tasks (choosing the correct row) confirm judgement but do not elicit the independent construction and adjustment of a tiled measurement, so they are a check, not a substitute.

A labelled static picture can show why a gappy or mixed row is wrong on tap, but it cannot let the child lay and adjust units; the corrective action stays demonstrated rather than practised, so use it only as a supporting scaffold.

An interactive drag-to-tile tool that flags gaps/overlaps and withholds a settled count is one effective way to make the consequence of a gap immediate; the same learning is achievable with real clips and a finger-sweep check. These are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not a required medium.
Measuring units along an object is a planar task; a 3D handling environment is not needed and adds handling cost without sharpening the gaps/overlaps/equal-unit ideas.
Keep real materials (paper clips, matches, ribbon, books) and physical or screen tiling as approximations of the same idea; neither is universally necessary.

When comparing lengths by their counts, hold the unit size fixed: a bigger count with the same-size unit means longer, but a bigger count made of smaller units on the same span does not. The counts as numbers can still be compared (8 is more than 4); they just do not show which length is longer unless the units are the same size.

activityReferences.title: How much taller? Measure, align, and find the overhang
Same unit first: the mixed-unit trap
Check questions: comparison word problems and 'by how much?'

startingActivity.title: How much taller? Measure, align, and find the overhang
learnerActions: Place two objects of clearly different height/length (e.g. a desk and a bookshelf) so both stand on the SAME baseline, with a ruler, metre stick or tape measured from zero at that baseline.
Measure both in the same unit (e.g. desk 118 cm, shelf 125 cm) and write each measurement with its unit.
Identify the strip of the longer object that sticks up above the top of the shorter one — this overhang is the answer to 'how much taller?'
Find the difference by subtracting the smaller measurement from the larger (125 − 118) and state the answer with its unit: 'the bookshelf is 7 cm taller.'

In a word-problem round, both measures are given (for example, stated in the problem's words in the same unit rather than read from the ruler), and the DIFFERENCE is the unknown: draw a comparison bar/tape diagram with two bars from a common baseline, mark the difference as the missing part, then write an equation with a symbol for the unknown difference (e.g. 32 + ? = 45, or 45 − 32 = ?) and solve it.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The difference is a real, measurable piece of length — the overhang between two lengths aligned at a common baseline — not just the fact that one object 'wins'. The answer must be an amount with a unit.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two bars aligned at a common baseline with the overhang marked as the difference
A number line showing both lengths from 0 and the gap between their endpoints
A tape/bar 'comparison' diagram with the difference as the missing part
An equation with a symbol for the unknown difference (32 + ? = 45)
commonMisconceptions: Gives only the comparison ('the shelf is taller') without quantifying by how much.
Subtracts the wrong way or mis-subtracts, or compares by lining objects up with mismatched endpoints.
Compares the bare numbers when the two measures are in different units (shelf in m, desk in cm).
Treats the difference as the sum, or adds when the problem asks how much longer.
constraints: The answer must state an AMOUNT with its unit ('7 cm taller'), not just a direction ('the shelf is taller').
Both measures must be in the same unit before subtracting; subtract the smaller from the larger so the difference is positive.

To read a difference directly as a visible gap, the objects must be aligned at a common baseline/zero, because mismatched starting points produce a wrong gap. When each object is measured separately from the ruler's zero, the two measurements can be subtracted without physically lining the objects up.
A static bar-model diagram can illustrate the overhang idea but does not let the learner measure and compute across new cases; use it as a reference scaffold alongside hands-on measuring.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which is longer, or multiple choice) can check understanding but do not by themselves elicit independent measuring, subtracting and expressing — include at least one task where the learner constructs the measurement and difference.

Interactive examples (dragging objects to a shared baseline, live-shaded overhang that updates as lengths change, auto-labelled difference) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.

activityReferences.title: Estimate–measure–revise with a benchmark referent
Interactive estimate-then-reveal loop (optional digital scaffold)
Benchmark reference cards (supporting scaffold)

startingActivity.title: Estimate–measure–revise with a benchmark referent
learnerActions: Before measuring, commit an estimate for a given object in an appropriate unit and say how you worked it out (e.g. 'my fingernail is about 1 cm, so this book is around 20 cm').

Anchor the estimate to a personal benchmark — fingernail ≈ 1 cm, US quarter ≈ 1 inch across, hand-span, 12-inch ruler = 1 foot, metre stick = 1 m (check your own stride against it; a child's stride is usually shorter than 1 m), doorway ≈ 2 m tall — and mentally iterate that unit along the object.
Measure the object and compare to your estimate: were you over or under, and by how much?
Record each estimate, the measured length and the difference on an estimate–measure–difference strip, so the gap is visible and comparable across objects.
State what you would change for the next estimate, then try the next object and check whether your estimates get closer.
Work across different scales (book → desk → whiteboard → playground) and switch benchmark and unit to match the scale.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A good estimate is a reasoned prediction anchored to a known length, not a blind guess; measuring then recalibrates the mental ruler, and the benchmark and unit must suit the object's scale.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Personal benchmark referents: fingernail ≈ 1 cm, hand-span, stride ≈ 1 m, doorway ≈ 2 m
A 'mental ruler' / mental number line of length magnitudes
An estimate–measure–difference recording strip
Everyday reference objects (an inch-long piece of gum, a metre stick)
commonMisconceptions: Wild guessing with no referent — numbers untethered to any known length, often off by an order of magnitude.
Unit/scale confusion — estimating a book at '20 m' or a room at '300 cm', muddling centimetres and metres.
Not committing before measuring — treats estimation as pointless and reaches straight for the ruler.
Never recalibrating — measures but doesn't compare with the estimate, so the mental ruler never improves.
constraints: Estimation should come AFTER hands-on measuring experience, so learners have felt real unit sizes.
Learners must commit a real estimate BEFORE measuring; reaching straight for the ruler turns estimation into a post-hoc guess.

Always include the compare-and-revise step (over/under and by how much), recorded on an estimate–measure–difference strip; measuring without relating it to the estimate does not improve the mental ruler.
Choose the unit and benchmark appropriate to the scale (cm for a book, m for the playground); the same referent will not serve all scales.
Benchmark reference cards are a supporting scaffold: they provide referents but do not supply measured feedback, so pair them with real measuring.

A fixed scored slider practice of 'estimate this length' items scored on closeness can exercise and assess the estimating skill, but on its own it lacks benchmark scaffolding and the explicit compare-and-revise loop; add these around it rather than relying on scored items alone.
Recognition-only or score-only formats do not by themselves elicit the learner's reasoning; include prompts for how the estimate was derived.

startingActivity.title: Drag-and-align: the chipped-edge ruler
learnerActions: Drag a ruler to measure a small object such as a leaf or pencil, where the ruler's end is chipped so the 0 mark sits a little inside the physical edge.
Notice that lining the object up with the chipped physical end gives a wrong readout, and that repositioning the object's end to the actual 0 mark gives the true length.
Watch the running unit-count and unit label update as you reposition, so the reading changes live until zero is aligned (or, for a scale that begins at a whole numeral, the offset is accounted for).
Work through a short series of broken-ruler puzzles whose scales start at a numeral other than 0 (e.g. start at 3, end at 12).
Use a tool-picker: match a pencil, a table and a room each to the most suitable instrument (ruler, tape, metre stick) and say why.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The number read names the units of space covered from zero, not from whatever end you happen to touch, and not the last mark the object reaches; different-sized objects call for different tools.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Centimetre / inch ruler
Metre stick and measuring tape
A 'broken ruler' whose scale starts at 3 (offset zero)
A child-made unit ruler built by iterating one unit
An annotated ruler showing 'numeral = units of space covered from 0'
commonMisconceptions: Starts the object at the '1' mark, or reads the last numeral touched — treats numerals as start-signals, not accumulated units.
Cannot cope with an offset or broken ruler; assumes measuring must begin at 0 or the physical edge.
Counts the marks / hash-lines rather than the spaces (unit-lengths) between them, giving a fencepost error of one too many.
Chooses an inappropriate tool — e.g. a short ruler to measure a room by repeated flipping.
constraints: Target ages roughly 7–8; procedural skill of selecting and using rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes in cm/m and inches/feet.
A fixed annotated ruler is a reference scaffold: it conveys the meaning of numerals but cannot rehearse alignment, repositioning, or live reading; pair it with active measuring.
A broken-ruler/tool-matching check is a discriminating assessment of the skill more than a builder of it; use it alongside hands-on tasks, not instead of them.
Reading or recognising a stated value does not itself elicit the independent act of aligning a tool and reading a length; keep genuine construction/measuring in the core tasks.
Live-recompute readouts, running unit-counts, drag-to-align, and tool-pickers are offered as concrete interaction examples to make the mechanism felt, not as required implementations.
When using paper or card unit-strips/rulers, treat them as physical approximations with slight thickness; the represented scale is an idealised line of iterated unit-lengths.
Distinguish the two offset cases: a non-integer chipped edge is handled by repositioning to the 0 mark, while a scale starting at a whole numeral is handled as end numeral minus start numeral.

Match reteaching to the error: a fencepost or 'start at 1' miscount needs reconnecting numerals to iterated units; an ill-fitting tool choice with sound reading needs the tool-to-scale habit, not re-teaching ruler mechanics.

activityReferences.title: One desk, two rulers: watch the counts differ
Same count, different length: the paperclip chains
Check and consolidate the inverse relation

startingActivity.title: One desk, two rulers: watch the counts differ
learnerActions: Before measuring, PREDICT: which number will be bigger when you measure the desk in centimetres versus inches? Say WHY.
Lay the inch ruler along the desk edge and count units as a tally climbs to about 47.
Lay the centimetre ruler along the very same edge and watch the tally race past to about 120.
Point to what actually changed between the two measurements — and confirm the desk itself did not change.
Toggle to a third, larger unit (metres) and watch the count shrink; say whether that fits the rule.
Complete the statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number' and 'larger unit → ____ units → ____ number'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number relative to a unit: the smaller the unit, the more of them fit, so the larger the number — even though the object is unchanged.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The same desk measured with a cm ruler and an inch ruler, the two counts side by side
Two rows of the same length tiled with small vs large units (many small / few large)
Regular vs jumbo paperclip chains (same count, different length)
A statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number'
commonMisconceptions: Bigger-unit-bigger-number: believes the larger unit (inch) gives the larger number because inches are 'bigger'.
Thinks the object itself is longer when the number is bigger — the cm measurement 'makes the desk longer'.
Smaller-unit-smaller-number: reasons a centimetre is small so it must give a small number, landing on inches.
Treats equal counts as equal lengths regardless of unit size (10 small clips = 10 jumbo clips).
constraints: The learner must GENERATE the two counts and make a prediction first; a static labelled image (e.g. '120 cm / 47 in' with a tap-to-reveal rule) states the idea but does not let the learner produce the counts or predict, so it belongs as post-activity consolidation rather than the core experience. This describes the affordance of each format, not a claim that other media cannot teach the idea.
Multiple-choice and slider checks can assess the relation, but the reason/explanation must be elicited — a 50/50 answer alone does not show the concept; require the justification tied to unit size.
Make explicit that the object did not change — only the size of the unit did — so a bigger number does not mean a bigger object.
The approximate counts (~120 cm, ~47 in) depend on the specific desk; treat them as illustrative of a real desk, not fixed facts for every object.
Use at least two units spanning different sizes (e.g. inch vs centimetre, then metres) so the relation can be seen to work in both directions.

learnerActions: Look at one physical length laid against two scales stacked together — e.g. a metre scale and a centimetre scale — each with its own counter showing how many of that unit fit the length
Make the length longer and watch BOTH counts rise, then say which count rises faster and which is always the bigger number

Explain in your own words why the smaller unit always gives the bigger count (one large unit holds many small units, so the multiplier equals how many small units fit one large unit — e.g. 100 cm in a metre)

Feed a value through a '×/÷' gate to convert between a larger and a smaller unit and back; use the km↔m case where the factor is ×1000/÷1000 because 1 km = 1000 m, and note that a different pair has a different factor (100 for cm per m)
Deliberately pick the wrong gate once and describe why the answer is an absurd size (e.g. 3 km wrongly divided to 0.003 m)
State the rule you observed: larger unit → fewer, larger units; smaller unit → more units, so larger→smaller multiplies
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Why larger→smaller multiplies: because a larger unit holds many of the smaller unit, the smaller-unit count is always the bigger number — the inverse relationship between unit size and count, observed rather than memorised. The exact multiplier depends on the pair (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km).

keyRepresentations: A two-column conversion / equivalence table
The same physical length shown against two scales of different unit size (so the differing counts are visible)
A place-value chart / prefix table (kilo–, centi–, milli–) tying metric conversion to ×10 structure
A '×1000 / ÷1000 machine' making the direction of the operation explicit
A number line or tape diagram for conversion word problems
commonMisconceptions: Converts in the wrong direction — divides when the larger→smaller move should multiply, or expects the smaller-unit answer to be a smaller number
Treats a compound measure like 2 m 30 cm as one number (230, or 2.30) instead of converting and adding
Over-applies base-ten to time — an hour becomes 100 minutes
Doesn't securely know the relationship (uses 100 cm in a km, 30 days in a week)
constraints: Establish the conversion relationships (1000 m/km, 60 s/min, 60 min/hr, 7 days/week) as secure known facts before drilling the procedure; a facts reference can stay to hand while the conversion direction is the focus.
Keep metric (base-ten, place value) separate from time (60s and 7s); do not over-apply powers of ten to time (an hour is 60 minutes, not 100).
The conversion multiplier is pair-specific (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km); do not let one example's factor be carried onto a different unit pair.

For compound/mixed measures, convert to a common unit BEFORE combining; never allow digits from different units to be strung together (2 m 30 cm ≠ 230 by juxtaposition — it equals 230 cm only after converting 2 m to 200 cm).

A static prefix/place-value chart with tap-to-reveal can teach the facts and base-ten structure, but pre-set content cannot itself run the live multiply/divide direction demonstration; use it as a facts scaffold, not as the main vehicle for the direction insight.
Recognition-only items (e.g. spotting a wrong conversion) assess judgement; include items where the learner constructs and explains a conversion to elicit independent production.

The manipulable two-scale demonstration is one effective way to make the inverse relationship visible; it is a proposal, not the only route — physical rulers, equivalence tables, and number lines can also make differing counts and conversion steps concrete.

startingActivity.title: Slide the digits across a fixed decimal point
learnerActions: Enter a measurement such as 3.5 km and choose the target unit (metres).
Before computing, answer the prompt: 'Is a metre bigger or smaller than a kilometre — so will there be MORE metres or FEWER?' State whether this means multiply or divide.

Watch (or physically move, using a place-value chart or Gattegno chart) every digit slide three places left while the decimal point stays nailed in place, so 3.5 becomes 3500, with place-holder zeros dropping in where needed.
Repeat for a case that keeps the decimal visible, e.g. 1.75 km to m, naming where each digit lands (the 1 becomes 1 thousand, giving 1750 m).
Do at least one divide case too, e.g. 4500 m to km, moving digits three places right to give 4.5 km.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The number grows (or shrinks) because the DIGITS move a fixed number of places, not because zeros are 'added' — so 3.5 km can never become 3.50 m.

keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart showing digits sliding across a fixed decimal point
Conversion tables (e.g. cm→mm: 1→10, 2→20, …)

commonMisconceptions: Confuses when to multiply and when to divide (converts to a smaller unit by dividing, or vice versa).
'Adds a zero' or manipulates zeros mechanically, which breaks with decimals (3.5 km → '350 m' or '3.50 m' instead of 3500 m).
Treats a mixed unit as concatenation (2 kg 35 g → '235 g'), a two-separate-numbers error.
Fills a conversion table by copying a pattern without understanding the ×10 relationship.
constraints: Secure fluency with ×/÷ by 10, 100 and 1000 BEFORE layering on conversion, to avoid overload.
Talk about the DIGITS moving one/two/three places while the decimal point stays fixed; never say 'move the decimal point' or 'add a zero'.

Practice tasks (fill-in conversions, matching equivalents, choose-the-operation items) are a strong companion for probing direction and zero errors but provide no live digit-movement feedback; pair them with the place-value chart work, which shows the transformation.
A static reference table or single worked example can show a result but does not let the pupil perform the conversion or watch digits move; treat it as reference only, not the main teaching vehicle.

A place-value slider/chart where digits visibly slide across a fixed point is proposed as a strong vehicle for THIS numeric transformation; it is not claimed superior for every topic. The content here is numeric, so 3D or spatial representations add little for this particular conversion skill.

Recognition-only responses (picking a correct conversion from options) do not by themselves show the pupil can independently reason about direction or move the digits; include tasks requiring them to produce and justify the conversion.

startingActivity.title: Dual-scale estimation playground
learnerActions: Place a bag of sugar (about 1 kg) on a kitchen scale reading kilograms, then estimate its weight in pounds before checking.
Drag a pointer on a blank pounds dial to your estimate, then reveal the true value and compare it against a double number line showing 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb.
Load 3 kg and watch both scales climb together; describe in words how the pounds number relates to the kg number (about 2.2 times), with a ratio/conversion table recording each kg–lb pair.
Use a ruler tool that overlays inches on centimetres: line up 1 inch and read off that it spans about 2.5 cm, then scale up (2 inches ≈ 5 cm).
Toggle 'is it exact?' to reveal the fuller value (e.g. 1 kg ≈ 2.20462 lb) and explain why the everyday answer is only 'about'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Converting between systems means scaling by a fixed multiplier (pounds ≈ 2.2 × kg; inches ≈ cm ÷ 2.5), and because the taught factor is rounded the cross-system answer is used approximately, so it is phrased as 'about …'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Dual-scale ruler (inches and cm side by side)
Kitchen/bathroom scales showing kg and lb together
Double number line
Ratio / conversion table

commonMisconceptions: Treats an approximate equivalence as exact (writes 1 inch = 2.5 cm and cannot say the answer is only roughly right).
Confuses which unit is larger, so converts in the wrong direction (multiplies when they should divide, or vice versa) because the larger number of cm suggests a cm is the bigger unit.
Struggles with unfamiliar imperial vocabulary and relationships (e.g. knows feet and inches measure length but not that 1 foot = 12 inches).
constraints: Introduce ≈ explicitly and contrast 'approximately equal' with 'equal'; expect and accept answers phrased as 'about …'.

Keep clear that the taught cross-system facts (inch↔cm, kg↔lb, litre↔pint) are all used approximately — their conversion factors are fixed but rounded for everyday use — while relationships purely within imperial (pound↔ounce, stone↔pound, gallon↔pint, foot↔inch) are exact.
Emphasise which unit is larger before converting, so learners judge whether the count should be more or fewer and avoid multiplying when they should divide.
Static dual-scale displays convey facts and referents but do not let the learner feel scaling; use them as reference or introduction rather than the sole route to the multiplicative idea.
Slider/multiple-choice practice checks recall and sense-of-size but does not on its own build the multiplicative feel; pair it with hands-on or tool-based scaling.
Target is a working approximate sense for estimation and sense-checking, not exact arithmetic conversion.

startingActivity.title: Move the digits, keep the point still (place-value conversion)
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart extended to thousandths. Write 3250 g in it, then convert to kilograms by sliding every digit three places to the RIGHT (dividing by 1000) while the decimal point stays fixed, landing on 3.25 kg; note that a holder zero is inserted only where place value demands it.
Before moving, state the unit-size reason aloud: 'Kilograms are the bigger unit, so there will be FEWER of them — I divide.' Then check the direction of the digit shift matches.
Convert the reverse case 0.45 km to metres (×1000), sliding digits three places LEFT to get 450 m; state that metres are smaller, so there are MORE.

Convert 5 cm to 0.05 m (÷100), sliding each digit two places to the right — a shorter example of the same digit-movement method with decimal notation; say why metres are the larger unit so there are fewer.
Confirm that 3.250 kg and 3.25 kg name the same quantity — the trailing zero after the last significant digit does not change the value.
Do a reasonableness check each time: 'Should this number get bigger or smaller?' and reject any answer that is orders of magnitude out.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A conversion moves the SAME digits across a FIXED decimal point; the point does not move. Converting to a larger unit gives fewer of them (divide, digits move right); converting to a smaller unit gives more (multiply, digits move left). 3250 g and 3.25 kg are one quantity; 3.250 equals 3.25.

keyRepresentations: Place-value chart extended to thousandths (digits slide, point fixed)
Powers-of-10 ladder mm×10→cm×100→m×1000→km
Double number line for the two units
Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of 10
commonMisconceptions: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals: 3250 g → '325 kg', or 0.45 km → '45 m' / '4.5 m'.
Reverses the multiply/divide direction, giving an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m).
'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point or treats 0.45 as the whole number 45.
Cannot articulate the powers-of-10 relationship, so treats each conversion as an isolated fact.
constraints: Reject 'add/remove a zero' and 'move the decimal point' as methods; teach movement of the DIGITS across a point that stays fixed.
Keep unit-size reasoning ('larger unit → fewer → divide; smaller unit → more → multiply') so direction is reasoned, not guessed, and pair it with a reasonableness check.

A fixed reference ladder of powers of ten can show the relationships but does not let a learner move digits or check direction themselves; use it alongside an activity where the learner performs the transformation (chart, writing, or spoken step-by-step), not as the only medium.

Matching, fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice items (including true/false decimal cases) can probe direction and the add-a-zero error precisely, but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the conversion; include tasks where the learner produces the converted value and justifies it.
Ensure a holder zero is inserted only where place value requires it (e.g. 0.045), and that trailing zeros after the last significant decimal (3.250 vs 3.25) are recognised as equal value.

An extended place-value chart to thousandths, a double number line between the two units, and a Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of ten are useful supports but are scaffolds; learners should also reason and state values without them to show secure understanding.

startingActivity.title: Recipe scaler: convert, operate, and track the unit
learnerActions: Take the problem 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour — how many grams are needed for 3 batches?' and FIRST write a rough estimate of the expected answer (about 2 to 2.5 kg, i.e. roughly 2000–2500 g).
Plan the steps on a bar model or double number line: decide which quantity needs converting and in which direction (0.75 kg → 750 g), then which operation (×3).
Execute either order — convert then operate (0.75 kg → 750 g, ×3 = 2250 g) or operate then convert (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g) — writing the unit on every line of working.
Compare the final answer to your up-front estimate: check both the size and the unit (2250 g is sensible for 3 batches; 2250 kg or '2.25 g' is not).

Repeat with a different context and step order (e.g. mass, capacity, length, time, money) so the method generalises, remembering that time conversions use 60 (minutes/seconds) or 24 (hours/days) rather than 10, 100 or 1000 (e.g. 1.5 hours = 90 minutes, not 150).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A multi-step measurement answer is only trustworthy when each quantity is converted correctly, the unit is carried through every step, and the final size and unit match a sensible up-front estimate.

Drops the conversion step or reverses its direction inside a multi-step chain (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 reported as '2.25 g').
Loses track across steps or never estimates, so an unreasonable answer (2250 kg of flour) passes unnoticed.
Treats a mixed/decimal measure as two separate whole numbers when operating.

Label the unit at every line of working so a stray 'g' vs 'kg' is caught, and keep the unit-size reasoning from earlier years; digit-movement (×/÷ 10, 100, 1000) only works for metric conversions and money (£ to p), not time, which uses 60 and 24.

learnerActions: Work with a double number line AND a matching ratio table, both with miles and km aligned from 0, showing the pairs 5↔8, 10↔16, 15↔24.

Scale the ratio up and down multiplicatively: state that 15 miles is 3 lots of 5 miles, so it is 3 lots of 8 km = 24 km; extend to 40 miles ≈ 64 km (×8), and confirm the ×1.6 'between the lines' multiplier.

Connect the pairs to a conversion graph: plot the pairs and confirm they lie on one straight line through the origin (with miles on the horizontal axis and km on the vertical axis, the gradient is about 1.6).

Then try a character's 'add 5 to both' shortcut (5 miles, 8 km → 10 miles, 13 km) and plot that point; notice it falls OFF the origin line (the true pair is 10 miles ↔ 16 km) and explain why the shortcut is wrong.
Use a compare task: place a 10 km race and a 6-mile run (≈ 9.6 km) on the same line and decide which reaches further (the 10 km race).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Converting means scaling the ratio 5:8 (multiplying), which keeps every point on the same straight line through zero; adding a constant to both quantities knocks points off that line and is wrong.

keyRepresentations: Double number line (miles and km aligned from 0)
Ratio / conversion table
Conversion graph (straight line through the origin, gradient ≈ 1.6)
'Spot the mistake' worked example exposing additive error
commonMisconceptions: Additive rather than multiplicative reasoning ('two more miles means two more km'; from 10 miles ≈ 16 km, adds 5 to both to convert 15 miles).
Thinks a kilometre is longer than a mile because the same distance is a bigger number in km, so converts in the wrong direction.
Treats 5 miles = 8 km as exact rather than approximate, ignoring ≈.
constraints: Treat the relationship as approximate throughout: teach ≈ explicitly and expect 'about' answers; 5 miles ≈ 8 km (true value for 15 miles is ~24.14 km), never exact.

A static aligned double number line with tap-to-reveal pairs conveys the fact pairs but cannot show the additive error in motion; it can still display a plotted additive point statically. Use it as a scaffold and make the multiplicative/additive contrast explicit.

A single selection-based spot-the-mistake item can assess whether reasoning is multiplicative but does not by itself build graph intuition; pair it with construction of pairs on a number line, ratio table or graph.
Keep the direction check concrete: a mile is longer, so the km figure for a given distance is always the bigger number — use this to sense-check every conversion.

activityReferences.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot
Interpret a given line plot: how many versus how long
Reference reveal: what each X and each position means

startingActivity.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot
learnerActions: Collect 6-8 small real objects (pencils, crayons, leaves, blocks) and measure each to the nearest whole centimetre, measuring from the ruler's zero mark, not from 1 or the end.
Record each measurement in a simple tally or frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot.

Notice how a line plot differs from earlier tally or category charts: here the horizontal axis is an ordered measurement scale with equal whole-number intervals and every value present, not a set of arbitrary categories you could reorder or leave out.

On a horizontal line, mark the scale as equal whole-number intervals across the full range of your data, including any whole-number value that nothing measured. Early on a line that is already pre-scaled can be provided as a scaffold so you focus on plotting; building the scale yourself afterwards is the fuller skill this topic is aiming at.
Place exactly one X above each object's measured value; when two objects share a length, stack a second X on top of the first.

If your scale marks are spaced 1 cm apart, keep an actual ruler aligned directly beneath the line, with its numbers matching your scale labels, so each X's horizontal position reads as a length on the same scale.
Answer two separate questions from your finished plot: 'How many objects were 6 cm?' (count the Xs in that stack) and 'How long is the longest object?' (read its position on the scale).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: On a line plot the sideways position of an X answers 'how long?' while the upward height of a stack answers 'how many?'. Unlike reorderable categorical charts, the axis is a ruler-like measurement scale: equal intervals with every whole-number value staying on it even when no object landed there, so the gaps stay equal.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The horizontal number line as a measurement scale (equal whole-unit intervals)
Stacked X marks, one X per object
A ruler aligned under the plot linking measured length to axis position
A tally / frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot
commonMisconceptions: Reading the height of a stack as the length ('the tallest stack is the longest object')
Drawing only the values that occurred and spacing them evenly, so a value with no data is omitted and the intervals become unequal
Measuring from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every length is off by a unit
Treating each X as one unit of length rather than one object
constraints: The core objective is a procedure: children must actually measure objects and construct the scale and marks, not only read or recognise a finished plot. A pre-scaled line is an acceptable early scaffold, but children should reach the point of building the scale themselves.
Children should generate and record their own data before plotting, so the plot displays data they produced.

The horizontal axis must be an ordered measurement scale: equal whole-unit intervals across the full range, with every whole-number value present even where no data lands — unlike reorderable categorical/tally charts.

Measure from zero with gap-free unit iteration; measuring from the 1 mark makes every length one unit too long, and measuring from the ruler's physical end can make lengths wrong by the size of any gap before the zero mark.
One X per object; two equal-length objects produce a stack of two at the same position. Each X represents an object, not a unit of length.

Interpreting a given plot and reveal-the-meaning references are supporting scaffolds: they can assess or clarify interpretation but do not exercise the generative measure-and-scale skill, so do not rely on them alone.
Keeping a real ruler aligned under the axis is a concrete device to link length to position; it is one effective option, not the only way to teach the link.

Separate frequency from length

startingActivity.title: Measure to the nearest quarter and build the fractional scale
learnerActions: Measure a set of ribbons or objects (about 5–6) against a ruler whose quarter-inch ticks are clearly marked and, at first, labelled with their fraction values (¼, ½, ¾).

For each object, name the quarter inch it rounds to out loud or in writing — e.g. 'this one is 2¾ inches', not 'the third line'; for one or two objects, also name the nearest half inch and notice that the two answers can be different.

Using the ruler to mark it, draw a number line at true scale (1 inch per whole number) that covers every measured length, and partition it into equal quarters between the whole numbers, so the marks run e.g. 2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3 in correct order and with equal spacing.
Place one X per object at its fractional value on the line.

Align the ruler directly under the true-scale plot, with the ruler's whole-inch marks under the matching whole numbers on the axis, so each ¼ tick on the ruler sits beneath the matching ¼ mark on the axis.
(Optional, on screen) Measure a ribbon that is 2¼ inches: drop its X and watch it settle one quarter-tick past 2, directly beneath the same tick on the ruler, making the shared subdivision visible.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: confirm 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and that 2½ lands at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).
Read the finished plot: e.g. 'how many objects were 2½ inches?' and 'how many were shorter than 2½?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The subdivision on the ruler and the subdivision on the plot's axis are the same partition of one unit into equal quarters; a measured length maps to a position on an equal-interval scale, and ½ = 2/4 is one position, not two.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A ruler subdivided (and labelled) in quarter-inches
A number line partitioned into equal quarters
A fraction strip or bar linking ¼, ½, ¾ to show equal parts and order
Stacked X marks, one per object
commonMisconceptions: Spacing the fraction marks unequally or out of order — placing ½ midway but crowding or mis-ordering ¼ and ¾
Measuring 'to the nearest line' on the ruler without knowing the fraction that line represents, so a tick position is recorded rather than a measured value
Carrying over the value-vs-frequency habit — reading stack height as length
Treating ½ and 2/4 as different positions on the scale
constraints: Use a ruler with clearly marked quarter-inch subdivisions, labelled at first, so children can name the fraction value of the tick they round to rather than recording 'the nearest line'.
Keep the ruler's ¼-inch tick spacing aligned with the plot's ¼ spacing so the tool and the axis share one subdivision.
Maintain the one-X-per-object rule established with whole-unit plots.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and 2½ at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).

A labelled reference image or tap-to-reveal plot is a scaffold for naming marks; being fixed, it does not by itself exercise measuring to the nearest quarter or constructing the scale, so pair it with hands-on measuring and plotting and fade it.

Reading-only tasks (ordering, counting on a given plot) assess interpretation but do not show whether a child can build a correctly spaced, correctly ordered quarter scale; include a construction task to cover that.

Snap-to-equal-spacing or tick-alignment feedback (whether on screen or via physically aligning a ruler under the plot) is an optional way to make the shared subdivision visible; it is not the only way to teach equal intervals.

activityReferences.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
Compute from a given plot: difference and total
Reveal equivalence on the eighth scale (reference scaffold)

startingActivity.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
learnerActions: Measure several real objects (e.g. seedlings or paper strips) to the nearest 1/8 inch using a ruler subdivided into eighths; include some objects that share a length.
Draw a number line marked in equally spaced intervals that each represent 1/8 inch, and plot one X per object at its measured value.
Mark where 2/8 lines up with 1/4 and where 4/8 lines up with 1/2 directly on the axis.
Find longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions, converting to a common denominator on the scale (e.g. 1/2 − 3/8 = 4/8 − 3/8 = 1/8).
Find the total length of all objects by adding each object's value with multiplicity — a stack of three Xs at 3/8 contributes 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, not '3'.
Predict how the total changes if one more object at 1/2 is added, then check (the total rises by 1/2 = 4/8).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An accurate eighth scale makes equivalences (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2) and common denominators visible, and totalling over a plot means summing measured values with multiplicity — which is different from counting Xs.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A ruler subdivided to eighths
A number line in eighths showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½)
Fraction bars for adding and subtracting like denominators
The plot itself used as a data source for computation
commonMisconceptions: When asked for a total length, adding or counting the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
Adding fractions by adding numerators AND denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
Spacing eighths unequally or not seeing 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
Counting a value only once when several Xs are stacked on it while totalling
constraints: Learners must construct the scale themselves and measure to the nearest 1/8 inch; a given-plot or tap-to-reveal task isolates computation or shows equivalence but does not exercise building an accurate eighth scale or measuring.
Scale-building should be assessed through actual construction; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of an equal-interval scale.
Keep the one-X-per-case convention, and ensure eighth intervals are drawn equally spaced so quarter/half ticks line up.
The total must be computed by summing measured values with multiplicity, not by counting Xs; keep frequency and value explicitly distinct.

Adding fractions that have the same denominator keeps the denominator unchanged (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8); adding denominators (giving 6/16) is an error. When denominators are related but different (e.g. 1/2 and 3/8), first rewrite them with a common denominator (1/2 = 4/8) before adding or subtracting.

An interactive panel showing live arithmetic (e.g. selecting a stack to lay out 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8) or overlaying quarter/half ticks is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required tool; the same reasoning can be done with a ruler, drawn number line and fraction strips.

Lengths from 0 on a number line, with jumps

startingActivity.title: Build a bar or ruler model, then read the equation off it
learnerActions: Read a result-unknown story, e.g. 'A rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now?'
Draw a bar (or ruler line) labelled 45, mark off the 18 cm that was cut, and mark the leftover piece with a □ to show it is the length you do not yet know.
Write a number sentence that matches the drawing, using a symbol for the unknown: 45 − 18 = □ AND 18 + □ = 45.
Solve and label the answer with its unit: 27 cm.
Show the two equations against the same drawing and explain why both describe one picture.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The unknown is a visible piece of the bar or ruler you can point to before you know its number, so the equation is a description of the picture — not a guess triggered by a word like 'cut off'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model (whole split into known part + unknown □)
Ruler / number-line drawing with jumps from 0
Equation with a symbol for the unknown (□ or ?)
Comparison bars stacked to show 'how much longer'
commonMisconceptions: Chooses the operation from a keyword ('longer'/'altogether' → add; 'cut off'/'left' → subtract) without modelling the situation, so comparison and missing-addend problems are miscalculated.
Writes the answer where the unknown symbol should go, reading '=' as 'the answer is' rather than 'has the same value as', so cannot represent 18 + □ = 45 before solving.
When drawing/using a ruler, counts the marks or starts at 1 instead of 0, so the represented length is off by one.
Drops the unit or draws a picture that doesn't match the quantities.
constraints: The learning objective is for the child to construct the model and the equation, so recognition-only tasks (choosing a finished sentence, tapping to reveal a completed bar) check understanding but do not elicit the independent construction the standard requires; use them as checks or worked-example references, not as the main activity.

Deliberately include comparison and missing-addend problems alongside result-unknown take-aways, especially structures where a keyword points to the wrong operation (e.g. 'Mia's ribbon is 12 cm longer than Sam's. Mia's is 42 cm. How long is Sam's?', where 'longer' appears but you subtract). Keyword strategies often give the right operation on result-unknown items, and even on some comparison or missing-part items such as '12 cm longer, how long is Mia's?' or 'how much was cut off?'. So check the structure rather than assuming every comparison or missing-addend item will expose keyword use.
Insist on a drawing that matches the numbers and on units (cm) in the answer, so the model and equation stay tied to the quantity.
When a ruler or number line is used, start length from 0 and count intervals, not marks; otherwise represented lengths come out off by one.

A draggable on-screen builder (e.g. sliding a cutter along a 45 bar so the leftover segment is marked with a □, or stacking two comparison bars to reveal a 12 cm gap) makes the unknown concrete and can accept both 45 − 18 = □ and 18 + □ = 45; paper bar/ruler drawings achieve the same modelling and either medium is acceptable.
Keep problems to one step and within 100, with both lengths in the same unit.

learnerActions: Measure two real quantities of the SAME kind — e.g. two lengths of ribbon in cm, or two beakers of juice in ml (250 ml and 400 ml), or two masses in g.

Combine the two measures on a number line / tape: place lengths end to end to read the total (e.g. 25 cm + 40 cm = 65 cm), or mark the two volumes along the scale to reach the total (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Write the answer WITH its unit (65 cm; 650 ml).
Switch to a subtraction task: use the same number line to find the difference between the two measures as the gap between them.
Decide for each worded problem whether you are combining the amounts (stack them / mark to the total) or finding how much more one is than the other (find the gap).

Meet the mixed-unit case: a 2 m length and a 30 cm length. Try to total them and notice you cannot simply write 32 — line both up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) and say what has to be true (same unit) before adding.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding measures means combining amounts and subtracting means finding a gap; a measurement answer is only meaningful with its unit; and you can only add or subtract measures that are in the same unit.

keyRepresentations: A number line / tape diagram for combining and comparing lengths

A measuring bench: measure two quantities, then combine them
An answer frame that always includes the unit (____ ml, ____ cm)
commonMisconceptions: Adds or subtracts across different units as if they were the same number (2 m + 30 cm = 32).
Drops the unit from the answer (250 ml + 400 ml = 650).
Muddles compound units, e.g. reads 3 cm 5 mm as 35 or adds 3 + 5 — not yet knowing 10 mm = 1 cm.
Applies the wrong operation — adds when the problem asks for a difference, or vice versa.
constraints: Keep all arithmetic within a single unit at this stage; delay formal mm–cm–m (and kg–g, l–ml) conversion to a later unit-conversion topic. The mixed-unit trap is used only to reveal that units must match, not to have the child compute a converted total.
Always require the unit in the answer; treat a bare number as an incomplete answer.

Keep length examples (ribbon in cm/mm), capacity examples (juice in ml) and mass examples (in g) coherent — do not label a volume as a 'length' or carry a length action over to a capacity or mass result.
The fill-in/selection check tests and states the same-unit rule but does not by itself build number-line sense; pair it with the measure-and-combine activity.
The reference diagram is a worked example: it cannot let the child measure varied cases or recompute at the same-unit trap, so use it to support, not replace, hands-on measuring and calculating.

Optional interaction examples (marking measured amounts on a line, a subtraction 'gap' mode, a running unit-bearing answer box, lining up mismatched units on one common scale) illustrate the mechanism; they are suggestions, not mandatory features.

When a child muddles a compound unit (e.g. writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 cm, or adds 3 + 5 to get 8), do not drill conversion now; keep calculations within one unit and let compound-unit fluency arrive with the later conversion topic.

startingActivity.title: Build the model before you compute
learnerActions: Read a multi-step measurement problem, e.g. 'A 2.5 kg bag of flour is shared equally into 4 tubs, then 150 g is taken from one tub — how much is left in that tub?'
Before writing any equation, draw a bar/strip diagram or number line that shows the quantities and how they relate (the whole 2.5 kg, the 4 equal parts, the 150 g removed)
Convert to a common unit where needed (150 g = 0.15 kg, or 2.5 kg = 2500 g) and note the conversion explicitly

Let the structure of your diagram tell you the operations: splitting the bar into 4 equal parts IS the ÷4 (each part = 2500 g ÷ 4 = 625 g = 0.625 kg), and marking off 150 g from one part IS the subtraction (625 g − 150 g = 475 g = 0.475 kg). Working in grams keeps the numbers whole, because 0.625 kg is in thousandths and Grade 4 decimal work usually stops at hundredths.
Estimate roughly first, then check the computed answer against that estimate and label the unit

Test transfer: if the same bag had been 3 kg instead of 2.5 kg shared into 4 tubs, predict whether each tub holds more or less and by how much before computing — the same partition-then-subtract model still applies
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The diagram generates the operations, so you never have to guess an operation from a keyword; partitioning a bar is division and marking off a segment is subtraction. Checking against an estimate catches off-scale answers, and the same model transfers when a quantity changes (e.g. a 3 kg bag still partitions into four equal parts).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Number-line diagram with a measurement scale
Bar / strip (Singapore) model showing part-whole relationships
A labelled part-whole diagram linking known and unknown quantities
A conversion table for units within a system (km/m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min)
commonMisconceptions: Keyword plucking — grabbing the numbers and applying the operation a keyword cues, with no model of the situation
Operating across mixed units without converting (adding 0.75 m and 95 cm as if the same unit)
Treating time as base-ten (handling 1 hr 45 min as 1.45; carrying at 100 rather than 60)
Misaligning decimal points or dropping/mixing the money symbol (writing $5.7, or $0.50¢)
Computing with no diagram or estimate, so an unreasonable answer goes unchecked
constraints: The target skill is modelling plus computing: learners must build their own representation, not only read or tap a finished one. Annotated worked examples and reveal-the-segment displays are exposition/reference scaffolds and should be followed by learner-constructed diagrams.

Fill-in-the-blank, slider and draw-the-jump response formats can assess computation and unit handling, but a sequence that only scores the final number cannot see whether the learner modelled the situation or plucked a keyword — so pair any such checks with observation of the build.

Interactive supports such as dragging quantities onto a bar or number line, partitioning a bar into equal parts, a unit strip that snaps g↔kg or cm↔m, and flags for off-scale answers are useful ways to make the model concrete and provide feedback; they are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tooling.
Refuse keyword shortcuts ('altogether means add', 'left means subtract'); require a model of the situation before an equation.
Insist on unit-checking (convert to a common unit before operating) and on labelling the answer with its unit and money symbol (avoid $5.7 or $0.50¢).
Treat time as base-60: 1 hr 45 min is not 1.45, and minutes carry at 60.
A fixed/static annotated example can still teach how a bar maps to an equation; it simply cannot be manipulated by the learner — scope its role to exposition rather than claiming it cannot teach.
Include transfer: once a model works, vary a quantity (e.g. 2.5 kg → 3 kg) and have the learner predict whether and by how much the result changes using the same model.

Explain-the-error dialogue: 'convince me on the line'

startingActivity.title: Dragging across zero on a vertical number line (thermometer)
learnerActions: Set a start value (e.g. −2°C) and an end value (e.g. 3°C) on a vertical number line scaled like a thermometer.
Drag a marker from the start up through zero to the end, watching the interval light up as two arcs meeting at zero: '2 below → 0' and '0 → 3'.
Read the running interval as it decomposes: 2 + 3 = 5, rather than a single subtraction.
Switch the context (temperature → sea-level cross-section → bank balance, e.g. −£120 below zero and £350 above) while the same number line stays, and repeat the drag.
Compare the positions of −5 and −3 on the scale and state which is lower and why.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is the sum of the two distances on each side of zero; direction (not the size of the digit) sets the order of negative numbers, so −5 lies below −3.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Vertical number line / thermometer spanning below and above zero
Horizontal number line with zero as the crossing point and interval arcs
Real-context strips: temperature scale, sea-level cross-section, bank balance line
Interval arcs decomposed at zero (−5→0 is 5, 0→3 is 3, total 8)
commonMisconceptions: Treating −5 as larger than −3 because '5 > 3' (ignoring direction)
Counting the interval across zero without including the step onto/over 0, or double-counting zero
Adding the numbers instead of finding a distance (−5 to 3 answered as −2)
Believing there is no number between −1 and 1 other than described, or that zero is negative/positive
Reading a fall in temperature as a rise because the digit gets 'bigger' (−2 to −8 seen as warming)
constraints: Keep the focus on ordering and measuring/counting intervals; defer formal signed +/−/× arithmetic rules to later (KS3) study.
Anchor every negative in a directed context (temperature, sea level, bank balance) so the sign denotes direction, not a smaller ordinary number.

A labelled thermometer with tap-to-reveal readings illustrates the scale but does not let the learner traverse and measure an arbitrary interval across zero; treat it as an illustrative scaffold, not the core interval task.
A multiple-choice or value-setting check consolidates and assesses the skill but does not by itself build the across-zero intuition; introduce the hands-on or annotated number-line work first.
Report intervals as positive distances; contrast 'the difference between −5 and 3' (interval = 8) with the individual values so distance is not confused with a single number's value.
Distinguish the ideal number line (direction and position) from any physical thermometer prop used to represent it.

Zero is neither positive nor negative; treat it as the single crossing point where an across-zero interval splits: count the steps (unit gaps) from the start to zero and from zero to the end, so zero is a boundary point, not an extra step.

startingActivity.title: Cut the rectangle, keep the factor
learnerActions: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle (3 rows of 6 tiles), then physically cut it along the grid line between the first 4 columns and the last 2 columns, making two sub-rectangles.
Match each piece to its product (3×4 and 3×2) and match the whole uncut rectangle to 3×(4+2).

Recompose the pieces and check the two areas sum to the whole.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A rectangle a×(b+c) split by one line across its (b+c) side, at the point between b and c, becomes two sub-rectangles a×b and a×c whose areas SUM to the whole; the repeated factor 'a' stays on both parts.

keyRepresentations: A partitioned rectangle / area model split into two labelled regions
The open array (regions labelled by dimensions, tiles not all drawn)
