startingActivity.title: Cover, count, and separate area from perimeter
learnerActions: Fill a figure drawn on squared paper with unit squares, snapping them edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps, and count them to state the area, e.g. 'area = 12 square units'.

Trace the boundary of the SAME shape separately, stepping round the edge and counting the unit lengths, and record the perimeter in unit lengths. This is a different kind of measure from the area. For a 12-square figure the perimeter number is also different (at least 14), but for some shapes the two numbers can match: a 4-by-4 square has area 16 square units and perimeter 16 units. Even then they measure different things.
Say aloud that the squares INSIDE measure area while the steps AROUND measure perimeter — two different measures of the same shape.

Rearrange the same set of (e.g. 12) tiles, joined edge-to-edge, into a long strip. Re-count the covering squares (still 12), then re-count the perimeter and compare. For example, a 3-by-4 rectangle has perimeter 14 units, but a 1-by-12 strip has perimeter 26 units. The area count stays the same whether or not the perimeter changes.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares covering a region; it is distinct from perimeter and is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A single unit square labelled '1 square unit'
A figure on squared paper filled with unit squares, counted
Congruent rectangles: one with unit lengths marked round the perimeter, one with the interior square units drawn
The same set of tiles rearranged into different shapes (area conserved, perimeter changes)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area with perimeter / length — judges the 'bigger' shape by how far it stretches or the distance around, not the surface covered.
Undifferentiated 'bigger' — calls a longer or taller shape bigger by one dimension without coordinating the 2D covering.
Thinks rearranging the same squares into a new shape changes the amount of area.
Gives area as a bare number without square units, or counts squares with gaps/overlaps.
constraints: Area answers must always be stated in square units (e.g. '12 square centimetres'), not as a bare number.
Unit squares must tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps for the count to be a valid area.

Static reference images (a labelled '1 square unit' and a 12-square figure marked 'area = 12 square units') are useful consolidation but do not let a learner rearrange tiles to experience conservation; pair them with hands-on covering and recomposition.

A sort/multiple-choice check can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction but is a recognition task; it does not by itself require independent construction or demonstrate conservation of area, so use it alongside covering and rearranging activities.
Keep the focus on 2D surface. A 3D setting risks conflating area with volume; if 3D is used, keep the measured attribute explicitly the flat surface.
The optional live counter, AREA/PERIMETER toggle, and rearrange mode are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms; squared paper and physical tiles achieve the same objective.

startingActivity.title: Trace-the-boundary L-shape with live missing-side reveal
learnerActions: Trace a finger (or pen) all the way around the boundary of an L-shaped figure, naming or ticking each side as you pass it so no side is counted twice and none is missed.

When you reach an unmarked side, work out its length from the labelled sides: the two shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side, so find a missing longer side by adding the two shorters, or find a missing shorter side by subtracting the known shorter length from the longer. Write the deduced length on the blank.
Keep a running total as you go; when every side is ticked, read off the perimeter in cm.
Notice the internal 'fold' line where the rectangles join: leave it out — it is not part of the boundary.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A hidden side length is not missing information: it can be recovered from the labelled sides, because the shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side. Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary, each side counted exactly once, excluding internal lines.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: L-shaped / rectilinear figure with some sides unmarked
Missing-side deduction (opposite sides equal)
Tick-each-side-as-counted method
Boundary-versus-internal-line contrast
commonMisconceptions: Forgets to find the unmarked sides and adds only the given numbers.
Cannot see that the two shorter sides equal the opposite longer side, so mis-deduces a missing length.
Includes internal lines, double-counts a side, or confuses perimeter with area.
constraints: Define rectilinear/compound shape explicitly (only straight sides, with sides always meeting at right angles, including the inward corner of an L-shape; rectangles joined) and use both terms.

Include figures with unmarked sides so the deduction step is genuinely required; fully-labelled shapes given to read off only practise addition, not the distinctive skill (the draw-your-own task, where the pupil labels all sides they create, is a separate production activity).
Mark/tick each side as it is added to prevent missing or double-counting a side.
Distinguish the boundary (perimeter) from internal split/join lines, which are excluded.
Keep perimeter (length, cm) distinct from area (cm2); address the common area/perimeter confusion explicitly.
Secure addition and subtraction underpin missing-side deduction; reteach these prerequisites if the pupil cannot combine the known lengths.

Tap-to-reveal or lit-side animations are optional scaffolds that illustrate the method but do not by themselves give the pupil tracing or counting practice — follow them with pupil-constructed working.
A spot-the-mistake multiple-choice item checks error-diagnosis but does not require constructing a full perimeter; include at least one open compute or draw task.

State the relationship precisely: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape SUM to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape, the two shorter sides along a direction SUM to the opposite longer side, and other composite shapes may have more than two parts on one side. Subtraction is only how a missing shorter side is recovered (longer minus a known shorter), not a restatement that the shorter sides 'equal' the longer.

startingActivity.title: Cut the L-shaped floor plan into rectangles
learnerActions: Look at an L-shaped room on a grid with its outer measurements labelled.
Draw a cut line to split the shape into two non-overlapping rectangles.

startingActivity.title: Dissection workbench: rearrange to reveal the formulae
learnerActions: Take a parallelogram whose perpendicular height from a top corner lands on the base. Cut along that height to remove a right-angled triangle, then slide it to the other end so it forms a rectangle of the SAME area. Confirm that base × perpendicular height is the area, because the rectangle's length and width are the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Take a triangle, duplicate and rotate the copy, and fit the two copies together into a parallelogram; observe that the single triangle is exactly HALF, so its area is base × perpendicular height ÷ 2.
Place or drag the height line so it meets the base at 90°, marking the right angle; check a line that is NOT perpendicular and explain why it is not the height.
Rotate the shape so the base is no longer horizontal, then identify which side is now the base and where its perpendicular height falls.
Work with a diagram that includes a decoy slant length (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8) and deliberately ignore the slant when computing the area.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The area formulae are consequences of rearranging shapes: a parallelogram is a rectangle in disguise, and a triangle is half a parallelogram, which is where the ÷2 comes from. The height is always perpendicular to whichever side is chosen as the base, and not every given number is needed.

commonMisconceptions: Uses the slant side instead of the perpendicular height, partly from believing every number given must be used.
Forgets to halve for a triangle (computes base × height and stops).
Thinks the base must be the horizontal or bottom side, so cannot identify base and height in rotated or obtuse triangles.
constraints: The height must always be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the chosen base (meeting it at 90°), never a slant side; have learners mark the right angle and examine lines that are NOT the perpendicular height.

Any side can serve as the base with its own matching perpendicular height; include shapes in varied orientations (including rotated and obtuse triangles) so learners do not assume the base is horizontal or at the bottom.
Tie the ÷2 to the two-congruent-triangles-make-a-parallelogram image so halving is meaningful; apply ÷2 only to triangles, not parallelograms.
Include decoy slant lengths so learners practise selecting needed lengths: a 'given' number is not always a 'needed' number.
Calculation/'who is right?' practice checks and consolidates fluency but does the least to build the dissection insight; it should follow, not replace, the rearrangement work.

Tap-to-reveal static diagrams can show the dissection steps but do not let the learner perform the rearrangement; a live on-screen manipulation or physical paper cutting lets the learner carry out the cut-and-rearrange themselves.
Paper cutouts have slight real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figures; distinguish the represented plane shape from its physical model.
Re-secure rectangle and parallelogram area first, as a prerequisite, if a learner has no sense of perpendicular height.

startingActivity.title: Discover π by unrolling the circumference
learnerActions: Take several circular objects (tins, lids, cups) of different sizes; wrap a string once around each and measure that length, then measure the diameter across each.

Divide each circumference by its diameter and record the result; notice the results are all close to the same value, a little over 3 (near π ≈ 3.14, allowing for small measurement errors), whatever the size of the circle.
Lay the measured circumference along a line marked off in lengths equal to that circle's own diameter, and see that it reaches to just past three diameters.
State in your own words: C = πd means the way round is 'a bit more than 3 diameters'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: π is the fixed ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14), so C = πd is almost a definition, not an arbitrary formula to recall.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A circle with radius, diameter and circumference labelled; the d = 2r link
π as the ratio of circumference to diameter (a string round a tin measured against the diameter, ≈ 3.14)
The circle cut into wedges rearranged into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (derivation of πr²)
A composite shape decomposed into a rectangle plus a semicircle
Unit labels distinguishing length (cm) from area (cm²)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing radius and diameter — substituting the diameter where the radius is needed (or vice versa)
Swapping the circumference and area formulae (using πr² for circumference or 2πr for area)
Forgetting to square the radius, or squaring as 'doubling' (treating r² as 2r or as the diameter)
Giving an area in linear units, or a circumference in square units
On composite shapes, using the diameter as the radius of the semicircle, or dropping a straight edge from the perimeter
constraints: Learners should be able to convert between radius and diameter (d = 2r) and to find the area of a rectangle before this topic; semicircle composite work also builds on perimeter/area of composite shapes.

Recognition and matching tasks (matching circles to formulae, multiple-choice with distractors) are useful for rehearsal and assessment but do not require independent derivation or application to a novel figure; they should supplement, not replace, the measurement, wedge-rearranging, and composite-construction activities.

A static labelled circle with tap-to-reveal can name radius, diameter and circumference and display both formulae, but cannot let a learner derive π, rearrange the wedges, or apply the formulae to a new shape — treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main learning activity.

Paper circles and string-and-tin measurements are physical approximations of ideal plane figures (paper and card have slight thickness); use them to approximate the mathematical circle and reason about the represented figure rather than the physical cutout.

Interactive features named here (roll-the-circle animation, drag-the-wedges tool, radius/diameter toggle, composite-shape builder, unit labels) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not mandatory; the same insights are reachable with physical materials and sketching.

startingActivity.title: Shear a parallelogram into a rectangle
learnerActions: Study a parallelogram on a grid labelled with base 8 cm, a perpendicular height 5 cm marked with a right-angle symbol, AND a slant side 6 cm.
Before computing, decide which length should multiply the base to give the area, and say why.
Move the sloping triangular overhang from one end across to the other so the shape becomes a rectangle; confirm the covered area is unchanged.
State the area: 8 × 5 = 40 cm² (the 6 cm slant is a decoy and is not used).
If a dynamic model is available, drag the overhang live and watch an area readout stay constant as the parallelogram becomes a rectangle.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A parallelogram rearranges into a rectangle of the same base and the same PERPENDICULAR height, so its area is base × perpendicular height — the slant side is longer and is never the height.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Parallelogram sheared into a rectangle; triangle as half a parallelogram (derivation diagrams)
Trapezium as the average of its two parallel sides × height
A prism 'extruded' from its cross-section along its length; cylinder as a circular cross-section extruded
The perpendicular height marked with a right-angle symbol, distinct from the slant side
Unit labels: cm² for area, cm³ for volume
commonMisconceptions: Using the slanted side instead of the perpendicular height for a parallelogram, triangle or trapezium
Dropping the ½ (triangle/trapezium) — applying the rectangle/parallelogram rule (base × height) to a triangle
Confusing area with perimeter (adding sides) or volume with surface area
Multiplying all the given lengths together for volume instead of cross-section × length
Muddling the units — cm² for volume, or forgetting square/cubic units
constraints: Always use the perpendicular height (at right angles to the base), never a slanted side; include a labelled slant as a deliberate distractor so learners must select the correct height.
Derive each formula from the rectangle rather than presenting it to be memorised; derivation and transfer (e.g. to a new prism or the cylinder) are the real objective, not recall.
Volume must be taught as one idea — uniform cross-section area × length — so the cuboid, triangular prism and cylinder are the same rule; do not let learners multiply every given length.
Keep units coupled to the dimension count: two lengths multiplied → square units (cm²); an area × a length → cubic units (cm³).

Recognition, matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and can reveal the slant-side error, but they do not by themselves elicit independent derivation or transfer; use them alongside tasks where the learner performs the rearrangement and applies it to a novel figure.

A static labelled diagram with tap-to-reveal can name base, perpendicular height and slant side and show the formula, but cannot let the learner perform the rearrangement or apply it to a new figure; treat it as a scaffold, not the main vehicle.

Optional dynamic or 3D features (live area readout while shearing, draggable parallel sides with a ½(a+b)h readout, slicing a prism to expose the cross-section, extruding a circle into a cylinder, cm²/cm³ unit toggles) make the mechanism concrete where available, but are not mandatory for the learning to occur.
Paper cut-and-rearrange versions (cut off the overhang and slide it to form a rectangle, or draw the diagonal to halve a parallelogram) are valid concrete realisations of the same derivations.
When discussing the circle cross-section, πr² is the exact area; 9π ≈ 28.3 cm² is a rounded value — keep the exact form where exactness matters.

startingActivity.title: Pour the same water back and forth (conservation)
learnerActions: Fill a tall thin glass with water and set an empty short wide bowl beside it, ready to pour the same water from one to the other.
Pour the water from the tall glass into the empty wide bowl and back again; notice the level is high in the glass and low in the bowl, even though it is the same water.

Predict first, then pour each of two mystery containers (secretly holding the same amount) into its own identical beaker and check: the levels come out about the same (small spills or drips can make a tiny difference).
Say aloud what happened: the tall one never had more, it just looked that way because the glass is thin.
Hit half-full and quarter-full targets by pouring until the water reaches a marked line (about half, about a quarter is fine at this age).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The same amount of water can look very different in differently-shaped containers; when the containers are different shapes, the height of the liquid (or the tallness of the container) does not by itself tell you the amount. startingActivity.title: Fill, count, record — then swap the cup
learnerActions: Fill a container cupful by cupful using identical cups, filling each cup to the same mark or brim, and keep a running count (e.g. pour until the count climbs to 8).

startingActivity.title: Decode the changing scale
learnerActions: Before reading any value, find two labelled numbers on the jug (or balance) and count the gaps between them.
Work out what one small step is worth, e.g. 100 over 5 gaps = steps of 20.
Read a part-filled scale by accumulating the steps from where the scale starts, not by counting lines (e.g. a level at the labelled 300 plus two more 20-steps = 340 ml).
Use a small number line of the steps (0, 20, 40, 60…) to track the accumulated value when the interval is unlabelled, counting up from where the scale starts.
Repeat across tasks where the interval changes each time — 10 ml, 20 ml, 25 ml, 50 ml — so memorising a single step size fails.
Say aloud 'what is one small step worth?' every time before giving a reading.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The marks mean nothing until you decode the step: the same mark position (e.g. the 3rd small mark above a label) stands for different amounts on scales with different intervals, so measuring is working out interval value, not counting lines.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Measuring jug / scaled beaker with variable interval size
Pan or dial balance for mass
Benchmark referents (1 g / 100 g / 1 kg weights; 1 ml drop; 1-litre bottle)
Bar model for one-step mass/volume word problems
Number line for the value of unlabelled intervals
commonMisconceptions: Counts the marks/lines as units ('measuring is counting'), so reads a scale by the number of small marks rather than the interval value.
Assumes each small interval equals 1 (or 10) when the scale actually steps in 2s, 5s, 20s or 50s.
Reads the nearest labelled number to the level (endpoint reading) without noticing the level falls between marks, or ignores where the scale starts.
Estimates with no sense of the unit (a textbook '5 kg') or picks the wrong unit (grams for a person's mass).
constraints: Keep word problems ONE step and in the SAME unit; exclude compound units and multiplicative comparison for this age.
Record measurements as approximate to a sensible degree of accuracy; estimation is checked against a measurement, not left as a guess.

A static labelled picture of a jug or a benchmark can scaffold what 1 kg or 1 litre looks like, but cannot make a child decode a changing interval or check an estimate against feedback; use it as a reference, not as the core task.

Recognition-only checks (choose-the-unit, read-off at a fixed interval, fill-the-blank for the 3×250 g problem) can probe understanding and act as a companion check, but do not elicit the pour-and-adjust feedback loop or independent decoding of a novel interval.

Pouring real water or loading a physical balance adds genuine physical feel; it is a useful complement to reading 2D scales, which can be practised without apparatus. However, handling real benchmark objects (e.g. a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle) is needed to build the bodily referent that estimation depends on.
Vary the interval size across tasks deliberately (10, 20, 25, 50) so 'what is one small step worth?' becomes a habitual check rather than an assumption of ones or tens.

startingActivity.title: Watch duration grow from a shared start
learnerActions: Start two events at the same moment and watch a visible timer or growing duration-bar under each until it stops
Name which event was quicker — the one with the shorter bar/time — and say how you know
Use a slower-speed toggle to make a walker go along the SAME path at a slower walking speed, while the timer runs in real time, and watch its duration-bar grow longer than before

startingActivity.intendedInsight: Duration can be seen directly — how long something takes on the clock — separately from how fast it goes, how far it travels, or how much happens during it. constraints: A static two-timer picture with tap-to-reveal can label quicker/slower but, being static, cannot animate duration growing independently of speed; use it as a scaffold, not as the moment that dislodges the confusion.
Selected-response/ordering tasks consolidate and check correct use of time language but do not require the learner to construct and justify a comparison in their own words.

Comparing duration is not primarily a spatial task, so a 3D representation offers little over clear timed comparisons here; this is a scoping note, not a claim that any medium is incapable of teaching it.

Keep comparisons fair: use a common start when finishing order is meant to show who was quicker, and only introduce different-start cases deliberately to teach that start time matters.

startingActivity.title: Order the day and slide the 'today' marker
learnerActions: Put pictures of the day's events — wake up, breakfast, school, bed — into chronological order.
Narrate the ordered sequence aloud using 'first… next… last' (e.g. 'first we wake up, next we have breakfast, last we go to bed').
The same drag-to-order can be used with story-sequencing picture cards: retell a familiar story in order, not only the daily routine, narrating it with first/next/last.

On a scrolling strip of consecutive days with a moveable 'today' marker (e.g. Tuesday–Wednesday–Thursday), start with 'today' on the MIDDLE day so both neighbours are visible, and say what happened yesterday (the day before) and what will happen tomorrow (the day after).

Slide the view forward one day, keeping 'today' on the middle slot: the day that was 'tomorrow' is now 'today', the day that was 'today' is now 'yesterday', the oldest day slides off and a new day comes into view ahead, so all three relative labels stay represented and keep re-pointing.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Yesterday and tomorrow are not interchangeable words for 'a day that isn't today' — they name a definite place relative to where 'now' sits, and they re-point as 'today' moves. Sequencing follows real chronology, not how exciting an event is.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A visual daily-timeline / sequence strip of routine events

commonMisconceptions: Swaps yesterday and tomorrow (both used loosely for 'a day that isn't today')
Reverses before/after, or uses 'next' for the last thing
Ties morning/afternoon to particular activities rather than the time of day
Sequences by salience (the most exciting event first) rather than chronology
constraints: Teach by modelling and eliciting USE; never ask a 4-6 year old to define a time word.
Anchor in the child's own daily routine, shared class events and familiar stories, and revisit the terms daily so the shifting deictic meaning is rehearsed in context.
Tie yesterday/today/tomorrow to concrete markers — what we DID and what we WILL do.
Anchor morning/afternoon/evening to the time of day, not to a single activity: afternoon is the time after midday until evening, and many different activities can happen then.

Treat early slips (swapping yesterday/tomorrow, reversing before/after, sequencing by salience) as developmental, expected and self-correcting with age and exposure — not as errors to drill or confront with a rule.
The static part-of-day timeline is a naming scaffold only: it does not let the child sequence or experience the deictic shift, so do not rely on it for the full objective.
Scored ordering/matching tasks cannot assess spontaneous spoken use in live context; combine them with listening for correct use in conversation.
Keep conversational exchanges short, concrete and child-led for this age range.

startingActivity.title: Time a real activity with start and stop aligned to the event
learnerActions: Pick a short, real activity to time (e.g. writing your name five times, tidying a small tray, building a block tower).

Choose the right tool: for an open-ended duration use a stopwatch or a seconds count/large seconds display; a fixed one-minute sand timer is best for checking whether something takes about a minute or comparing against its known span.
Hold the visible timing tool ready.
Count '3-2-1 start' and start the tool at the exact moment the activity begins.
Stop the tool the instant the activity finishes (on the last action).
Read off and say the duration in simple terms, e.g. 'about half a minute', 'about 40 seconds', 'a bit more than a minute'.
Repeat with a second activity and compare which took longer.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 'How long' is a quantity you can capture with a tool by aligning start and stop with the event, not a feeling guessed from how fast or how effortful the activity was.

keyRepresentations: Sand timers of known durations (1 minute, 3 minutes)
A stopwatch or large seconds display
A number line / counting track of seconds
A one-minute timer paired with a count to 60
commonMisconceptions: Judges duration by speed or by how much happened, not elapsed time (carried from comparing durations)

Reads the number currently showing as the duration, ignoring where timing started
Thinks 'a minute' and '60 seconds' are different amounts
constraints: This is a procedural, embodied skill: assess by WATCHING the child start and stop the tool with the event, not by asking them to recite the procedure or a fact. Reciting '1 minute = 60 seconds' is not by itself evidence they can measure.

Prefer sand timers first — duration is visible as the sand falls — before digital stopwatches; a fixed sand timer and a stopwatch give different experiences (checking a known span vs capturing an open-ended duration) and can be compared, with neither being universally necessary.

A recognition/ordering quiz (reading a stopwatch value, ordering activities by length) can check whether a child reads a duration, but does not elicit the act of measuring — starting and stopping in step with an event — which is the main objective.
A static labelled timer image can name the parts of a tool but does not let the child time an event or watch a duration accrue; use it as a scaffold, not as the performance itself.
Sand timers and stopwatches are concrete tools; a screen bar/ring display is one optional representation of the same idea, not a replacement for timing a real activity.

activityReferences.title: The hour hand's double lap: why a day is 24 hours
Closing the hour at 60: the non-decimal grouping

startingActivity.title: The hour hand's double lap: why a day is 24 hours
learnerActions: Move the hour hand slowly round an analogue clock from midday, naming the hours aloud as it passes the numbers.
When the hand returns to 12, pause and count: that first lap covered 12 hours (midday through to midnight).
Send the hand round a second time, now naming the night and morning hours, and track a day-strip that fills behind the clock — one half for the first lap, the second half for the second lap.
Write down the total: 12 + 12 = 24 hours in a whole day and night.
Line a 12-hour clock up beside a 24-hour clock so that, for example, 1pm matches 13:00, confirming the numbers 1-12 get used twice.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A whole day is 24 hours because the hour hand goes round the 12-number clock face twice — once from midday to midnight and once from midnight to midday — so 12 + 12 = 24, not 12. One lap alone is 12 hours; it takes two laps to make a day.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Analogue clock face
A number line marked in minutes and hours
A day-strip showing two 12-hour halves (day and night)
A 24-hour clock shown alongside the 12-hour clock
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a day is 12 hours because the clock face 'stops at 12'
Over-applies base-10 — treats 1 hour as 100 minutes, 90 minutes as 9 hours, or half an hour as 50 minutes
Fails to regroup at 60 when adding times (3:40 + 30 minutes = 3:70)
Muddles which unit is larger (minute vs hour)
constraints: Target the fact and its use, not the astronomy: the Earth-rotation cause of a 24-hour day is a different topic and is not the learning objective here.
Keep one-lap=12 hours and two-laps=24 hours distinct in all learner-facing wording; never state or imply that the hour hand goes 'once round' in 24 hours.

Recognition-only checks (multiple choice, fill-in) confirm recall and can catch some regrouping errors, but they do not by themselves show the learner can explain the double sweep or regroup a fresh duration — pair them with a 'why' prompt that elicits the reasoning.

A static labelled clock or day-strip, or a character/dialogue, can state the facts but does not let the learner watch the double sweep or the 60-grouping happen; treat these as lighter scaffolds, not replacements for counting/tracking the motion.
Explicitly contrast time with base-10 (60 not 100) rather than assuming learners will transfer money reasoning correctly; the base-10 over-application is the main error to pre-empt.
Half an hour is 30 minutes because half of 60 is 30; do not let '50 minutes' (half of 100) stand as an acceptable answer.

startingActivity.title: Timed race from a shared start line, then order the duration bars
learnerActions: Run or watch two or three timed events that all begin at the same common start (for example three sand-timers started together, or three classroom activities timed with a stopwatch).
Watch each event's duration grow as a bar (or sand-timer level) and note the moment it stops.
Arrange the finished bars/timers into order from shortest to longest duration — the order is simply the bar lengths.
Explain how you decided, pointing to the measured length rather than how fast or exciting each looked.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: How long an event lasts is read from its measured duration, not from how fast, far, or exciting it was. With a common start, whoever stopped first took the shortest time.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Stopwatch / sand-timers giving a measured duration
Duration bars laid side by side for ordering
A common start-line for fair comparison
A daily timeline for sequencing intervals
commonMisconceptions: Judges duration by speed or distance (faster/further = longer) — the time-speed-distance confusion
Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took longer', ignoring the start
Orders by how exciting or memorable an event was rather than its measured length
Treats a bigger clock-number at the end as a longer duration
constraints: Learners this age cannot yet calculate elapsed time, so comparison must rest on measured or timed evidence (stopwatch, sand-timers, duration bars); a common start is required only when fair finishing-order reasoning is used to judge who was quicker.

Ordering by how exciting or memorable an event felt is common at this age and often improves with repeated measured evidence; respond by re-lining-up the measured durations side by side and reading the order off the lengths.

A static two-timer picture with tap-to-reveal can label longer/shorter but does not let the child measure and order events live; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for timing and arranging real durations.
Spoken commentary can invite comparison but does not itself supply the measured evidence that settles which event took longer; pair any discussion with timers or measured lengths.
Timer-reading comparison and matching are recognition tasks: they verify a decision but do not require the learner to independently run and measure events, so include hands-on timing too.

startingActivity.title: Build the jumps on a number line
learnerActions: Start at the first time (e.g. 2:50) on a blank number line.
Make the first jump to the next o'clock (2:50 → 3:00, a +10 jump) and say the number bond to 60 that produced it (50 + 10 = 60).
Make whole-hour hops next (3:00 → 4:00, +1 hour).
Add the remaining minutes (4:00 → 4:10, +10).
Keep a running total of the jumps to assemble the duration (1 hour 20 minutes).

Compare this count-on method with column subtraction: line up 4:10 − 2:50 and notice the minutes column needs borrowing, and that borrowing as if there were 100 minutes in an hour goes wrong, because the minutes are base-60, not base-10.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Counting on from start to end — bridging the o'clock, adding whole hours, then the remaining minutes — gives the duration reliably, and column subtraction misleads across the hour unless you remember an hour holds 60 minutes, not 100.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Blank number line with jumps (to next o'clock, whole hours, remaining minutes)
Analogue / digital clocks showing start and end
Number bond to 60 for the bridging jump
commonMisconceptions: Uses column subtraction of end minus start, which breaks across the hour boundary
Thinks a later end time automatically means a longer duration
Works in 100s not 60s (treats the minutes as base-10)
Counts in the wrong direction or forgets the bridging jump to the o'clock
constraints: Use number bonds to 60 (not 100) for the jump to the next o'clock; the minutes column does not carry in base-10.

Analogue/digital clocks showing start and end, and a blank number line with labelled jumps, support the method; a static worked number line can only annotate one example and cannot let the child build the jumps.

Comparing durations depends on first calculating each duration; do not judge 'longer' by the later end time.
Keep every feedback example consistent with its activity's stated setup, or state explicitly that a slip is general to any start/end time.

activityReferences.title: Count on along a number line to find the end time
Fill the gap to find a duration
Decide the direction before you jump

startingActivity.title: Count on along a number line to find the end time
learnerActions: Read a word problem such as: 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?'
Draw a blank number line and mark the start time (2:15).
Make a first jump that bridges to the next o'clock: +45 minutes to reach 3:00.
Make a second jump with the remaining minutes: +2 to reach 3:02; label each jump and read off the end time.
Repeat with a harder bridge: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Jump +20 to 4:00, then +15 to reach 4:15.
Check the end time on a clock face.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Adding a duration means counting FORWARD from the start; bridging to the next o'clock first makes the hour roll over correctly, so you never write an impossible time like 2:62 or 3:75.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Blank number line with labelled jumps
Clocks marking start and end
The 'bridge to the next o'clock' jump
commonMisconceptions: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
Column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
Counts in the wrong direction (subtracts a duration instead of adding, or vice versa)
Overshoots or undershoots the o'clock bridge (base-10 slip)
constraints: Pupils should already read and record time in seconds, minutes and hours and compare durations before tackling these word problems; if they write times with 60+ minutes, revisit how 60 minutes rolls the hour over before continuing.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items about elapsed time can check whether answers are correct, but they do not show whether the child built the jumps or bridged the o'clock; pair them with a 'show your jumps' task so the method is visible.
A fixed worked-example diagram can illustrate the jumps but does not let the child build them in either direction; use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
A spoken or dialogue format can pose word problems and prompt reasoning, but still needs the child to actually draw and label jumps so the method is practised, not just discussed.

An interactive number line where jumps are dragged and a clock rolls over as each jump lands can make the hour roll-over visible in real time; this is one helpful presentation, not a requirement — the same learning can happen with pencil-and-paper number lines and a physical clock face.
Always state the known times explicitly (the start time for end-time problems, both times for duration problems, and the end time for start-time problems) so the direction of counting is unambiguous.

startingActivity.title: Wind the clock and watch the hour hand slide
learnerActions: On a geared teaching clock (one where turning the minute hand drives the hour hand in proportion), start at 7 o'clock with the minute hand on 12 and the hour hand exactly on the 7.
Slowly turn the minute hand clockwise (the way clock hands normally go: 12, 1, 2, 3…) round the face to the 6, and watch the hour hand crawl away from the 7 toward the 8.
Stop when the minute hand reaches the 6 — half a turn round — and check where the hour hand is: it sits exactly halfway between 7 and 8.
Say the time aloud as 'half past 7', naming which hand told you it was a HALF (the minute hand, half way round) and which told you the hour (the hour hand, past the 7).
Repeat starting from several other o'clock positions (3, 9, 11) so you see the same halfway pattern each time.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: At half past, the hour hand is dragged halfway between two numbers by the minute hand's half turn; 'half past 7' means 'half way past 7', not 'hour hand on 7 or 8'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A geared analogue clock
Blank clock faces for drawing hands
A clock with the two hands colour-coded (short = hour, long = minute)
A half-circle sweep showing the minute hand's half turn
commonMisconceptions: Puts or expects the hour hand exactly on a number at half past, instead of halfway between
Confuses the minute and hour hands (reads or draws the wrong one)
Reads half past by the number the hour hand is nearest rather than the one it has passed (half past 3 read as half past 4)
Reads the clock as a bare number, matching a hand to a numeral, ignoring what each hand measures
constraints: Use a geared or linked clock so the hour hand moves in proportion as the minute hand turns; a clock whose hands can be set independently will not show the proportional relationship and may reinforce the hour-hand-on-a-number error.
Establish o'clock (minute hand on 12, hour hand exactly on a number) before introducing half past (minute hand on 6, hour hand between numbers).
Always pair reading with drawing: given a time, draw both hands; given a clock, say the time.

Matching clocks to times by selecting among ready-made options is recognition, not construction; it does not reveal whether a child can place the hour hand correctly between numbers and should be followed by actual drawing.

A static labelled clock (e.g. tap-to-reveal names of the hands) can introduce which hand is which, but cannot show the two hands moving together or catch a mis-drawn hour hand; treat it as an introductory scaffold, not the main activity.
Colour-code the hands (short = hour, long = minute) and name each hand's job to help prevent swapping their meanings.

startingActivity.title: Count round the clock in fives
learnerActions: Starting at the 12, count the minute marks in fives round the clock, saying the running total at each number: 1→5, 2→10, 3→15, 4→20, 5→25, and so on.
Label (or tap, if using an interactive clock where each number lights its running five-count) each number with its minute value.
Then read a real clock showing 3:25: minute hand on the 5, hour hand between the 3 and the 4 but not yet halfway, so the hour is still 3. State the minutes as twenty-five, not five.
Repeat with other 'past' times to five minutes.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The number the minute hand points to is NOT the number of minutes — each number stands for its multiple of five, so the minute hand on the 5 means 25 minutes, not 5.

keyRepresentations: A clock with the 5-minute counts marked around it
A past/to split clock (right = past, left = to)
A geared clock for the hour-hand position

commonMisconceptions: Reads the minute-hand number directly (minute hand on 5 → '5 past' not 25 past; on 2 → '2 past' not 10 past)
Confuses quarter past and quarter to
After half past, keeps counting 'past' (35 minutes past) instead of switching to 'to' (25 to)
Names the wrong hour for a 'to' time, or puts the hour hand on a number instead of partway toward the next
constraints: The objective requires pupils to both tell AND write time to five minutes including quarter past/to, and to draw the hands — so recognition-only matching tasks must be followed by independent construction (drawing hands, writing the time).

A static labelled clock can show the five-counts but cannot demonstrate the 'past'→'to' switch dynamically or check a learner's drawn hour hand; use it as a reference, and still have learners draw and move hands.
A geared or movable clock is valuable for showing the hour hand's gradual position between numbers, which a fixed picture cannot be adjusted to demonstrate.
Spoken rehearsal of times supports the language but does not replace reading, writing, and drawing on actual clock faces.

When introducing the digital form of 'to' times, note that the hour numeral stays as the earlier hour (quarter to 4 = 3:45) even though we name 'four' when speaking — a common point of confusion to handle explicitly.

startingActivity.title: Drag the minute hand and watch the count-in-fives and digital readout
learnerActions: Drag the minute hand around a moveable-hands clock and watch a 'count in 5s' tape (5, 10, 15, 20...) unroll around the rim as a digital readout ticks alongside.
Pause when the minute hand reaches the numeral 4 and confirm the tape and readout say 20 minutes, not 4 — then do the same for numeral 8 (40 minutes).
Watch a vertical 12-to-6 line shade one colour on the right (past) and another on the left (to), and read 3:40 aloud as 'twenty TO four'.

Flip an a.m./p.m. toggle that slides a marker along a day-strip so the SAME hand position recurs 12 hours later — once in the morning (e.g. 8 o'clock breakfast, a.m.) and again 12 hours on in the evening (p.m.).
Write the shown time as h:mm using a colon with its a.m./p.m. label (e.g. 3:25 p.m.), then rewrite it in 24-hour notation (e.g. 15:25; 8:05 a.m. = 08:05).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Each clock numeral stands for its five-times value, 'to' times are named against the next hour, and every clock position recurs 12 hours later, so each clock time happens twice in one day, split at noon and midnight.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Analogue clock with moveable hands
Counting the 12 intervals in fives (5 times-table)
Vertical 12-to-6 partition for past/to
12-hour digital display (h:mm)
A daily timeline split at noon and midnight for a.m./p.m.
commonMisconceptions: Reads the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes (points to 4 -> '4 minutes past')
Confuses times past and times to the hour
Insecure 5 times-table blocks fluent counting of minutes
Writes a decimal point instead of a colon (3.25)
Thinks there are 100 minutes in an hour, so 50 past 3 = 50 to 4
Confuses a.m. and p.m. (1 a.m. 'should be' 1 p.m. because it feels late); doesn't know noon/midnight or that each time occurs twice a day
constraints: Secure recall of the 5 times-table underpins fluent counting of minutes; weak recall blocks fluent counting of the minutes, so rehearse it alongside clock reading. (It does not by itself block the past/to or a.m./p.m. reasoning.)

Write digital times with a colon (the convention used here; some styles write 3.25 with a full stop, but the separator is never a decimal point); the hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so '50 past 3' is 'ten to 4', not '50 to 4' via base-10 reasoning.
'To' times must be named against the NEXT hour (3:40 = 'twenty to four'), decided by whether the minute hand is left of the 12-6 line.
a.m./p.m. must be grounded in the noon/midnight split and the fact that each clock time occurs twice a day, not in how 'late' a time feels.

The static tap-to-reveal face and the conversation are scaffolds: the first cannot move hands or convert to digital; the second cannot show the reading method. Use them to support, not replace, work with moveable hands.
Recognition, matching and sorting tasks check and rehearse the rule but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading from scratch or physically set the hands.

startingActivity.title: Count on from the last five on a moveable clock
learnerActions: On a clock with moveable hands and a minute scale (tick marks), set the minute hand to a target such as 43 minutes.
Find the last 5-minute mark the hand has passed (40) by counting the fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40.
Count on the extra single minutes from there: 41, 42, 43 — do not count all 43 ticks one at a time from the 12.
Check the hour hand: notice it has moved about three-quarters of the way toward the next numeral, and say the hour as the number it has LAST passed.
Try another near-the-hour example: set 9:57 — the hour hand is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9 because that is the number it has last passed.
Read the whole time aloud (e.g. 'forty-three minutes past seven' / 'seven forty-three').
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The quick, reliable way to read exact minutes is to land on the nearest 5-minute mark below the hand and count on the remaining minutes, and to read the hour as the numeral the hour hand has last passed.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Analogue clock with a minute scale (tick marks)
Counting on from the last multiple of five
Number line for past-to-to conversion; part-whole bond to 60
Paired analogue and digital displays
commonMisconceptions: Counts individual minutes from 12 to the hand instead of counting on from the nearest 5 below (slow and error-prone)
Multi-step 'minutes to' reading breaks down (miscounts the bond to 60)
Reads the hour as the numeral the hour hand is nearest, so 7:43 becomes '8:43' (hour hand almost on 8)
Reads a digital time literally rather than converting it (says 'seven forty-three' but can't render it on analogue or as a 'to' time)
constraints: A static labelled clock can display one worked time but does not let the child rehearse the count-on procedure or watch the hour hand travel; use it as a worked example, not as the main practice.
Prompted oral readings (a character asking 'what time is it?') can elicit answers but do not reveal HOW the child finds the minutes; pair them with tasks where the method is visible.
Recognition/matching tasks assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading or set the hands; include writing and hand-setting for production.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: lighting the 5-minute marks in groups up to the last interval in one colour, then single count-on minutes in another colour; a toggle that rolls the reading round a 0–60 number line to show the 'to' form; an hour hand that creeps toward the next numeral so the child must read last-passed. These are illustrative, not required.
When scaffolding a child who counts single minutes, do not reteach clock reading from scratch — prompt them to the nearest five and count on.

activityReferences.title: Walk the 24-hour day-line and watch the two clocks agree
Decide before-or-after-noon first, then convert
Match and build a conversion table
Timetable word problems that force the right decision

startingActivity.title: Walk the 24-hour day-line and watch the two clocks agree
learnerActions: Move a marker along a day-line running from midnight 00:00 through noon 12:00 and back to midnight, watching a 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) readout and a 24-hour readout change together as the marker moves.

Stop the marker just before noon and just after: just before, both displays read 11:59 (11:59 a.m. and 11:59); at noon both read 12:00 and only the 12-hour LABEL flips from a.m. to p.m. (so it shows 12:00 p.m., not 1:00). Then move on past 1 p.m. and watch the 24-hour clock tick to 13:00 while the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. — this is where the 12-of-difference first appears.
Stop at midnight and read both displays; confirm the 24-hour clock shows 00:00 (a new day starting), not 24:00, by looking at what it shows one minute before and one minute after.

For a chosen afternoon time from 1 p.m. onward, read the 12-hour value, then the 24-hour value, and state the relationship: 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' — noting that the 12:xx noon hour is the exception, where both forms still read 12.

If a day-line is available, use its paired displays and boundary labels at 00:00 (midnight, new day) and 12:00 (noon); if not, draw the day-line on paper, mark 00:00, 12:00 and 24:00->00:00, and write both forms side by side for several times.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The +12 / -12 relationship is not an arbitrary rule but the afternoon and evening hours continuing to count on past 12; noon and midnight are fixed boundaries, the 12:xx noon hour still reads 12 in both forms, and the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 straight to 00:00.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Paired 12-hour and 24-hour digital displays
Analogue clock for representing a converted time
A 12-hour to 24-hour conversion table
The 24-hour day-line (00:00 midnight -> 12:00 noon -> back to 00:00)
commonMisconceptions: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
Adds 12 to a.m. times too (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38')
Writes midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00
When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m. on the answer
constraints: Target age roughly 8-9 (Year 4); procedural measurement objective: read, write and convert between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks.

Always decide before/after noon FIRST; add 12 only to p.m. times 1:00-11:59, subtract 12 only from 24-hour times 13:00 onward. a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 are NOT given +12 — they keep their hour, with a leading zero only for single-digit hours (9:45 a.m. -> 09:45, but 10:15 a.m. -> 10:15); the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is written 00:xx.

The 12:xx noon hour stays 12:xx p.m. — do not subtract 12 from it; noon is 12:00 and midnight is 00:00, never 24:00. At noon both forms read 12:00; the 24-hour ticks to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. only when passing 1 p.m., so the 12-of-difference begins after the noon hour, not at noon.
24-hour times always show four digits; single-digit hours take a leading zero (09:45, 06:38).
Always label a.m./p.m. on a 12-hour answer.

Matching and multiple-choice recognition confirm a learner can identify correct conversions but do not by themselves show the learner can construct conversions unaided; pair them with activities requiring the learner to produce conversions in both directions.

A static paired-clock poster can label the two formats but cannot show the marker crossing noon or the boundary behaviour; treat a drawn or printed day-line as a static scaffold and have the learner reason through the noon/midnight transitions aloud.
An interactive day-line is one helpful representation, not the only way to teach this; a hand-drawn day-line, a conversion table, and analogue-clock work are valid concrete alternatives.

startingActivity.title: Multiply-then-combine with a conversion machine
learnerActions: Take a mixed quantity such as 3 hours 25 minutes and convert it: multiply the whole units by the rate (3 × 60 = 180 minutes), then add the remaining 25 to get 205 minutes.
State out loud whether you counted up or multiplied, and why multiplying is faster.
Work a reverse conversion: take 150 seconds, group it into sixties — two full groups of 60 make 2 minutes, with 30 seconds left over, giving '2 minutes 30 seconds'.
Test the tempting '100 to a minute' idea against grouping real seconds into sixties, and describe what goes wrong.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Converting units of time is multiply (by the fixed rate) then combine the remainder — not counting up — and for seconds, minutes and hours the grouping is 60, not 100.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Conversion tables (Days-Weeks, Years-Months, Minutes-Seconds)
The x60 / x7 / x12 rate as a known-fact chain (36 ÷ 6 = 6, so 360 s = 6 min)
A number track for counting leap years / weeks
A bar model splitting a mixed quantity into whole units + remainder
commonMisconceptions: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
Assumes base-10 (100 seconds in a minute, 100 minutes in an hour)
Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
Converts a mixed quantity by ignoring the remainder or the second unit
constraints: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (×60, ×7, ×12), not repeated addition; for mixed quantities convert whole units × rate, then add or keep the remainder.
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, not 100; the 100-to-a-minute idea should be shown wrong against real grouping, not merely stated wrong.
Handle reverse conversions by dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s), not rounding or dropping the leftover.
Keep exact rates (1 week = 7 days, 1 year = 12 months) distinct from the approximate month-to-weeks relationship; month lengths vary from 28 to 31 days.

Choosing a correct option in a matching or selection item checks reasoning but does not by itself demonstrate independent construction of the method; include tasks where the learner carries out and shows the conversion.
A fixed conversion poster or table can display the rates but does not let the learner compute and see the remainder form; treat it as a reference scaffold rather than the main activity.
A bar model (whole units + remainder) and a number track for counting weeks/leap years are optional representations that can scaffold the split and the counting, not required mechanisms.
Illustrative interactions (feeding units into a ×rate step, grouping seconds into sixties, a toggle offering the base-10 reading) are ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.

activityReferences.title: The looping days wheel: jump in anywhere, go both ways
Zoom from a day to the year: nesting made visible
Count across the calendar: dates and weekdays together
Daily calendar talk: functional use in conversation

startingActivity.title: The looping days wheel: jump in anywhere, go both ways
learnerActions: Spin or turn a days-of-the-week wheel and watch it roll past Sunday straight back to Monday, so the week never 'ends' — it comes round again.
Tap or point to any day (e.g. Wednesday) and name 'the day after' without singing from Sunday.
Answer 'what's after / before X' questions starting from a day in the middle, moving both forwards and backwards.
Optional: tapping a day lights up the day after and the day before so the child can check their answer against the wheel.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The days form a repeating cycle you can enter at any point and travel in either direction — not a one-way song that must restart from the beginning.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A wall calendar / month grid
A days-of-the-week wheel showing the cycle
A year strip divided into 12 months
Birthday and seasonal anchors on the calendar
commonMisconceptions: Recites the sequence but can't start from the middle ('what's after Wednesday?') without restarting
Cannot work backwards through the days/months
Doesn't grasp nesting — treats week, month, year as unrelated, or a year as vaguely 'a long time'
Treats the cycle as linear — nothing comes after Sunday or December
constraints: The core objective is functional use — random access in both directions, grasping the cycle and the nesting — not rote recitation of the days/months chant.

A static calendar with tap-to-reveal facts names the parts but does not itself show the loop or let the child count across dates; use it as a naming scaffold and pair it with a cyclic representation and a counting task.

Selection/ordering/multiple-choice items check knowledge of sequence and relative length but do not elicit independent spoken or calendar use; include at least one task where the child counts on a real calendar and names the date and weekday aloud.

The looping wheel and nested zoom are concrete ways to make cycle and nesting visible; they are suggested affordances, not the only valid medium — a page-turning calendar, year-strip, or verbal routine can serve the same purposes.

Rote recitation without random access, weak nesting, and a linear (non-cyclic) view are largely developmental for this age: build the structure visually and with daily practice rather than re-drilling the chant or confronting the child with a rule.

activityReferences.title: Advance a four-year calendar cycle and watch February change
Build the leap day from the Earth's orbit
Group seconds into minutes at exactly 60
Recall and sort the facts

startingActivity.title: Advance a four-year calendar cycle and watch February change
learnerActions: Step through four years one at a time on a calendar dial or a strip showing four Februaries in a row.
On years one, two and three, note that February has 28 days; on the fourth year watch a 29th day appear and the year-counter go from 365 to 366.
Say aloud what changes and what stays the same across the four years, then predict which upcoming calendar year will be the next leap year.
Tap or reveal each month in turn to pop up its length, and sort or describe the uneven 31/30/28 pattern as a shape, not just a list.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 'Every four years' is not an arbitrary rule to memorise - the extra day actually appears only on the fourth turn, and February is the month that gains it, while month lengths follow a lumpy repeating pattern.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A wall calendar / year-strip divided into 12 months
The knuckle mnemonic for month lengths
A stopwatch or number line marked in seconds
A four-year calendar cycle showing February gain a 29th day
An Earth-orbit model linking the year to one revolution
commonMisconceptions: Assumes all months are the same length (e.g. 30 days each)
Treats the leap-year rule as arbitrary, unconnected to the Earth's orbit
Over-applies base-10 to seconds and minutes (90 seconds = 0.9 of a minute; 1 minute 30 seconds = 130 seconds)
Thinks February always has 28 days
constraints: Fact-recall items (naming months, stating '60 seconds', multiple-choice on leap-year frequency) check recall and classification but do not by themselves elicit the causal explanation of leap years or the regrouping skill for seconds/minutes; always pair recall with a 'why' or a conversion task.

A static calendar or year-strip with tap-to-reveal month lengths can name the facts and show the irregular pattern, but cannot run the four-year cycle or demonstrate the 60-grouping dynamically; use it as a naming scaffold, not as the full objective.

A character explaining months and leap years can introduce the facts; the four-year cycle and the 60-grouping may be easier to follow through a worked or observed sequence, though the cited sources do not establish this comparison. Treat the character as an introduction scaffold.
Keep the orbit model focused on the quarter-day accumulation; the objective is the leap-year fact and cycle, not full orbital mechanics.
Mnemonics (knuckles, '30 days hath September') aid recall of month lengths but do not teach why leap years occur; treat them as memory aids only.

learnerActions: Set up a shopping problem: two items at 65p and 20p, paying with £1

startingActivity.intendedInsight: In a multi-step problem each number along the way means something specific; the answer is only right when you name the quantity the question actually asked for and check it is reasonable in context.

The worked-example walkthrough is a scaffold: it illustrates the process but does not elicit the child's own representation choice or an independent sense-check, so it should not replace build-and-check practice
The dialogue/shopkeeper activity should never be scored

This objective involves money/measurement/time, which is not spatial-3D, so a 3D build is not specifically matched to it; this is a fit note for this objective, not a claim that 3D media teach nothing in general
Arithmetic check: 65p + 20p = 85p (the interim total, which is the COST), and since £1 = 100p, 100p − 85p = 15p is the CHANGE; keep these two quantities distinct in every representation

startingActivity.title: Till total: more coins is not always more money
learnerActions: Drop real coins (or coins onto a running-total mat/till) one at a time and watch the TOTAL VALUE build up.

startingActivity.title: Build a target several ways with a live-updating total
learnerActions: Take a target amount (e.g. 50p) and drag or place real-denomination coins into a tray until they reach the total.
Watch a running total so you can see when the tray reaches exactly 50p.
Once a valid way is found, record it on an organised board or list of 'ways to make 50p', then find another distinct way.
Work from the largest coin first, or swap a coin for equivalent smaller ones, so the search is organised rather than random.
Only real coins are available on the shelf (no 8p), so every solution is one that could really be paid.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Many different coin sets can share the same total value; building each one and watching the total confirm the target makes 'equal value, different coins' directly visible.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Real coins arranged into equal-value sets
A part-whole model (total = these coins / those coins)
An organised list or table of combinations
Swapping one coin for equivalent smaller coins
commonMisconceptions: Uses a non-existent coin (e.g. an '8p') to make a total
Finds combinations unsystematically, repeating some and missing others
Tracks the number of coins rather than their total value
Thinks a set with more coins must be worth more, so two ways can't be equal
constraints: Use only real coin denominations; there is no 8p (or 3p) coin, though any total can be built from the coins that do exist.

Systematic enumeration develops with age and practice: treat random searching not as an error to punish but as a cue to model one system (largest coin first, then swap down) and record each way on an organised list.
Recognition and sorting tasks (choosing which given sets make a total) check judgement of value but do not require independent construction of combinations; include building tasks for production.
A static 'ways to make 50p' poster can display combinations but does not let the learner build or swap them; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main activity.

Assess by watching HOW combinations are generated (systematic vs random, real coins vs an invented coin) and by asking why two different sets are equal — this distinguishes secure combining from guesswork and catches the more-coins-means-more-money misconception.

startingActivity.title: Give change at a role-play market stall (count up with coins)
learnerActions: Set up a shop: a toy priced 35p, a 50p coin to pay with, and a pot of mixed coins.
Count UP aloud from the price to the amount paid, placing a coin into a change tray at each step: '35… (put in a 5p) 40… (put in a 10p) 50'.
State the change as the coins you built: 'The change is 15p — a 10p and a 5p.'
Check by counting the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid (35p + 15p = 50p).
Repeat with other friendly prices (e.g. 45p paid with 50p gives 5p), then extend to the source worked example 27p paid with 50p, counting 27→30→50 to give 3p + 20p = 23p.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Change is the DISTANCE travelled from the price up to the amount paid — it is the total of the jumps you make when counting up (here 5p + 10p = 15p), not a take-away you have to work out on paper. The coins themselves record how the change was reached.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Real/realistic coins counted into the hand (coins as a record of the steps)
Empty number line showing change as jumps from price up to amount paid
Part–whole (bar) model: amount paid = cost + change
A shop/role-play till context
commonMisconceptions: 'More coins = more money' — thinks a fistful of small coins is worth more, so gives too many or judges having-enough by count not value.
Adds the two numbers (price + amount paid) instead of finding the difference, because early teaching over-emphasises 'take away' and difference is not recognised as subtraction.
Loses the running total or miscounts when bridging through a multiple of ten while counting up.
Counts single pennies one-by-one inaccurately instead of using coin values.
constraints: Keep amounts to friendly values that bridge a single multiple of ten first (e.g. 35p→50p), then extend once secure.
A tap-to-reveal picture of coins can serve as a reference to coin values; it does not let the child carry out or get feedback on the counting-up procedure, so it is a scaffold, not the main activity.
Recognition/short-answer checks assess the answer, not the method; they do not elicit the independent counting-up construction that is the objective.
Running-total bars (anchored at the price), number-line jumps, and a change tray are optional supports to make the gap visible — offer them to illustrate the mechanism, not as mandatory steps.

Keep the value of the change coins distinct from the running total: the change coins total the difference (e.g. 15p), while the running total counted on from the price reaches the amount paid (e.g. 50p).
Always have the child check reasonableness by counting the change back onto the price to rebuild the amount paid.

startingActivity.title: Build a price with coins and record it correctly
learnerActions: Look at a price tag (e.g. 75p, or £1 and 50p) and choose real or on-screen coins to make exactly that amount
Say the running total by VALUE as each coin is added — e.g. '50... 70... 75' — not by the number of coins
Write the amount down in a correct form, then write it a second way if possible (150p / £1 and 50p)
Check your written amount against the rule: never put £ and p together
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An amount of money can be built from coins by adding their values to a target, and the same amount has more than one correct written form, but £ and p are never written together.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Price tags and till displays showing £ and p
Real coins combined to make a target amount
A 'say it / write it' pairing (150p to £1 and 50p)
A part-whole model of an amount split into coins
commonMisconceptions: Writes £ and p together (£1.50p, £50p)
Muddles the two symbols or which side the symbol goes
Reads 150p and £1 and 50p as different amounts (misses the equivalence)
When combining coins, counts the number of coins rather than their value toward the total
constraints: At Year 2 the central rule is recording pounds and pence separately and never writing £ and p together. The objective and the verified NCETM convention accept forms such as £1.50 and £1.00 (but not £1.50p); accept £1.50 as correct. The White Rose scheme (verified:false in the row) suggests Year 2 avoids decimal notation and uses 'and' (£5 and 30p); treat that stricter 'no decimal' guidance as unverified and do NOT use it to reject £1.50.
Keep any pence component below 100p when writing the split form (£1 and 50p, not £1 and 150p); this does not forbid the all-pence form 150p, which is a valid written form throughout.
The same amount has more than one correct written form (150p = £1 and 50p = £1.50); accept any correct form and treat them as equal money.
Assess by listening for correct USE in context — avoid asking the child to define a symbol in the abstract, as stated in the source's assessment approach.
A static price-tag poster or tap-to-reveal image can label £ and p but does not let the child build amounts or use the symbols in context; treat it as a labelling scaffold, not the main task.
Recognition/matching items check and rehearse the convention but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or real-context use; combine them with building and speaking tasks.
Interactive feedback examples (till display writing the running total, rejecting '£1.50p', 'say it two ways' toggle) are optional proposed illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.

startingActivity.title: Shop till: total, pay, and count change up
learnerActions: Choose two or three priced items (e.g. a £2.60 car and a £1.85 book) and total them, building the total step by step (£2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45).
Pay with a £5 note and work out the change by counting UP from the total to the note, drawing each jump on an empty number line: £4.45 → +5p → £4.50 → +50p → £5.00, so change is 55p.
Collect the change as actual coins into a tray; when the pennies/pence in the tray reach 100p, physically exchange them for a single £1 coin and re-read the amount as one quantity.
Repeat for a single £3.47 item paid with a £5 note: count up £3.47 → £3.50 → £4.00 → £5.00 = £1.53.

Record the change in £ and p notation (e.g. £0.55, 55p), then say the amount in a place-value-honest way suitable for Year 3 (e.g. 'fifty-five pence'); avoid reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds (e.g. 'three point forty-seven' for £3.47). Reading the digits separately ('nought point five five') is also acceptable and is the decimal reading the cited research recommends.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Change from a note is a short counting-on jump from the total to the note, and an amount in pounds and pence is ONE quantity because 100p exchanges for £1.

keyRepresentations: Empty number line for counting-on change from a note
Real coins/notes with 100p→£1 exchange
Part–whole (bar) model: note = total cost + change
Place-value columns (£ | tenths/10p | hundredths/1p) shown aligned by the decimal point
commonMisconceptions: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers (adds the pence column past 100 without exchanging, or writes £3.7 for £3 and 70p).
Notation errors — omits the decimal point, mixes units (£3.47p), or writes pence as if pounds.
Attempts change from £10 by column subtraction and makes 'take smaller from larger' / subtract-across-zeros errors instead of counting up.
'Most coins = most money' persists, and reading '£2.47' as 'two point forty-seven' reinforces the two-separate-numbers error.
constraints: Treat each money amount as ONE quantity: insist on exchanging 100p for £1, never carrying pence past 99 without exchanging and never writing three digits after the point.

Teach change from a £5/£10 note primarily by counting UP (finding the difference) on a number line; reserve column subtraction for cases without the across-zeros trap and only when done correctly with exchange.
Never present an incorrect money form (£347, £3.47p, £0.55p, pence written as pounds) as a correct option in a learner task; use such forms only as clearly labelled non-examples to be rejected.

Read amounts place-value-honestly for Year 3 ('three pounds and forty-seven pence', 'fifty-five pence'); the pitfall to avoid is reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds ('three point forty-seven'). Digit-by-digit decimal reading ('three point four seven') is acceptable and is the reading the cited research recommends.
Recognition/selection checks confirm notation and reasonableness but do not elicit the independent counting-on calculation; pair them with hands-on totalling, change-finding and recording.

The National Curriculum's non-statutory Year 3 notes and guidance say pupils record pounds and pence separately, with formal decimal recording of money introduced in Year 4; introduce the £3.47 form deliberately alongside its meaning, and expect some learners to still record pounds and pence separately.

Illustrative interactions (total bar, number-line jumps, 100p→£1 animation, coin tray) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and must not be treated as the only valid medium; coins, paper number lines and spoken rehearsal achieve the same purposes.

activityReferences.title: Proportional-coin workbench: build value and make change
Coin denomination reference with the size/worth contradiction

startingActivity.title: Proportional-coin workbench: build value and make change
learnerActions: Place coins onto a mat; as each coin is placed, it opens into its worth shown as unit-squares (dime = 10 squares, nickel = 5, penny = 1, quarter = 25) while a running total counts on by value.
Set the small dime beside the fatter nickel and compare the stacks of squares: the dime's 10 squares visibly outstretch the nickel's 5.
Build a target amount such as 30¢ in more than one way (e.g. three dimes; or a quarter and a nickel) and compare the coins used.
Switch to a make-change task: an item costs 40¢; pay with coins totalling 46¢ and count up the 6¢ change.
Count a mixed handful (2 dimes and 3 pennies) by counting on from the largest coin: 10, 20, then 21, 22, 23.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A coin's worth is a number of cents you count on, separate from the coin's size or how many coins there are; proportional value makes 'smaller but worth more' visible and concrete.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Proportional value strips / 'proportional dollar' (a coin laid over its worth in unit-squares)
A number line or hundred-square for skip-counting coin values
A coin-value reference (penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, dollar 100¢)
A part-whole bar for making change (cost and amount paid)
commonMisconceptions: Value = size: a bigger coin is worth more (nickel > dime; five pennies > three dimes)
Value = count: each coin counts as one, or all coins are counted by ones regardless of denomination (unitary thinking)
Cannot switch counting patterns — counts 25, 50, 75 then cannot shift to +10 for a dime or +1 for a penny
Notation errors — mixing $ and ¢ ($0.50¢, or $5 for a nickel), or writing 5¢ as $5
Overusing one denomination (all dimes) because counting by tens is easiest, rather than realistic combinations
constraints: When making a coin's worth visible, use a proportional representation (each coin shown as its worth in unit-squares) rather than relying on a realistic play coin, since a coin is not a concrete representation of its own value; real/realistic coins remain useful for diagnosis and handling.
Introduce denominations a couple at a time to limit how often the counting pattern must switch.
Build skip-counting (5s, 10s, 25s) and place value before totalling mixed collections.
Model 'counting on' from the largest coin and correct $/¢ notation, including 100¢ = $1.
A static denomination reference establishes facts but does not provide totalling or make-change practice; use it to support, not replace, hands-on value building.

Selected-response or slider checks can reward a correct number without revealing the size/count reasoning behind it; pair them with a 'show me why' step or hands-on value work. A check of this kind can assess totalling and comparison but does not itself elicit the proportional-value reasoning.
Real or realistic coins are useful for diagnosis and handling, but when teaching the size/worth contradiction, add a proportional value representation so worth is seen apart from size.
