activityReferences.title: Measure bench: estimate first, then check
Convert before you compare: the balance that tips
Money as one quantity: totalling £.p
Benchmark estimation across length, mass and capacity

startingActivity.title: Measure bench: estimate first, then check
learnerActions: Face a task: three priced items (£2.45, £1.30, £0.75) to total, or two measures to compare.

Round each amount to something friendly (£2.45≈£2, £1.30≈£1, £0.75≈£1) and commit a rough estimate BEFORE seeing any exact answer — for example drag a slider or write the estimate down and lock it in.
Keep benchmark referents in view while estimating (a £1 coin, a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle) so the estimate is anchored rather than guessed.
Only after the estimate is committed, reveal/compute the exact total (£4.50) and look at the gap between estimate and truth.
Decide out loud whether the exact answer is reasonable: does it land near the estimate (about £4)? If not, treat that as a flag to find an error.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An exact answer that lands far from a sensible estimate signals a likely error; landing near it makes the answer plausible, though it cannot catch every small slip (e.g. £4.40 instead of £4.50). Estimation is a deliberate step before calculation and a checkable habit afterwards, not an afterthought.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Benchmark referents (metre stick, 1 kg mass, 1 litre, £1 coin) for anchoring estimates
Double number line / bar model for comparing across units
Place-value columns aligned by the decimal point (metric measures and money)
Rounding number line for estimation before exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Compares across units by digits alone, ignoring the unit ('1200 g > 1.5 kg because 1200 > 1.5').
Skips estimation and so cannot judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.
'String-length thinking' persists in totals — treats £2.45 or 2 m 30 cm as two separate whole numbers when adding.
Rounds after calculating rather than before, or rounds the wrong way, so the estimate is useless as a check.
constraints: Estimation must be committed BEFORE the exact value is revealed or calculated — otherwise it cannot serve as a check and becomes an afterthought.

A labelled picture or benchmark image can show what a metre, 1 kg or £1 looks like, but on its own cannot run the estimate-then-check loop or a unit conversion; use it as a referent, not as the full activity.

Recognition/ordering formats (choose-the-heavier, order these) can rehearse and check each skill crisply but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own free reasoning; pair them with prompts asking the learner to state and justify the estimate and the conversion.

A 3D balance or container adds physicality to mass/capacity comparison but is optional; the core reasoning (convert, compare, estimate) is numeric and not inherently spatial, and is not needed for money or estimation.

Interaction examples (slider to commit an estimate, a balance that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips, double number lines, decimal-aligned place-value columns) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory tools.

Role-play dialogue does not by itself require the learner to carry out the estimation or unit conversion this objective targets, so on its own it may not elicit the procedural steps; if used, direct it to prompt the learner to state and justify an estimate rather than relying on it to teach the procedure.

activityReferences.title: One array, four facts
Partition to derive a harder product
Predict which column moves
Classify by properties, not by how it looks

startingActivity.title: One array, four facts
learnerActions: Lay out 24 counters as 6 rows of 4 and state the multiplication it shows (6×4=24).
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn and read it again as 4 rows of 6; say why 6×4 and 4×6 are the same 24 dots seen two ways.
Cover one factor: with 24 shared into 4 rows, read off how many are in each row (6) to get 24÷4; then read 24÷6 the same way.
Say in your own words how knowing 6×4=24 means you already know 24÷4 and 24÷6 without counting.
Try a second fact family (e.g. 5 rows of 3) and derive all four facts from the single array.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: One rectangular array holds a whole fact family; multiplication and division are the same structure read different ways, so a known product gives the related quotients without recomputing.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Rectangular array / area model for the multiplication-division fact family
Three-digit place-value apparatus and arrow cards
Property checklists and Venn-style overlapping shape sets
Distributive splits (7×8 as 7×5 + 7×3) shown on a partitioned array
commonMisconceptions: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite knowing 6×4
When adding 100 to a three-digit number, changes the wrong column or mis-carries
Classifies shapes by orientation/appearance (a rotated square becomes a 'diamond'; only a 'pointing-up' triangle is a triangle)
Thinks a derived fact must be checked by counting because facts feel separate rather than connected
constraints: The teaching aim is the transfer habit 'which fact that I already know helps here?' — reaching the right numbers is not enough; the child should explain why one fact yields the others.

A fixed reference diagram of a fact family or distributive split can annotate and explain, but cannot be rotated or re-covered by the learner; a manipulable array lets the child test that a turned array re-reads and that covering a factor reveals a quotient. Use static diagrams as support, not as the sole route to the deriving habit.

Matching or derive-the-answer tasks (from 6×4=24, give 24÷6) can check whether facts are treated as connected, but a correct answer may be a recomputed one; always pair with 'which known fact did you use?' to distinguish deriving from recalculating.

Carrying is an exception to 'only one column changes': when adding 100/10/1 causes a carry, the named column fills and rolls into the next place. Address this explicitly rather than teaching 'the other columns never change'.

Fact families and three-digit place value are quantitative; 2D shape classification by property needs the 2D figure and its properties. These do not require 3D models, though a 3D context is not forbidden where genuinely useful.

Optional interaction examples (tap to highlight 6×4, rotate the array to read 4×6, cover a factor to reveal a division, a predict-then-check place-value wheel, live recolouring of a checklist while rotating a shape) make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.

startingActivity.title: Build, extend, and name the unit of repeat
learnerActions: Continue a given model pattern, e.g. red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue — carry it on further with cubes, beads, or drawn shapes.
Circle or box the part that repeats and say where the pattern 'starts over'.

Name which items are the SAME and which is DIFFERENT: for red, blue, blue the two blues are the same and the red is the different cube that starts the chunk (spoken in order: different, same, same). The plain 'same, same, different' chant maps most cleanly to a two-same-then-different unit such as AAB.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that repeats; the pattern is the unit, not just the next item you could add.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Colour/shape cube or bead strings
The unit of repeat circled or boxed
ABB / AAB units contrasted with AB
'Same, same, different' labelling of the unit
Number sequences and skip-counting as patterns
commonMisconceptions: Extends a pattern by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping that there is a repeating unit.
Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer (makes ABAB for an ABB model).
Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit plus extra items that break the unit.
constraints: A static pattern with the unit highlighted (e.g. tap to box the unit and reveal which items are same/different) is a useful reference, but a fixed display on its own does not let the child extend, abstract, or isolate the unit; pair it with building/doing tasks.

Sequence and fill-in-the-blank response formats can check 'what comes next' and 'circle the unit', but risk rewarding visual matching; always add an abstraction (new-materials) task and a smallest-unit task to go beyond appending.
Extending a pattern can be achieved by visual matching without understanding; use the abstraction and smallest-unit tasks to distinguish surface copying from structural understanding.
Use units beyond AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation and may revert to AB on longer units.
A partially correct pattern (one full unit plus stray items) is a transitional, emerging state — do not treat it as simply wrong.

The 'same, same, different' chant describes a two-same-then-different unit (AAB); for the ABB example (red, blue, blue) name the two blues as the same and the red as the different start rather than chanting the phrase in order over it.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: swapping to a new colour set for the abstraction task, a 'shrink to the smallest tower' control, laying the new pattern under the model for unit-for-unit comparison, and flagging reversions to AB. These are suggestions, not required mechanisms.

Hands-on construction is central for building and abstracting patterns; conversation can support prompting an explanation of the rule alongside that construction, without being treated as a substitute for it.

activityReferences.title: Number-line step machine: lay equal hops that stride past zero
State a rule precise enough to rebuild the sequence
Check every step, not just the last term
Negative terms in real below-zero contexts

startingActivity.title: Number-line step machine: lay equal hops that stride past zero
learnerActions: On a horizontal number line with zero in the MIDDLE (positives to the right, negatives to the left), set a starting number and a signed step.
Lay each term as an equal-sized hop along the line, one tap/hop at a time: e.g. start 5, step −2, so 5 → 3 → 1.
At the next hop, watch the marker stride the SAME distance straight past zero to −1, then −3, −5, −7 — the step never changed, so the sequence simply continues.
Commit to a rule in a 'state the rule' box in the form 'start at ___, add/subtract ___ each time'; if you type only 'goes down', answer the prompt 'by how much, and from where?'.
Repeat with a decimal preset (start 2.5, add 1.5) and confirm the identical equal hop works for tenths: 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, 7.0, 8.5, 10.0.
Take a 'predict the 10th term' challenge that rewards using the rule/structure rather than counting on one by one.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A linear sequence has one constant signed step; because the step never changes at zero, the sequence does not stop or bounce — it continues into the negatives. A rule that names BOTH a start and a signed amount uniquely rebuilds the whole sequence, and the same structure covers increasing, decreasing, whole-number and decimal cases.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line with zero central (positives right, negatives left)
The term-to-term '+d / −d' arrow chain drawn under the numbers
A temperature scale / number track for below-zero contexts
A position-vs-term table
commonMisconceptions: States the rule vaguely ('it goes down') without the amount, or gives the amount but not the starting number
Treats a decreasing sequence as a different phenomenon rather than as adding a negative each time; notices only increasing sequences
Believes the sequence 'stops' at zero — doubts that negative numbers exist or that you can go below zero
Reads or writes a negative term wrongly, e.g. −1 written or read as 1 (the raised minus sign not recognised)
Fixates on the last term and imposes a familiar pattern (4, 7, 10, 13, 16 → 18 as 'even numbers') instead of the constant step
constraints: The rule must name BOTH the starting number and a SIGNED amount (e.g. 'start at 5, subtract 2 each time'); 'goes up/down' alone is not acceptable because it cannot uniquely rebuild the sequence.
Treat a decreasing sequence as 'adding a negative each time' — the same structure as an increasing one — rather than as a separate kind of sequence.
Use a horizontal number line with zero in the MIDDLE so that continuing past zero is seen as a continued equal step, not a bounce or a stop.
Include decimal and fractional steps so 'add 1.5' is treated as one ordinary equal step, exposing pupils whose constant-step idea only holds for whole numbers.

A static reference poster (worked +1.5 chain, tap-to-reveal rule, zero-crossing example) is useful for consolidation but does not let the child continue their own sequence or experience the equal hop past zero; use it as a reference card, not as the generation task.

Recognition/selection items (fill-in-the-blank continue-the-sequence, slider placement, sequence ordering, multiple-choice rule with an 'add 4 vs subtract 4' distractor) check the skill but recognition alone does not elicit independent production; use them to assess, and pair with open generation to build the skill.

A slider item that asks the pupil to place the next term just past zero (e.g. −1), and a decimal continue-the-sequence step, are useful for catching the 'stops at zero' error and the whole-number-only limitation respectively.

activityReferences.title: Generate, align, and compare two sequences
Make ordered pairs and plot them
Test whether the ×2 depends on the starting number
Tape diagram for 'twice as much'
Check and sort: additive vs multiplicative, table-to-graph

startingActivity.title: Generate, align, and compare two sequences
learnerActions: Write out the first six terms of Rule A (start at 0, add 3): 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15
Write out the first six terms of Rule B (start at 0, add 6): 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30
Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so position 1 sits above position 1, position 2 above position 2, and so on
For each column, compare Rule B's term with Rule A's term in the SAME position (vertical comparison across the two rows, not along one row)
State the relationship multiplicatively: 'B is twice (×2) A in every column' and explain why — Rule B adds 6, which is twice the 3 Rule A adds, and both start at 0
Check what happens to the difference between corresponding terms down the columns (6−3=3, 12−6=6, 18−9=9…): it is not constant but grows, while the ×2 ratio stays the same in every column
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The two sequences are related by a constant factor (×2) at corresponding positions. 'B is 6 more' does not describe the relationship, because the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (0, 3, 6, 9, …) — so no single 'add a number' rule fits every column. 'B is twice A' holds in every column instead, and here this works because the step 6 is twice 3 and both sequences start at 0.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two-row table of corresponding terms (positions aligned in columns)
The (x, y) ordered-pair notation drawn from corresponding terms
First-quadrant coordinate grid with points on a ray through the origin
Tape / bar diagram showing one quantity as twice the other
commonMisconceptions: Describes the relationship additively ('the second is 6 more') instead of multiplicatively ('twice') — defaulting to additive comparison, which only fits the first pair because the difference actually grows (3, 6, 9, …)
Compares term-to-term WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) instead of between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counting up-then-across
Tries to guess a single hidden rule underlying both sequences rather than generating each from its given rule
Assumes the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone, and keeps applying it even when the two sequences do not both start at 0
constraints: Keep both rules GIVEN; the task is to generate each sequence from its own rule and then find the relationship, not to guess a hidden rule.
Compare CORRESPONDING terms column-by-column (vertical, across the two rows), not term-to-term within a single sequence.

The clean ×2 relationship between corresponding terms depends on the starting numbers as well as the steps: here it works because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0 (in general, Rule B's start must be twice Rule A's start). Do not present 'twice' as following from the steps alone.

The difference between corresponding terms is not constant — it grows (0, 3, 6, 9, 12…); do not present 'B is 6 more' as a true relationship that holds for a specific early pair. It coincides at most at a single column, and the honest contrast is 'difference grows' versus 'ratio stays ×2'.
Respect (x, y) order when forming and plotting pairs: Rule-A term across (x), Rule-B term up (y).

Recognition and sort/match/fill-in checks confirm the skill but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction of generating two sequences and coordinating them into pairs and a graph; use them after construction.

A consolidation summary (a two-row table beside a pre-plotted line with the ×2 annotated and facts revealed on tap) can tidily review the result, but a fixed display does not let the learner generate the terms or watch the growing difference against the constant ratio themselves; treat it as a review aid, not the main task.

Optional interactive supports that make the mechanism concrete: taps that fill each row ('add 3' / 'add 6') with corresponding terms locked in columns; a toggle between a '+' view (drawing the growing difference 3, 6, 9…) and a '×' view (showing the constant ×2 in every column); auto-plotting each column as an ordered pair that lands on the ray through the origin; and a 'change the starting number' control to reveal that the ×2 breaks when the starts no longer fit it (e.g. A starts at 1 while B starts at 0), and holds only when B's start is twice A's start. These are illustrative, not required mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Dual-engine generator: the same sequence built two ways
learnerActions: Build a sequence term-to-term: set a start value and an operation (e.g. start at 1, add 3) and generate the chain one step at a time.
Build the same sequence position-to-term: type a rule such as 3n−2 and substitute n=1,2,3,4,5 to light up each term under its position.
Switch a sequence between the two modes and confirm the numbers are identical.
Press 'jump to the 50th term': in position-to-term mode the answer for 3n−2 appears at once; in term-to-term mode the machine visibly grinds through the 49 predecessors first.
Drag the coefficient of n in 3n−2 and watch the inter-term step change to match, so the coefficient is seen to equal the common difference.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A term-to-term rule chains from the previous term; a position-to-term rule substitutes the position number into a formula and so reaches any term (e.g. the 50th) directly without listing the earlier ones. In a linear rule such as 3n−2 (of the form an + b), the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Position-to-term table (positions n=1,2,3,4 above; terms below)
Dual display: term-to-term arrows vs position-to-term substitution
Differences row and ratios row written under a sequence
Graph of terms against position (constant difference = constant steepness)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a position-to-term rule as a term-to-term instruction (reading 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2'), so the first term is wrong.
Classifying by 'it goes up' alone, failing to distinguish arithmetic from geometric or to spot a non-constant difference (1, 4, 9, 16).
Confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.
Assuming a later term can be reached by multiplying an earlier one (10th term = 2 × 5th term).
constraints: Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' sequences — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n=1,2,3,… , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
The practice/quiz set gives retrieval practice and scoring but does not by itself build the position-vs-term-to-term insight; pair it with generation and discussion.
A static side-by-side reference of the two rule types is a useful worked example but cannot recompute for a learner's own rule; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main generative task.
Interaction examples (mode switching, jump-to-50th button, coefficient dragging, live differences/ratios rows) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.

activityReferences.title: Flip-the-groups: the total that stays put
The ten hiding inside a teen number
Read the repeating unit, not the last item
Does swapping always work? Adding versus taking away

startingActivity.title: Flip-the-groups: the total that stays put
learnerActions: Drop 3 counters in one bowl and 2 in another; count the running total of 5
Swap the two bowls past each other so it now reads 2+3, and watch the total counter
Say out loud whether it is still 5 and how you know, in your own words
Answer the adult's prompt: 'Is it still five? How do you know?' — aiming for 'same numbers, just swapped round, so I don't need to count again'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The whole (5) stays fixed while the parts trade places, so swapping the order of an addition cannot change the total — you don't have to recount.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten-frame (a teen quantity fills one frame + spills into a second, showing 'ten and some more')
Paired counter groups that can be physically swapped to show 3+2 = 2+3
Repeating object/colour/shape sequences (AB, ABB, ABC)
Rekenrek / bead string grouped in fives and tens
commonMisconceptions: Treats 2+3 as a brand-new problem after solving 3+2, recounting from the start rather than seeing the order swapped
Over-extends 'order doesn't matter' to subtraction, expecting 5-3 to equal 3-5
Hears a teen number as one indivisible word ('fourteen') with no sense of the ten inside it
Continues a repeating pattern by copying the last item rather than reading the repeating unit
constraints: Do not state the rules (commutativity, 'ten and some more') and ask the child to repeat them; arrange experiences so the child notices and articulates the regularity in their own words.
Do not drill commutativity as a memorised rule when a child recounts; the habit of reusing structure matures with repeated side-by-side exposure.

Tap-to-reveal or labelling tasks ('ten and four' on a filled frame) can show the fact but do not let the child do the swap and watch the total hold, which is where the noticing happens; use them as scaffolds, not the place the concept is learned.

Prediction/matching checks can indicate whether a pattern was noticed but do not reveal whether the child saw the structure or guessed; use them as a light check after hands-on work, not as the primary teaching.
Assess by whether the child RECOUNTS a swapped fact, not merely whether they reach the correct total — both a child who recounts and one who reuses the answer can reach 5.
The swap/invariance claim is scoped to addition (and totals of combined groups); explicitly flag its boundary at subtraction rather than letting it generalise.

startingActivity.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one
learnerActions: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Doubles and near-doubles on ten-frames / cubes (double + 1)
Hundred square and place-value cards for ±10
Number line marked with equal repeated steps (+5)
Bead strings for repeated addition patterns
commonMisconceptions: Recomputes 6+7 from one, not seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly (adds 2, or doubles the larger number)
States a rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing
Subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones instead of dropping the tens digit
constraints: This is a META/mathematical-thinking topic for ages 6-7: the goal is the derive-and-check habit, not just correct totals. Listen for reuse of a known fact and the adjustment, not just the answer 13.

Fill-in or sequence-continuation checks can show whether a correct answer was produced but cannot by themselves reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned, recalled or guessed; always pair with 'which fact did you use?' and treat them as a follow-up to hands-on building, not a replacement.

A static near-doubles card or annotated −10 column can illustrate the move for reference, but does not let the child adjust the quantity or test a self-stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Bound the −10 rule explicitly: it lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — this specific 'drop the tens by one' rule does not generalise to −1 or other amounts.
Do not confirm or correct a child's sequence rule for them when the aim is building the checking habit; prompt them to test the next case instead.

activityReferences.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
Use a table pattern as a reasonableness check
Describe and test a sequence rule

startingActivity.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
learnerActions: Face 8×7 shown as an array 8 rows tall and 7 wide.
Cut the 7 into 5 and 2 (drag a divider, fold a paper array, or draw a line) so the array cleaves into an 8×5 block and an 8×2 block.
Read off 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then combine the two blocks to get 56.

Try a different way to reach the same answer: 8×8 − 8 = 64 − 8 = 56 (take one group of 8 away from eight 8s). Compare which way you prefer and why — this uses one fewer group of 8, which is a different idea from cutting the 7 into 5 and 2.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A 'hard' table fact can be assembled from facts you already own; the array makes the decomposition (distributive idea) visible rather than relying on recall or skip-counting, and the 8×8 − 8 route is a distinct alternative strategy (adjusting from a near fact), not another split of the 7.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Arrays / area model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid highlighting column/row patterns (evens, digit patterns)
Number line with equal repeated steps for growing sequences (+50)
Hundred square shading multiples to reveal their pattern
commonMisconceptions: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts instead of deriving them from known ones (8×5 + 8×2)
Splits the derivation wrongly (8×5 + 2, forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8)
Accepts an unreasonable answer because the pattern check (multiples of 4 are even) isn't applied
Over-generalises a pattern from a few cases without testing, or reverses it wrongly (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)
constraints: Build tables from known facts and visible pattern, not rote memorisation alone; always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'

Arrays and grids should be things the child acts on (cut, fold, shade) so the derivation and pattern are visible; a pre-split array or fixed shaded grid with tap-to-reveal annotations can illustrate and reference the method but does not let the child choose the split or test their own candidate answer against the pattern — treat it as a scaffold.

Recognition/selection questions check whether a child can identify a correct split or sort numbers, but do not by themselves require the child to construct a derivation unprompted; pair with a spoken or written 'why' and with open construction tasks.
Open discussion alone supplies nothing to split or shade; pair talk with an array, grid, or number line (a practical pairing, not a claim that talk cannot support reasoning).
These are flat number-and-pattern ideas; a 3D presentation is not needed and may add load — this is a practical note for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
Pattern-as-check establishes that an answer is plausible (e.g. even, within a range), not that it is exactly correct; keep both the derivation and the check.
Keep the 8×5 + 8×2 array split distinct from the 8×8 − 8 near-fact route; both reach 56 but they are different strategies (decomposition vs. adjusting from a known neighbour).

activityReferences.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
nth-term rule tester for a linear sequence
Generalise a structural fact and find the case that disproves a false rule

startingActivity.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
learnerActions: Start with a triangle (angle sum 180°). Add one side at a time to make a quadrilateral, then a pentagon (convex shapes); for each, split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Keep the hexagon back as a fresh test case.
Record in a running table: number of sides, number of triangles, and angle sum. Notice the sum climbs by a steady +180° each time while the triangle count stays at (sides − 2).

Explain WHY: in a convex polygon, from one vertex you can reach the n−3 non-adjacent vertices by diagonals, so an n-sided polygon splits into exactly n−2 triangles, and its angle sum is (n−2) lots of 180° — reason the rule from the structure, don't just fit it to the numbers.
Write the general rule in words ('two fewer than the number of sides, times 180°') then in symbols: (n−2)×180°.

Verify on a case you did not build the rule from: test a hexagon — (6−2)×180° = 720° — and check it matches the measured/added angles. Then stretch it: a decagon (10 sides, 1440°) and a 100-gon — does it still make sense?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The angle sum is (n−2)×180° BECAUSE the polygon decomposes into n−2 triangles — a rule explained by structure, and confirmed by testing a new polygon rather than trusted on faith.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Polygon triangulation (an n-gon splits into n−2 triangles)
Position-vs-term tables and the nth-term expression
Linear-sequence graphs/number lines showing constant difference and offset
Algebra tiles / area models for operation-property generalisations
commonMisconceptions: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce an nth-term rule for a far term
Assumes direct proportion — e.g. angle sum is n×180° or the 20th term is 20×(first term) — ignoring the −2 offset / start value
States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so errors go uncaught
Fits a rule to the given cases that fails to generalise (a pattern that works for 3, 4, 5 sides but wasn't reasoned from structure)
constraints: Verification is not optional: every stated generalisation must be tested on a fresh specific case before it is trusted. Do not let a learner stop at a rule, and do not simply confirm a rule for them — ask for the verifying case.
Guard against the direct-proportion misconception explicitly: n×180° for angle sums and 20×(first term) for the 20th term are the key errors to surface and refute, not avoid.

The rule must be reasoned from structure (a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex is n−2 triangles), not merely curve-fitted to 3, 4, 5 sides; a pattern that happens to fit the given cases but wasn't reasoned may not generalise.

A static triangulation diagram or a pre-filled table is a useful reference for showing the decomposition, but by itself it does not let the learner conjecture a rule and test it on a new case — pair any static display with an actual conjecture-and-check task.

An interactive explorer or a well-designed quiz (deriving the rule, finding a far term, and selecting the case that disproves a false rule) can each be used during teaching, not only for assessment; choose by what the learner needs to do, not by assuming one medium alone can teach generalisation.

3D representation is unlikely to be needed here because polygon angle sums, linear sequences and operation properties are flat/symbolic; it may add handling load rather than insight for this specific content. This is a scoped judgement about this topic, not a universal or verified claim about 3D.
Area models/algebra tiles are an optional representation whose fit is strongest for simple binomial products; do not present them as a verified or required method for the cubic cancelling pattern.

Explain WHY the feature must continue
Vary the step to discover the roles of start and step
Growing shape patterns and position-to-term

startingActivity.title: Generate, then colour by parity to spot a hidden feature
learnerActions: Take the rule 'start at 1, add 3' and write the first eight terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22.
Mark each 'add 3' jump between consecutive terms (on a number line or by an arrow) so the step stays constant.
Colour or mark each term as odd or even and describe what you notice about the sequence of colours.
Record each term in a table with two columns: term number (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and value, so emergent features line up next to their positions.
Predict whether the 10th term will be odd or even, then generate it and check.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A rule states a step, but the generated sequence can show a feature the rule never mentioned — here the terms strictly alternate odd, even, odd, even — and a table or parity colouring makes that feature visible.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: T-table (term number ↔ value) — exposing emergent features
Growing shape/dot pattern — term number as a count
Number line / hundred square — visualising step patterns and parity
Colour-coded terms (odd/even) to make features pop
commonMisconceptions: Applying the rule inconsistently or miscounting steps when generating terms.
'Explaining' a feature by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Assuming a short-run feature always holds without justification (over-generalising).
Confusing the term-to-term rule with a position-to-term rule.
Not distinguishing the starting number's role from the step's role in an emergent feature.
constraints: The aim is both skills together: generate accurately AND notice-then-explain a feature not stated by the rule; listing correct terms alone does not meet the objective.
Explanation must be structural (why the feature must continue), not a restatement of the observation.
Distinguish the term-to-term rule (the step) from a position-to-term rule; keep the starting number's role separate from the step's role.

Response formats that only ask a learner to pick the correct explanation from options can check whether they can distinguish a reason from a restatement, but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing and voicing their own structural justification; use them to assess, and pair with tasks where the learner generates terms and explains in their own words.

A static exemplar table and growing-shape picture can anchor the idea and reveal a feature, but cannot let the learner vary the rule and test how emergent features change; provide that experimentation separately.

Interactive examples (auto-colouring terms by parity, a table filling in as terms are generated, a reveal-the-reason prompt, changing the step to compare) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tools.
Do not over-generalise a short-run observation; require justification before accepting that a feature always holds.

When judging whether a target value can appear in an arithmetic sequence, reason from the step's effect on remainders/divisibility, not from parity or units digit alone, since those surface features can be insufficient (e.g. 30 is even and ends in 0 yet cannot appear in 1, 4, 7, 10, …).

State the role of the step precisely: an odd step makes terms alternate in parity while an even step holds a single parity; the start only sets which parity begins the sequence, so avoid saying terms 'settle/lock to a value' in the alternating (odd-step) case.

startingActivity.title: Pair and light the grid: building every meal in order
learnerActions: Start with 3 starters and 4 mains and first PREDICT how many different meals you think are possible before listing any — write down your prediction and say whether you think it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.

Begin by pairing starters and mains in any order you like, recording each meal you make in a two-way grid (starters down the side as rows, mains across the top as columns) by marking the matching cell.
Look at the grid: check whether random pairing has left scattered marked cells with empty gaps, or whether you tried to mark any meal twice. Ask yourself: have I found them all? Can I be sure?
Now switch to a fixed order: hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn (filling a whole ROW), then starter 2's row, then starter 3's row, until every cell is marked with no gaps.
Count the completed grid as rows × columns = 3 × 4 = 12, and compare this with your earlier prediction.
Explain how you know you have found every meal, and why the total is 3 × 4 rather than 3 + 4.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Working in a fixed order — fix one choice, run through every option of the other — guarantees no combination is missed or repeated, and the complete set fills a grid whose total is rows × columns, the product of the options.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two-way grid / table (one category on the rows, the other on the columns)
Tree diagram (a branch per first choice, a sub-branch per second choice)
An ordered list generated by holding one choice fixed
The multiplication statement 3 × 4 = 12 read off the grid
commonMisconceptions: Lists haphazardly, so combinations are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
Cannot tell whether all the combinations have been found
Predicts the total by ADDING the options (3 + 4 = 7) instead of multiplying (3 × 4 = 12)
Changes both choices at once (e.g. only the diagonal S1M1, S2M2, S3M3), losing track of the rest
Believes there are only a handful, stopping before the set is complete
constraints: A completed grid or tree with reveal-on-tap can SHOW the organised set and the product, but if the learner does not build it or test completeness themselves, the systematic search and the product structure are presented rather than discovered — use it as a worked example, not as the main learning activity.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. selecting the total, filling one missing combination) verify the skill but do not elicit the learner's own systematic enumeration method; keep an open construction task where the learner generates and orders the combinations themselves.
The structure here is inherently a flat two-dimensional grid or tree; a third spatial dimension is not needed and can obscure the rows × columns count.

A role-play dialogue may discuss the systematic method, but on its own it does not require the learner to generate and order the combinations themselves; if used, pair it with actual listing and grid-building so the learner produces the enumeration.

The additive error (3 + 4 = 7) must be confronted directly, ideally by a predict-before-building step and by reading the total as the grid's area (rows × columns), not merely noted as a possible slip.

startingActivity.title: Two routes, one gap: linked part-whole and number line
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole bar with whole 10 and known part 8, and a number line beside it.
First try to count BACK from the whole by the known part (back 8 from 10) to find the missing part; notice this is fiddly for some pairs.
Then start at the known part (8) and hop UP to the whole (8→9→10), counting the jumps to find the gap.
See both routes highlight the SAME gap of 2, and read the two printed sentences 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10 together.
Repeat with a close-number case such as 12 − 9: count back nine steps, then instead start at 9 and hop up 9→10→11→12 (three easy jumps), and see 12 − 9 = 3 printed above 9 + 3 = 12.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A subtraction and its unknown-addend twin ask the same question — the missing part of a whole — and counting up from the subtrahend is often the shortcut, especially when the numbers are close.

commonMisconceptions: Believing subtraction can only mean 'take away / count back', so refusing to count up.
Not seeing 8 + ? = 10 and 10 − 8 = ? as the same question.
Counting back inefficiently for close numbers (12−11 counted back eleven steps) and making errors.
Confusing which quantity is the whole and which is a part in the part-whole model.
Treating the answer to 8 + ? = 10 as 10 (writing the whole) rather than the missing part.
constraints: Target ages 6–7; this bridges take-away toward the additive structure of subtraction.

The static part-whole picture and the matching/missing-number tasks consolidate or anchor; they do not let the child freely toggle between the take-away and count-on views, which the linked model provides.

Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and strategy choice; they do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken or written justification of why the two questions share an answer — pair them with an explanation prompt.

Teach counting up explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close; do not present it as universally faster — for a pair like 12 − 3, counting back three is quicker, so prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are.

startingActivity.title: Balance the equation: find the missing number
learnerActions: Work with a balance or bar model showing 245 and an empty box on one side and 380 on the other, with the beam tilted.
Try putting 380 in the box and observe that the side becomes far too heavy (245 + 380 = 625) — much more than 380.
Adjust the box until the two sides match, finding 135, and say in words why 135 balances it.
Use a number-line route for the same problem: start at 245 and count on to 380, noticing the jump is 135.
Repeat with the unknown in other positions, e.g. □ − 120 = 250 (answer 370) and 500 − □ = 340 (answer 160), deciding each time whether the missing quantity is a part or the whole.
Check every answer by substituting it back into the original equation (does 245 + 135 really equal 380?).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same value; the position of the unknown (part vs whole) decides whether you add or subtract, and you can verify an answer by putting it back.

Always require a substitution check against the original equation.

A static diagram is a reference only: it cannot let the child test candidate values, so it supports but does not replace manipulable or written solving.

startingActivity.title: Balance-scale equation bench
learnerActions: Model the story 'Maya has 3 packs of pencils plus 5 loose pencils, 26 pencils in total' by placing 3 identical unknown boxes (each labelled n) and 5 single cubes on the left pan, against 26 cubes on the right pan.
To find what is inside one box, keep the scale level: remove 5 cubes from BOTH pans, leaving the 3 boxes on the left against 21 cubes on the right.
Share the remaining 21 equally among the 3 boxes, and open a box to reveal 7 inside each.
Write the matching equation 3 × n + 5 = 26 next to the balance, and state in words what n stands for.
Substitute n = 7 back: check that 3 × 7 + 5 = 26.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The letter box held a NUMBER (7) all along, and it could only be found by doing the SAME thing to both sides, so '=' means genuinely balanced. The +5 is undone before the ×3 because the +5 is the last operation built — undo the last operation first — and removing it from both pans keeps them level.

Balance scale (both sides equal)

Operator view of '=' — 'the answer comes next' — so the equation cannot be run backwards
Ignoring order of operations — adds the 5 before multiplying, or reads left to right
Undoing the two steps in the wrong order (dividing before subtracting)
Accepting an answer without substituting back to check
constraints: The letter must be treated as a NUMBER we do not yet know (how many in a pack), never as the object or a label for it.
'=' must be read relationally ('is the same value as'); the equation is a balance, not an instruction to 'work out the answer'.

startingActivity.title: Build the pair-finder: sweep one unknown and watch the pairs appear
learnerActions: Before starting, compare a + b = 12 with a + 7 = 12: how many answers does each have? Notice that the one-variable equation has a single answer but the two-unknown equation has many.
Start with a + b = 12 (whole numbers, greater than 0). Set a = 1 and work out b; record (1, 11). Set a = 2 and work out b; record (2, 10). Continue in order: a = 3 → b = 9, a = 4 → b = 8, and so on.
Record each pair in an ordered two-column table (a | b) so completeness is visible.
After listing, answer: 'How many pairs are there? How do you know you have found them ALL?' State the justification: 'I tried every value of a from 1 to 11 in order.'

Optional interactive version: drag a slider for a that moves in whole-number steps from 1 to 11 and watch b recompute live so a + b = 12 always holds; each pair drops into the ordered table AND lights a point on a grid. Sweeping the slider fills the table in order while the separate points line up along a straight line — showing at once that there are many solutions and that stepping a through every permitted value catches them all.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An equation with two unknowns has a whole family of solution pairs; stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order generates every pair and lets you prove the list is complete.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ordered two-column table of (a, b) pairs
A 'fix one unknown and step it' systematic list
Bar / part-whole model for a + b = 12
The pairs as points on a straight line (bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations)
commonMisconceptions: Treats it like a single-answer equation — finds ONE pair and stops, as if a and b are unique fixed unknowns
Searches unsystematically, so pairs are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
Ignores the constraints — includes 0, negatives, or non-whole values when only positive whole numbers are allowed
For 2x + y = 20 mishandles the coefficient, treating it as x + y (offering pairs like (3, 17))
Cannot say whether the list of pairs is complete
constraints: Establish FIRST that there are many pairs, not one — contrast a + b = 12 with a one-variable equation like a + 7 = 12.
The ordered two-column table (or a 'fix one unknown and step it' list) is essential for judging completeness; recording pairs out of order defeats the purpose.

Recognition-only or fill-in-the-blank items (complete-the-pair, categorise valid vs invalid, 'how many pairs?') can check the skill but do NOT by themselves build the systematic, exhaustive search; the learner must generate and order the pairs independently.

A static completed table beside the line of points can display the full solution set, but it does the discovery for the learner — they do not generate the pairs or test completeness themselves. Treat it as a reveal/illustration, not as the generating activity.
Plotting the pairs as points on a straight line is a bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations; keep it linked to the ordered table so the pattern connects back to the stepping method.

Interactive slider/toggle/point-lighting features named above are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the underlying learning (stepping one unknown in order, computing the partner, justifying completeness) can also be done with pencil, paper, and a hand-drawn table.

startingActivity.title: Balance-scale solver: keep both pans level
learnerActions: Represent an equation as two pans: unknown-boxes (x) and unit-weights, using 'anti-weights' (zero-pairs) for any negative amount. Set up 8x − 6 = 2x with the −6 shown as six anti-weights on that pan.

Choose an action (add or remove the same number of units, using zero-pairs where a pan has none to remove; remove an x-box; halve everything) and apply it to BOTH pans at once; watch the scale stay level.
Try a one-sided action on purpose and observe that the scale tips — that move is not allowed because it breaks the equality.

Solve 8x − 6 = 2x: remove 2 x-boxes from each pan to reach 6x − 6 = 0, then add 6 units to each pan (cancelling the six anti-weights) to reach 6x = 6, then divide both pans into 6 equal groups (÷6) to reach x = 1.

Use an anti-x-box for −x, plus unit zero-pairs, to model 5 − x = 6: remove 5 units from both pans to reach −x = 1, then swap every item on both pans for its opposite (multiply both sides by −1) to reach x = −1, so the negative solution is something you build and see rather than distrust.
Write down each balanced state as its own line — one true equality per line.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The only way to keep the scale level while stripping it down to a single x is to mirror every move on both sides — that mirroring IS the solving method, and a negative result is a legitimate, visible outcome.

keyRepresentations: Balance scale (unknown-boxes and unit-weights; same action on both pans)
Algebra tiles with zero-pairs for negatives and unknown-on-both-sides

commonMisconceptions: Treats subtraction as commutative: 5−x=6 solved as x−5=6 giving x=11.
Considers positive numbers only, so rejects or never reaches a negative solution.
Run-on / operational equals sign: writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then'.
Mishandles the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x): stops at 'unlike terms' or subtracts incorrectly.
Performs an operation on one side only, unbalancing the equation.
Thinks every equation has exactly one solution (misses none/infinitely-many).
constraints: Each written line must be a single true equality; forbid run-on chains like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1 or 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 where the '=' means 'and then'.
Every operation must be applied to BOTH sides; operating on one side only unbalances the equation and makes the line false.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line or zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; 5 − x is not the same as x − 5.
On a balance model, represent any negative amount (e.g. the −6 in 8x − 6) with anti-weights (zero-pairs) so the pans and the written equality stay consistent.
For the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the same term from both sides (e.g. subtract 2x from 8x − 6 = 2x to reach 6x − 6 = 0).
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Discuss that an equation may have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many (e.g. the identity 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6).

startingActivity.title: Bar-model translator with a numerical reality check
learnerActions: Read a comparison statement such as '4 times as many cats as dogs'.
Before writing anything, answer 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12) and build the picture: a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar.
Write the equation that fits the picture: c = 4d (equivalently 4d = c), where c = the number of cats and d = the number of dogs.
Test it: set d = 2, check that the equation gives c = 8, and confirm the picture agrees.

Deliberately try the reversed equation 4c = d, set d = 3, and see that it demands c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, not the 12 cats the picture shows, and fewer cats than dogs. Notice that d = 4 gives c = 1, a whole number but still fewer cats than dogs, so compare with the picture rather than only checking for a whole number. Explain why this shows word-order matching is wrong.
In a second mode, turn a 'think of a number' process into an equation step by step, e.g. 'think of a number, double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Reading words straight into symbols left-to-right is NOT the same as modelling the relationship; testing an equation against counts built from the situation (3 dogs → 12 cats) reveals a reversed equation, which predicts fewer cats than dogs and sometimes even a non-whole count such as three-quarters of a cat.

keyRepresentations: Bar model (a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar)

commonMisconceptions: Reversal error via word-order matching: '4 times as many cats as dogs' → 4c=d, mapping words directly to symbols instead of modelling the relationship.
Letter-as-object/label (static comparison): treats c as 'cats' and reads 4c=d as 'four cats for each dog', with '=' meaning correspondence not equality.
Writes an expression with no equals sign when an equation is required.
Mis-orders operations in a process translation ('double it and add 5' written wrongly), ignoring order of operations.
constraints: Letters must stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats'); the object-label reading drives the reversal error.

Always close translation with a numerical test: substitute a value and check the equation gives the count you predicted from the situation (e.g. 3 dogs → 12 cats). A non-whole count of objects is a warning sign, but a whole answer alone does not prove the equation is right (4c = d with d = 4 gives c = 1).
An equation requires an equals sign expressing equality; an expression alone is not an equation and the equals sign does not mean correspondence.

Matching and fill-in-the-blank checks are recognition tasks: they assess and rehearse but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and defend an equation independently — pair them with construction.
A fixed annotated example is a scaffold; it does not itself run the try-and-test cycle, so follow it with learner-generated translations that are tested with numbers.
For comparison statements, build the quantities (e.g. 'if 3 dogs, then 12 cats') before writing the equation, rather than mapping words left-to-right.

activityReferences.title: Expression translator: build, read, and evaluate

startingActivity.title: Expression translator: build, read, and evaluate
learnerActions: Build an expression from word tiles such as 'the number', '×5', '+4', and 'brackets', and watch the symbolic form assemble alongside.

Enter the two readings 'add 4 then multiply by 5' and 'multiply by 5 then add 4', and substitute n=5 into each using a substitution box: confirm 5(n+4) = 45 and 5n+4 = 29, so the two readings land on different numbers.
Use a tap-to-unfold panel to open 3y into y+y+y and y² into y×y, then substitute y=4 to check (3y = 12, y² = 16), distinguishing coefficient from power.
Test a deliberate misreading: enter 3y as 3+y and let the tool evaluate both to expose the mismatch.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Notation obeys the same order of operations as arithmetic, decided by brackets and structure rather than left-to-right word order; a letter is a hidden number, so '3y' and 'a²' are shorthand for repeated operations, not new symbols read like a sentence.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Repeated-operation unfolding (3y → y+y+y; a² → a×a)
Word ↔ symbol ↔ area-model card sets (Swan/MAP translation task)
Substitution check (replace the letter with a number to test a reading)
Bracket-as-grouping diagram contrasting 5(n+4) with 5n+4
commonMisconceptions: Reading/writing expressions left-to-right, ignoring order of operations (writing '4 + n × 5' for 'add 4 then multiply by 5' instead of 5(n+4)).
Misreading the symbols: 3y as 3+y (or a two-digit number), a² as 2a or a×2, ab as a concatenated number rather than a×b.
Treating the letter as an object/label ('a' = apple) rather than a number, which blocks operating on it.
Mis-grouping with brackets — reading 5(n+4) as 5n+4, or (n+3)² as n²+3².
constraints: A letter stands for a NUMBER; every notation convention is shorthand for an arithmetic operation, testable by substituting a value.

Word ORDER does not set the order of operations — brackets and structure do: 'add 4 then multiply by 5' is 5(n+4) (=45 at n=5) and 'multiply by 5 then add 4' is 5n+4 (=29 at n=5); keep these distinct.
Separate coefficient from power explicitly: 3y = y+y+y (so 3y=12 at y=4) while y² = y×y (=16 at y=4); 2a = a+a while a² = a×a (so at a=3, 2a=6 but a²=9).
Juxtaposition means multiply (ab = a×b, not a concatenated two-digit number); a/b means a÷b; brackets group, so 5(n+4) ≠ 5n+4 and (n+3)² ≠ n²+3².
The matching/multiple-choice format checks recognition and discrimination but does not by itself elicit independent construction of an expression; pair it with a build-or-write task.

The annotated reference card and read-aloud dialogue are scaffolds: the card cannot let a learner build an expression or watch a misreading evaluate, and reading aloud rehearses interpretation but does not by itself elicit written symbolic construction.
Interactive panels, substitution boxes and tap-to-unfold reveals are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; the same learning can be reached with paper, cards, and spoken substitution.

activityReferences.title: Build and number-check an equation from a worded situation
Travel the full loop: words → formula → table → graph → interpret
Spot the reversal and the misplaced structure

startingActivity.title: Build and number-check an equation from a worded situation
learnerActions: Read a worded situation such as 'there are six students for every teacher at a school'.
Define each variable as a quantity: 'let S = the NUMBER of students' and 'let T = the NUMBER of teachers'.
Assemble an equation from the letters, numbers and operations that links S and T.
Test the equation by substituting a real case: put T = 2 into your equation and work out S. Ask whether the answer is sensible for the situation.

If the equation gives an impossible result (for example 6S = T gives S = 1/3 of a student at T = 2, and fractional values 1/6, 1/3, 1/2 … for T = 1, 2, 3; even when it gives a whole number, such as S = 1 at T = 6, that means fewer students than teachers), revise it so it models the relationship, not the word order.
Once the equation checks out, fill a table for T = 1, 2, 3 and plot S against T.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An equation must model the RELATIONSHIP between quantities, not the left-to-right order of the words. Writing 6S = T for 'six students per teacher' copies the word order; substituting T = 2 then demands S = 1/3 of a student, which is impossible. Flipping to S = 6T models 'six times as many students as teachers' and produces a sensible, growing table.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: The four-way link: word problem ↔ expression/formula ↔ table of values ↔ graph
'Let [letter] = the number of …' variable definitions
A numeric check of a proposed translation
Graph features (through-origin, gradient) read back into the context
commonMisconceptions: Reversal error: translates 'six students per professor' as 6S = P (mirroring the word order) instead of S = 6P.
Letter-as-label: treats the letter as the object ('s = students') rather than the number of them.
Mirrors the word order rather than the relationship's structure (e.g. 'add 5 then double' → 2n + 5 instead of 2(n + 5)).
Reads a table or graph as isolated points without interpreting the relationship in context.
constraints: Variables must be defined as quantities — 'let S = the NUMBER of students' — never as labels ('S = students'); a letter that names an object cannot be substituted with a value.
Every proposed translation must be checked by substituting at least one concrete case before it is trusted.

A side-by-side display of situation, equation, table and graph can illustrate the links but does not require the learner to perform the translation or expose a reversal; use it as a reference, not as the main task.

Recognition and matching tasks check whether a learner can identify a correct translation but do not elicit independent construction and self-correction; include at least one task where the learner builds an equation from scratch.

A live checker that substitutes a case and flags contradictions (e.g. demanding a fraction of a student), an auto-filling table and an auto-plotting graph are useful optional supports that make the loop self-correcting; they are illustrations of the mechanism, not required tooling, and the same numeric check can be done by hand on paper.
Distinguish multiplicative 'six per' relationships (S = 6T, through origin) from additive 'six more than' relationships (S = T + 6, intercept at 6); do not conflate them.

Describe the reversed equation's failure accurately: 6S = T yields growing student counts that are fractional for most teacher numbers (1/6, 1/3, 1/2 … for T = 1, 2, 3), and fractional students are impossible. Even its whole-number results (T = 6 gives S = 1) contradict the situation, because they give one student for every six teachers instead of six students per teacher. The numbers do not shrink.

startingActivity.title: Build an equation from an expression (card-sort workspace)
learnerActions: Start with 2a + 3 sitting on its own and say aloud whether there is anything to 'test' or 'solve' — establish that it just names a value.
Drag an '=' and the number 11 alongside it to form 2a + 3 = 11, and say what has now changed.

Sort a set of six cards into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (e.g. 2a + 3, 2a + 3 = 11, 2a + 3 < 11), pointing each time to the =, <, >, ≤ or ≥ as the deciding feature, or saying that no such sign is present for an expression.
Substitute candidate values of a into 2a + 3 = 11 to test whether the statement is true or false; confirm it is true only at a = 4.

Also do an Always / Sometimes / Never true card sort, TESTING each statement by substitution rather than trying to 'solve' it, and recognising that one counterexample rules out 'always' (and one true case rules out 'never'), but checking a few values alone cannot prove 'always' or 'never' — give a reason for those.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The equals sign turns an inert value (expression) into a statement that can be true or false (equation) and therefore tested; an inequality is also a testable statement, and here (2a + 3 < 11) it is true across a whole range of values (a < 4) rather than at a single answer.

keyRepresentations: Card sort into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (and Always/Sometimes/Never true)
Balance scale for the equals sign as sameness

commonMisconceptions: Calls any algebra string an 'equation' and expects to 'solve' it, even with no equals sign (writes an expression when asked for an equation).
Reads '=' operationally ('= means work out the answer'), so rejects 8 = 3 + 5 or treats an equation as an instruction rather than a statement.
Conjoins terms / treats a letter as an object, so miscounts terms or reads 3a + 2b as a single quantity (or '5ab').
Treats an inequality as if it were an equation with a single answer, ignoring the range of values it describes.
constraints: This is a LANGUAGE objective for ages 11–12: the goal is precise USE and justification of vocabulary, not memorised definitions; always require the learner to say which category and why.

Categorization/matching/multiple-choice checks (sort statements into expression/equation/inequality; match term to coefficient; 'which change turns 2a+3 into an equation?') assess the distinction efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of an equation from an expression — use them after, not instead of, the build-and-test activity.

A static labelled 'anatomy' (tap the =, a term, a coefficient to reveal its name) works as a reference glossary but does not stage the expression↔equation transformation that carries the key insight; this is a limitation of a glossary-style reference, not an impossibility of static media.

Optional interactive features (greyed-out 'Test it' button, truth-lamp, value sliders, balance scale, colour-coded signed term boxes, number line for inequalities) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; none is mandatory and they should not replace the learner's own stating and justifying.
A balance scale and value substitution are approximations of 'both sides name the same value'; keep the represented idea (sameness/testability) in focus rather than the prop.

startingActivity.title: Build the rule from a growing pattern
learnerActions: Work through an illustrative growing shape or matchstick example such as 4, 7, 10, … and rewrite each term to expose structure: 4 = 1+3, 7 = 1+3+3, 10 = 1+3+3+3. Here the fixed start 1 is the zeroth term and the repeated +3 is the coefficient, giving the rule 3n + 1.
Apply the same technique to the target sequence 3, 7, 11, 15: identify the repeated group (+4) as the coefficient of n and the fixed starting part (the zeroth term) as the constant.
Find the zeroth term by stepping back one step before the first term (for 3,7,11,15: 3 − 4 = −1), and state the rule as 4n − 1.
Complete the sentence frame 'As the value of n increases by one, each term increases (or decreases) by ___' and connect that difference to the coefficient of n.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The nth-term rule reads structure directly from position: the coefficient of n IS the common difference, and the constant is the term at position zero — found by stepping back one before the first term, not the first term itself.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Growing shape / matchstick patterns (the repeated group = coefficient of n, the fixed start = constant)
Position-vs-term table with an explicit '0th term' column
The 'as n increases by one, the term changes by d' sentence frame
Plotted terms on a graph (steepness = common difference; points not joined)
'Set the rule equal to the target and solve' for membership testing
commonMisconceptions: Uses the common difference as the WHOLE rule: writes n + 4 (or just 'add 4') for 3, 7, 11, 15 instead of 4n − 1
Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — assumes a sequence going up by 3 must contain multiples of 3
Whole-object method: finds the 100th term by taking the 10th term × 10, or claims the 10th term is twice the 5th (only true when the line passes through the origin)
Gets the sign wrong for decreasing sequences: writes 4n + 6 for 10, 6, 2, −2 instead of −4n + 14
Attends to the term-to-term rule instead of position, so cannot reach a far term without listing
Over-generalises from only-increasing examples, treating decreasing sequences as a different kind
constraints: The nth term is new learning at KS3 and must be built from — and sharply distinguished from — the term-to-term rule, which only gives the next term.
State explicitly that the coefficient of n equals the common difference and the constant is the zeroth term (one step back before the first term), not the first term.

Keep any term decomposition consistent with its own sequence: 4=1+3, 7=1+3+3, 10=1+3+3+3 illustrates 4,7,10,… (rule 3n+1, zeroth term 1); for 3,7,11,15 the repeated group is +4 and the zeroth term is 3−4=−1, giving 4n−1.
Always verify a proposed rule by substituting n=1,2,3 before accepting it; a rule that gives the first term correctly can still fail later (common for wrong-sign decreasing cases).
Deliberately include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences; the coefficient of n is the SIGNED difference, so decreasing sequences have a negative coefficient.
Membership must be decided by solving rule=target and accepting only a whole-number position, never by surface features such as parity or resemblance.
When plotting, read steepness as the common difference but do not join the points — non-integer positions have no meaning.

A static annotated diagram is a consolidation/reference scaffold: it does not let a learner test a wrong rule against the real terms or independently jump to a far term, so it should follow, not replace, derivation and verification.
Recognition/selected-response items check fluency but do not elicit independent construction of the rule; use them after building activities, not instead of them.

Live-manipulation features (sliders, test-all lights, jump-to-n, membership solver) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete but are optional; equivalent work can be done with tables, graphs, and pencil-and-paper substitution.

startingActivity.title: The sort that refuses to merge (algebra-tile bench)
learnerActions: Start with a jumbled heap of a-tiles, b-tiles and unit-tiles mixed together.
Drag identical tiles together so they stack and label themselves (three a-tiles become '3a', two b-tiles become '2b', five unit-tiles become '5').
Deliberately try to press an a-tile onto a b-tile — notice it will not fuse and springs apart; you cannot build an 'ab' tile this way.
State the finished result as three separate stacks: 3a, 2b, 5, and say aloud that this is fully simplified.
Switch on a negative-coefficient mode where red 'anti-tiles' cancel matching tiles, e.g. show how 3b − b leaves 2b.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Unlike terms genuinely cannot be merged, and the leftover collection of separate terms IS the complete answer — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Algebra tiles (an x-tile, a y-tile, a unit tile — only identical tiles stack)
Sorting groups / columns by term type
Area square for a² vs a bar for a (why powers differ)
Signed-coefficient bar model
commonMisconceptions: Conjoins unlike terms to 'close' the expression: 3a + 2b → 5ab or one number, because an open sum feels unfinished (lack of closure, Collis).
Combines terms with the same letter but different powers: 3a + 2a² → 5a² or 5a³.
Loses or mishandles a sign when collecting: treats −b as +b, or 5a − 3a as 8a.
Drops the variable when combining: 3a + 5a → 8 instead of 8a.
Letter-as-object thinking (a = apple) that makes a + b feel like it should be 'ab'.
constraints: Insist on same letter AND same power: 3a and 2a² are not like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached before combining: in 4a − b + 2a the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds letter-as-object thinking and licenses conjoining (a + b = 'ab').
Make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms — an expression is an object, not an unfinished instruction.

The tap-to-reveal labelled expression is a vocabulary scaffold: its fixed example cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting or construction. Pair it with tasks where learners build and sort.

The categorisation/selection check uses recognition and selection; recognising a correct form does not guarantee a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so also require learner-produced simplifications.
Algebra tiles and discussion offer different experiences (manipulation vs articulation); neither is claimed here to be the only way to fix the closure misconception.
Watch written working rather than only final answers: a merged single term, a wrong sign, or a dropped variable each show as a distinct final line.

activityReferences.title: Split the rectangle: area model of a bracket
Expand, then check by substitution
Expand within a larger expression (order of operations)

startingActivity.title: Split the rectangle: area model of a bracket
learnerActions: Draw (or manipulate) a rectangle labelled width 3 and length (2x + 5).
Split the length at the '+' into two parts, producing two regions: a 3-by-2x region and a 3-by-5 region.
Label each region with its own area: 3×2x = 6x and 3×5 = 15.
Gather the two areas to write the total: 3(2x+5) = 6x + 15.

Now take a new example with a negative multiplier, −2(x−4), and split it into one part for each term inside the bracket. A length of −2 is not a real side length, so treat the grid as a signed diagram, not a literal area: write it as (−2)×x + (−2)×(−4), reasoning that a negative times a negative gives +8, so the result is −2x + 8.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Seeing the bracket as TWO regions answers 'why does the +5 not just come along unchanged?' — the multiplier covers every region, so every inside term must be multiplied, and the sign of a negative multiplier is applied to each term.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Area/grid rectangle split into one region per inside term
Arrows fanning from the multiplier to each term
Number substitution check (evaluate both forms at x=1)
Signed-multiplier annotation (−2 × −4 = +8)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies only the first term inside: 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 (documented as 2(n+3)=2n+3 being judged correct).
Sign error with a negative multiplier: −2(x−4) → −2x−8 (fails to flip the second sign).
Confuses × with +: 3(2x+5) → 3+2x+5, or adds the outside number to the coefficient (3×2x → 5x).
Leaves the expression unexpanded or unsimplified after multiplying.
constraints: Expansion with sign handling is a procedure built through practice with feedback; recognition-only tasks (choosing a correct answer from options) can diagnose errors but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an expansion — include tasks where learners write the full working.

A static labelled area diagram can show the split and support reasoning, but it does not let the learner carry out expansions across varied cases; pair any fixed diagram with learner-produced expansions to build fluency.
The area/grid model is inherently planar — the two dimensions represent multiplier and sum. Keep it in 2D; introducing a third dimension would misleadingly suggest volume.
The correct results to preserve are 3(2x+5) = 6x + 15 and −2(x−4) = −2x + 8 (NOT −2x−8). Any practice item or distractor must treat 6x+5 and −2x−8 as errors to be caught, never as acceptable answers.

When checking by substitution, prefer a non-zero value (e.g. x=1) or use more than one value so that a correct constant term cannot mask an error in the variable term; x=0 is acceptable only when the error being caught lives in the constant term.

activityReferences.title: Build the rectangle with the largest common side: the reverse area model
Factorise then expand-back: the routine check
Annotated worked example: where each number comes from

startingActivity.title: Build the rectangle with the largest common side: the reverse area model
learnerActions: Take the tiles for 12x + 8 (twelve x-tiles and eight unit tiles) and try to arrange them into one solid rectangle.

First try a common side of 2: notice the result is a long 2-by-(6x+4) strip. Check whether each row could be split again into equal parts — it can, because 6x and 4 both still divide by 2, so the strip can be regrouped into a taller rectangle. That means 2 is a common factor but not the highest, so 2(6x+4) is not fully factorised.
Now try a common side of 4: the tiles form a compact 4-by-(3x+2) block with nothing left to share, giving 12x + 8 = 4(3x + 2).
Divide EVERY original term by the factor you pulled out (12x÷4 = 3x and 8÷4 = 2) and write each result inside the bracket.
Use an 'expand back' action to re-spread the rectangle into 12x + 8 and confirm the product equals what you started with.
Repeat with a shared letter: arrange x² + 3x and find that the common side is x, giving x(x + 3).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The highest common factor is 'the biggest common side that leaves nothing left to share', so fully factorised means no common factor remains inside the bracket; factorising and expanding are inverse moves.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Reverse area/array model (terms arranged into a rectangle; common side = factor)
HCF via prime factors or factor lists of the coefficients
Expand-back check (product → sum)
Side-by-side expand/factorise pair showing the inverse relationship
commonMisconceptions: Takes a common factor that is not the HIGHEST: 12x+8 → 2(6x+4) instead of 4(3x+2) — 'factorised' but not fully.
Drops or fails to divide a term: 6x+9 → 3(2x) or 3(2x+9) (the 9 not divided).
Only spots numeric factors and misses a common variable: x²+3x left unfactorised or written 3(x²)... .
Does not check by expanding, so an incorrect factorisation goes unnoticed.
Confuses factorising (→ product) with simplifying/collecting (→ fewer terms).
constraints: 'Fully factorised' means no common factor (number or letter) remains inside the bracket; stopping at a smaller common factor is incomplete.
Every original term must be divided by the factor and appear inside the bracket; a dropped or undivided term is the classic slip.
Always verify by expanding the product back to the original sum before accepting an answer.
The annotated worked example is a fixed scaffold: it displays the parts but cannot let the learner search for the HCF by building, so pair it with learner-constructed factorisations.
The array/rectangle model is planar; representing it in three dimensions can misleadingly suggest volume, so keep it two-dimensional.
Selecting the fully factorised option or answering yes/no about completeness checks recognition; require learners to produce the factorisation and expand it back to evidence independent construction.
Distinguish factorising (produces a product) from simplifying/collecting like terms (produces fewer terms).
