startingActivity.title: Build the expansion on a 2×2 grid
learnerActions: Draw a 2×2 grid. Write the terms of the first bracket down the left of the rows (e.g. x and +3) and the terms of the second across the top of the columns (e.g. x and −2).
Fill each of the four cells with the product of its row term and its column term, writing the sign explicitly: x², −2x, +3x, −6. Keep a running tally of how many of the four cells you have completed.
Identify the two middle like-terms (−2x and +3x) and collect them (−2x + 3x = +x) to write the simplified answer x² + x − 6.
Connect it to numbers: set out 12 × 13 as (10 + 2)(10 + 3) on the same grid and check the four cells add to 156 (100 + 30 + 20 + 6).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A product of two binomials has FOUR products before collecting; the grid gives every product its own cell so none is forgotten, and it is the same idea as grid multiplication of two-digit numbers.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 2×2 multiplication grid / area model (four cells, one per product)
Algebra tiles arranged as a rectangle
The numerical grid analogue, e.g. (10 + 2)(10 + 3) for 12 × 13
Substitution check (put x = 1 into both forms)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms, MISSING the two middle cross-products, e.g. (x + 3)(x − 2) → x² − 6
Squares each term of a squared bracket: (a + 3)² → a² + 9 (or (a + b)² → a² + b²), forgetting the 2ab middle term
Sign errors with negative terms — applies a false 'same sign in the middle' rule, or drops the minus on a cross-product
Miscollects or mis-multiplies the middle/constant terms (e.g. 3b + 4b handled wrongly, or 3 × 4 written as 7)
Leaves the answer uncollected as x² + 3x − 2x − 6 instead of simplifying to x² + x − 6
constraints: Collecting like terms is a required final step, not optional: x² + 3x − 2x − 6 is unfinished and must be simplified to x² + x − 6.
Directed-number fluency is a prerequisite for the signs; reject the false 'keep the same sign in the middle' rule and multiply signed terms explicitly (+3 × −2 = −6).
Always treat (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3); never square each term separately.

FOIL and similar mnemonics can give correct answers but hide the distributive structure and do not generalise to longer products; if used, tie them explicitly to 'every term × every term' via the grid.

A static filled grid or a selection-based check can present and check expansions but cannot, on its own, surface a learner's own missing-middle or sign error — pair them with tasks where the learner constructs the four products.
A static worked grid is a reference and a selection-based check is a check; neither elicits independent construction, so use them alongside build-it-yourself practice.
The 2×2 area/grid model is planar; representing it in three dimensions would suggest volume and obscure the four-product structure.

startingActivity.title: One equation has many answers; two equations share only one
learnerActions: Take a single equation, e.g. y = x + 1, and list several pairs that satisfy it: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (10,11). Confirm there are infinitely many such pairs — together they form the line.
Now add a second equation, e.g. y = 2x − 1. For each of your pairs from the first list, test whether it also satisfies the second equation.
Find the one pair that satisfies BOTH. Check (2,3): 3 = 2+1 ✓ and 3 = 2×2−1 = 3 ✓. Check (4,5): 5 = 4+1 ✓ but 5 ≠ 2×4−1 = 7 ✗.
State the solution as the PAIR x = 2, y = 3, not a single number.
Plot both lines on one set of axes and mark the intersection; confirm it matches the pair that passed both substitution tests.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A solution to one linear equation alone is any of infinitely many pairs on its line; when the two lines are neither parallel nor the same line (as here), 'solving simultaneously' narrows this to the one pair shared with the second equation, which graphically is where the two lines cross.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two lines on one set of axes with the intersection point marked as (x, y)
A table of pairs satisfying each equation, with the shared pair highlighted
The substitution check: the solution put back into both equations
Parallel lines (no solution) and coincident lines (infinitely many) as edge cases
commonMisconceptions: Uses only one equation — offers any pair that fits one equation as 'the solution', ignoring the second.
Reads the solution as where a single line crosses an axis, rather than where the two lines meet each other.
Gives only one value (x or y) instead of the pair.
Trusts an inaccurately plotted intersection without checking it by substitution.
constraints: A static labelled two-line graph displays the intersection but does not, on its own, prompt the learner to test both equations; pair it with hand-substitution or an interaction so learners actively verify both equations. This is a design observation, not a ranking of one medium over another.

Interactive green/red checker panels and point-dragging are optional ways to make the simultaneity test vivid; the same insight is reachable by tabulating substitutions by hand. Do not treat any one interface as required.

Selected-response (multiple choice/matching/categorising) items can detect the one-equation misconception but, on their own, exercise recognition; pair them with a required substitution justification to exercise reasoning and production.
A third spatial dimension is not needed for two lines in a plane and can obscure the intersection; keep the representation on a single set of axes.
Always verify a graphically read solution by substituting into both equations, since poor scale or unlabelled axes can yield an inaccurate reading.
Connect the graphical intersection to algebraic methods (substitution, elimination) as alternative routes to the same shared pair; the graphical read alone is approximate.

startingActivity.title: Formula-on-a-shape: watch the bracket do its work
learnerActions: Set the length and width of a rectangle (for example with sliders), and evaluate P = 2(l + w) step by step: add length and width inside the bracket FIRST, then double.
Trace the perimeter round the edge of the rectangle as the formula computes, and check the traced path closes back on itself.
Toggle a 'double first' version that shows what 2×l + w would do — a path that traces both lengths but only one width, so it stops one side short and never closes round the shape.

Flip to a triangle whose top vertex lies above its base and place it on a rectangle with the same base and height (on screen or with a paper/card cut-out). Cut or drag the leftover pieces of the rectangle to show they exactly cover the triangle (for a right-angled triangle, two identical copies make the rectangle), so the ½ in A = ½ × b × h is seen as the triangle being half that rectangle. (A paper cut-out has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat, zero-thickness triangle; it still shows the half-area relationship.)
Optionally lay the formula out as a function machine so the sequence of operations the formula specifies is explicit.
State, in your own words, what each formula computes and what each letter means before substituting.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The bracket's order is not arbitrary here: adding-then-doubling walks the whole boundary and closes it, while doubling-then-adding misses one width and does not. The ½ for a triangle is the visible fact that a triangle has half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.

keyRepresentations: The shape itself with the formula overlaid (perimeter traced round the edge)

commonMisconceptions: Ignores the bracket / order of operations: P = 2(l + w) computed as 2×l + w (e.g. 2×5+3 = 13 instead of 2×8 = 16).
Omits the ½ in a triangle's area, giving b×h (24) instead of ½×b×h (12).
Confuses perimeter and area formulae, or uses the wrong measurements.
Attaches wrong units (perimeter in cm², or no units).
Reads a worded formula incorrectly and mis-sequences the operations.
constraints: Perimeter and triangle area here are planar (2D) quantities; a third dimension is not needed and can mislead toward surface area or volume, so keep the representation flat.

A paper or card triangle cut out and rearranged against a rectangle with the same base and height has slight thickness and is an approximation of the ideal plane figure; use it to show the half-area relationship, not as a literal zero-thickness shape. This is also noted in the activity where the paper model is proposed.

startingActivity.title: Plot and read on a four-quadrant grid
learnerActions: Given a target coordinate such as (-3, 2), place a point by first moving horizontally along the x-axis to -3, then vertically along the y-axis to 2, and check whether it lands on target.

Immediately after plotting (-3, 2), plot (2, -3) and compare where the two points land: note that swapping the order of the two numbers (each keeping its own sign) sends the point to a visibly different quadrant.
Switch to reading: a point is shown already marked on the grid, and the learner states its coordinates as (x, y) with correct signs.
Repeat with on-axis points such as (0, 2) and with negative and fractional values so plotting and reading are both rehearsed.
State what one grid line is worth before each plot or read, practising with grids where each line represents 1, then 2, then 5.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The order of the two numbers and the sign of each carry independent meaning: (-3, 2) and (2, -3) are different points in different quadrants, and the interval each grid line represents must be checked before counting.

keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines forming the Cartesian plane, origin labelled
'x-axis first, then y-axis' read against the origin (the 'corridor/stairs' rhyme holds only in the first quadrant)
Sign-by-quadrant grid: (+,+) | (-,+) | (-,-) | (+,-)
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting/reading (y, x) — takes the vertical value first (the single most common coordinate error).
Sign/direction error: counts the wrong way for a negative value, landing a point in the wrong quadrant.
Misreads the scale: assumes each grid line is one unit when it is 2, 5 or 10, or reads two differently-scaled axes as if identical.
Over-relies on the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic and is stranded when a coordinate is negative (goes 'up the stairs' for a negative y).
constraints: Work in all four quadrants from the start rather than adding negatives after first-quadrant practice.

Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch only; once negatives appear, prioritise 'first coordinate on the x-axis, second on the y-axis', because the rhyme breaks for a negative y (plotting (4,-5) means along then DOWN).
Always state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially where grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10, or where the two axes use different scales.
Rehearse both directions — plot from given coordinates and read coordinates off a plotted point — so fluency is not one-way.

A static labelled plane or reference card can help name quadrants and locate the origin but does not rehearse the act of plotting or reading, where the procedure lives; use it as a reference alongside active plotting.
Recognition-only or read-back-only responses confirm accuracy but do not by themselves build the plotting sequence; pair them with active placement.
Squared paper and drawn axes are a fully adequate substitute for any on-screen grid; the interactive examples are illustrative, not required.
A third spatial dimension is unnecessary for this planar ordered-pair concept and risks adding load without clarifying the two-axis sign-direction link.

startingActivity.title: Rebuild-the-expression substitution with a sliding value
learnerActions: Take the expression 3a² − 2a and first rewrite the implicit operations explicitly: 3×a×a − 2×a, or 3×(a)² − 2×(a).
Choose a value for a and drop it inside the brackets so the expression becomes 3×( )² − 2×( ), e.g. 3×(5)² − 2×(5).
Evaluate in order: resolve the power first, then the multiplications, then the subtraction. For a=5: 3×25 − 10 = 75 − 10 = 65.
Repeat the same expression for a sequence of values — try a = 3, then a = 0, then a = −2, then a = 1/2 — writing out every step each time.
For each value, note alongside what the two parts (a² and 2a) came to separately, and watch how a² stays non-negative while 2a goes negative as a crosses zero.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Substitution means replacing the letter with its value while preserving the encoded operations; brackets protect negatives so (−2)² = +4, and a² (=a×a) behaves differently from 2a (=2×a).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Function machine / 'substitution machine' (value in, result out)
Area square for a² (a by a) contrasted with a bar of length 2a
Bracket-inserting template: 3×(  )² − 2×(  )
Table/spreadsheet of values for one expression
Number line for negative substituted values
commonMisconceptions: Concatenation: substitutes to make digits, e.g. 3a with a=4 read as '34' instead of 3×4=12.
Reads a² as a×2, e.g. a² with a=5 evaluated as 10 rather than 25.
Ignores order of operations after substituting, e.g. 2+3a with a=4 done left-to-right as (2+3)×4=20 instead of 14.
Drops brackets on a negative value, e.g. (−2)² evaluated as −4 instead of 4 (−x² vs (−x)² confusion).
Assumes a=0 makes every term vanish, forgetting constants.
constraints: Choose an expression that contains BOTH a square and a coefficient, e.g. 3a² − 2a, so the a² vs 2a distinction and the sign rules both come into play.
Always substitute the value inside brackets, especially for negatives — (−2)² not −2² — so the sign is protected.
After substituting, treat the result as an ordinary arithmetic expression and apply order of operations (powers, then ×÷, then +−), boxing each term first.

Deliberately sample positive, zero, negative and fractional values; each exposes a different error, and the negative case is decisive because it requires keeping the bracket AND knowing two negatives multiply to a positive.
Include transfer to at least one unfamiliar formula (the curriculum scope covers scientific formulae) so the procedure is shown to generalise beyond the practised expression.

A completion or selection check (fill-in-the-blank, set-the-value, or pick-the-answer with distractors like 34 and 10) confirms the procedure but does not by itself elicit independent step-by-step construction; pair it with open working and talk-through.
A tap-to-reveal worked example can show one substitution's steps as a scaffold, but the learner still needs to perform the procedure across several values to build fluency.

Live manipulation (sliding a value through positive, zero and negative while the expression auto-rebuilds and brackets snap around the value) is an optional way to make the a² vs 2a difference and the (−2)²=+4 behaviour visible; it is one helpful presentation, not a required mechanism, and the same learning can be reached with written working, a number line for negatives, or a table/spreadsheet of values.

startingActivity.title: Build the line from a table of values
learnerActions: Take the equation y = 2x + 1 and complete a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = -3, -1, 1, 3, 5).
Plot each (x, y) pair on axes and join them.

keyRepresentations: Table of values → plotted points → straight line
y = mx + c with m (gradient) and c (y-intercept) annotated on the line
Distance-time graph where the gradient of the line is the speed

commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation (the line goes up, so the person went up a hill).
Slope-height confusion: judges the line that is HIGHER on the graph as faster/greater, rather than the STEEPER one.
Gradient/intercept swap: reads c as the slope or m as where the line crosses the axis.
Believes every equation gives a straight line, and is surprised that y = x^2 curves.
constraints: Matching, multiple-choice comparison, and categorisation confirm understanding but do not themselves build the dynamic link between a parameter and its visual feature; use them after exploration, not instead of it.

A static annotated y = mx + c diagram (tap m to highlight steepness, tap c to highlight the crossing point) can summarise the gradient and intercept on one line but cannot itself show the pivot-and-slide; it works as a recap card after dynamic work, not as the first teacher of the relationship.

The slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions must be confronted with a case where the higher line (at the compared time) is the slower one; a single rising line can reinforce rather than break 'higher = faster'.

When using Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10, compare at a time before the lines cross (they meet at t = 5, both 30 m); t = 4 gives Maggie higher (26) but Emma steeper and faster, with Emma pulling ahead after t = 5.

Interactive sliders, a live-redrawing line, and a synced value table are optional ways to make the equation-to-graph relationship concrete; the same insight can be reached by hand-plotting several lines and comparing them.
Require learners to state reasons, not just answers, when judging which runner is faster — the reason is what distinguishes gradient reasoning from slope-height reasoning.

activityReferences.title: Build the line and measure its gradient
Confront rise-over-run, sign, and scale pitfalls
Rearrange to y = mx + c and confirm against the line

startingActivity.title: Build the line and measure its gradient
learnerActions: Take a linear equation and fill a value table with at least three (x, y) pairs, then plot each pair as a point.
Draw a straight line through two of the points and check that the third plotted point lies exactly on it; if it does not, find and fix the arithmetic or plotting slip before continuing.

Choose two clearly placed lattice points on the line and form a rise-over-run triangle: moving left to right, count the rise (vertical change: positive if up, negative if down) and the run (horizontal change, across) in axis units, then compute rise ÷ run.
Repeat the measurement using a wider pair of points on the same line and confirm the ratio is unchanged.
State what the gradient number means in words, e.g. 'the line rises 2 units for every 1 unit across'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Gradient is rise-over-run measured in axis units and is a property of the whole line: it does not change depending on which two points you pick along the line.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Table of values grid feeding plotted points
Rise-over-run triangle drawn between two lattice points on the line
y = mx + c rearranged from ax + by = c
The same line drawn on two different scales to show gradient is invariant
commonMisconceptions: Rise/run inverted: computes run-over-rise (horizontal ÷ vertical) instead of rise-over-run.
Gradient sign error: reads a falling line as a positive gradient, or draws a rising line for a negative gradient.
Scale-dependence: judges the gradient by the line's visual angle rather than by rise-over-run measured in axis units.
Rearrangement error: mishandles 2x + 3y = 12 (e.g. y = 12 - 2x, forgetting to divide the whole side by 3, or a sign slip).
constraints: The learning objective is DOING the translations (filling tables, plotting, measuring, rearranging), not recognising finished results. A static annotated worked example (table → line → gradient triangle) can support reading the chain and serve as a reference, but does not let the learner rehearse the translations; treat it as a scaffold, not the main experience.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice gradient reading, ordering pre-written rearrangement steps) can check a distinct sub-skill but do not elicit independent construction of a line or an equation; pair them with tasks where the learner plots and rearranges themselves.
Gradient must be judged by counting rise and run in axis units, never by the line's visual angle, because a stretched or squashed axis changes appearance without changing the gradient value.
Always generate and plot at least three points and verify the third lies on the line.

Optional interactive supports can make the mechanism concrete without being required: an auto-plotting table where each entered pair appears as a point, a draggable rise-run triangle that reports rise, run and their ratio, a toggle that redraws the same line on a different axis scale, and a step-by-step rearrangement checker with the plotted line confirming m and c. These are example affordances, not mandatory tools.

A two-variable linear relationship is planar; adding a third spatial dimension does not aid table-to-line translation or gradient calculation. An open in-role dialogue format is poorly suited to rehearsing plotting, measuring and rearranging, though spoken explanation of reasoning can still support a learner.

activityReferences.title: From number to letter: rearrange with identical steps
Divide the WHOLE side, not one term
Undo multiplication by dividing, not by sign-swapping
Harder structures: denominators, roots and the subject appearing twice
Spot the flawed step, transfer, and verify by substitution

startingActivity.title: From number to letter: rearrange with identical steps
learnerActions: Solve the numeric equation 3x + 1 = 10 step by step, writing each inverse operation you apply to both sides (subtract 1, then divide by 3) to reach x = 3.
Now take y = 3x + 1 and rearrange it to make x the subject using the SAME two steps: subtract 1 from both sides, then divide the whole side by 3, reaching x = (y − 1)/3.
Write out, side by side, how each line of the numeric solution matches each line of the algebraic rearrangement.
Finally rearrange the general form y = mx + c for x, undoing +c first, then ×m, to get x = (y − c)/m, provided m ≠ 0.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Changing the subject is exactly the same balancing technique as solving an equation; the letters simply stand in for the numbers, so the inverse operations and their reverse order are unchanged.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 'Same to both sides' balance layout
Function-machine / inverse-operation chain run backwards
Original vs rearranged formula checked by substitution
y = mx + c rearranged to x = (y − c) / m
commonMisconceptions: Applies the inverse to only part of the side: y = mx + c → x = y − c/m (divides only c by m, not the whole (y − c)).
'Swap side, swap sign' over-generalised to multiplication/division (y = mx → x = y − m).
Sign error when moving a term across (subtracts where it should add or vice versa).
Mishandles the subject when it is in a denominator, under a root, or appears twice.
constraints: Learners must actually construct the rearranged formula and carry out the inverse steps themselves; recognising a correct answer or reading a worked example does not demonstrate independent rearrangement.
A fixed worked inverse-operation chain can show the method but does not let the learner perform the balanced steps or catch a left-behind term; use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
Error-spotting and fill-in-the-blank tasks check recognition and completion; pair them with at least one rearrangement built from scratch to evidence full competence.

Use substitution with several suitable values to look for errors, but justify equivalence by valid algebraic operations. Agreement at one value does not prove a formula identity, and division or root operations require domain conditions.

When the subject is in a denominator, under a root, or appears twice, require the extra structural step (multiply up, apply root/power inverse, or collect and factor) rather than treating these as routine single inverse steps.
The substitution check only discriminates if the learner computes the known output from the original formula first, then substitutes it into the rearranged form.

State each harder-case formula and its restrictions. Forx=(y-c)/m requirem!=0; forr=k/t obtained fromt=k/r require the originalr!=0 andt!=0 for this rearranged form; for t=(v-u)/a requirea!=0; form=(y-c)/x requirex!=0. Handle excluded zero cases separately. Root/power examples must state domains and any sign choices.

activityReferences.title: Plot y = x² from a table that includes negative x
Line versus curve: contrast y = x with y = x²
Read roots and explore hill/valley and shifts with an auto-plotting table and sliders
Recognition checks: classify, count roots, and order by height

startingActivity.title: Plot y = x² from a table that includes negative x
learnerActions: Before plotting, predict the height of y = x² at x = −3 and write down both the value AND your reason.
Complete a table of values for y = x² across x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, computing each y yourself.
Plot each point, then join them with a single smooth curve (not straight segments).
Compare the point at x = −3 with the point at x = 3: notice both sit at height 9.
State in your own words why the two sides of the curve mirror each other.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Because (−3)² = 9 = 3², (−2)² = 4 = 2², and so on, the negative-x points land at the same heights as their positive partners, so the graph is a smooth U-shaped parabola symmetric about the y-axis with its lowest point at (0, 0) — not a straight line, because the amount y increases grows as x moves away from zero.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Table of values including negative x → plotted points → smooth parabola
The parabola with its axis of symmetry and turning point (vertex) marked
Side-by-side straight line (y = 2x) and curve (y = x²) from their equations
x-axis crossings shown as the roots / approximate solutions
commonMisconceptions: Expects a straight line (or draws one), not distinguishing a quadratic from a linear function.
Squares a negative wrongly ((−3)² = −9), so the left branch is plotted below the axis and the symmetry is lost.
Joins the plotted points with straight line segments rather than a smooth curve.
Reads only one root, missing the parabola's second, symmetric crossing.
constraints: The table of values must span negative and positive x (e.g. x = −3..3) so symmetry and the turning point emerge from the numbers, not from assertion.

Points must be joined with a smooth curve, never straight segments; if a learner draws chords, add intermediate x-values to force the bend — this is a drawing habit to scaffold, not a concept to reteach.
Learners must compute squares of negatives correctly: (−3)² = (−3)×(−3) = +9, not −9. Distinguish (−x)² from −(x²).

When describing the rate of change over a table that includes negative x, say the step sizes are not constant — shrinking toward the vertex and growing as x moves away from the vertex (x = 0 for y = x²) — rather than simply 'growing'.

Recognition checks (classification, multiple-choice, ordering) assess whether the parabola is recognised but do not elicit independent graph construction or an explanation of why the graph curves; pair them with the plotting and explanation activities.

A static annotated parabola is a useful reference but a fixed picture cannot be manipulated to show the curve emerging from a table or the hill/valley flip; treat it as a complement to the dynamic and hand-plotted work.

The coefficient sliders, straight/smooth toggle and auto-plotting are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the essential learning (table with negatives, smooth plot, symmetry reasoning, reading roots) can be done on paper.

Full understanding requires relating symmetry, curvature (rate of change growing in size as x moves away from the vertex, which is x = 0 for y = x²) and the x² term together — not just producing a U-shape or knowing negatives square to positives in isolation.

activityReferences.title: Live percentage bar over a settable amount
Hundred-grid reference for landmark equivalents
Fluency and context-step rehearsal

startingActivity.title: Live percentage bar over a settable amount
learnerActions: Set the whole amount to £40 on a percentage bar and move a marker to 25%; read off the shaded amount (£10) and a separate sale-price readout (£30), so discount and remaining stay distinct.
Build 20% of 60 by stacking two 10% benchmark blocks (10% of 60 = 6, so 20% = 12), watching the arithmetic appear as you combine them.
Keep the marker at 25% but change the whole from £40 to £80 and observe the pounds answer change from £10 to £20 — the same percentage, a different amount.
Try each target percentage two ways where possible (e.g. 1/5 of 60 as 60 ÷ 5, and 20% of 60 as double 10%) and compare.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of the whole, not a fixed amount: changing the whole changes the pounds answer. Benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) can be combined to reach any whole-number target percentage, and the discount is a different quantity from the sale price.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Hundred-grid (10×10) with a fraction shaded, read simultaneously as fraction, hundredths-decimal and percentage
Bar model / percentage bar marked at 0, 25, 50, 75, 100% aligned with the whole amount
Double number line: amount on top, percentage on the bottom, for scaling to any percentage
Benchmark toolkit table: 50% = ÷2, 25% = ÷4, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100 with worked combinations
commonMisconceptions: Base-neglect: treats a percentage as a fixed amount independent of the whole — '25% off means £25 off' or '20% of 60 is 20'.
Denominator-as-decimal / faulty equivalent: converts 1/5 to 0.5 (copies the 5) or thinks 1/5 = 15%.
Rote 'divide by 100' with no meaning: divides by 100 and stops, or divides by the wrong number (e.g. by 20 for 20%).
Solves '25% off' by finding 25% and forgetting to subtract, giving the discount as the sale price.
constraints: Always require interpreting the answer in context: '25% off £40' means find the discount (£10) then the sale price (£30), not just compute 25% of 40.
Teach percentages of amounts via combinable benchmarks (50% halve, 10% ÷10, 1% ÷100, 25% ÷4), e.g. 20% = double 10%, so children reason rather than recall an isolated rule.
Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent means per hundred' stays visible; connect the divisor to the fraction (20% = 1/5 = ÷5), not to the percentage number.
Address base-neglect directly by varying the whole: 25% of £40 vs 25% of £80 gives different pounds for the same percentage.

A static/tap-to-reveal hundred-grid is a reference scaffold for the recall set; it does not let the learner vary the whole or compute a percentage of a chosen amount, so it is not sufficient on its own for the problem-solving evidence.
Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and fluency but do not elicit independent construction of a method; use them alongside tasks where the learner builds and explains a calculation.
A shopping role-play can motivate the context, but the calculation and model-manipulation must be where the doing happens, not just talked about.

Distinguish the forgot-to-subtract error (calculation correct, interpretation incomplete — scaffold the re-read, do not reteach percentages) from genuine misconceptions (base-neglect or faulty equivalents — reteach the meaning).

activityReferences.title: Same percentage, different whole: resize the base
Bigger percentage, smaller amount: compare across different bases
Writing and checking the three forms
Predict, count, reconcile: '50% is always 50?'

startingActivity.title: Same percentage, different whole: resize the base
learnerActions: Set a percentage (e.g. 50%) and shade that proportion of a 10×10 hundred square.
With the whole set to 20, read off the actual amount (50% of 20 = 10); then change the whole to 200 and read the new amount (50% of 200 = 100).
Describe what stays the same (the proportion / the shaded half of the square) and what changes (the actual amount) as the base changes.
Alongside the shading, write the percentage as a fraction n/100 and as a decimal, and locate it on a 0%–100% number line.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A percentage fixes the PROPORTION of a whole, not a fixed number; the actual amount depends entirely on the base, so you must always ask '% of what?'.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred square shaded to the percentage
Four-way link: percentage + fraction n/100 + decimal + 0%–100% number line
Bar model of a whole partitioned to show a percentage of it
Landmark strip (0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) against fractions/decimals
Two different-sized wholes each showing '50%' to expose the role of the base
commonMisconceptions: Base-neglect: treating a percentage as a fixed number independent of the whole ('50% is always 50 / a lot').
Reading a percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator ('24% means 1/24', '40% means 1/40').
Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writing 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
Believing 100% is the maximum — that you cannot have more than 100%.
Thinking a bigger percentage always means a bigger amount, regardless of the base.
constraints: Always tie the percentage to a named whole: ask '% of what?' every time an amount is computed, so the base stays visible.

A fixed/static hundred square annotated with 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 is a useful reference and can illustrate 'parts per hundred', but it cannot itself vary the base; base-dependence is best experienced by changing the whole or by comparing two different-sized wholes.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. choosing 'Jo is right/wrong') check understanding but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and justify the amount; include tasks where the learner computes and explains.
Include single-digit percentages (5%, 9%) as well as 40% so the decimal placeholder error cannot hide behind cases like 40% → 0.40.
Simplify fractions (40/100 = 2/5) only where it is natural and does not obscure the 'out of 100' meaning that defines percentage.

Establish landmark percentages (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) alongside their fraction and decimal equivalents, and seed deliberately that percentages can exceed 100% so '100% is the maximum' does not take hold.

Any base-comparison example used with learners must be arithmetically correct and must actually demonstrate the intended point (e.g. 10% of 500 = 50 truly exceeds 80% of 60 = 48); do not reuse the source row's '90% of 60 = 48' figure, which is wrong (90% of 60 = 54).

startingActivity.title: Squash-mixing bench: one mixture, two descriptions
learnerActions: Build a mixture by adding whole 'parts' of concentrate and water into a jug (for example 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water).

As each part is added, read two pictures that update together: a twin-bar showing concentrate beside water (part to part) and a single stacked bar showing the whole mixture with the concentrate shaded (part to whole).
Complete two sentence frames about the SAME mixture: 'the RATIO of concentrate to water is __ : __' and 'the PROPORTION that is concentrate is __ out of __'.
Then 'say it another way': express the proportion as a fraction, a percentage and an 'out of' phrase (for 1 part in 5: 1/5 = 20%).
Change the recipe and say whether the ratio and the proportion change.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The same mixture is described two different ways depending on which picture you read: for 1 concentrate to 4 water, the 1 sits against the 4 in the twin-bar (ratio 1:4) and against the whole of 5 parts in the single bar (proportion 1 out of 5). Ratio compares part to part; proportion compares part to whole; the whole = the sum of the parts.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Two side-by-side coloured bars (part-to-part) contrasted with one part-shaded whole bar (part-to-whole / proportion)
'For every ___ there are ___' sentence frame linking language to the ratio
Squash/paint mixing jugs or coloured counters (concrete part-to-part)
A double-headed 'same proportion' triple: fraction 3/5 = 60% = 3 out of 5
An enlargement pair of shapes labelled with the scale factor
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' interchangeably, as if they mean the same thing
Reads a part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: hearing 'red to blue is 2:3' and saying '2/3 are red' (should be 2/5)
Treats 'proportion' only as everyday 'a large proportion' (a vague amount) rather than a comparison of part to whole
Confuses 'scale' / 'scale factor' with a difference (adds a fixed amount) rather than a multiplicative enlargement
constraints: The objective is linguistic and relational: require the vocabulary in the child's own explanations rather than accepting a correct number with vague words.
Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context and 'for every' speech before any colon notation.

Reveal-only labelled examples and sort/fill-in tasks are scaffolds: they support recognition and reference but do not by themselves require the child to generate correct descriptions unprompted; pair them with building and spoken tasks.
Keep ratio and proportion contrasted on the SAME situation so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole difference is heard and seen, not memorised.
The whole used for a proportion is the SUM of the parts (1 concentrate + 4 water = 5), so the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5, not 1 out of 4.

Scaling the amounts (e.g. 1:4 to 2:8) leaves the ratio equivalent (2:8 = 1:4) and the proportion unchanged once the whole is recomputed (2+8=10, so 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5); use this to test real command of the language.
'Scale factor' is multiplicative (every length times the same number), not an added difference.

activityReferences.title: Build a percentage from benchmark chunks
Compare mode: percent of WHICH base?
Scored practice set with a base-ignoring distractor

startingActivity.title: Build a percentage from benchmark chunks
learnerActions: Treat a bar as the whole amount (e.g. £360 = 100%) and partition it into ten equal 10% chunks.
Find 15% of £360 by taking one 10% chunk (£36) and half of another (5% = £18), then combining them to read £54.
Say aloud how each benchmark is found: 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 5% = half of 10%, 25% = ÷4, 50% = ÷2, and combine (e.g. 35% = 25% + 10%).
Record the matching equivalence each time: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15, and check the decimal point is in the right place (0.15, not 1.5).
Progress from friendly multiples of 5 to any percentage, and later to a single multiplier (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Finding a percentage of an amount is assembling friendly known pieces, not recalling an opaque rule; 'parts per hundred' stays visible on the bar.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 100-square (each cell = 1%) and a bar split into ten 10% chunks
Benchmark fact ladder: 10%, 5%, 1%, 25%, 50% and how to combine them
Percentage bar model (whole = 100%, shade the required part)
The equivalence triple 15% = 15/100 = 0.15
Two labelled bars of different totals for comparison (percent of WHICH base)
commonMisconceptions: Compares two percentages while ignoring their different bases (assumes 30% off always saves more than 25% off, whatever the prices)
Misplaces the decimal when converting: treats 15% as 1.5 (or 6% as 0.6), giving a tenfold error
Cannot assemble a percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of 10% ÷ 2
Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount rather than a proportion of the given whole
constraints: 5% is HALF of 10% (÷2). It is not the amount ÷ 5, which gives 20%, and it is not 10% ÷ 5, which gives 2%. These are common slips to pre-empt.
Always make 'percent of what?' explicit in comparison problems — a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount, so compute the actual amounts.
Check decimal placement: 15% = 0.15, not 1.5; misplacement gives tenfold errors.
The static 100-grid is a benchmark reference, not the main practice: fluency and comparison require the pupil to compute across multiple cases, not just view one worked example.

The scored set consolidates and diagnoses; recognition-style items can check whether an answer is right but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction, so they supplement rather than replace the bar work.

Bar/grid models are representations of proportion; keep the numeric meaning (parts per hundred) explicit so pupils do not treat the picture as the whole method. Percentages and fractions are comparable as numbers (e.g. 0.15 < 0.30) irrespective of any base; it is the actual amounts they produce that depend on the base, so when comparing represented portions use a common whole.

activityReferences.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
Same percentage, different wholes — 50% of two bags
Convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage
Express one quantity as a percentage of another, and compare

startingActivity.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid (100 cells, each cell = 1%), shade 45 cells and write the result three ways: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45.
State in your own words what '45 out of 100' means by pointing at the shaded and unshaded parts of the grid.
Shade a second grid partly to show more than one whole: fill one full grid and 50 cells of a second, and write 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes.
Convert a small percentage carefully: shade 7 cells and record 7% = 7/100 = 0.07 (watch that it is 0.07, not 0.7).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A percentage literally means parts per hundred, so it is the same quantity expressed as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal; 100% is 'one whole', not a ceiling, and percentages can go beyond it.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 100-grid (each cell = 1%), shaded to show a percentage as a proportion
Fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence triple (45% = 45/100 = 0.45)
Two differently-sized bars/quantities with the same percentage shaded (relative-to-whole)
A 100-grid plus a partial second grid to show >100% (150% = 1.5 wholes)
'A out of B, restated out of 100' bridge for expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount (50% is 'the same amount' regardless of the whole), not as a proportion of its base
Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is seen as a maximum rather than 'one whole')
Mis-converts between forms: 7% → 0.7 (decimal misplacement), or 0.45 → 4.5%
Confuses 'A as a percentage of B' with 'B as a percentage of A', or which quantity is the whole (the base)
constraints: Keep the base explicit at all times: every percentage is 'of' some whole; when amounts are involved, state the whole before computing.

Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition of equivalent forms but do not, on their own, show the learner can produce conversions or justify the proportional reasoning; pair them with learner-constructed answers and spoken/written explanations.

A static shaded 100-grid is a strong, honest picture of the 'per hundred' definition and the equivalence triple; to let a learner test that the SAME percentage yields different amounts on different wholes, they need to act on at least two different wholes themselves (compute, shade, or physically share), whether with paper grids/bars or an interactive model.

Optional interactive supports — a grid whose fraction and decimal update as cells are shaded, a side-by-side panel shading the same percentage on two differently-sized bars, a drag-past-100% mode onto a second grid, and an 'A as % of B' tool that restates A/B out of 100 — make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same learning can be reached with paper grids, drawn bars, or shared counters.
Distinguish the diagnostic prediction step from the explanation: the reason given BEFORE observing is what reveals the absolute-vs-proportion view.
Do not teach '100% always beats 50%': supply a counterexample, e.g. 100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) is fewer than 50% of a 40-sweet bag (20), so 50% of a larger whole can exceed 100% of a smaller one.
Percentages compare proportions directly because each one is restated out of a common whole of 100. Comparing the actual amounts still needs each whole: 50% of 40 (20) is more than 100% of 10 (10).

activityReferences.title: The price-changer: every change is a multiplier
Reverse percentages: undo by dividing
Does it cancel out? Chaining changes on a changing base
Simple interest on a fixed base

startingActivity.title: The price-changer: every change is a multiplier
learnerActions: Start with a value shown as a bar (drawn on paper or on screen), e.g. £240, apply a 15% increase, write the change as a single multiplication ×1.15, and read off the new value (£276).
Apply a 20% decrease to a value and write it as ×0.8; write a 6% decrease as ×0.94 (100% − 6% = 94%).
Deliberately contrast ×1.15 with ×1.5 and ×0.15 for a 15% increase, stating which is correct and why (100% + 15% = 115% = 1.15).
Match pairs of multiplier cards and check which pairs multiply to 1 (e.g. ×1.25 ↔ ×0.8), noticing the multiplier that UNDOES a change is its reciprocal.
OPTIONAL interaction if a live tool is available: drag or set the percentage and watch the bar grow/shrink while the displayed multiplier and new value update together.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A percentage increase or decrease is one multiplication by (1 ± r/100), not an add-on or subtract-off, and the decimal multiplier must be built carefully: a 5% increase is ×1.05, not ×1.5; and finding 6% OF a value is ×0.06, not ×0.6 (distinct from a 6% decrease, which is ×0.94).
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Decimal-multiplier form of change: ×(1 + r/100) and ×(1 − r/100)
Paired multiplier cards showing reverse = reciprocal (×1.25 ↔ ×0.8, product 1)
Bar model where the original is 100% and the change adds/removes a shaded strip
Reverse-percentage arrow: original →(×0.8)→ new, so new →(÷0.8)→ original
Simple-interest table: same interest (r% of P) added each year for t years
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage change as addition/subtraction rather than a single multiplication (e.g. 240 + 0.15 or 240 + 1.15 rather than ×1.15)
Reverse-percentage error: to find the original before a 20% discount, adds 20% of the SALE price back on (64 + 20% of 64) instead of dividing by 0.8
Assumes an increase then a decrease by the same percentage returns to the original (subtracts percents: 20% up then 20% down = no change), not seeing the base has changed
Builds the wrong multiplier: 5% increase as ×1.5, or 6% as ×0.6 (decimal misplacement)
Computes simple interest on a growing balance (compound) or forgets to multiply by the number of years
constraints: A scored set of items (fill-in-the-multiplier, a reverse-percentage selection item with the '£64 + 20%' add-back as a distractor, a true/false on 'up 20% then down 20% returns to start' where the misconception is the incorrect option, and a simple-interest item with a compound distractor) can diagnose which model a learner holds, but selecting among options does not by itself elicit the independent construction of a multiplier or a dividing-by-the-multiplier method; include tasks where the learner writes or builds the method.

A static worked example or tap-to-reveal diagram (e.g. tap +15% to reveal ×1.15, tap a reverse problem to reveal ÷0.8) can present the method as a reference, but it is fixed and cannot be re-based by the learner, so the 'base changes under you' insight is better met by actually applying a sequence of changes and tracking the new base.

A shop/bank persona dialogue can pose sale and interest problems and raise the 'does it cancel' challenge, but learners still need to carry out the multiplier computation themselves rather than only hear it explained.
Keep the base fixed for simple interest; do not let it drift into compound unless deliberately contrasting.

When checking reverse-percentage answers, require a reversal test (apply the original percentage change to the found original, e.g. reduce it for a sale or increase it for a price rise, and confirm it returns to the given value) rather than accepting the numeric answer alone.

activityReferences.title: Scale a mixture and compare adding versus multiplying
Build a bar model to find one share
Solve varied missing-value problems and catch the additive trap
Talk it through: is it still the same drink?

startingActivity.title: Scale a mixture and compare adding versus multiplying
learnerActions: Meet the problem 'red:blue is 3:5 and there are 15 blue — how many red?' alongside a visible outcome such as rows of beads or a paint shade produced by the ratio.
Scale the ratio up a ratio table (3:5, 6:10, 9:15) and watch two bars (one per part) grow together, stating the multiplier that turns 5 into 15 (×3) and applying the same ×3 to red to get 9.

Try two contrasting moves on the mixture: 'add 10 to each part' (giving 13:15) and 'multiply each part by 3' (giving 9:15), and observe which move keeps the mixture/shade the same and which changes it.
Say in words why multiplying by 3 keeps the same relationship but adding 10 to both does not.

As an optional extension beyond the integer-fact objective, keep red:blue 3:5 but switch to a measurable paint mixture: with 12 ml blue the multiplier is 12÷5 = 2.4, so red = 3×2.4 = 7.2 ml. This shows that building up in whole groups of 3:5 cannot reach the answer. (A bead count could not be 7.2, so use continuous amounts here.)
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The two quantities in a ratio are linked by a constant multiplier, not a constant difference: scaling both parts by the same factor preserves the relationship, while adding the same amount to both breaks it whenever the two parts are unequal.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar model with equal blocks per part (find one block = the share/multiplier)
Ratio table showing the constant multiplier down the columns (3:5, ×3 → 9:15)
Double number line aligning the two quantities at 0
'For every a there are b' grouping with counters/cubes
Arrow diagram showing '×3' mapping ratio to real amounts
commonMisconceptions: Additive/constant-difference reasoning: 'blue rose by 10, so red rises by 10' (or 'the difference is 2, keep it') instead of scaling by a constant multiplier
Applies the multiplier to only one quantity, or adds the multiplier instead of multiplying
Uses the wrong direction (multiplies when should divide to find the multiplier, or vice versa)
Build-up strategy that works for whole-number cases but collapses when the multiplier is non-integer
constraints: This is procedural problem-solving: learners should construct and solve problems and state the multiplier, not merely recognise a correct answer from options.

Build-up (repeatedly adding the ratio unit) is a valid stepping stone and should be extended toward the multiplier ('how many groups of 5 is 20?'), not discouraged. Non-integer multipliers, where whole-group build-up fails, are an optional extension beyond the integer-fact objective and should use measurable (continuous) quantities.

A worked example that only reveals one scaling (e.g. tap to show ×3) is a reference scaffold; it does not by itself give practice solving varied problems or confronting the additive alternative, so pair it with learner-constructed solutions.

Scored item sets with additive distractors (e.g. 17 for 2:5 with 20 known) can check and diagnose the additive misconception, but selecting a correct option does not by itself require the learner to produce the method or justify why the multiplier applies to both parts, so pair them with learner-constructed, explained solutions.

Vary which quantity is known, include non-unit multipliers and scaling down, and offer non-integer multipliers only as an optional extension with measurable quantities (or ratios not in simplest form that give whole answers, e.g. 4:6 with 15 → ×2.5 → 10), so correctness does not depend on whole-number build-up alone.
Keep each activity's ratio consistent within its own worked examples (e.g. activity 1 stays 3:5), so learners are not silently switched between different ratios mid-task.

activityReferences.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts
Explain and check the shares
Short questions to consolidate the routine

startingActivity.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts
learnerActions: Take a ratio such as 3:5 and draw an empty strip (a tape/bar diagram) to represent the whole quantity.

Decide how many EQUAL segments to cut the strip into so that both children's parts together fill it exactly (try 3, 5 or another number and check), then explain in your own words why the sum 3 + 5 = 8 is the simplest count that works.
Place the total quantity (40) across the strip and work out the value of one segment: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Colour 3 segments for the first child and 5 for the second, then read off 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 5 = 25.
State what fraction of the WHOLE each child gets: 3/8 and 5/8, and check these sum to 1 (and that 15 + 25 = 40).

In a second round, turn chained language ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam, Sam three times as many as Jo') into one ratio Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6 by making the smallest quantity one part, then build that 10-part bar before sharing.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The ratio a:b needs (a+b) equal parts, so each share is a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole — not a/b. One part is the building block; chained comparisons must become a single ratio before sharing.

keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram cut into a+b equal segments

Sharing equally, ignoring the ratio (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each).
Finding the value of one part but forgetting to multiply each share back (reporting the number of parts, or one-part, as the answer).
Unable to combine chained comparisons into a single ratio, so treating 'twice as many' and 'three times as many' as unrelated.
constraints: A static labelled bar model (cut into a+b parts, with tap-to-reveal values and part-to-whole fractions) is a useful reference/scaffold, but it does not let the learner cut and check their own segmentation — the choice of how many segments is where the key misconception surfaces, so include an activity where the learner decides the segment count themselves.
Recognition/short-answer questions assess and reinforce the routine but do not elicit independent construction of the bar or the shares; use them alongside, not instead of, the building task.
Always convert chained/multiplicative language into a single ratio (using the smallest quantity as one part, and scaling up if needed so all parts are whole numbers) before sharing.

Keep the part-to-whole fraction explicit (3/8 and 5/8 for 3:5) and contrast it directly with the wrong 3/5 to fence the misconception — and when demonstrating why 3/5 is wrong, in EVERY learner prompt and feedback item apply the misconception's own rule (3/5 and 5/5) so the contradiction (exceeding the whole) is visible, rather than its correct complement (3/5 and 2/5), which wrongly looks consistent.

startingActivity.title: Ratio-divider on a tape diagram (forward direction)
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 1:2:3 and cut the strip into the SUM of the parts — six equal segments for 1:2:3, not three.
Let the quantity (e.g. 180) distribute across the equal segments and read off one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
Colour 1, 2 and 3 adjacent segments to read the shares 30, 60 and 90, then add them to check they return 180.
Repeat with a two-part ratio (e.g. share £60 in 2:3: 5 parts, one part = 12, shares 24 and 36, summing to 60).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A three-part ratio 1:2:3 needs six equal parts, not three; dividing once by the total number of parts and then scaling each term is the whole routine, and the shares must add back to the original quantity.

startingActivity.title: The fraction-of bench: convert units, then form the fraction
learnerActions: Start with two quantities in different units, e.g. 45 minutes and 2 hours, and say in words which quantity is the whole (the one after 'of' — here 2 hours).
Before writing any fraction, convert both to a common unit: split the 2-hour bar into 120 minute-segments and highlight the 45.
Form the fraction from the shaded bar: 45 out of 120, then simplify the equivalent-fraction chain 45/120 → 9/24 → 3/8.

In a second round, take 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours: shade 3 hours against a 2-hour whole bar so the shading runs past the end of one whole and spills into a second bar; read the fraction as 3/2.
State what 3/2 means here in words: '3 hours is one and a half times the two hours' / 'more than the whole'.
Check yourself with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours should be 1/2 — confirm your method gives it.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Both quantities must be in the same unit before forming a fraction, the quantity after 'of' is the denominator, and the comparison fraction can exceed one whole when the first quantity is larger.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Bar / double number line with both quantities in a common unit (45 out of 120 minutes shaded)
The sentence frame 'a as a fraction of b = a/b' with 'of' → denominator

Equivalent-fraction simplification chain (45/120 → 3/8)
commonMisconceptions: Writing the raw numbers without converting to a common unit (45/2 for 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours).
Putting the quantities the wrong way round — ignoring that the quantity after 'of' is the denominator.
Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so being unable to accept or interpret a result greater than 1 (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2).
Forgetting to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly, leaving the comparison obscured.
constraints: Always require a 'same units?' checkpoint before any fraction is written; converting to a common unit must precede forming the fraction.
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2, 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m = 3/2) so learners accept and interpret improper results.
Simplify and then interpret the fraction in words tied to the situation ('3/8 of the two hours'); do not leave it as a bare number.
Selection/recognition items confirm the rule and surface distractors but do not elicit independent construction of the common-unit comparison; pair them with hands-on forming.

startingActivity.title: Talk it through with a market-stall trader (or science reporter)
learnerActions: Respond in-role to a character who throws real situations at you and listens for the right word: '3 apples for £1 — what do we call this, and what are its units?' (target: it is a rate; its unit rate is 'pounds per apple', found by sharing £1 across 3 apples ≈ £0.33 per apple — or equivalently 3 apples per pound).

When you label 'more workers, fewer hours' as direct, answer the follow-up: 'I add two workers and the time drops — are those two quantities moving the SAME way or opposite?' and revise to 'opposite — and if every worker works at the same rate, doubling the workers halves the time (workers × hours stays constant), so it is INVERSE proportion.'
Describe at least one directly proportional situation, one inverse, and name a rate aloud WITH its units (e.g. '120 miles in 2 hours is 60 miles per hour — a rate/speed, miles per hour').
Say a full sentence that explains WHY, e.g. 'as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it in a constant ratio, so it is direct proportion.'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A term is pinned to the behaviour it names — you decide 'direct' vs 'inverse' by checking whether the quantities move together in a constant ratio (direct) or oppositely with a constant product, so doubling one halves the other (inverse), not by spotting the word 'more'. If neither holds, the relationship is not proportional. A rate is incomplete without its units.

keyRepresentations: Frayer-style word map (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples) for each term
Paired example/non-example situation cards (direct | inverse | neither)
Unit tags for each compound measure (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³)
Sentence frames ('as … increases, … so this is … proportion')
commonMisconceptions: Using 'proportion' in its loose everyday sense ('a large proportion') rather than the mathematical multiplicative meaning.
Labelling any 'more → more' situation 'direct proportion' and failing to identify inverse proportion (more workers → less time).
Using 'rate', 'speed' or 'density' without units, or treating 'ratio' and 'rate' as interchangeable.
Confusing 'scale factor' with an additive change rather than a multiplier.
constraints: Always attach units when using rate/speed/density (mph, m/s, kg/m³); a rate stated without units is incomplete.
Teach each term through examples AND non-examples that fence its boundary (direct vs inverse vs non-proportional), with active use rather than rote definition.
Contrast the everyday and mathematical senses of 'proportion' directly so the technical multiplicative meaning is distinguished from loose usage.

Rehearse the direct/inverse distinction in full sentences ('as one increases the other decreases so that their product stays constant — doubling one halves the other — so it is inverse'), not as a label guessed from 'more'. One quantity going down as the other goes up is not enough on its own to make it inverse.
Direct proportion requires quantities that increase together IN A CONSTANT RATIO; 'both increase' alone is not sufficient and may be non-proportional, so keep 'neither' a live category.
Give learners the terms to USE in describing and solving problems, not to define in isolation (e.g. compute the speed of a car doing 120 miles in 2 hours and NAME it a rate).

The term map is a consolidation/reference scaffold: it supports recognition but does not require independent production of the term in a novel context, which the productive tasks and assessment target.

A multiple-choice or categorisation check verifies correct selection; it does not on its own elicit the independent spoken/written USE of a term that is the main objective — pair recognition items with explain-and-generate tasks.

startingActivity.title: Ratio simplifying bench with a shape-stays-the-same check
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 12:8 and simplify it by repeatedly choosing a number to divide BOTH parts by (e.g. ÷4 straight to 3:2, or ÷2 to 6:4 then ÷2 again).
Watch two scaled bars drawn beside the numbers: as 12:8 becomes 6:4 becomes 3:2, the bars keep the same shape/proportion, showing the relationship is preserved.

Use a 'can this go smaller?' indicator that stays red while a common factor greater than 1 still divides both parts and turns green only when none does, so 'simplest form' becomes a testable end-state.
Then snap the 3 and 2 blocks together into one whole of 5 and read off the part-to-whole fractions 3/5 and 2/5 from the total number of blocks.
For a decimal or fraction ratio (0.5:2, or 1/2:1/3), first apply a scale-up step (×2, ×10, or a common multiplier) to reach whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2), then simplify.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Simplifying a ratio keeps the same 'for every' relationship with smaller numbers; simplest form means no common factor remains; and converting to a fraction uses the whole (a+b) as the denominator.

commonMisconceptions: Stops before simplest form — divides by a common factor but not the HCF (12:8 → 6:4 and leaves it)
Reverses the order relative to the wording (writes girls:boys)
Converts a:b to fractions using the other part as the denominator (3:2 → 3/2) instead of the whole (3/5)
Simplifies by subtracting a constant from both parts (12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7) rather than dividing — an additive slip
constraints: Keep order fixed to the wording: boys:girls must be written boys-first, to prevent order reversal.

Simplest form is reached once both parts have been divided by their highest common factor, either in one step or in several smaller steps; always check that no number other than 1 divides both parts again (e.g. 12:8 ÷4 = 3:2, and 3 and 2 share no common factor other than 1). Stopping at 6:4 is not simplest form.
The part-to-whole fraction uses the TOTAL of the parts as the denominator (3:2 → 3/5 and 2/5), never the other part (not 3/2).
Decimal or fraction ratios must first be scaled up to whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2 via a common multiplier) before simplifying.
Contrast the ratio 3:2 with the fraction 3/2 aloud so a:b is not misread as a/b.
Simplifying must preserve the relationship by dividing, not subtracting: 12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7 is an additive error that changes the 'for every'.

The scored practice set checks recognition and fluency but does not elicit the full independent simplifying procedure; it complements active manipulation rather than replacing it. In a fraction-of-the-whole item, keep the incorrect options genuinely distinct in value (e.g. 3/2, the part-to-part reading, versus 2/5, the other part's share of the whole), not numerically equal forms of the same error.
The fixed worked example is a reference only; it cannot be manipulated across many cases and so does not build fluency by itself.

startingActivity.title: Proportion lab: drive one quantity, watch the other
learnerActions: Work with three switchable scenarios: pens & cost (4 pens £6 → 10 pens £15, directly proportional); taps filling a bucket or workers digging a hole (inversely proportional); and a phone plan of £15/month + £0.20/min (linear but NOT proportional).
Before changing anything, PREDICT where the next point will land on the graph and what the paired value should be — write or say the prediction and your reason first.
Change quantity A (e.g. with a slider or by choosing a new value) and watch quantity B recompute, with the point plotting live on a graph while a ratio table fills in alongside.

In the phone-plan scenario, double the minutes while predicting the cost will also double; observe that the plotted point lands below your prediction and the traced line clearly does NOT pass through the origin.
In the inverse scenario, halve the number of taps and observe the fill time double, with the curve bending away from the straight line you expected.

Apply two quick tests out loud: 'if one quantity is zero, is the other zero?' (a first check for direct proportion; it is needed but not enough by itself, so also confirm that the ratio stays constant) and 'does doubling one halve the other, keeping the product the same?' (inverse-proportion test).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Quantity B's response to driving quantity A reveals the structure: in direct proportion the ratio holds (and the line goes through the origin), in inverse proportion the product holds (one goes down as the other goes up), and in linear-but-not-proportional situations a fixed charge means the line misses the origin so doubling fails. Proportionality is a property to test, not a default to assume.

keyRepresentations: Ratio table / double number line (direct proportion — scale columns by multiplying)
Graph through the origin (direct: straight line) vs decreasing curve (inverse)
Product-constant table for inverse proportion (e.g. speed×time = distance held fixed)
Three-bin sorting mat: directly proportional | inversely proportional | neither
commonMisconceptions: Illusion of proportionality — treating every relationship as directly proportional, applying y=kx to situations that are linear-but-not-proportional (phone plan with a fixed charge) or inverse.
Confusing direct and inverse: expecting 'twice as fast' to mean 'twice the time' rather than half the time.
Additive rather than multiplicative scaling: going from 4 pens to 8 pens by adding the same amount to the cost instead of doubling it.
Believing any straight-line graph shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
constraints: Delay the formulae y = kx and xy = c until ratio-table and product-constancy reasoning is secure, so learners reason about structure rather than substituting into a memorised triangle.
Scale direct-proportion tables by multiplying, never by adding a constant difference.
Build direct proportion from ratio tables and double number lines so the unit rate (e.g. cost per pen) stays visible.

Selection and sorting tasks check whether a learner can discriminate the three families, but recognition-only responses do not require the learner to construct or drive a relationship; pair them with the hands-on predict-and-drive work.
The fixed reference triptych shows cues and supports consolidation but cannot let a learner vary one quantity and watch the other respond; treat it as a reference, not the first encounter.

When using the taps/inverse example, state the idealisation (equal constant flow per tap, fixed bucket volume, no overflow) and be precise that the constant product is taps × time (equal to the one-tap fill time, 60 s), not the volume itself.

Optional interaction examples (a slider driving a value, a live-plotting point, a ratio table filling alongside, tap-to-reveal properties) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; the essential requirements are prediction-before-observation and side-by-side contrast of the three families.

startingActivity.title: One ratio, three costumes — and what breaks under 'add 4'
learnerActions: Work with the ratio 1:3 (e.g. red:yellow paint) and extend a ratio table: 1:3, 2:6, 3:9, 4:12, scaling both quantities together.
For each new row, plot the point (x,y) on a coordinate graph and note that the points fall on a straight line passing through the origin (0,0).
Observe a perceptible constant-ratio context alongside: in an idealised, thoroughly mixed model, a paint swatch mixed in that ratio keeps the same orange shade as the batch grows.
Name the same relationship in three forms on this one example: ratio 1:3, fraction/multiple (y is 3 times x; x is 1/3 of y), and linear function y=3x with gradient 3 (the gradient equals y÷x).

Switch the rule from multiplicative (y=3x) to additive (y=x+4) and watch what changes: the graph's line no longer passes through the origin, the plotted points leave the straight proportional line, and the swatch shade shifts row by row.
State in your own words which quantity stays constant in each case — the MULTIPLE stays fixed for a ratio relationship, while the DIFFERENCE stays fixed for an additive one.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A ratio is a single multiplicative idea wearing three costumes (ratio a:b, fraction a/b, straight line y=kx through the origin); its signature is a constant multiple, not a constant difference. When the quantities scale, the difference changes but the multiple — and the colour, the ratio and the gradient — stay the same. An additive rule breaks the line-through-origin and changes the shade, which is what separates it from a ratio.

keyRepresentations: Ratio table with the constant multiplier visible down the columns and the a:b relationship across
Double number line aligned at 0 (equal ratios line up)
Straight-line graph through the origin (y = kx) with gradient = the ratio
The triple 1:3 = 1/3-relationship = y = 3x shown together
Paired multiplicative vs additive tables for contrast (y = 3x vs y = x + 4)
commonMisconceptions: Reads a relationship additively — fixes on the difference between a pair of values ('y is 4 more than x') instead of the constant multiple
Sees the constant multiplier for whole-number rows but cannot express it as a ratio, fraction, or y = kx
Confuses the part-to-part ratio a:b with the fraction a/b of the whole
Thinks any straight-line graph shows proportionality, not noticing it must pass through the origin
constraints: Target age 12–14 (KS3); this is a conceptual objective about ratio notation and multiplicative relationships.
Ground the abstraction in at least one perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' can be seen, not merely asserted.

The invariant is best surfaced by varying values and watching what stays fixed; a static annotated triple (table, ratio, graph) can summarise and reference the connections but does not itself let the learner vary quantities, so use it as a summary rather than the sole discovery activity.

Sorting, matching and prediction tasks can check and consolidate translation between forms but are recognition-level; they do not by themselves require independent construction of the invariant, so pair them with activities where the learner scales the quantities and states the relationship.

Express the linear form as y=kx where k (the gradient) is the constant multiple y÷x; for ratio 1:3 that is y=3x. Do not write the gradient as a/b (which for 1:3 would give the incorrect 1/3); a/b=1/3 is the separate fraction reading 'x is 1/3 of y'.
Keep part-to-part ratio a:b ('x is 1/3 OF y') distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of total x+y); do not let learners write the fraction with the total as denominator.
Double number lines must start at aligned zeros for equal ratios to line up; a ratio table does not need a 0:0 row, though including one can show the link to the origin on the graph.
A straight-line graph shows proportionality only when it passes through the origin; a line not through (0,0) represents y=kx+c, not a ratio relationship.

Live recolouring, a rule toggle (y=3x vs y=x+4), draggable/extendable table rows and linked plotting are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are examples of interaction, not required mechanisms.

startingActivity.title: Double-number-line scaler: find one unit, then scale
learnerActions: On two parallel lines locked by a rate (e.g. kilograms against cost in pounds, £), slide to mark 3 kg opposite £12.
Use a 'find 1 unit' action to collapse the lines to 1 kg = £4, then slide on to 5 kg and read off £20.
Switch to a recipe mode: scale ingredients by ×6/4 (e.g. 200 g flour for 4 people → how much for 6?) shown on a bar model.
Switch to a shape mode: halve every dimension (×1/2) and read the new measurements.

Try the 'additive trap' toggle: add the same number to both lines (3 kg + 2 = 5 kg, so £12 + 2 = £14), then compare with the locked-rate result of £20. Notice that adding matching amounts instead (2 kg and its value, £8) keeps the lines aligned and gives £20.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Scaling and rates are proportional, multiplicative relationships: finding the value of one unit unlocks any target amount, and adding the same difference to both quantities does not preserve the relationship.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Double number line (two quantities scaling together) — core rate/scaling tool
Ratio table — unit value and scaled values
Bar model — fraction scaling of a quantity
Scale-factor arrow (×6/4, ×1/2) linking original to scaled
commonMisconceptions: Scaling additively — adding the difference in people/kg instead of multiplying by the ratio (recipe for 6 = recipe for 4 + 2 portions of everything, done wrongly).
Not finding the unit value, so unable to scale to a new amount.
Inverting the rate (£12 per 3 kg treated as £3 per kg).
Confusing scaling up with down, or mis-applying ×1/2.
Treating rate problems as unrelated to multiplicative comparison / fractions.
constraints: Scaling must be taught as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with additive 'add the difference' change.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Include at least one non-integer scale factor (e.g. 4→6, factor 6/4) so learners cannot rely on whole-number multiples; the unit-value route always works.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness of the unit value (e.g. 50 g per person, not 0.02).
This topic is the launchpad for formal ratio and proportion (a separate domain); keep it grounded in known multiplicative-comparison and fraction ideas rather than introducing formal ratio notation.

The worked exemplar and quiz are scaffolds/checks: a fixed image and recognition items cannot by themselves elicit independent solving of new problems, so pair them with activities where the learner constructs the solution.

The 'additive trap' toggle and live sliders are optional devices for making the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and manipulation is not asserted to be the only way to learn this.
