startingActivity.title: Enlargement studio: grab, scale, and compare with additive mode
learnerActions: Work on a grid with a non-square rectangle or triangle whose aspect ratio is locked. Drag a corner to enlarge it and watch a live scale-factor readout while every side multiplies by the same factor and the angles stay unchanged; for a rectangle enlarged from a fixed corner, notice the dragged opposite corner moves along the original's diagonal, showing it is the same shape.
Fill a ratio table alongside (old side | new side for each pair) and check that the same column multiplier appears for every pair of corresponding sides.

Flip to an 'additive mode' that instead ADDS your chosen number to each side of the non-square rectangle; observe it stretch lopsided and fall off the original's diagonal — it is no longer similar. Compare directly with the multiplicative result.
Turn on a grid-tiling overlay: with a scale factor of 2, see FOUR copies of the original tile the new shape; with a factor of 3, nine copies fit — connect this to area × k².
If a scaling touches only one side, use the flag that highlights the unchanged side and correct it so every corresponding side is scaled.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Enlargement multiplies every corresponding side by the SAME factor, preserving shape and angles; adding the same amount to each side of a non-square rectangle distorts it. Because the shape grows in two dimensions, area scales by k², not by k.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ratio table pairing corresponding sides (old side | new side), scale factor as the column multiplier
Overlaid/nested shapes on a grid showing the enlargement from a centre
Area grid showing k² tiling (double sides → four sub-rectangles)
The scale-factor arrow (×k) applied to every corresponding side
commonMisconceptions: Additive enlargement — adding the same amount to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor (distorts the shape; the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error).
Treating 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or as 'congruent/identical', not checking that all sides share one ratio.
Believing that doubling the lengths doubles the area (area actually scales by k²; MAP Enlargements documents this as a persistent error).
Applying the scale factor to only one side, or using new÷old for one pair and old÷new for another (inconsistent direction).
constraints: Establish the definition — same shape, equal angles, ALL corresponding sides in one ratio — and contrast a true enlargement with a stretched copy BEFORE any calculation.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair (new ÷ old), then apply the SAME factor to every other side; make 'multiply by the same number' explicit.

A static nested-shapes diagram with tap-to-reveal '×k per side' and 'area ×k²' can consolidate the rule as a reference card, but does not let the learner manipulate and watch the additive distortion occur; use it after, not instead of, hands-on work.

Multiple-choice/recognition items (e.g. choosing which pair is similar) assess discrimination but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of finding and applying a scale factor; include fill-in and show-your-working tasks for production.
Keep the direction of division consistent (new ÷ old) within a comparison, and sense-check whether the answer should be larger or smaller before computing.
The 3D solid-scaling activity is an optional extension that goes beyond the 2D similar-shapes objective and must not be the main teaching artefact.

Illustrative interface features (locked aspect ratio, live scale-factor readout, additive-mode toggle, diagonal check, tiling overlay, ratio table, single-side flag) are examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory requirements.

The additive-mode distortion demonstration should use a non-square rectangle, since a square keeps its shape under equal additions; present the additive result (e.g. 21) only as a flagged error, never as a valid answer option.

startingActivity.title: Measure, scale and convert on a map
learnerActions: Read the scale ratio aloud before calculating, e.g. 'one centimetre on the map is 25000 centimetres in real life' — emphasise that both sides share the SAME unit.

Measure the map distance between two points (e.g. two villages 8 cm apart on a 1:25000 map). Optionally, drag a ruler on a map and use a live panel that unfolds measured map-cm, multiplication by25000, then the cm-to-m-to-km conversion, with the scale bar alongside for checking.
Before calculating, estimate: real life is bigger than the map, so map→real MUST multiply — predict roughly how big the real distance should be.
Do the unit conversion as a deliberate final step, tracking units: 200000 cm ÷ 100 = 2000 m, then ÷ 1000 = 2 km.
Apply the scale to the whole measurement, keeping both quantities in a common unit — do not scale only part of the problem.
Cross-check against the scale bar on the map and against your estimate: is 2 km between villages sensible?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Scale is a consistent multiplier: going from a map measurement to the real distance means multiplying by the scale denominator for this reduced map; the reverse means dividing. commonMisconceptions: Forgetting the unit conversion — leaving the real distance in centimetres (200000 cm) instead of converting to metres/kilometres, or converting with the wrong factor.
Going the wrong direction — dividing a map measurement instead of multiplying (or vice versa), producing a real distance smaller than the map one.
Misreading the ratio — treating 1:25000 additively, or reading it as '1 cm = 25000 km' (unit slip).
Applying the scale to only part of the problem, or mixing map units and real units without a common basis.
constraints: Practise BOTH directions: reading a real distance from a map (multiply) AND creating a scale diagram (divide). A procedure learned in only one direction is not yet secure.

For real-distance questions requesting kilometres, show the explicit conversion chain with units (cm to m: divide by100; m to km: divide by1000). Do not stop at an unconverted centimetre value for those questions. Scale-drawing lengths may appropriately be given in centimetres.
Read the ratio as a same-unit multiplier — both sides of 1:25000 are the same unit — to block additive readings and unit slips like '1 cm = 25000 km'.
Apply the scale consistently to the whole measurement, keeping map and real quantities on a common-unit basis; do not scale only part of a problem.

The annotated/reference map is a scaffold for reading and consolidation; it cannot provide practice in measuring a self-chosen distance or in drawing to scale, so it should not be the primary teaching activity.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check whether errors are spotted; they do not elicit the independent construction of a scale drawing, which requires the learner to compute and draw the lines themselves.

A live-computing map tool and interactive layout are optional means to make the measure-scale-convert and divide-direction feedback immediate; the same learning can be reached with a paper map, ruler, scale bar and squared paper.

startingActivity.title: Rate workshop: best-buy, two-leg journey, and km/h↔m/s converter
learnerActions: Best-buy station: compare two shelf tags (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20). Put both onto a shared 'cost per 100 g' line and state which is cheaper.
Two-leg journey station: assemble a journey of 60 km at 60 km/h then 60 km at 40 km/h, and — before doing any arithmetic — predict the average speed for the whole journey.

Now compute it: write down the time each leg takes (60÷60 = 1 h and 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km) and total time (2.5 h), then average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h). Compare this with your prediction and explain the gap.
Converter station: turn a km/h figure into m/s as two visible steps — ×1000 (km→m), then ÷3600 (per hour→per second) — tracking units so they cancel on screen.
Sanity-check magnitude: 36 km/h should come out as about 10 m/s — a fast cycling/sprinting pace, well above a walk — not 0.6 or 600.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A rate is 'how much for exactly one', computed by dividing the right way round; average speed is total distance ÷ total time (not the mean of speeds) because more time spent at the slower speed pulls the average down; conversions are a tracked chain, not a single memorised factor; and fair comparisons need a common per-unit basis.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Double number line pairing the two quantities (e.g. km against hours, cost against grams)
Ratio table for scaling a rate up and down and for unit conversion
Unit-rate label ('£ per 100 g', 'm per s') as the object of comparison
Distance–time context for average speed (total over total)
commonMisconceptions: Averaging two speeds directly (60 and 40 → '50') instead of using total distance ÷ total time.
Dividing the wrong way round when forming a rate (time ÷ distance for speed, or cost basis inverted).
Comparing unit prices on different bases (price of the big pack vs unit price of the small) and concluding the cheaper total is the better value.
Botching km/h↔m/s by using a single wrong factor (e.g. ×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000÷3600 chain.
Treating the formula triangle as the concept — getting a number without knowing whether it should be bigger or smaller.
constraints: Derive every compound measure as a unit rate first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table before introducing any formula.
For best-buy, insist on a common basis (cost per 100 g, or per item for both products) rather than comparing raw price to raw size.

Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong; include the equal-TIMES counterexample where the mean IS correct, so pupils learn the precise condition rather than a blanket 'never average speeds'.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked, not a single memorised factor; include a magnitude sanity check (e.g. 36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling; use the triangle only with care if at all.
The reference card is a consolidation scaffold: it holds facts but does not let the learner perform or check a calculation, so it must not be the sole activity for this procedural skill.

The short check records which answer was produced and surfaces specific slips, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the full method; pair it with the paper performance task.
Density and unit price follow the same multiplicative 'per one' structure as speed; comparisons and conversions should be modelled on that shared structure rather than treated as separate rules.

startingActivity.title: Linked board: one rate, three views that move together
learnerActions: Enter or accept a rate such as 3 kg → £6 and watch a ratio table, a double number line, and a coordinate graph populate for the SAME example.
Plot the proportional pairs on the graph and draw the line; confirm it passes through the origin.
Drag a point to 5 kg and read £10 simultaneously on the table, the number line, and the graph.

Point to where the constant '×2' appears in each view: the gradient of the line (£2 per kg), the multiplier from each kg entry to its £ entry in the table (3 → 6, 5 → 10), and the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6).
Flip a 'fixed charge' toggle (e.g. add a standing £2) and observe the whole line lift OFF the origin while staying perfectly straight; state whether it is still proportional and why not.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: All three representations encode the SAME constant multiplier, and the origin — not mere straightness — is the test of proportionality.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0)
Ratio table with a constant column multiplier
Coordinate graph: straight line through the origin (gradient = the rate)
Overlay contrasting a through-origin line with a not-through-origin line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any straight line — or any rising graph — shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
Not aligning the double number line at 0, so equivalent ratios don't correspond.
Reading a graph as isolated points and being unable to interpolate an unknown, or swapping the axes when reading off.
Believing the graph need not start at (0,0) — missing that zero of one quantity means zero of the other.
constraints: Multiple-choice identification and tap-to-reveal items assess or rehearse recognition of cues; they do not by themselves elicit the independent production of an origin-anchored line, so include a draw/plot task for full mastery.
An annotated fixed graph cannot be freely manipulated; pair it with a task where learners plot, drag, or draw so the constant multiplier is explored, not just viewed.
Always keep double number lines aligned at 0 and scales consistent, or equivalent ratios will not correspond.
When introducing the fixed-charge contrast, state the setup explicitly (e.g. £2 standing charge plus £2/kg) so learners attribute the lifted line to the non-zero start, not to a changed rate.

When asking learners to draw a 'different' line, ensure the chosen rate is genuinely different from any line already on the axes (£1/kg, not £2/kg, against a given £2/kg line), so the task is coherent.

In-role dialogue and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits here: the relationship is inherently 2D (two quantities, one plane), and drawing/reading a graph is a visual-spatial task; these are design judgements for this topic, not universal rules.

activityReferences.title: Tile the square metre: deriving the k² (and k³) factor
Multi-step conversion as a tracked chain

startingActivity.title: Tile the square metre: deriving the k² (and k³) factor
learnerActions: On a 1 m square, mark how many cm fit along ONE side (100), then work out how many cm squares tile the whole square (100 × 100 = 10 000). State the equivalence 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
Convert 3 m² to cm², showing working: 1 m² = 100² = 10 000 cm², so 3 × 10 000 = 30 000 cm².

Extend to volume: picture a 1 m cube filled with cm cubes along each edge (100), so the whole cube holds 100³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Decide whether 1 m³ equals 100, 10 000, or 1 000 000 cm³ and justify your choice — the correct answer is 1 000 000; 100 is the trap of applying the linear factor and 10 000 the trap of applying the area factor.

If using an interactive bench, enter the value and units and watch a 1 m square flood with a 100×100 grid as the counter climbs to 10 000; optionally switch to a 3D mode that stacks cm cubes in a 1 m cube up to a million — these visuals are optional illustrations of why the factor is squared/cubed, not required mechanisms. A printed grid may be used the same way; treat it as a thin physical approximation of the ideal square metre.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When a length scales by factor k, area scales by k² and volume by k³, so converting area/volume uses the square/cube of the linear conversion factor, not the linear factor itself.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Tiled-square / stacked-cube diagram showing k² and k³ (1 m² = 10 000 cm²)
Conversion chain with the factor written on each arrow (h → min → s)
Place-value / decimal grid for cm↔m
Double number line pairing the two units
commonMisconceptions: Converting area/volume with the LINEAR factor — 1 m² = 100 cm² (should be 10 000), 1 m³ = 100 cm³ (should be 1 000 000).
Going the wrong direction — multiplying when converting to a bigger unit, so the number grows when it should shrink.
Stopping a multi-step conversion partway (hours to minutes but not on to seconds), or using a wrong intermediate factor (e.g. treating an hour as 100 minutes).
Decimal place-value slips when moving between units (5 cm → 0.5 m instead of 0.05 m).
constraints: The target objective requires pupils to construct and show conversion working (especially the squared/cubed factor and each chain step), not merely select correct answers; recognition-only items assess classification/selection but do not elicit independent construction, so pair them with a produced conversion.

Interactive visuals (flooding a 1 m square with a 100×100 grid, stacking cm cubes in a 1 m cube, factor-on-each-arrow chains that refuse skipped steps) are optional illustrations of the mechanism; they are not the only way to teach the k² / k³ idea. A static tiled-square diagram with reveal of '10 000 cm² in 1 m² because 100²' can consolidate the fact but does not itself let a pupil run and check their own conversion.

A paper/card cm-square cutout or printed grid has slight thickness and is a physical approximation of the ideal (zero-thickness) area model; use it to count tiles but keep the represented square metre distinct from the cutout.
The 3D cube-fill is a volume-focused extension; most of the topic is handled well with 2D grids and chains.
Decimal place-value accuracy (to three decimal places) is a precision requirement; a place-value chart and convert-back check are prompts for accuracy, not a conceptual reteach.
Direction must be sense-checked against relative unit size: converting to a smaller unit increases the number, to a larger unit decreases it.

startingActivity.title: Tell the literal robot where teddy goes
learnerActions: Direct a friendly robot (or puppet/character) to place teddy somewhere, e.g. say 'put teddy by the box'.

Watch the robot do EXACTLY what the words say — 'by the box' only means near the box, so the robot might put teddy behind it, in front of it, or beside it — so the ambiguity can produce a result that is not where the child meant.
Refine the instruction to a precise positional word ('on top of the box', 'behind the box') and check the robot now gets it right.
Repeat with a comparison round: ask for 'the tower with MORE blocks' rather than 'the bigger tower', to distinguish taller from more.
Say, in the child's own words, why the exact word helped the robot understand.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A vague everyday word (like 'by' or 'big') often fails to pin down the meaning; choosing a precise word (on top of / behind; taller / more) lets a listener do exactly what you intend.

constraints: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation.

Build informal→formal: accept the child's own words ('pointy', 'curved', 'big') first, then introduce and reinforce formal words gradually; have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than simply supplying it.
Pair each word with the action or feature it names (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) so vocabulary is grounded, not recited.
Treat interchangeable use of 'sides' and 'corners' as a developmental stage that resolves with exposure, not an error to drill or mark wrong.

A picture-word matching or tap-to-reveal task can check or prime recognition but does not by itself elicit the child producing or refining language; use it as a warm-up alongside the directing/dialogue activities, not as the sole vehicle.
The spatial-scene activity supports only the positional strand; it does not exercise comparison or shape-name vocabulary.

Diagnostic prompts deliberately use an ambiguous word (e.g. 'by') so the vagueness is detectable; a precise word like 'behind' would not reveal whether the child attends to precision. Responses are surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.

When naming a square, use the properties that define it (four equal sides and four square corners), so a non-square rhombus is not accepted as a square; the teaching point is that turning a shape does not change its identity.

startingActivity.title: The curious listener who wants to know HOW
learnerActions: Solve a within-10 problem such as 5 and 3 using counters (physical objects or on-screen draggable counters).
When asked 'how did you get 8? show me!', move or point to the counters to re-enact the method — for example, 'I put 5, then counted on 3 more'.
Hear the method echoed back as a little story ('first you put 5, then you counted on 3 more, so you got 8') and notice that explaining = showing the doing, not repeating the answer.
Watch the listener solve a problem its own way — sometimes by a muddled or wrong route — and answer 'do you agree with how I did it? how can you tell?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: 'How do you know?' is answered by demonstrating the method, not by restating the answer; and a method can be judged by whether its steps make sense, not only by whether the final number is right.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters moved to enact and show a method
Ten frame and part-part-whole drawing
Number sentence alongside the objects
Spoken sentence stems ('first… then… so…')
The describe → explain step of the NRICH reasoning ladder
commonMisconceptions: Restating the answer ('because it's 8') when asked 'how do you know?' instead of showing the method
A quiet or brief response mistaken for weak reasoning, when it is really communication that lags
Judging a peer's work only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the method makes sense
Believing 'showing your working' means writing the sum again rather than revealing the thinking
constraints: The target is demonstrating AND beginning to evaluate a method — not producing a single scored answer. An answer-only, scored format can record only the final result and cannot capture showing or telling a method, and it tends to reward the answer-restating this topic must move beyond; if used at all, treat it as a check of the final result, not of the reasoning.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a modelling scaffold: the child watches rather than demonstrates, so it must be followed by the child producing and narrating their own method.

Separate reasoning from its communication: when a child is quiet or brief, judge whether they need help thinking or help putting it into words, and support that thread. Do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation.
Elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects, pointing, and drawings; accept these as valid ways to show working rather than requiring written sums or rich sentences.
At this age, full critique of a peer's reasoning is only emerging; expect the child to begin attending to steps (e.g. 'can you show what I did?') rather than deliver a complete evaluation.

Showing arithmetic working here does not need elaborate 3D spatial environments: simple concrete arrangements such as counters and ten frames are useful for showing a method, but complex spatial/3D manipulation is not needed for this objective, though it may serve other topics.

startingActivity.title: Weigh the sentence: does '=' balance?
learnerActions: Take a friend's working, 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 = 15, and look only at the middle part: 7 + 5 = 12 + 3.

Using identical cubes (each cube weighs the same), place 7+5 cubes on the left pan and 12+3 cubes on the right pan of a pan balance and observe which way it tips (left holds 12 cubes, right holds 15, so the heavier right pan sinks and the lighter left pan rises — it does not balance).
Say aloud what '=' promises: both sides weigh the same.
Decide whether 7 + 5 = 12 + 3 is true or false, and explain using the balance.
Make both sides the same a different way, e.g. check that 3 + 5 = 6 + 2 (both are 8).
Complete an open sentence like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 by making the pans level, and say what number balances it (7).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same amount; it is not an arrow pointing to the next answer. A running chain like 7+5=12+3=15 misuses '='. A balance that tips or levels makes this relationship visible.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Pan balance / balance scale for the equals sign
True/false and open number sentences
3-D shapes with face, edge, vertex labelled and handled
Measurement answers written with units (12 cm, 3 kg)
Comparison statements with >, <, =
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' operationally as 'the answer is / and then', writing running chains like 7+5=12+3=15 (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Fills 8+4=□+5 with 12 (the total so far) or 17 (everything added), not 7
Omits units, giving '12' for a length that is 12 cm — treating the unit as optional (CCSS)
Describes 3-D shapes with 2-D or loose words — 'corner' for vertex, 'side' for face, or calls a cube a 'square'
constraints: The equals-sign strand is the priority: most primary children read '=' operationally, so teaching must directly confront the running-chain error with true/false and open sentences, not assume the relational meaning is obvious.
A true/false or unit-completion sorting check identifies the error pattern but does not itself elicit the child's reasoning or show why '=' means balance; pair it with discussion or balance work.

A labelled static picture or reference card can display finished, labelled examples but cannot let the child balance a sentence, attach a unit, or rotate a shape; use it only as a reference, not as the main learning mechanism.
The spatial 3-D shape strand (face/edge/vertex) benefits from a handled solid or rotatable model; the equals-sign and units strands are not spatial and need the balance and unit-naming work instead.

Physical solids have real thickness and can be picked up; an on-screen 3-D model is a rotatable representation. Both support the vocabulary strand through different experiences; neither is uniquely required. Do not teach 'can be picked up' as the test for a solid — ask instead about the mathematical shape and its named parts.
Recognition/sorting items alone do not elicit independent construction — have the child build balanced open sentences and state units themselves, not only pick from options.

startingActivity.title: Convince-me dialogue: catch the broken step
learnerActions: Listen to or read a plausible-but-wrong worked chain, e.g. a partner says: 'I did 71 minus 46. I couldn't do 1 take 6, so I did 6 take 1, that's 5, then 7 take 4 is 3, so 35.'
Point to the EXACT line where the thinking first goes wrong (the digit-flip), rather than re-solving and comparing totals.
Say WHY that line breaks, grounded in place value: 'you can't flip the digits; the 1 is really part of 71, so you exchange a ten to make 11, and 11 take 6 is 5.'
When challenged with 'how do you know?' or 'why does exchanging fix it?', keep going until the objection becomes a because-chain.
Then construct a correct chain aloud for 71 − 46, starting from what 71 really is (giving 25).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Critiquing someone else's error forces your own reasoning to become explicit: a vague 'that's not right' can be turned, under questioning, into a because-chain you did not know you had.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Fraction bars / area models for size arguments (more equal parts ⇒ smaller pieces, so 1/3 > 1/5)
Place-value equipment or a written column layout for locating an exchange error
A because/therefore sentence frame turning a list of facts into a chain
Derived-fact number strings (6×10, 6×2 ⇒ 6×8) shown as a linked sequence, not isolated facts
commonMisconceptions: 'It's wrong because the answer's different from mine' — judges a peer's argument by answer-agreement rather than by finding the flawed step
Checking one example and treating the rule as proved for all cases
Restating the method louder instead of giving a reason why it works
Believing a longer fraction/denominator names a bigger piece (1/5 > 1/3)
constraints: The productive half of this practice — constructing a multi-step argument and explaining a flaw in the child's own words — requires construction and talk; a scored fixed-answer format can test RECOGNISING a correct argument or spotting a flagged flawed step, but a 'spot the flawed step' multiple-choice item should be used only as a warm-up and its score should not be treated as evidence of the reasoning practice.

Static compare-and-annotate pairs are scaffolds: they can show and label arguments but cannot elicit the child's own chain or respond to their reasoning. Follow them immediately with construction or critique.

Error analysis is the practice: finding one clear faulty step and explaining it is the goal, not re-solving and comparing answers. Keep critique pointed at the shared representation so it targets the reasoning, not the person.
Scribe/revoice a child whose reasoning outruns their words; do not judge reasoning by fluency of telling or score it.

Distinguish an argument-skill gap from a prerequisite gap: if a child endorses 'always take the smaller from the larger', reteach the column-subtraction exchange concept with base-ten equipment before expecting critique of that algorithm.

This guidance is medium-flexible: a live partner, scribed classroom talk, paper worked examples, or a screen workspace can all carry it. Interaction examples (tile snapping, tapping a step, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative, not mandatory.

startingActivity.title: Tiling to find the unit for area
learnerActions: Enter or write the area of a rectangle, e.g. '63'.
Fill (or draw) the rectangle with unit squares that tile it exactly, counting the squares.
Revise the answer to carry a square unit: '63 cm²' or '63 square centimetres'.

startingActivity.title: Testing factor vs multiple with arrays
learnerActions: Take the statement '6 is a multiple of 12' and test it: try to build 6 by stepping up in 12s (12, 24, 36...) — it never lands on 6.
Now test whether 6 fits INTO a 12-array (arrange 12 as two rows of 6, or six columns of 2) — it does, evenly.
State the corrected sentence: '6 is a FACTOR of 12' (equivalently, '12 is a multiple of 6'), and say why.
Repeat with a second pair: is 24 a factor or a multiple of 12? Build it by stepping up in 12s (12, 24) to show it is a multiple.
Write the definition in your own words: a factor fits into a number exactly, with no remainder; a multiple is a step in that number's times-table.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A factor divides evenly INTO a number, while a multiple is built FROM it by multiplying — so direction matters and the terms are not interchangeable.

Presents an estimate as an exact value, omitting 'approximately'
constraints: Sort/label and 'read the notation' screener items can efficiently flag factor/multiple and index errors, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the child's reasoning about the definitions or independent construction of the corrected term — pair any screener with a task requiring the learner to explain or produce.

A unit-cube model is useful for grounding 'cubed' and cm³, which is genuinely spatial; factor/multiple and most of this band are not spatial, so a 3D model is a companion for the volume-notation strand only, not a general requirement.
Drawn dot-squares and unit-square/cube diagrams are concrete approximations; distinguish the counted squares/cubes from the quantity (area/volume) they represent.
Estimate-tagging ('approximately') depends on the task being genuinely an estimate — do not apply it to exact measured or computed values.

startingActivity.title: Sort algebra cards by the role of '='
learnerActions: Sort three cards — '3x + 5', '3x + 5 = 11', 'V = l × w × h' — into three bins labelled expression, equation and formula.

For each card, say out loud what makes it belong there: Does it have an equals sign? If it does, is it a statement of equality that is true only for particular values of an unknown (one you solve), or a general rule relating quantities that holds for any values (a formula, which is a special kind of equation)?

Explain the consequence: an expression can be evaluated (worked out once you know the value of the letter) or simplified, but not solved, while an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved (find the unknown that makes it true).
Test the boundary with a non-example question such as 'Is 3x + 5 an equation? Why not?' and 'What single change would turn 3x + 5 into an equation?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The presence and role of '=' is the defining feature: an expression has none, an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 asserts equality for a particular unknown value (and can be solved), and a formula is a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities for any values. The precise term changes what you are allowed to do with the object.

startingActivity.title: The confident conjecture champion (adversarial dialogue)
learnerActions: Face an in-role character who asserts a universal claim with total confidence: 'Multiplying ALWAYS makes a number bigger — I've tried 3×4, 5×6, 10×10, works every time. So it's proved, right?'
Decide whether piling up more agreeing examples settles it, or whether you must HUNT for a case that breaks the claim.
Produce and state a decisive counter-example, e.g. '6 times a half is three — that's smaller, so it's not always,' and explain why that single case is enough.

When the champion patches the claim ('okay, multiplying always makes bigger OR the same') test the patch again: × 1/2 still shrinks it (so it breaks the patch), while × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch now allows.

When the champion defends a flawed fraction division ('just flip the FIRST fraction') locate the faulty step, say why it fails, and give the correct method (invert the divisor — the second fraction — then multiply).
Answer the champion's probes: 'Is that a proof or just examples?' and 'Does the opposite — the converse — also hold?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A universal claim is destroyed by one honest counter-example, while confirming cases cannot prove it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers); constructing arguments and critiquing flawed ones are the same reasoning practice, and a claim is not the same as its converse.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: A single well-chosen counter-example as a disproof object (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3 against 'multiplying makes bigger')
Chained angle-fact diagrams (angles on a line / in a triangle / vertically opposite) building to a proved value
Scaling picture of multiplication (× less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) to reason about product size without computing
A because/therefore proof frame linking givens through steps to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes bigger / division always makes smaller' — the whole-number generalisation that fails for factors below 1
Confirming a conjecture with examples and calling it proved (empirical proof scheme)
Confusing a statement with its converse ('if square then 4 right angles' ⇒ 'if 4 right angles then square')
Inverting the wrong fraction in division, or 'dividing straight across', and critiquing only by the odd-looking answer rather than the faulty step
Believing a proved geometric result holds only for the specific diagram drawn
constraints: Insist on proof by chained fact, not measurement: measuring is only for checking a value, never for establishing that an angle MUST be a given size.
A proved geometric result holds generally, not only for the specific diagram drawn — make this generality explicit so learners do not think the proof applies only to one picture.

Reward finding the single breaker over listing confirming cases; explicitly name the asymmetry (one counter-example disproves an 'always'; no number of confirming cases proves it unless every possible case has been checked, which is impossible for claims about all numbers).
Keep the claim/converse distinction concrete: 'if square then four right angles' is not the same as 'if four right angles then square' (a non-square rectangle breaks the converse).

Recognition and selection tasks (pick-the-breaker, tap-the-step) are scaffolds; they do not elicit a learner-constructed proof chain or a flaw explained in the learner's own words, so do not treat a correct selection or score as evidence of the full reasoning practice.

If a learner endorses 'multiplication always makes bigger', treat it as a genuine false belief: reteach multiplication as scaling (for a positive starting number: × less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) with a picture, not only the argument skill.

When a learner suspects a rule is false but cannot yet find the counter-example, prompt the search ('what if a number were less than 1? try a half') without handing over the answer — the deductive instinct is forming.

The flawed fraction-division cue is 'invert/flip the first fraction'; it must always be presented as the error to find and critique, never as a method to follow — the correct method inverts the divisor (second fraction) then multiplies.

Any conjecture used in a sort must have a determinate truth value as stated; if a claim's truth depends on scope (e.g. 'more sides, bigger angles' depends on angle type and regular vs irregular), state that scope inside the activity so the sort is fair.
Static annotated examples and reveal cards cannot respond to a learner's own implication errors; pair them with dialogue or discussion.

activityReferences.title: The tool tray: 8 + 7 and 3 + 2

startingActivity.title: The tool tray: 8 + 7 and 3 + 2
learnerActions: Face the problem 8 + 7 with a tray offering cubes, counters, a ten frame, and fingers; pick a tool and use it to solve.
If you choose fingers and try to show 8 and then 7 more, notice you pass ten and run out of fingers before you reach the answer.

Try the ten frame instead: place 8 (nearly filling one frame), then split the 7 — 2 completes the first ten, and the remaining 5 go beside the full frame (or into a second frame), giving 'fill to ten, then five more — fifteen.'
Say why your chosen tool helped: e.g. 'it shows the gap to ten' or 'the fingers ran out'.
Now solve 3 + 2 and decide which tool fits — discover that fingers work perfectly here, so the best choice depends on the numbers, not on a favourite.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Choose a tool and strategy because they help with the particular problem. Showing all15 objects at once on one finger each exceeds ten fingers, but counting-on with fingers can still solve8+7. A ten frame offers another useful structure: the gap to ten. Accept a valid strategy when the learner explains how it helps.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Ten frame (rows of five/ten expose the gap to ten)
Cubes / multilink (joinable and splittable)
Counters
Fingers
Five frame
commonMisconceptions: Reaches for the same familiar tool (usually fingers) every time regardless of whether it fits — e.g. fingers for 8+7
Uses the tool to get an answer but cannot say why it helped — treats it as a ritual, not a thinking aid (EEF)
Becomes reliant on the tool and cannot attempt even a small, known fact without it (EEF)
Thinks the ten frame is just somewhere to put counters, missing that its rows of five and ten show structure
constraints: The goal at this age is the dawning judgement that a tool is FIT for a purpose, not fluent tool use — value the fit-reason as much as the answer.
Keep tools as temporary scaffolds: model solving a small, known fact without a tool afterwards so reliance does not set in.

A child who insists on a tool for a fact they genuinely already know (e.g. 2+1) is likely showing reliance on the scaffold rather than a conceptual gap — gently invite them to try without the tool to build confidence, and only revisit counting if the fact turns out not to be secure.

A 'meet the tools' reveal and a single 'which tool is best?' recognition item can introduce or feed into the work, but they do not elicit the child choosing, using, and justifying a tool, so they are not the main vehicle. A lucky pick on a recognition item can score full marks without revealing the reasoning.

Compare3+2 and8+7 and ask what each tool or strategy makes easier. Directly showing every object on one finger runs out above ten, but a child may use fingers successfully for counting-on; accept a correct method with a clear fit-reason rather than requiring one tool to fail.

startingActivity.title: The thinking partner who won't take a number yet
learnerActions: Listen to a tiny within-10 spoken story from a friendly partner character, e.g. 'Three frogs were on a log and two more hopped on.'
Before giving any answer, retell the story in your own words and say what is being asked ('what are we trying to find out?').
Show the story with counters/frogs or fingers ('show me with your frogs') so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Work out an answer for a solvable story, then answer the partner's closing question: 'Does your answer make sense in the story?'
When the partner occasionally tells a deliberately silly story ('...so what colour is the pond?' or '...so how old is the cat?'), catch that it cannot be worked out and say why.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A word problem is a situation to understand, not just numbers to do a sum with; sense-making and a reasonableness check come before and after calculating.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters the child physically moves to enact the story
Part-part-whole picture (two groups combining into a whole)
Simple bar or strip drawing linking the known and unknown quantities
Numberless word-problem staging (reveal the story, then the question, then the numbers last)
A four-move frame: understand → represent → solve → check
commonMisconceptions: 'I look for the special word — altogether means add, left means take away' (keyword strategy, applied before the story is even read)
'Every problem is just a sum with the numbers in it' — computes an answer even for an unanswerable or nonsensical story (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate)
Restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for
Treating being stuck as 'I can't do it' rather than a cue to represent the story a different way
constraints: Comprehension first: have the child retell the problem in their own words and say what is being asked BEFORE any calculating.

Never teach cue-word rules ('altogether means add', 'left means take away'); build understanding of the situation, not word-to-operation mapping. Cue words misfire when the word points the wrong way — e.g. a 'more' comparison story whose answer is actually found by subtracting.
Represent the situation concretely (counters, fingers, a simple drawing, or a simple bar/strip drawing linking the known and unknown quantities) so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Deliberately include the occasional unanswerable or 'silly' story so children learn not every set of numbers yields a sum; keep most stories genuinely solvable.
The tap-to-reveal worked example shows the routine but has the child watch rather than do it; use it as a companion, not the main practice for a habit that must be practised.

Scored, speed-oriented quizzing of multiple sums is unsuitable here: it can score the final number but not 'made sense of the story', and it reinforces the compulsion to calculate. A single reasonableness item is acceptable; a battery of sums is not.

Making sense of a word problem is a comprehension task, not a spatial one; a 3-D handling environment is not recommended for this topic because it adds handling cost without serving the comprehension-first goal. This is a scoped suitability judgement, not a claim that 3-D adds nothing in general.
When a child is stuck, scaffold by offering a representation ('let's put out the counters') and naming the move ('when it's tricky, we show it a different way'), rather than reteaching the concept.
Watch for restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for.

startingActivity.title: Build the story, then flip it
learnerActions: Listen to or watch a short story: 'Five ducks bob on a pond, then two more paddle in.'
Drag/place five cubes into the left of a part-whole frame and two into the right to match the story.
Watch a bar form across the top and the sentence 5 + 2 = 7 appear, with the '5' marking the first cubes and the '2' marking the newcomers.
Point to which cubes are the 5, which are the 2, and show the whole group.

'Flip it': take a pile of cubes already split (e.g. 4 and 3) and invent a story the picture could tell — then notice the SAME cubes could be 'four birds and three more' OR 'seven birds, three flew off'.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The model carries meaning in both directions: numbers stand for ducks, the joining stands for adding, and the child can travel from world to symbol and back — the model is not a picture of an answer but a thing that holds a relationship.

keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes for acting out and combining/separating
Five-frame and ten-frame for structuring the quantities
Part-whole picture: two groups lined up with a drawn bar beside them (the bar model's earliest form)
Simple number sentence (with +, −) as the symbolic end of the concrete→pictorial→abstract bridge
commonMisconceptions: Treats the model as a picture of two separate amounts, not a relationship — lays out 5 and 2 but cannot say which is the whole or show the joining
Loses the exact quantities when telling a story from objects ('some ducks and some more') instead of preserving 5 and 2
Produces the total by counting all but cannot point to the parts or the action inside the model
Picks the operation from a word ('more' → add) rather than from what happens in the situation
constraints: The productive core is CONSTRUCTING the model and explaining what each part represents, and working the translation BOTH ways (situation→model and model→story). Recognition-only tasks (e.g. 'which number sentence matches this picture?') can at most serve as a brief warm-up; a correct match does not show the child can build the model or map the parts, so do not read a match score as evidence of quantitative reasoning.
A fixed reveal/tap scene is a worked example only: it cannot let the child do the two-way translation or vary the quantities. Use it before the builder, not as assessment.

Assessment should not stop at the total: both a reasoning child and a compute-only child may say 'seven'. Listen for the mapping (which cubes are the 5, which the 2) and the joining action, which are hard to fake without the meaning.

When a child tells a vague story that loses the exact numbers (e.g. 'some ducks and some more'), do not mark it wrong — the reasoning may be present while the language of quantity is still forming; scribe/revoice to recover the precise numbers.
Do not let the child pick the operation from a word ('more' → add); connect the operation to what actually happens in the situation (putting together = addition, taking away = subtraction).

startingActivity.title: Act the story on cubes, then read the answer back
learnerActions: Listen to or watch a short story, e.g. 'I had 5 apples in a bowl and I ate 2 of them'
Show the story with counters/cubes: start with five, then physically remove two to model the eating as a taking-away
Optionally arrange the counters on a five-frame or ten-frame to structure and see the quantities clearly
As the model settles on three, say or build the matching number sentence 5 − 2 = 3
Answer the question 'three what?' by saying 'three apples left' and pointing to the three remaining in the model
Check the model against the story: 'Does what I did to the cubes match what happened to the apples?'
startingActivity.intendedInsight: The model must preserve the ACTION of the story (taking away), not just the numbers; and the answer is three apples still in the bowl, not the bare number 3.

keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes acted on to show joining or taking away
Simple drawings that show the action of the story
Dictated or written number sentence (5 − 2 = 3) tied to the story
Five-frame/ten-frame to structure the quantities
commonMisconceptions: Models the numbers but not the action — draws 5 and 2 as if adding when the story takes away
Gives a bare number ('three') without saying what it means about the apples
Accepts an answer that contradicts the story (more apples after eating some) — doesn't check the model against the situation
Draws the objects decoratively without preserving the quantities in the story
constraints: Model the ACTION, not just the numbers: 'ate 2' must be shown as removal, and the model must be checked against what actually happened.
Always read the answer back into the story ('three apples left'), not as a bare number — the interpret-in-context habit starts here.
Work both directions (story→objects and objects→story) so the model is understood as standing for the situation.

A static tap-to-reveal scene (tap apples to see '5', tap eaten ones to see '−2', flap reveals '3 left') can present one worked example mapping a situation to a number sentence, but it is a scaffold: it cannot let the child act out the situation, vary it, or build their own model.

A scored 'which sentence matches?' item tests recognition and does not by itself elicit the child building a model that preserves the action or interpreting the answer in the story; use at most as a brief warm-up, not as the main activity.
Interpreting-the-answer-back is developmentally just emerging at 5-6: a bare 'three' with no meaning should be modelled and invited, not marked wrong.
Counting and simple change stories are not inherently spatial/3D work; concrete objects and drawings are sufficient models.

startingActivity.title: Model a shop story, then make the return trip
learnerActions: Read a shop story, e.g. 'Sam has 20p in his purse and buys a sticker costing 15p. How much change does he get?'
Build a bar model of the situation: 20 as the whole, split into a 15 part and a mystery (change) part; or write a matching number sentence.
Work out the missing part to land on 5.
Complete a mandatory 'what does your 5 mean?' step: attach the unit and quantity, finishing the sentence '5p change'.
Pass a reasonableness check before the answer is accepted: decide whether a candidate answer could possibly be true in the story (e.g. flag that change greater than the amount paid is impossible).
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A calculation is not finished when the number appears; it is finished when the number is read back into the story and checked for whether it could possibly be true. You cannot end up with MORE money after spending some.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Part-whole and comparison bar models for two-step problems
Number sentence with units attached to the quantities
Number line for measurement/money jumps
Simple diagrams of the situation (coins, ribbon lengths)
commonMisconceptions: Stops at a bare number without interpreting it in context or attaching a unit
Grabs the numbers and applies the operation a keyword suggests, without modelling the situation
Doesn't sense-check — accepts an answer that can't be true in the situation (change larger than the money paid)
Reports the wrong quantity (gives the total when the question asks for what's left)
constraints: Every numerical answer must be interpreted in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') — the interpret-in-context half of MP4 is the core objective, not an optional extra.
Reason about the situation before computing; resist keyword-stripping ('take away means subtract'), which the CDE guide identifies as a cause of suspension of sense-making.

A static worked example (story, bar, answer, and a 'what it means' flap) can illustrate the return trip but does not let the child model or sense-check for themselves; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.

Recognition-only scored items check getting the number rather than interpreting it in context or judging reasonableness, and can reward the compute-and-stop habit; a short 'is this answer reasonable?' item can still be useful during teaching, but keep the modelling and interpretation work open and constructive.

A reasonableness gate, slider, or shopkeeper character are optional ways to make the sense-check concrete, not mandatory mechanisms; the required learning is the interpretation and the check themselves.

Where a learner shows number-grabbing errors, reteach by modelling the real situation on a bar before any operation; this connects to the prerequisite skill of representing the situation rather than grabbing numbers/keywords (CDE).

startingActivity.title: Choose, build, interpret back: a modelling workbench
learnerActions: Take a situation such as 'a £40 jacket has 25% off — what does a shopper pay?' and first choose which representation exposes its structure from a palette: percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line, or ratio table
Build a percentage bar: partition the 100% strip into quarters, shade off one quarter (the discount), and read what remains
State explicitly what each number refers to: £10 is the discount (25% of £40), 0.75 is the proportion of the original price remaining, and £30 is the price paid
Pass an interpret-back gate: state the final answer with its unit (£30) and check it is reasonable — a sale price must be less than £40

Re-run the same process on a room-carpet problem (choose a scale diagram, apply the area formula, and give the area in a squared unit that matches the length unit of the measurements — e.g. a 4 m × 3 m room needs 12 m² of carpet) and a recipe-scaling problem (choose a double number line, answer in grams)
Notice which representation you reach for — if you grab a single bar for a rate problem that has two varying quantities, ask whether it hides structure
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When the question asks what the shopper pays, the answer is the part that STAYS (£30), not the part taken off (£10) nor the bare proportion (0.75); and a model is chosen to fit a situation's structure, with every answer returned to its real units and sense-checked.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Percentage bar model (100% strip partitioned for discount/increase)
Scale diagram / scaled drawing for area and length
Double number line and ratio table for scaling and rates
Area/perimeter rectangle with l, w labelled and formula alongside
commonMisconceptions: Gives the discount amount (£10 off) when asked the sale price (£30), or leaves the answer as a decimal (0.75) never returned to pounds
Confuses area and perimeter — adds sides when the situation needs area, or reports the carpet answer in cm instead of cm²
Applies a percentage as a raw number ('25% is 25') rather than a proportion of the specific amount
Picks a representation by habit rather than fit, so a rate problem gets a single bar that hides the two varying quantities
Scales additively (adds the same amount) instead of multiplicatively when enlarging a recipe or shape
constraints: The modelling cycle is the objective: choosing a representation, computing, AND interpreting back with a reasonableness check. A scored step that accepts a bare correct number cannot force or observe the representation-choice and interpret-back, so use such checks only for isolated sub-skills (e.g. percentage of an amount) that feed the real modelling task.

A static labelled percentage bar or scale diagram can prime or remind what a representation shows, but on its own does not let the learner choose, compute, or interpret back; treat it as a reference card, not the teaching vehicle for the practice.

Keep area and length as distinct quantities with distinct units throughout; the area uses a squared unit (m² or cm²) that matches the length unit of the measurements and must not be reported as a length.

Every percentage answer must return to the real quantity the situation asks for, stated with its unit (e.g. the £30 a shopper actually pays when the question asks for the price paid) — never leave a bare 30, 75, or 0.75.
Enlarging a recipe or shape is multiplicative (scale by a factor), not additive (add the same amount); watch for additive scaling.
The room/coverage activity is an optional scaffold for learners who confuse area and perimeter, not a required step for every learner.

activityReferences.title: Order the coaches: when 8.2 is the wrong answer

startingActivity.title: Order the coaches: when 8.2 is the wrong answer
learnerActions: Take the real job: 328 people need to travel to a match; each coach seats 40. Build a ratio table or double number line, or divide, and land on 8.2.
Make the rounding decision explicitly: do I round? which way? to what accuracy? and WHY — state the reason before trusting the number.
Check the consequence of rounding down: 8 coaches × 40 = 320 seats, leaving 8 people with no seat. Commit to 9 coaches and justify it by those stranded people.
Explain in your own words why the SITUATION (a coach is indivisible, nobody can be left behind) decides the direction, not the nearest-whole rule.
Try the exact-division contrast: if only 320 people travelled, 320 ÷ 40 = 8 exactly, so no rounding decision arises — notice the dilemma only appears when the division leaves a remainder.

Try a variant that rounds the OTHER way: 'how many FULL crates can we pack from 328 apples, 40 to a crate?' — here you round down to 8 full crates (8 apples left over). Explain why the direction differs.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A computed decimal must be interpreted back against the real question; whether and which way to round is a judgement the context makes, not a rule applied on autopilot. The same arithmetic rounds up for coaches and down for full crates, and when the division is exact (320 ÷ 40 = 8) there is no rounding decision at all.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: Double number line and ratio table for ratio/rate and proportion
Bar model for part-whole ratio and comparison
Labelled 3D diagram with volume formula (V = l×w×h / B×h)
Scale factor / scaled drawing for similar shapes
commonMisconceptions: Reports the bare quotient (8.2 buses) and never rounds to the whole buses the situation demands, or rounds the wrong way (down) leaving people stranded
Rounds by rote to the nearest whole/decimal place regardless of what the context needs (money to 2 dp, buses always UP, lengths to sensible precision)
Reasons additively about ratio/scale (adds the same amount to both quantities) instead of multiplicatively
Blurs volume with area or length, or reports cm³ answers in the wrong unit
Chooses a tool by habit (single bar) that hides the two covarying quantities in a rate/ratio problem
constraints: The learning objective is the situated judgement of whether/which-way/how-precisely to round, plus choosing a structure-matched tool — not just producing a correct quotient.

A check of an isolated computation (compute a volume, simplify a ratio) assesses the component skill but does not elicit the independent rounding-in-context decision; use such checks only as sub-skill feeders into a full modelling task. A bare '8.2' can score as correct arithmetic while being the wrong real-world answer.

A static labelled diagram can illustrate a finished model or serve as a reference for what each tool represents, but does not itself host the computation, tool-choice or rounding judgement that is being taught.
Keep units explicit through volume work (cm vs cm² vs cm³) and interpret the final quantity as a real capacity.
Always include a reasonableness pass: estimate first, then check the computed answer sits near the estimate and makes sense in the situation.

Include at least one round-up case (coaches), one round-down case (full crates), and ideally an exact-division case (no rounding needed) so the direction is read from the situation, not fixed as a rule; avoid teaching 'always round up in word problems'.
Physical cube-packing and on-screen models offer different experiences of volume; do not claim one is universally necessary or that a diagram cannot convey capacity.
When the proportional set-up or the interpret-into-context step is missing, a flagged earlier prerequisite topic should be revisited; confirm the correct prerequisite linkage before relying on it.

startingActivity.title: Build-your-own 'plan-it' workspace with a red herring and an estimate-first step
learnerActions: Meet a problem revealed a piece at a time: first the story, then the question, then the numbers (a staged, numberless-to-numbered reveal).
Build your OWN representation by dragging parts onto a canvas to map the known parts to the unknown — a bar/strip diagram, or a number line to show the jumps — rather than using a pre-made diagram.

Identify and physically set aside the irrelevant number. For example, in 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers; 8 children go home. How many children are left?' the 3 teachers are not needed (this one is a single step, 24 − 8 = 16, chosen to practise spotting a red herring).

Practise the sequencing on a genuinely two-step version, e.g. '8 children go home in the morning and 6 more go home at lunch; how many are left?' — here finding 16 is only step one (24 − 8), and 10 is the answer (16 − 6).
Before computing, set an estimate ('about how big will the answer be?') to create a reasonableness benchmark.

Compute, then compare the answer to your own estimate; when the answer lands far from the estimate, re-check — did you stop after step one, use the spare number, or (in problems where order matters) do the steps in the wrong order?
Return to the still-visible model to complete or fix the second step.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Planning, relevance-sorting, and self-checking become things the child does and watches on a live representation, rather than rules they are told. Keeping the whole situation visible helps the child notice when they have stopped after step one on multi-step problems, and comparing to a self-made estimate can make an unreasonable answer stand out.

Choosing the operation from a cue word rather than the problem's structure

When illustrating multi-step work and stop-after-step-one, use a genuinely two-step problem (two operations); a single-operation problem with a distractor exercises relevance-sorting but not step sequencing.
Build-your-own representations are the target; being handed a pre-made diagram or watching a worked example are scaffolds and must be followed by the child planning and building independently.

Scoring final answers rewards fast computing and does not assess planning, relevance-sorting, or reasonableness reasoning. startingActivity.title: Estimate-first multi-step solver with inverse check
learnerActions: Take a two-step problem, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' and arrange it as two connected sub-problem cards in the order you will solve them (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), adding more cards only if a longer problem needs them
Before computing, state 'about how big' the answer should be — set an estimate benchmark (e.g. 'about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left')
Solve each sub-step in order, keeping the whole plan visible

After you have an answer, work backwards through the story (inverse) to see whether you return to the starting number: put back the pencils that were sold, 120 + 4×50 = 120 + 200 = 320. Undo the actions in the problem, not just your own calculation, because undoing a wrong calculation (e.g. 320 − 50 = 270, then 270 + 50 = 320) would still get you back to 320
Compare your answer against your own estimate: if it is wildly off, treat that as a signal to recheck both the answer and the estimate
If an approach stalls, deliberately re-represent the problem a different way — for example switch between a strip/bar diagram and a number line that sequences the jumps — rather than stopping
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Decomposition is something you physically arrange and sequence, not a rule triggered by a cue word; the estimate and a backwards check that undoes the problem's actions (not merely the child's own calculation) are two separate signals that can catch a wrong-order or wrong-operation answer.

keyRepresentations: Bar / strip diagram decomposing a multi-step problem into sub-parts
Number line for sequencing multi-step jumps
Estimation / rounding to a benchmark before computing
Inverse-operation check (work backwards to the start)

commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy on multi-step problems — tying a word to an operation and applying operations in the wrong order
Computing an answer with no estimate and no check, accepting answers that are wildly off (compulsion to calculate)
Believing that if the first method doesn't work, you're simply stuck (no strategy-switching)
Doing the sub-steps but not connecting them — losing track of what has been found and what remains
constraints: Teach problem structure (schema), not keywords: cue words like 'left' can trigger the wrong operation or wrong order on multi-step problems.
Always require an estimate benchmark before computing and a check (an inverse that undoes the problem's actions, or a different method) after — revise if they disagree.
Normalise strategy-switching: a stalled first approach is a cue to re-represent the problem (e.g. swap a strip diagram for a number line), not evidence of failure.
Worked, reveal-only examples are scaffolds or references: they show the decomposition and check but do not have the child sequence steps or perform the check — pair them with independent practice.
Scored linear items can assess estimation and wrong-order spotting but do not elicit independent decomposition or self-monitoring and tend to reward fast computing; do not use as the primary task.

Interactive affordances (sequenceable cards, estimate slider, backward-working inverse panel, reasonableness gauge, 'try another way' button) are optional illustrations; the learning can be done on paper with drawn diagrams and written checks.

This multi-step arithmetic content is not spatial, so a 3-D environment adds set-up cost without a clear benefit here — a judgement for this specific content, not a general claim that 3-D media add nothing elsewhere.
At this age children develop the habit with teacher support; independent strategy evaluation comes later, so expect to scaffold the plan-estimate-check routine.

startingActivity.title: Build the sub-structure and bracket the answer
learnerActions: Take a multi-step problem such as 'A rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm. You colour 3/4 of it. What is the coloured area?'

Before calculating, name and sequence the sub-steps in order (first find the area, then find 3/4 of it) — arrange them as cards or a written plan so the order comes from the structure, not from a word
Build your own bar/strip or area diagram of the problem to expose its sub-structure
Before computing the fraction, state an estimate: is 3/4 of the rectangle less than half, about half, or more than half? Record it
Compute the sub-steps (area = 8×5 = 40; then 3/4 of 40 = 30)

Check the answer against your estimate and the whole: 30 is more than half of 40 and less than the whole 40, so it is sensible — if an answer comes out bigger than the whole rectangle, or below your 'more than half' estimate, return to the area diagram to find where a sub-step went wrong
Replay the same problem as equations and compare: which strategy made the structure clearer here, and why?
startingActivity.intendedInsight: Multi-step answers should be bracketed for size before and after computing, and a self-built diagram makes the order of sub-steps and the reasonableness of the result visible; strategy choice is a felt comparison, not a fixed rule.

Computing with no estimate or reasonableness check (compulsion to calculate) — e.g. a fraction-of-quantity answer larger than the whole passes unnoticed
Doing the sub-steps but not monitoring — losing track of what has been found versus what remains, or failing to combine sub-results
Defaulting to one strategy (always equations, or always drawing) regardless of which fits the problem
constraints: Teach structure/schema, not keyword-to-operation matching: keyword matching fails on multi-step problems (reported match rate under 10%).
The child should identify and name the sub-steps and state a plan themselves before calculating — do not pre-decompose the problem for them.

startingActivity.title: Estimate-first complex-problem solver
learnerActions: Take a three-step problem, e.g. finding a percentage of a large quantity that also requires a unit conversion, and lay it out as separate sub-step cards so each step is visible.
Build your own representation for the key step: a double number line or bar model for the percentage step, a strip diagram for a fraction step.
Before computing, round each number and place an estimate into a benchmark band (e.g. round 4,832 to about 5,000, so 4,832 × 7 should be about 35,000).
Compute each sub-step, then compare the computed answer against your own estimate band, and against what makes sense in context (e.g. a 'part' of a fixed group cannot be more than everyone in it).
Keep a running 'found so far / still to find' tracker so you don't lose your place across the steps.
Work backwards with an inverse operation to confirm or fix the answer.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: An answer can be rejected by your own estimate and by plain context, not just by a teacher. Estimation and magnitude sense become tools you trust, and a long problem stays manageable when its sub-structure is laid out and monitored.

commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy on complex problems — operations chosen from words, wrong order
No estimate/reasonableness check — accepting a computed answer that rounding would flag as wrong (compulsion to calculate)
Weak magnitude sense — accepting a percentage over 100% or a 'part' larger than the whole as a valid answer in context
Losing track across three or more steps — not monitoring what has been found versus what remains
constraints: Scored, linear question formats and recognition-only items can probe estimation and magnitude judgements but do not themselves elicit the planning or monitoring of a long solution; use them alongside full problem-solving work, not as a substitute.

A tap-to-reveal worked example shows the estimate and inverse check but the child does not perform the planning or checking; treat it as a modelling scaffold and always follow with an independent attempt.
In the reasoning-partner activity the partner must prompt and never supply the steps, or the monitoring routine is not rehearsed.

A percentage over 100% is impossible only as a 'part' of a fixed whole group (e.g. pupils who passed). It is perfectly valid when the whole is a reference unit that can be exceeded (e.g. 250% of a jug = 2.5 jugs). Do not teach 'over 100% is always wrong'; teach the distinction.
Optional interface features (reasonableness gauge, benchmark band, running found/to-find tracker, double number line) make the mechanism concrete but are examples, not mandatory components.
Complex numerical problem solving here is not inherently spatial; a 3D spatial treatment was judged a poor fit for this objective, though this is a design judgement rather than a general rule.

startingActivity.title: Set it up before you solve
learnerActions: Read a ratio, proportion, or algebra problem, e.g. 'Flour and sugar are mixed in the ratio 3:2. A baker uses 750 g of flour. How much sugar? Then she scales the whole recipe by 1.5 — how much of each?'
Before touching any numbers, label what is KNOWN and what is UNKNOWN in the problem

Build a representation of the relationship first: a ratio table, a bar model, a double number line, or an equation with a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 parts flour = 750 g, so 1 part = 250 g, sugar = 2 parts = 500 g)
Only after the relationship is represented, carry out the computation to find the missing quantity

State an estimate for the answer as a benchmark (e.g. scaling by 1.5 means each quantity ends up about half again — one and a half times — as large, so flour becomes roughly 1100-1150 g and sugar roughly 750 g)
Check the result with an inverse operation and compare it to the estimate
Say what the answer means back in the problem's context, including what a negative or fractional result would represent
startingActivity.intendedInsight: When you represent the relationship first, the structure shows which computation will find the missing quantity: a ratio table or bar model makes clear what one part is worth and how many parts are needed, so you resist the pull to simply combine the given numbers.

keyRepresentations: Bar model / ratio table for ratio and proportion

commonMisconceptions: Compulsion to calculate interfering with algebra — combining the given numbers instead of representing the unknown and setting up the relationship
Keyword strategy on complex problems — operations chosen from words, wrong order
No estimate/reasonableness check on decimal-division or proportion answers
Stopping at a number without interpreting what it means in context (e.g. a negative or non-integer answer)
constraints: Represent the relationship (ratio table, bar model, double number line, or equation with a letter for the unknown) before computing; an optional design is to keep the compute/number pad locked until a relationship is represented, so the child cannot grab and combine numbers immediately. The lock is one optional way to enforce represent-first, not a required mechanism.

Always estimate a benchmark and verify with an inverse operation, especially for decimal-division and proportion answers; a reasonableness gauge comparing the answer to the estimate is a useful optional cue.
Always interpret the result back in context (what a negative or fractional answer means) rather than stopping at a number.

Worked-example and match-the-set-up tasks are scaffolds/checks: they do not require the child to independently plan and construct a full multi-step solution, so pair them with tasks where the child does the representing, estimating, and checking.

A scored selection format can check recognition of a correct set-up or a reasonable answer size, but does not by itself elicit the generative planning and representation of a multi-step algebraic/ratio solution; use it as a supporting reasonableness check alongside production tasks.
Avoid teaching keyword-to-operation matching as a strategy; it fails on complex multi-step problems.

activityReferences.title: Up-and-across reading with the scale stated first
Finding both roots of a parabola
Intersections as shared solutions, and checking read-offs

startingActivity.title: Up-and-across reading with the scale stated first
learnerActions: Before reading anything, state aloud what one grid square represents on each axis (e.g. 'each square is 1 unit' or 'each square is 2 units').
For a plotted curve, draw a line up from a given x-value to the curve, then across to the y-axis, and record the estimated y.
Read a value to the nearest sensible fraction of a grid square, writing it as a band (e.g. 'between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single over-precise figure.
Re-read the same physical point after the grid interval changes (e.g. squares now worth 2) and note how the number changes while the point does not.
startingActivity.intendedInsight: A read-off value depends on the axis scale, so checking the scale comes before trusting any number; a value between grid lines is an estimate given to a sensible interval, not an exact figure.
startingActivity.selectionStatus: 作为适配起查项；不宣称首个活动覆盖全部目标

keyRepresentations: 'Up and across' reading lines drawn onto the graph
x-axis crossings as roots/solutions; intersection of two graphs as a common solution
Real-world axes (distance-time, cost) with a clearly labelled scale
A read-off shown as a band ('between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single false-precise figure
commonMisconceptions: Reads against the wrong scale (assumes each square is one unit) or reads off the wrong axis.
Gives a single false-precise value instead of an estimate to a sensible interval.
Stops at the first x-axis crossing, missing a parabola's second root.
Confuses where a single line crosses an AXIS with where two graphs intersect each other.
constraints: Report read-offs as estimates to a sensible interval (a band), not false-precise single values; the task is approximation using the axis scale.
State each axis scale before reading; do not assume one square equals one unit.

A static graph with pre-drawn read-off lines can demonstrate the routine but does not let the learner perform the reading across many different values, so pair any worked reference with active reading practice.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice on 'how many solutions') can check understanding of root count but do not by themselves elicit the learner drawing and executing the up-and-across reading; include tasks where the learner produces the reading lines and values.

An interactive draggable marker is one way to rehearse the routine and make dual roots salient; it is an optional scaffold, not a requirement — the same routine can be taught with pencil-and-paper reading lines on a printed graph.
